when the content is just so rich without any stupid fillers and distractions.

I'm not someone who gravitates towards platformers or cute games in general but despite been both of these, Ori and the Blind Forest has been a delightful experience! The art is rich with colour, originality and well executed, evoking a hand drawn cell animation look that is fluid and natural. The soundtrack varies from mournful to joyously animated, complimenting the fast and freeform platforming experience. The story is fairly simple and is told effectively through the perspectives of different characters, the main character Ori left mute except for cute barks and grunts.
I would recommend any person who enjoys quality games to give this game a try, even if they do not typically enjoy platformers or prefer a different atmosphere for their games.

As any review that has credibility, I'll point out the pros(+)/cons(-) of this game for the sake of impartiality so it's up to you decide if it's worth. In my view, the pros are greater that the cons, so that's why this is comming with a thumbs up.
In summary, SRS is a 2004 race game (this steam version was released in 2005) that features an underground import racing scene, on which the player's main objective is to gain respect on the streets and affection of various females in the city.
+ This game has a killer idea of gameplay, in which you have 3 types of racing: 1. Crew Meets, 2. Street Challenges and 3. Random Encounter. In Crew Meets, you have 3 pre-requisites to meet in order to enter a racing series: Respect Amount, Ante Cash (to build the final prize) and the car horsepower. When these are attended, you may enter the series of 3 races. Before each one of these races, you decide whether to place or not a reserved bet on a specific racer to boost your money earnings. These bets are per race and not related to the total prize made by the ante cash of the 4 racers. The others two types are similar and simpler. To compete in them, you need the cash the rival is willing to bet. The higher his car specs are compared to yours, higher is the amount of cash required to race (for instance, if its a skyline versus a skyline, the bet is x thousand, but if it's a skyline versus a celica, the wager would go up to 3x thousand). The difference between 2 and 3 race types is in the way you trigger them. While 2 is in a specific spot within the map, 3 is triggered when you eventually find a racer in free roam and you flash your headlights at the rear of his car. The customization options require effort in tunning because all can be bought and installed in your car since the very beggining; you only need the cash to get it. But that is not probably the best idea bacause equipping your car with all that can be purchased may overpower the car, rendering it uncontrolable, easy to crash and slower than the competition as it burns tires for a quarter mile at the slightest touch on the throttle. A balanced car is needed to raise the win rate and finding the thereshold for power/control in each car is different and very rewarding for those who like motorsports (as myself). "But where is the killer part in the gameplay until now?" "All this I have seen in other racing games blabla..." Now just imagine all this I have said with these aspects: SRS features a car damage model that forces the player to drive carefully. Heavy damage impacts car performance and heavy repairs cost money to the player. Depending on the price of the car and the amount of destruction, fixing the ride will drain the most (if not all or even more than) of the earnings from their last race. All of this with no restart feature! That's right people NO RESTART! If you lose a race, you will lose the money and your girlfriend - if you had any riding with you - and that is genious. Weaklings don't survive on this hardcore simulation of life game, and I say that because in life you have only 1 shot at pretty much everything, and this games does just that, and it does beautifully, unlike any other from any other genre.
- For the weak spots, I will state the lack of polish and a deeper care for the excellent idea the game promotes. The game has a fair amount of cars and customization options (given the limitations of the platforms originally intended to run this game) but the carrer mode is very short and generic. There are only a handful of short cutscenes to give the player a feedback on the overall progress and the story itself is a little out of place. The driving feels different for each car as they have different wheel drive configurations, weight and engineering, but that isn't very convincing in this game. The physics lack trimming to convince the player the car is actually going through the surface, the graphics are dated and the city plays static and dead. In some regions is always night time and in others always day, the police A.I. is abnormally retard and you can count in your fingers the people found on the streets and sidewalks on the hole district.
With these comments stated, I finish this review giving a score of 8.5/10 to this game. I know the game looks dull, unfinshed and unpolished, but my score is this high because of the concepts this game offers. The removal of the restart feature makes you enjoy and live trough every corner of the game, and crashing makes you rage just like if you did in a real car. You know it can't be undone and it's going to cost a lot. With 14 hours of gameplay on this steam version and hundreds more in the XBOX version, I can safely assure you, seen that I have experienced countless other racing games from before and after SRS time, that this game is the best at it's genre, and I strongly recommend it to virtual racing and car tuning lovers just like myself.

After playing Wolfenstien: The New Order I couldn't wait to play New Colossus. Now I have played it and it's become my favourite campaign to play in 2017 and of all time alongside with Batman: Arkham Knight and Transformers: War for and Fall of Cybertron.
The story: It is awesome, that's it. The story is serious at times when it comes to topics like racism and child and domestic abuse or
but also fun and carefree. The characters are very fleshed out, they aren't one dimensional where you'll forget about them at the end. You're going to remember them even if they only have short screen time, especially Blazkowicz. When you play as him it feels like you are him with his thoughts and his emotions. This game is an unfortunate example how review bombs can misrepresent a game as a whole. i waited a month to get the game because i thought that it was a broken game and needed to be patched. when in reality, less than about 30% of people playing the game experienced game bugs! my friend pre-ordered the game and it ran ultra smooth on his beastly dual xeon + 1060. it ran just as well on my computer, which has has a standard combo of a ryzen 5 and 1050 ti. we experienced no crashes or framerate drops at normal or even medium high graphics. many of these review bombs were upvoted simply because people like riding these bandwagons and causing hype; while looking at these reviews, i noted that over half of the people upvoting them had never even played the game!
valve is right to be looking into the review system and making changes...(lol. i would be suprised if this very review got downvoted to oblivion because i mentioned it)
im glad that the game is up  to a "mostly positive" standing; it is what it deserved from the start.
When it comes to gameplay, this game enduces so much nostalgia; i bought the new order last year after promising my 13 year old self i would buy it as soon as i got my own rig; almost 4 years later and the new order convinced me i had to get the sequel. while certainly not as intense as the first game, the new colossus still provides an amazing experience, adding many mechanics like better stealth, explosive weapons, and a refined perk system.
the narrative is the best part of this game by far; with 4 hours of cutscenes, bethesda is intent on telling an all american story of freedom. while there are no boss fights like in the new order, i found the ending to be just as satisfactory, if not better than the mediocre ending of the new order.
all in all im very happy with bethesda on this title, all they gotta do is get rid of all their creation club boolshet and they will have regained my trust.

Bears more than a passing resemblance to Sunless Sea, and manages to be sufficiently different to be worth checking out.
: A dark portion of a multiverse; this universe is called The House. From what I've seen so far, it's a post-apocalyptic wasteland of ruins, possibly-cursed locations, giant mushrooms, unexplained statues, large rocks, pirates, travelers, and more. All shrouded in darkness. The description of "rooms" makes you think The House will be a little more interesting than it is. Many of the rooms are essentially empty, or have a repeated random encounter, which can lead to some monotony. This is broken up with the occasional city (all rather unique) and other places of interest (the unmoving star, the burning god, etc). You will also get glimpses of other universes. The setting is imaginative and the pacing is decent. (Making money through trade, however, is less straightforward than Sunless Sea.)
: Usually something to be avoided. It's sort of turn-based - interesting but not well-explained. In the beginning your weapons/hull aren't good enough for you to survive most encounters anyway. You'll spend a good portion of the game running from potential enemies.
: There are a wide variety of lively characters. You have a few customization options for yourself, although for the most part you're stuck with the job of poet/writer/journalist/explorer. Your goal is to escape The House - if it's even possible. You run around in a steam locomotive with spidery legs.
Other stuff:
+ It seems the developer has patched most of the significant bugs. (June 2017) You can still find bugs. Some minor, such as NPCs passing through objects. I did experience one major bug: going through a door but then somehow it was locked after I passed through, which made me stuck in the doorway. I could see into the next room, but couldn't go forward or back. I was forced to exit the game in order to continue. (I was able to replicate this - just head east from Phobetor Quinn until you encounter a locked door, then head south.)
+ Music and graphics are decent.
+ You can save your game often, and you should, in case something goes wrong. (Autosave can't always help you.) I kind of wish there were more available save slots.
+ At the moment, this is part of the Steam Summer Sale, and costs just over $6. This is a good price point for people on the fence.
+ The available endings are satisfying and intriguing. I think for most people it'll take 10-15 hours to beat the game. 20+ if you do more exploration and don't focus on getting to the end ASAP.
Overall I would say Sunless Sea is the better game.
is more forgiving and has a bit more in the way of character interaction. If you like exploration games or Sunless Sea, you'll probably like this game too. Read the game's description: what you see is what you'll get.

Played for a fairly short amount of time, so take what I have to say with a grain of salt, but this game, from the 20 minutes I played, is so similar to Sunless Sea that it's hard to avoid making direct comparisons. And, from the 20 minutes, every part of this game is just worse. And Sunless Sea, as much as I loved the story and roleplay, I ultimately decided wasn't a good game.
Still, I was quite surprised at how many flaws lept out at me so quickly into the game. Resolution limited to 1920x1200 when I'm on a 4K monitor means everything is hard to see. You can scale up the text, but that's it, so all the other UI elements seem too small.
No option to control mouse sensitivity also seems extremely strange.
But the kicker for me? One of the main reasons I disliked Sunless Sea was that, ultimately, it was a choose-your-own-adventure game with vast amounts of monotonous travelling interspersed. Sure, early on the tension of not knowing if you'll reach the next refuelling point is intense, but I know from experience with Sunless Sea that it eventually wears off, and I expect the same would hold true here. The one thing which I was holding out hope for was the combat system in House. Sunless Sea's combat was just awful, while this one purports to take inspiration from FTL, which is one of the best games of all time.
Sadly, it just doesn't seem well implemented. No apparent shortcuts to make movement / targeting faster, coupled with a semi-realtime combat, just sunk the ship for me.

This is what I wanted Sunless Sea to be. More choices, better characters, less downtime. The gameplay isn't amazing by any means, but it's incredibly immersive.
EDIT: After playing a few more hours, I'm going to stick with a positive review but only slightly so. It's still more enjoyable to me than Sunless Sea due everything I said originally. The writing is really good, and there are a lot of strong stories.
The problem is that traveling in this game isn't fun. The scenery gets repetitive, the events are minimal, combat is subpar, and it doesn't take an insigificant amount of time to move between cities. After a while, it feels like I'm moving between squares than between an otherworldly dimension. While I enjoyed the writing and story based approached to leveling, I'm putting this game down because the gameplay is just too weak. My positive review stands because this the right game for someone with more patience than me to suffer through some of the game's tedium.

5/10  Not the best by far, but not the worst solitaire game either.  Wait for a sale, is my advise, and only get this if you've played just about all the other solitaire games out there.
I suspect this was made longer ago than other solitaire games.  It feels more bare bones than others.  And the number of cards you get on some levels is off.  For instance, you need to uncover a hammer to turn over cards with stone on them but I kept clicking and clicking on the deck and not getting the card I needed.  Now there are wild cards you can use.  They are numbered and one time use.  So you could use one of those if you have the one you need to continue.  And in the store you can buy a random wild card.   That was the first red flag that popped up in my head.  Hmm....this might be one of those game that was phone/tablet game with in-app purchases and they want you to buy more wild cards.  On Steam this cannot be done so we are stuck with the way it is.  YOu'll have to do some grinding to build up your wild card deck and money to buy special help items.  That's another red flag, becauase I did not gain enough money to buy all the help items!  That is the first time that's happened to me in a solitaire game.  Usually by the last level one has already bought them all.
Graphics look older and are just ok.  Nothing special.
Sound: I don't know because I turned it off to listen to my own music while playing.
Final thoughts:  Since Steam only has a yes/no review system I'm giving it a tentative yes.  I only give "NO"s to really, really bad games.  This one is just for solitaire fanatics who have played everything else and need something new to play.  Not the best by far.  But not really the worst.  I've seen one that is blatantly skewed to in-app purchases and they didn't change it for Steam.  This one isn't as bad as that, just middle of the pack (heh, heh, nice pun, eh? pack?)

I'm a pretty big fan of solitaire games. I play them to relax and, at the same time, exercise my mind a little. Too bad Avalon Legends doesn't really allow you to do either.
In a baffling design choice, you're unable to choose to replay a level you didn't do well on, making getting perfects almost impossible. Which is bad enough, but even just doing well is very difficult, as your hand is often 80 to 90% cards you don't need and won't use. I have literally found myself in situations in which I could remove almost no cards as all, because there wasn't a single useful one in my hand. It was particularly common to find the same card over and over and over. Not that the game cares at all if you've left almost every card on the board. For a solitaire game this frustrating, the actual goals it asks you to achieve are so easy you can do poorly on every single stage and still complete them.
There isn't much else in the way to allow you to strategize, either. You're given a paltry few wild cards, and most of the time they're barely worth using, since they won't get you far. There are items you can buy that give you abilities, but most of these are pretty useless, being things like giving you 1 more undo, or something similarly pathetic.
The story in the game isn't even interesting enough to keep be going. There's just nothing fun about this game.
I know I can't expect every solitaire game to be Faerie Solitaire, but I can certainly expect them to be better than this.

Pros:
-Decent combat system, had a solid spin on the Arkham-style combat that wasn't just counter-counter-counter. System and encounter variety encouraged usage of all special abilities, also encouraged varying tactics and not spamming the same button 3 times over and over. A little slower than I would've liked at times, not the GOAT, but solid for sure. Bigger effort than♥♥♥♥♥♥like Assassin's Creed by far.
-Overall strong music, 1 or 2 tracks that are super memorable and compliment the action well
-Cool, interesting settings for the levels, nice color palette variety that all still fit the near-future cyberpunk-ish theme
-Not too short, not too long
Cons:
-Story conceptually decent, but not well executed. While the overarching narrative was there, a lot the pieces seemed strung together poorly.
-Mixed bag voice acting, main character VO was alright but a lot of the supporting characters sucked.
-Non-combat parts of levels were very dull a lot of the time. There's too much sticky-climbing style platforming to get you point A to point B.
-Unsatisfying ending imo
Neutrals:
-Very easy. If you play games at all, you should probably play this on hard. I played through on normal because it seemed like the type of story-driven game I just wanted to zip through and wasn't sure how much I'd like it, or if it was good enough to where I'd care about honing a technique / repeating stuff. If I'd had more knowledge going in, I for sure would've gone hard -- I was basically never even close to a combat death including boss fights, the entire game. Difficulty doesn't scale steep enough and never got challenging for me. (All non-combat sequences where you could die are OHKOs from environment etc , guessing difficulty doesn't affect any of that)
_____________________
Overall, I'd say it was alright. Not a super fantastic game (and kinda forgettable... get it) but I got a fun enough 10 hours. If you enjoy the occasional linear action-adventure story to relax to, go for it, it's not a terrible option.

To sum it up in a word, Exploration.  With a capital 'E'.
I rarely get hooked into a game on this level.  I recently went at least two years without experiencing it.  The dry spell is now over.
The last game similar to this I spent any time in was Freelancer.  This is an improvement over that in just about every imaginable way.
I have read a lot of reviews.  I'm learning that they often paint a distorted picture.  This game obviously has a unique history in that regard, since they launched it half-finished at full price a year ago.  Glad I didn't get it then (I've developed a habit of not buying anything at release).  The reason I picked it up was that I heard the Atlas Rises patch/expansion was awesome, and it was on sale.
Holy what the wow.  For my 25 bukaruus or so, I have now gotten over 27 hours of pretty much nonstop enjoyable gameplay, and I'm only 8 achievements in, still on my first ship, and haven't ventured more than 2 warp-jumps away from where I started (with one quest-related exception).
I'll say it again-- the free, open Exploration is unmatched.  Going from fumbling around to fix your sad, broken junk to mastering multiple levels of ship control and continually acquiring new ways to overcome challenges is a powerful feeling.  It stays with you; I'm even looking at the real world differently.  Beyond this, the art and music are fantastic, the writing is way beyond what I expected (to the point of messing with your head, I love it), and I always feel like there's something more to look forward to.
Downsides?  If you don't like resource gathering (i.e. Minecraft) you may have trouble with this one.  However, there are a lot of things to gather for different reasons, and you can choose how much of that you want to do to some extent.  Inventory space is cramped, and you will have to manage the heck out of it, at least initially.  I personally like this pressure - it forces you to streamline and incentivizes seeking upgrades - but some may find it tedious.  It would be nice if sentient NPCs had better A.I. (they're more like Morrowind than Oblivion/Skyrim), but dialogue and animation are quite good and there's so much else to do that I honestly don't miss it.
Is it worth full price?  At this point, it would have been for me.  I had no idea going in, though.  If you're an explorer type who likes sci-fi, enjoyed Minecraft and had fun with any of the Elder Scrolls games, DEFINITELY buy it if it's on sale.  You get elements of all those, plus a spaceship to fly and fight with in different ways.  You can even forget everything else and just play your own version of Asteroids while building up hoards of cash and ship upgrades-- a simple home base and finding a spaceport are all you need.
I'm just having such a blast for the first time in a long while and wanted to share it with the world.  I quit a nearly 3-year Hearthstone addiction (the main game I kept playing during this time) and I'm so glad.  If you're still unsure about buying it, put it on your wishlist NOW.  It will be waiting.

This is a pretty fun Sega Genesis Simulator. I really like how you can look around an old style bedroom, and the animations for the putting in of game cartridges.

What you get here is a customized emulator for several classic games that provides simplified settings menus (menus look like game menus instead of emulator settings) within a nice 3D approximation of some bedroom some 90s kid may have had. The coolest thing about this is seeing the games you've purchased lined up on a shelf while being given the option to select between them. All game switching, loading, etc is done from within the 3D environment, which makes it extremely easy to play 1 game, save your progress, and switch to something else.
Overall, I like the experience I've paid for over simply grabbing the game files online and loading up an emulator. I missed out on the whole SEGA Genesis era, so I can't speak much to nostalgia aside from the few games I've previously played. I've encountered no real issues so far in terms of the performance of the games I've purchased.

The developers of this game have an excellent talent for aesthetics and music. It doesn't quite extend to the writing (mostly mechanical stuff like punctuation; the story itself is a pretty fun cheesy power metal romp).
However, the real flaw is in game design:
- Enemies, even the most basic enemies, soak up an enormous number of hits.
- There appears to be an elemental weakness system (???), but there's no rhyme or reason to what enemies are weak to what, other than what you are explicitly told. No consistent color scheme, animation, or other visual cue, nor is there a special sound effect for hitting a weakness.
- The elemental "upgrades" are given to you at the *start* of levels where none of the enemies (as far as I can tell) are weak to that element.
- The basic sword with no elemental enchant is often the best weapon. It is faster and deals more damage than elemental weapons to many enemies (killing the annoying knife ghosts in 1 hit rather than 2+).
- Switches and moving platforms are often set up so that you have to wait for them to complete a full movement cycle to board them.
However, the thing that made me put the game down out of sheer disbelief was a section in a later level with "flaming skellywags" (skeletons with fire sword/shield). These enemies have multiple annoying mooks accompanying them that knock you out of animations. Furthermore, an NPC cheekily tells you that ice will counter their fire magic. Equip the ice axe and go to town, right?
- Their sword slash instantly kills from full health.
- Their shield blocks all damage while they aren't attacking.
- You can't simply walk back and forth to bait an attack, since they have a pulling effect that extends a fair distance in front of them.
- Ice magic shots do nothing special.
- Charged ice magic shots do nothing special.
- Pulling off the extremely slow charged-up heavy attack with proper timing does nothing special.
- Blocking their attacks with the ice axe achieves nothing (it one-shots you anyway).
- Parrying and countering with the ice axe requires 3 (!!) iterations plus some extra hits. Remember, if you slightly mistime your parry you die instantly.
- There are TWO of these, plus mooks, in a row in the span of one save point. And *then* there's a durable enemy with a ranged attack that leaves a lingering AoE effect, placed right after the second skeleton.
Dying to the instant death traps is pretty amusing, the game looks nice and has decent music and compelling theming. The wolf level is definitely the best one.
However, it is frustrating, more than a little abstruse, and lacks polish in enemy, level, sound, and boss design. I wouldn't pick this up if I were you, but I look forward to what this developer creates in the future.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifices main focus is the narrative Senua, the loss she has suffered and her battle with mental illness. This has all been done exceedingly well. The lore, the psychological affliction of senua and backstory of the game are all very well researched and executed within the game. Couple that with brilliant sound design and a fitting art direction, and this game has the power to draw you into an immersive and rich experinece.
The only issue I had with the game was its lacklustre combat system and puzzles. Yes, towards the second half (3-4 hours in), the puzzles did get better and more interesting. Combat, however, remained stale.
Overall, the game is certainly entertaining to play. It did stir up thoughts and emotions as you would expect from any interesting piece of media. I would recommend people play it. Especially if you see yourself as a gamer who likes to support new and different titles. Ninja theory have shown they do deserve that support from the care they poured into this product. However, I would not recommend it for everybody. It isnt for everyone since as a game its main focus is narrative. Combat and Puzzle solving only fulfil a minimum level of requirement here For some this may be a larger issue since they may have certain expectations when playing games. Hellblade sometimes feels more movie then game (story telling vs. gaming).

What an impressive game! Almost disturbing, but not in a bad way.
In short:
PROS: Great story, beautiful graphics, superb sound (put your headphones on!), nicely balanced horror (I'm not at all a fan of the genre and I still liked it).
CONS: Fighting is a bit dull, linear story (limited replayability), some contrasting graphic quality between elements of the game.
More comments:
The story is very rich and has many layers, both obvious and also beneath the surface. The main quest gives the game a driving force, but the lore stones are very interesting and the unfolding of Senua's character throughout the game is just brilliant. It's as linear as a book.
Graphics are quite impressive (on a GTX 1070 card). Senua looks, moves and reacts like a real person. Motion capture and facial expressions are the best I've ever seen on any game (and even better than the CGI on some major Hollywood productions). The way images react to Senua's experiences, morphing and even breaking apart sometimes, play nicely with the story. Lighting plays an important role. That being said, some bits (like the "moving hands" on the walls here and there) look a bit unpolished, contrasting with the nicely rendered parts.
Sound may be one of the best aspects of this game (headphones on!). Music and sound effects are good, but the way how the voices in Senua's head "dance" around her and interplay with everything is amazing. The voices reveal her thoughts and feelings in a third-ish person, mock her, encourage her (and give handy gameplay hints, such as "behind you!" and "defend yourself!").
The only real downside was the fighting, which I found rather simple and repetitive, but I had the easy setting turned on (it was not what attracted me to the game, anyway). Most fights, with the exception of boss fights, felt like an unnecessary distraction from the story.
If this game was in VR, I'd have needed to change my pants a few times (not because of the fights), but it would have been worth the trouble.

Hellblade's strengths are often scratched by its weaknesses.
Where Hellblade is stongest is in its artistic expressions: visceral sights and unnerving sounds. Where it's weakest is in its game design: puzzle solving. Namely, the game relies far too much on uninspired "find the symbol in the environment" to solve a puzzle and move the game forward. It's repititive. It gets old fast.
Looking past this, though, and you'll discover a game full of passion. One that isn't afraid of itself or its material.
An interesting game, just one that needed better game design.

Ugh, it is at these times that I really don't like the very low dimension and spectrum of Steam reviews. Pretentious Game isn't a game that I would wholeheartedly recommend to buy, especially not at full price, but it's not really a bad game by any means. At $2 price point, I would definitely recommend it, but at its full price of $5? That I'm not sure.
The game is short, really,
short that you can finish it at 15 minutes. Comparing even to the extremely short Sakura Spirit visual novel, the game worth even less than it in terms of worth by playtime mileage and development efforts. There is nothing really original about it, either, other games has done something to this effect and better. The ending is also another problem, as it feels like it came out of nowhere. If the game had been longer, all of the problems with this game would really be solved.
Now, why do I still recommend it? Because I simply really really like the gameplay and narrative's connectment. One of my biggest gripe over JRPGs are that they are often disconnected in terms of story and gameplay, the gameplay feels meaningless and only serve as padding rather than something genuinely fun or challenging (exception exists, of course). Meanwhile, this game's presentation of narrative and gameplay really boosts each other up. The narrative, short as it was, gives a greater meaning to the gameplay as well as be the instruction while still being a story that doesn't break the fourth-wall, and the gameplay boosts the story as it feels like we're enacting the story ourselves.
I like the concept, even if it's starting to get overdone, and considering that sales data are the language of video game financing and investment, I would rather pay for these kind of games to be made more than many other Tripple-A games. Not to mention that it means supporting the developers whom we can see from this game and their next game to be a creative bunch, perhaps had they had better support before, this game would have been longer and better.
At the end of the day, Pretentious Game is a flawed game, but it is a flawed yet meaningful game that I would definitely prefer to support than mindless games that are neither fun nor meaningful. If you have some spare money, go buy this game, if there is a sale on it, definitely go buy it.

Because the other thing I've underestimated is the game's difficulty! **Please keep in mind that this Review is simply a matter of opinion, based upon certain facts of the game [age/PC requirements/etc.]**
SRS, Where to begin on this?.. First and Foremost, If you're looking for a game thats entirely seamless and has top of the line graphics on the vehicles, You may as well stop this review, and head to another page, as this game is nearly 10 years old now (Came out late 2005).
With that aside, SRS has many features that even most current games do not give you the luxury of changing anymore.
The Pros:
1) Get to Customize your car [i.e. weight reduction (for carbon fiber peices), A Body kit (sadly, only 1 for each car i have tried that is... beside the stock body), Underglow (to which you can change between about 8 different colors), Body+Rim paint, etc.]
2) You get to choose which parts can go onto the car, they have about a 18 parts from real life authenticated part manufacturer's that you can use to upgrade your car with, turning that 343HP Nissan GT-R, Into a 918HP AWD Road Beast ;)...
3) The game is fairly realistic in its driving (except the fact you can obviously keep driving after hitting someone going 120... but hey, its a video game), But on that note. You dont want to go around and wall grind around corners like alot of people do in NFS. It makes for a very costly repair bill after your races.
4) ^ In note with that, It honestly makes you a consious driver, As you NEED to avoid obsticicles if you want to start earning money toward that awesome car you're waiting for, Giving it that realistic feel. (Repair bills are a B!@#$.)
5) What it adds over the other games, Is the fact you can free roam everywhere without limitations toward the map. (But the map in its own is fairly small and rugged)
6) Races are gauged by a 'Respect' system, You earn respect by running races quickly and cleanly, And throwing in a bit of spice to mix the pot.
7) [and probably the best/most reason everyone whose played the game prior for] The girls. Yes, As you race, you get the chance to earn yourself a Girlfriend, (18 in total, all unique, their own descriptions and they even went as far as to add comments as to what they like) Each girl has 3 Videos of them dancing as you race with them tagging along with you. (Except for one, which i heard is bugged with only 1 video, unsure as to which one so far)
The Cons:
1) The graphics are pretty out-dated (but hey... its 2014, and this is a 2005 game, still not the worst..[could always go back to GTA2?.. bahaha])
2) The maps are small.
3) There is no real story to the game.
4) To those of you whom play RPG games, This Racer has a 'Grinding' feel to it. As you end up repeating alot of races in order to get the car/upgrades that you desire.
5) The modifications are pretty limited, (both tuning wise and cosmeticly)
6) A (decent, but) Small quantity of vehicles to choose from. [If you are into muscle/luxury cars, and dont like racing with anything else, dont bother with this game, as it deals with mainly tuner styled cars (save for the Lexus IS300)]
7) The game goes by fairly quickly, I've got just under 9 hours on record currently, and i already have the 2nd most expensive car, and beaten nearly every race perfectly.
8) Is meant as a keyboard game, Not fully integrated for PS3/xbox360 controller use.
All in all, I would definately recommend this game for those of you who are nostalgic with old racing games (weather it be this one specifically or racing in general) But would definately just add it to your wishlist untill it comes on sale, unless you're die-hard for those videos ;) haha.
**As a side note, For anyone who plays/buys the game, keep in mind that upgrading and buying high-end modifications for your vehicle wont always make it the fastest, weather the fact its a bug in the game [which would not suprise me] Or just the way the designed it.
As an example. I've got the Mitsubishi Lancer Evo VIII ('04 model) [which is unlocked before the '02 Evo VII]. Did a few minor modiciations to it, bringing it from the 200HP or so it started at, up to 814HP. It will go 0-60 in 2.5 seconds, But the top speed maxes out at a measly 160mph (claims 162, but i couldnt pull it off, even downhill).
While on the other hand, I have a Mazda RX-7, which has about 740HP, but maxes out at a stunning 190mph.

“A House of Many Doors” is for those who enjoy text-heavy games, and can put up with some fairly tedious, but atmospheric, exploration in order to experience tons of pretty great writing and world building.  While the world map can seem somewhat empty and repetitive at times, the story sequences that you will be spending most of your time on more than make up for it.
The obvious comparison to make with this game is with the earlier game, “Sunless Sea”, as the two games have some obvious similarities in gameplay and storytelling.  Compared to that game, HoMD is considerably less difficult, and more accessible, due to allowing multiple save files and the ability to reload at any point, even after a game over.  As a result, this game never really gives the same sense of dread that “Sunless Sea” gave, where you knew that any major mistakes on your end could be catastrophic.  On the other hand, it also means that a simple, careless error doesn’t mean having to start the game over from scratch and going through the repetitive early game portions again and again.  Overall, anybody who enjoyed “Sunless Sea” should definitely give HoMD a try, as it’s fairly likely they will enjoy this one as well.  It’s similar enough to feel familiar, but definitely has its own unique charms.
It took me about 24 hours total to complete the game with one of the endings, doing as many of the optional sidequests and storylines that I came across.  However, there were whole sections of the map that I never explored, and many sidequests that I never even started.  If you compound that with the fact that the majority of the sidequests in the game have multiple solutions and story branches, this is a game that I can definitely see myself going back to in order to either continue playing or start again from the beginning.  Some of the earlier reviews here, as well as other commentary I’ve seen online, seem to indicate that the game suffered from some performance issues shortly after launch, such as crashing and broken sidequests.  Most of these seem to have been fixed since then, as I never experienced the latter, and only had the game freeze up on me once.

It's funny that when I was playing Sunless Sea I thoguht to myself "I would like to make a game like this," and apparently this author was thinking just the same thing.  Unfortunately, this game makes me think I was right not to.
The art: The city art is nice, with just a but of an impresisonistic style.  But there isn't much of it, just the city itself.
The graphics: On the other hand, are quite poor. And I don't just mean because it is an indie.  The millions of areas you have to slog through between the towns are procedurally generated.  And as is all too common in procedurally generated levels, are VERRRRRRY repetative.  I mean, the 500th time you come across some abandoned extra-dimensional gas station sitting next to an Easter Island statue, they really lose their appeal.  And that moment is 15 minutes into the game.
The audio: Actually takes away from the boring graphics, by which I mean it makes them worse.  Your train already looks like a little wind up toy moving across a dirty living room, so why did they have it the same sound effect as one?!  Especially if it is supposed to be this giant steam engine.  Its annoying whine as it piddles along gets old fast.
The mechanics? Well, good luck finding them out.  The tutorial blows by with no way to access that info later.  Hope you wrote it all down, or God help you if you want to know what any of your oddly named stats do the rest of the game, or what any of your people do in combat.  For that matter, good luck trying to determine how much inventory you have of an item you are selling to a merchant.
The writing: Well, it's pretty good.  An extremely original and cool concept, with fun variety from place to place.
Sadly I could not recommend this game, but if this writer teams up with the right game design crew in the future they might accomplsh something great.

When I saw Bethesda's logo, I already knew.
For better or worse, this game was about to be broken. And being a Bethesda game, of course, it didn't disappoint on that front. Though, sadly, it wasn't broken in an entertaining way.
First problem of all was realising the game couldn't handle the alt-tab. Game crashes when alt-tabbed if you don't play in windowed mode. No amount of trying to fix it helped, disabling the Steam overlay did nothing, for exemple. Now, having a game not able to handle alt-tabbing in this day and age is unforgiveable. I would maybe understand if it was for a low budget game, but come on, the drat thing has been pushed like a hot product since months. It's especially bad seeing previous Wolfeinstein games DID handle alt-tabbing without any problem. How can you manage to actually make your technology go backward, I will never know...
To top it, game was actually crash heavy. It loved to crash in particular in some level transitions, and sometimes when cutscenes were involved. I think breaking the scripting of some ennemies also can do that, like for exemple hiding and trying to sneak kill them, rather than fight them openly like the game seems to want you to do.
But what about the game itself? Well, the game itself is a decent FPS with a poor stealthing system, and which is ruined by collectibles.
I know, you don't HAVE to look for every single collectible or secret, but I'm sure I'm not the only one with an OCD and who tries to go for a 100% against my better judgement. Besides, some of the concept arts for the game are helleluva cool. To the point when you see the difference between concept art and what the game does, you feel a bit sad for the artists. I will be damned if the guys and/or gals didn't have vision for that game. The way collectibles are signaled on your map only when you kill area commanders, forcing some horrible backtrack, and the fact sometimes it also doesn't mark everything on said map(which also doesn't show all area and allow you to switch between the map of each), makes the whole experience pretty horrible. This is made worse by the fact you can't alt-tab to check guides and such so you don't spend half your life looking in every cook and granny to find a stupid postcard.
Stealth is also an offender and I can't really make sense of it. Sometimes you will pass on the side of a guard pretty close with no cover, and they won't see you, and sometimes you will move behind crates in a dark spot while crouching and get noticed by a guard on the other side of the subway station up a flight of stair through what I assume is a crack between the crates. Maybe. You can actually spray guards with overheated bullets machine pistols and no one will hear anything despite the guards screams. Yet, fire a laser behind 5 walls in a remote part of the map and everyone will come running. And seeing how brutal the combat can be, by which I mean how much damage you take, believe me when I say stealth is really important.
Game is pretty brutal and gory, and it some way it's satisfying and fun, in others, it's more... Well... Disturbing. But I guess that's the whole point to make you realise how evil the nazis are. That point is nailed in your brain quite a lot during the game. You don't need to tell me game, I would have shot the ennemies anyway, you know. I appreciated the upgrades systems and how they allowed different ways to access different zones of the levels to sneak and surprise the ennemies. It's interesting and reminded me a tad of Deus Ex(the good ones).
The story is well... It's pretty meh honestly. I didn't have any motivation to do things at any point. I did them because it was a way to progress toward the end, but that's pretty much it. The game totally failed to give me any drive to do what I was doing. The new characters aren't that good to me except Sigrun maybe. Liked the poor girl despite the fact the game insisted on trying to treat her like the fat girl comic relief. Game did have some pretty funny moments, so I at least give it that. Really, it's not a game that should be taken seriously at all anyway. Actually that's quite related to the issue, the game fails to accomplish anything as soon as it tries to be dark and serious. BJ monologues are pointless. The whole political aspect, while necessary seeing the setting, and interesting honestly, isn't treated like it should, or more precisely, not treated by the right characters. It's basically hearing the voices of all the extremes shouting at each other. And while it's intresting to see the point of view of such radical characters, it's also opening 10 cans of worms at the same time and having them draw borders before engaging in a free for all.
Gameplay wise I also felt the whole akimbo gun system is poorly implemented. Switching between weapons, in which hand, and if it should be handled with one or both hands is really bad on the fly. It makes adapting to the ennemies in front of you harder, which turns already difficult fights in worse fights. The backtracking to accomplish side mission is neither a good idea nor really welcome. This is not the recent Hitman, guys. Those levels don't have the sheer potential to bring new things to the table each time you replay them with different targets and entry points. If you want to do stuff like that, bring your game in open world. That will do you more good.
There is a correct game underneath all that, but the problem is, it's just the same old that was already done with only few good additions. The problems the game has don't manage to really compensate for that. The story feels like it was half Max-Haassed.
As a result the end product is barely worth the 20 euros I would usually determine as the price for such a game. Maybe get it for that price if you don't plan to suffer through the collectibles and manage to find the drive to play both timelines, but otherwise, you may want to consider taking a rain check or wait for it to go even lower.
A pity really, I expected more from this game after the 2 previous ones.

After finishing this game, my standards for story-based games rocketed sky high (pun completely intended). I have yet to experience the same tear-jerking, heart-wretching emotion that To The Moon kicked me in the shin with.
Your adventure begins with two keen and quirky scientists, Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts. From the very start, these partners-in-crime pull you in with their witty personalities and constant (yet amusing) banter toward each other. The overall humor seeded throughout the game is perfectly timed and extremely entertaining and original.
During the story, you are brought into many curious situations as you try to piece together the mysterious life of Johnny Wyles, a dying old man whose only (and last) request is to go to the moon. The only plausible way he can fulfill his wish is to do so artificially, and he receives this help from Rosalene and Watts.
With every moment you play, you are lead through bliss, sorrow, amusement, secrecy, tragedy, grief, hope, and many more. The raw sentiment I have for this game is purely overwhelming, and I highly recommend this game to anyone who has a soft spot for rich story. If you enjoy adept humor, cleverly-written characters, wonderful graphics, and excelling originality, this game is definitely for you.

I really wanted to like this game. I came away middling. The music's enjoyable as a fan of heavy metal (if a bit generic) and the controls are damn solid. I like the parry mechanic a lot. The story is pretty barebones. Warrior resurrected. Gets his sword. Meets the BBEG. Does the thing. Fights the thing. Gets to the BBEG. That's about it.
The thing I hated was the level design, specifically the art. It took all the most glaring aspects of death metal and black metal album covers and slapped that over the world. Sometimes it's fine. The Wolf levels and the intro level are fine for the most part. A LOT of the level design is just too visually busy though. Like I said, aspects of album covers: so you have lots of pointy, almost monochrome visuals (the last level in particular is almost nothing but red) with very little contrast. It feels like frustrating game design as a lot of deaths in some areas were because my eye didn't catch something until JUST before it killed me. I think the metal-centered art style would've benefitted heavily from more contrast and color usage. You want a sea of spiky, thorny, evil looking things in the world? Okay, just keep your color palettes appropriate. Album art is album art, you just have to stare at it but playing a game requires clarity for the player. I know I'm harping on that a lot but this was the worst aspect of the game.
I was more than fine with going in with a Dark Souls mentality: death is just going to happen, it's gonna suck when you're near a checkpoint but it happens, oh well, move on. So combat was fine in that regard. Character models seemed fine. Sometimes the camera was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but that was mostly for platforming segmets where things were going up or down and the camera wasn't keeping up or showing you enough. Annoying but not unreasonable.
Also, I originally found this game listed under Metroidvania titles. It's really not. Your two weapon upgrades are given to you at the start of the levels you need them in and the medallion is really the only thing you have to look for. Beyond that, there's no reason to explore, there's no upgrades, and the levels are linear. I don't remember any branching paths. So if you found it that way, it's NOT really a metroidvania. You get a hub world but it doesn't really serve a purpose except you can choose which order to tackle the areas in.
So, overall, I can't really recommend this to anyone. I played it, I finished it, I doubt I'll ever pick it back up. I would, however, be curious to see what the team does with a sequel. They have a lot of potential.

Slain: Back From Hell is a tough but awesome hack and slash platformer.
From the gritty faux-pixel art graphics to the pumping heavy metal soundtrack this game is a joy to look at and listen to. The backgrounds, characters and their animation are brimming with setpieces and cool ideas. The game is tough as nails in some places but never gets frustrating due to the careful placement of checkpoints. Some sections take some more tries than others but the game offers the perfect balance between difficulty and reward. In a time where the roguelike genre reigns supreme in indie games, I was pleasantly surprised that this game offers a manually designed experience that offers a reward from skilled play that is not lessened by unfair chance encounters.
The controls are pretty tight, but could be a smidge tighter. Playing this game on a Playstation controller, I found it necessary to switch to D-Pad controls instead of thumbstick because the game would frequently register a thumbstick release as a short impulse in the opposite direction (missing dead-zone would be my guess), which caused the hero to turn the other way. D-Pad solves this problem though and for a classic game this would be the recommended method of control anyway.
The gameplay itself is super fun, in part because the sound effects are very well designed and each hit has a nice crunch to it. There aren't a lot of attacks to choose from but the normal attack chain, the charge attack and the mana shot offer a good range of experimenting to find the right tactic for each combination of enemies. The elemental attacks that are added later in the game require to find each enemy's weakness so there is a good amount of discovery all in all without too much fluff.
All in all Slain: Back From Hell was a big surprise for me as I didn't have very big expectations. It has become a personal favourite right away.

Recently, I decided to play Slain: Back from Hell once more. I forgot to leave a thumbs up the last time I played though, so here we go!
I like this game a lot - it has great visuals, music, tight controls and solid platforming.
But it's pretty obvious that not everybody's gonna love it. Gloomy heavy metal, stylized scenery, characters and dialogues - it's not everyone's cup of tea.
Besides, the game is very difficult, although player's death never breaks the pace - you just instantly resawn on the last checkpoint and continue forth. Not even music stops to accentuate player's death. Think of Super Meat Boy where you died many times, yet kept playing because failure does not waste your time - you respawn and try again until you succeed.
If you love metal and difficult games - this one's right up your alley! Would recommend!

What you see there is a hub. You buy games separately and this program/game appears in your library so you end up running it all through it. Sega released it way before Steam had DLCs system or reviews so they work kinda funkily. If you want to write reviews for those games, check Chapter 6 in this guide:
It's a good guide for other questions too.
Anyway, I think that Sega Classics packs started to come out around 2010 for a while before getting them all onto Steam. You can look up at the bundle on store page to see all the games. All of them, aside from Sonic CD, are bare-bones emulation of Genesis versions. Save states, sure. No online multiplayer. The emulator is based off ancient JEnesis, but personally I think of it as "fine enough". I mean, sure barely anybody gets the sound chip right not to mentioning that each model of Mega Drive sounded slightly differently. At least back then. I don't think that it supported x-input (Xbox controller input method).
Plus, Sega misconfigured it at times. For example, Golden Axe 3 doesn't have the second player enabled. I kinda write review for each game individually slowly so I am going to write in those if there is anything wrong.
None the less, that launcher is still available. Just choose "Simple Launcher" when attempting to launch it. It runs good so I stick to it.
Though, I have to warn you, it seems that if you load the emulator-side save state then you will not be able to do in-game saves properly.
And uhh, Genesis is a name of Mega Drive in US region.
In 2016 Sega with d3t developer has released the update. Let's call it Bedroom HUB. Now for additional 1 Gigabyte download, albeit if you plan to use "simple launcher" you can just delete bedroom files later on, you get another thing on top of emulator. Bedroom simulator that runs in Unity and is just a glorified menu for same emulator, nothing more. And it also lags for many. Albeit I think that some have found solution to make it run smoothly. Otherwise, eh. Different config options. You can make TV screen flat in options, by the way. Emulator has it's own mistake in config, mostly Alien Soldier runs too fast here. Sound is a bit screwed. Otherwise bleh, more of waste.
Albeit made a news by creating workshop that allows hacks to be uploaded. Of course it mostly means that randoms just uploaded a bunch of hacks off Internet that isn't their so if Sega wanted to support content creators then they kinda failed. And no, Simple Launcher doesn't support workshop. Have to workaround.
And uhhh, there are trading cards. Just in case you are a snotty capitalist. No achivements tho.
Thankfully, update also included uncompressed ROMs of purchased games into hub's folder so you can just grab them, claim that you have DRM-less version and run it on your own emulator. I think this is what they are for. At least until GabeN comes into your house and says that according you Steam agreement you only own rights to playing purchased games on Steam service. But who knows, I am derping.
And yep, just 58 or so games out ot whole library. You see, just because something came out on Sega Genesis doesn't mean that Sega owns it. These games are a selection of those that Sega has published itself. Or developed. Or owns. Or second-party with devs permission, I think. It's not like they can claim anything.
So as much as I think that Adventures of Batman and Robin is one of the best games around, it's still a licensed game that was made by a third-party company that also went to bankrupt almost immeditly. Good luck figuring that out.
However there are few games from Sega missing like Monster World 4, that had translated version on Virtual Console I think, or Super Hang-On. So yea.
Less begging and more discovering what is already here tho, okay?
And well, what can I say. Genesis wasn't a jRPG power-house like SNES, albeit few it has are one of the best, like Phantasy Star 4. Genesis wasn't a shmup power-house like TurboGrapx-16, albeit few it has are one of the best. But this collection has only Bio-Hazard Battle which is more of a hidden gem.
What Genesis did have is games that cater toward 90s-Arcade style gamers. As well as many quality games from various genres that gamers sadly have trouble to remember because most of them were part of a single brand-franchise, like when you throw kart racing as Sonic spinoff, and thus don't feel as important. Just the way that our memory works. Maybe a fast platformer. Maybe a mix of strategy and action or the port of the first ever traditional RTS. Maybe best games in beat-em-up genre. Or fast explosive action in shoot-em-up.
None the less, most of those games were arcade-like, short and hard. Almost no story outside of manuals. By the way, read manuals, either find original scans or check in the root folder of Sega Classics, there are some. How else people would figure out that you can slow your jump down by holding up in Wonder Boy Dragon Lair. Games themselves explain nothing. You aren't going to find any cool endings. Neither stuff to unlock. Devs back then expected you to play and replay games because for game process itself, not to unlock concept art. You come one day after work, you play game for a hour, you get game over, you stop playing game happy that you got enjoyment, you move on to the next day.
Also, silly thing: some games has high score list. But no way to save anything. Hue.
Also, regarding to controller. Most games used 3-button default controller while later games used 6-button controller that added X, Y, Z above A, B, C. And there is Mode button that if you held when launching console then it would switch it back to 3-button mode. It was rarely used by games.
And what else can I say. Genesis came out to the West in 1989 or so, marketed as upgrade over your old Nintendo (meant NES) that could give games that were almost as good as arcade versions, managed to beat TurboGraphx-16. Still managed to survive until 1996 when Sega decided to focus on the 32-bit generation and SNES was running around, thinking that it has won on the empty battlefield. Rocked with quality games and good 3rd party support. Had Sega-CD addon while Nintendo fans had to wait 10 more years for CD-based games and 32X that was like alternative to putting processor chip into every cart, costed overall less this way on theory. No, Sega CD or 32X aren't emulated there, Sonic CD is a separate port-remake on PC game engine. Blast Processor that allowed for beat-em-ups with big sprites and more than 3 enemies and enough power for rare software scaling, awesome funky sound chip that wasn't being forcefully filtered and bigger resolution than SNES (unless using high-resolution mode that allowed only 16 colors). Tho there are almost no multiplatform games here so no one cares anyway.
What I want to say is that it's an underrated console and that you should play more games than just Sonic.
Like, try Phantasy Star 4 or Bio-Hazard Battle, as mentioned, they are totally awesome.
Or try action-RPGs like Landstalker and Beyond Oasis.
Or get into fairly forgiving tactical jRPGs that are Shining Force games.
ToeJam and Earl is unique split-screen rouge-like slow exploration game to hang out with a friend in coop.
Streets of Rage series are the kings of Beat-Em-Up and Gunstar Heroes is awesome take on Shoot-Em-Up genre with unique weapon combination system and difficulty that isn't completely brutal, albeit it has higher one.
Take on immersive hard journey in Ecco the Dolphin.
Discover obscure (non mainstream) stuff like Gain Ground, Bonanza Bros or Decap Attack. Or Kid Chameleion.
Most importantly, try Shinobi games that includes Shadow Dancer. Those will blow your socks off, I promise.
And do Flicky.

That's the biggest waste of potential I've ever seen.
CONS:
1.The idea is freaking amazing: What would happen to a society that can control memory? Imagine, people could remember things that never happened, do horrible things because of false memories, become obedient soldiers, or maybe memory-addicts.
Instead, this game is like "Screw that, let's just make them all bad, mad people and get on with it!". Nothing sophisticated, everything is blunt and obvious.
2. The characters. Again - a huge potential for interesting characters (do I trust him because remember thing that didn't really happened? How can i know what's real?) that's gone to waste.
I didn't feel connected to none of them. The good guys were simply good without reason, the bad guys evil without reason. When a character died or suffered, it was like "Meh".
3. Paris. Again, that's a lovely idea - a game in futuristic Paris! The thing is, when non of the characters speaks French, or even in a French accent (Damn, Nillin has a BRITISH accent!), the names aren't French, nothing feel French - it's just New York with the Eiffel Tower and the prison is named La Bastille. That's about it.
Also, you can't explore, and you are led like a moron in a very specific line and you can't go back. Pretty frustrating.
4. Cut scenes. You can't skip them, and in some parts that you have to go over again and again until you make it, every time you fail and start over, INCLUDING THE GOD DAMN CUT SCENE!
Overall, I did want to finish the game and expected a plot twist, but I was disappointed.
But that doesn't mean this game has some good features, too:
PROS:
1. The memory remixes. This is the only part that reached the full potential I expected from DONTNOD - you need to find the delicate spots and you change a person - turn him to your side, make him kill himself, make him go mad. That's the best part of the game, but it happens only 4 times in the whole thing.
2. The battle system. It has its obvious flaws (hard to aim at a specific enemy and you have to finish a combo fighting the exact same enemy) but the sensen mechanism is unique and interesting. You can build you own combos and pick your own fighting style - healing, damage, or special moves.
3. Boss fights. Many boss fights weren't only about fighting, but also about thinking outside the box and finding actual weak spots. There were a lot of boss fights, so this made the game a little more special and not repetitive.
The bottom line - it sure as hell isn't worth the 30$ price. Not even 10$.
Maybe 5$ if you really don't have anything else to play. Hope that helped!

This game seems to be getting a lot of praise, I guess due to it dealing on a high level with psychosis (to be clear for those who do not know, "high level" means "on the surface", "tip of the iceberg"), and while it has a decent narrative, as a game, it fell short of expectations. A completely linear game, in a very static world, with repetitive and unimaginative "puzzles", and a combat system that, to me, felt almost like QTE, due to its simplicity, lack of movement, and the awkwardness of the camera while in combat.
The game is very short, and it would be much shorter if it weren't for the "puzzles" and the inability of the character to sprint: the character can only jog or walk.
I keep writing "puzzles" in quotation marks, because these aren't really what I would call puzzles (then again I was a long time player of The Secret World): you walk around trying to find shapes in the world, with the occasional maze thrown in here and there.
Personally, I'd have enjoyed Hellblade a lot more as a narrative, had I just been able to jog through the story, clicking the occasional lore piece, instead of being stopped every so often to look around for shapes while not being able to run, and fight the same very few enemy types over and over again using a subpar combat system.
The graphics are good, the sound is good, the animations are good, the art is good, but for me, not good enough to make up for the limitations of the actual gaming portions of the game. As it is, I have not finished the game, and I don't think I will.

Finished the game in 11 hours over roughly three days with exactly 50% achievements and something like 80% in-game completion. It piqued my interest immediately and kept it for the entire story. Normally I multitask while gaming, but within the first two minutes I had turned off everything else and was giving Ori and the Blind Forest my full attention. It's a fully engrossing game and is a treat on every one of the senses.
+Beautiful artwork, music, and sound design.
+Tight controls and movement that feels good.
+Level design that teaches you how to play. Not mind-numbingly easy, but fair.
+Steady learning curve; new things are introduced at a perfect pace. The game allows you to die if you're an idiot, but it does not allow you to avoid learning something.
+Good story, and a great storytelling style. A few interactive cutscenes alongside non-interrupting one-liners as you explore the world.
+Good characters, there aren't many but they're all endearing as ♥♥♥♥.
-Endgame is endgame. I'd hoped to go back and 100% the world map after the main story, but you're not able to play after finishing. In restrospect, I realize that it warns you before entering the last dungeon, something to the effect of "We may not be able to return from this place!" but I missed it because I was skipping over the nav fairy's dialogue. Which brings me to
-The nav fairy, Sein. Above, I mentioned the good storytelling style, which honestly could have done a fine job of telling the story on its own. However, your little ball of light companion has a lot of expositional lines and is the only character to freeze your game and talk to you in a text box. Honestly the game would have been fine without it. Sein's lines feel super annoying and handholdy in a game that otherwise really knows how to show rather than tell.
-Each dungeon has an escape portion at the end with an advancing hazard enforcing your speed. They're definitely quite fun and utilize all of the things you learned in the dungeon, taking the place of a boss fight, but they definitely feel unfair. I died maybe a handful of times in the overworld (my fault), but my deaths in-game totaled something like 500 pretty much solely because of the escape parts. It's a little too much of a change of pace from the overworld in my opinion.

I like this game, but I have to object to it on the terms that is is too similar to Sunless Sea (The development team for Sunless Sea assisted the team for A House Of Many Doors). The only people I could recommend this to are those that have played Sunless Sea and want more of the same before Sunless Skies comes out. Sunless Sea is more polished and HoMD has a quite frankly unintelligible combat system. It seems like it wants to be Faster Than Light, but no indication of the area of effect of enemy shells is given, nor an explanation of the abilities of crew members. Enemy ship shells fall without any indication of where they will land so there is no point in using action points to move crew members out of the field of fire instead of using those action points to DPS the opposing ship into wreckage.
The map is unnecessarily huge. You can traverse thirty+ squares (or more, if you're unlucky) of nothing but random objects until hitting a location. The locations and events are the entire appeal of this game, it makes no sense to make you slog through map squares where nothing happens before you get to the good stuff. It's also very easy to evade random encounters.
The randomly encountered objects also are far too limited and become routine. Oh, there's an abandoned house. Time to press-gang another crewmate.

A magnificent experience, period. Complaints of emptiness or boredom are all but unfounded, and the bugs are all but gone. It's a fabulous world packed with crannies to scuttle through and you'd be rather a silly ♥♥♥♥ing goose to pass it over.

tl;dr:  if you haven't played Darksiders II, if you dig hack-and-slash, if you like games that tell big stories and if you don't mind your games to be a little... glitchy then I'd say go for it.  I highly doubt you'll be disappointed, especially when it's on sale.  If you already own it, there's nothing new here (save for an even higher difficulty setting) that warrants another purchase but it
look nicer than before.

Cons
What, you want more?  Okay then, but know that there's no possible way I can be objective about this game.  I've put over 150 hours into the original.  I loved it so much, I was
to buy it again when Nordic released the Deathinitive edition.  I even bought the soundtrack.  On CD.  From Amazon.  Because that was the only place I could pay for it at the time.  Yeah, it was that bad.
See, I loved the art, the world and especially the STORY of the original Darksiders so when the sequel was announced, I was eager to get my hands on it and eager to see what would be done with Death.  Darksiders II brought everything I wanted and a whole lot more.  Where Darksiders I was pretty straightforward hack and slash, Darksiders II brings a richer, deeper world that invited exploration and a more meandering playthrough.  Where power was gained strictly through item collection in Darksiders, Darksiders II brought a bit of a role-playing element in with character levels and a reworked loot and ability system.  And where War was a straight-up
, Death is a more complicated character, with a wry-sense of humor delivered with pitch-perfect gravelly voice acting.  For me, the art, the monumental soundtrack (so good I need to hit it twice in this review), the cinematic set pieces and the sweeping plot arc of the story all added up to a game that was much, much greater than the sum of its parts.  Little wonder I've spent more than a solid week's worth of time playing it.
I'm sure I'm coming off as more than a bit of a fanboy here, and it's a fair cop.  I'm also sure that the Darksiders franchise isn't everyone's cup of tea and I won't begrudge anyone their preferences on that front.  But that said, and just for the record,
since Nordic
decided to get the band back together and make another sequel, I'm there.  Buying the Collector's edition...
, which, c'mon devs, take a hint!  Even if I don't know how they plan to top Death's story with
Fury.  Don't care.  Hell, if I lived near the dev team I'd probably bring them coffee and pizza or other reasonably-priced alternatives in my free time.  You can practically hear me squeeing with glee at the very idea of it now.

Just finished my first playthrough - this review will be mainly focused on how I think this game compares to the original darksiders.
Although I wasn't as immediately engrosed in the story as I was with the original darksiders, darksiders 2 grew on me as I progressed past the initial levels, where the game picks up pace. I'd say that, compared to the first game, the story arc is less fleshed out although I haven't completed any of the side campaigns/ quests as of yet.
However, in terms of the combat system, visuals, loot system and level design, darksiders 2 is far better than the original (especially with 1080p in this version).
- Combat is much quicker than the original and gives you some options: 2 skill trees, differing secondary weapons, item stats etc. which is really awesome compared to the more linear progression in the first game.
- Boss battles are less frustrating while still being challenging and equally epic. This was welcome after the nightmare ♥♥♥♥-fest that was Stygian ;-;
- Visuals are the big thing in this re-work of the game. Originally they were 720p (I think bc it was made for last gen consoles, then ported over) however now they are 1080p and the game has had many other visual elements (animations especially) improved.
- Loot is done in a more traditional RPG style rather than the linear progression in darksiders. It's not /that/ great but certainly a welcome improvement.

Another title I picked up during a Steam sale, Running With Rifles is a fairly unique game with interesting elements and surprisingly good replayability. It may not quite last long enough to justify the wholesale price, however.
Running With Rifles is a stylized 3D isometric game, and for the most part its almost cell-shaded graphics work quite well. Interestingly, the soldiers themselves are not 3D models, but are instead rendered with voxels. This gives them an odd look compared to the rest of the game, but it works out in the end and is evocative of classic Army Men toys. Running With Rifles is one of those games that, due to its art style, won't really become obsolete in graphics, and I definitely like the style they chose to follow.
The weapon and vehicle sounds are all distinct, but I will note that they aren't as powerful sounding as you might expect. This adds on to the feeling of being a toy soldier, with weapons producing odd pops and clicks instead of the thunderous report you might expect out of an M107 or Desert Eagle. The music is limited, and will become repetitive, but what they do have is catchy and upbeat, while still fitting the setting of the game.
I was surprised by the performance of this game, and unfortunately not in a good way. I got a much lower framerate than I would've expected - barely playable at all - on a laptop despite the seemingly low-end requirements of the title, so I would suggest trying the demo before you buy it to see how it runs on your system.
In Running With Rifles you take on the role of a single infantryman inside of a massive army, a cog in the machine. Each battle take place across locations about the size of a Battlefield conquest map, and features a very nice frontline system with multiple objectives and headquarters locations. Battles take place between either two or three factions, and players will receive two forms of currency for contributing to their side's chances of success. The first is requisition, which is used to buy items at armories and call for air support. The other is experience, which allows the player to be promoted. Promotions allow for new weapons to be used and new supports to be called (ranging from a vehicle drop to heavy artillery), and eventually allows the player to start commanding a squad. This progression doesn't make the player feel like a one-man-army, however; most unique weapons are exceedingly rare, and are lost forever on death. Armored players are only protected against one or two more bullets than those unarmored, and damage is represented using a unique system: When a soldier is hit with a bullet, the game determines, via a percent chance that varies from weapon to weapon, whether the soldier instantly dies or lives. All in all, gameplay is fairly unique and is the biggest contributor to the game's longevity.
The game's singleplayer revolves around a large, persistent campaign, where the player's faction seeks to conquer the entire region. The region spans every major map of the game, as well as several special campaign missions. Much of the time, you'll only face one enemy faction, but there are situations where you'll have to deal with two. The AI isn't genius, but they're competent enough in the field and put up a good fight; much of the time, if the two or three AI armies are left alone on relatively even ground, they will settle into a frontline-based stalemate for large periods of time. The campaign is a great way to learn about the game, and it is humbling in a way for a new player to expect to be able to hop into a vehicle and deal some heavy damage and instead be met with an angry
from the crew within. The final two missions can be somewhat aggravating, but the whole experience is quite enjoyable.
The game features two main gamemodes for multiplayer; either adversarial or cooperative. The latter of those two is the only one really played as of this review's publishing, which is a bit of a shame but is understandable; experienced players have an unfair edge with their rare weaponry and better knowledge of game mechanics compared to newer ones. The cooperative gamemode  is extremely punishing, and sees one whole faction of players square off against an AI onslaught, both sides having the goal of conquering the battlefield. It is persistent, as well, so you can save your gear, resources, and experience between matches and slowly collect interesting weapons. Another good way to extend the game's lifespan.
This game features Steam Workshop support, and already plays host to a wide variety of modifications. I am disappointed that there is a lack of custom maps, as that is the area which needs the most new variety in my opinion, but the new settings (ranging from the Great War to Mass Effect) still do the trick, and it's fairly easy to start making modifications without having to download development tools.
Running With Rifles is a fun isometric third-person shooter that is set back slightly by its lack of new maps in updates, but nonetheless can provide quite a few hours of good fun in singleplayer and many, many more in multiplayer. If you're interested in a more brutal, large-scale shooter than usual, definitely consider it, but maybe wait for a sale, as its $14.99 price tag is a bit much considering how much content it has. It's one of the few games I can think of that also has a good demo on Steam, so if your interest has been piqued by this review, I would definitely suggest downloading it and trying it out before you buy.
