This game is a literary treat like few others. It will make you feel like a Victorian Marco Polo skittering through Italo Calvino's Invisible Cities on a giant bugtrain, while sipping on some of that cosmic horror and understated dark humor blend perfected by the Fallen London gents (is it possible to talk bout this game without mentioning them? probably not).
In my opinion, despite being less polished, this is the superior game - more enjoyable to play (and forgiving) than its siblings Sunless Sea and FTL, more densely packed with ideas and atmosphere than anything I have played in a long while, putting to shame many projects with much larger writing teams (Torment, looking at you).
With so much sterling prose to read (a mind-boggling amount from a lone author), it really does not feel like the House had to be padded with so much empty space. I understand that the vast spaces are meant to create a pacing, and a sense of danger as you pick a random direction and venture as far as you can, hoping your fuel, hull and sanity will endure until you reach some harbor.
Unfortunately, there really is a little too much of that, and I feel like all I will ever experience from this game is a tiny fraction of what it has to offer, as the perspective of 10 more minutes of backtracking through mostly empty rooms for the next two bits of dialogue in some questline has become more grating than the reward. But perhaps it is fine - the House is too big for one person, and I have seen more than enough to be content.
Another issue is being asked in various quests to find random assortments of items, and not being given the slightest idea of where they might be found - I spend a couple of hours in vain looking for an oscillating prism to help the rebellious Heart of a Prince, and had to fail this intriguing questline, only to find such a prism by chance an hour later. Some sort of oracle to help with finding things would have been hugely appreciated.
Still, this game deserves all the praise I have to give. I was sold when I learned you play as a poet, journalist and museum curator. But the real heroes here are the cities, the locales, the diseases and the gods. (oh boy are there gods aplenty in that House). I dearly envy a mind capable of birthing that level of brilliance by the metric ton.

TL;DR: Not entirely polished, but an excellent narrative game with superb writing. A cosmic horror fan should especially buy this game.
I am going to actively avoid mentioning certain other games, because I think that this game deserves at least a few reviews that take it on its own merits and not in comparison to others.
Though the launch was a bit rough, with a lot of bugs rearing their heads, the dev put out 18 patches in a short time to clean up almost every bug and detail. Now this game plays pretty smoothly and it really is a fun time. I always find myself thinking "Oh, I have things to do, I'll get to the next location and save and quit." And then that repeats as at each location I uncover new steps and new things to do, new trails to follow. It is very easy to lose track of time by just following the many stories that come up so naturally through gameplay.
Pros:
Excellent writing
Lots of moral choice and ambiguity, even surrounding what seem like horribly callous or malicious acts. I stole a mother's memories of her children and it didn't even seem like the worst idea.
Not terribly grindy. Access to a few resources might be rather specific, but the basic things you need are relatively easily obtained, so progress occurs at your pace.
Unique world with a variety of interesting interpretations of various ideas and themes.
Cons:
There are still a few bugs, especially surrounding dialogue in certain dreams.
Controls and scenery during travel are a bit rough. Turning can be weird if you have a lot of carts.
In-game documentation is a bit sparse. You only get to see what your stats do one time, to the best of my knowledge. Make sure you remember it.
Pro/Con: Depending on how much directness you like in your cosmic horror. This game does not shy away from brutal and awful events being described quite plainly. Much cosmic horror takes an 'averted eyes' and euphemistic stance on dark events; this game definitely does not. While I find that a refreshing approach, some of the events have surprisingly made me feel upset. I rarely feel so attached to a game or character that I get emotionally involved in events to that degree, so I am overall pleased with that sort of connection. Others might be less enthused with that directness.

So this is a quality exploration game. The writing is good, and the atmosphere is spot on. I honestly love it. However, that isn't to say it's not without its flaws. pros:
-Fantastic writing
-unique premise
-nice turn based FTL inspired combat system
-very similar to sunless sea (which I loved) but with better pacing and not nearly as unforgiving
cons:
-bugs. Jesus christ the bugs.
Yeah that's pretty much it. I would have no complaints if it were not for the bugs.
While the game may be buggy, you should take into consideration the fact that the studio is only one guy. He can't find every single bug himself, and that's where the players have come in. He's been remarkably communicative with the players and has even followed up with specific bug reports after patching it. I have to applaud him for his proactive approach to communicating with the community, and lots of large studios could really learn a thing or two from him.
All in all, and for all its bugs, I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. It's clever, its interesting, and you can seduce a 10 mile high tower of conjoined crows. What more could you ask for?

I was trying to decided whether to give this a thumbs up or down and, in the end, it boiled down to the fact that I couldn’t think of anyone I know who I could honestly say "yah, get this, you'll enjoy it". This is one of those games that needs a 'neutral' response.
The controls are responsive and the art style is neat. When I died I never felt like it was because the game cheated me, it was always me not pressing the right button at the right time. Despite the game teetering back and forth between brutally difficult and yawnfully boring fights, it was interesting enough to get me to keep playing to the end.
Unfortunately there is little substance to the world and zero replayability if you get 5 [vaguely] hidden items (which have a lackluster reward for obtaining).
- I'd have to say the worst part was the game music. I'm not a hard metal fan and the music was not very atmospheric. I turned it off on the second stage and played Castlevania music instead.
- Next on the chopping block is some of the cringeworthy dialogue. The game tries really hard to be "in character" but some of the dialogue is so bad I couldn’t help but wrinkle my brow in a "that’s really the best you had?" thought.
- The combat gets a little samey after a few levels as well. There's a damage-type mechanic that adds basically nothing to the game and you really have no way of knowing if one type is better than another on a specific enemy unless you're told by the hag or count the number of hits it takes to kill them with each type. Whether you do or don’t bother with the damage type (there's a neutral damage type I spent most of the game using instead with little issue) the only two things you really do the entire game is the charge attack or the block-counter; everything else does so little damage (or leaves you vulnerable) even with the correct type that its not worth the time to use.
- And the last, minor but noteworthy aspect that kept me from recommending is that there is no advancement. There are no powerups or additional moves you gain that allow you to vary up how progressing through the levels or fighting enemies occurs, you really are fighting solely to get to the next nearly identical fight so you can get to the next nearly identical fight. Getting your first damage type seems cool until you realize its almost entirely cosmetic and getting the second feels even more disappointing.
In conclusion, the game was worth the couple bucks I picked it up for and I hope the developers make another game taking what did and didn’t work in this one to their next creation. That being said, I still can't picture anyone in particular I would honestly tell to spend money on this game.

I really wanted to like this game. It seemed to be one of those nice trips back to when video games were pure fun. But unfortunately this title isn't fun at all; it sucks. It holds a good concept at the very best.
I've lost like 30 minutes dealing with a skeleton who would kill me with a couple of blows. Until I realized that I should simply duck and attack (I tried to back dash/guard but it's useless). Now imagine yourself fighting a creature twice your size and all you do is to duck and swing your sword. That's no strategy. That's ridiculous! And you have to go like that for 15 blows or so. One mistake, you die. In my opinion this is not difficulty for I didn't have to evolve/create strategies. I just duck and swing. I had to get on my knees and blow it - doesn't sound so hardcore now, does it? And just for the record, this enemy exists in all levels I've put myself through so far.
Platform/action, stage-by-stage games should have at least two things in their absolute best shape: jumping and combat. To be honest I would settle for tight controls. Everything else would be fine. If only the controls were good I wouldn't care about repetitive enemies, repetitive levels, tiresome dialogs, big frame drops depending on the level you're in etc.
So my frustration is even bigger because the game has actually several good things like the music and sound, the characters, power-ups. The plot is fair enough. But failed the most fundamental aspect of video games: human interface.
I even had to change my MO of finishing every game I start. I couldn't take it. I'm sorry. I was slain by this game (pun intended).

FPS Perfected. It would not be a stretch to say that CoD’s initial try at a modern FPS not only set the groundwork for how big the franchise is today, but has also inspired the genre to be as big and as multi-player focused as it now is. Out of all the games on the 50% off list, this will be the one you’ll least regret.
From a single-player standpoint, IW finally stuck to telling a single narrative and it worked. It was the first game that, to me, felt like a purposeful story. Characters were made to appear more personable, but don’t really stand out until later on in the franchise. Team AI hardly got in the way while also being useful, and enemy AI was firm but fair. Although it would be unfair for me to criticize the game for its monotony in killing hordes of enemies, it would have been nice to be able to do so in more creative fashions (i.e. more AC-130-like levels and levels that required more driving or stragegy). Luckily, this is expanded upon in the franchise and was still more than I could have ever asked for out of a game that’s almost 10 years old.
But the obvious winner and the main reason why this game has more players on it than the latest installment of the franchise (Infinite Warfare(IW)) comes down to its multiplayer. Nostalgia aside, the maps, weapons, and well-designed perk systems still hold up and are emulated in your most cherished FPS. The challenge systems for weapon attachments and XP were also a nice touch, including the implementation of camos and golden weapons. Even though the graphics aren’t on par with today’s titles, there’s still enough content in there to keep you engaged. It just bites that the prestige system was only on console systems and the latest remaster - but I still won’t give in to that darn cash grab with IW.
Whether you buy it to relive the glory days, or you’re buying it to see what a genre-defining FPS is like - there’s no reason to not have this title in your library.

I'm usually hesitant when it comes to buying games that have really good scores because I was afraid that I'd be one of those people that wouldn’t enjoy them. When I happened to stumble upon some gameplay footage of Ori and the Blind Forest, I was immediately hooked to try this game out. All I have to say is: man, is this one hell of a good game, from the art direction to the music to the gameplay; everything about this game is truly spectacular, and I can definitely see why so many people gave really good remarks for the game.
Story/Plot:
I’ll give a one-sentence synopsis of the game’s story without any spoilers. The story takes place in the forest of Nibel and the goal is to help Ori – an orphan and a white guardian spirit – and Sein – ‘the light and the eyes’ of the Spirit Tree – revive the Spirit Tree and restore a decayed forest back to its former beauty; but something is trying to stop you from doing so. There is a narrator who speaks at certain points throughout the game. Overall, following the story and being told by the narrator really engaged me to keep playing and I really enjoyed every single part of it. Just a small warning that if you're going to play through Ori and the Blind Forest, you may experience what people call 'the feels' during your experience, because I know I did. (10/10)
Graphics & Music:
Now these two points are where the game shines the most. The art style really reminded me of Hayao Miyazaki (the mastermind of many well-known Ghibli films), especially with a certain character in the prologue. Then I looked up this game and realized that the art design was inspired by him as well as other works like The Lion King and the Iron Giant, films that I really enjoyed as a child. The art for the environment is one of the most beautiful art styles; it’s really compelling and I very much enjoyed seeing how beautiful the game looks. I can say the same for the music, which is why I included music along with the graphics. The music is mostly orchestrated and/or piano, and the music always sets the perfect mood in each section of the game and in many of the scenes. I’m a sucker for video game music, especially when there’s orchestra and/or piano involved, and this game is no exception. These two are what made the immersion of exploring the environment such a great experience for me. (10/10)
Gameplay:
As a 2D platformer, there’s a lot to know about the gameplay mechanics. Ori is the character you control to traverse and explore the forest, while Sein is in charge of keeping you safe from any foes and obstacles that come your way (Ori will be able to have abilities of his own later in the game). There are collectibles in the game, such as abilities and upgrades for Ori and Sein (many of which are required if you want to explore everywhere), health shards, and energy shards. You can save the game either through save points, which are found in certain spots; or you can create Soul Links (which require enough energy cells) to serve as your checkpoint. The player can also collect ability points to purchase very useful upgrades, which must be purchased in the order they’re presented. The traversing combined with what appears to be a fighting Navi (Legend of Zelda) was what made Ori and the Blind Forest felt very Metroid-esque to me; which isn't a bad thing at all.
As much as I didn't want to give any faults for Ori and the Blind Forest, there are two reasons why I deducted one point in this category. The first reason is about the difficulty of Ori and the Blind Forest: there is only one difficulty and that one difficulty is pretty difficult as it is. The game does get harder as you progress through the story; so you’re required to take extreme caution traversing the environment as one single mistake may lead you to your doom. So depending on what kind of player you are, you may have some frustrations trying to complete certain parts of the game; because I know I have. I believe the Definitive Edition adds different difficulties for you to make the game easier or harder than it already is. The second reason is in regards to the instructions. After the prologue, you take control of Ori, and the game kind of throws in everything that you need to know about how to play the game at you all at once. So you may forget a thing or two, and I definitely forgot one of those things. Though it led me to frustration in some parts of the game, I always find that it’s my fault for the mistakes that I made and not the gameplay; and that’s definitely tells me that the gameplay is enjoyable. (9/10)
Overall Verdict:
To be honest, despite what everyone has been saying, I really was not expecting too much out of Ori and the Blind Forest. But now that I've just completed the game at the time of this review, I was blown away with everything that this game has to offer; and immediately convinced me to make it one of my favorite video games of all-time. The art and the music are the two main points of this game that I believe make Ori and the Blind Forest a truly spectacular game. I really enjoyed following the storyline and exploring [almost] every part of the environment while clearing obstacles. Even if you're not a huge fan of platformers, I think that Ori and the Blind Forest is definitely a game worth trying; and I though I would recommend this more to those who like platformers, I definitely give this game a high recommendation.
Overall Score: 9.5/10

Ori and the Blind Forest is an example of how a Metroidvania/Platformer should be made. The artwork is amazing, the sound track matches the game perfectly, then controls are tight and responsive and it contains a plot that makes sense and compels you want to finish it. It doesn’t need weeks to play (10 hours should get you through the game without using a guide), but it can be rushed much quicker- in under 3 if you are very skilled.
I won’t go into the plot, suffice to say it’s a story of loss and sacrifice, and goes about explaining it in a way that doesn’t overwhelm the player, but fleshes out all the characters so you have an understanding of why things are happening.
The environments are well designed and if it’s your first run through or 50th, you can see little additions here and there that still balance out the area after you have picked up certain upgrades. As mentioned the controls are very responsive, you don’t accidently jump off a cliff in this game, but using a controller is a must.
The soundtrack deserves a review just for itself, it’s just that good.
My only gripe with Ori and the Blind Forest is how hard some of the area’s become- we are talking super meat boy spikes of difficulty here. These aren’t gradual build up’s, they spike from relatively easy to stupid hard in one screen. Fortunately, this isn’t often (just enough to keep you wary). If you are hunting the 100% achievement, then this might be an issue for you (unless you like pain).

This is actually the first time a game has dragged me across the threshold to write a review. Not because it's so good, but because so many things irked me.
To start off with the good:
+ Great story = I don't know many near-futuristic games like these and I found the story intriguing, really made want to play on.
+ Setting = By now almost every city & town in America has been a setting for one game or another. Nice to see Europe being the main stage for once, with Neo-Paris as the theater.
+ Graphics = For a game that's 4 years old, it has some really great graphics. With my GTX1060 6GB OC I was able to play it rather smoothly (only some odd drops in FPS).
And that's about it for the good. Up next are, for me, the most disappointing/annoying things:
- Camera = While being in the larger areas poses no problem in gameplay, when you get into combat in tight areas, the camera doesn't exactly work in your favour. It's mostly all just manual repositioning, since the camera will just stay on one side and kind of sidescrolls with you.
- Gameplay = This game has taken 'make it difficult, but also help the player out from time to time' for developing games a bit too literal. While you are treated like a moron in the 'free-roam' (come back to that later) and you are guided everywhere, the combat is just ridiculously infuriating. They start introducing new types of units gradually, but in the last 30% of the game or so, they just start to spam the electrified enemies, who hurt you if you hit them. And you will hit them, as the targeting of attacks is just horrible. There has been a couple of times where she (Nilin) would hit the electrified enemies while I was trying to hit the normal ones (to heal myself with), killing me because I was already low health.
- Immersion = You don't really get immersed in the game, as it's actually quite empty. You can't really free-roam (heck, in crisis-situations some moves even feel stupid), as you are forced to take the ledges that show an arrow, while there are perfect ledges right next to it that you can't get on to. None of the NPC's can be spoken to, except for the ones relating to the mission.
TL;DR = it just feels like they started making this game with big ambitions, realized they had no money for such a big project and just gave up halfway through the development. It's a game that tried to be a combination of Deus Ex and Assassin's Creed, but failed to imitate both. The one (kinda) unique thing they did, remixing memories, was fun but appeared only 4-5 times.
Buy it on sale, but don't pay more than €5 for it.
I'd give it a 5.5/10, as I did enjoy the game somewhat. Really just disappointed, because I can see the potential.

A game that received better than average support when it came out, but didn't make waves - unlike a game the same studio, DONTNOD, would make later,
, that became a hit for story-focused gamers everywhere. And because their name was on this game, I wanted to give it a whirl.
I honestly had a hard time at first getting into this game. It's almost claustrophobically linear at times - curious nooks and crannies to possibly explore, and yet the main character can't even walk into the debris from a painfully obvious invisible wall or swing to a ledge Infamous-style a bit further over that looks identical in every way; combat, that was inspired in its design by Godhand and similar fighting/character action games, feels slow and clunky despite the movements themselves being fluid, and the moves not adding much to the flavor of fighting in comparison to relatively uninteresting enemy types (at least for fight scenes); and the music, while certainly enjoyable and recognizable, can be hard on the ears at times with its techie distortions.
But I remember how the game opened - and I was determined to see the rest of the story through. And my goodness, was it worth it. It's clear to see where DONTNOD's strengths are, and that's in their storytelling. The setting of Neo-Paris in the end of the 21st century, rebuilt after global collapse, with its harsh contrast of post-war urban wasteland and new shining towers is something to behold, and this game loves to presents its vistas - perhaps a little too often, but each time a grand splendor of the world beyond. And with a new time, comes a new technology: Senzen, the digitization - and commoditization, degredation, and augmentation - of human memories. Backstory of the world and the view of its inhabitants is told through text articles, human encounters, and in-game advertisements for different fantasy systems all based on Senzen technology. And with this technology, there is now a new form of terrorism - The Errorists, thieves and modifiers of memories, in opposition to this new "utopia" being built.
And you play as a woman, Nilin, who finds herself in a mental asylum scenario, her memories taken from her, and you are suddenly given the chance to escape... and rediscover who you are. Every step of the way is rough, as it should be for the path Nimble Nilin treads, but each reveal, each twist, is intense and well done, even if you see it coming. Which, I have to say, about half of them I did, and still felt it hit me.
Oh, and there are a few game mechanics that, once I got used to the controls, I really liked from a story perspective.
If you are a story lover and like eye candy, and don't mind doing a bit of slogging and log collection to get it, definitely play this game. At some point, setting up your Presens (hit combos) will click, you'll get used to the combat, and it will be one less thing you really think about as you seek more of the story for its conclusion. Because, really - once the game gets out of the way, the story is gripping.
Play with a controller, though. The controls are♥♥♥♥♥for mouse and keyboard.

*Minor spoilers ahead*
This game is about making your way through a mansion with 1000 rooms. It's an interesting idea and the various setpieces that pay homage to other horror classics were pretty cool. There were some tense moments and I admit I jumped a few times. The place where the game falls short is that there are too many empty rooms. You start out getting save points every 50 rooms. Levels consist of wandering through 15 empty rooms, finding a setpiece that sets up some story and lets you explore to get a key to proceed. You get chased by something for 10 rooms, then stumble on through more empty rooms until the save point. At room 300, save points start to appear less often (every 100 floors). The same basic pattern repeats, but now you are punished for death by having to redo many more rooms if it happens that you die in a late stage before the next save. I completed the game in about 3 hours or so and my opinion is that it could be about 500 rooms instead of 1000 and simply have fewer empty hallways to slog through. The game is free, so might as well give it a try.

Short version: This game is due for another name change, to "10 spooktacular rooms and 990 empty hallways."
I like the concept of this game, and I enjoyed it for about 100 rooms. But after an hour of "this room again," it started becoming very grating to see the same things and hear the same 'spooky creaky door' soundbytes.  As for the actual content in the rooms that weren't empty, the reviews oversold the game for me; I was really expecting something more as I progressed, but that expectation never materialized.
I think this game could be something really good, but as of right now, it could absolutely stand to be pared down to 500 rooms of cute terror. There's a lot of room for potential, but nothing to fill in the space.

This game feels like a huge backward step for the Wolfenstein series.  Everything in The New Colossus feels like a substantial downgrade from its predecessor.  Stealth has been nerfed heavily, with more or less any kill sending guards into an alarm state with no clear way to cancel.  Blazkowicz is far more vulnerable than he has ever been, even inside a suit of power armour, meaning most fights are spent in cover - completely antithetical to The New Order's approach to combat.  There are fewer weapons, and what you do have feels wholly ineffective on any difficulty, with enemies taking multiple shots to even stagger.
On a technical front the game is also pretty disappointing.  Unlike The New Order or The Old Blood, which featured huge, imposing vistas showing the scale of the Nazi threat, The New Colossus is content to place you in cramped, poorly designed corridors filled with superfluous detail that will frequently cause the player to get stuck.  Don't expect anything near the grandeur of Castle Wolfenstein or the London Nautica
On the plus side, the writing is as good as it ever has been, but the problem here is in spite of the game having a genuinely good story to tell, it completely overshadows the gameplay.  The New Colossus is maybe 60% story and 40% gameplay, and I genuinely feel like the developers, if given the skillset, would have rather made a movie than developed a game.
In summary, this is a game that sold itself on killing Nazis, yet does an astonishingly poor job of letting the player do so.  It is short, unambitious, dull, rote, mean, stingy, but most of all just generally disappointing.  Machinegames can do better.

Much like the first one, I had a lot of fun with Wolfenstein II. The game looks pretty as hell, and the environments are some of my favorite in an FPS. The new characters mesh well with the old cast, forming a continuity that makes me invested in not just their successes, but also how they interact. Sigrun was a surprise favorite. The story was fantastic. Setting the game in America made everytime I killed a Nazi feel just that much more patriotic. Essentially Wolfenstein II is just The New Order turned up to 11, especially when it comes to the superscience and drama.
There aren't many new guns, but there are more than a few new abilities introduced that sweeten the gameplay just enough to keep it from being stale without turning into a different game.
That said, there were a few problems.
I beat the game in about nine hours, which felt short for a $60 game. Now that's not a horrible return on investment insofar as hours of fun, but there wasn't nine hours of content. The game is just hard, but not always in a fun way. New Order's difficulty was fun. This sometimes ekes into trial-and-error you-just-wanted-to-pad-the-length difficulty. That said, it's entirely possible I just need to git gud.
I also had a weird problem where the hit feedback just wasn't enough. Between the audio and visuals, there were a lot of times I just did not realize I was being shot until my health got low enough that the screen got really red. Even when I was aware I was being shot, I rarely knew from which direction. I would say Sunless Sea and A House Of Many Doors are like siblings.
Clearly the same family, but really quite different characters.
A House of Many Doors is the bigger one - the map really comes off as bigger, though divded into sections, a bit similar to Binding Of Isaac.
It is also the more talkative sibling - there is simply more writing (but excellent writing, no less).
It has a worse taste in fashion - the UI has many smaller quirks and issues and is rather inefficient at times, which can be a bit annoying.
It is a bit more clever than it's brother - instead of action combat, combat in this game is turn based and allows you to apply some actual tactics and send people around. Nice!
It is more merciful - you can save at (almost?) any time and have different save slots.
It is a worse dancer - The controls range between working fine and "why does this feel so weird to control", some of this is related to the UI issues.
It is insane - I mean, even more so than Sunless Sea. Wonderful.
If asked which one I would recommend more, I'd have kind of a hard time. Sunless Sea is more polished, no doubt. But give this one some more time & publicity and I am sure the developer can iron out many of the remaining issues.
But either way, you can't go wrong with buying A House of Many Doors.

If A House of Many Doors looks like an eerie amount like Sunless Sea, you're not mistaken - but there's good reason for that. Failbetter Games (the devs of Sunless Sea) apparently financed half of this game, and the primary developer worked on it in their offices. Once you understand that, the connection to Sunless Sea makes a lot more sense, and rather than a knockoff, it feels like a sister title to Sunless Sea.
That said, it's certainly a bit more rough around the edges than Sunless Sea. While most of the UI and mechanics are the same, there are some differences. The art isn't nearly as polished, and the gameplay isn't quite as fun. Rather than exploring a map that changes each playthrough, you explore a series of tiled rooms (similar to Binding of Isaac) where the locations stay the same. There are some randomized events on each tile, but for the most part they're visually uninteresting and static. The combat, too, is a drag. The mechanics are a bit like FTL, except not in real time, and it's best avoided as it's never particularly fun or rewarding. That makes exploring the world in A House of Many Doors more of a chore than the almost meditative experience it was in Sunless Sea.
Still, despite these flaws, it's absolutely worth playing simply because the writing is absolutely phenomenal. It's just as good as Sunless Sea, yet unique with its own tone. Despite the bland gameplay, it's a world you want to explore, that's easy to get lost in - which is a huge accomplishment.
If this is the beginning of a series of "Sunless-likes" I couldn't be more happy. It's been a long while since I've found anything so enchanting and transporting in the world of gaming, and it's great to have something to fill that gap while Sunless Skies goes through development.

I have not played this game much yet so I can't really speak to overarching plot or pacing, but I can speak to tone and character, both of which House of Many Doors has in abundance. HOMD is as excellent and lovingly crafted as the delightful Sunless Sea (is that the wrong word, given the genre? should I say delightfully dreadful instead?), from which HOMD draws a lot of inspiration. I very highly recommended it if you enjoy rich, narrative games with strong mechanics that help drive the pace without masking the story.

Do I recommend this game? Yes!
Do I recommend buying this game? Only if you want to support the developer, otherwise play it for free!

This game visualizes some of the most detailed of pixels I've ever seen and it's not hard to see how much effort has been put in to flesh that out. From the hellish background and environment to the death animations, it's a sight to behold. Slain: Back from Hell does seem to possess the heavy metal theme going, since I do get a Black/Death/Extreme Metal kind of vibe through the visuals alone.
It wouldn't also be a surprise to know that most of the soundtrack consists of metal-sounding tunes. That's a plus too.
This game however, despite all of that - is just not fun. It's a trial and error game where you're going to die a bunch of times, trying to compromise with the level of unfairness. Have you ever had an obstacle of a level hurt you? Those hands you're supposed to jump on? Yeah you can get hurt by those even though they help so that you could reach higher places. What the hell is that about? I've actually died a couple times because of those damn things and thinking that since it's an object that'll help me, I can't get hurt by it. That's not the case in Slain, apparently.
The bosses are fun as hell to fight. The enemies? Not so much, moreso, the opposite. I can't tell you how much I hate those ♥♥♥♥ers who hurl energy shots at you. You can parry them back, but it takes a while to kill them with their own shots. Much less, it takes a little to kill them even with your own attacks. How are you supposed to feel powerful in this game if you have difficulty killing even lesser enemies? It doesn't make sense.
Those wolf guardians? Screw them too, because they require precise timing to get hits in on them. Charging your attack, in particular against them, requires a narrow opening to make it. What I hate the most about them is that they can delay their attacks until you get close. They'll begin summoning a energy wolf form that they'll sick on you and if you distance yourself away, the energy infront of the guardians will still be going. It is until you get closer, then they'll attack. It gets pretty annoying dealing with this.
So, the point of the matter is, dealing with the big things in Slain isn't so much of a problem. But it's all of the smaller things littered about in this game that make up for this lacking trait. Dealing with those smaller things may see you just getting killed over, over and over again. Gets boring quick.

It's no secret that this game looks fantastic. If you're into the SNES era pixel graphic aesthetic, there's no doubt you're drooling over over the screen shots and as good as those look, the game only look
in motion due to some gorgeous dynamic lighting effects. The music is good, the controls are responsive, the story isn't intrusive, this game has
everything going for it!
Unfortunately, the actual gameplay kinda sucks. It's not that it's overly challenging; you're given generous re-spawn points, infinite lives and there's almost no spawn delay, you can even "restart from checkpoint" at will from the menu. It's not that combat isn't engaging; you have a range of options to deal with everything the game throws at you and there's a large enough variety of enemies to keep things fresh, even the palette swaps have some interesting twists. The game doesn't even rely on unfair tricks or excessive trial and error deaths or anything silly like that.
The problem with the game is that it's
tedious. Every enemy and I mean EVERY enemy is either a massive damage sponge or flying. Basic skeleton enemies don't even die from your standard issue three hit combo! When you're dealing with big enemies it takes either multiple counters or charge attacks to take them down, and while it's reasonable to not simply be able to one shot them, basic attacks do so little to them that it's hardly worth sneaking them in. The result is waiting,
of waiting.
There are two primary types of sections; long corridor sections and climbing sections. When dealing with the former, you often encounter unit spawner protected by big enemies. Since big enemies basically require use of multiple slow calculated charge attacks or counters, this basically results in kiting everything back, killing the big thing, then slowly advancing to the spawner because everything it spawns takes about two attack combos. Sometimes you can rush the spawner but it's the exception. In some cases you can use your magic to stun the basic enemies and chain counters off it, but not all basic enemies allow this function.
The climbing sections are a bit more interesting, but often include major level design flaws. I'm talking about things like dissolving platforms that don't respawn and a switch that's required from progression and easy to miss on the side you came from. Normally this would be absolutely intolerable but the generous checkpoints make it somewhat forgivable, it's still just more time you can expect to have to waste though.
There's one boss in particular that highlights everything wrong with this game and it's the...
The game's not terrible, but it's deeply flawed. If you're OK with tedious gameplay and you're a game design student, this game is probably worth buying, just to deconstruct.

4/5

Slain got re-released after it quite literally went through development hell the first time round due to negative reviews stemming from it's difficulty & lousy controls. Now, with a fittingly appropriate new name and a few tweaks here & there Slain ' Back From Hell ' was resurrected once more. It's style reminded me of classics of old, such as Ghost 'n Goblins / Altered Beast / Splatter House, with it's distinct levels & imaginative bosses. Here, the developers have stitched all that together with a sprinkling of the bloody macabre & thumps you with head banging Heavy Metal rifts, producing an all together new kind of beast. On reflection, the game is still cursed with sluggish & poorly thought out controls, which frequently hinders the fluidity this game deserves to be dishing out. Added to that is it's unforgiving difficulty, where you feel like you're just progressing through sheer luck, rather than any skill gleaned by perseverance. Its a shame, as this game has a lot of good ideas going for it, and I wanted this game to succeed. If more blood, sweat & tears from the developers were applied, it would have remedied all these shortfalls. I hope it's successor ' Valfaris ' fares far better, and the lessons are learned.  As it stands, Slain: Back from Hell will remain a game worthy of a few minutes of your curiosity … nothing more.

Remember Me is one of those middle-of-the-road games that neither impresses very often nor messes anything up.
Take the story for example - it doesn't take itself seriously enough to deliver a hard dystopic sci-fi vision, and it's not funny or light-hearted enough to work as a great adventure. It features an interesting if hard-to-grok concept - memories are now interchangeable, and also can somehow gives you superpowers and make you invisible? I'm not really sure how it works, but the lore is there to read for those interested in its far-fetched ideas. There's just enough of a plot to want to see it through to the end, but the characters are really uneven, with some cartoonish Japanese-style charicatures thrown in with some truly abysmal voice actors (save for the main character - she's good) and some pathetic action movie one-liners. With such an uneven tone, I couldn't really recommend playing for the story. Although it's worth mentioning that there are 4 "memory remix" sequences, which are interactive cutscenes that feel pretty well acted and directed compared to the rest of the game's cutscenes and dialogue. Since they're interactive and wholly original from a gameplay standpoint, they definitely stand out in an otherwise mediocre story.
Or how about the environments? They are well-detailed, with very strong art direction and an eye for photography - the use of color and lighting can be spectacular even by today's standards. And yet, they boil down to a series of linear corridors, ledge sequences, and combat spaces that very rarely loop back in on themselves. If you look closely at the backgrounds - and you might because they are beautiful - you will see geographical inconsistencies, such as passing through your typical loading corridor and suddenly emerging in a completely different place with different buildings around you. It's like each piece was designed to be as beautiful as possible without any thought given to how they interconnect. Trying to keep a mental map in your mind of where you are in relation to where you've been is useless, so your brain will go into autopilot before long. That missing engagement with your environment, combined with a distinct lack of set pieces, means the game is quickly forgettable as you progress through it.
The combat is perhaps the most uneven part of the game. On the plus side, it feels really polished and fluid, and the enemy variety is actually pretty decent. You will have to juggle through all of your powers and combos regularly, and each combat encounter feels pretty different. The presentation is also top-notch, with some awesome animation and music that reacts real-time to how well you're performing. (The finishing moves in particular have a really neat sense of violence without showing any gore, as your character grabs people's heads and savagely rips their memories out, represented by bursts of digital fluid and color.)
And yet, some of the basic mechanics will make you raise your eyebrows. The unique gimmick here is the "combo lab" - you essentially choose what each button in your preset combos does, whether it be recharge your health, cool down your super powers, or deal extra damage. These can be chained together and even give you exponential benefits. Sounds good and can be satisfying reaching the end of combos, but the combat system constantly gets in your way. You can only combo on one enemy at a time, and if you get hit by or hit a different enemy, you lose the combo chain. Since enemies group up and hit you pretty frequently, the auto-targeting system doesn't do a good job of keeping you locked in with one enemy, and you will often break a combo midway through and start punching the wrong guy because that's what the game thought you wanted to do. Either having a hard lock function or allowing you to keep your combo going against multiple enemies would have made much more sense and kept the fluidity up to a Batman Arkham standard.
Beyond that, you have a checklist of action-adventure gaming tropes that found their way into the game and add very little to the experience. Collectibles - check. QTE's - check. Uncharted-style climbing paths - check. Boss fights - check. Very easy puzzles - check. The part where the helicopter chases you with a machine gun - check. The sewer level - check. The entirely predictable plot twists - check.
I could go on, but maybe 2 people in the world will read this far, and nobody cares about old games that didn't sell well, so I'll keep it simple.
Remember Me is enjoyable to play through, but it doesn't do anything interesting enough to warrant a strong recommendation. It's glitch-free, polished, stable, fluid, and at times gorgeous, but feels uneven and a bit safe in terms of what it tries to achieve. The fun is there, the visuals are there, and it's a really easy game to suggest for a weekend with nothing else going on, but don't expect to be blown away.

This game is a trip, and definitely has a meaning to it.
There are few games where I'll think about real life, consequences, and the result of everything that's happened so far, but Remember Me definitely hit the note. It's odd to play the game and view the memories of your family in the past, only to alter what they remember for your "personal" benefit.
It makes you think, "What if we had this ability in the real world?" Though I'm glad to say we don't.
Remember Me shows through the story that removing your bad experiences in life can lead to living a life that isn't worth living at all. It shows you that everything that has happened made you into who you are today, and removing those memories removes yourself. Nilin, thoughout the game, recovers the memories that were stolen from her and realizes that the pain that people have been through needs to stay with the people, not locked up where "it didn't happen at all."
Gameplay-wise, while the combat can get repetitive pretty quick due to the two-button combo system, walking around the environments were a pleasure visually to look at. The linearity of the game will definitely put some people off, and the parkour mechanics aren't as refined as, say, Mirror's Edge, but it works out for this game.
This game has become one of my favorites, and I'll definitely be doing a replay of it for collectable hunting and to enjoy the story again. I recommend everyone play it for the story, at least. Crank down that difficulty and immerse yourself in a world where you could have the ability to bend anyone's memories for your own enjoyment and benefits ... and realize how bad of an idea that could be.

Large Combat Combos never came into play for me
They should have utilized the memory altering mechanics more often

FIrst off im not really going to go into detail about what makes this game good as many many many of the reviews already go through that. The art style and music and voice acting are perfect. The memory redux and other nifty things the game has throughout are pretty good as well. There are some pretty glaring issues though.
First off the game is 100% linear which by itself isnt a BAD thing.
Second, the game has a tendency to be very unclear with directions even being this linear. This shows itself more once you got the pocket lock thing later in the game.
Third, and pretty much the biggest of the three, is the combat. Want to know how to take an purely unique combo system and make it frustrating? Slow unlocks, throw massive groups of enemies, have no real defense system in play.  I have never in my life seen a game that punishes its players so harshly for learning a new ability or just getting more powerful in any way. They throw HORDES of enemies at you making essen fury pretty much required in every fight, which wouldnt be to bad a thing if it didnt just throw the combo system out the window. Pretty mcuh every fight is essen fury, essen stun then gg. If you try to fight without them it will be kinda rough without just doing the basic 3 hit combo. Wait till you get to the elite guys oh boy thats fun. remember the essen stun? yeah theyre immune! and so is 80% of the enemies you face now. Oh , and when you hit an elite you take damage as well so the only way to kill them reliably is with full healing combos which do very, VERY little damage. What to say about A House of Many Doors? Well let's start by describing some of the experiences of my alter-ego Elizabeth.
Elizabeth grew up pretty much within the Pauper's College of the City of Keys. She doesn't particularly recall her parents and none of the professors, porters, students and other assorted irresponsible adults of her youth seemed to know anything about them. She ended up both the ward and student of the College gradually growing up and progressing in her studies. One day in her late teens or maybe early twenties she had seemlessly made the transition from student to professor, seemingly without anyone noticing or actually offering her tenure. Her knowledge of and fascination with the occult made her one of the College's foremost experts on the subject, though her interests ranged much wider than that. For a few years she was happy and glad but eventually she began to unearth half-forgotten myths that hinted at something more. Not merely another locked door within the House but a door out of the House altogether. She tried so very hard to put these incessant whispers to bed but what is seen cannot be unseen; well unless the Governor's Men and their damned memory boxes come. She did consider that option... But no she would simply find the rumors again and be infected with them again. Her only choice to put them to bed was to set out to discover once and for all if they were true or false. So she gathered together her guineas, all her savings for professors do not earn that much, and brought a ramshackled fifth-hand kinetopede complete with a ragtag crew of oddballs and screwups. Then she set off into the dark.
Since then she has fought with memories thieves to regain her own mind and gained more than she bargined for. She delved into forgotten depths to converse with gods and oil-rigs alike. She has gazed into the minds of fallen god-things buried deep beneath the ground. She has gazed upon the magnificant Kelp Fortress where the shark-people do dwell and through both dilligent study and prudent assistance gained access to their hidden districts. She facillitated an escape from the dreaded Kennedy Yard but, to prove she wasn't a traitor to the City, then handed over a long-lost weapon of terrible destruction and swore to keep secret where she found it. She has destroyed a gestalt psychosomatic entity that inhabited the unconscience of an entire species and facilitated their exploitation whilst being central to their entire culture and is still haunted over whether she brought liberty at too high a price! She has lost so many days wandering the Screws and come close to joining so many of the cults found within there that her crew are seriously contemplating banning her from ever returning. She has written several highly acclaimed novels, sanitised versions of her own adventures, but it is her secret poetry that truly elates her soul! She has shared it with almost no-one bar a handful of the Poet-Knights during one of her drug-fueled sojurns within their keep. Not that she normally takes substances but, with the Poet-Knights, 'tis only polite to get stoned out of your mind. You'll understand if you choose to met them.
Here are the barest bones of a mere handful of Elizabeth's adventures through both the light and the dark of the House. If you don't want to start adventuring there yourself yet then this game probably isn't for you because, more than almost any other game I've played (including Sunless Sea), A House of Many Doors is a game about story and stories. There is an overall narrative arch within the game, which is itself interesting, but more importantly there is such a bewildering array of stories to explore beyond that narrative arch. Hundreds of thousands of words of them (the game contains over 350,000 words). Your character advancement is to a large extent driven by writing poetry about your adventures (no actual poetic ability required; the game has a procedural poetry generator). Secrets and experiences are key currencies in the game (moreso probably than guineas, the actual monetary currency). So yeah it's incredible go buy it now.
That all said, you should be aware that the game is a one man job so bugs persist because it is impossible for one man to QA a game of this size with this many interacting events. They are being squashed at a truly prodigious rate though. Combat, contrary to all the analogies to FTL, is entirely turn-based with you taking 4 actions per turn to aim guns and move or otherwise command crew. The fact many people believe it to be similar to FTL (which was real time with pause) may explain why so many people find the combat hard! :p Though it certainly can be risky in the early game. Otherwise mechanically it is pretty similar to Sunless Sea.

Street Racing Syndicate was originally released back in 2004 on pc and all the major consoles. Considering this pc port was made the same year, it's alright.
As a street racing game, it's pretty average, all things considered. Most of the races are pretty straightforward, you buy upgrades for your car between them, and you can drive around the city freely between races to find secrets. However, I greatly appreciated the feature that allowed you to instantly start any race from the map so you don't have to drive all the way there. Why more modern racing games still don't have that as a standard feature is beyond me.
If you're going to buy this, remember it's a 10-year-old pc game and they made no effort to update it. The max resolution you can achieve is 1260 x 960, so it won't look great on most modern setups. However, it still has a lot of scaling capabilities, and all the buttons can be freely remapped without any trouble. I managed to get my xbox 360 controller running without much of an issue, though I'd suggest manually setting the keys yourself because the default layout is a little weird.
All in all, it's a pretty average game. If you're looking for something fun to play on a really outdated pc, or you just like street racing, you could do a lot worse than this.

The story arc is pretty traditional, but the climax is done so well that it really lends itself to the medium. The music and voice acting are top-notch.
I don't know, this game is easily a 9.5/10 for me.

I initially bought this game as a skeptic after watching the third trailer, where images and quotes are faded in and out of the screen, I thought; there's no way a videogame could be so moving as described in the testimonials, so I had to try it for myself.
From start to finish I was glued to this game, forcing myself to take one break- it was almost 4AM, with an 8AM day coming... The game takes you through Senua's quest to find Dillion, her love, and fight The Darkness. I won't get into the mental-health side of things, as I don't find myself well-versed in that subject, but experiencing the visions and hallucinations Senua goes through was super intense and really made you feel for her. Cutscenes are the only time you'll feel really safe.
The voice acting in this game is absolutely amazing and the visuals are stunning!
Puzzles: I've seen some complaints around forums about the puzzles in this game, and I will admit they are a little odd and strenuous,
but I believe they add to the feeling of hardship you're supposed to see in Senua's mind as she struggles with the difference between what's real and what's her imagination.
I had only one minor issue with this game that do absolutely nothing to take away from the story, but I believe it's worth mentioning.
Combat.
Combat felt oddly repetitive and easy, I found myself easily mowing down enemies after noticing their few basic attack types.
The game does a great job of keeping your fights super-intense through use of visuals, sound, and other elements that present themselves throughout the playthrough. Also, Senua only has a few (maybe 8 or 9) attacks. Maybe I didn't explore the combative side enough, but after a while I began to notice the same exact combos rolling out over and over, and I guess I expected more attention to stuff like that coming from the same Devs who developed Devil May Cry. There are definitely differences in the way this game uses combat to drive the story, which is a smart move by the devs, but I feel like there could have been
All-in-all I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a great story backed up by fun gameplay and audible/visible candy.

I think the claims of high difficulty are greatly exaggerated. This is game is tough, ya. There will be a few parts where you get ticked off and have to relax and rethink your approach. The thing is, the game gives you many different ways to deal with different threats, it's a matter of reflex and strategic thinking deciding what to do and sometimes just basic muscle response. You can send projectiles back to their source, you have a screen clearing magic spell, you have a very handy parry and counter attack that does massive damage, a quick back dash, multiple weapons and small little fireball spell.
I agree on this point though, if so many people are having trouble with this they should have added some kind of difficulty level. I also wish there was some kind of heal inbetween checkpoints. Most of the time the checkpoints are pretty liberal but there are instances of you slashing your way through hordes, only to die right before the checkpoint cuz of some butt ugly ghost that flew in from nowhere.
The graphics and music are awesome, in my opinion the controls are precise and the jumping for the platform bits works fine. Don't listen to anyone comparing this to Dark Souls, it has nothing in common. People just use that term to describe a game that is hard.
There is also a lot of variety inbetween stages, not just visual, but different gameplay mechanics. Just wait for the big white wolf and you'll see what I mean ;)
Overall, if you don't mind practicing a bit and getting to learn the timing on different enemies with your counter attack, I'd buy it. If you're looking for something a bit more easy going with less stress, maybe just download to try it out and if you don't like it, get the refund.

'Slain' is a throwback to games like the original 'Castlevania' - a platformer with somewhat limited scrolling hack and slash action.
I won't go into the story, mainly because (a) its a load of guff so far, and (b) because truthfully I haven't seen that much of it.
Depending on your tolerance for very retro gameplay, this is either a nails challenge where you'll "git gud", or a fiddly and tedious pain in the backside.
You mistimed your jump and an offscreen fireball or enemy appears that's heading straight for you? tough luck! You're gonna take that hit....and the impact will bounce you into a pool of goop that kills you instantly. Big fun!...if you're a masochist.
Whilst the checkpoints are reasonably spaced it's not enough to combat the frustration of these 30 year old gameplay mechanics. And although the platforming and general enemies are quite a nuisance, the first boss was fairly easy, which was a surprising disappointment.
Instead of an epic battle you get a lacklustre affair, and where you'd think the challenge would be fairer leading up to the boss - it instead poo poo's on you from a great height, with clunky action.
I would say it's a pity as 'Slain' looks pretty decent, controls fairly well with a few neat touches to the combat such as reflecting enemy projectiles, and is capable of being fun in small doses.
But this kind of game is really more of an acquired taste, than a bad one as such. For me though, after an hour or so of playing it I wasn't really fancying experiencing the rest of the game.
I'll probably finish it at some point, though it will most likely carry on being a bit of a chore and therefore not one I can wholeheartedly recommend.

This is an extremely tough game to review. By all accounts I should be angry at the game, but it absolutely scratches an itch. The game tells a wonderfully woven story, but is so laden with bugs and far, far too similar to another game, Sunless Sea.
I have a very love/hate relationship with this game. I was obsessively playing through the crashes to desktop every 20 minutes to see the next bit of story. I would play for 5 hours trawling back and forth, keeping affairs spinning in a host of different cities, and then get hit by a game bug deleting a bunch of documents and saves for other games, including a hundred hour baldur's gate save.. and then when that got fixed I came back for more. What finally made me give the game a negative review is, after beating the game the alternate way, it packed up for good. It removed all options to play itself, deleted all saves, and left me with a quite expensive paperweight. It is a design choice that leaves me baffled and angry, rather than satisfied.
If this game was released Early Access, that would be one thing. You would know what you were getting yourself into, a kind of work in progress, something to opt in to if you couldn't wait to play this game. This thing was released as a full product with a thousand different bugs, crashes, typos, dead conversations, uncompletable quests, and poor gameplay choices. And every time the creator has updated, they've left a comment saying 'okay, this time I've absolutely got all of them', and every time you play you get another dozen crashes and bugs.
The saving grace of the game is the wonderful pacing and story. There is a great gameplay loop of exploring further and further afield, adding new adventures and current affairs to your world view, then coming back to your home base to restock. Very few things can be completed in one pass, and every pass you do you'll probably discover a new location and new quest, some new thing to discover and explore, some new relationship to form or happening in a city. You very much feel a part of the world, involving yourself in the politics and lives of many other players, from insects to gods to princes and emperors, to cults and ghouls and miners. You can side differently in their struggles and affect the world around you in a real, permanent way. There is an obsessive, 'well just one more trip so I can see this thing' feeling that kept me playing long hours and through countless crashes and bugs.
With all that said, there is another game that does all of this and more, a great deal better. Sunless Sea. Now if you've played Sunless Sea, you'll find endless similarities in this game. It's a bit more than a passing resemblance. All the interesting loops in the game, from going out to collect current affairs, to secrets and gossip as commodities, to narrative driven towns and cities and crew, to fuel and sanity meters and vehicle maintainance - they're all cribbed from sunless sea. The setting for both games is the same period of time, that victorian steampunk macabre. With very little tweaking, anything in House of Many Doors would fit quite comfortably in Sunless Sea. House of Many Doors has no real improvements on Sunless Sea, in fact they've somehow managed to make the combat (sunless sea's worst feature) even worse. It's cribbed off another better game, FTL, and swings wildly on chance and first hits.
It all begs the question - why not just play the better, bug free, game?
For me this game scratched an itch, but the experience was deeply marred by constant crashing and bugs. For most people looking for a narrative driven world exploration, there are better games out there for a similar price. If you've already played sunless sea and maybe a month or two has passed from this review, enough time to fix all the bugs, it could be worth checking this game out - just don't play the alternative ending, or your game is no longer playable.
A fun game with lots of potential, but it's still very buggy. I'd give it a 3/5 at this point, but once all the bugs are smashed it'll easily be a 4, 4.5.

With a near-identical implementation as Sunless Sea, A House of Many Doors (HMD) manages to stand on its own myriad, scuttling metal legs, thanks to its phenomenal worldbuilding and impeccable narrative.
Players of Sunless Sea will find HMD a familiar experience, and newcomers will pick up on its basics intuitively. You navigate the world in top-down view, following the movement of your armored vessel as it explores a grid-based series of interconnected rooms, collecting items and experiences to fulfill tasks and fund your exploration. Cities and outposts are your destinations, richly realized through Harry Tuff's evocative text and Catherine Unger's bold, monochromatic illustrations. Cities offer a suite of activities, while outposts and other points of interest offer fewer, but every one is a narrative treat.
The map is immense. Unfortunately, the hundreds if not thousands of rooms between loci of civilization are nearly devoid of interest, housing only the occasional non-player vessel (both hostile and neutral), or red-haloed points of minor interest (derelict cottages, cairns, etc) that offer random rewards or hazards and an accompanying gobbet of text.
And make no mistake, no matter what you do in HMD, the text is the true goal and reward. Tuff's writing is by turns evocative, grotesque, and surreal, portraying his patchwork world in a manner that never feels cumbersome to read. The mysteries of the House are revealed through narrative-driven quests (dubbed 'concerns' in the framework of the game), and HMD offers a main storyline that frames the central mystery of the House, as well as hundreds of ancillary stories revolving around locations and crew members. Some of these are resolved within a few clicks, while others will have you navigating pages of branching choices and outcomes, or scuttling your armored vessel to all corners of the House as you seek exotic reagents. None of these 'side quests' feel grindy or burdensome - every one has a distinct narrative with its own suite of weird and wonderful minor characters. Most have branching paths, and there's a commendable effort to make these choices impactful, allowing for as many outcomes and intentions as possible.
A game like Sunless Sea and HMD is only as good as its text, and Tuffs really has spared no effort on HMD's novel-length script. I must commend him again for an exhaustive attention to detail, as the game consistently refers to my crew members not just by their name but their quirks and characteristics. For example, when an event in the City of Bridges left a woman grievously wounded by a growing tumor-like metal shard heading for her heart, you have the option to call in your Surgeon. When my Surgeon was the alchemist Char, she informed me that was she good for making explosives and the occasional poultice, not actually cutting someone open, and I was returned to my former suite of choices, minus the surgical consult. When my Surgeon was Rotherford, the disenfranchised doctor, I was able to have him save the woman via emergency surgery. Most games would have left the option fulfilled by having a surgeon, any surgeon, but Tuffs cuts no corners when it comes to making your crew members feel like their own distinct pieces of the game's world.
If I've mentioned Sunless Sea several times before, there is a reason for that: HMD is an unapologetic spiritual successor to Sunless Sea, and was made with office space, mentorship, and funding by the developers behind Sunless Sea. I was relieved to find that HMD does not use the StoryNexus engine behind Sunless Sea; despite Sunless Sea's similarly laudable narrative and world-building, I found the game engine to be far from user-friendly, entirely too bogged down by the way it quantifies story progress by obscure numerical qualities and banks upon banks of tiny icons. I find HMD's user interface much more accessible, on the whole.
HMD feels more gratifying to navigate than Sunless Sea, with the ponderously slow zee vessels replaced by a swift many-legged kinetopede that can outrun some enemies even without upgrades. You start with a full complement of crew members (even if their stat bonuses are paltry), depleted sanity isn't terribly punishing outside of combat, fuel burns slower, there is no hunger - HMD is a more forgiving game because you are expected to stick with one save and one captain instead of cycling through generations of expendable captains. I tend to get invested in characters, so I prefer this approach.
Make no mistake, the game isn't fast-paced either on the world map or in combat (a turn-based affair similar to FTL, and something I generally avoid with great success, so I will say no more on it), but if you had any frustration regarding Sunless Sea's pace or punishing losses of progress, HMD should feel more comfortable.
Finally, if I mention Harry Tuffs by name several times in this review, it is because HMD is a one-man undertaking in its design, coding, and writing. This lends it a cohesiveness I often find lacking in studio indie games, where one can often find the seams between content where different writers or teams worked on different parts of the game. HMD is seamless in this regard, and it lends it a subtle but appreciable quality.

This game looked really intriguing: nice chiptune soundtrack, charming pixel art that still sticks to NES limitations, and random generation to keep it fresh. While these features are executed well, I found the gameplay to be severely lacking, esp. if you compare it to the NES titles it's drawing from.
To put it succintly: the combat is just not fun. A good deal of enemies simply walk at you, but because of how quickly you can swing your default sword you're in no real danger of them ever hitting you. Most fights boil down to an enemy trying to walk into you while you mindlessly mash attack until they die. The only enemies who pose any threat to you are the tiny ones who either dash at you or shoot at you, often at the border of the camera before you can see them. While this is accurate to how a lot of old titles played, I don't think it's very good game design. The bosses seemed a bit better, I'll admit, but there's just so much tedium in between them.
Then there are more minor quibbles: chests that spawn in when you clear a room can damage you for some reason, and there is no indication of where they're going to spawn from. Who thought this was a good idea? It's like a kick in the shins for doing the challenge they set out for you. The upgrades didn't seem all that necessary given how easy the game was; I'm sure they become more relevant in subsequent runs but again, you need to draw the player in enough for them to want to actually do that. While random level generation is a fun idea, I think it's a big reason this game feels so dull to me; more deliberate enemy placement would feel more interesting, but because you can't replicate a level designer's intelligence that easily the game has to make up for it by adding artificial difficulty with the aforementioned tiny enemies.
To put it succintly, this game absolutely feels like something that would've come out on the NES; unfortunately this extends to the limited gameplay and artificial difficulty. Castlevania, a game this clearly had some inspiration from, still holds up today because of the depth in fighting (you can't just spam attacks and expect good results, you actually have to time it out) and fiendish yet fair level designs. If you're really patient then you may be able to get something out of this, but personally I can't recommend it: for those of us with limited free time, the "it gets better X hours in" argument is not going to cut it

J. Kyle Pittman's games with Minor Key Games are hyper-polished platformers, comparable in every way to the best and brightest bits of Zelda II: The Adventure of Link. The world of Gunmetal Arcadia (and its hand-crafted prequel, Gunmetal Arcadia Zero) follow on the heels of Super Win the Game, using the classic platforming mechanics and CRT emulation for a roguelike tale of elven factions at war, hives of evil critters, and a monstrous queen spreading its evil with the Seed of Unmaking.
As with other roguelikes, levels are randomly generated while following predictable patterns. There are only four chapters and four endings with all but the final boss pulled randomly. A single successful playthrough should take around 40 minutes. It'll take a while, however, to get to that first successful run, with my first taking 13 attempts over 3.75 hours. There are legacy aspects -- bonuses to make your run easier -- that hold over from one playthrough to the next, but only the next. (This means, a single failed run could set you back pretty far if you rely on those stacked bonuses.)
Over the course of the dungeons, you'll run into many genre staples, including shops and inns, faction outposts and monster traps. Factions offer another welcome layer of complexity, however small: By joining either the warriors or the academics, you gain access to exclusive items and massive discounts when you come across their outposts. You'll be forced to ignore the opposing faction's offerings if you join one, as they loathe one another and will force impossible price hikes to opposing members.
The randomly-generated levels don't hold up quite as well as the hand-crafted ones in the bite-sized prequel, but the game as a whole offers more content, and the legacy aspects and random surprises in each playthrough make this an improvement over Zero. It's also not terribly difficult, but Gunmetal Arcadia emulates the absolute best of the NES: There's a strong sense of nostalgia to playing Gunmetal Arcadia, even though it's its own original property. It just feels fantastic to play, and has become a go-to when I'm in the mood to cozy up and play vegetable.
I love both sides of Minor Key Games. J. Kyle and David Pittman both create their own unique, fantastic games, and Gunmetal Arcadia fits right alongside the best of the indie gaming scene. Support these devs and play it.

Instead of simply walking and having the story told to you, you actually use the story to see how you could advance the gameplay. You figure out how each stage is completeted through the text that's presented to you and it makes for a really interesting experience. It can be quite rewarding and compelling when you figure out how to get to the level by interpreting the text correctly. The game is also not afraid to break its own rules in order to keep the core gameplay interesting.
While it's not the most in depth game, it most certainly lays down a very interesting template that more games should follow.

Pretentious Game Review
TLDR:  Wait for a sale / bundle or play the flash game versions.
I guess having pixel blocks as characters is a thing now?  I just finished Thomas Was Alone and played this only to find it is much of the same.  However that's not a bad thing.
Pretentious Game is not for everyone.  It is not a hardcore platformer, it's not a puzzle platformer (though there is some puzzling), but it does get artsy as so many indie games do now.  It only took me a hour and a half to beat it.  I can't tell much of the story because I don't want to spoil it, you're better off playing it yourself.
As for the gameplay you'll have to manage Tetris blocks again and jump on top of each other (or of course platforms) to get to the end of the level.  It isn't too hard, if you get stuck just try a different method or jump around until something happens.  At times it does break the fourth wall, for example it forces you to simply wait for ten seconds or turn the music off at like two levels.  Unfortunately that's as interesting as it gets in the gameplay part, but just like Thomas Was Alone you're playing it for the story.  Music is nothing special either, it's like one sad piano track playing over and over (or at least that's what it sounded like to me).
Just keep in mind you have to use the keyboard as there is no controller support (as of now).  Use Joy2Key if you must.  Last thing I'd say is wait for this to be in a Steam bundle or a good sale, it's simply too short and unrewarding to pay full price for.  However if you get the chance and want an easy game to kill an hour with, Pretentious Game is a good choice.
PS It looks like this is originally a series of flash games and an IOS game.  I guess you can sample this game elsewhere.  Also supposedly there is going to be more levels added in the future.  I'll keep this game installed for a few more months, if it updates then I'll play those and revise this review if necessary (doubt it though).

The original Assassin's Creed was released by Ubisoft in 2007 for the Xbox 360 and PS3, and was later ported to the PC. It spawned 9 sequels and 17 spin-offs, but was it a good game?
Firstly, the presentation. Assassin's Creed nailed the setting straight on the head, faithfully recreating the Third Crusade and creating a very atmospheric experience that later entries in the series have struggled to match. Each city has its own unique flavour and the whole game is rendered beautifully for its time using Ubisoft's brand new Anvil engine. This game was one of the most graphically advanced games of its day. I wish I could say the same about the immersion. Although the atmosphere is great, the immersion is often killed by low-quality audio files such as fuzzy NPC dialogue, or the fact that the HUD covers about a quarter of the screen (there may be an option to change this though).
The gameplay was actually quite innovative for its day. The idea of hiding in plain sight without the use of a disguise was not really explored until this game came out. Also, the free-running mechanics were great and fun to use. However, the combat is really just too easy, as you can easily fight 15 opponents by holding the block button and countering attacks for an instant kill. This is probably why the game's later levels are so ridiculous, forcing you to fight 30 or more opponents just to add difficulty. This causes many of these later levels to become quite tedious.
The story isn't great, but it isn't bad either. You play as Desmond Miles, a stupid idiot who turns out to be descended from a whole load of assassins. Most of the game is spent reliving the memories of Desmond's ancestor, who is tasked with killing nine individuals who cause pain and suffering. It works well on paper, but the assassination missions cannot be accessed until you do 3 side tasks that are always exactly the same, so it can get repetitive, an issue that was fixed in the far superior sequel.
Overall, I'd say it's worth playing, but only to give the later games some backstory.
