Alright, about 42 hours of gameplay, having completed the game once on deathinitive difficulty, here's what i think so far.
This game starts off great
- It has some nice puzzles, that would occasionally stop me in my tracks and and consider looking up a walkthrough, but was definitely beatable without one.
- Combat feels nice, it is definitely an improvement from the last game. they have removed the blocking all together, and opted for dodging, which i can fully understand, as it was never obious as to what could be blocked and what couldn't. At times the game felt like it was just throwing more and more enemies at you to try and make it harder, but mastering dodging and fighting system it ended up feeling like it wasn't just being unfair but that i simply just weren't familiar enough with it at the time.
- The game is very visually appealing and runs fairly well. getting about 70 to 90 fps, with maxed shadow quality and no antialiasing, on a 970 running a 1440p screen, which is reasonable compared to other games.
- The only issue i have is that tabbing out can do one of three things, 1. Nothing. 2. Break sounds making only some sounds play and the rest of the time leave you in silence. 3. Crash the game. i'd recommend either playing the game in windowed, or downloading the "Windowed borderless gaming" app, since the game does not support borderless windowed on its own.
- The game has a random loot drop system which i don't feel the game needs at all. It scaled weirdly and doesn't give you much freedom. For the most part it's just: sell your old junk at the vendor and then buy the item with the highest damage or highest defense. You get given special items sometimes when finding secrets or defeating bosses, but because of the nature of the leveling and scaling of the items, they almost immediately become useless or are already useless when you get them. There's a bit of health steal, and critical hit values you can take into account near the end, but it just feel like the game would have been better without the random loot and leveling.
- Since the game has a leveling system it also has skill points. Which i don't understand, at all. It starts you off with 2 choices, giving you almost no points to do what you want, but when you get further into the game it you suddenly have too many skill points to use on skill you don't want, and can't really use anyways because of the energy system. I would much rather have seen some kind of cooldown, but even then it would feel like they are stepping away from what works to try to appeal to a broader audience.
- As far as i can tell, all the secret achievements are just: "complete this, beat this, do this" and you should get them all from just playing the game, they're just hidden to not spoil the game i assume.
But sadly, despite my love of the game at the start it drops off near the end, even feeling like a chore at times.
-Almost all puzzles are thrown out of the window, it has 2 puzzle areas in the last 2(and a half) worlds, where as the first 2 probably had about 10-20 each.
-One of the puzzle mechanics it adds is really just super disorienting, but could still easily just be beaten with trial and error, it didn't feel great at all, it wasn't even obvious that i was progressing, i was just running back and forth being confused, only to suddenly be done.
-It straight up has a third person shooter area. The world doesn't have any puzzles at all, it's just your running around with a gun shooting large hoardes of monsters with a really mechanicly broken gun. The area can be beaten with melee combat but it doesn't feel like that was taken into consideration or tested for at all. And even if you do use the gun, the enemies actively try to get behind you, making you have to take your eyes off of about 20 enemies to deal with one enemy punching you in the back, only to leave you surrounded. The controls for the aiming on controller are also terrible might i add, it's either moving wasy too slow or way too fast, there is no midpoint. It would probablt be a lot better with mouse and keyboard, but the entirety of the the rest of the game plays a lot better with controller, and there is no easy way to change from keyboard to controller without restarting the game.
-Through the last 2,5 worlds with about 10 puzzles it has 5 bosses, where as one of them is repeated 3 times in the shooting segment. Neither of them really felt good to play. It didn't feel like i was learing attack patterns, and finding out when to attack, it felt like i was throwing my head against the wall again and again untill i won.
- Random enemies would be boss level hard for no reason, with one of the summoning a massive rapidfire stunning firestorm which it could summon again as soon as the first one ended, leaving you running away from it, with no chance to attack it. This would happen in small areas with no real room for dodging, and it would even throw more than one of this enemy at you at a time.
I wish i could give the game a "maybe" but i guess i'll let the 20-30 first hours speak and say that i recommend it.
If you really like these kinds of games or really loved the first one, then get this one, but i can do nothing but recommend you lower the difficulty near the end to make it less of a hassle.

When game development trends started shifting toward games that embrace difficulty, I was indifferent toward the movement.  I grew up on NES and Sega Genesis games that were tough, not just to be challenging, but out of necessity.  Every game was a big investment and people weren't going to be happy to knock it out in a short amount of time.  Today, as games are developed borrowing elements from stuff like Dark Souls, it can seem like some developers use difficulty itself as a mechanic rather than the challenge being a product of other mechanics.  Slain: Back from Hell is one of those games.
It's strange to say something like “difficulty as a mechanic,” but let me explain before you call me crazy.  It seems to me that some games intentionally set you up for failure in order to meet the qualifications to be called a “difficult game.”  For instance, there are several moments in Slain where you hit a checkpoint and then completely out of nowhere with no prior indication, a trap or creature will kill you.  It sort of reminds me of the design of Super Meat Boy where you may not recognize something new in a level and it will take you out.  Except in that scenario, you're set back what amounts to a handful of seconds rather than what could be a couple of minutes of already challenging gameplay.  Those moments feel like the developer saying to themselves “this will show them it's a hard game!”  But to the player it's just another frustrating moment where you had no way to avoid it, forcing you to replay something that may have only been interesting the first time through.  Having players repeat content, even on a relatively small scale, can really make that content less compelling.   You start to see every tiny flaw in other parts of the game.
Those flaws aren't numerous, but given that the game threw them in my face so much I think it's worthwhile to talk about them.  The first is that the controls can feel unresponsive at times.  Jumping, it seems, is very well done.  Platforming portions flow well because you're able to navigate as you would expect and the designs have just enough forgiveness to ward off the need for perfect jumps while still giving a reasonable challenge.  However, when it comes to attacking, countering, and dodging, there's a thin layer of resistance that shows up at the worst times.  Blocking, for one, has an extremely small animation that you can barely tell is active.  The action is necessary for the countering aspect of the game (which in itself can feel weak) requiring you to time these imperceptible blocks to coincide with enemy attacks.   Dodging seems to be affected just slightly enough by your attacks to ensure that you won't be able to use it reactively, only proactively.  Attacks, in general, are quick and work well, but with the requirement to use them so liberally on even the most basic enemies in addition to deflecting projectiles, the animations start to feel too cumbersome – especially in the basic combo structure.  Though as far as I could tell there was only one combo involving three consecutive hits.  These things wouldn't really be much of an issue if Slain didn't so often have you retreading territory and fighting the same enemies over and over.
Slain does have several positive qualities that warrant mentioning.  The aesthetic of the environments, enemies, and all the detail within is extremely well done.  The entire art style is unique for a 2D platforming game and feels like it was inspired by classics like Diablo and perhaps Bloodborne.  If you're in to that sort of macabre and gruesome design, this game delivers that by the bucket-full.  In addition to that, it has a noteworthy soundtrack of quality metal songs that feel right at home with the visuals.  There are a few times that I felt it got a little too soft, but most of the time it was spot on.  Also, in general, the game's overall presentation was carefully crafted.  Interfaces and menus work well and without much of an investment in a tutorial, the game was easy to pick up.  It really isn't missing anything you'd want from a game of this nature.
Reading all of this you'd probably get down to this point expecting me to turn you away from this game  to find something a little more appealing overall, however I am actually going to recommend this, but with some caveats.  If you're a fan of Dark Souls-style games, this title may end up working for you.  It's more than anything like the classic Castlevania games from many years ago, but of course with a lot more pixels.  Fans of those games would probably see this as an homage to those NES classics.  While I personally will probably take it slow in my efforts to finally beat it, since the frustration of failure gets to me quickly, I most likely will commit to it.  This is because I think, at its core, it's a well-made game that still has some flaws.  Don't get it if you want your platformers light-hearted and simple.  Be aware that you're going to probably get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥trying to get through the normal enemies of the game.  Also, I recommend using a controller (and not throwing it) even though the game seems to point you, without explanation, toward keyboard controls.  It will take some effort to discern what buttons are being represented since it doesn't seem to pre-map itself to the ubiquitous Xbox controller like many indie games.  I had to rebind weapon switching since it seemingly was mapped to nothing.  But if this game checks the right boxes for you, it's well worth picking up when it's next on sale.  The default price may be a little steep for what you get, but it has many times been discounted well over 50%, so wait for that.

TL;DR: This game is buggy. This is being fixed by the day as updates come up constantly, and eventually it will not be buggy. But the game itself--its concept, its execution, its style...makes it worth playing through the bugs.

I'll start with the obvious - if you've played and enjoyed Sunless Sea, you'll like this. If you haven't, but you're a fan of narrative-heavy stories and top-down exploration, you're going to enjoy yourself here.
House of Many Doors is something of a surreal experience. You're a captain who's had his (or her, or their - the game offers no opinion on your gender, which makes the romance options interesting to say the least) memory stolen, and you want it back. Moreover, you want out of the House, horrific, soul-sucking dimensional parasite-thief that it is, and you're willing to scuttle around in your kinetopede (think unholy union of crawly insect and... snake train? Idk) until you've found your way out. Write bizarre procedurally-generated poetry as you try to untangle your epiphanies into some semblance of order.
Beings from mythologies both old and entirely new will attempt to move you around like a piece on a board. Blimps full of crazed fanatics will try to eat you, or worse. So much worse. The game honestly delights in showing you just how awful some ways to die are. Friends will sleep with you, turn on you, and beg you for help with their own storylines, not necessarily in that order. And sometimes, if you're lucky, a goat-man will make you a really nice cup of tea.
Play the game, if only for the nice tea. I'm sure it's out there somewhere. Just... try not to die on the way.

The first thing I did in A House of Many Doors was to click around hte UI, not sure what to do, and accidentally disable my heart-light. Apart from plummeting me straight into darkness, which was spooky enough, it became instantly obvious that this was Not The Right Choice when a...a THING started to emerge in what had been the glowing circle of the heart-light. It was obviously coming closer and it was truly awful to look upon, and I knew I had to get away.
I did not. What it did when it got to me was much worse than violence.
After a few false starts, I made it to a city of spires out in the northeast. In poking around its abandoned eminence, I met a nest-beast horror of fishy viscera hanging from a ceiling that agreed that it was too depressed to eat me because it couldn't get a date with the river, and sent me on a quest to to retrieve sumptuous oils and romantic vintages to woo her with. From other experiences so far, that seems to be House's jam: mismatched levels and slightly subverted expectations, harmless ghouls and merciless angels and mutants who're happy being herniated but do want a date.
Also of note that House, unlike Sunless Sea whose engine it's based on, isn't permadeath--if there's an Iron Man mode I didn't spot it, and the game doesn't discourage you from using its save slots. That system waaas interesting for SS, but it's sort of a relief to have a weird dark deep adventure that hasn't been balanced around the idea I'm going to have to do it all over again if I'm exploded.
For Sunless Sea fans or people who wanted to like SS but found it a little too repetitive over its repetitive deaths, House of Many Doors is definitely worth a snag, and a steal at the price. For those who didn't dig SS, House is an entirely new setting with refocused combat and a clearer interest in letting its players make progress, so anyone into interactive fiction or subterranean freakery ought to give it a shot, too.

Thermite is composed of powdered aluminium and powdered iron oxyde (III). Mixed together and ignited, this exothermic reaction creates A LOT of energy, mostly heat and light, and can cut through steel like butter, hence the perfect angled cuts. Since the products of this reaction are Al2O3(s) + 2Fe(l) (liquid because of the high temperature), it's really easy to trace it back to the original source: thermite. Finished my first playthrough a little while ago..... both The New Order and The New Colossus are great stories with characters you care about and want to know more about.... looks AMAZING....... and the actual meat of the game- the combat- is terrific as well.  One usually wouldn't associate "Great Storytelling" with "Wolfenstein", but with these last 2 releases (didn't play The Old Blood so can't comment on that) Machine Games have solidified themselves at the higher end of the storytelling spectrum and the combat mechanics are second-to-none.
The complaints about this game, in my opinion, are wildly overblown.  There seems to be a trend of hating on sequels lately..... but I digress.  I've heard that this game is too short.... but it took me a little under 30 hours for a full playthrough on whatever the hardest initial difficulty was.... and I still had quite a few collectables and side-missions to do.  This game is essentially More Wolfenstein: The New Order- with some extra odds and ends.  If you liked the first game and it's quasi-over-the-top story and combat then you'll feel right at home here.  I can't see someone saying "Gee, I really liked the first game but The New Colossus was just awful."  TNC just broadens the excellent Perk System, adds in the ability to mod weapons, gives you some fun new toys nicely spaced throughout the campaign, throws in some side missions.... it's another yummy serving of Wolfenstein with some extra goodies.
I had heard that there were modern-day political overtones in the game.... which I absolutely HATE because when I'm gaming I don't want to be reminded of the real world usually.  That said- I think it's more of a case of seeing what you want to be there or think is there.  The game takes place in the 60's in America and with that in mind I found everything to be acceptably within the bounds of what I would expect.
In short.... Great combat.  Great story and characters.  Looks and sounds great.  High replayability because of some early story branching.... but mainly because it just FEELS good in combat. This is the type of game that, even after it's been in your library for a few years, you'll pull out again when you are looking for a good FPS campaign.

Patch 1.3. It's good. Really! The game is much closer now to what people expected at release. Yeah, they should have labeled the game early access, and no, it's still not worth full price. Base building, vehicles, portals, space stations that are no longer weird, empty shells with a single alien staring at you. All for free, too.
It's got problems, of course... survival is till tedious. The core philosophy of the game still doesn't make sense. The game demands tribute and grinding to do ANYTHING. A million players could visit a million planets and still not see 1% of the galaxy. Yet the developers insist on putting blocks to any progress and exploration. They cannot guarantee their algorithm will make every trip interesting - that's fine! Procedural at this scale is hard - so why bother? You build a warp cell to hop to a system that is a single barren planet and you have to make another.
Want to move base? Great, you lose 50% of everything you grinded for. Unless you want to dismantle everything manually and somehow find the inventory space for it all.
Even using the new portal system requires searching nooks and crannies for glyphs.
I still recommend it. When you find an amazing planet and call it home, build a cool base, find other players, it works, even without all the nonsense of "every atom procedural". There's an interesting idea that's marred by developers worried about players seeing too much content, for no rational reason.
Buy it cheap, slap some mods on, heck use a trainer if you have to. Light up if you want. Sean Murray's insane vision is kind of here.

There's a good game in here somewhere, but a number of poor design annoyances spoil it, making it a chore to play.
Pros:
- Looks amazing
- Well optimized
- Good voice acting and writing
- Snappy, enjoyable gun play
Cons:
- Awful checkpointing. Some levels don't have checkpoints at all, others checkpoint in terrible places, like in front of 3 enemies when you only have 30 health.
- The game wants to promote run and gun gameplay, but makes the main character too fragile to carry it off
- Levels are confusingly laid out and designed, meaning you have to frequently check a map or HUD hint to know where to go next.
- Damage indicators are poorly implemented, making it hard to find which direction you're being shot from. You often don't even notice the indicators until you've lost most of your health.
- The game has execution aniations, but you take full damage while using them, turning something that could have been fun and visceral, and turning it into a foolish risk you need to avoid.
- Stealth and Alarm system is confusing and inconsistent
The game has obviously been made with a lot of love and care, and it's a shame that some knuckleheaded design issues spoil what cold have been my game of the year.

Ok. So I'm just going to come right out and say this. I enjoy No Man's Sky. As you can see, I've put 44hrs in and I'm loving it. That being said, do NOT buy this except on sale. This game is fun, but it's not worth the $60. I was lucky to get it on sale and I'm glad I did. If you are wanting a game that is instant gratification, do not buy this game. This game is about exploring. Yes, you do shot things, but it's about discovering the unknown. Learning the history of this universe and learning the history of the Travelers (you). Having played a bit, I now understand why the game resets when you reach the center of the galaxy. It makes sense and adds a layer of meta to the "story"
Why I don't think it's worth the $60:
It doesn't have enough content. It may in the future, but it's hard to know what Hello Games is really gonna do (and not do). If you want a game that plots out an entire galaxy and has stellar (pun intended) graphics that is worth this much, I recommend Elite Dangerous.
Pros:
Interesting concept.
Exploration!!!
Like the graphics. Their wierd and quirky and fit the style of the game.
Diverse climates (watch out for the storms!).
Portals.
Cons:
Exocraft. They look good, but are really kind of frustrating to use on some planets. I rarely use them and just use my ship to go where I need to go. I wish I could take them with me (ala Elite Dangerous) but the only way you can get one is to build an Exocraft bay on the planet. It's cheaper to just fly and spend the Plutonium on your jump jets. Some materials seem to require the exocraft, but honestly, I haven't needed any of that except for base building and exocraft upgrades. Speaking of upgrades, exocraft have limited slots and none of them are technology, so if you add upgrades, you seriously impact the already tiny cargo. Also, driving them is awkward. You steer by moving the mouse (same with flight) and it's difficult sometimes.
Glitches. Some of the glitches mess things up. Like my base planet lost most of the textures and then everytime I tried to fly in my ship on that planet it would chunk (even when the textures were loaded and I had exited and restarted the game). This last time, I lost some of the sounds (jetpack and multitool).
Space Combat. Is a pain. On the PC, you're using mouse and keyboard which is great for walking around but space combat is icky.
Dispite those glitches, I'm really enjoying it. I know that Hello Games oversold this game and they still haven't lived up to their promises, but their doing something now, so hopefully it will get there. If not, I'll still enjoy it as I only spent $20 to get it.

I'll try to keep this short. As of this review, I've put over 60 hours into Gunmetal Arcadia. Its combat system is clearly inspired by Zelda II for the NES, and I happened to like that game a lot. Let me be clear, though: the game's combat isn't nearly as deep as Zelda II, but I still quite enjoyed it. You can even get an item that allows you to stab down in mid-air, allowing you to basically pogo on enemies.
The game itself is procedurally generated across four chapters. You cannot save and quit, so you'll have to complete a game in one shot. Fortunately, this can be done in less than an hour, but I would have appreciated the ability to suspend my game like in FTL or The Binding of Isaac Rebirth.
You never know what sort of items and weapons you'll get as you progress through the game. Aside from the Combat Bracers, which allow you to stab up and down, most of these are upgrades to your character's stats, so they don't feel too exciting after a while. There are also subweapons, sort of like what you'd find in Castlevania games: axes, daggers, boomerangs, etc. They are useful, but honestly I found myself just killing everything with my swords as I got better at the game.
You'll come across shops that will sell many of these items and subweapons. There are also inns that can fully restore your health for a price. I've found the former to be quite helpful, while I rarely use the latter (although I'd be lying if the inn hasn't saved me a few times). The shops also sell keys, which are necessary to open locked doors. Since it's all procedurally generated, though, you never know what's behind that door. Will it be a room full of enemies you have to kill for a treasure chest? Perhaps it's a shop? Or maybe, just maybe, you blew that key on an inn (and you already have full health).
Your other weapon in the game is bombs. These can be used to kill enemies or destroy certain parts of the environment. Sometimes there will even be a hidden door, but it's always obvious when a door is hidden behind destructable tiles; and destructable tiles are relatively uncommon anyway. I tend not to use my bombs for anything other than one of the final bosses, and even then it's not really necessary.
Most of the enemies in the game are not challenging on their own, but certain combinations of enemies can really beat the crap out of you. There are simple slime-like enemies who just leap towards you, and then there are bipedal enemies which try to slash at you and can be a little more troublesome. The bosses do offer a little more challenge, especially one of the final bosses.
Gunmetal Arcadia also features the Legacy system, where your previous playthrough affects your next run. Die early in the game, for example, and you'll start the next game with a little extra armor. You killed most of the enemies? In your next run, you'll start with an item that boosts your damage. Initially this made me think of Rogue Legacy, but it's a lot different in that most of this stuff only affects your subsequent run. It's a fun system to play around with, and it's also how you face different end bosses.
Gunmetal Arcadia features a few characters to choose from, all of who have different starting stats and items. They all play the same for the most part. At this point, I prefer to play as Grackle, who starts off with the Combat Bracers.
I mentioned earlier that I put over 60 hours into the game so far, but honestly, I think I would have gotten my fill at 20 if it weren't for the achievements. I've been trying to get the final achievement since around hour 37. I complete the game almost every time I play it now. I do enjoy it, although I'd put it below several other roguelites I've enjoyed like Spelunky, The Binding of Isaac, FTL, etc. If someone were to ask me where the game could be improved, I'd reply with an extremely unhelpful and vague "add more variety." Occasional different levels, maybe more types of enemies?
If you like the sound of this game, but would prefer the game without the procedural generation, the developer has also made Gunmetal Arcadia Zero. It's technically a prequel to this game, but I didn't feel like I missed out by playing this game first. It actually made my single playthrough of Zero really easy.

Worth owning. Based mainly on the Humble Store (DRM-free + Steam key) release.
Gunmetal Arcadia is part of what appears to be a series of games by Minor Key Games. Each of the playable characters (one of which is unlockable and from a different Minor Key release) has a back story, of which Vireo, from GAZ, is ellaborated upon in the intro. The intro shows the events of Gunmetal Arcadia Zero, which was actually released AFTER Gunmetal Arcadia.
The game mechanics of Gunmetal Arcadia are similar to those in Gunmetal Arcadia Zero, except that Gunmetal Arcadia is rogue-like and features five (one must be unlocked) playable characters. The combat and platforming are very 8 bit Castlevania-ish. The graphics look ripped straight out of the 8 bit NES era. The randomly generated environments mean both variety and a bit of chaos. The different playable characters aren't as varied in mechanics as one may expect. If you like Gunmetal Arcadia Zero's gameplay, but want more challenge and less predictability, Gunmetal Arcadia might be your cup of tea.
Like many indie games with a retro aesthetic, Gunmetal Arcadia is fairly accessible. The controls, which work with XInput controllers, are simple: jump, attack, sub weapon, bomb, and a D-pad or thumb stick. The hardware requirements are pretty low. Windows, Mac, and Linux (Ubuntu/Mint) are fully supported. Steam Achievements are challenging, yet attainable. Thus, Gunmetal Arcadia isn't too daunting to new comers.
Played on Linux Mint 17.3 64 bit, with Nvidia GT 720 graphics, and a Logitech F310 controller set to XInput.

This. This game. If ever you wanted:
•	A game which argues the point that games are works of art
•	A game that can change the way you perceive aspects of your life
•	A game that will make you feel something that no one else could explain to you
•	A brilliant soundtrack to listen to while looking at the stars at night
•	A game that is worth every cent
You have come to the right place.
But be forewarned, you will need
•	8 to 10 hrs
•	A heart, mind, ears, posable fingers and thumbs
•	Tissues, LOTS of tissues.
The story
To the Moon is the first instalment in what will soon be a trilogy of games. It follows the story of Dr Eva Rosalene and Dr Neil Watts, two Memory Traversal Agents that are called out to help a terminally ill Johnathan Wyles (aka Johnny), to achieve his life-long wish to go to the moon. The reasons behind his wish are slowly revealed to you as you travel through Johnny’s memories and visit each stage of his life to help grant his wish.
Gameplay
The game runs mainly on point-and-click mechanics, but there are times that you will need to use the keyboard in some fairly unconventional ways from time to time. The scenery and the graphics of the game are that of 16-bit 2D platformer with a similar look and feel to early 3rd Person RPG’s. You won’t have to rush after anything, but you will want to move as slow as possible so you can truly appreciate what is happening. Trust me, this will take some time to understand.
Music
I am a sucker for symphonies and the score for To the Moon is excellent. It sets the tone for the story so well, and as it pulls at your heart strings and toys with your emotions; it will be the hand on your shoulder throughout the story especially once everything is put into context. The opening is euphoric and the song “Everything’s Alright” will put the bittersweet bow on this fantastic gift of a game.
Overall 10/10
I finished this game over three days in 7 hours. I was so eager to find out what happened next that by the time I got to the end, I desperately wanted to find out what happened next; only to find there was nothing more to see. If you have any younger siblings (I personally have a younger brother), this game will make you want to hold them a little closer. For those in relationships, you will appreciate what you have even more so after playing this game. Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice has by far the most generic title of any game I've played, but I loved it anyway. This is the first game I've ever played that convinced me, a jaded bipolar kid that spent time in juvy, that games really can make real use of the 'interactive' part of 'interactive entertainment' when telling a story.
It's what happens when you cross a walking-sim with an action game and tie it together with an amazingly executed exploration into mental illness as both a narrative and gameplay element.
The mental illness that I and everyone else rave about isn't like the monologue in Dear Esther: it has real, tangible impact on the combat, puzzle solving, world traversal, atmosphere,
serves as the basis for the entire narrative. You could say that H:SS wouldn't, no
, exist without it.
Basically, it's not some tacked on extra trying to make the otherwise-standalone game more inclusive, but it's also not the only thing going for it.
All that said, if you're a gameplay gamer (my term for anyone for whom gameplay is the be all-and-end-all of a game) you will most likely hate this game.
The combat relies on lock-on functionality. Lock-on only combat is horrible on a controller and probably even worse on KB/M, which is why almost every game with lock-on functionality also has a soft-lock that tracks which way the thumbstick is facing.
This game uses the lock-on only system.
This means that, when groups of enemies show up, getting the game to focus on the right enemy can be needlessly difficult and even get you killed. And as others have said, the puzzles are entertaining almost exclusively because of the commentary the voices provide. They're far from challenging and all around just boring.
But the combat's not all bad. It can actually get pretty deep for having only four buttons that actually do anything (light attack, heavy, dodge, block). It's not something you'll notice facing off against early game enemies but when it gets more difficult, the combos and counters you can fluidly perform, as well as the dodge that will break you out of an in-progress attack, can actually provide for some pretty deep encounters.
I suck at these sorts of games (shooters are more my bailiwick, though I've been branching out) so it took me a while to get to that point, but someone more accomplished should be able to pick up on the subtleties earlier on (for instance, I saw one person counter a particular boss during an attack that had killed me half a dozen times, leaving the boss stumbling and open for attack).
And there were a few puzzles that required actual thought, and even relied on some pretty cool and seemless visual trickery.
H:SS is indisputable proof that lower budgets in modern times doesn't mean jack. This game is, in a word, gorgeous. The texture work, the details, the lighting and particle effects, it's all amazing.
No, it is not the second coming of Crysis, but the primary goal of any graphics technology is to sell the creator's vision, and this game does that spectacularly. The character designs are all fascinating, unique, and clearly cultural, while the environments, from the darkness drenched forests to the moody beaches littered with the skeletal remains of broken ships, all help sell this game's vision So it doesn't really matter that it doesn't have every single one of the latest technologies.
Basically, the game looks amazing. I played on Medium and my brother, who pretty much stopped gaming last gen, actualy asked if this was really what games looked like now.
Lastly, for a game that attempts to portray schizophrenia, the voice acting has to be up to snuff. It just has to. If even one of the voices constantly speaking inside your head doesn't meet the standard, then it doesn't matter how high the developer's ideals or how deep their research, it
break the illusion and it
turn what could have been an amazing concept into just another mismanaged game with high aspirations.
This game doesn't have that problem.
of the performances were amazing. Even the mad cackling sounded genuine, and that has almost never happened in
form of media. Heck, even the main character, Senua, who is voiced
by a complete novice that hates acting, sold the crap out of her role.
If all you care about is gameplay, or if clunky gameplay sours your experience of every game that has it, look elsewhere. If you're someone that cares about the experience of the whole package and are willing to brush off the dirt to see the diamond underneath, get this game. It's worth it, in more ways than one.

The negative thoughts we have build up in our minds. They weigh heavily on our conscious and given enough time alter your personality, and your memories. In the dark underworld of A House of Many Doors, these negative thoughts come in the form of a physical disturbance. In the form of  a frightening parasitic world where your very memories can be stolen, destroying what makes you, you.
Your journey starts as one of these unfortunate plundered minds. A leader to a group of scavengers and keeper of one of the many Keys to the doors of The House, you learn your memory has been stolen by one of the many groups of mind thieves who scour the wastelands. In order to act as an effective leader, you'll need your memories back and so you take off in search of the bandits. Finding this box of memories and reclaiming it is just the beginning, however, as it turns out to be only a small part of a much larger and ominous plot that sends you off into the world in search of answers.
The world is constantly living and moving around you through the tales told in every interaction. Talking to crew members while on the map opens many personal quests and stories for your crew members from cynical skeptics who think they've seen everything of worth to booze-hound surgeons with rumors of occultist organ harvesting. Each member has their own set of dialogue trees, their own varied personalities, and own ways of effecting the story based on the answers and reactions you give them. The inhabitants of the towns you visit also carry unique stories to either ignore or become a part of, and for the more dastardly of wanderers can even be taken prisoner for your future endeavors and profits.
As you whisk yourself from each sprawling and crumbling monument or town, you and your crew navigate the darkness of the overworld in your mechanical centipede-like locomotive. Your creaking mass of Steampunk looking steel crawls between each section of the map as various debris and relics litter each field, and sometimes memory-hunters or grotesque creatures appear to search you out. And in some cases depending on the quests you are given, you will search these foes out for answers or rewards. Coming into contact with one of these aggressive elements on the map sends you into a tactical battle, not unlike FTL. You'll go head-to-head with other kinetopedes utilizing the skills of your crew members, protecting vulnerable and important sections, and facing off with your accumulated and equipped arsenal.
The stories are decided through Choose-Your-Own-Adventure style branching choices in dialogue and events. Each choice provides your adventure with specific outcomes tailored to the personality and decisions you've given and made for yourself. Every outcome has its own consequences, or sometimes if you're lucky or witty enough, rewards. Within a single sitting I had lost crew members to dark possessions that drove them to their suicides, taken human passengers as captives for profits from slave traders, and had romantic relations with questionable entities such as a shark dude and an oil-rig. I could go on and on about the many strange and creative adventures I had been a part of, but it would only spoil the beautiful tale-crafting that makes up the core of House of Many Doors.
I was up all night, sleeplessly weaving and being a part of extraordinary tales. By the end of my trek, which is still churning on somewhere in the game's world for when I return, I had ferried so many strange and colorful passengers with such odd and extraordinary pasts and personalities. I had accumulated a mass of the oddest items from occultist tools to otherworldly relics. Even better, I had a museum built in my name to keep all of my obscure and otherworldly findings in, encouraging me to search the most mysterious places possible. I had seen and learned so much, yet the inner-working of this dark underworld where parasites feed from the energy of other dimensions mostly remained a mystery still to someday be discovered.
Such limitless imagination, and from the mind of one sole developer. The world has its own dreamed up calendar system, its own social hierarchies, and a world map filled with incredibly diverse and awe-inspiring regions that change location with any playthrough. The art is outstanding, music is melodic and memorable, the tactical combat is addictive, and most of all the stories crafted by your adventure will worm their way through your mind when not even playing as infectiously as the parasites within. It's a game every lover of tales will remember and think about for a long time.

I don't write reviews often, but I was a massive fan of Sunless Sea and its expansion, Zubmariner, and felt like I had to give this game a shot. I feel bad for inevitably constantly comparing this game to Sunless Sea, because they're two very different worlds, but there aren't too many games like these released. To describe what this game is, though, a Sunless Sea comparison is adequate.
Simply put, if you enjoy narrative-focused games, you'll enjoy A House of Many Doors a LOT. The writing is atmospheric, and the rather pretty background artwork for each of the locations adds to the general feel of things. Perhaps something that adds to this game's charm is much cleaner interface than Sunless Sea. Prompts are consistent in their reward/foreshadowing text, which makes things feel more fair. I personally feel as if skill/stat balancing is done better than Sunless Sea as well.
Combat is decently in-depth as it is right now, and certainly more strategic than Sunless Sea's "smash your boat into them and scintillack-fire-fire-fire while riding their♥♥♥♥♥" Unfortunatley, I have to say that travelling process is a little bit less engaging than Sunless Sea, as the world is divided up into a massive number of grid-like rooms. The start-stop-start camera pan as you skitter across each room can get a bit iffy, as elements of the GUI sometimes obscure the top parts of the room. The actual moment of REACHING your destination, however, is something I found much more satisfying in A House of Many Doors. It honestly had a Dark Souls kind of feel upon reaching a new location, which I love.
In addition, the crew member quests in this game surpass Sunless Sea's. They help you get to know your crew characters, and I'll find myself choosing to keep crew members with lesser stats simply because their stories are compelling, and I don't want to let them go. That's a great impact for a story-based game to have! While there are crew management elements that could be improved on (talking to crew while docked, for instance, unless I just haven't figured out how to do that), any objections are minimal compared to how good the story is.
Relevant criticisms: This game does seem to have shipped with a few bugs, but those seem to be being rapidly patched. If you want a great soundtrack like Sunless Sea, you're not going to get something THAT good. I personally place a very low emphasis on sound or music in a game, especially a narrative based one like this, but if you're an audiophile or something you probably won't be a fan.
I bought this game and have played it for 10 consecutive hours. I see myself putting in at least another 40. The sheer number of discoverable locations is surprising - I'm not sure exactly how it compares to Sunless Sea islands, but it feels like there are more. I have certainly not discovered everything yet, which is really impressive as I'm getting the impression this game was made by a very small (maybe 1 man?) studio. This game is definitely worth the $12.99 price tag. If it's ever on sale, pick it up without a second thought.

Despite all the negative reviews about bugs, this game has had more updates, patches and bugfixes in under 24 hours than many AAA games get in a year after launch. It may not be perfect, but the game runs just fine about 99% of the time.
If you liked Sunless Sea, you'll like this game. If not, well, you still might like this game. Besides, where else can you play as me? Plllllaaaayyyy meeeeeeeee.

As promised, I have updated my review. The developer of this game has and is doing an admirable job fixing the bugs that have plauged it. At the time of writing I cannot say that they are all gone, but all my recent playsessions have ended of my own accord, not a crash, so that's a shining mark considering how the game used to run for me, though the map is still very laggy.
So, now I can confidently and honestly say that this game is a good game. I am very much enjoying it, and look forward to completing it. All of its stories so far have been interesting if not engaging, and it is a solid game if you're interested in this genre.
There is only one major bugbear I have left with this game, and that is that getting around can become fairly monotonous and boring. In trying to keep this brief, I will say that rooms start to look very similar, and their base tileset and appearance doesn't change often enough to stay varied. The encounters are also very few in these rooms and you will see all of them in every area fairly quickly. I suspect that the high rate of enemy spawns is to compensate for this, but in order to balance the difficulty of combat your starting vessel can outrun every enemy, meaning that even the enemy encounters begin to feed into the monotony. I would personally prefer less avoidable but fewer enemy encounters, rather than every room be the same routine of running circles around whatever enemy happens to be crawling through it.
The monotony lifts immediately upon arriving in a location, however, which are so far, vaired, memorable, and interesting, with lovely art. It's just the stretches between them which begin to become grating.
In terms of grind, at least compared to SS, there seems to be little (at least as far in the game as I am).
The mark that Failbetter has left on this game is unmistakable, but to dismiss this as a clone would be unwise. There is great difference in these worlds, just not on the surface. It would also be needlessly flippant to dismiss this game as "tiding you over until Sunless Skies" as I've seen some people do. It is another solid entry in a niche but wonderful genre, and the more it gets fixed, the more earnestly I recommend it.

Slain offers exactly what you'd expect: typical 2D action elements coupled with old-school difficulty. It's the kind of game that doesn't excel in any one particular area, nor does it really disappoint in any one area. It's an average game through and through, and because of that, I cannot recommend this game at full price.
It's a very short, basic experience, filled with typical hack and slash gameplay and not much depth. While I can appreciate the beautiful sprites, the buckets of gore, and the heavy-metal music, Slain simply doesn't offer enough value or variety to warrant a full-price purchase. There are only three available weapons, which aren't exactly unique or fun to use, and there's only a smattering of levels to tackle.
If you can catch this one at 50% off or more, I'd say dive in, but anything above that price just isn't worth it.

For the price of admission the game's "ok". I can neither recommend nor not recommend it. Basically it's a 2D Hack and Slash game with some very light elements of platforming. The pixel art, while not breathtaking, is generally good, colour palette is also ok. The Metal theme, however, falls completely flat on its face and I wonder why the developer even bothered. There's some mild rock music playing in the background and after defeating a boss you "honour the metal Gods" by pressing X...wow. Doesn't help that the soundtrack for each level and boss fight seems to be the same.
Speaking of combat, this game is trying to emulate Dark Souls levels of frustration. You can easily die in 2 or 3 hits depending on the enemy, you can be knocked off platforms, knocked out of attacks, etc. Likewise you can also stagger enemies of which there is quite a good selection for the only 5 or so levels. Skeletons, huge skeletons, wolf beasts, acid spitters, ravens, sorcerers, vampires, you name it.
What I got out of the game is that you basically have to learn spawn points and position of enemies for each section and then repeatedly hammer your head against that section to make it to the next check point (which completely refills your health and mana and from which you can easily continue when you want to play the next day by the way). It's not that the game's combat is difficult, it's just incredibly easy to mistime a swing or get overconfident (how many attacks can I weave in before I have to dodge back?). You have basically 3 attacks: a regular swing, a charged attack that takes incredibly long to charge and actually requires perfect timing to unleash (too short or too long and it will just fizzle out, usually resulting in you getting smacked), and a "block attack", wich also requires precision timing (just like DS). Basically every enemy with a melee weapon, including bosses, in the game can be parried for massive damage. You should learn to perfect this attack, because it is the most important one. Other than that you can also reflect projectiles by hitting them, which is also a almost mandatory skill, and shoot bolts of mana, which can be charged or charged even further to wipe the screen (costs all your mana) of most enemies. Oh, you can also duck and attack, which I only needed to do in one level, since the enemies were literally children...yep. Dark. Later on you also get a fire and an ice weapon, which deal increased (or decreased) damage to certain enemies.
The game also features a boss at the end of each level, most of which are actually fun, apart from the ♥♥♥♥ing Mother Beholder! ♥♥♥♥ you...
But once you learn their attack pattern they usually devolve into rinse and repeat and try not to get hit until you whittle their HP down. Still, entertaining.
Since the game is only about 4 hours long and most of that time will be spent dying and repeating sections, unless you're just really good, then you can finish the game probably in under 2 hours, I would only get it during a sale.

Slain wasn't the best game I've ever played. I must admit that I was very excited to play this game after watching the trailer.
Let's start off by stating the obvious.
The pixel art & animations are beautiful, truly some of the best I've ever seen.
The atmosphere and the overall theme is perfect, it's really jaw–dropping how beautiful this game is.
The music is fantastic, but it ends up feeling pretty repetetive because you hear the same tracks over and over.
So let's talk about the not so good parts of the game.
The combat in some cases feel pretty stiff. There's no way to animation cancel which I think would be essential in a game like this. For example, you cannot jump or move around while in an attacking animation. This might not have been such a big problem if it wasn't because of how long the attacking animations really are. This makes the difficulty of the game feel unfair, it feels like all the difficulty is the game's stiff combat system.
The enemy placements feel very cookie-cutter and not strategic whatsoever. For those of you that have played the original Castlevania (1987) for the NES might know how strategic every enemy placement was and accommodated for the player's move-set. I felt like while I was playing Slain enemies just spawned both infront of me and from behind, like the game developers expected you to be able to have a fair fight but your move-set just isn't built around that. It works very well in 1v1 combat but not when you've got enemies all around you. Sure you've got magic that can pretty much blast all enemies off-screen but that should be seen as a last resort.
You don't get any power-ups that feel useful. Just a few sword enhancements really.
A few more minor annoyances is that when you die you'll see a screen saying "You've been SLAIN" This is completely unnecessary and just wastes your time, it really should just re-spawn you immediately.
Another thing is that after you've died and re-spawn by your checkpoint you still have to go through the dialogue all over again. It confuses me how something like this was left in the game.

, I was basically trying to run this on a potato (Geforce GT 640), but after a slight upgrade (Radeon R7 360), now it runs a lot better than ever before.
The original game is basically unplayable with it's default Vsync feature, because it only enables double buffering (if it dips below 60 fps, it immediately sets itself to 30 fps), wich is easily fixable if you disable it in-game and force it through your graphics card drives (or RadeonPro in AMD's case), but even after that fix, it still feels slightly stuttery for how the game was programmed.

So uh... Yeah, disregard my original thoughts about the technical issues I had with this game.

***SPOILER-FREE REVIEW***
"Remember Me" is is a title of a beautiful cyberpunk action-adventure game published by none other than Capcom and developed by Dontnod Entertainment. The reason why I wanted to arise attention to this title is because of those two powerful words that the whole plot revolves around.
You are Nilin, a woman in her 20's captured and imprisoned in an ultra security prison called "Bastille Fortress" situated in Neo-Paris, where here the prisoners are being brain-washed by Memorize. A corporation that commoditaze memories for the grater good, under the control of a vicious woman called The Dame and her husband. In the present you are about to get all your memories wiped out of your own brain by a machine but, a strange guy, Edge ( as if he's not edgy enough through the whole game ), saves you or shall I say creates a distraction in order for you to escape the facility. In the meantime while you are fighting your way out of the chaos, hoping to get to your destination and old friends, Edge tells you that you are an Errorist ( sounds very accurate like "terrorist" ), a memory hunter, even the best. What this means is that Nilin practically has the gift steal and change memories. I know, sounds pretty cool till now, until the games has a dark turn when you realize that in the future missions and actions that you will make, will destroy the lifes of innocent people in order for the Errorists to achieve their goals and destroy the government from inside. Of course everything is not that easy. Nilin is a smart girl and even tough she has a couple of loose screws she always finds a way to change the outcome of every past mistake. Some enemies will become allies and vice-verse, you will take part of this great adventure where a troubled woman paves her way into finding her true self and uncover the secrets that lurk in the 2084's Paris. But most important: Who exactly is Edge?
The story is original and the plot thickens the more you progress creating an amazing world full of mystery and suspense. The game is set in 2084, Neo-Paris ( which I found it pleasantly surprising since Paris is an unconventional setting found in games ). But every beauty has its flaws like the dark sewers and gritty slums hidden by the privileged world. And here come Memorize. A corporation that created a brain augmentation "Sensen" that has the power to access the mind of almost the entire population in order to ensure the control over it by sharing their memories on the net or erase the tragic ones, establishing an immense control over the entire state. And Nilin with the help of her friends has to stop it.
Well here is the problem. If you don't know anything about this game and you are wandering why the hell a game published by Capcom with an amazing narrative is so underrated. Here is you answer: THE COMBO SYSTEM. Gosh I don't even know where to start. I get it, they thought it would be an original thing to let the player create his own combos, with healing, CDR etc. and it would've been an interesting thing if it wasn't this bad. The 3rd moves are tasteless and not satisfying at all which makes the whole process annoying, boring and you end up spamming the combinations for the entire game trying to kill weak Sabre Force soldiers. Also the shooting system is just good enough to be acceptable.
OK so I know what you heard. It's an open world game and you like that well jokes on you. It's not what you think! Neo-Paris is alive, fresh, futuristic and what else and I don't get why the developers choose to take this from us and not letting us to explore it on our own. With all the parkour inspired by Assassin's Creed you can't even interact with the shops and people around you. The game just doesn't give you the permission to access this great things since it wants you to apparently finish the story sooner. Low blow guys, low blow.
With this so called "open-world" the are collectibles to find around which I liked them. They help you increase your health and fighting capabilities.
The graphics look fantastic and the design is very well detailed. The world is vibrant. From the great skylines and cyberpunk architecture and glamorous infrastructure of the buildings and interior designs to the gritty slums infested with Leapers. Beautiful.
The character designs are great. I like Nilin and her entire outfit, hell, i even searched the jacket on eBay to see if I can get one for myself. But the fact that I couldn't customize absolutely nothing really disappointed me.
As for the soundtrack I really enjoyed it. Fit for a futuristic environment that lets you sink into this fast paced adventure.
Remember Me is a great game that through its amazing narrative tells us that life will never be easy and we have to live with the memory of our failures and achievements in order to evolve and learn from our mistakes. As humans, we have to accept the obstacles and scars that various events that life threw at us and move on, become better, stronger. And as a society we have to remain united, helping each other overcoming the danger that lurks beneath, not by changing the past and cover it with lies and facades, but by staying together.
I can totally understand now why this game was this underrated. The story and setting is very complex and unique but all this is ruined by the gameplay and the huge price. Nonetheless I got over it and I came to the conclusion that the game is made to be enjoyed for its plot and meaning. So I recommend this game to be played purely for the story and be bought at a discount.

Bad Combo System. Mediocre Shooting Mechanism. No interaction with the city or the people in it. Can't skip cut scenes. Huge Price.

This is a direct port of a game made for mobile phones and tablets. As such, there is no keypad support, no fullscreen; only one mouse button and the option to connect to facebook. I mention the lack of keypad support because as of this moment, after traveling a mere 26 tiles (most of which were in a circle) my car has been stuck between two tiles for the past forty minutes, spinning its wheels endlessly as the map continues to change around it. Without an in-level menu screen my only options are to exit the game entirely by closing the window or to wait until I run out of gas. The latter seems like it's going to take a while, and having already left to make and subsequently eat breakfast, I figured I could write a review while it runs in the background.
Racer 8 is a clone of the classic game Pipe Mania (or Pipe Dream in the US), only instead of using sections of pipe to redirect sewage (or "flooz") to a designated point, you click on sections of raceway to direct a small car around a map towards where you think a checkpoint or the finish line might appear; and unlike Pipe Mania's unobstructed view of your handiwork from above, Racer 8 gives you an isometric view of its cluttered, constantly-shifting raceways. And they are cluttered; part of the difficulty of these "puzzles" is that the game doesn't want you to see them, and even without rain, snow, and night driving, you'll have plenty of trees, penants, and banners obstructing your view. Clicking the Move Camera icon pauses the game and lets you get a better view for a few moments, but it won't let you get the best view for this kind of puzzle, that being from above and without so many stupid trees in the way.
Even in those levels where you can see the road, any kind of planning or strategy is impossible. The goal of the game is to drive your car through the checkpoint tiles and, eventually, the finish line tile, but those tiles don't actually spawn at the start of the map; they show up at some prespecified time in a part of the map you have no way of knowing you should be heading towards, which makes the directions to "head to the finish" a bit of a cruel joke on the part of the developers. After that you have Men at Work signs, which section off one specific tile and change it into a random tile type. This isn't a problem when it chooses a tile a ways away from you or behind you, but it can instead choose to turn the tile directly in front of yours into a straightway facing the wrong direction and cause you to crash instantly. It might also turn it into a two- or three-way fork, which give no clear visual indication of which way the leadfooted elderly person driving your car is going to turn. Knowing which way Ardy Leadfoot is going to turn outside of the tutorial requires either some degree of prescience, or the unexplained Co-Driver upgrade, which at least gives you two tiles of warning.
It was after buying the Co-Driver upgrade that I realised I had enough for the Auto-Driver upgrade. You would think you already had one, what with the car being beyond your control, but what it really does is rearrange the tiles in front of you so you don't crash, doing so at speeds beyond human ability. Yes, essentially you can upgrade the game to play itself, which I take as a sign that even the developers knew nobody would want to play this buggy piece of garbage.
Pick it up for free if you can, farm it for the cards, then never touch it again.

I'm really quite sad about this game. AT first, I played a browser based flash game called Arcanorum, but then, one day, it wouldn't come up, so I did a little research and found that it was sometimes taken down for being a clone of this game. Excited, I bought it, hoping for a fuller, more satisfying experience.
What I got instead was a massive downgrade.
Even sadder, is that most of its issues seem to come from too much detail, and poor design choices. First, foremost, most obvious and most harmful is the profusion of effects. There's smoke, dust, flames, steam, rubble, you name it. Also flags, for some reason. But the more ornate your craft gets (and I have never quite known why it happens), the more obscuring the effects become. Couple this with the huge flashes of effects that appear if you land a decent-or-harder hit on anything and the whole area is obscured, leaving you blind and giving the AI a big advantage.
Similarly, there are a number of damaging effects that are difficult to see or recognise as such, such as the seemingly-unavoidable rifle shots from balconies or the bombs dropped by some things or even parts of killed machines that explode violently if you hit them too hard.
Another unfair advantage some enemies get is that they don't follow the same rules as you do. As the trailers show, you swing your weapon(s) by moving yourself, but some enemies do not have this limitation and their weapons just seem to constantly move towards you regardless of their movement, making them very difficult to avoid and even harder to land hits past.
Another problem is the lack of structure. There seems to be a small "hub world" where you can practice on a wooden block, and buy consumables and weapons, but how you buy what weapons is poorly explained and I was only ever able to bring up the buying UI for one choice at a time, meaning I had to buy it in order to view any others in the hopes of finding an improvement to what I had, which I never did.
The sensitivity of the movement controls are poor, which is very bad when they're heavily involved in its single core mechanic.
I feel that the strongest part of this game is the 1:1 or 1:Many combat against foes similar to oneself, so the fact that most levels are instead about some other objective, such as killing small, weak buzzsaw robots or using a low-level hammer to hit rocks as high up as possible breaks the pace.
A smaller gripe is that I couldn't follow the story at all, as it was entirely tell-don't-show and used names in an unfamiliar style that I found impossible to remember. Except Giar, I think that was in the flash game.
Speaking of which, the saddest thing is that the flash game had almost NONE of these problems.The physics were slightly dodgy until you got past the rock-on-a-chain weapon, like in this one, but the graphics were clean and easy to read, the enemies were all similar to the player, the shop menu between levels was easy to navigate and, while the weapon tree wasn't clear, it was still easy and satisfying to buy your way along one specific line, even if it did switch between hammers, axes, a sword and then end on a spear out of nowhere. The movement controls were also decent, much smoother and more responsive than this game, and the story was slightly more followable, as a simple story of an empire and rebel group who both think they're doing the right thing.
Overall: a proven good and enjoyable premise ruined by bad design.

My feelings on this game are mixed, but if I really consider it carefully, I have to say that I dislike more about the game than I like.  If I boil my thoughts down to their most basic elements, I have only 2 major points to make: one compliment and one complaint.
Compliment: This is one of the most (if not THE most) visually gorgeous games I have ever played.  The visuals are incredibly, unbelievably, shockingly beautiful (with all the graphical settings maxed out).  I could go on and on and on about how amazing this game looks, but you really just need to see it for yourself.  Also the voice acting is spectacular; some of the best I've ever heard.
Complaint: My main problem with this game are the explanations... in that there are none.  None.  At.  All.  There are no explanations of ANYTHING in the game.  There are 3 sub-pieces to this complaint, so I'll break them down to keep it organized.
1) Combat: None of the combat mechanics are explained in any way.  You are simply left to wonder what you're supposed to be doing.  How do the combat mechanics work?  Figure it out as you go.  It literally took me until the second-to-last section of the game to understand the "focus" mechanic in combat because it was simply never explained and it took me that long to understand how to use it by a combination of coincidence and trial and error.  That is not good game design.  Tutorials matter.  Tutorials are important.  Otherwise you end up with frustrated players.  Also the combat is samey, uninspired, clunky and repetitive.  More than anything, the combat is just a chore you have to slog through in order to continue the story.  Because it's the story that we're REALLY here for... and I'll get to that later.
2) Puzzles: The same goes for the puzzles; there are basically 2 broad types of puzzles in the game and in neither case do they explain how to work them.  It's not TOO hard to figure out what you're supposed to do, but until you figure it out, it can be VERY frustrating.  Again, the issue is no explanation at all.  You just gotta figure it out.  As before, the lack of tutorial decreases enjoyment and increases frustration.  Bad game design.
3) Story: "Hello darkness, my old friend..." or in this case, "hello no explanations, my old disappointment" (hmm, not quite as catchy, is it?).  The story they're trying to tell is a simultaneously epic and personal tale of love, loss, determination and literally walking to hell and back for what matters most.  But it ultimately falls flat because it's told confusingly and disjointedly, from multiple perspectives and by multiple people... at the same time.  I kept waiting, expecting that there would be SOME point where they'd connect the pieces of the puzzle together for me and make sense of all the flashbacks and ramblings.  Nope.  By the time the game ended, I had no idea what really happened.  Was it real?  Was it all a delusion?  Is Senua dead?  Is she alive?  Did she dream it?  Is she telling the story to someone after the fact?  All of the above are viable potential conclusions, because... again... nothing is explained.  So very little ends up making sense other than the very broadest swaths of the story they're trying to tell.  And one other very minor gripe would be that there are numerous typos in the subtitles as of version 1.0 (I believe that's the version I have; can't tell).
[sigh]  I wanted to like this game.  I really did.  The reason I have such strong feelings about it is because with a few SIMPLE fixes, the game could have been amazing.  But as it stands, I can't recommend it, because it left me feeling disappointed on too many fronts.
