If there is one word to sum up Gunmetal Arcadia in one word, that'll be "pleasant". It's both pleasant to look at and to play. And approaching it with a "just another NES/SNES throwback game" it also is a pleasant surprise that Gunmetal Arcadia is much better than what I thought ti will be, "just another retro entry".
Gunmetal Arcadia, is a 2017 action-adventure platformer rogue-like game. Think of it as Zelda II with elements from titles like FTL and Binding of Isaac, take what's make those games fun to play in the first place, combine it with spot on visual and sound direction, and then you have an all around solid entry of throwback NES game.
I never start my review of a game discussing the sound, but I have to for this one, because for me the soundtrack is the one that hook me first instantly when I start this game up. Upon hearing the retro 8 bit menu soundtrack, I feel nostalgic. It's so catchy and melodic, so infectious and it will most likely stuck inside your head. It applies to all level soundtracks. Gunmetal Arcadia strikes a really sweet balance between the 8-bit simplicity and the complex and layered feel of modern game soundtrack. Fun and hype is written all over it, even the slower tracks. The sound direction itself overall is pretty great and convey the retro feeling pretty well.

There are a lot of modern retro game published out there and only a few that can capture it really well, and Gunmetal Arcadia is one of those few. Just like music that accompanies it, the title screen and its presentation are the things that gives me a strong first impression that continues onward. Gunmetal Arcadia has a strong retro art style with a smoother touch to give it a more modern feel that adapts well with modern screen. Honestly, as awesome as these retro classics are, most of them don't translate well to my monitor, without some calibration, I can't play it more than 10 minutes. It's not the case with Arcadia. it looks perfectly great as it is. Every chapter has its own, certain feel to it, though most of them lack some kind of personality and definite diversity to it, that might be tied up with the randomly generated world that I'll touch later on. Effects and sprites work are, while not the best , they're well done, with good variation and they're also nicely animated.
The premise is simple, it's your good old fun and simple action-platformer game with added depth from the rogue-like elements. Gunmetal Arcadia takes those simple NES games and give it a new spin to keep things interesting. Like the typical rogue-like, the difficulty, even in the first level can be off putting for some people, though I think Gunmetal Arcadia is the easier one of the bunch. Arcadia is less grindy, and more about seamlessly traverse from one level to another, keeping the fast and fun spirit of the classic platformers. Destroying enemies and some environments, do some exploration to find treasures in hopes of getting some good loot or simply more gold to buy equipment really adds to the replay value. You can feel the difference of various stat booster and weapons, dare I say most of them are rather game changing at it's nature.
One of the most interesting feature in this game is the Legacy system which is a system where you'll be granted an initial stat booster that could help you advances through the game. What's the interesting part in this? It's the joy of discovering how trigger these events to gain it and sway it to your advantage. Weapons and stat boosters are varied and they have a very straightforward description. to keep in tow with its "fun, fast, and simple" premise.
Enemies, and most especially bosses, are varied and each of them has an attack pattern for the player to learn and deal with it accordingly. It's something to be expected and a bare minimum of both a good platformer and rogue like, and I must say, while its nothing spectacular, Arcadia delivers, it delivers it really well.
Gunmetal Arcadia also has a surprisingly good amount of customizable things in Option like a customizable CRT mode, and display customization. There's also a controller support with a comfortable and familiar default key bindings.
For most of the time, the randomly generated world works on Arcadia's favor. It keeps the game fresh, challenging, and unpredictable with definite predictability, though just like the vast majority of games that use a procedurally generated level, sometimes there are platform and ladders that goes to nowhere, an item shop behind a treasure room that is behind a healing inn, and stuffs like that, it doesn't occur often, but it grinds my gear when it does. The biggest downside of this system however is the lack of level design, resulting to somewhat bland background, and overall level that lacks personality. The other one is the random placement of enemis can result to some scenarios when it's almost impossible to cross an area without getting hit.
A more minor problem is about the different characters that you can select. They're not that different both in design, playstyle, and the stat differences are not too meaningful. I'd really like to see a more striking difference between those 5, maybe like inital weapon, speed, damage. jump height, etc.
Gunmetal Arcadia is one of the better and more unique retro styled game. Combining the fast and fun pacing of old platformer with depth of a rogue like, you'll find quite a good challenge in this title. It's easier than a rogue like and harder compared to most platformers, though its largely due to  the random generated world, at some run you can only hope that the system gives you a good level layout. It captures the retro feel, especially its hype and fun music and its art direction really well, but it lacks the personality presents for each level, because of its random nature, thus lacking a unique and intricate hand-crafted level design. Gunmetal Arcadia both delivers as a platformer and a rogue like, but it doesn't goes beyond that, again, except for the vibes.
For a $9.99 game, you'll get a well made modern-retro game with a good amount a replay value, and it can be addicting if you're into rogue-like / rogue-lite. It needs some polishing here and there, sure, like the bland background and probably adding some more parameters to prevent a few nasty effects of procedural level generating to occur, but other than, playing this game is quite a blast.

This is a very iffy yes. I was a fan of the original Gunmetal Arcadia Zero, as a nut for Zelda 2-alikes, and I liked what it was doing with the worldbuilding, the factions, etc. So Gunmetal Arcadia expanding on that was definitely appealing to me. But Arcadia doesn't expand so much as re-do.
The game goes in a rogue-like direction, with new music, the ability to play as different characters, and lots of new stat-boosting upgrades. There are factions to join, which will affect how much things cost to sell/buy in certain shops. The game is still linear-with-exploration like Zero and like Odallus the Dark Call, but the levels are randomly generated. The level design needs work, with rooms that have ladders/platforms that lead to nowhere. Tricky jumps in the air across temporary blocks that.. lead to nowhere. At one point I encountered item shops on back to back screens, then went through a locked door to find... an item shop. This is the kind of random generation that really frustrates me. It shouldn't feel so obviously randomized. It's not organic at all. It's not always this bad but when it happens it definitely warrants a side-eye.
If you die in this game, unlike Zero, you have to start over from the beginning (in a newly-generated world). But the Legacy system will give you perks upon starting over based on what happened in your previous run; what factions you joined, if you didn't join a faction, if you fell in combat, etc. Which can confer bonus hearts, temporary hitpoints (shields), or stat boosts. It's not a grind-to-win game, thankfully. They're just a minor boost to give you a little help getting off the starting block.
Each item and faction shop carries some sort of stat boosting item, weapon, or subweapon. They can increase your movement speed, attack speed, jump height, attack damage, attack multiplier, etc. One upgrade lets you attack vertically (including the infamous pogo-attack of Zelda 2). There seems to be a double jump (which I didn't run into). Subweapons work like Castlevania (stars being your ammo), and range from straightforward dagger-style attacks, to spread shots, spiraling orbs, rising tridents. Some of these return from Zero, while others are brand new. An interesting addition to the subweapons converts your stars into a random item. Sometimes it's a heart, or bombs, or even an enemy.
Like in Zero, each level has a mid-boss and a final boss. On each run, the bosses you face are randomized with the exception of Anathema at the end. These bosses are all pulled from Zero. It's possible that there are brand new bosses that I missed, but from my playthrough of the game (getting to Anathema and everything), it was all repeats from the first game. Similarly, if you are a fan of the CRT effects of Minor Key Games' other titles, it's here as well, with the ability to create presets as well. Even the areas themselves are based on the regions from the first game, including the very cool hive world, with platforms made of organs and ladders made of intestines.
That's why it's best to think of Arcadia as a re-imagining of Zero rather than a sequel or expansion. While Zero was a flat-out old school retro game, Arcadia is the modern take on the same type of game. For me, personally, I prefer Zero, but I also can't deny that people LOVE these kinds of games so I would not want to sway people from it just because of a personal preference. If things go your way you can get a really good run. My big run got me to two rows of hearts/temp HP and 4 stars in a lot of stats. I just prefer hand-crafted level design and that'll never change. Minor Key Games has never really failed me, though. I continue to look forward to and support their future stuff.

An NES-style action rogue-like/rogue-lite with a good balance of predictable and unpredictable elements. Depending on your skill level and knowledge, perhaps not every run will end with victory; however, bonuses are granted on your next run to give you a better chance. Learning what triggers these bonuses is a rewarding experience, due to the fact that their causes and effects are clearly explained in-game.
Game-feel is top-notch, but you might find a new character to control stiffly because you need to pick up some upgrades; movement speed and jump height upgrades work wonderfully because you can instantly feel a difference when you pick one up. There are four characters  available at the beginning, with a fifth character being unlockable. One thing I would like to see is more information about the characters at the selection screen. I would also appreciate more diversity in the characters themselves.
The story and world are conveyed seamlessly through small dialouges, quick cutscenes, and brief item descriptions. There is not an over-bearing or melodramatic plot; like the gameplay, you wil have to do some detective work to find the deeper lore.
This is a rogue-like, so to a certain extent your fate is determined by what the game decides to give you. However, there is a definite predictability to the game, and the system that is there is fun to learn. You will need to be able to adapt to what the game gives you. You will need to experiment with items to discover synergies and find out what kinds of builds have the potential to beat the final boss. You will have to be willing to die, but this process is ultimately very rewarding and satisfying.
If you enjoy games like NES Castlevania, Zelda II, FTL and Binding of Isaac, I strongly recommend Gunmetal Arcadia.
If you want a linear NES-inspired action game with excellent game-feel, and no rogue-like elements, check out Gunmetal Arcadia ZERO.

Gunmetal Arcadia is a challenging action platformer with roguelike elements that come in the form of random level layouts, random store items, and permadeath. When you start the game you have the choice of choosing between 4 characters, each of which have different loadouts and stats. One character for example, has more health and can jump higher than the others, another starts with a long reaching weapon, but starts with low health.
The game takes place within 5 chapters, each consisting of 2 levels, with each level ending in a boss encounter. Throughout these levels you will encounter stores, some of which are owned by 1 of the 2 factions, you can prescribe to. Prescribing to a faction is done by buying a free sigil from a faction's store, and accumulating these will give you buyer discounts and seller bonuses when interacting with them. The negative to this, is that the other faction will do the opposite and boost their prices instead, and pay you less for what you sell.
The items you can come across can be straightforward like different primaries (all melee), secondaries (which are all projectiles that consume ammo), though the majority of items you will encounter will be stat boosts that can increase your health, your ammo or bomb capacity, or your actual stats, such as bonus damage, jump height, walk speed, etc. There are activatable items as well that function just like your secondaries and consume ammo when they're activated. Some of these items for example can make you invincible, or allow you to recover health. There are also other items that can give you new passive abilities like double jump or the ability to attack above and below you etc.
The game controls pretty tight with some decent air control, and the hitboxes are pretty much as they appear on screen. Gameplay wise it's pretty standard for an action platformer with your main goal of defeating the final boss in the last chapter. A big thing is the fact that there is permadeath, so if you die during a run, you'll have to start all over. There is a benefit to this in that as long as you don't abort a run and instead die trying to get as far as you can, your next run will always be given some type of starting reward, whether that's a shielded heart (which function similarly to blue hearts in The Binding of Isaac), an item, or an extra heart etc. Regardless of the rewards, you can accumulate them.
Though with all this said, there are cons to the game. One con is how some enemies don't have tells or at least appear to not have startup frames when they attack, which makes them unpredictable, and this also goes for a few bosses as well. Another con has to deal with one enemy in particular that flies above you and drops a hook. Sometimes this enemy can spawn too low, making damage unavoidable. One last con only happened to me once in my 8 hrs so far, and that's when the only path I had to progress through a level was completely blocked off due to the randomness of level generation. Despite this occurence, I don't think It's that big of a deal because the likelihood of it happening appears to be extremely low, and I believe the devs can easily patch it out.
In conclusion: Gunmetal Arcadia is a standard roguelite action platformer with high replayability, that's worth a shot if you're up for the challenge.

SUMMARY: A moody, "literary sandbox RPG" set in a bizarre patchwork dimenions.  Though a bit unpolished, it's compelling and extremely well-written, with plenty of twists and turns, a lot to do, and multiple ending.
You may have heard some concerns about the game's polish.  There are some. However, this is also a game where I was able to seduce a one-eyed undead woman at a bar inside a hollow tree before dropping off a passenger at a city of slavers where I was looking to forment a rebellion.  I also found a dog from another world, fixed an election, and now a guy who exists in two tmelines at once wants to sleep with me.  So I'm forgiving some polish issues.
So let's get the questions out of the way:
1) The launch was buggy and there were some polish issues.  The author worked his backside off on those to fix them in the first few days.  As of this writing there's still some bugs being quashed and new features being added - it's actively supported.
2) It's inspired by Sunless Sea and Fallen London but is very much its own world and own thing, with it's own feel and sensibilities.  In fact, some of its other influences will surprise you when  you find them . . .
3) It's probably one of the best-written and most imaginative games you'll play, period. For sheer gut-punch emotional impact I'm going to put it up there with Personal 4, Fallen London, and a few other games.
OK, done there, good.  On with the review.
House Of Many Doors is a sandbox "explore-trade-interact" RPG in the vein of "Pirates," its inspiration "Sunless Sea," and more.  Highly literate, atmospheric, and story-driven it's probably a game that means "Sunless Sea" is a genre now, kind of like GTA became.  Sunless Sandbox?
You play an adventurer and writer who was born in the House, a dimension that steals from other dimensions and stashes parts of them inside itself, a giant structure of connected rooms.  In this dark, mysterious place are cities, places, people, and even gods and natural laws pilfered from elsewhere.  Despite the chaos, civilizations have managed to arise in this place over the centuries and do what civilizations do - write, fight, expand, study, and die.
You decided to explore it, though as you come to after a pirate attack it's not going quite as planned.  Soon, depending on what you want to do you might search for missing memories, follow a god, battle pirates, or become a news reporter.  Or just get to know all your crew and seduce them as you travel around in your Sex Train.
There's a LOT to do in House of Many Doors.
Gameplay consists of:
1) Wandering through the "cells" of the house in your "Kinetopede."  This is pretty simple if fast-playing.  Most of it involves looking for glowing signs of interesting stuff or dodging enemies.
2) When you can't or don't outrun enemies (which isn't too hard especially if you build a high-speed Kinetopede) you fight them in a kind of turn-based FTL-style combat.  Combat is interesting, though not as well explained as it could be.
3) In cities and major locations you can trade, interact, upgrade your kinetopede, sell, buy, and indulge in all sorts of adventures and stories.
4) You interact with your crew to improve abilites and follow their stories, and if you want, get romantic with them.  Not all of them are romance options, many have complex and interesting stories with multiple endings - not all of them good or happy.
5) Actions unlock all sorts of other actions, stories, challenges, and more.  One posession, one choice, one test might send you down a whole other story. Part of the game is figuring out what unlocks other parts.
6) You can take on a variety of jobs and tasks; preach about a god, write for the news, smuggle information, start a civil war.  Played right almost any path is rewarding.
7) You can write in the game.  Get experience for writing poetry, compose a mangum opus, be a news reporter. and more.  Experiences and news are like items - you can acquire them, combine them, and use them to achieve various goals.
So when it comes down to it, yes the game is good, in some cases exceptional, and in a few groundbreaking.).  There's a lot to do, a lot to explore, many options.  It's brilliantly written and incredibly evocative.
There are flaws as mentioned.  The launch was buggy.  The game has a lot of polish issues, little things that could have made it easier, or irritating design choices.  It has, pretty much, the very issues you'd expect to find in an indie game.
However, it's a very impressive game.  So the question is, who is this for?
* If you like indie games and games that get truly imaginative and outrageous, it's hard not to reccomend it.  This is everything we expect from a good indie title, something that doesn't just push the boundaries, it pushes them off a cliff - especially in the area of writing and worldbuilding.  It's existence is a reminder of how good game writing can be and how a world can come to life.
* If you want a change from the same-old-same-old  sandbox-explorer type games.  This is a change, especially with the plot and the unusual choices.
* If you're looking for AAA type polish, no you won't have it.  This is an indie game, with it's limits.  It's also an indie game so it gets over many OTHER limits, but it has its flaws.
* If you're not sure of the whole sandbox-literary-rpg mix it's not a good starting point.
* It'd probably make a good gift for an indie-loving friend.
House of Many Doors isn't for everyone.  But the fact it exists makes the gaming world a little more interesting for all of us.  If you think it might be for you and are willing to invest some time getting to know it, it'll probably be worth it.

First order of business:
1) YES THE GAME IS BUGGY AF
2) I can't stop playing because it's so damn addicting
I have a hard time finding a game that will hold my attention for more than a couple hours. Long gone are the days of playing an RPG for 36 hours straight while home "sick" from school. Instead I often find myselff playing an hour of a cheap Steam game, then moving on and never looking back. So to find this gem of a game on it's release day has been a breath of fresh air.
As you will see from other reviews, dev blogs, forums, etc... the game in its current state is still fairly buggy. I made it about 12 hours before I had any crashing, whereas others had it fairly early on.
the one-man dev team
has already addressed these issues and has been working around the clock to fix them. Mr. Tuffs has been all over social media and the discussion forums taking note of any and all issues, fixing them, AND answering all the questions players have had. So hats off to him!
With that being said, this game is an absolute delight. I have been able to easily look past any minor technical glitches. Hell, I haven't really minded the crashes either. The story-telling in so in depth that it completely enraptures your senses. Almost every conversation you have gives you a multitude of choices that can lead to nearly infinite possibilities. Some moments are blood-curdling terrifying
, some are sombre and filled with melancholy, and some are so bizarre and outlandish that they are down right hilarious (looking at you Tybalt). This game is very text heavy, which makes me feel better about already spending 15 hours on it. It's no different from reading a book, right? And that's just it. This game feels like I am delving into an interactive book series filled to the brim with adventure, heartache, war, and glory.
The artwork is absolutely moody and gorgeous. At first I was unsure how I felt about a lack of imagery (example, you won't see a character portrait for each and every new face you meet), but the writing is done so well that it is easy to conjure up your own visualizations. Combined with an impressive, atmospheric score that is reminiscent of what Ramin Djawadi did for 'Westworld', each new location you visit immediately gives a sense of what it's all about. Maybe it's a nice safe haven or a seedy stopover for romantic pirates, or maybe you shouldn't stop in this room at all.
The characters themselves feel completely fleshed out, even those who technically don't have flesh. With character driven plot-points and missions, I quickly felt deeply connected with all members of my crew. While the lower deck crew just seems like a revolving door of bodies (seriously can they just for once not fall prey to the darkness?), the upper deck crew feels like that lovable rag-tag bunch of miscreants from all your favourite stories and shows.
Admittedly, I had difficulty getting a grasp on battles at first. Although there is a bit of a tutorial, I still had no idea what I was doing. I hope in the near future a full tutorial can be constructed, as I feel this will aid the gameplay tremendously. However, once you figure it out, battles are quite fun and IMO have the best music in the whole game (think 1920s carnival). Because battles are not random encounters, you can easily avoid them if you'd like. However, not every ship/creature/dirigible/kinetopede is an enemy, so why not try saying hello to all of them.
Overall, I am completely enamoured with this beautifully creepy, gothic, witty, and inventive game. It needs some polishing here and there, and could have benefitted from some early access time, but things happen and that's life. I have the utmost faith in the developer that all issues will be handled, so I encourage everyone to give it a shot. With the right support and backing I can see this game reaching cult status, especially due to it's replayability.
Ciao for now! I have to get back to fixing a ghoul election, seducing an oil rig, and aiding a mad underwater scientist destroy the House. XoXo

Being a fan of the Cyberpunk genre I was looking forward to exploring a new gritty futuristic city with all the hi-tech and low life the genre usually comes with, and while I do enjoy the rendition of this futuristic Paris it's pretty much the only thing I enjoy from the game. The game is more "techno-magic" than traditional cyberpunk. Instead of implants and gadgets it's all about colorful lights that do the craziest things, from whiping memories to manifest physcial bolts that can hurt and manipulate physical objects. Some of your kicks can also heal you. Yep, you're a 21st century magician, which for me hurt immersion a lot.
Looking past that I tried to get myself into the actual gameplay. I quickly noticed on big issue, the camera. It's a mess. To zoomed in on the character and slow and laggy while you're actually allowed to use it yourself. The game takes control of it way to often and the angles presented aren't always the best, forcing you to sometimes fight out of view. During in-game cutscenes it often shakes, not much but enough to be noticable and very annoying, even nauseating at times.
The game is quite linnear with very little to do and with the help of invisible walls everywhere there's no real exploration. There's very little logic in pathing pathing as you can sometimes jump serveral meters across rooftops but seconds later cannot jump over a chair. It forces you to take a predefined path, which luckliy is clearly marked, otherwise I'd be lost because of how confusing it is sometimes. Bossfights are also prescripted and uneccesary long. The game doesn't want you to think ... at all. I even find the story, which many others enjoy, dull. Maybe it's the "techno-magic".
Graphics are quite nice on the highest setting. Nothing spectacular but I'm not picky, and the performance is generally good. The prerendered movies are on the other hand blurry, low-res and film grain is overused. While the music is generally good, some tunes played at certain moments in the game feel oddly out of place. The game runs stable and I haven't had any crashes or really gamebreaking bugs.
If you're really curious about the game, pick it up on a sale, run through it and forget about it. I do not see any replay value for this title.

Remember me takes us to world where memories are now an available commodity for indulgence of everyone. A world where memories can be managed at will as well as the consequences when such technology is abused due to greed. Remember me can be described as a game with great concept and story but yet falls flat due to its underwhelming gameplay and design.
Pros:
Stunning visuals and atmosphere
The visuals of remember me are no short of amazing, with it depicting neo-paris in a highly immersive way. With large skyscrapers and immersive npcs going on with their lives. Throughout my experience, i could not help but feel how natural the npcs were acting as well as the amazing scale and cyberpunk design the city had. It felt real and alive as compared to other games i had played before. The visuals age well too despite it being released in 2013.
Amazing concept
The idea of having memories as a commodity can only be described as thought provoking and refreshing. This concept helped compliment the already immersive world and helped in creating the subtle areas of the game's story.
Cons:
Too linear
However, one of the issues remember me suffers from would be its linearity. Throughout my many years of gaming, remember me can be described as one of the most linear i have ever experienced. Often the world begs to be explored with its amazing immersion and design but yet i often found myself following the paths set by the developers with often little to explore due to the game often locking me out upon reaching a certain checkpoint. Pathways are often blocked off as well in order to prevent the player from exploring which further adds on the game's flaws. This could be attributed to the developers removing the area to further optimize the game, however it only serves the detract players from the game world. Another problem that further adds on the game's linearity would be the implementation of prompts on where u can jump or climb which further reduces exploration during the ingame puzzle sections. IMO, the linearity of remember me is one of the reasons that crippled the game and prevented it from being replayable as there isn't an incentive for players to return upon completion.
Short campaign
Campaign is disappointingly short as well. Players can expect to clear the game in about 8-9 hrs which imo is way too short for game that was planned to be released for 60 dollars. The game is not replayable as well which further reduces it value.
Redundant combat system
One of remember me advertising points would be its self customizing combat system. However, do not be fooled by this. Different moves in this game do not matter except for the pressens it has. Pressens in this game can be described as moves with certain functions such as being able to heal upon hit or perhaps do more dmg. It however, makes the combat system poor as creating of combos often lie in the pressens they have instead of the different moves the game offers which are merely different animations. Combat system is highly repetitive as well which causes fatigue in the later levels.
Lack of enemy variety
Remember me also suffers from a lack of enemy variety as enemies are often reused again and again throughout the story. This occurs alot, even in the boss fight sections which dampens the variety of ways players can approach their enemies.
Underwhelming sections
Throughout the story, players will experience several memory remixes where Nilin (Main protagonist) can alter the memories of selected indviduals that play major roles within the story. This sections are highly interesting and allow players to delve further into the story. However, such sections occur far too little and often are too short leaving me feeling underwhelmed upon finishing them.
Conclusion
Despite stating more cons than pros, i would still recommend this game due to its merits. It might not be one of the best games i have played, however its creative concepts and thought provoking concepts holds a special place in my heart. If you are deciding whether to play this game, do consider the following:
Is the game on sale?
Do you like thought provoking stories?
Do you like Sci Fi games?
If your answer is yes, then this game is for you.

Games that attempt some level of deeper meaning are often derided as “walking simulators” or “Not a Game” so it's nice to see a game come right out and say, this is a Pretentious Game.
Pretentious Game is a minimalist platformer much in the vein of Thomas was alone but instead of the voiced narration, each level is accompanied by a single line of text not only detailing were you are in the story but also describing how to get through the level.  This is a very nice trick, while some of the levels are esoteric it best, that single line of text will always lead you to solving the puzzle of each level.
The story revolves around A man, his wife, his mistress, the resulting children and even you the player all represented as boxes of various colours and how their various lives intertwine. Each level usually revolves around moving one of the story's players to either the other side or to one of the other characters but with a trick.  For example one level revolves around the character feeling invisible, so they are, only a little puff of dust is visible where they land.  While another claims the character has become self absorbed and only thinking of herself so the screen is zoomed in very close to the player and you can only see the close surrounds making the level much more difficult than it should be.  A nice little commentary on today's narcissistic culture.
The game is very short and I'm not sure if I can recommend paying full price, all three chapters and the epilogue will take less than an hour and there is no real challenge in the platforming.  I really enjoyed it but what each player will get out of it will probably depend on how the story affects you, but hey, we were all probably in love with a pink box at one time!
Amusing for the 20~ minutes I played. If you get it in a bundle give it a go, otherwise the title of the game gives a good indication what the price will get you.

Pretentious Game sets itself up from the onset as something of a farce; a parody of games accused (whether justifiably or not) of being pretentious, overselling and alienating themselves by trying to tell a story that pretends to be deeper than it really is. In this way, PG had the chance to be a clever commentary on how many perceive these games, but instead it falls nauseatingly over itself in its attempts to make the most unquestionably pretentious game the internet could think up.
PG is a story of lost love; soul mates turned divorcees, children abandoning their mother, players losing themselves to drunkenness, and death taking them all in the end. It's depressing to say the least, or it could be if it managed to make me feel anything at all. PG constructs itself as a tone deaf joke; content to paint a shallow picture of life with its simplistic blocks, never stopping to attempt to reflect the real joy and heartache we all experience, while reveling in its own self loathing. Any narrative that's left is nothing more than one individuals misguided view of reality, stemming either from their own experiences or what they perceive them to be like having not experienced them firsthand.
It almost seems irrelevant to talk about PG's gameplay, as through 45 minute game it changes and breaks its own rules so often for the sake of its rubbish narrative that's there is little left to define it by. It's a platformer that attempts to hide its blandness behind worthless dialog and an abundance of underdeveloped mechanics, lacking in every regard and managing to be incredible tedious despite how little you are required to do to complete levels. There's nothing here I could pick out as engaging or original, similarly matching the narrative its emptiness and attempts to emulate other games but barely scratching the surface of their design.
Despite the loathsome name, I had hope that Keybol's square love story would be more than first impressions lead me to believe. Instead it's exactly what it says it is: a pretentious game that completely misses the point of the games it is making fun of, while simultaneously showcasing how tone deft many are to other games dubbed as "pretentious". It's memorably only for its failure at being nothing more than a misguided incarnation of overbearing, forced emotion and lopsided mechanics used improperly to move the story along. As a stalwart defender against the internet's unwavering determination to call everything deeper than the average shooter a pretentious mess, I say without reservation that yes, this is a pretentious game that should be ignored and forgotten in the hopes others don't use it as a blueprint for anything more than how not to attempt to say something deeper with a video game.

Splitted into 4 or 5 chapters or so. The first one or two Interestingly break with some conventions and purposefully ask the player to ignore rules seemingly set up previously. The following chapters switch perspectives between various "charactes" (which are personified in similar ways as done in "Thomas Was Alone") and tell their interweaving relationships. It's about (flawed, unfullfilled) love, loss, misunderstanding and about some fates ending and others beginning. It's even more minimalistic than Thomas Was Alone. There is only one music track, no narration/voice acting, and barely any other audio. The game is offering less varied visuals than Thomas Was Alone. It was an interesting play, but a short one. Steam tells me I have 1 hour on it, should be about right, and I'm done with it already. Not sure if I would recommend it to buy at it's current full price for it's shortness and lack of challenge. It's very easy to play, mostly relaxing, except for the last chapter which has more difficult platforming parts, they are becoming some detailed jump work and spacebar hitting towards the end. Some of them may be close to frustrating, one or two for the wrong reasons perhaps, like your "character" clipping through boxes he jumps on into pits of fire. More chapters seem to be planned. The story could be seen as finished mostly, though the last chapter leaves some questions open regarding the perspective of one character and so I'm curious to see some more chapters added.

Excellent and unique title. Control the flying machine with the mouse movement, spin a wide variety of massive, physics-based weapons and brutally crush everything in the sky. Moderately simple, but extremely entertaining and satisfying game.

I unabashedly adore this game, albeit its many flaws.
At its core, everything is controlled by mouse movement for better or for worse (and it goes both ways). Starting out can be incredibly frustrating, as its purely reliant on understanding the movement system and how to use it to attack (With little in the way of instruction). However, once you get the hang of it, it becomes enjoyable to crush your respective weapon into an enemy; Ripping off armor, cleaving a monster in two, or smashing someone into a wall.
As you progress, you get different weapons to use as well. A pickaxe, hammers, maces, curved swords or giant ones that have extra weight to them, and plenty of chained weapondry that depends entirely on momentum. On top of this, you can carry 2 weapons at a time, either swinging them wildly or locking them together that makes you adapt to a different way of swinging all together. Any way can be deadly if you know how to properly control it, and each offers different playstyles.
While the story itself seems very mashed together, it offers several paths to go through that offers different rewards that make it somewhat worth playing through several times as the fights are different and focused on the different enemy types. There are other modes as well that award weapons and gems that grant effects like fire, freezing an enemy, or phasing to weapons.
Small things are noted in things like titles such as if you try to kill everyone you come across, or if you choose to spare everyone after they defeated, or if you are more keen to decimating swaths of monsters.
The audio and music isnt overly impressive, but it feels like it fits the game, and the hits are matched in power and sound satisfying.
The major complaint i'd hold over the game is the UI and resolution being extremely clunky to work with. The game doesn't like to work outside of its set resolution and will stick to its windowed mode, which would effect each person and their screens differently.
Overall, you'll love or hate the game if you enjoy its physics based combat system, which relies heavily on practice and dedication to learn its unique control method (That again being reliant on the mouse and momentum).

IF YOU ARE HARD OF HEARING THEN PLEASE READ THIS!!
Picked this up in the Steam Sale as I started playing AC games when Black Flag was released. I have played them all since then and loved them all equally, yes, even Unity. So thought I would pick up the earlier games so I could fill in the blanks in the story of the Assassins V Templars. However, upon starting my game with this first entry into the series I have found that this AAA game has no subtitles - not a deal breaker to  most gamers, but I have 80% hearing loss in both ears and therefore the dialogue is incredibly hard to follow. I should be able to get by and can find a lot of the dialogue of the cut scenes on the various Wiki's, but it certainly breaks the immersion. Now I understand there is no way these will be added so many years after the game was released, and I also understand that all AC games from AC2 onward are fully subtitled, but leaving this hear (pun intended) so others who are hard of hearing understand before purchasing that it will dull the game playing experience somewhat.  Surprised that a game of this size and with the production budget available it had omitted to add subtitles. Thankfully this has changed a lot in the past ten years with even small indie games sub-titling important dialogue. I havent played enough to form an opinion of the game itself, but I am sure it will be as good as the others in the series.

Let's begin after the introduction mission. The leader of the brotherhood in Masyaf will send you out to Damaskus (I think) to kill someone (after you completed a few side tasks),
who as a character fells just like that. Someone. After your job is done you go back to Masyaf, where the leader now has two someones in two towns for you to kill. Great! And this without exxagerating goes on like that. Oh and the Desmond storyline also couldn't keep me playing.
Although I have to say the lack of an interesting story would not be a problem, if the gameplay would be fun. I bought this game because after playing  "Mark of the Ninja" and "Dishonored" I thought: "Hey this stealth genre seems quite fun!"
Well... the thing is that the stealth gameplay elements in this game feel like a small addition the devs thought may be interesting. Stealth gameplay elements are imho not integrated well whatsoever, wich is a shame for a game that communicates to you that alarming your enemies is a bad thing and getting rid of them is a pain in the ****.
Oh, and there seems to be no way to skip cutscenes, wich, again, usually is not a problem for me, but dialogues in this game are so mind-bogglingly boring, partly because you kind of know what is going to be the important content, that leads to the next task even before you have ever seen the character.
Plus, every nanny you safe from two mideast-hooligans tells you who else she is going to bore stiff with this 20 second monologue, which gets really annoying after you have heard it the fifth time.

- Story was enjoyable until probably the very end... but definitely before the series went crazy

"Colossal Disappointment" about sums this game up. If you played TNO and want more of the same, don't bother. Just play TNO again. If you never played TNO and want a fast-paced but methodical and thought-provoking game, play TNO.
The characters, quite frankly, are a pathetic effort. I've never seen such one-dimensional excuses for writing, and after TNO's heart-wrenching and memorable cast, every new character in this game is completely uninteresting and/or utterly infuriating. The few likeable characters that ARE in this game are the ones that have either been shoehorned in from the previous game such as "easy-going black man" or "loveable idiot", and the ones that actually do have a reason to be here have been exaggerated and painted into caracatures of themselves or downright stripped of all depth, such as "wacky jewish engineer" and "love interest". The one character they didn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ize was seen for all of five minutes during the start of the game.
The level design was *okay*. It wasn't hideously bad; it has its pointless dead ends and misdirections, as does any mediocre game. It was also not even remotely close to equal with TNO. There are no more dangling-off-a-bridge vertical platforming sections, or legitimately puzzling water manipulation parts, or tense behind-enemy-lines stealth levels. You just get plonked in a confusing and underwhelming series of industrial-looking boxes and buildings, shoot things that move and try not to get shot - because you WILL die in about six hits - pick up their loot and move on to the next room.
Speaking of enemies, what a ♥♥♥♥ing joke. Grunt soldiers are still just grunt soldiers, but one of the most iconic features of TNO - the colossal mostly-bulletproof plate-metal hulks with heavy machine guns and ominous visages - have been replaced by flimsy predictable jesters that walk slowly toward you firing akimbo spud guns at your general direction until you sneeze at them at which point they are blown into the winds like tissue paper. No more horrifying building-sized mechs, no more skull-grating mechanized voices that chill your bones and still your heart, just tedious cardboard cutouts to throw your corpse at until it works.
Oh, and the Laserkraftwerk is just a lump of ambiguous grey mass with 3 pointless upgrades and no more plasma cutting.
tl;dr: Just play TNO again.

When you think of a character driven, story focussed experience do you think of a 7 foot slab of gravelly voiced meat, dual wielding shotguns and blasting Nazis on the moon? You don’t? Well buckle in, as Wolfenstein 2 has some very optimistic views when it comes to narrative investment.
The New Order managed to (just about) get away with telling a somewhat compelling story in a world of ludicrous cartoon Nazis, giant robot dogs and secret moon bases, possibly because it used the rickety plot as a framework to hang the rest of the game off. Like ID luminary John Carmack I typically treat the plot in an FPS with roughly the same respect I treat plot in porn – nice to have, but ultimately not why we’re here. The problem with Wolfenstein 2 is that this tortured narrative plays out over the course of unskippable ten minute cutscenes, and there’s a LOT of them.
The New Colossus has tonal whiplash so severe it’s a wonder its empty head hasn’t been severed entirely. One minute we’re fighting the equivalent of Skeletor in a snappy uniform, the next apparently the game decides its going to be Grave of the Fireflies. The game starts with BJ as a child being forced to shoot his dog by his racist, sexist, anti Semitic dad. I laughed, but I don’t think I was supposed to. When your villains are so cartoonishly evil it’s basically impossible to tell a story with any nuance whatsoever, so it’s better to go stupid or go home. Strangely this dissonance seems to only afflict the first half of the game - eventually the game seems to wholeheartedly embrace the ridiculousness of its narrative and is all the better for it.
This strange wobble in quality also extends to the gameplay – the first half of the game is so poorly balanced and designed compared to the second half I have to wonder if they were made by entirely separate teams. In those early levels the stealth just doesn’t seem to work properly – I’m not sure whether it’s a change to the mechanics or just that many levels don’t really support a stealthy approach very well. Once you’re spotted every enemy within a 30 mile radius knows your exact location, and guards are either completely blind or psychic.
So a lot of the time you’ll be relying on the gunplay to carry the day, and there’s no doubt that at its best it’s good, clean Nazi killing fun. Even here though in some ways it feels like a step back from TNO. My biggest problem is the lack of feedback – it can be difficult to determine where fire is coming from and it’s not always clear just how much damage players have taken until they suddenly keel over dead. Player speed and accuracy on the move seems to encourage fast paced running and gunning, but hitscan enemy weapons alongside deceptive player fragility quickly punish you for playing that way. The difficulty in general is very schizophrenic, particularly during the first few levels with some seriously brutal difficulty spikes, though the game improves drastically as it goes on. Many of those early encounters (and some whole levels) just don’t feel very well designed, with poor signposting – I found myself lost more than once, and you will often find hidden entrances and routes well after they would have been useful to you.
Overall my impressions of TNC were somewhat variable - until the halfway point I was all but ready to give up on it, but those latter levels are easily as good, if not better than anything in TNO. It’s a shame that this style of game is such a dying breed – a 50% discount a month after release does not speak to healthy sales or a bright future for the linear, single player game.

Private Edwin Williams was no soldier. In fact, he cried like a newborn girl when he received
letter, the sole piece of paper that every man dreaded. He was drafted, without ever given a chance to truly say goodbye to his loved ones. Edwin pushed his feelings far behind his mind; he had much more pressing matters at hand. "1 minute!" shouted Benny Adams, his tough-as-nails Sergeant.
Edwin asked himself. Was he ready for his first battle, ready for his first kill? Whether it was his body quivering uncontrollably, or the vibration from the squad's armored vehicle, he was unsure. He glanced quickly from side to side, gazing at his comrades' petrified faces. His hands gripped tightly at his rifle. His lungs rose and fell rapidly, sucking in as much air as possible. "Oi, Private Edwin!" called Corporal Douglas Smith, his cocky, dauntless comrade. "I think we have a traitor in our midst." Edwin stared at him, puzzled. "See," continued Smith, who sat on the left side of the vehicle. "Brownpants!" Smith bursted out laughing, but Edwin detected a faint shakiness in his voice. He checked his weapon for the umpteenth time. "Brownpants, 12-o'clock!" shouted Sgt. Adams, whose voice was immediately seceded by a barrage of bullets, which splattered against the heavy vehicle. Douglas burst into another laugh as the rain of bullets continued to wreak havoc on the armor. "OMG! Rocket!" the Sergeant screamed. The rocket exploded on the left side of the vehicle, and suddenly, the Corporal's pestering laugh ceased forever. Light flooded through the new hole in their previously armored vehicle. Edwin, alongside his Sergeant and the rest of the squad (minus Douglas), jumped out, screaming as they unleashed their weapons. All of Edwin's fears, all his sadness, disappeared as he prepared to slaughter the Brownpants. His teeth grinded together, his hands tightly clenched his weapon, his eyes gazed forward. He stood up, screaming as he trained his weapon towards the enemy squad. There were nine of them, all looking at him...
SFC. Quincy Brooks was a good soldier. he had 4 men under his command, and was leading his squad to flank the Brownpants at the beach.
, he assured himself. He and his men hid behind the shelter of a large rock. He peeked ahead, spotting a large Brownpants infantry squad. His men made ready, and double-checked their ammunition. Suddenly, Brooks gave the order, and they charged forward, screaming like mad men. The Brownpants hesitated and positioned themselves to defend, giving the fellow Greenbelts the perfect opportunity to strike from the front. A barrage of grenades and bullets mowed the infantry squad down. Only one enemy soldier remained, who cowered into the sandbags. He spoke something quickly, and sounded like, "This is Brown 2-1."
Brooks mused to himself. He aimed his rifle and popped the guy twice in the chest and once on the head. Everyone jumped with joy and fired their guns in the air. "We did a bang-up job now, didn't we, Cap?" said Corporal Jenkins, Brooks best soldier in his squad. "Wait... Everyone shut up!" Quincy shouted. A certain hum was in the distance, and suddenly, it grew loud. The roars were followed by the distinct whistle of falling bombs. SFC Quincy Brooks knew exactly what that Brownpants had called...

Great story and setting, and very responsive dev.  That's right folks, this is the work of a single developer!

The positives:
1. An absolute ton of areas. I was blown away at how many different cities/locations there were, and they just kept coming. Exploring is rewarded, and you are often given valuable items from exploration in and between areas, making pacing far better than in Sunless Sea. You can log in for half an hour and still achieve some clear goals.
2. The NPCs are well written and have a number of quirks and quests connected to them, and their own stories. There also seem to be a great number of them.
3. A lenient hold system feels slightly but not damagingly restrictive.
4. The story is interesting, and even having 'completed' the game, there are things I feel like going back to explore/figure out. Definitely very content rich.
I edited out the negatives, because the core of this type of game isn't really the "game", which is just a framing device to sell and limit access to the story. Man the achievements for this game. "Beat the game without Dying" which only 0.1% of players have after presumably 5000+ people who played the game. Basically, the developer made a joke and nobody gonna get completion for this game. You will have better luck beating Battletoads blindfolded.
It is not much of a platformer. All you have is a basic jump and a back-dash which does not give much mobility. 90% of the game is the just timing your attack and counter-hit. Hope you can kill them before they kill you. There are some secret areas but for the most part, the game is rather linear. Even though the game is focused on combat that part is also lacking, to say the least. Aside from basic attack, you have charged attack which is too slow for the pace of the game. You will get some powerups such as different weapons that deal extra damage to specific enemies ( and...they don't really change how you play )
Overall pretty generic mechanics and not all that interesting. Skill in the game is mostly gained by trial and error instead of good judgment. Usually, there are too many enemies on the screen to apply any strategy on the go. You will mostly progress by dying over and over until you know exactly what to do.
There are some beginner traps but you can spot them visually. It may not seem like a big problem until enemies start to bounce you back into instadeath spots. One of the sections in the game took me maybe 40+ respawns and was the only level 2. It is kinda like birds in Castlevania feeling multiplied by 3. Since the game has a lot of tedious button mashing, restarting the same section over and over is not particularly fun.
Checkpoints can be pretty unforgiving. It seems like the game always wants to push it one step too far out of your comfort zone.
In some spots, I am not even sure if it is possible to avoid damage. Like you are completely surrounded by enemies with a bunch of projectiles coming from both sides. The only solution sometimes is to take few hits on purpose and get to one side of the screen.
So the game teaches you to use block which by the way has extremely poor consistency in the game. Some of the regular enemies, go right through with no indication. Even if you do block the damage reduction is abysmal. I find it easier to either avoid close combat completely or rely on charge/counter hit. Counter-Hit is the name of the game. You need it to get through many big enemies but even if I time it to animation it just works 33% of the time. It depends on the enemy but you cannot rely on the damn thing even though you have to do it consistently throughout the game.
This is one thing that game does flawlessly. Some of the coolest pixel gore in the business but it might be hard to enjoy aesthetics when the game requires so much focus. Everything has a METAL theme which makes constant deaths appropriate. I like the occasional boobies, very nice touch. Animations look great and there is a good variety of enemies and levels.I also like the small story bits and interactions between characters.
I generally do not hold the difficulty against the game but it could use some "difficulty settings". The gameplay depth is not even that deep or unique in any way. The saving grace for me and the only reason I can recommend it is the fantastic pixel art. Hard games are fun when frustration is balanced by fun gameplay but here you get a lot of frustration and a lot of tedious repetition.

I tried to look for positive areas in this game. I even (initially) gave the game a 'tentative positive review' in the hopes I enjoyed the game more due to either; understanding mechanics more, or mastery of controls.
After nearly 2 hours of gameplay I am more than confident that the game no longer deserves a thumbs up.

Extremely simple. Both a positive and negative, except the delay on attacks is ridiculously frustrating. A jumping attack (simultaneously) is faster than a standard standing attack. Parrying feels extremely inconsistent with some types of enemies. This often gets you killed, or losing half your health in one attack.
The game revolves around taking on enemies using one of two important tactics; Either parrying an attack, which creates an opening for a (pretty weak) counter attack, or, Normal-attacking projectiles to shoot them back toward the attacker.
The frustrating point here is the game constantly pits you against groups of enemies in inescapable rooms where you are fighting a mixture of ranged and melee enemies. You simply cannot parry and normal attack at the same time ...all of the time.
Which brings me to another glaring issue; There are times you just cannot avoid damage.
Okay, there are frequent health/checkpoint areas, but my god! These locked-in horde rooms where enemies resurge repeatedly and you must try and parry/attack 15 enemies that surround you, and you cannot touch a single enemy without being damaged, and you are mid-parry on one enemy while two projectiles race toward you from either side. You are left with either tanking damage from a projectile, or scoring an axe to the face.
This is a frequent occurence. And an annoying one. It feels tactless. It doesn't give you a sense of "wow, I earned this win".
Oh no. It makes you feel like "how in the hell was I lucky enough to get through that?!"
And please believe me when I say; "Some wins in this game feel like pure luck".
There are sections of the game that feel like they tried to add in something "different" or "cool" in an attempt to break up the monotony. But it ends up feeling empty.
One example being an after-boss 'bit' where you can press a button and make your protagonist do the devil sign and some head-banging for a second or two. Which seems pointless. The game attempts to build this really 'heavy-metal-rock' vibe as though your character is some metal-god. Except, every time you die, the protagonist wails like a 13 year old kid getting the belt from daddy.
Finally, enemies take way longer than necessary to kill. Eight or nine hits to kill a basic, recurring enemy? Or 5 Parry/counter combos on a common enemy? A hard game isn't turning the enemies into damage-soaking tanks.
It gets boring quickly.

Slain isn't the worst game I've played, and it sure is pretty as heck, but the difficulty spikes can be so annoying, and the instant deaths so cheap feeling, that I just can't recommend it. Which is a shame, because damn does it look nice.

The things I found most annoying:

The flame-shooting statues, and one of the bosses, have no 'tell' animation when they are about to fire. This is a head-scratching oversight in a game where every other attack does, and the game is built around parrying attacks and deflecting projectiles.

The game doesn't get harder, it just has massive difficulty spikes. Typically these are rooms that lock you in and spawn a bunch of monsters. These end up being harder than a regular boss because an enemy that needs parrying can end up sharing the same space with an enemy that needs its projectiles deflecting, and there is no way to separate them. On their own most large enemies are easy enough to learn and deal with, but shove several together and their logic becomes desynchronised. Luck got me past most of these encounters, not skill.

Everything takes slightly longer to kill than is actually fun. Some large enemies need parrying 3 times or more (one will even insta-kill you if you miss the timing just once), smaller enemies still take 3 hits to go down, and bosses take way more hits than is actually fun, making defeating them one part learning their attacks, and 8 parts mental attrition.

There are smaller irritations. Checkpoints are sometimes too far apart, one of the bosses was an utter sod, the level design is actually quite dull even though it looks darn pretty, and the 3 weapon system just feels uninteresting.
I'll stop there.

Ultimately, dogged insistence on finishing it, and a desire to see the next level of lovely pixel-art kept me playing, but now that I'm done I have zero desire to go back. Hopefully for their next game they spend as long on the gameplay as they do on the art, if not longer.

To the Moon is more than just a game, it is an experience. I honestly feel bad for anyone who has not experienced this game as it has become one of my favorites of all time!
Kan Gao has created a masterpiece in To the Moon that few games ever eclipse. From the absolutely perfectly crafted soundtrack to the intricate and emotional storyline this game has it all! I laughed, I cried, I felt bewildered, and I felt enlightened throughout playing this game.
I have been through this game personally 3 times, 2 on Steam and once on Android and each time I have realized different subtle aspects of the storyline or dialogue I have previously missed. I recommend this game highly and have had several friends play through it as well and they loved it too!
The soundtrack is simply amazing and fits each "scene" of the story very well. It makes you remember each part of the story when listening to it after completion of the game. I listen to the soundtrack while doing my college studies due to its relaxing nature.
The story takes simple objects and makes them pivotal accessories to the storyline. I won't post them here so as not to spoil them, but what other game can make something as simple as a jar of pickles so memorable!? XD
I would highly recommend you don't spoil the game for yourself by watching others play it on youtube. It is truly an experience that you will carry and want to share for many years to come.
To the Moon stands tall with other story-driven games (that I recommend very much) such as:
Valiant Hearts: The Great War
Ori and the Blind Forest
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons
Kan Gao's other game "A Bird Story" is another great story-driven game that I recommend as well. It is shorter and not "as" good as To the Moon, but also a fantastic game. The soon-to-be-released "Finding Paradise is looking to join To the Moon as an extraordinary experience so be on the lookout for it when it releases!
One might say I'm "obsessed" with To the Moon because I have purchased the game on both Android and Steam, bought the digital comic, and soundtracks as well. Well this game changed quickly.
The first 2:30 hrs I played of this game were awful. I'd heard it was good, so I gave it a shot, and it was rubbish. The movement was screwed up, I could barely control my character it felt, yet it was still incredibly generic. The main problem I had, however, was the combat. I'm not someone who dislikes combat in games, but the combat here was an absolute disaster. The main (and only viable) weapon was the Spirit Flame, which is targetted. The movement didn't allow me to safely bypass enemies, meaning every time I encountered one, I simply had to sit out of range of its attacks and spam left click until it died. It was bloody boring. Because of the general squishiness of Ori and how much I disliked the controls I just kept dying over and over, until 2:30 hrs into the game where I got to the Ginso Tree and unlocked Bash.
Then everything changed.
Bash is undoubtedly one of the best, most unique, well designed, well executed etc abilities I've come across in a long time. I almost immediately stopped hating the game,  having fun with the Bash ability, only wishing it had been unlocked sooner, and the Ginso Tree escape sequence was some of the most fun I've had in a long time. It was perfect difficulty, where it felt like a challenge, but I was still able to (just about) beat it on my first try, and it seriously felt like playing a whole new game.
The reason I liked bash so much was because it basically counteracted everything I disliked about the game. The movement felt smooth from then on, and being able to dodge enemy projectiles and do what I wanted from there almost single-handedly fixed the combat system. (still hate those slimes that shoot three projectiles at a time as I can't bash off them). The other abilities were obviously not as game-changingly good as Bash, but some of them (such as Kuro's feather) really helped the gameplay experience. At this point even things which weren't directly affected by Bash still felt improved, such as Ori's lack of durability.
About level design, I thought the first part was crap obviously, but after unlocking Bash I enjoyed most of it. Unfortunately the second escape sequence was a bit of a downer as no matter how cool the atmosphere is, when the only mechanics are holding shift to go up and trying to figure out where I'm supposed to go it's kind of ruined, at least for me.
As for the story and soundtrack, the story wasn't that compelling for me, mostly because it's not really something I was valuing throughout the game, it feels a bit incomplete and I still hate that annoying little **** Sein, but I really enjoyed most of the soundtrack, even though a lot of it was based off the same melody.
If we're ignoring the pre-bash part of the game, I very much enjoyed it overall, and would definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys this kind of game. (didn't think I would be saying that lol)

I was one of the many saps that preordered this game, and for console no less (because I had an incapable pc at the time).  I was also one of the many that rushed back to GameStop (when I still went there) to get absolutely nothing when everyone realized it was a sham and they gave nothing for the trade in (or less than usual).  I was extremely disappointed that at what seemed was going to be an adventure filled with wonder turned into a ridiculous circle of grind with no point except to get stuck in an endless circle of grind.
I bought a PC, and a few random games to mess around with to see the notable differences between console and PC, and was still seeing this game pop up in my queue.  With every update, it seemed like they were working in the right direction, but I didn't want to drop 60 bucks on it AGAIN.  When it came around to being on sale after the Atlas Update, I figured what the hell, I can drop 20 bucks on it and see what happens.
The difference between now and launch is night and day.  Yes, there are still more fixes and changes that need to be made, and that are probably already in the works.  Yes, it still needs optimizations.  But, it is SO much closer to the game that was promised to us at release.  Planets have their own personalities, their own landscapes, weather patterns, and wildlife that could be/not be a threat.  They are building on more multiplayer aspects that while still in infancy, show promise.  The development team here deserves a lot of credit for their perserverance and dedication to a game that many had written off and expected to disappear into the night.  Sitting down at a game that once bored me after 25 minutes, I find myself losing hours at a time in exploring different planets and mining materials to make products to sell to markets and find the next best ship/weapon/mining tool/blueprints/upgrade.
I'm still weary on whether or not I would pay full price on it, but the fact that I'm on the fence instead of deadset against it as I was a short time ago says something.  Just looking at the recent reviews that aren't bogged down by all the raging neckbeards with their blinders on should tell you something.  I would whole-heartedly recommend snagging this game if it is on sale, and I would recommend not taking advice from someone about this game who hasn't played it since the Atlas update, as they will probably steer you in the wrong direction.  I hope Hello Games continues to improve and keep hard at work at a game that has come MILES, against all the odds and people in the world who were very much against them.

I've had the game since Alpha and followed the progression. The game has a solid campaign with a big overview map and a last boss map. You can play these maps over and over and try different routes and tactics.
I've played mostly Coop so I can't speak for the PVP part, which I don't like. Against the NPC and AI, the game is like a single player experience except you can have friends help you out and push. PVP is a different story because you can't hide in grass and if you see your enemy, they most likely see you.
There's 2 combat vehicles for all teams which is an APC and a tank. You can have a HMMW flown in which is not part of the team's assets.
The game uses RP points as currency for buying weapons and assets which is a solid balanced currency. Most enemies drop RP worthy loot upon death and you recover these items and sell them. Gaining RP is also fairly easy, just stay in a capture zone and kill enemies.
One thing to note about the combat is that there is no health system in the game. Each gun has a probability to hit at a certain range and if it goes past 100%, the target dies. In order to prevent death, units can wear body armor which gives 2 chances of surviving a hit and a third which puts the unit down for a medic.
Pros and cons:
+ 32 player servers where each player can have a maximum of ten AI squad mates which allows for 320 units of in game units for a team + the stationary AI units that defend points.
+ Large variety of weapons and balance.
+ Large maps with close quarters.
+ Lengthy battles (one map can last 4 hours).
+ Cartoon style.
+ Good performance with 32 players.
- Unlimited tickets for teams (Yes, this is a con, after killing 300 waves of enemies that can't be halted it gets tedious).
- No smoke grenades or deployable smoke screen.
- APCs and Tanks looses health from grenades.
- Somewhat rage inducing.
The game looks cheesy but it's very fun and very serious.

Have you ever wondered, what would a proper story-based dark fantasy game be like without leveling up? Without chore lists? Without dress-paragliding circuits or Windscreen wiper combos or dating calendars or tactical, color coded, hotkey-assigned, turn-based shenanigans to divert our overdeveloped left hemispheres from the truths of life, death and the mists in-between?
Buy this title! It’s delightfully raw in those respects.
I confess, I bought this video game right after watching the "Accolades Trailer". Forget those vividly stunning or epically edgy first impressions for a moment and look beyond, hey, even forget that Senua seems to be striking all kinds of hot and bothered poses and… probably having all sorts of wild thoughts at the same time… so what Senua? The first thing that got me into it and the thing that I eventually came to admire the most is that it seems to have some kind of undiluted higher meaning about it. And yes, after more exposure, it also seemed refreshingly intriguing that it decided to purposely ignore a great deal of the usual collection of noisy, tired, vain, gamey gimmicks that plagues the medium (which most of the times serve only to trivialize the more tangible content and to detract from it with petty tags and quantifiers). Those things are most definitely not going to be missed at all in this game.
My mind is ready abandon all notion of micromanaging and lucid cognition.
Give me an existential journey through a dark otherworldly setting, with a genuinely powerful atmospheric thematic and with breathtakingly intense visions, so I can take it seriously. A relatable character which is constantly engrossed by soul tearing emotional conflicts, so I can grow fond of her as a 3D person and care about her trials. A taste of clean and personal artistic expression (with personal, I mean completely off-the-grid, full-screen, anti-roommates, single-player-only gameplay, so no 12-year-old tea-baggers allowed). A true escape, free from all sorts of mundane currencies, far away from the tedious grind of unimpressively demeaning tasks or the intrusive HUDs that keep track of them and of any other kind of Unnecessary Metagaming Garbage. Give me all of that and I will remember it forever as a rare artistic masterpiece similar to Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice.

After seeing a negative review of this game,even though the majority like it,I wanted to make a review talking about what a GREAT horror game this is.
First of all,it's free.I really see no reason why you shouldn't get it just to try it out.
Karamari Hospital (The DLC) costs just under $6,but if you enjoyed the game I would recommend the dlc.
Now,I'm gonna get into the main review.
The game itself does have a lot of references,but that's what makes it great.
The game doesn't feel like it "stole" these concepts from anything,the closest it gets to other games/movies is slight references.
1.If you find jump scares scary.GET THIS GAME.
2.If you are unsure,try watching Markiplier or someone play it,that's how I found out about it.Just make sure you only watch a bit,so that the game still has some surprises.
3.I found I rarely died from enemies,but that was because I was absolutely terrified of them,and wouldn't get near them.
TIME TO TALK ABOUT THE ENEMIES!!
(I won't say them all,just some stuff to know)
(Possible Spoilers)
Specimen 1.The main specimens take the form of cardboard cut outs,at first they aren't scary,but later into the game,I began to fear them more then the actual enemies.They jump scare you,but the do it ALL the time,and it's terrifying.
Specimen 2 and 3 chase you around,they aren't the scariest.
I skipped a bit of the game,(I'm gonna replay it all soon),so I missed the specimen 4 and 5 parts.They still look spooky though.
Specimen 6 is well...The bane of my existence.Specimen 6 is probably one of the scariest monsters in the game,as he will stalk you down,and slaughter you.His death screen terrified me,and his area contains a lot of Zelda references,which I quite enjoyed.Just,when you play the game,BE READY FOR SPECIMEN 6.
Specimen 7 isn't really scary.But it confuses you,and makes chase's with other monsters MUCH HARDER.
Specimen 8 is the deer god.Things in his area start out fairly un-scary,but then 8 shows up,and the terror begins.Although not one of the scariest,he is probably on the most memorable.
Specimen 9 randomly appears if you spend too long in a room.I have never encountered him before,
[spoileri] He re-appears as the final boss of the game,whom you battle with an axe.It is fun,and similar to the Ganon battle from LOZ:OOC.[/spoileri]
Specimen 10 is featured in a cool 'futuristic' area.I don't entirely remember him,but I remember he is VERY hard to run away from.
Specimen 11,who I refer to as the 'beef god',is one of the scariest enemies in the game.I remember him from let's plays of the game,so maybe I was just nervous when I entered his area.The area he is in is a fast food restaurant area.
There is a lot to do before meeting him,but it is very unnerving,especially since the music is terrifying.
Specimen 12 the 'old man' or 'the mansion' is one massive room.It takes the place of a mansion,where you complete various tasks while running from the 'old man'.It was very fun,and scary.
Specimen 13 who I call 'the siren' is a monster very similar to Kaernk from 'Amnesia:The Dark Descent'.You must frantically run to different crates floating in a flooded room in order to escape the siren.It was really fun,and the area before was very scary.
That raps up the review of the monsters,but I have a few more things to say.
1.The game doesn't have amazing graphics,but that kinda adds to the horror.
2.The game has A LOT OF REFERENCES,which is one of the best parts of the game.
3.THIS GAME IS TERRIFYING.(atleast if jumpscares scare you :3)
I would definitely recommend this game.

This game is one of the worst PC ports I've ever seen. It crashes all the time for no clear reason. I did some research, and apparently the game cannot manage a save file if it becomes larger than 300 kb. This wasn't a problem with the vanilla game, but the DLC makes the save file much larger than it would be normally. The only solution I've seen is to limit how many chests you open, how many items are in your inventory, and how many DLC's you load or play. Otherwise your game will crash as soon as there's too much data for it to handle.
*Edit: Maximum save file size is not 600 kb, it's 300 kb. Changed number in review

There's also a lot of utilities and boss battles that are very intriguing and fun to use. However, at various times in my playthrough, I hit points where I couldn't interact with something to advance the storyline such as talking to someone or placing a lantern on a statue, reloading the game fixed this thankfully. Somewhere in the middle of the game I also lost the ability to run and could only move forward if I wiggled my analogue stick forward but I was able to run again around an hour later. Worst of all, the game would crash at very random points, such as using a revolver on the final boss or loading a new area, but the crashes were never consistent which made it even more confusing. There was also a point where the game would always crash after the cutscene where you talk to this angel which was very annoying, it seems the problem was leveling up after completing that quest so I needed to level up beforehand.

Remember me is a good game, but falls short of being a great game for a number of reasons. To its credit it has a great story, full of moral ambiguity, internal conflict, and a plot twist here and there. Combat is fun, as you'd expect from the "Arkham-like" mechanics, and allows you to repurpose combos to emphasize damage, healing, cooldown, or cloning any of the previous effects. There are memory remixing segments that allow you to alter details of someone's memory to change the outcome, which are fun, if not a bit combersome.
There are some disappointments, though. There are quite a few unskipable cutscenes in every level, so even if you're on a second playthrough to finish collecting or whathaveyou, you'll still  have to sit through the whole story which, for me killed replayability. Climbing and platforming can be fun, but rarely offers more than one path. Also its pretty short, bout 10h. Still fun though, no regrets.
