4/5 Heavy friggin' Metal.
Based heavily on the
(DRM-free) release, so my Steam stats don't reflect my time with SLAIN.
SLAIN is every bit Heavy Metal. From the dark imagery to the sense of forboding to the tough-as-nails combat, SLAIN goes hard and heavy and expects you to do the same. Taking a cue from old school platformers, such as the Castlevania series, SLAIN mixes platforming with combat and a bit of environmental puzzle solving. The graphics, while in the pixel art vein of contemporary indie titles, are remarkably beautiful and atmospheric. The music captures the dark and dramatic atmosphere every bit as much as the visual aesthetic does. Check points are fairly spaced. Deathtraps are as unforgiving as the mini bosses. The only thing knocking a star off of SLAIN would be simplistic combat and a few cheap enemies. In multiple ways, SLAIN is a game with a classic Heavy Metal vibe to it.
Played on Linux Mint 17.3 64 bit.
2.4GHz dual core CPU.
Nvidia 3100M (256MB) graphics.
Logitech F310 controller set to XInput.

I wouldn't really call it challenging, I didn't feel like my skills improved over time. It's an exercise in patience with gorgeous graphics.
The first few levels start out well enough but you only have a 3 hit combo attack, 1 magic blast and a block counter for the entire game. You are given a fire sword and ice axe later on but they function exactly the same, some enemies and bosses take a little more damage (represented by a subtle audio queue of all things) but they are essentialy just a change in appearance. There are a very small number of collectibles in the game, but nothing alters or improves your character in any way.
Probably the worst thing, is so many deaths feel like you did nothing wrong, its just the game being sadistic. Your character feels less like a Metal Warrior badass and more like Dave, the guy who works at the local dry cleaners and only wears Black Sabbath shirts and really could use a haircut. 3 hits is about the most you can take, and that's not including the multitude of 1 hit deaths you'll suffer from traps, pits and enemies. These aren't "Oh I see what I did wrong" its "Oh that blood spewing wolf demon spawned on top of me I see"
By the end of the game I was playing not because I was having fun, but because I'm stubborn and hate feeling happy. The music isn't anything noteworthy, the gameplay is so one note, by the end I felt like you do when you finish watching porn and have that sort of dirty/guilty feeling.
There are much better "Old School" platforming games that are challenging and fun, I'd recommend Oniken, Odallus The Dark Call, Shovel Knight, or stabbing yourself with a pen like Matt Damon does to that guy in the first Bourne movie.
This is the second release of this game and although mechanics were improved from the first time (which you have to give props to indie devs who would take the time to do that, I think it still needs some more time to truly be a product I'd recommend. I feel the art was the main focus, and it definitely looks absolutely fantastic, but personally I just found it wasn't to my liking. Here's hoping their next product, a side scrolling shooter from what I've seen, is better, because I'm sure the devs can make something great.

I wasn't entirely sure what to expect when I picked this game up, but wow...glad I did.  Here's the breakdown:
Combat is ROUGH.  Every single wiff or screw up will get you punished hard and when death can happen in just a few hits, you learn to take things slow and steady.  Timing is everything.  Learning the animations is the key to success here and there are plenty of enemies to test your *metal*.
The environments and art might be some of the prettiest I've ever seen in a sidescroller.  The devs clearly took a lot of pride in creating the world and filling it with some insanely metal stuff.  Blood lakes?  Got em'.  Gargoyle statues?  Yep.  Spike traps covered in rotted flesh?  Mhmm.  Intimidating stone fortresses?  You bet your♥♥♥♥♥  Combined with the enemy and character design and modern effects, this game is a visual masterpiece.
Music?  Metal as fu-
Story?  You've been awakened to slaughter legions of the damned and rid the world of their pestilence.  'Nuff said.  The dialogue is great when it's there and Bathoryn feels like a total badass right from the start.  Headbanging after a well-slain boss is a nice touch.
Overall, it's a brutal heavy metal journey that retro sidescrolling fans are guaranteed to love.  I got it on sale, but I'd honestly have had no problem paying the full price for the kind of quality and attention to detail displayed here.  Do it.  You won't regret it.

Hammerfight is probably the best physics based fighting game you'll ever come across.
In Hammerfight, you play as a pilot operating this strange barrel/helicopter hybrid that uses maces, hammers, swords, axes, and even guns to fight other barrel/helicopters, monsters, and machines. The story is really text heavy, so I chose to ignore it, but the gameplay is excellent. Using only your mouse, you use the movements of your mouse to pilot the machine, and you swing your weapon through the momentum of your character. This is the epitemy of "easy to control, hard to master", and it takes a long while to get used to the controls, but it is extremely satisfying to be able to smash a bad guy across the map and have him explode when he hits a wall. There's also these "Song Stones" you can augment your weapons with, which gives you an edge in battle. These song stones range from turning etherial to avoid damage to freezing enemies with your blows and shattering their weapons and armor.
This game has amazing physics, despite having few bugs, and is an absolute blast to play once you get past the difficulty curve.

This is a unique game that has the potential to be a truly fantastic experience if you "house rule" the game a little bit.
At its core, Hammerfight is a mouse-driven, purely-skill-based game of arena combat in which players fly 2D flying machines with various freely rotating weapons attached ranging from swords to hammers to guns. The use of the mouse to directly control the flying machine, almost as if the machine is a cursor, results in a unique and skill-intensive game that is fun and addicting. It also supports the use of multiple mice for multiplayer arena duels, which I highly recommend.
The problem with Hammerfight is that, if you follow its mouse calibration procedures to play the game "correctly," the responsiveness of the flying machines to the mouse movements is so slow that the game is unplayable. I believe that Hammerfight has largely failed because of this one flaw (yes, there are other interface problems and annoyances, but the sluggish and unresponsiveness of the game when "calibrated" kills it). Therefore, the house rule: IGNORE its calibration procedure and instead set it to make the mouse as sensitive as you can. If your mouse is too sensitive in-game after you do this, only then lower the sensitivity until it feels right. Yes, your cursor will move with ridiculous speed in menus once you do this, but it makes the game not only playable but truly excellent.
Once you've successfully ignored the game's attempts at imposing ridiculous limits to your control, it becomes a challenging but very doable game of arena combat with an interesting world (albeit a cliched story) and an absorbing game mechanic. This in the only game that I've ever played where, when I quit playing, I had to readjust to a reality that wasn't rotating about my center of gravity as Hammerfight requires--an experience I usually only notice after a day of skiing and I still feel the world rocking back and forth even though I'm not moving.
I suspect that, had the game's calibration made the flying machines very responsive to mouse input instead of making the machines fly like the Avenger's hovercarrier in a dogfight, it would have become a minor classic. That one flaw killed it, and those who don't try to get around it by messing with the calibration are missing out on a unique and absorbing game. You can get around that problem, though, and you should.
If you like to fight with hammers, then this is the game.

I was one of the many saps that preordered this game, and for console no less (because I had an incapable pc at the time).  I was also one of the many that rushed back to GameStop (when I still went there) to get absolutely nothing when everyone realized it was a sham and they gave nothing for the trade in (or less than usual).  I was extremely disappointed that at what seemed was going to be an adventure filled with wonder turned into a ridiculous circle of grind with no point except to get stuck in an endless circle of grind.
I bought a PC, and a few random games to mess around with to see the notable differences between console and PC, and was still seeing this game pop up in my queue.  With every update, it seemed like they were working in the right direction, but I didn't want to drop 60 bucks on it AGAIN.  When it came around to being on sale after the Atlas Update, I figured what the hell, I can drop 20 bucks on it and see what happens.
The difference between now and launch is night and day.  Yes, there are still more fixes and changes that need to be made, and that are probably already in the works.  Yes, it still needs optimizations.  But, it is SO much closer to the game that was promised to us at release.  Planets have their own personalities, their own landscapes, weather patterns, and wildlife that could be/not be a threat.  They are building on more multiplayer aspects that while still in infancy, show promise.  The development team here deserves a lot of credit for their perserverance and dedication to a game that many had written off and expected to disappear into the night.  Sitting down at a game that once bored me after 25 minutes, I find myself losing hours at a time in exploring different planets and mining materials to make products to sell to markets and find the next best ship/weapon/mining tool/blueprints/upgrade.
I'm still weary on whether or not I would pay full price on it, but the fact that I'm on the fence instead of deadset against it as I was a short time ago says something.  Just looking at the recent reviews that aren't bogged down by all the raging neckbeards with their blinders on should tell you something.  I would whole-heartedly recommend snagging this game if it is on sale, and I would recommend not taking advice from someone about this game who hasn't played it since the Atlas update, as they will probably steer you in the wrong direction.  I hope Hello Games continues to improve and keep hard at work at a game that has come MILES, against all the odds and people in the world who were very much against them.

To the Moon is truly something special.  More of an interactive novella than a game, it tells a thought provoking story that examines love and loss, anguish and remorse, the nostalgia of youth as seen from the pillar of old age, and the human experience in general.  The story follows two doctors who specialize in constructing and implanting memories into a dying person with the purpose of fulfilling one's last wish.  This is accomplished by travelling through the subject's memories backwards from old age to childhood, gathering a series of objects in each memory in order to unlock the next.  Finding these mementos is the only real gameplay element, but works to advance the story in a simple and satisfying way.  To say anymore about the story would be a disservice, but the characters and themes are relatable, the story captivating and unique, the dialogue charming and believable, with the humorous banter between the two doctors working more often than not.  The graphics are reminiscent of the RPGs of old, a la Chrono Trigger or the older Final Fantasy games, and the old style visuals serve the themes of nostalgia present throughout the story and nicely compliment the old school JRPG-esque dialogue.  The game clocks in at around five hours, just long enough to tell the story it sets out to tell without blatantly spelling out the themes and leaves it up to the player to fill in the blanks.  The music particularly stands out, as the soundtrack is beautiful and brilliantly compliments an emotional tale.  As other reviewers have said, this is a game that will likely affect you emotionally, presenting a story that acts as a magnifying glass on one's own life and memories and is likely to stick with you for a time after experiencing it.  Equal parts comedy and tragedy, To the Moon will leave you with a smile on your face and a mist in your eyes, heavy thoughts and a heavier heart.  Easily and highly recommended.

We were moving, digging the enemy out of their heavily entrenched position, which used to be a mansion on a cliff, a beach protruding from its east. The beach was heavily defended, but every direction besides it was even more defended. The beach was our best option.
We got in our truck, various trucks moving in, including a mobile supply truck and reinforcements truck. Moving in, we walked onto the beachhead to die. Around a hundred of us died on that beach within the first five minutes, us all having no other option but to scrabble forward, as strong as we could possibly be in that sort of situation.
By the time we reached the cliff, we had lost hundreds more. We charged, throwing everything we could at them from every angle. A special operations team had managed to pierce the mansion's defenses, took down their radio communications and called in paratroopers. A few of them died before they hit the floor, but they had crippled the defense. The hundred or so of us charged in, furious at the beachhead.
When the government actually got to the beachhead, it was a horrific sight. They found no captives, but only the gutted,  dead,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in corpses of what could be called the enemy. Hundreds of us didn't come home, and many families ended up with no mother or father to hold them tight, and tell them that everything would be okay.
I was one of the lucky ones, but I'm saddened to say that though. I am warred constantly by the thoughts that maybe someone else deserved to live instead of me. I wasn't ever important, besides my mother, father and grandfather. The dead had wives, children. They should have lived, I should have died in their place. I hope that one day, the sound of gunfire hitting the body of a marine will be the last thing I ever hear.

Possibly the scariest (but not the best) horror game I've played so far. I dare you to finish the entire game in one sitting during a black night, like I did. Man, I will never forget that.
Gameplay is somewhat similiar to one SCP-082-B has. You do not need to solve any complicated puzzles and such, but as you progress, game will pump more and more fear into you, slowing you down and preventing you from progressing any further. The whole point is having guts and bravery to push forward and to prepare for any and all unknown horrors that await you. The rooms are randomly generated, and yes, you need to pass 1000 of them. Just like the floors in SCP-082-B.
If occasional jumpscares and creepy atmosphere doesn't kill you, something else will. The threat in this game comes from creatures called "specimens". These specimens are (obviously) on loose and as you go on, you will encounter more and more of them. They are usually a reference to other popular horror games, like Silent Hill (there are a lot of references in game to be found). They also have their own ways of slowing you down and making it difficult to escape them, such as laying down pools of slime that slow your movement or causing distortions to confuse you (they even hide doors). Most of them are considered as a ghost entity and those can go through walls, meaning that in some room its guaranteed that you will take a hit, but there are ways and tactics to avoid that.
The weapon in this game is 95% useless, so forget about turning around and fighting the specimens, it won't work. Specially the one who will punish such violent behavior. Its mainly used to remove obstacles and fight weak, non-specimen enemies. Only becomes actually useful at very near end of the game.
Graphics are unique and have a "HD look" on them, kinda like in a Sphax BDCraft texture pack style. Music is spooky, and its made in Fruityloops studio if anyone wondering (noticed some FL presets here and there).
I highly recommend that you give it a try. Hell, I recommend you stay awake for one night and play the entire game, its an experience that you will never forget. Shivers that you'll never able to shake off. But also, a huge thanks developers for making this game and to whoever took time to read my review. I reward you with a hint: never stay in one room for too long. You are being.. followed... (No, seriously, don't).

Slain: Back from Hell is a fantastic game. The overall presentation is what makes this game a great experience: Sound, Music , Visuals, Enemy Designs and Animations are blending together perfectly. I really enjoy this game just from the atmosphere it creates.
The game has received some very negative comments here and I can understand the pain the players have felt while getting slapped in the face from some encounters in it. However, while I felt some frustration along the way, so far every encounter had some underlying solution to it. Usually trying to approach enemies in different ways will bring you quickly through the game. After reading about the Highlands here in the reviews I was prepared for the worst. But the frustration didn't came as expected. It's an enjoyable experience, despite the typical rage moment you get if you can't get past an enemy for a while. People are quickly blaming game design if they fail in a game. I blame that on getting pampered by UX Designers for the past years with No-Fail designs. Sometimes a game doesn't have to hold your hand the whole way through.
There are some flaws that haunt the game. Some checkpoints are placed perfectly to save you from a hard passage and some are placed far away just to make your life hell. They can result in a repetetive spiral where you're fighting the same skeletons over and over to reach the part that you actually struggle with. These remind me a bit of Dark Souls 1 and Megaman Zero, because they're equally challenging and addicting. One thing Souls does better than Zero though is that you can skip and bypass stuff more frequently, creating a more sandbox-y experience. Slain does offer some hidden passages and jumps, but usually it wants you to follow a certain pattern to reach the next checkpoint. While that doesn't make the game bad, I would like to play a sequel that offers a bit more freedom.
People are pointing out that there is skill lag in this game. There isn't. If you swing a sword, you'll have to wait a fraction of a second to swing it again. Almost every game with a combat system plays that way. Of course attacking randomly will make you miss the timing to reflect a projectile coming your way.
I also read that the attacks given as tools to get through the game are useless. They're not. I'm using every single one of them because I need them.
It's worth every buck. The combination of art, gameplay and soundtrack is fantastic. You might value games differently, but please don't promote buying games only on sale. If you can throw 60 bucks at a game like For Honor and get disappointed, maybe buy some Indie Games full price next time and get surprised by how charming they are.

The initial release of this game was rocky to say the least. But after waiting a whole year to try again, and numerous promises from the developers that it had been "fixed", it's still wholey unplayable. For those not familiar with Slain, it's a mashup between Castlevania 1 and Rastan, much closer to the latter than the former. The game is intended to be "Nintendo Hard" and is very unforgiving for that reason. So from a very basic glance the game did a perfect job recreating the game play of the two while adding a kvlt metal style. But when you peel back the surface there is just WAY too much poorly programmed gameplay to consider this game playable.
Take Castlevania. It's hard, but it's predictable enough to learn how to play. The timing of the whip, jumps, and enemies is consitent. Puzzles are visually obvious (exluding those stupid fake blocks), and gameplay is consistent. You learn to play the game early and are challenged at mastering that knowledge as time goes on. Basically, it's Nintendo Hard.
Slain is a different beast. The challange doesn't lie in learning controls and then mastering them. It lies in very odd timing, standing still for long periods of time, and mashing buttons to perform combos. The problem, however is that the timing has to be precise. Now if this were once or twice per enemey, that would be fine. But most enemies take between 3 and 12 (yes 12) repititions of pricisely timed actions in order to kill. Most of the time a single failure causes death. Imagine if you were playing Guitar Hero where 1 failure resets the song, and there was no way to change this. It's not fun, and it's absolutely not what this game was going for. What really happens is that as a player you are shown one game at the start, but expected to play a different game that feels like shoving tooth picks up your fingernails after the first few enemies.
Combat is terrible. All of the combat available to the player is essentially useless. It appears that they were added in because animators had free time and wanted to draw more frames. Basically you use cut scene atacks and air attacks. Everything else will get your killed.
Why? Because the visuals of the animations are the only thing that matter. Meaning that something that SHOULD reset an animation never does. So you can never rely on which attack you will get next. Sometimes you do the normal swipe. Sometimes you lunge into a pit of koolaid that kills you. Enemy animations are especially deceptive. You sometimes reset them to the start of their animation, but most of the time something that otherwise disables an enemy causes their strongest attack to happen anyway. There are even ways to get strong attacks to cause damage 3 times in 1 hit. Which would be a forgivable glitch if it didn't invovle the only effective way to cause damage, blocking to start cut scene attacks. There is no clever skill of learning controls and outsmarting your enemies. No, your only hope is that mashing a button at the right time happens to work, because the last 72 that you did work, but for some unknown glitch the timing was off by a split second this time... and you died.
Takeaway? Gameplay programming is as kill. Don't skimp on it.

This game has all the trappings of a Soulslike. Dark atmosphere, a parry/riposte system, lots of style, beautiful, etc etc. The main thing it's lacking? Options.
The straw that broke the camel's back for me was a certain sequence in the Highlands. It was a gauntlet style room, and has possibly the worst combat situation design I've seen, ever. It's almost as if this specific area was DESIGNED to be as hard as possible... not because of the actual challenge, no. But because to all outward appearances, it is utterly incompatible with the game's controls.
Let's start it out with:
STAGE 1: Surrounded by skeletons.
This stage is pointless. You head to the middle of the room, and skeletons spawn around you. These are easy enough to dispatch, and it mainly serves as a way to make you waste mana just to get past the tedium of wailing on them. The only thing that matters here is WHERE you kill the last skeleton.
STAGE 2: Like Stage 1, but with projectiles.
As soon as you kill the last wave of skeletons, a dialogue prompt appears, and then a bunch of other skeletons appear in roughly the same places, added by mage skeletons on the left and right. Here are the problems with this:
-If you kill the last skeleton while partially to either side, they will spawn either on you or around you, causing instant damage since you have no defense for both sides other than your 'smart bomb' move, which costs the entire mana bar, meaning you cannot use projectiles before or after, without farming it by parrying or charge attacking enemies ad nauseum.
-If you kill the last skeleton while in the direct middle, skeletons will appear around you and the mages will attack from both sides. Again, since you have almost no defense from both sides at once, it is incredibly likely that something will hit you.
-If you kill the last skeleton while on the far right or left, you will spawn safely, but there is still a buffer of skeletons between you and the nearest mage, who will constantly fire while you're trying to deal with the skeletons.
Now would be a good time to mention that the mages continually back up away from you, and their attacks have almost no start-up.
It would also be a good time to mention that there is not enough jumping room, both horizontal and vertical, to jump over skeletons without taking damage.
Are you starting to see the problem here? The only thing you can do is continually mash attack, or try to snipe with your woefully limited magic, maybe peppering a parry/riposte or charge attack every now and then if the relentless mages give you any time at all.
It's tedium. But even this was excusable. This was the kind of thing that's happened before.
The real problem happens in
STAGE 3: Plague Dog Master
This stage consists only of a big skeleton, accompanied by a dog. The dog shoots exploding low-arcing projectiles at the player that must be reflected by attacks at close range, or produce a highly damaging toxic field. The big skeleton blocks most blows, and so the only way to reliably damage him is to parry and riposte him. If you are attacking while he attacks, you will most certainly be damaged.
Take notes, game designers. This is, without a doubt, the best way to demonstrate flaws in your own combat system: introduce two enemies simultaneously who must be countered in mutually exclusive ways. In order to kill the skeleton, you must parry and riposte him, which requires that you are not attacking. In order to protect yourself from the dog, you must attack within range of the skeleton.
If you are attacking, the skeleton will kill you. Its sword goes right through yours.
If you are trying to parry, the dog will kill you. Its projectile is unhindered by your block.
If you are FINISHING a parry, the dog will still kill you. Once you come out of the "riposte-finisher' animation, you will be hit by the toxic cloud.
And to top it off, they are both slowly advancing on you in a small room. They are too tall to jump over without taking damage. The player literally does not have any other options.
In some games, tedium can be excused by beauty, plot, or moments when the game shines. The game does not have enough of the first, a forgettable second, and as for the third, for the 6 hours I've played this game, I cannot think of one. I was waiting for that moment, but it never came.
A marginal improvement over the original, but still does not fix many of the technical and performance issues. Frankly unacceptable-and all the worse because the game itself is fantastic.

If you're a fan of deep storylines, spectacular vistas, amazing sound track and detailed character development, you'll really like this title. Incredible world design, high quality voice acting and an engaging plot really make this game stand out. There are only a few things I can say are wrong with this game, and they only minorly detract from the overall experience.
The combat system is fairly tedious. It consists of a customisable combat system, where you choose the attacks that go into the combo, but they are still fixed to kick or punch per combo slot. Meaning there's really not that much customisation to be done, and it doesn't really feel like it has all that much impact on combat, you still click the same buttons in the same order pretty much over and over. There is a secondary system to combat, a set of special abilities that trigger special combat modes. Called s-pressen, I've only unlocked 1 so far, and it does add a little more diversity to combat, it's possible that further unlocks might do the same, but I'm not sure I can see how. One big positive I can say about the combat is it looks great, the combat animations are seemless and flow together beautifully, but the combat just feel like it's lacking something to make it as engaging as the story, and I find myself just waiting for combat to end.
The game (outside of the story telling) mostly consists of jumping/climbing puzzles. So far though, they're proving to be linear and unchallenging due to the overlay telegraphing where you need to go next. Most games I've played in the past that involve this kind of puzzle use subtle visuals to show where you can jump to. This game basically hand-holds you through the entire thing with bright yellow chevroned markers telling you your next move. This, to me, is one of the negative effects of this game clearly being developed primarily for the console market (this is also reflected in the controls).
As I stated, the game feels like a console port. Playing with a controller might be an advantage, although the mouse/keyboard controls aren't terrible. There seems to be issues with camera angles when using mouse/keyboard, they can spin out of control sometimes, or flip weirdly. I'm playing on the highest difficulty, and I feel like there's zero challenge, it's just lucky the story is so engaging.
Pros:
Cons:
Overall Remember me has an engaging story, looks beautiful and has great voice acting to tie it all together into a well crafted title. It's only letdowns are overshadowed greatly by it's positives. I can definitely recommend this title to those that love a good story.

I tried to like this game, I really did. I liked the story; it was fairly engaging (if a bit confused) and the game world was somewhat intriguing. However, the gameplay was just overly frustrating and tedious. The mouse controls never seem to work like they should and just feel clumsy. The AI doesn't help as they frequently seem too perfect, making the game feel completely unfair. Its a shame because the concept was impressive.

I will recommend this game for those of us who love the Assassin's Creed games. Good story and wonderful graphics for its time. If you're just getting this game and have never played it, you will enjoy the story and the gameplay (most of the time, hopefully).
With that being said, I will move onto the pros and cons portion of this review:
PROS:
- Beautiful graphics with zero FPS drops.
- Good storyline that will have you hooked and have you wondering what will happen next.
- Fun parkour and stomach clenching goodness (like that famous Leap of Faith move).
- Once you get the hang of it, the combat is extremely fun and challenging.
CONS:
- Very glitchy. There will be many cases where the game will disagree with the controls I demand, and I go flying off of something I didn't even aim for. I have gotten killed from Leap of Faiths not being rendered correctly as well. I also had an issue with Memory Block 0 where you have to throw a dude into a specific location. I would do so, and the game would brick itself and continuously reload the tutorial without the dude reappearing with it. I had to start over several times before it finally registered that I was passing that sequence.
- Since I played this game on the Xbox 360 originally, I thought it only fair to go ahead and get my Elite controller out and play. Forewarning, you WILL have to redo almost every single control button if you decide to use a controller versus the mouse and keyboard. The buttons were not mapped accordingly as the game had intended them to be, BUT that could also be from me using an Elite Xbox One controller (which has several different buttons to map from) versus a standard Xbox controller.
- You will need to make sure your machine is compatible with this game. Though it's older, it is still graphic intensive. You need a good processor (as it recommends, you will need at LEAST a dual core processor), and a decent graphics card wouldn't hurt too much.
The only reason I gave the con list more detail is due to the fact that I do want to help some people out who are considering buying it and/or having similar issues to what I was having. This game is old, and it has its fair amount of issues, but it is definitely worth the purchase regardless. You might have moments of "WTF?!" while you're playing it, but as I recall, the 360 version was like that as well. A lot of people have said AC2 is better simply because the controls are smoother and the glitches are less frequent (which is true coming from someone who has played both of them). Still, though. Whether it be for nostalgic purposes, or you're wanting to get into where it all began, I highly recommend you buy this game.

Gameplay is solid, but here's where the first part is already better in almost every aspect, and with no innovation whatsoever at best. The New Colossus has been advertised as the "ultimate Nazi-occupied America" resistance simulator, and it is - to an extent. I thought Frau Engel would be a really amazing antagonist, and it is; in The New Order and the first phase of The New Colossus. She is absent for most of the game, and you don't even keep her in mind.
New characters are nice, but none of them develop further, and even B.J. feels bland, considering how badass he always was. Maps are really nice, but here's the kicker, the HUGE majority of them are buildings, when most of the game's ads showed otherwise, and you never really feel like you're in America at all. Felt great to go to the diner, but that was just an interactive cutscene (one that was part of one of the first and more well-known ads for TNC, actually!), because right after that? That's right, you go underground into yet another grey, Nazi-garbed building.
Collectibles are a-plenty, and even though I always love a good set of them (TNO, I'm looking at you), these ones are annoying to get to, and the in-game maps aren't helpful AT ALL to at least get to them and be done with that particular place.
Side-missions are mindnumbingly added as pure filler content, with no excitement involved, for as soon as you kill everyone in the phase, you just aim to grab said collectibles, roaming through a lifeless place.
I'm utterly disappointed in what was called to be one of the best games of the year, if not the decade, and I'm a big fan of the franchise. Them releasing the DLC's shortly after didn't help.
Verdict pains me to no end, as it is a 6/10 for me. Just like I said in my Homefront review, this does feel like a prologue; once you get to the end (?), you realize it was a massive build-up fitted in a relatively short game, filled with not-so-bad cutscenes. I would've settled with another TNO considering what we've been given.
Bethesda, you better step up and redeem yourselves with the third installment of the series. To quote Angry Joe, "you done ♥♥♥♥ed it up!".

With the gameplay being weaker, the graphics seeming blander, how's the story? In a few words? It's♥♥♥♥♥♥

Well the first game had some silliness to it, we even saw that in BJ's character. He took the situation as a whole seriously, but was still able to crack a few jokes and be lighthearted about a few things. But when he wanted to be serious, you knwe it was on. He seemed pained and bruised by everything that had happened to him, but still went on, because he had to. Now instead of a few real characters, with their flaws, hopes and their own motivations, we have a big roster of bland characters, each with a few quirks and absolutely idiotic dialouge.
While the first game had a character like Wyatt (or Fergus) loosing it because of the pressure of trying to the defeat the Nazis, has the second game a sassy black woman calling every white person a racist, an unfunny paranoid guy worshipping a toilett and BJ himself becoming a bad Max Payne knockoff, spouting suicidal dialouge while technically being the biggest badass in the solar system. Entry 1:
I've begun keeping this diary more as a way of pinning my thoughts down than as any real record of events. For who would read them? It's clear to me I'm in some kind of Faustian hell. Who I once was or where I came from is gone from my mind. Clearly I wasn't born in Courthouse and clearly I had a life before Courthouse, but memory fails me. They're coming again...

Entry 2:
I nearly forgot I had begun this diary. Time has no meaning anymore which is why I'm merely numbering my entries. I've lived and died countless times with varying duration, but always the same cruel result. I have managed to wrest some kind of checkpoint from the demons who torment me on this acursed plane. Some kind of new starting point in this engagement no doubt engineered only to taunt me and further my anguish with the false hope of progression. Progression? Is there a goal here beyond this mindless reincarnation to dance with the hordes of masked foes who soak up my aggression with mocking disregard? Footsteps. They've located me...

Entry 3:
A door opened. I know it did. I heard it somewhere behind me as I struggled to contain my spilled guts before the light faded again and I was placed at the beginning for another cruel trial. As the second of the two giants fell to the desperate vollies of my Hammergewehr there was a sound of creaking wood and more rushed footsteps. More footsteps? More? But is there a way out of this room? Is there a world beyond Courthouse? Spotted again...

Entry 4:
I can feel the carpet burns. I can't explain it. There are no marks but it's as though psychosomatically I've recorded the hundreds of dashes across these floors onto the virginal skin of this immortal body. Over the rail, run and slide. Pickup the ammo, hello friend. Over the rail, run and slide. Hello armor, how much of you will I be allowed to keep as I clamor up this clumsy crate and over the rail. Run and slide. It burns, but they won't give me the dignity of upright movement. Run and slide. Run and slide. Hello Hammergewehr. Always cold to the touch even though it feels like you are forced from my white palms for only seconds at a time between runs. And slide...

Entry 5:
I was through the threshold! There is more to this world! I went to the place of the others. There is more to Courthouse. There's a whole world outside of it I just know it! How many hundreds of lives have I lived in such ignorance? There must be more. Keep to the routine. Run and slide. Hello Hammergewehr...

Entry 6:
It is hopeless. There is no outrunning them. Courthouse is too strong. It won't let me go. It needs me. The pain is non-existent anymore. Death is just a momentary confusion before the reset. Didn't I just pick up armor? How was I so absurdly unaware of my physical state? The walls are closing in. I think I'm losing my mind...

Entry 7:
I'm upstairs. There's an upper level with cover that does not splinter at the slightest touch. There is an actual wall behind me. I feel it with my hand every now and again. No enemies sneaking up behind me. The small comfort is peculiar. I've got a Lasergewehr and what appears to be all the armor and health I can carry. I can't be sure. It's been ages since I was able to scrape together this much dignity for myself. The enemies seem lessened and are currently unaware of my location. I am terrified. Not of death as we are old friends. I'm terrified of progression. I'm terrified of leaving Courthouse. What could possibly be out there? What will I do with myself now? Courthouse is all I know. The man who came to Courthouse is dead. He died a million miserable deathes. I am Courthouse. I have always been Courthouse. I kiss the baluster next to me. Courthouse tell me what to do? I place the barrel in my mouth...

Entry 8:
No! I will advance. Whatever lies ahead I will meet with renewed vigor and determination! I am not Courthouse. Courthouse is just a prison of my mind! My name is B. B something. An icon appeared after the last enemy fell. I almost didn't notice it through the tears and my own hoarse screaming. A door. An action. Agency. Progression. A way forward. I turn the knob...

Entry 9:
It was all a dream sequence. A dream sequence? Ffffff...
This game rocks. Fix your difficulty spikes! Playtest or something...
If you enjoyed the first game you're almost certainly going to enjoy the sequel. Buy it!

This is one of the best games I've played in the past 20 years.
I stayed away at launch because of all of the negative reviews and drama. It looked to me like the devs were a bunch of scammers who took the money and ran. Fortunately, I was wrong. I decided to give the game a try at the release of 1.3 because the reviews were positive and it was 60% off and I'm so glad that I did. The game starts out simple - you're on a planet walking around on foot to find resources to repair your ship - but progressing further into the game you realize there's so much to do.
You're finding resources to repair your ship, now you need resources to refuel your life support, you'll also need resources to sell, there's a lot more of the planet to explore too, and several planets in the system and they're all different (maybe some are hot, some cold, some have acid rain, some are paradise), now you can warp between systems, now you can warp in a different way that I won't spoil, wait now you can "warp" in another way, oh look other species that you can't understand so you have to interact with them to learn bits and pieces of their language, don't forget to upgrade your multitool so gathering resources is faster, now your ship is kind of slow and has few inventory slots so you need to buy another one or maybe find a crashed one and repair it, now pirates are attacking you, oh look side missions and now you can hunt the pirates instead, running low on personal inventory slots so you better find some drop pods to upgrade it, don't forget to find a planet that you want to make your home and build a base on it, oh now you're doing missions for your home and you discover that you can make a farm and create other vehicles, now you're in a large battle in space to protect a huge freighter - wait you can buy the freighter and store multiple ships in it, time to explore more planets and - wait this planet doesn't like anything like that last hundred that you've seen and that doesn't look like a real tree...oh and don't forget the main story, which is actually compelling.
The point I'm trying to make is that there's a ton of content and you will absolutely get your money's worth. Highly recommended.

We were moving, digging the enemy out of their heavily entrenched position, which used to be a mansion on a cliff, a beach protruding from its east. The beach was heavily defended, but every direction besides it was even more defended. The beach was our best option.
We got in our truck, various trucks moving in, including a mobile supply truck and reinforcements truck. Moving in, we walked onto the beachhead to die. Around a hundred of us died on that beach within the first five minutes, us all having no other option but to scrabble forward, as strong as we could possibly be in that sort of situation.
By the time we reached the cliff, we had lost hundreds more. We charged, throwing everything we could at them from every angle. A special operations team had managed to pierce the mansion's defenses, took down their radio communications and called in paratroopers. A few of them died before they hit the floor, but they had crippled the defense. The hundred or so of us charged in, furious at the beachhead.
When the government actually got to the beachhead, it was a horrific sight. They found no captives, but only the gutted,  dead,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in corpses of what could be called the enemy. Hundreds of us didn't come home, and many families ended up with no mother or father to hold them tight, and tell them that everything would be okay.
I was one of the lucky ones, but I'm saddened to say that though. I am warred constantly by the thoughts that maybe someone else deserved to live instead of me. I wasn't ever important, besides my mother, father and grandfather. The dead had wives, children. They should have lived, I should have died in their place. One of the most intense and fascinating narrative adventure I've played. Splendid visuals (it's really amazing how such a small team managed to build this from scratch on the engine), sublime art direction and, above all, an incredible sound design that masterfully uses voice actig, atmosphere, music and all kinds of distortion effects to make this game even more captivating.
The portrayal of mentall illness (the subtle and ambiguous depiction of psicosis, not only as a condition but also as a profond and personal perception of reality) in the context of norse mythology makes it even more interesting and moving.
The well balanced pace, the smart absence of HUD and the clever ways in wich the game teaches the player to progress contribute to make this a smooth yet terrifying journey under the skin and inside the mind of the main character.
Heavily inspired in other psicological horror games such as the original Silent Hill games, Amnesia or Dark Souls, Hellblade manages to have its own identity and stile with a smart mix of environmental puzzles and thrilling combat sections. Exploration is encouraged through narration and the unnerving manipulation of Senua's inner voices.
Some may claim that some mechanics are a little too clumsy in some sections (specially combat) or that the level design it's a little too linear and sometimes excesively guided. But this small details cannot possibly obscure the many virtues of a daring game that offers a unique and refreshing adventure that leaves a heavy impression after being finished.

First time I've ever been motivated enough to post a review for a game, though this is something more than that.  As far as storytelling, character development, setting, atmosphere, sound, visuals, and acting, this is top tier.  I personally enjoyed both the combat and the puzzle challenges because I think they both contributed to the experience as a whole, they 'fit' with the rest of the game and worked together with everything else.  This is a powerful work of art and was worth every penny.  It kept me playing to the end the same way that the best novels keep you up late into the night wanting more and more.  The feature that is included about the making of the game is really great and gives you insight into how much forethought and research went into this game.  In an age of SWBF2's, Senua is exactly what we need so desperately.

I salute Ninja Theory and their take on creating a game like this. Mechanically the game is very simplistic in design and button layout and pretty forgiving in combat. I think the biggest element Hellblade brings besides touching on a taboo subject is that the entire thing is about perspective from the beginning to the end and every challenge in between. The story telling and writing is wonderful especially if you enjoy any kind of Norse mythos, and Senua is a very fleshed out and believable character whose story you want to see the end of. The game in total is around 6 hours depending on difficulty and player. There's not a lot in the way of replayability and actual game play mechanics, but that by no means should diminish your outlook on Hellblade. It's a wonderful story and well worth the price to support an Indie dev that showed they can't take a step into a mine that no one's really touched on. Without a doubt I recommend Hellblad: Senua's Sacrifice to anyone who loves a good story and to have an interesting perspective shown to them.

This game is a rather unique experience. I see it not as a traditional game but more as a medium to dive into (and educate about!) the topic of mental illness an how its affecting people.
I won't write about the game in detail as this game is best experienced with as little knowledge as possible. You don't even get a ingame tutorial, HUD or any of that 'modern' stuff. Just play it and experience it on the way.

In the end you will get a lot to think about (the game, mental illness in general, even about yourself) for only ~ 8h of gameplay.
By creating a unique atmosphere (which is quite emotional like LiS or 'To the Moon') the true value of Hellblade lies not in the superficial first experience of playing this game, slaying monsters, beating bosses, but in the narrative, touching story and surprisingly fresh way of portraying mental illness in a hero.

The character model is closer to the frame than in most other thrid person adventure games, at first this felt odd and wished I could change the FOV in game, but after a few minutes it grew in me.  The close camera serves to make the experience more intimate as if you were living it through Senua's eyes, yet not a 1st person experience.
I played this game with In Ear Monitors and would strongly recomend the use of headphones!!! The voice acting is another strong point for this game. The voices have different volumes and are very expresive without becoming "theateresque".  After a few hours in, the voices feel very real... in an uncanny way, they feel in your head lol
The cutscenes incorporate real acting video overlays on top of in game rendering to create a very beautiful and seamless experience.  It feels very cinematic!  While we are talking about visuals the game has a "photomode" in which you can pause the game and explore tha environment and compose beautiful images!
In terms of combat I played the game on the hardest difficulty, it's quite simple in concept but it felt odd with the original mapping for kb+mouse so I made it fit my liking. Short version: Hellblade relies on the burgeoning popularity of mental illness as an artistic subject to create story. It is on rails, has an unresponsive and unreliable combat system, and its puzzles are only challenging because of the difficulty in moving about the landscape. The only redeeming factors are the art and sound design. If you are looking for an interactive movie and are willing to put up with an awful combat system, buy this game. Otherwise, stay clear.
Long:
I purchased this game because I was intrigued by all the positive reviews it was getting and the description of it as a "triple-A Indie" title. The opening credit sequence was interesting, though it took far, far too long. The world introduced in that sequence is lushly designed and the sound design is truly wonderful, doing an excellent job of making the player feel the annoyance of hearing voices. It was too good at that, in fact, because I became annoyed after about five minutes of play and stayed that way for the next ~2 hours.
After the credit sequence, it was an additional 25 minutes before I was able to make a *choice* about what to do--and even that choice was false (one must return to that point and complete the other fork in the path as well). I am not strictly a player of open-world games, and I do appreciate story. The impression that I got from this work, however, was that the designers were intending to create an interactive movie rather than a game, or perhaps they forgot what they were doing along the way.
Sure, if you fail in combat you must try again and your progress can be lost if you fail too many times, so there is valorization of outcome (win in combat = hurray). Unfortunately, combat is an annoyance even worse than the voices in your head, not due to the difficulty of the enemies, but rather to the unresponsive and unreliable nature of your limited moveset. If you win in combat, the story proceeds. You do not choose how or where to go.
Speaking of choosing where to go, the beautiful (if muted) world feels wasted because Senua (the player character) cannot explore everywhere it looks as though she can explore. Some ledges that are chest-high are fine for her to climb on; others that are about knee-high are not. Some gaps between trees are passable and others are not. This served to add to my annoyance--it was clear where one should go to unlock the next piece of each puzzle, but finding the "right" path along the terrain out of all the apparent ways one could travel? Needlessly arduous. Add to that the fact that Senua's fastest gait is a half-hearted shuffle, and frustration builds quickly.
I was hoping that at some point the challenges would become fun, but instead of the good parts of Myst and Dark Souls this game combines the worst of both. I regret my purchase and will seek a refund.

B.J.'s badass monologues are back - along with brutal, frenetic gunplay, and a cast of quirky characters who fight at your side. The New Collossus begins five months after the events of New Order. Nazis have occupied the United States, and while the country is mostly under their control, there are pockets of resistance fighters. B.J. teams up with a capable group.
If you're a fan of New Order, then you will definitely enjoy this one, but I will give New Order the slight edge in entertainment. The New Collossus just doesn't feel as fresh as the first. Still, the game has its brilliant moments, including one of the craziest execution sequences I've ever seen in a game or even film. It's honestly incredible to me that this game was even made, considering its massive budget. There are hours and hours of cutscenes joining the action sequences, so understand that the game is entirely story-driven. This is a good thing though, as the writing is fantastic, and you care about the people you're fighting with.
The gameplay is fun and fast-paced, albeit repititve at times, and I wish it was a bit more polished. Personally, I think the gunplay is a notch below a game like Doom, but it's still fun and gory.
I was disappointed with the abrupt ending and it's on the short side, but it's a game that wants you to take your time, immerse yourself in the enviornment, and I'd also recommend playing on a harder difficulty (although you will suffer cheap deaths). It's one of the most unique single player games I've played, and if you're a fan of story-driven games in any capactiy then this might be one for you to pick up.

This is one of the best games I've played in the past 20 years.
I stayed away at launch because of all of the negative reviews and drama. It looked to me like the devs were a bunch of scammers who took the money and ran. Fortunately, I was wrong. I decided to give the game a try at the release of 1.3 because the reviews were positive and it was 60% off and I'm so glad that I did. The game starts out simple - you're on a planet walking around on foot to find resources to repair your ship - but progressing further into the game you realize there's so much to do.
You're finding resources to repair your ship, now you need resources to refuel your life support, you'll also need resources to sell, there's a lot more of the planet to explore too, and several planets in the system and they're all different (maybe some are hot, some cold, some have acid rain, some are paradise), now you can warp between systems, now you can warp in a different way that I won't spoil, wait now you can "warp" in another way, oh look other species that you can't understand so you have to interact with them to learn bits and pieces of their language, don't forget to upgrade your multitool so gathering resources is faster, now your ship is kind of slow and has few inventory slots so you need to buy another one or maybe find a crashed one and repair it, now pirates are attacking you, oh look side missions and now you can hunt the pirates instead, running low on personal inventory slots so you better find some drop pods to upgrade it, don't forget to find a planet that you want to make your home and build a base on it, oh now you're doing missions for your home and you discover that you can make a farm and create other vehicles, now you're in a large battle in space to protect a huge freighter - wait you can buy the freighter and store multiple ships in it, time to explore more planets and - wait this planet doesn't like anything like that last hundred that you've seen and that doesn't look like a real tree...oh and don't forget the main story, which is actually compelling.
The point I'm trying to make is that there's a ton of content and you will absolutely get your money's worth. Highly recommended.

tl;dr: My personal Goty2017, for having one of the most lovingly crafted settings, characters, story presentations and heartachingly beautiful and terrible depictions of mental illness, sheer strength and will I've ever seen. It is not flawless, but the wonderful experience offsets its minor flaws.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a singleplayer and story-driven third-person game where you take control of the titular Senua on her quest through the Norse afterlife of Hel, battling her own mind as much as the external threats of wondrously designed and animated Norsemen and even Gods themselves. So let's look a little closer at this title, shall we?
This is a bit of a mix of things. On Senua's quest, you will be driving her through a mostly linear path with minor exploration options. While the trailers mostly focus on cutscenes and combat, the most time consuming gameplay comes from a slowpaced yet truly gorgeous exploration of the scenery, solving a variety of puzzles primarily based around finding ways to align certain bits of scenery with other bits in order to see patterns emerge. Be it outright shards of reality itself seen in a way so it patches a broken bridge, through seeing shadows cast in the shape of a particular rune or wandering until two trees form the shape of another when seen over each other, this will probably be the most time consuming of gameplay and I suspect it may be frustratingly slow for some players, but in the context of this game I personally found it pretty much exactly the right pace, speed and difficulty.
These slower puzzle sections are punctuated by bits of combat, as Senua displays her fearsome skills with the sword against absolutely magnificently designed monstrous and towering norsemen. The combat can rightly be criticized for being a bit basic and some find it repetitive, but I must say that's genuinely offset by the sheer level of presentation. The animation is absolutely top notch and the combat feels impactful and weighty, while aided by brilliant sound design.
The camera will remain claustrophobically close to Senua and your vision is severely limited, adding to the tension and stress of it all as enemies most certainly won't hesitate to strike at you from your blind spots. This is where another aspect of the game's design comes in and I will cover that a bit later under audio.
If it was merely exploration and combat on offer, I probably wouldn't have enjoyed the game as much as I did, but Ninja Theory breaks things up very nicely by offering a varied set of challenges all the time. The base recipe of getting Senua from A to D via B and C remains much the same, but the devil is in the details. In one section you may be close to blind, another overwhelmed by far too many solutions, a third you must venture from light to light in a panic and in a fourth you may rise above it all in a fury worthy of the norse gods themselves. From a basic recipe, we're subjected to a very engaging variety of gameplay at a pace that may feel a bit slow, but I definitely feel helps present the story and feel the game aims for.
Senua's psychosis makes for an incredibly compelling immersion into her world, and leveraging it for gameplay like Ninja Theory has done is masterfully done.
This is not merely a hack'n'slash combat game. This is so much more.

What this game displays vividly and proudly is that there's so much more to visuals in a game than simple technical graphics settings and technology. Ninja Theory has leveraged a gorgeous engine, with great power, and shows how important -design and skill in presentation- is. This game's visuals repeatedly managed to take my breath away. I've seen better textures, I've seen better smoke effects and fire and so on and so forth, but I have very very rarely seen presentation this good.
The character designs, the world design and uses of various effects is absolutely top notch and I can only conclude that this game is a labor of love for the developers. This is one of the absolutely better looking games out there and I'll gladly pit it against the AAA games of this year in that regard.
Coupled with great use of mo-cap, this game presents itself in a breathtaking fashion.
As the game warns you when you fire it up, it highly recommends headphones to truly enjoy the binaural recordings used, and I can definitely vouch for the impact a good sound system has on this game. Senua's mental illness manifests in many ways, one of them through the presence of voices doing anything from mocking, advicing, fearing for her and exposing parts of the story and boy oh boy are they immersive and unsettling.
The voice acting is absolutely top notch and so much has gone into the sound design here. The norse theme of the game is coupled with an absolutely stunning soundtrack that grips you tight when it must and merely raises the hair on your neck when it wishes.
This is not merely a matter of presentation though, as the voices in Senua's mind actually serve gameplay purposes as well. Sometimes they will warn you when an enemy is about to strike you from outside your view, or they will give you hints about what you must do next or where to go.
... but be warned, they might not all have your best interests in mind.
This is the part that I wish to extoll the virtues of the most, yet can't really tell you much about because it would spoil the experience. Let me just say that Senua is one of the most compelling characters I have seen in all my years of gaming from the good old Commodore 64 and until today. Lovingly crafted all the way from the conception through writing and visual design, and acted magnificently by her actress, she grips your heart and... well, in the end all things must be let go.
A great main character is plunged into a fantastically designed Norse Hellscape, exploring everything from her own mind and delusions, and through the challenges of both mental illness, grief and philosophy.
The final hour or so of the game had me in a deathgrip and by the time the end credits were rolling I was exhausted and genuinely shed a tear at the conclusion. One of the very few games I've ever sat through the credits of, and this is genuinely a story that you should experience. Everything spoken of above comes together in a polished and gorgeous way, telling a story you will never have heard or seen elsewhere.
A story of mental illness, an exploration of character, mythology, courage and fear presented magnificently by Ninja Theory in what I can only assume has been a labor of love. I have almost nothing but good things to say about it, but will have to almost grudgingly acknowledge that this is not a game for everyone. If story doesn't matter to you or if puzzles frustrate you, or you don't have the patience to just take in gorgeous settings and scenery... this may not be as good to you as it was to me.
But if you care about any of these things... Senua will take you on a journey you will never forget.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a game I've been wanting to play for a while and I'm glad that I finally bought it. The game provides a thrilling and unique adventure filled with puzzles and monsters, accompanied by a beautiful soundtrack and some of the best voice acting I've ever heard in a video game. Well worth the money, even at full price. Highly recommended you play with headphones!
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is an award winning Indie game made by a team of roughly twenty people. The things that they have accomplished in this game are outstanding. I'll start with the base of the game. In Hellblade, you follow a young Celtic warrior, Senua, in her quest save the soul of her once love, Dillion, from the Norse goddess Hela. The game is heavily inspired by Scandinavian culture, as well as Norse mythology and has Senua travel into places such as Helheim later on in the game.
What makes this game so unique is the main character's mental health condition, Psychosis. The game heavily focuses in this area and has created an accurate representation of the mental illness. This is due to the developers working closely with experts on the condition as well as people who have experienced Psychosis. Throughout the game you will hear voices, otherwise known as "Furies". These voices will sometimes guide you and assist you through combat, but can also try to deceive you. The main character, Senua, sees her condition as a curse known as "the darkness" and refers to it as such throughout the game. Senua struggles to come to terms with her illness many times in the game, causing her to be in a constant battle of her own inside her mind. The way this is performed in the game, is spectacular and has been commended by users and critics alike.
The story starts off with a cinematic of Senua travelling across water to an island. This cinematic is accompanied by one of the voices acting as the narrator of the game. We learn that Senua is travelling to the island to save the soul of her dead love, Dillion, as she carries his severed head as a vessel for his soul. To do this, she must defeat the goddess, Hela, in her realm called Helheim. As you progress through the game, you are accompanied by other characters such as Druth, who will tell you stories, and the Darkness, what she thinks is the core entity of her curse.
When you reach a certain part of the game not far from the start, you are greeted with a so called perma-death system. Rot appears on Senua's arm, and will continue to grow up her arm everytime she dies. If she dies too many times, the rot will supposedly grow to her head and kill her, deleting the save file. Bearing in mind, the game tends to trick you throughout the entire story. Whether you choose to believe this perma-death system, is up to you.
The game's combat system has many different opinions across the community. Personally, I think it's brilliant. Although it is rather basic, it still provides some of the most exciting moments I've ever experienced in a video game, whether it be dueling bosses or fighting off massive hordes of enemies. The ability to focus during combat provides an interesting twist to the gameplay.
Visually, the game looks stunning. The attention to detail is very high and gives off a very convincing setting. Some parts almost feel real, though I guess that has more to do with other parts of the game accompanied by the graphics. The animations are also worth a mention too. The cutscenes are entirely performed by the voice actors using motion capture, which increases how realistic the game looks and feels.
It is highly recommended that you play this game with headphones. I cannot stress this enough! You will not get the same experience if you play without headphones. I'm sure the game is still good without them but it is even better with headphones.
What the developers have achieved with sound is also worth a mention. As shown in the in-game documentary, the voices in Senua's head were recorded using a binaural microphone. This involved the actors walking around the microphone so the sound was coming from different directions which the game was praised for by many people. The pressence of these voices really gives you an idea of what living psychosis is really like.
The soundtrack to this game is beautiful. No doubt about it. The right songs are always used at the right times, and bring some of the most memorable experiences I've ever had in a game, especially the final boss song.
Of course, like all games, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is not without its faults. A common glitch of not being able to open doors properly affected me a couple of times near the beginning of the game, which forced me to restart the game.
Part of the game involves you doing a series of trials, also known as Odin's Trials. In my opinion, the second trial is ridiculous. It starts off alright, but when the house starts to burn the game barely gives you an idea on what you have to do. I died many times on this stage, resulting in me having to look up on the internet what I have to do, breaking the immersion a little bit.
Overall, this has to be one of the best games I have played in a long time. What I love about it the most is that it felt real. There were times where I completely forgot I was playing a game. The story is gripping and the atmosphere of the game, although dark, feels so realistic. The combat, although basic, is exciting and challenging at times. The characters are realistic, accompanied by brilliant performances and voice acting, adding to the realism.
I think everybody can relate to the main character a little bit. Although not everybody has psychosis, everybody at some point in their lives has had or is having their own struggles that have affected them in some way. This is why I recommend for everybody to try this game, no matter what genre you prefer. You're bound to find something to her that you can relate to. Honestly, the actress who played her deserves an award. Somebody with no acting experience to have achieved something like this is outstanding.
Without a doubt, this game for me is my game of the year of 2017. I would recommend it to anybody, even at full price. Just remember to play with headphones! It brings me a little bit of hope for the gaming industry, and I hope we see more games like this in the future. Thank you Ninja Theory, and to everybody involved in the production of this masterpiece!

TL;DR: Decent game with some great aspects that is sadly ruined by bad design decisions, mostly concerning the controls. A lot of wasted potential, because lets face it: challenging games can be fun, dying a lot can be a great motivator, but if your worst enemy is the botched input and bland repetition, is becomes a chore pretty quick.
The good:
- Lovely art-style! The game looks fantastic, lots of detail and it really comes to life. This is the one reason I actually kept playing for longer than I wanted to.
- Great soundtrack. Maybe a bit repetitive, but it certainly fits the game-play and the game-world.
- Diverse levels. The different levels, or stages, are always interesting and never bore you.
The bad:
- While the enemies are pretty diverse over all, most of them come in great number and you will fight the same enemy-type over and over. And since their animations are very basic, you will see the same enemies, going through the same motions, over and over again. And no, a different color on an enemy doesn't constitute a "new" enemy,
- Your attack options. Again, pretty limited. Sword or flaming sword, the attacks look and sound always the same, not much you can change here.
The ugly:
- The controls are infuriating. No, there is no delay in the input, but it feels that way. Your character always has to finish his animation before he will accept a new input, meaning very often you try to react to something but you can't, because you are still stuck in your previous animation. And in very tense situations, this quickly goes out of hand.
You never seem to be able to do what you want to do, because you always have to wait. One second you hit an enemy with your sword, when you see a magic projectile approaching. Now you need to react: either deflect it or jump over it. But because you were hitting the enemy right before you could see it, you are still caught up in the animation and you will get hit. There is nothing you can do about it.
This quickly gets annoying and then infuriating.
Such a beautiful game with actually decent game-play gets completely ruined by the botched animation timing. Maybe they thought it wasn't hard enough before, but I don't like games that make your worst enemy the input controls. No matter how beautiful they look like.
If they fix the animation-input issue this game is a 5/5, now it maybe a 3/5 if you love this type of game, but for most ppl it will be a 2/5.
Short, but very good. Definitely worth the $13 dollar asking price, especially if you enjoy a challenge and collecting achievements.

Hammerfight is a simple game, swing your mouse around to fly and swing your weapon. The right movement for control is hard to pick up at first, but it gets easier as you learn. As you continue through the game, you find more new elements that aid you in fighting and add complexity to the techniques you can use to beat up opponents. You pick up new weapons that suit a variety of play styles such as swords, axes, hammers, flails, and more. You can even mix and match these weapons for all sorts of combinations. The gems add another layer of complexity by enchanting your weapon with various attributes. Armors, bombs, ballistas, and all sorts of other components are also available to be used. You end up switching around all sorts of equipment trying to create a machine that best fits you, whether it be a speedy swordsman slicing everything, a slow and heavily armoured juggernaut with a massive flail to smash enemies, or even a long range fighter that precisely aims and snipes out targets from afar.
This game is still fun long after you complete the various routes in the story mode to just crush some guys in the arena mode and take out some stress.

Criminally underappreciated! This game is packing more quality pound for pound than most others. It's a real diamond in the rough, and it certainly is rough, but it offers so much that you can't find in other games. I don't think that there's any other game that uses its thematic style, for one thing. It seems vaguely middle eastern but not really, vaguely steampunk but not really. It's just endlessly interesting. The engine, too, is astounding considering how little it's talked about. It's so robust that it enables crazy things to occur. I once hit a guy so hard that, in the endlessly looping arena, he passed over my head multiple times before he hit the ground. It really is amazing. The game has so much replay value, too. You start out with only the ability to do your story missions as an almost nameless grunt, but you unlock the ability to buy weapons and go on hunts. Eventually you're decked out in ornate armor and weaponry, with titles so long that they take half a minute to list. It never stops being satisfying. Definitely buy this game. 5 bucks is a steal.
A few vital bits of information, though:
- When you first load the game up, go into the options menu and set your DPI as low as it can go. It often gets set too high and players can hardly move. If you've set it properly, then the cursor should be very sensitive in menus and your craft should be quite responsive. You should be able to swing your weapon in a circle without removing your mouse from the center of the pad.
- When you first get to choose which mission to take, choose the harder worm hunt mission. Doing it unlocks a game mode that's incredibly profitable and supplies you with powerful stones that you otherwise can't get.
- You can spare people by either lowering their health until the bar turns red or disarming them and knocking their weapon away. Given how cluttered and dangerous the ground gets during battles, you'll want to be hitting people upwards. Giving them more time to fly will often make it so that you won't be credited with a kill even when they land on a sword and explode. Knocking their weapon away works way better, though. If you manage to launch it outside of the level boundaries (usually up, but sometimes to the side) then the enemy will bloodlessly retreat unless it can find a new weapon. There are no fights against humans in which you have to completely kill them, but sparing them doesn't influence the story.

With elements of games like Mirror's Edge, Oni and Assassin's Creed, Remember Me still introduces enough original game elements and ideas to be worthwhile. But all three of those games do a few things really well, which make them classics. I can see why Remember Me didn't do as well, since it also has some serious flaws.
Nothing that gets in the way of basic gameplay or finishing the game (which took me about 12 hours on the medium setting, with an 85% completion (so, that a lot of the collectibles and plenty experimentation in the memory remixes). But the combat gets a bit dull and is effectively too easy once you figure it out. A combat system similar to the Arkham series or Shadow of Mordor, but it lacks the depth and variety of those and the upgrades you unlock don't really change the game. It's nice that 'crafting' new combos can really help out in some battles, but it never feels really satisfying.
Visually, it's engaging, although the levels feel a bit small at times and the layout and maps not very realistic. The camera can get a bit annoying at times, but on the whole it behaves well enough. The decor is nicely done and it certainly has its own flavour. Given that you'll only spend about 10-15 hours in it, it's more than enough.
The playtime is a bit of an issue though. For a campaign, 12 hours isn't very long. It's fine, but even a game like Mirror's Edge then offers a lot of replay values with challenges, score boards and speed runs. The Arkham series did with a very extensive challenge system as well and offers an open world with insane amounts of collectibles. Remember Me doesn't offer all that much beyond the basic game.
Al that's fine, but I would recommend buying it when it's one sale. Remember Me had the potential to be great, but it's writing, overall value and gameplay design flaws make me a bit sad for what it could have been. Still recommended.
