I have mixed opinions about this game. The graphics are nice and the music is good and atmospheric, but when I first launched the game I was wondering if it was developed by the same people as Tiny Bang Story. To my surprise, apparently not, although Mr. Pumpkin Adventure is extremely similar to it. Others have pointed out that it's also similar to Amanita Studio's works. What I'm trying to get at is that this game is not very original.
The puzzles feel too random at times, half the time there are no clues from the actual level, but you just have to sit there and spend ages trying to decipher each individual puzzle. This bothers me a lot since it makes the game incohesive,  as if they just started out with nice graphics and then slapped on some puzzles for good measure. On the other hand, that also means there is a great variety of puzzles if you only came for that aspect.
If you care about a good story then steer away from this game. The fact that the game is developed by a Chinese studio is no excuse, since there are other brilliant Chinese puzzle games that have better translation, such as Flood of Light, and  other games by non-native English speakers that are way better than Mr Pumpkin Adventure. The comic strips open a window of opportunity for the development of a good story, but the writing makes no sense.

Mr. Pumpkin Adventure is a very math and programming heavy bizarre Chinese-made point and click adventure with way too many references to everything the creators clearly loved. On one hand, it has a really great strange style, that can remind you a bit of Machinarium, but is, at the same time, distinctly Chinese. It looks and sounds interestingly and it's weird surreal story with little comic book cutscenes between chapters are extremely charming. But then, there are puzzles. Which start as something interesting and fun, but later devolves really heavily into advanced math knowledge, references to movies and things that you might not know and will have to search and committing other "game design sins" of puzzle making.
Which, in the end, really killed the game for me. I went about halfway without even considering to use a walkthrough, but using internet for help, because getting a set number out of a formula of 4 other set numbers is not a task I can solve on my own. But then had to almost exclusively play with the walkthrough in the later parts of the game, apart from some more obvious and not too obscure puzzles. It's charming, it's bizarre, it has all the potential to be amazing, but unless you are into the same things the creator of this game was, I don't think you'll enjoy this journey.

Helmet Heroes… where do I even begin? Well, let’s start from the beginning to give you as much information about this game as possible. When I first saw Helmet Heroes I thought it was a cute 2D side-scroller. I clicked download and started going through the reviews since I was going to be playing this with a group of friends later. Of the 205 positive reviews, quite a few of them either talk about the game getting good after level 100-200 or that they can’t even load the game and are asking for help. After looking at the reviews I head towards the features of the game. The game lists “Around 40 enemies to do battle against.” Remember that number because its important for later. All in all, that’s not a very good first impression of the game.
With the game fully downloaded its size was less than 50 Mb, which caught me off guard so I booted it up expecting another download. To my surprise, the game quickly booted and I was put on a character creation screen which is where things started going downhill even faster. The first thing I notice is the music, which isn’t bad, just repetitive. The next thing I notice however, is the graphical glitch on the screen from the character creation. I cycle through the different looks until I finally find one that doesn’t have a graphical glitch. At this point my character looks like an old Asian lady, but I didn’t really care what I looked like since I was playing with three other guys. We all chose a different class with me getting the archer class. Of the other classes, two of them are ranged characters with only one class being a melee type. They are: warrior, mage, and cowboy.
Once we got into the game we all added on another as friends and started looking around. Everyone has crappy looking weapons, but that’s to be expected of being level 1. We start looking and walking around and see a little green glob that looks to be like an enemy. The three ranged guys all try to shoot at him, but none of us can aim. Yes you read that right, you can’t aim in this game. Over half of the game is slopes and you can only shoot in a straight line. As a stubborn person I chose to keep using my ranged weaponry whereas everyone else swapped over to using swords because the classes only affect the starting points. Any class can use any weapon, everything is just decided by level whether or not you can use it. Getting past the blaringly obvious graphical glitches next to trees and the inability to aim, we start exploring and find a couple quests. One of which is kill every monster in the game. All 40 of them.
We completely missed the tutorial and managed to make it into the next region exploring complaining about the unchanging music. As we manage to get into the new area, someone notices that there are a lot of options in the top right that none of us had looked at yet. The character menu has all the character stats and most of us were ready for a level up by this point so we took a minute to explore the menu. There’s also a map if you can call it that. In reality it’s just a bunch of colored blobs next to one another. After laughing at it and trying to figure out where we are, we give up and keep exploring. At this point we do one damage to the mobs and are incapable of killing them. We eventually die and are teleported to the “nearest” safe haven, which was farther into the dangerous area. At this point half our squad gives up because we're trapped in an area in which we can’t easily get out of without dying.
In the building we spawn into when we die here is a weapon and armor shop. This is where the game starts getting racist. The vendor sells “Mexican shirt”, “Mexican Pants”, and a “Sombrero”. All of which only put points into artillery, which is guns. We can’t buy anything here though because everything is thousands more than what we can afford..
If that’s not bad enough to deter you away from this game, there are also several other issues this game has. The experience is sticking out of the experience bar and is out of sync. Most mobs and players are desynchronized so you never know where someone or something actually is. Sprinting takes three mana per tick and you can go into negative mana if you don’t have a multiple of three for your mana. Trying to alt tab out of the game breaks the resolution and then has a large black bar on the right side.
I would strongly suggest you don’t waste your time in this game.

Oh boy where to begin on this one. I went into this game expecting something mediocre. Not good, but something that would have some positive qualities that might be interesting to study. After all, I have had some good experiences with "mixed" reviewed steam f2p games in the past, so when I got some friends together to play this none of us could have expected what terrors we were in for. We should have actually read the positive reviews before assuming that steams "40% Positive" rating was accurate, because the vast majority of the thumbs-ups are either people saying that the game "only gets good around level 100" or "I can't get the game to boot up, making a positive review to seek help"
Me and my friends load the game up, and are already greeted with an indicator of quality right on the character creation screen. The majority of the hairstyles have clipping errors and there are weird lines at the edge of each sprite. This glitch is present in almost every sprite in the entire game, and the fact that something this simple hasn't been fixed (i'd assume its just fixing some clipping errors on a spritesheet) then that speaks measures to the overall quality of the product.
Me and my 3 friends decide to all take one of the classes. 3 of the classes are generic fantasy classes (Warrior, Archer, Wizard) but then you have a Cowboy who is completely differently themed and uses actual real world guns like an AK-47 or Mac10. This tells us a few things. 1: This game does not have a very consistent theme (Most likely trying to appeal to the edgy kids who want to use guns) and 2: This game will rely heavily on ranged combat (3 of the classes are ranged). Now this may not seem like a bad thing, but when you realize a few things about the combat this turns into one of the most frustrating combat I've experienced in any game (We will go more into on combat later.)
We load into the game and are placed in the "tutorial" aka a sign that tells you how to move and use a basic attack, nothing else. There is a bunch of features we never learned about, such as how to heal or sprint (which you should never do by the way, it uses 3 mana per second out of the 20 I had, and there is no way to restore it other than going to a healer in town). We tried to attack the first enemies, and everyone just fell apart. Movement was the slowest I have seen in any game, however if you jump you move almost twice as fast so we just moved about the game in a constant spinning animation. We attempted to kill the first enemies, which were on a slope down from the "tutorial" sign, and the flaws in the combat became apparent.
You cannot aim in this game. All attacks must be shot directly forward. Now, if the game was designed around this (such as the flat area in a game like Maplestory) it wouldn't be a problem, HOWEVER this game has the worst possible design for a combat system like this. Almost all enemies are on a slope, which means that if you are playing a ranged character you can't hit them. Because 3 OF THE 4 CLASSES are ranged, this turns combat into a battle against the controls instead of the actual enemies.
We decided to keep attempting to push through the game, although most of us just equipped swords to get around the awful ranged combat. We have been given no direction, so we open up the map to see where we should be going and then Our. Jaws. Dropped. The map screen is literally 20 single colored blobs placed randomly on an empty screen, and there is no indication of what each area is, how they connect, or where you even are on the map. The map is quite literally, just a 3 year old's art project that tells you nothing and you have to attempt to figure out what it is even supposed to represent.
So, the combat is unbearable, we have no direction, and the map is something even Dora the Explorer would scoff at, so all that is left for us to do is keep going right until we find something interesting. We find an NPC who gives our first quest sweet! Too bad that the quest is to kill EVERY ENEMY IN THE ENTIRE GAME. That is clearly not going to happen for a while, so we keep heading to the right, and eventually end up in a new zone. In this zone, we can't even deal a single damage to the enemies and they eventually kill us. However, instead of being teleported back to the last area in a safe zone, we respawn further into the area in a town where we are now surrounded by high level enemies and a store that costs 100x more than the money we have.
At this point my party gave up. I could go into detail about the many glitches and game design flaws, but I feel the point is made. Things like abilities not activating unless you press the key multiple times, high level players being able to spawn enemies that instantly kill you in safe zones, but at the end of the day there is no point in wasting your time with this game. I was curious where all the positive reviews had come from, but when I found some other players I finally knew. All of the players I met talked in horrible spelling and it was clear the game was full of children who didn't know any better games to play. Overall, a massive thumbs down. This game doesn't even deserve a 40% positive rating, its one of the worst things I have played in a very long time.

HAIL TO THEE, FELLOW KEYBOARD BARBARIANS!
You know the routine all too well. You've been out in the caves all day, grinding away on scallywags and fiendmounds and mutant flying barfing testicles, and now you've returned to your grimy yet lovable village with a sack full of dosh. How to spend your hard-won scrilla this eve? On rusty tankards brimming with filmy ale? On the intoxicating fleshes of lords and ladies of the night? Or on SLAIN: BACK FROM HELL?
Well my mutually murderous head-banging brethren, without further ado, allow me to expound on this game's fine, dull, and downright blunt edges!
THE METAL
† Just look at those 16-bit gore-filled graphics! They're so true to the spirit of metal, you'll puke your guts out.
† Flaming sword! Giant ice axe! Regular sword! And mana blasts and totally angry electrified Venusaur vine blast (or whatever)! Yes, these weapons are metal indeed.
† Your long-haired protagonist dude lord is named Bathoryn—a totally boss reference to the most metal band ever in the history of the universe.
† Dying a lot can be funny—and vivid! After those wretchedly crisp graphics and backgrounds, Bathoryn's many death animations are some of the best and most hideously thoughtful design elements in SLAIN.
† Headbanging after popping a broadsword cap in a boss's demonhide is soooooooooo insanely satisfying—especially since this game is soooooooooo hellhoundishly difficult.
THE GOTH
† So let's talk about the difficulty, shall we? Other reviewers have said SLAIN hearkens back to the death-filled,  save-sparse NES days of yore. Not quite, my brosephs in arms. I'd say this game's difficulty spiritual successor is none other than Shinobi for PS2...but without all the crazy jumps and intensely plotted levels and enemy-filled screens that made you want to drop your ninja sword, don an empty KFC bucket and smash your worthless dome against the wall.
† *a heavy chug-a-chug-a-chugging can be heard in the distance* Is that the sound of some fresh hellbeast grinding its many cacophonous tendrils of doom across the landscape? Nah, that's just some guy who used to be in a respected metal band turning 30 seconds of banal metal chords into a "soundtrack." But hey, at least it sounds heavy, because that'll totally persuade you to keep grinding when all that gnarly grinding gets to be too much of a grind!
† If SLAIN is really Metroidvania, then where are all the transformative power-ups? Where are the items that alter gameplay mechanics? Where's the dank mystery? And where in the bloody demon fetus is the heavy metal Mother Brain?!? (Trick question, my fellow murderous space bounty hunters! Mother Brain in Super Metroid is already more metal than Burzum.)
THE EMO
† More hole-riddled than an old corpse, more clunky than a wicker man come to life, and more rank with the stench of stereotypical ye olde-y overwrought pseudo Middle English, lo, 'tis the ungainly writing of SLAIN! Wooothebadman suggested the uncredited writers probably wrote this tripe on a cell phone, and the only way I could show my agreement more is by cutting off my arm and beating myself to death with it—such is my conviction of the truth of this statement! Verily, never in all my thousands of years have I read a statement more shot through with the skull-splitting knell of truth, O my amigos of annihilation! Not only are the plot and dialogue completely uninspired and unnecessary, they're also atrociously edited and inconsistent in their language—sometimes we get Middle English-style words, sometimes we get modern English words, and by the folly of Darkthrone, sometimes we even get futuristic English in the form of abbreviations! Time travel is sooooo metal! *NOT!*
† Hey, you know what's really emo? Being so overburdened with ennui that you can't fully coordinate your body. SLAIN's controls are sluggish like a demon snail—Bathoryn always takes a second to respond. Or maybe he's is just really out of shape—he was dead after all, my flesh-splitting fiends. But if you die and your fleshbag is preserved by dark magick, do your muscles retain their original werepanther-smashing might? Or do they go slack? Inquiring necromancers want to know!
† Lastly but not leastly (and tremendously beastly), there's one element to SLAIN that defines its shortcomings: repetition. It's so metal, we must say it again: repetition. It's so true to the spirit of this game, we must say it once more, this time in a hut-crushing guttural growl that swells and swells to a timbre that thunderbolts the Skullthorn Mountains into rubble as it's joined by a Golgothic choir of the unholy chanting REPETITION REPETITION RE-PE-TI-TION until the blood curdles in our very veins and our eyeballs sprout teeth and gnaw off our skullcaps and free our brains to stretch their sore legs like a satanic froggy gone a-courtin' because DAYYYYYM, THESE LEVELS ARE ALL THE SAME!!! Oh look, another dreary stretch of platforms that were seemingly untouched by playtesters! Oh look, another small horde of pointlessly simplistic enemies to splatter joylessly! Oh look, another unbalanced miniboss that's more difficult than an actual boss! Oh look, another batch of thoughtlessly placed traps! Oh look, another chance to perform the SAME. THREE. ATTACKS. OVER. AND. OVER. AND OVER. AND. OVER. AND—
That's enough right there, my weary marauders!
TL;DR: Save your ducketts, save your keyboards, and save your mental muscles for a mightier, more worthy quest!

A positive review with caveats:
Basically, Remember Me is best played for its story, not its gameplay. A lot of the mechanics that are implemented are introduced in halfsteps, and really only the puzzle elements manage to shine. Combat doesn't have a lot of variety and can be hollow, but the mechanics have an easy, breazy kind of flow that can be pleasurable at times, with its weaving between enemies through a flurry of strikes and dodges. The platforming is essentially just go this way we tell you and there's a bit of a corridor effect at times. There can be some replayability in terms of collectibles, as well as an interactive story element that involves remixing memories, but really the memories still funnel you towards a goal and alternate endings to them are just what could happen as opposed to giving the player input in the story.
The story it tells, though well-trodden, is an emotional and personal one towards the main character, with some interesting developments near the end.  It's for these reasons that it has its merits and though the developers tried to make an innovative game, a lot of those efforts fall flat. But with all these things taken in mind, the game is enjoyable. Though it's not a revolution, the things it does aren't done badly, and at the end of the day, about 8-12 hours of fun can be had with this game. It's definitely worth a buy, but so long as it's on sale.

So many, so, so many flaws in this game. The difficulty curve is as bouncy as Commander Keen on coke and has some of its nastiest peaks very early on. Parts of how the game works are barely explained at all. The story is more concerned with how many different setting archetypes it can throw in a pot (is it steampunk? Cosmic horror? Science fiction? Arabian Nights?) than with making sense. The huge UI obscures far too much of the screen when you're playing. I had to edit a config file to get the mouse sensitivity to a level where it feels good in gameplay, and at that level menus are barely usable because the cursor jumps around dozens of pixels from the slightest bump. Etc, etc..
But none of that matters when, once you get into the game, it's just *that* satisfying to whack things with heavy weapons. Hits *connect*. Bits of armor go flying off, a good hit might detach an enemy's weapon, and over time in a long fight what's left of the devastated landscape gets covered with refuse. It's a beautiful game, too, with stylish and well presented 2D art that will hopefully prove timeless.
Just, you know, it takes a little while to learn the game. And you might have to tune some settings, and even after tuning them, things will be a little bit weird and clunky. Yet so damn satisfying.

Check out the other negative reviews for some valid criticism which I basically share. I'd like to highlight two things that bugged me about it.
First, the typesetting. For a game as text-heavy as this, more care should have been taken to make the text look good and readable. Instead, we get a hotch-potch of fonts and styles, for instance in the dialog boxes (emphases sometimes done in bold, sometimes italics etc), the character spacing is notably off quite often, and don't get me started about the memento preparation mini-game. I'm aware that this might be a limitation of the engine, but that's no excuse in my view. For a game that has great pixel graphics for the most part, the quality of the typesetting really stands out in contrast.
Second, the music. Yes, it's good, atmospheric, at times even original. But in some tracks, some instruments are painfully out of tune, as well as some parts of the voice in the ending song. It's probably been produced on a low budget, but it's still way too noticeable for me.
Other than that, it just didn't grip me as it apparently did a lot of other people. I found the storytelling, humor and background graphics enjoyable, but that's about it.

Part 2 of the DOOM prequal series that explains the nazi-killing origins of DOOM Marine.
A fantastic sequel to the first solid entry in the series. The shooting feels great, and the story flows at a perfect pace. The game reminds me a lot of how Half-Life 2 first felt back in the day, at least structurly. There is nothing comparable to the plot however, and if you thought the first game was over the top, this takes it to a whole new level.
Talking points:
Regarding complaints about the difficulty - This game is tough. I played on the normal difficulty and died a couple times through the game. If you're not a seasoned FPS player, definitely drop it down to the easier ones. The challenge is very rewarding though, and the only complaint I have is that you take damage without much notification, so your only warning you may be about to die in a firefight is BJ grunting. Keep an eye on your HP/armor, and you're fine.
Regarding the inconsistent themes - This game goes all over the place. From one moment you're being thrown into a shocking and horrific scene with characters you know, the next is campy pulp fiction material. Some people see this as wildly inconsistent, but I felt it all fit together (mostly, Anya's stuff is... strange) in a way that only Wolfenstein could.
Regarding the political themes - There are definitely jabs at current politics all throughout the game, especially in newspaper clippings and letters. A personal favorite is one man writing to another telling him to "look at that crazy buffoon in Germany. Have you seen that guy? He won't last more than a year with those tirades of his." While the general theme of killing Nazis is what Wolfenstein has always been about, it certainly has been more about the current american political crisis. If you're a sensitive alt-right snowflake and someone making media challenging your views is going to hurt you, best stay away. :^)

Anyone who bought this game a year ago for £60 has every right to be annoyed at the game they received.
Fast forward a year to the Atlas update and we are now closer than ever to the game that was promised.
The story arc provides a relaxed introduction to the various game systems but without entirely handholding. So far each planet I have visited feels and looks different enough to fuel the belief that the universe is as diverse as promised albeit the alien presence of bases and the ever present (and annoying) sentinel drones reduce the feeling of being the first person to visit. Fauna and creatures follow a pretty similar aesthetic but there is enough variety to maintain the diversity. Exploration rewards with units (in game currancy) and though not massively lucrative does encourage sightseeing. Different atmospheres lend further credibility to each planet and promote the need to seek various upgrades for your space suit. Weather effects are somewhat lacking at present.
Transition into space is seamless but I find the fixed FOV (first person no option for head movement) restrictive especially after games like Empyrion.
As such space combat feels clunky and space travel very 'on rails'. Similarly there seems to be very little in space to explore apart from repetitive asteroid fields and space stations. The cookie cutter design of the space stations wears thin quickly and I would like to see more variety here.
The game has a relaxed feel and is more akin to Subnautica rather than Elite or Empyrion. I genuinely enjoy space hopping around the planets and discovering new creatures. Mining is also very lucrative for earning units.
Overall MMS as it is now is a lovely game and with enough to do right now to easily justify the £15 I paid. Longevity is going to be its biggest hurdle for the future but hopefully they can find a way of making content infinite as well?

A Co-op mode is what lured me in to buy the game. The first few playthroughs were an absolute blast on a full 32 player PvE server but after 8 hours in total I had the feeling seeing it all. It becomes repetitive, tiresome and even boring. The magic of the game wears off quickly.
The reason is the enemy AI. Once you know how the enemy AI behaves you will experience the same battles over and over again. Besides that when you have a small amount of players in a server the battle will often turn out into a stalemate which essentially results into a tiresome grindfest which can take hours to complete.
The majority of your deaths is the result of enemy suicidal rushing tactics. You will rarely lose firefights by enemy tactics but often as a result of you being outnumbered and outrushed. They will rush you even if it means death for them. When they rush they do not use any suppressive fire at all.
Rushing in outnumbered with a jeep and jumping out when they park it in the midst of your army. Another example is when you are on top of a building and enemies keep climbing up the ladder while I just popped 6 of them at the top end who were doing the same. The enemy does not react to your suppressive fire at all so there is no need using it.
You will frequently encounter the situation where you run into an enemy squad in the middle of nowhere while doing a large flanking manouvre. It is like they are being dropped on the battlefield just outside your view. The game has great potential in PvP mode which is unfortunately dead. After 15 hours of total playtime I have absolutely no desire to come back for more due to its repetitive/predictable nature.

Spooky´s House of Jumpscares (I refuse to call it "Spooky´s Jump Scare Mansion") Is one of the best indie horror games
I´ve ever played.
The game starts pretty innocent, and I thought it would be your typical walking simulator with little "boo!" internet images to try and scare you along the way. That´s what the developers want you to believe.
I was so wrong.
There´s such a cool variety of worlds, and the monsters are pretty original and differ from each other a lot. Pretty original because, just like the levels, you can clearly appreciate where the inspiration came from.
It only took me about 3 hours to finish the game, but these were some of the best 3 hours I´ve ever spent on an indie horror game like this.
The formula is pretty simple. You´re tasked with the objective of going from room to room, until eventually crossing all 1000 of them. Most of the time, not only in the beginning but during the whole game, you walk through rooms that have nothing of interest. Maybe a chair or a couple paintings, but that´s it. This, accompanied with your creepy music and your ocasional carboard cutout jumpscares, really builds up the tension of wether the next room will be normal or a COMPLETELY different experience. Hell, there´s even little game rooms with arcade games in them, and you also get save points every 50 rooms or more depending on how advanced you are in the game.
I don´t want to describe the monsters or the worlds inside the game, ´cause I want you to experience it all for yourself. Make sure you don´t spoil yourself anything.
I don´t really find the game to be that replayable. In my opinion this game is a one time experience.
To end this review, I really enjoyed this game. I would recommend it to everyone that wants something that´s actually scary, as in "PARANOID AS HELL, ALWAYS CHECK YOUR BACK" scary. Really the only flaws I can find about the game are the lack of replayability and the duration for it, but overall, I guarantee you a really good time with the game.

I was in a weird position. I was actually about halfway done with the standard edition of the game when the Deathinitive came out, promising better game play and stuff. At first, word on the street was that you couldn't copy over your save file. So I said, it's probably better if I finish the original first. So here's what happened. I came across a crippling bug: I was unable to open a void walker portal towards the very end of the game. It was supposed to just open, but wasn't responding to me. I saw online that one other guy had this problem and in the end gave up on the game. I was afraid I'd have to do the same. I restarted the application, and it was stuck on the load screen. I was so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥because I couldn't finish this amazing game, due to a stupid bug. Eventually after the Kubler-Ross 5 stages of grief, I accepted it and realized this was probably the time to start playing the Deathinitive Edition. And that's when things got crazy.
I downloaded Deathinitive and saw that it had a save slot already for the exact location that I was in in the Standard Edition when the bug hit. I loaded it and it worked! I was able to finish the game I started on the Standard Edition and am now current in New Game+ in the Deathinitive. Overall, the graphics so-called improved graphics in this edition are not all that impressive. In most cases I don't notice a visual difference. However, my PC goes into maximum overdrive like I'm playing Arkham Knight on the highest settings and becomes very loud. I don't think the graphics justify the extra heat.
So bottom line: This is a really great game and I hope everyone can enjoy the Darksiders franchise. I am really excited about the possibility of a DS3!

Hammerfight is a bit old, challenging but fantastically creative, deep and fun physic-based fighter.
Instead of controlling humans, you control a helicopter to what various deadly melee weapons are attached to, everything from simple rocks trough axes and hammers to swords. There are also guns, although they are difficult to aim and I never used them much. You control the helicopter in 2D space with the mouse alone, occassionally using either botton or the keyboard for shortcuts.
The good bits:
- very satisfying to smash things.
- Simulated physics on many things: there are sometimes destroyable walls, fire and enemies seem to hurt each other. You can knock enemies into each other.
- physics feels fairly intuitive and the game gives you hints.
- large weapon selection (even of plain old flails), plus extras like throwable weapons and armor to help vary gameplay.
- a singleplayer campaign with a story where you can make choices (either it affects the story or gameplay, like getting things).
- variety of gameplay in singleplayer mode. Sometimes you make desperate last stands, sometimes you play mini-challenges.
- extra modes (unlocked during story) that allow you to be in the arena, on a hunt or just allow you to buy things like weapons or extras.
- local multiplayer with multiple mice, althugh I have not tried this.
Cons:
- cannot increase resolution, you are stuck on one.
- bad GUI blocking parts of the screen, there are pictures of coins (of varying worths) rather than clear numbers (you have to go to a merchant to see how much money you have). It does not help that during fights the mandatory flags and such crap confuse your view of what's happening.
- minor bugs, sometimes you get stuck during a cinematic.
- problematic visual design: the art has an interesting, somewhat realistic look but can get confusing during battle. This may be deliberate, such as smoke and stuff obscuring vision (and this is with FX turned off!).
- enemy AI in one-on-one can be dissapointing (although I might have just become that good).
- game can be difficult. I consider myself somewhat of a veteran player and even I lose many games due to bad luck or momentarily losing track of what's going on. Enemies with explosives are a nightmare.
- you switch sides of blades (axes and swords) with the same botton you throw things, terrible idea.
- the game really needs an inside encylopedia, the story does not always establish context well and throws a lot of fantastic terms around that you have no idea what they mean. Sometimes it makes the story difficult to follow.
If you are looking for a action-heavy, challenging and fun physics game I heavily reccomend this game.
That said, this is a game that could really benefit from a HD remake, with some cleanup on design, better view of what's going on, better GUI, some fine-tuning of several features, a few more modes (hammerball anybody?), etc.
A few suggestions for new players:
- try to keep your weapon in motion. Don't just make circles but try learn how to do balanced positions to allow you to strike with minimal wind-up, such as just balancing your weapon side-to-side.
- try to make attacks with an opposite spin on your weapon than your attacker's (if he is flinging it clockwise, fling yours counter-clockwise and vice versa).
- try to learn how to follow-up on attacks, such as attacking with one spin and continuing to attack that has an opposite spin.
- use your momentum and the enemy's to your advantage. You can make your enemy fly right into a well-controlled flail.
- many weapons, particularly bladed weapons, give the most damage when they just touch the enemy without sucking up your momentum.
- you can "cheat" a little by decreasing the set mouse resolution. Just don't do it too much and lose fine control.
- heavy flails are good starters, they damage both monsters and armored opponents. I find swords the most difficult, particularly against armored opponents.
- during a mission, you are given the choice to fight an adult sophit (the thing you had to fight without your lantern). Do so and you'll get a gem that heals you as you use the weapon you put it into, making those long arena sessions survivable. Put it into a very good weapon, preferably something like a colossus or a relic sword.

It's simple, challenging fun with a lot more flavor than it needs.
Very highly recommend it, it's a cheap little gem in the rough.

Overall this is well worth the play.
On the positive side, the graphics are gorgeous - excellent thought and effort put into making a dystopic Paris.  I especially appreciated the attention given to colors in the game and the use of the black & white motif.  The fight sequences are worthwhile, simple combos easily executed - though as others have said, after a while it does get a bit monotonous.  The premise of the game (a tyranny based on the collection & sale of memories) and the story execution is pretty good.  Throughout the game there are some nice touches here and there worth noticing; I would have liked to see more.  The first play through is a good bit of sci-fi action.
On the negative side, the game does get a bit dull after the first playthrough so hunting down achievements is a bit of a grind (if you are into that sort of thing).  The cut scenes, although beautifully rendered, cannot be skipped - so you have to watch every one of them again and again.  Finally, I have a problem with any game that uses the autosave feature as does this one.  It prevents a player from screwing up their game and saving right before they get clobbered or right after they've screwed up some crucial element of the story, true, but it also prevents the freedom to stop / start the game when the player wishes or to pick up at a specific point in the game rather than at the beginning of a save sequence.  Consequently, if you miss a certain achievement or you want to play only one section of the game (say the memory mixes) you cannot so do but have to play the entire boring chapter over again.  Nuts to that!!!
Everything taken into account, though, I'd rate this game as worth a try.

Assassin's Creed could easily have been one of the best games of 2007. It is, without question, impressive on several fronts. But developer Ubisoft Montreal took some missteps along the way and squandered the immense potential of its pseudo-stealth action title. A bad story, repetitive gameplay elements, and poor AI lead to the downfall of one of the more promising games in recent memory. Assassin's Creed could have been one of the great games of this generation. Instead, it turned into just another action title.

The original Assassin's creed is a blast to play even to this day. Now don't get me wrong, this is far from the best game ever made, it certainly suffers from certain problems, but let's not go too fast ok?
Let's start with the few bad things I found about this game:
-The game is, like you may have heard already, really repetitive. I won't spoil the story, but throughout the game you'll be doing the same things over and over again.
-The combat: I thought the combat was a bit too slow. The best and quickest strategy is to just wait for the guards to attack you so you can either throw them to the ground or execute them immediatly. Otherwise you'll be blocked most of the time, especially in the late game.
The 'Meh' things in the game:
-/+The free-running is just okay. As expected with the first game in the series, it's far from flawless and rather slow. Whereas other Assassins (except for maybe Ezio) will climb up buildings and what not with monkey-like speed and skill, Altaïr will only just carefully climb whatever is possible to grab.
-/+The atmoshpere of the cities is somewhat lackluster. People will respond to you and your actions, but after a few hours you will have heard all the lines the people have to offer. Same with the guards and the people who are yelling speeches on the markets (I can almost quote the entire text about 'The English King and his army of infidels')
-/+The main cities you will visit are much the same. Acre is the only one that's somewhat different in style and peopel that walk around because it's ruled by the Crusaders, but Jerusalem and Damas are bassically the same.
And now, the things I really enjoyed:
+ The stories of both Desmond and Altaïr are very enjoyable. Desmond's story is not as complicated (and downright awful) as it is right now and it wasn't boring at all. Altaïr is also an enjoyable character. Not very deep or anything, but good enough. Which brings me to my next point:
+This is probably the only Assassin's Creed where you actually need to follow certain rules. You HAVE to follow the creed, it plays a large role in this game (a role I hope to see return in Origins). Not only are you not allowed to kill civilians (part of the creed), your behaviour will also be monitored by the guards. So if they see you climbing a wall, they'll most likely pull a sword out of their♥♥♥♥♥♥and chase you because what you're doing is not allowed. It adds a sense of realisme to one of the most unrealistic game franchises ever made.
+The setting. I LOVE medieval times, especially the period of the crusades. I also like how all cities are divided in 'Rich-Middle-Poor' districts, which I find really fitting.
+You won't be beaten to death by appearences of famous people in this Assassin's creed. In fact, there is only ONE guy in here, who you'll only see once or twice in the entire game for less then 5 minutes.
+Your assassination targets are also somewhat interesting in how they always tell their motives when they're killed.  Every single target will also have a significant build-up through the missions you must complete in each memory segment.
+The missions, although repetitive, are still really fun and somewhat varied. I only found 2 or 3 missions that annoyed me because of either the controlls or how the mission was set up (I HATE the mission where you must kill archers without being seen. ♥♥♥♥ 'em)
I usually rate games by how much they irritate/bored me at certain points. I'm happy to tell you that I never really got bored of the game and I only got frustrated a couple of times in the 15 hours it took me to complete the game (with all missions cleared except for the flags around the cities).
In points, I give 'Assassin's Creed' a 7,5/10. It feels very different from the Assassin's Creed meta that started with the sequel and the good definitely outweighs the bad. I even enjoyed it more then I did AC2.

on it's own merits it could probably be seen as a fantastic game, but everything feels lacking except for the visuals.

nowhere near as enjoyable as a villain as deathshead was.
She feels like a holdover from the last game, maybe because they couldn't think of a better villain or didn't want to actually having fun with the concept of Nazis having won the war and having a Mecha life-support Hitler or something.
-the characters don't feel nearly... well they don't feel like people any more with a few exceptions.
Max Hass is probably the most likable one out of the entire bunch.
Even BJ himself, his depressive monologues really weigh on my patience; constantly going on about feeling death come closer, how he wishes he was as strong as another character... he feels like a deflated shadow of what he once was in the previous game.
While probably fitting thematically it doesn't go well with making the entire experience enjoyable as a game.
I never once thought to myself “these people are ones I would like to know in life”, or even in the context of the world in game I never thought “I would want to fight alongside these people”.

You cannot play this game as if it were DOOM or any other wolfenstien game for that matter, you probably want to play this game as if it was a rainbow six game.
You're far too squishy, even with a suit of power armor that makes you a supposed bad♥♥♥♥♥ it's like you never got off that wheelchair.
You are going to rely on cover and the lean mechanic to shoot these enemies if you get caught sneaking, you are going to die more often than not before you can say “sturmgewehr” if you go guns blazing after being detected and reinforcements are called in.

Anything from the old game is either gone or a weapon you can't store in your inventory.
Everything else is just a gun that you can upgrade with things that could've been made into a different more interesting gun, like that slower fire but more powerful shot for the SMG?

I want to like this game but I just can't, it feels like they took the previous game as a template and colored in the picture with “what if we did the nazi moon base again but it's a planet this time? People would love this”.
They tried to jump the shark that they jumped previously in the new order with a straight faced grimace instead of a “let's kill Nazis and have have fun every step of the way” smirk.

Why is this a video game?
The story is the main selling point of To the Moon. And it's pretty good if a bit cheesy at the end. My only real complaint would be the two controllable characters, Neil and Eva, who are way over the top for my taste.
So, where is the problem? I think this game would have been better without the tacked on gameplay elements. What does any of it add to the game? Why am I throwing pots at zombies with awkward controls? Why am I solving logic puzzles that, thematically, couldn't be farther removed from the story? Why am I collecting orbs by exploring when there is barely anything to explore? The walking speed is agonizingly slow, and I found myself constantly bumping into obstacles that don't look like obstacles. Just let me continue with the story! This is not fun to play.
Alternatively you could control this game with the mouse like a P&C adventure. But the mouse sensitivity is going through the roof because this game is running in 640x480 stretched to fullscreen. Which also means that, if you want to get the correct aspect ratio you will have to set your monitor manually to 4:3 mode. And even then you will get a blurry image that ruins the otherwise beautiful pixel art. The only other option is to hit Alt+Enter and play this in a tiny 640x480 window. I would have liked to play this in 1280x960 with crisp 2x2 pixels. But there is no real options menu, no resolution options, no scaling options, no filters, nothing. You can't even take normal screenshots because there is no Steam overlay. This is amateurish, even by 2011 standards.
My recommendation: Buy it on sale if you a curious about the story, or save yourself the hassle and watch a longplay.

I'm not entirely certain how to properly express how I feel about this game. Its been a constant companion since the day I found it, a source of comfort and frustation in equal measure.
I say frustation because without a shadow of a doubt, this is one of the most buggy and janky games I have ever played, filled with small and large annoyances and questionable design decisions that plague me even after I have become familiar with each and every eccentricity.
Yet the game is amazing, revolutionary. When you swing a sword, you must learn the character of the weapon to land a proper blow. When you make a critical hit, its because the blade slipped in between your enemy's plates. All of the mechanics and moves of combat emerge organically from the detailed physics model which can accurately react to the clashing of different materials, with different characteristics and shapes and produce a result that feels right on an instinctive level. Sharp blades get stuck in wood and slide off of metal. Maces drag you around and can knock the weapon from an enemy's hand if they strike at the right angle. The use of each weapon to the fullest extent is requires so much skill that entire other games could be made on the basis of each one. Bullets will ping off your armor and spark off your weapon.
The art and music is beautiful, the world is a steampunk middle-eastern environment that is unique and to me personally a great joy in the face of endless medival European environments. The story is equal parts impossible to follow, disjointed, full of strange unexplained terms, fascinating, atmospheric and moving.
I would give a great deal indeed to play another game that built upon these mechanics, but until that day comes I know that at least Hammerfight will always be to hand.

The combat in this game, which is the real reason to play it, is really fun, and I haven't seen other games like it . You use entirely the mouse to swing your weapons and deal damage. That said, the story was quite short, though you can redo and pick a few different routes, seems like... and it wouldn't be a problem if the arena afterwards were more fun and more fleshed out. I liked the idea of it, but not only is it lackluster but it's way too hard. Some enemies can throw bombs that hit you even from pretty darn far away, and it's really hard to do anything about it besides one stage. If it was just hard, that'd be one thing, but it feels a bit unfair.
I recommend it just for the first while of fun, at least on sale.

Great game, great concept, but has some really wonky problems that you have to be aware of.
Pros:
Immensly satisfying to do well in, the gameplay is very fun at the lowest leveel (nothing but a rock on a chain) and still very fun (but very different) at higher levels (armor, consumables, ranged and melee, fire aspect...)
Some very fun mechanics for battles, including the best ear ringing effect I have yet seen. Environments are partially destructable, and they used this to full effect (some campaign missions have you break through walls, faling debris can damage you...)
Amazing single player campaign- choice based, different experience for different choices (took me about 4 run throughs to explore the options).
Art style is a hit or miss- I personally liked steam punk arabic? or whatever this is, but i can very clearly see why many people wouldn't like it. See cons. The universe too is well developed, it actually had me interested in the world as well as the gameplay.
Cons:
some artistic decisions are very controversial, and there is no ability to disable them. Emoticons and text appears when you land solid hits, and you can't disable them. Coins fly around too.
Multiplayer is funky to get working. look to other reviews as to that- I didn't explore it much. (they have dual mouse support????)
---------------------------IMPORTANT----------------
Mouse sensitivity is roughly equivelent to difficulty level in this game!!
spend a LOT of time messing with the in game mouse sensitivity function!
you will have to find a sweet spot, where you ship doesn't feel unbearably slow, or you don't have to lift and reset your mouse.
however: the game can become boring and far too easy on other settings; the mouse sensitivity can straight up increase your speed and agility. In a game where inertia and dodging are key, this makes a HIUGE difference.
After reading a few of the negative reviews, I bet they had their sensitivity wrong, and never thought to change it.
----------------------------------------------------------
I recommend trying this game out, even if you just get the single player out of it, it will be worth it. If you can grab it on sale, even better.
remember to adjust the mouse sensitivty often, makes the game much more fun. Thanks for reading this far!

A Co-op mode is what lured me in to buy the game. The first few playthroughs were an absolute blast on a full 32 player PvE server but after 8 hours in total I had the feeling seeing it all. It becomes repetitive, tiresome and even boring. The magic of the game wears off quickly.
The reason is the enemy AI. Once you know how the enemy AI behaves you will experience the same battles over and over again. Besides that when you have a small amount of players in a server the battle will often turn out into a stalemate which essentially results into a tiresome grindfest which can take hours to complete.
The majority of your deaths is the result of enemy suicidal rushing tactics. You will rarely lose firefights by enemy tactics but often as a result of you being outnumbered and outrushed. They will rush you even if it means death for them. When they rush they do not use any suppressive fire at all.
Rushing in outnumbered with a jeep and jumping out when they park it in the midst of your army. Another example is when you are on top of a building and enemies keep climbing up the ladder while I just popped 6 of them at the top end who were doing the same. The enemy does not react to your suppressive fire at all so there is no need using it.
You will frequently encounter the situation where you run into an enemy squad in the middle of nowhere while doing a large flanking manouvre. It is like they are being dropped on the battlefield just outside your view. The game has great potential in PvP mode which is unfortunately dead. After 15 hours of total playtime I have absolutely no desire to come back for more due to its repetitive/predictable nature.

When the game first loads, you fly through the actual game map of the giant galaxy you start in. Each star has planets that are procedurally generated with different terrain, animals, vegetation and it’s really cool to see what the procgen cooks up.
You start with a crashed ship and no memory. It is up to repair it using only the resources around you. Finally blasting into space with no loading screen is really fun and never gets old. Throughout your explorations, you never know if you will land on an extreme planet and be hunted by robots, be blasted out of space, or find a paradise full of dinosaurs.
The art style and music in this game are both amazing.
The story and lore of this game are interesting and I am really into it. It is delivered in adventure game style text. This may be a turn off for some but it reads like a great sci-fi novel. I like this because of the nostalgic feel and greater depth that written word provides. Know what you are getting into though.
As you aim to upgrade your weapon, ship, and suit there are times where you could fall into a pattern. Few upgrades are required to enjoy the game but if you are obsessed with upgrading everything NOW you could feel a grind. There are different ways to gain money, blueprints, and better ships so you can mix it up and have fun.
For now, I think the game would be more enjoyed by the chill explorer rather than someone looking for a fps slaughter, though the space battles and combat can get crazy. It is definitely not primarily a space shoot 'em up. I have not played survival mode (hard mode) yet and I hear that can get really intense though. I wouldn't recommend this game for young kids as there is mining and inventory management that is typical of a survival game (gets easier with upgrades), and the text that they may be too young to appreciate.
Importantly, this game is being updated consistently by the devs. The love they have for the game is clear. Check out some of their GDC lectures on Youtube to see what I mean. The latest update was huge and has been really fun. The initial release was controversial but the game is now really solid.
I am around 70 hours in now and still feel like there is so much more to discover. The community is great and has even grouped together at the galactic hub in game. I really think this a very special, stand out game. If it sounds like your type of thing, I do recommend it. Also check out the NMS subreddit if you need more research.
Edit: I finished the story that came with the last update. I never expected to care about the characters in a sandboxy game like this. I became invested in the story and the ending impacts your game, although the journey is better than the goal, and leaves you to continue to explore the game afterwards. I can't wait to see what else they do with the game. There is huge potential here.

Unless I'm out of the loop, A Wolf in Autumn diverges away from Szymanski's Moon Sliver/Music Machine universe. If you've played those games, you know what you're in for with this game. Of his walking puzzle narratives, this is probably the prettiest looking one, particularly the opening stage set inside a forest.
Unlike the "Moon" saga, A Wolf in Autumn focuses strongly on metaphor. That's not to say the "Moon" saga didn't have metaphors in it - it does - but there is a distinct difference between what happens in the Moon saga and this game. I won't say anything more.
I still recommend this game, but of his walking puzzle narratives that cost money, this was probably my least favorite; I think it may have less to do with the story of this game and more to do with the fact that I want more of the "Moon" saga storyline. I absolutely love those two games (Moon Sliver; Music Man), and would always love Szymanski doing more stories that are connected to that world.
On its own merit, A Wolf in Autumn is a good $2 game and still gives food for thought. I think it is less complicated than the Moon saga, which may be a good start for gamers who would like to see a little more of what Szymanski is about if they liked Fingerbones.

Do I recommend it? It's hard to give a yes or no for this "game". It costs $1.99, and the best way to describe it would be a "slice of life" interactive psychological horror short story that lasts about an hour. I wouldn't say it has any redeeming social quality, nor does it  have anything particularly meaningful to say, but rather opens a brief window into a psychologiclaly disturbed woman's mind, played out through the experience
of her young daughter.
The writing is fairly pretentious, post-modernist stuff.
The puzzle mechanics and interface are clunky; you can hold one item at a time, and clicking on something else attempts to use the two items together; your hands must be free to use something you click on by itself. This can be somewhat irritating if you're holding something and try to open a door, as you try to use the object on the door.
The game is very easy, giving broad hints about what you need to do at every turn, and in many cases leaving multiple copies of the items you need to solve the next puzzle strewn about. The art style does the job without being exceptional, giving a surreal experience at game start with a blown-out high contrast pallette, devolving into creepy brown and green later.
I would not recommend this to anyone looking for a game. If you're into the slightly creepy walking simulator sort of experience and have $1.99 to spare, sure, go for it. I'm giving it a thumbs-up for delivering on what it promises.

I agonised over whether to recommend this game or not, and having completed it I've finally decided, on balance, that it's worth your time.
A classic case of ambition exceeding ability. This game has some incredibly forward-thinking ideas about gameplay, story and how to integrate the two. The combat takes a bit of getting used to, but once you get the hang of it it's challenging, deep and complex. Unfortunately, the platforming is merely competent but unremarkable, and sometimes impeded by awkward controls and camera angles - particularly unfortunate given that there is much more platforming in the game than combat. The "memory remix" sequences are an amazingly innovative gameplay concept: it's just a shame that they aren't explored further, instead serving as a sort of "mini-game" to break up the gameplay.
The story has a lot of interesting ideas about psychology, futurism, the relationship between the corporation and the state and other weighty themes, there's a lot of effort put into worldbuilding, and the family dynamic had the potential to be quite moving. Alas, the story is let down by some of the worst dialogue I've heard in a game intending to be taken seriously. The voice acting is mostly dreadful as well, aside from the actors who play Nilin, Scylla and Charles, who somehow manage to elevate the dreadful dialogue. The ending is a bit disappointing, but reasonably logical at least. The story is a little bit tonally uncertain as well, with some comic relief characters who seem rather out of place. As noted in other reviews I've seen, initially it looked like the game was going to address some of the ethical grey areas of its storyline and characters, but by the end it seemed to have largely abandoned that plot thread, which was a shame.
Aside from that, excellent visual aesthetic (I was particularly fond of the use of glitches and datamoshing, and the AR elements used to fill in backstory, even if the latter resulted in the screen getting a bit cluttered at times) and decent (occasionally excellent) soundtrack.
Well worth your time if you want to play a very inventive and imaginative sci-fi game: just be prepared for the execution lacking somewhat. I hope they release a sequel to address these flaws.

was revolutionary when it was first released over a decade ago. To date very few games can hold their own as well, with a solid plot and graphics to rival many modern titles.

In short Assassin's Creed has:
+ A brilliant storyline (into the protagonists' ancestors past)
+ Very detailed environment to explore (within cities)
+ Complex combos leading to satisfying combat results
+ Spectacular and very fluid movement across rooftops
+ Diverse sounds and voice-overs (mix of English, French, Turkish etc)
+ Each assassination assignment is unique
+ When Ubisoft was still decent (no external login hassles)

- A handful of repeatable mini-games/races across rooftops (boring after a single try)

- The ending can accurately be described with the emoji "meh"!
- No steam achievements or trade-cards
-----
TL;DR: Assassin's Creed still holds its own quite well to-date, even though later iterations have improved the game considerably. With an intriguing and original storyline, fluid combat, exciting rooftop chases (influenced by the Prince of Persia classics) and a lot of assassinations, it is a gem worthy of a place in everyone's library. Highly recommended!

Having recently decided to play through the series again, I thought it high time to review each game as I go in what is one of my favourite game series ever. This is what I think of Assassin's Creed.
The game still looks decent for a game released way back in 2007, albeit showing its age in a number of areas. The cities themselves are wonderfully crafted and is a joy exploring on the ground or on high across the rooftops with the series' famous parkour free-running. The present day story, often dismissed as an unnecessary distraction, is in my opinion the driving force for the series. I liked the main character, Desmond Miles, as he is forced by the evil Abstergo corporation to use the Animus to relive the memories of his ancestor centuries ago. That ancestor is Altair, an Assassin operating in the Holy Land at the height of the Third Crusade. Altair starts the game as an unlikable arrogant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bag but grows into a compassionate man as the game goes on. This premise involving the Animus back when it released was something truly unique, and I remember being enamored with the game. However, the ten years since then have not been kind to it.
This game is repetitive. I said it. The Assassin's Creed series is infamous for its use of collectables and filler content to compliment its story so this might not sound so strange but unfortunately it is in the story and main missions that it suffers this. The story consists of hunting down and assassinating nine targets to regain your lost status from the beginning of Altiar's story. Each assassination consists of going to each city, one of Jerusalem, Damascus or Acre, speaking to the bureau leader and doing the same three or four activities to learn about the target and assassinate them. It sadly doesn't cut it in 2017.
Towards the end of my run of the game, I found myself rushing to finish it. What was once a favourite of mine was now a chore to complete. This might sound like I don't recommend this game but I still do. The things you can do, the movement, the gear and the variety of missions is very limited compared to its sequel and beyond but the set up of the story for future titles and introduction to the series is worth at least a playthrough to experience it for yourself. At around 10 hours, it's the shortest game in the series. Perhaps that's a good thing.
And remember...nothing is true; everything is permitted.

Is this game a joke?
When you hitting repeatedly the attack button and then hit the jump button, what do you expect? Hm? Nothing? Correct! Because this is what happens: nothing!
When you hit the attack button twice or ten times in the air, what do you expect? Correct! Only one single hit! One SINGLE hit! Because... why?
When you come down, after a jump, you can't attack for a second or so! Again... why?
Do you know the situation, where you want to jump from the edge of a cliff, but instead fall off? Yes, this is the kind of game.
In this game it's all about timing, as if you going to win a fighting beauty contest or something.
The same type of enemy can have different attack timings. You think you can hit it twice, but... nope, this one shoots earlier.
Until you learn all the patterns and all the tricks, you repeatedly play the same passage over and over again. When you finaly manage to pass it, you don't have the feeling you did it with you SKILL, but because you just KNOW all the movements of your enemy. You basically predict the future, which is absolutly unsatisfying.
If you step in blood, you die. Because... why??? Or is it lava...?
PS: Oh, yes the soundtrack: it's a short tune playing over and over. I wouldn't call it a track. Or was it because I died so many times and had to listen to the same short part repeatedly? Anyway I switched it off. Then you hear some ambient sound, like wind, which is good and atmospheric (not like the music!).

Great game, great concept, but has some really wonky problems that you have to be aware of.
Pros:
Immensly satisfying to do well in, the gameplay is very fun at the lowest leveel (nothing but a rock on a chain) and still very fun (but very different) at higher levels (armor, consumables, ranged and melee, fire aspect...)
Some very fun mechanics for battles, including the best ear ringing effect I have yet seen. Environments are partially destructable, and they used this to full effect (some campaign missions have you break through walls, faling debris can damage you...)
Amazing single player campaign- choice based, different experience for different choices (took me about 4 run throughs to explore the options).
Art style is a hit or miss- I personally liked steam punk arabic? or whatever this is, but i can very clearly see why many people wouldn't like it. See cons. The universe too is well developed, it actually had me interested in the world as well as the gameplay.
Cons:
some artistic decisions are very controversial, and there is no ability to disable them. Emoticons and text appears when you land solid hits, and you can't disable them. Coins fly around too.
Multiplayer is funky to get working. look to other reviews as to that- I didn't explore it much. (they have dual mouse support????)
---------------------------IMPORTANT----------------
Mouse sensitivity is roughly equivelent to difficulty level in this game!!
spend a LOT of time messing with the in game mouse sensitivity function!
you will have to find a sweet spot, where you ship doesn't feel unbearably slow, or you don't have to lift and reset your mouse.
however: the game can become boring and far too easy on other settings; the mouse sensitivity can straight up increase your speed and agility. In a game where inertia and dodging are key, this makes a HIUGE difference.
After reading a few of the negative reviews, I bet they had their sensitivity wrong, and never thought to change it.
----------------------------------------------------------
I recommend trying this game out, even if you just get the single player out of it, it will be worth it. If you can grab it on sale, even better.
remember to adjust the mouse sensitivty often, makes the game much more fun. Thanks for reading this far!

This is one of the best physics-based action fighting game that I've ever played. To make things easier, I'll list out the pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
-Cheap and reasonable price.
-Small size. Only takes a minute or two to download the whole game.
-Great, smooth yet chaotic physics-based gameplay. So far, I haven't encountered any glitches, and the physics of the game is overall pretty smooth. You can definitely feel the weight of the weapons as you're swinging them around and crashing them into your enemies, let alone when a bunch of other machines are doing the same thing.
-Grim mode is awesome. It's essentially a casual mode where you fight flying worms, giant bees and a bunch of other random demonic creatures from hell. Mass-killing a ton of monsters by swinging around gigantic axes or maces is very stress-releasing, too.
-Decent storyline. Not much to say, I'm just kinda glad the game at least has some story to it.
-Can't really explain it, but there's just something very satisfying about swinging a flail at full momentum and hurling it towards a machine/ monster, hearing that majestic crushing sound and watching the guts/random metal parts and coins raining down upon the glorious battlefield.
-There's a multiplayer feature too, if you have a bunch of other mice that you can connect to your PC.
Cons:
-You need a large mousepad that is glued to your table in order to comfortable play this game. Otherwise, expect the mousepad to constantly move around.
-The gameplay is too chaotic for co-op missions since in a game where you're mostly ramming yourself towards the nearest guy on the battlefield, friendly fire is near unavoidable. This is especially problematic in Grim mode, since the other hunters can unexpectedly and suddenly ram into you. In most of these missions, 50% of the damage you take comes from your allies.
-Explosives are very uncontrollable, especially when a bunch of people are using them at the same time. Again, this is an even bigger problem when even your allies are using explosives.

This forces you to play smart and your playing really impacts the game.
Unfortunately, it kinda stops being so fun after about 2 campaigns, because nothing (xp and rp) carries over between games and once you get past 10,000 xp there's no incentive to level up really, because you unlock everything (I made it past 50,000 in a single campaign, so there's a lot of room for upgrades). After a while you just get bored and end up cheating yourself some rp and carpet bombing the map. Also a lot of the maps have quite a bit of blank space that really should be filled.
This isn't really that bad though, because you can just come back in a month or two after the boredom has worn off and do it all over again. Also the devs are still updating it, so there's usually some new stuff to play around with.

No Man's Sky is simultaneously a great example of how not to market your game, and how through hard work and dedication the developers can turn around public perception among those who own it. It's the game that should have been at release. But that's not to say it's complete yet.
Better inventory UI. Why can't I sort my items, or move around my technologies?
The ability to transfer exocraft items to your exosuit. It doesn't make sense that I can transfer items to my ship on the other side of the planet yet I can't make immediate use of items that's literally inside the vehicle I'm driving.
Trading Posts should provide shelter from hazardous elements.
Actual orbiting planets and a star you can travel to instead of it being separated by infinite distance.
For the love of Atlas, please include lush planets that don't have hostile sentinels for those of us in Survival or Permadeath mode so we can build bases there in peace. Or at the very least add a progression system where you can gradually eliminate the population of sentinels on a given planet.
Multiplayer interaction with other players is currently limited to seeing an orb at their xyz position and voice chat. While Hello Games is headed in the right direction, I'd like to see them expand this feature to see actual player models and to make environment changes viewable by other players. Hopefully this will also mean pausing the game won't freeze the environment around you, which means you'll be able to tab out while growing your farms.
Space battles (and events leading up to it) could use a bit more variety. It gets repetitive seeing the same type of transmission warning you to pay up or engage in combat. I'd like to see a branching story mode involving a space campaign fighting for the system authorities. Also, please disable friendly fire when coming to a freighter's aid.
Better creature/fauna AI. I'd also like to be able to do more with them than feeding them, such as have them aid me in combat or take them with me to a habitable room in my base. Maybe even sell them on a black market for a high price (and risk losing standing with the system's faction).
I'd like to see more variety among space stations. They all look pretty much the same. Also would like different things to do in space stations depending on the system economy. A destitute space station should be near vacant, while a prosperous one could have a boisterous marketplace filled with walking NPCs.
The ability to rename systems/planets/flora/fauna/etc. For a price.
Adjustable ship POV, maybe also allow third person view.
Despite the complaints I have about the game, I've had countless hours of enjoyment exploring unknown worlds and absorbing the lore of the recently revampled story missions. I bought it for $23 on sale, and I'd say it's definitely worth that price for the amount of time I've played. For $60 it's a bit of a hard sell, but if a casual space exploration game is your type of genre then I say go for it in lieu of its flaws. I'm giving this game a "pretty great, but not done yet" and leaving a positive review in the hopes that it encourages Hello Games to continue their appreciated work to address the concerns of the community.

I am normally hesitant to deal with games that handle such harsh topics as A Wolf in Autumn does, for two reasons: either they are too psychologically painful for me to handle (I'm kind of anxious) or they just... aren't a good example, or a considered portrayal, of mental illness, or the many real world topics that indie horror games often try to deal with. Even large studio-made games can fall victim to turning mental illness into fodder for a horror story, when the people living with such conditions know far too well: their lives are no ugly plot twist.
A Wolf in Autumn is, gladly, neither inconsiderate nor badly written. It forms a complex portrayal of all the characters within, however gruesome their actions; the game tries it's hardest to paint a picture of them -their pain and fear and the things their experiences drive them to. At the same time, it is not apologist and does not try to excuse the characters actions to the audience in the process of explaining their motivations. It deals with incredibly harsh topics such as
bluntly; with care where needed, but also making no attempts to hide the gruesome horror of the situation the game's child protagonist is experiencing.

Game Review: ★★★ (3/5 Stars)
A Wolf in Autumn is a remarkably surprising game. You play a nine year old who finds herself locked inside a shed in a fenced area in the middle of the forest. As you manage to break out of the wooden shack that is your prison, you receive a message from your mother, warning you about the dangers of moving about. It is now your choice whether to listen or to continue exploring.
Upon choosing the latter, we find ourselves in a short but deed storyline unlike any other captivity story that I have previously encountered. Nothing turns out to be quite the way I expected it to and I assume it would be the same for most anyone who plays this. Having played Fingerbones first there is a resemblance between the two games - obviously since they're both made by the same creator.
The graphics are quite nice, and a little odd with unusual color combinations on every-day items. The atmosphere is therefore unique, sometimes relaxing and sometimes creepy. The riddles are a bit weird for me personally but I liked having some trouble passing through the game - it kind of added to that feeling of helplessness and confusion one has the impression the girl must have felt.
Altogether a very nice indie game, although sometimes a bit annoying with systems like for example only being able to pick up a single item at a time and not being able to interact with anything while carrying it.
