Please note that I played Darksiders 2 in it's entirely when it came out on Xbox 360, the time I spent with this version was meant for me to get a look at the remastering job.
Darksiders 2 Deathfinitive Edition is perhaps the best or maybe the worst subtitle to ever grace a video game. Nordic Games, who purchased the IP from the now defunct THQ, may have chose this name ironically, making fun of the plethora of remasters that have graced this generation, or maybe they actually thought it was a good name making this more of a tragedy than a comedy. I’ll be honest, what you’ll get out of the Deathfinitive is largely dependent on whether or not you’ve played Darksiders 2 before. The remastering job done by Gunfire Games is commendable, however, they touched up a game that arguably didn’t need touching up. The great setting, over-the-top story, and intuitive combat are still present however, and if this is your first experience playing Darksiders 2 this is currently the best version to pick up.
Darksiders 2 has a distinct visual aesthetic that is the result of the original developers, Vigil Games, hiring a comic book artist as the art director. This produced a larger-than-life dark fantasy theme that gives the characters, world, and combat a very unique look. Because of the stylized graphics Darksiders and Darksiders 2 have aged very well; if the art style had been more realistic and grounded this could be a different story, however, the remaster job here almost goes to waste as a result. I have to be honest, I had to do a direct comparison in order to see a difference between the two. While the lighting has certainly been enhanced and textures are sharper, the overall aesthetic of the game is still exactly the same, enhanced by the visual upgrade, but by no means creating a new experience. In short, the Xbox 360 and Playstation 3 versions of this game still looks fantastic and getting the Deathfinitive Edition for just the graphical upgrade may not be the best idea.
But maybe you haven’t played Darksiders 2 and you are looking to give it shot? That’s great because, in my opinion, this one of the best original franchises to come out of last generation and Darksiders 2 is the better of the two games. The series is famous for its derivative nature, taking elements from other franchises then combining them and twisting them into something unique and often time successful. The combat is typical combo-driven hack and slash fare similar to God of War or Devil May Cry. You do upgrade your abilities through an RPG mechanic that has you putting points into either offensive or defensive abilities depending on your play style. There is also a loot system that feels half-baked and unnecessary; it really just becomes a game of making sure you have the best armor or weapons equipped rather than strategically picking the right item for the right situation and it’s probably the only real issue I have with the game. The previous game had you focusing more on upgrading existing equipment rather than constantly picking up new items that drop from fallen enemies and chests. The world is structured similarly to a Legend of Zelda game where you have a large hub world with smaller dungeon areas branching off from it. In order access new areas you must acquire new gear and it always feels like you are progressing. All in all the gameplay loop is satisfying and keeps you entertained for the 20 or so hours it takes to complete the game. Combine that with a fairly standard yet entertaining dark fantasy story, memorable and well voiced characters, and an appropriately epic soundtrack and you have the making of a terrifically entertaining experience that is well worth your time.
It is difficult to review a remaster especially one for a game that only came out 3 years ago. The work that went into remastering this game is commendable, but ultimately wasted when you directly compare it to the previous versions. And while it is nice to get a Darksiders game on the current gen consoles, the experience feels some what incomplete without the first game. You won’t be totally lost diving into Darksiders 2 first, but there are references made to characters and events that may make newcomers wonder what they missed by not first playing the original. And there is almost nothing here for seasoned fans of the series. Nordic Games has been honest stating that they are releasing this game to gauge interest in a sequel, but I wish they had done more to entice the old audience to re-purchase the game. Including the first game or making a worthy collector’s edition would have gone a long way, but as it stands Darksiders 2 Deathfinitive Edition is a bare-minimum effort that really only makes sense for newcomers or the most die-hard fans looking to support the franchise in anyway possible. All in all Darksiders 2 is a fantastic game on its own and this version does nothing to diminish what I believe to be one of last generation’s hidden gems.

I seriously regret telling my local RPS club I would look into this software (I scoff at the thought this could "teach" an aspiring athlete). Simply, the core gameplay is plagued, one could not count the issues. Yes, even with the extra fingers of a siamese twin.
Most notable is this shovelware's lazy reliance on RNG, not unlike many lowly RPS sims. If the devs stopped there it could pass as a free (albeit ugly) timewaster, but ASSwHOLEtone GAYmes decide to trash a classic with some "modern" additions. I simply cannot fathom why they decided on ommiting a "classic" mode without the "Streaks", "Score" or Health Bars.
Much has already been said about this title's aesthetic. I personally like the look (I'm no graphic design designer by any means). I even thought the song was catchy. However, not one RPS enthusiast I showed this to could hold in any vomit.
"Rock Paper Scissors '''''''Champion'''''''''" lacks, like a corpse without a coffin.
You will find no simple AI assessing moves, nor making a typical guess (Noob? Beat them at the start with paper).
In case you didn't know, pro players spend hours upon hours honing their knowledge of "tells". Nowhere in this game will you see anything of the sort. Hear me out plebs, this is important:
Thumb positioning in the pre-game fist could be a giveaway for rock. (If my suggestions are taken onboard, keep this to the easy difficulty, anyone in a legit "championship" knows (some may even bluff/double bluff a new facewith it).
The animations could be given more frames, and hint to the moves early on, this allows a predictive counter, providing one can  move milliseconds late. The current control scheme is set out much too rigid for anything of the sort, which is a pity. I have seen many people bluff rock, only to snap out two scissorblades of fingers (a semi legal, but respectable technique).
"Rock Paper Scissors" is much more like a duel in a Western than this game's casual clicking.
You will find no depth or redeeming value here, what I have witnessed deserves a fetid 0/10
However, I will be analysing the game in the further weeks. Current scorn aside, this abomination could be quite purposeful in some sly "modern art", a topic to which I hold much enthusiasm. I can imagine it's context for satire of our society post Hilary Clinton's inauguration. Therefore, I will be scanning this game for twists, hidden messages, or alternate endings.
This review will be updated should the onion have more layers. Cutting deeper I just leak tears of dissapointment, but I want to prove or disprove any improvement. Maybe this is like the tasty fried onion in a hotdog. God forbid I bite this onion raw.
Adieu

On Saturday, I played the game To the moon.  A really good one! I cannot calm down until now. But how it can be so moved？
First, gameplay. It's no doubt that To the moon is good, but is it a good game or a good story? Many players have the same question like me. One obvious reason is that its gameplay is so simple (collect and puzzle) that it's more like an interactive novel rather than an RPG game. In another word, in the game, gameplay serves for narrative instead of the opposite. And this situation becomes a more complex question. As the video “Nintendo stated” provided in TGP，Nintendo believes game first (Gameplay first). They even ask writer to set story according to the certain gameplay. So, the question is what the standard of the good game is? At least, we cannot judge from the relationship of gameplay and narrative. In TGP, Prof. Ouellette stated that there are two types of game development, which one is Top Down, another one is Bottom Up. Obviously, To the moon is the former, which developed from story narrative to dynamics to mechanics.
Second, emotional experience. To the moon provide a unique and strong emotional experience. From the beginning, it has a mysterious atmosphere and a lonely feel. As the story developed, it looks like John bears unhappy marriage and takes care of River. And it’s confused why River crafted paper bunnies and what her illness is. There even some happy when I saw John and River riding. However, when Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts learned the truth, it becomes a deep emotion mixed with regret, sympathy and move. The reason “to the moon” and the yellow and blue paper bunny are thematic dissonances, which are powerful and successful. River is not a weird woman but a girl who loved John so deeply. What’s more, excellent soundtrack (such as main theme “To the Moon” or “Everything’s Alright” ) by Kan. R. Gao promotes this emotional experience.

I can't recommend RWR enough. So far, I've been plaing about 10 hours, singleplayer only. Think of it as Battlefield 2 from above. You start out as simple soldier of your chosen army (there are 3 factions, roughly representing USA, Russia and EU; with different weapons). You are on a large map (some of them are well known from the Battlefield series), the main objective is - like in Battlefield - capturing one area after another, until you control the whole map. The great thing is that your comrades (and there's plenty of them) will fight, regardless of what you do. You can take a jeep and drive around the map, you can go full Commando and try to capture an area in the enemy hinterland or you can go for a secondary objective that will randomly pop up (capture and bring back an enemy cargo truck, free prisoners, destroy an enemy radio tower and others).
With each kill you gain XP, which allow you to slowly level up and increase in rank. Every 1.000 XP one further soldier is assigned to you, so that you can form a powerful squad (you can, however, always decrease your squad size, down to the point that you're fighting alone - helpful for stealth missions). Also with increased rank you're able do buy and equip different weapons and equipment. You can pick up enemy weapons (bosses will drop rare weapons; these are not overpowered, you'll always be fine with your standard equipment). You can call in reinforcements, mortar and artillery strikes, vehicles and more to turn the tide of a battle.
When you die, which happens a lot, you respawn at a spawnpoint (open your map before respawning to selectanother one). You keep your money, rank and XP, but if you had a rare weapon or other precious loot, you'll have to hurry to your corpse and retrieve it. Combat is challenging - if you don't wear a vest, you'll be dead after one or two hits. Line of sight plays an important role, the terrain isn't flat. If you just try to rush into the enemy, you'll die; you have to make use of crouching and laying prone, cover, stealth and tactical squad manouvers in order to overcome an equal or superior enemy.
I haven't played multiplayer yet, but the SP alone would have been worth the price. I'll update the review when I'm further in the game.

A Wolf in Autumn follows the trend of David Szymanski's last two games (The Moon Sliver and The Music Machine) of dropping the player into a strange and slightly unnerving environment with little to no explanation for why they are there or what they should do about it. While leaning further into the use of color and shadows that set the mood so well in The Music Machine, this game also places a heavier emphasis on puzzles than his previous games which makes A Wolf in Autumn feel even less like a walking simulator than its predecessors. However, a total lack of explanation regarding the game's mechanics and simplistic controls can make for painfully obtuse puzzles, stalling the narrative instead of enhancing it. The traditional game mechanics could use some work, but the foreboding atmosphere and the thought provoking quality Szymanski is so adept at infusing his games with is present in full force here.
A second playthrough of this hour-long game is useful both for understanding the cryptic dialogue of the beginning in the context of the game's conclusion and also for catching all those things that might have been missed while stumbling around trying to understand how the game works. The experience is quite short and very little is ever revealed, leaving the player to guess at its full meaning. Whether that's because A Wolf in Autumn asks the player to really reach for their own understanding or it's just trying to hold onto its mystique by being vague, the ending left me shaking and eager to pour over what meager details were given for answers. So how ever it came about, the experience is potent and thus effective either way. And that's what matters.

An interesting, albeit short, horror game about neurosis (as far as I can tell)
While I’m sceptical about the use of text in the beginning, things soon get interesting, coming together a twisted fairy-tale about the main character’s (Autumn) personal issues with her mother.
There's a lot of symbolism going on. It's also a rare example of psychological horror that puts psychology first. Further, it's easy for us to appreciate as the player because the discordant sound effects creates an oppressive atmosphere to play match the characters' inner turmoil.
That’s arguably where the game stands out most. The gameplay parts are slightly more rudimentary (a lot of walking around and picking things up).
So yeah, I'd recommend it if you like experimental and bleak.

The modern take on the Wolfenstein series has always struck me as an odd one.  It seems to ferociously  push itself toward this hardcore run-and-gun action packed game with dual wielding and huge explosive weapons, but at the same time rewards you for crouching and sneaking around picking off enemies from the shadows.  Even the original game suffered in part from this identity crisis, but only in Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus does this form itself into an issue that is really a detriment to the game.
Between Wolfenstein 1 and 2 there was a little game called Doom that hit the market and said to the world “you don’t need to pay attention to the story, just blow things up,” and so we went ahead and did that.  We all forgot that Wolfenstein: The New Order and The Old Blood to a lesser degree showed us that there can be some story in there with all of our action and it’s at least worth checking out.  So when the time came for Machine Games to craft a true sequel, they had a choice to make.  Do they embrace this love of raw action and carnage that Doom all-but-perfected (and was still a strong element in Wolfenstein) or do they double down on what sucked so much of the joy out of The Old Blood and try to will the idea of stealth and story side-by-side with explosive action.   Well, it seems they chose the latter and ended up with a game that tells a really compelling story, but somehow lost even more of the fast paced gameplay that the original reignited in the modern AAA game arena.
BJ Blazkowicz returns to his role of Nazi massacre in a very mild way.  The entire first half of the game, for story reasons, has you hamstrung and limited in your ability to fight head on with any reliability.  Perhaps in an issue of inherent difficulty, you’re practically forced in to the slogging tedium of the stealth gameplay because any attempt at a frontal assault means you’ll most likely be put down in a handful of enemy shots.  It imprisons you in what, for me, was the least enjoyable type of gameplay from any of the games in this rebooted series.  When you have, from the onset, the ability to dual wield every weapon, you want to run out and lay down hot lead until nothing moves, but that’s something that is punished far more than it is rewarded.
The story, mostly told through cutscenes, ends up stealing the show.  It’s almost as if the gameplay itself was sacrificed to make the story more interesting and easier to feel invested in as you desperately try to ‘take America back’ from its complacent occupants.  The characters involved are developed more completely and the events they are wrapped up in are meaningful and give them a little more dimension.  While some of the plot points *definitely* require a suspension of disbelief, I can’t say I was at any point disappointed with the wild twists and turns that I got to experience.  It became even more frustrating that the game itself was so disappointing because the writing and voice acting throughout the narrative really raised the bar.
Queen lyrics aside, one of my biggest issues with Wolfenstein was crashing and bugs.  I actually stopped playing for a while and waited for a patch to see if it resolved anything, but even after some were released it would still get a fair number of crashes to desktop and lockups.   At one point the bugs and artifacts on the sky was so bad I could barely play.  Another time I crashed while trying to start a mission every single time until I restarted the game in safe mode.  Even playing more recently, I still locked up the entire game on a death and had to restart.   I don’t recall these issues with the previous game and I’m unsure why they are so prominent this time.  I can’t judge the game too harshly based on these issues since games usually get fixed after some time, but it is a very frustrating thing to see a AAA title suffer from such bothersome issues like this.
Along with this, it seems from a design and mechanical standpoint, the game lost some of the feeling of quality and the smooth player experience.  The option to dual wield weapons of different types put a very clunky set of steps in switching weapons – which can be quite important if you need to minimize time that you aren’t firing since it’s easy to die in the seconds that a reload takes. Even more frustrating are the designs of many maps.  Some ranging from that is the grey/brown equivalent of Fallout 3 to the repetitious labyrinthian underground bunkers of many mid 2000s forgettable shooters.   I don’t recall a single moment in The New Order that I was ever as lost as I was on the regular with The New Colossus.  There will be broken buildings that loop around with dead ends and blocked doorways that have a single small exit you have to find before moving forward.  Many levels seem to just arbitrarily slow you down so you can’t rush through what is actually relatively limited in scale and enemy saturation.   It actually seems as though the entire game is fully of speed bumps so that it can make it three times as long.  Side quests exists in the game to toss you back in to the same maps with minor changes (like time of day and some broken buildings) and the main content really doesn’t last all that long.
If there’s one piece of advice I hope I can offer Machine Games, it’s that I hope they can take a cue from id Software and move future Wolfenstein games in the direction of Doom.  Give players the option to be rewarded for being aggressive play just as much as they’re rewarded for stealth approaches.  The New Colossus shows that modern AAA games can still exists with unique and well-told stories, but also is a shining example of how important good QA testing and gameplay design can be to tear down something great.  If the game had managed even get on the same level as its predecessor, it would have been easy to recommend, but because it comes up short and adds in a heaping spoonful of functionality issues, I can’t say this game is worth buying now or any time in the near future.  Perhaps when it’s extremely cheap it would be worth checking out assuming it has become stable, but by then this review will be buried under hundreds of others and not as relevant as a more up-to-date perspective.

Just finished the game on "Call me Terror-Billy" Difficulty (Very Hard but not the Hardest), and I'm truely baffled by some of the negative reviews on here.
From start to finish, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is an EXCELLENT sequel to Wolfenstein : The New Order.
You've got the same great fast-paced, think-on-your-feet, skill-based shooter mechanics from the first game, along with several new abilities that really help to mix things up a bit.
On "Call me Terror-Billy" Difficulty, I died many many times, but I never felt cheated. Every time I died, I died because I messed up. The enemies all feel very fair and balanced, each with their strengths and weaknesses. Learning the quirks of each of the enemy units as you progress is satisfying, and helps you learn to mow down hoards of Nazis with greater and greater efficiency.
The storyline is fantastic. You've got all your old friends from the first game, plus many new friends. Both the interactive and non-interactive cutscenes were incredible. Voice acting is excellent, dialog is excellent. The whole time I felt like I was right there, hanging out and fighting alongside my pals.
Mick Gordon is back at it with another killer soundtrack that perfectly captivates the adrenealine rush of the combat sequences.
The game itself is linear in nature, but does allow the player to return to previously visited sites to pick up additional collectables and secrets. Level design for the most part is very good throughout. Great attention to detail in the environments, from all the little readable notes scattered throughout the game, to the cluttered, lived-in interior of Eva's Hammer. There are thousands upon thousands of little details. Cracks of humanity hidden amongst the grit, many of which will go unnoticed by the player, but together they combine to keep the immersive feeling of the game that much stronger.
All in all, I definitly felt that I got my money's worth on this one, and am looking forward to the future DLC and any potential sequels.

Assassin's Creed is a fascinating filler-fest that has very little to do with assassination.
Assassin's Creed presents itself in a dual narrative.  You are Desmond Miles; a New York bartender and kidnapping victim who awakens on the cold metallic slab of the Animus within the minimalist architecture of the Abstergo Corporation.  Taken against his will, Desmond is unceremoniously greeted by the abrasive Doctor Vidic and his assistant Lucy.  As a child, Desmond belonged to a small enclave of Assassins; a secretive brotherhood of trained from birth killers.  Although he ran away at the age of sixteen, Abstergo has tracked him down for research.  A breakthrough discovery by has revealed that DNA acts as a memory archive, and the Animus as been developed and built for the express purpose of being able to decode and read the ancestral memories of whoever is put into it.  Desmond's DNA holds a secret of great importance to Abstergo, and faced with either being thrown into a coma and his mind forcefully sifted through, or voluntarily reliving the life experiences of his ancestors to assist the research team; Desmond chooses the latter.  Thus his mind is thrust into the twelfth century boots of the Assassin Altair.  Belonging to the Assassin Brotherhood located in the Holy Lands, Altair is a skilled but arrogant killer working under the direction of Master Al Mualim in their battle against the Templar Order and any other men deemed "evil" during the Third Crusade.  Altair's conceit leads to instant failure, and he is stripped of all rank and equipment, save for a sword and assassin's blade.  Offered a chance at redemption, he must track and assassinate nine men of power and misdeed; each assigned by Al Mualim.  What follows is a genuinely philosophical tale.  Like all people, Altair's targets, powerful as they may be; are men.  They have hopes, dreams, doubts, and fears.  The Holy War ravages the land, and Altair is faced with a line dividing friend and foe that is either too blurred or too thin to make out.  Are his killings just?  Are they any less evil than the acts commited by the men he hunts?  Are lies meant to stop the war any worse than the illusions that started it?  Much of Assassin's Creed's story may not rest well with a person, depending on how religious they are, but for the rest of us; its an interesting look at the morality and sacrifices men uphold to build a better world.  And that's before you even figure in the crazier surprises the game will throw at you.
Assassin's Creed is a third person action game with a unique free-running mechanic.  Holding down the freerun button allows Altair to leap, climb, mantle, and dive in a ridiculous number of animations.  Buildings with the proper handholds are easily scaled and leaving the slower guards behind by leaping from rooftop to rooftop is a breeze.  Altair's actions are entirely automatic and based upon what you're running him towards, but aside from some occasions where the man does absolutely none of the things you want him to do, it works incredibly well for world navigation.  Climbing will eventually begin to feel like a chore though.  Furthermore, the trained from birth assassination prodigy can't swim, so stay well clear of deep water.  Altair can swing his weapons, block, throw knives, riposte enemy attacks, grab enemies to be shoved in any direction, and he can flee if necessary.  The combat itself is incredibly simple.  Altair's sword swings a little slower and does a little more damage while his dagger swings a little faster and does a little less.  The differences are negligible.  He can also make use of his hidden blade.  Usually intended for stealth kills from behind, sudden frontal attacks on unsuspecting foes, or drop attacks from above; the blade can be used as an instant killing riposte in combat.  However, the blade can't block.  This makes using it come at a price if you aren't spot on with your counters.  Even then, the combat presents little challenge.  The kill moves however, are instant, efficient, and brutal.
Each assassination runs the same way as the last.  You enter one of the Holy Land's three cities and begin scouring the city by climbing tall structures to get a handle on your surroundings.  Scanning the enviroment from these heights reveals investigation opportunities on your map.  Each contract has six opportunities but only three are necessary for Altair to get the green light on his kill.  None of the investigations are particularly engaging and they repeat the same hand full of missions again and again and again.  Repitition and filler are the name of the game.  Tall structures not only repeat the same few towers over and over, but the automatic climbing means you won't even get the satisfaction of being challenged to scale them.  The assassination attempts themselves are varied in theme and target, but all come down to getting in close and pressing the insta-kill button.  After that, it's a mad dash back to HQ as the city goes on alert.  Players must lose their pursuers and hide by either concealing themselves or blending with the crowd until the heat dies down.  The cities are connected by the winding valley of the Kingdom, a wide open spiderwebbing canyon filled with more towers to climb but not much else save for the next facet of repitition.  For the absolutely die-hard collectors, Assassin's Creed comes stocked with no less than four hundred twenty flags scattered across the realm as well as sixty Templars to kill, numerous towers to climb, and several dozen citizens to save from the hilariously tyrannical guards of each city.  Altair is a murder powerhouse and can't go five seconds without stabbing five men in the streets.  By the time you reach the target you intend to kill, you'll probalby be wading in blood.  All of these distractions are best ignored, and the gameplay experience is far more gratifying if you rail gun it down the main story path while avoiding distraction.  Each sucessful contract garners a new skill or piece of equipment, and you even get to see Altair's outfit change as he gains more and more abilities.
Here the game is a mixed bag.  From a visual design standpoint, the cities look incredible.  Entire metropolises loaded up on my PC in seven seconds and standing above them on some tall tower gives a great sense of scale.  Bustling crowds fill the streets and the environments are rich in detail.  On a macro scale, the cities are each unique and laid out in very hand-crafted ways, but up close you'll start to see a lot of familiar people, towers, buildings, and details.  They also fail to really differentiate themselves.  Although you'll visit the rich, middle, and poor districts of each realm; outside of color grading, they all just feel like another dusty twelfth century Arabic cityscape.  Animation is absolutley stellar.  It's not always perfect and sometimes things don't quite fit, but faces are highly expressive and filled with life.  Every single conversation in the game, big and small, has its own animation which lends an excellent sense of body language to characters.  And then there are the little things.  Cloth cuffs slide down upraised arms.  The shadows of clouds grind across the landscape.  Droplets of blood scatter from a newly whetted blade as it exits the opposite side of the man it was thrust into.  The game is chalk full of these things.  None of the music is anything I'd much care to listen to on its own, but it all blends perfectly to set the tone while in game as monks whisper and choirs sing.  For all the good it does, Assassin's Creed hits major technical pitfalls.  Entire populations will pop-in only a block away from you.  Shadows are so jagged that they might be used for assassination right up until you stand directly on top of them.  Only then do they smooth.  These things are unfortunate but not deal breaking.  Also great stabbing noises.

It was a good experience, I enjoyed the story layout (memory blocks visualised as DNA strands), the amount of detail put into every location (there are only 4 cities and some patches of open kingdom between them, but they're big enough that the game isn't boring), the combat (which starts off simple but gradually adds another modicum of complexity as you progress, which
make fighting easier since attracting a mob is suicide in earlygame but mandatory in lategame), and the organised assassination notes (to offer you a way to stealth assassinate targets without the city guards on your tail constantly - although you can brute force your way through as loudly as you want with the exact same overall outcome, if you can survive it).
It is a little flawed though:
Definitely worth a buy, and I get why it's regarded as a modern classic. Sales are coming soon too, so you can pick it up then for like £2.

The Annual Lazytown Spring Smash Potluck was tomorrow or so Robbie had been informed. It was something of an explanation to how Robbie had ended up here in his life, walking along with Sportacus with bags of groceries. He didn't understand it but it was an explanation.
To begin with, Sportacus was not particularly good at walking alongside someone while carrying groceries. Point of fact he wasn't particularly good at carrying groceries at all. In order to flippity flippity flop around town, he needed his hands free, and that left Robbie trailing along behind him, lugging cloth grocery bags loaded with supplies.
This is what Robbie's life had been reduced to; carrying someone else's groceries. Strike that, carrying someone else's groceries and listening to that person explain what they were going to do with them. Some sort of fruit salad, Robbie had gathered, not that he was about to ask.
"…of course you don't have to eat it, but maybe you could try it? I think you'll like it, maybe, and…"
Groceries. Sports candy. All in the bags, along with one small cake, delicately frosted in white and purple icing, for him alone. Although knowing the local brats Robbie was likely to be suckered into sharing at least some of it. That blond kid was particularly good at sorrowful, pleading eyes when it came to sweets.
Sportacus jogged back to him, still rambling on about what he was going to mangle his fruits into for the potluck and utterly unbothered that Robbie only grunted in reply. "…and I was thinking about making those little sandwiches, the kids like them last time…"
He'd never have done this before, Robbie thought sourly. He'd never even been to The Annual Lazytown Spring Smash Potluck; he'd always managed to sleep through the blasted thing. How was it Sportacus always managed to get him to do things like this?
Shopping for fruits and veg, no, get it right, shopping for sports candy, going along with Sportacus for potlucks, for crying out loud. Worse, they were going back to Robbie's bunker with all of it and Robbie wasn't even entirely sure why. Yes, yes, he had some kitchen space cleared out now, one section of his counter marked off with masking tape that meant none of his machine parts were allowed to enter the sterile area. And yes, he had somehow grown a collection of knifes and utensils and bowls; the blasted things seemed to have sprouted from nowhere and now they lived in the masking tape zone.
It still seemed like it would be easier to make whatever it was Sportacus was babbling about in his airship, but that would mean Robbie would have to climb up a ladder carrying bags and that was a level of no that couldn't be properly expressed in words.
At his bunker, Robbie set down the bags with a sigh, only half-listening to Sportacus yammering on about fruit salad and sandwiches and whatever else was flittering through his mind.
Why did he do these things for Sportacus, Robbie wondered idly. It made Sportacus happy, true, but…it made Sportacus happy. Something about that clicked in Robbie's head, like a faulty gear suddenly snapping back into place. It made him happy, it delighted him when Robbie did things with him. Shopping for his sports candy, going to the Annual Lazytown Spring Smash Potluck, tinkering around with small inventions in the park while half-watching Sportacus playing with the children. It made Sportacus happy and when he smiled at Robbie, it felt like…it felt…well. Sportacus being happy made Robbie happy.
Realization came with the force of a smack between the eyes. Sportacus was humming to himself, sorting through the bags and making neat piles out of the fruit and he was here in Robbie's bunker doing this because Robbie wanted him here.
"Sportacus, I think I'm in love with you," Robbie blurted and he couldn't have held the words back with both hands.
"Hmm? Oh, thank you. I love you, too," Sportacus said absently, studying the row of bundled vegetables and fruit as though he were planning out a schematic of health. Probably he was.
That...was not the right reaction. Robbie blinked at him, mouth agape, and then demanded, "Didn't you hear me? I said I love you."
Sportacus glanced at him, "Yes, of course I heard you. I said thank you, didn't I? And I love you, too."
Robbie stared. "But--"
"Don't tell me you're only just realizing this now. We've been going out for weeks." Sportacus turned to look fully at him, setting the loaf of organic stone-ground wheat bread aside.
Robbie straightened instantly, looking down his nose at Sportacus who had the audacity to look amused. "Of course not!" Robbie scoffed, "I just realized I hadn't said it out loud."
Sportacus's smile gentled. He rose up on his toes and pressed a light kiss to Robbie's mouth, hardly more than a peck. "Of course you have. I always hear I love you when you're speaking." He turned back to the splayed vegetation. "Now, do you want to help me slice these or did you have a project you wanted to work on?"
"I…" Robbie faltered. He did have a project he could be working on and he was making a new outfit for the potluck because there was no point in attending an event if you weren't prepared to dress for it. Sportacus was already peeling the bananas, slicing them into even chunks as if it didn't matter to him in the least what Robbie chose…and why would it. Apparently, he knew how everyone in the room felt before even they did.
"I can slice them." Robbie washed his hands before gingerly taking the little green carton of strawberries. His slices weren't as even as Sportacus and sometimes he got little pieces of the leaf in it but he managed the entire carton.
Sportacus smiled at him, soft and sweet, when Robbie handed over his uneven strawberry chunks and added them to the bowl. "Thank you, Robbie, these are perfect."
Not perfect, not at all, but Sportacus was still smiling, humming to himself, and he didn't so much as glance up when Robbie started slicing the grapes to add to the bowl. They were making fruit salad together and tomorrow they would be at the Annual Lazytown Spring Smash Potluck together and it would be everything that Robbie dreaded it would be. And everything he hoped it would be.
Maybe, just maybe, he could hear 'I love you' when Sportacus spoke, too.

If you're not sold on the setting of this game you probably won't enjoy it, but if you're a sci fi fan looking for a unique storyline with at times great-looking graphics and a great soundtrack with well-written dialog and can look aside from some repetitive combat and one-note character portrayals, you may want to give this a go.
The game's story is set in a futuristic, more Utopian than Dystopian world as you ascend from an early slum section to the opulence of the city Paris above. The game does an excellent job of depicting a futuristic, well-kept society tearing itself apart more behind closed doors via shady organizations than outright chaos in the streets as seen in other futuristic sci fi.
The gameplay itself consists of very light platforming sequences comparable to Enslaved, Prince of Persia, and Uncharted type depth with the next area to jump to often being highlighted by some variant of color if you look closely. Combat-wise Remember Me is very reminiscent of the Arkham titles (for better or for worse.) You have  punch/lightattack kick/heavyattack block and evade actions against throngs of enemies in hand-to-hand combat. What is there looks good. There is a combo system present which is more blab than anything all that rewarding or useful (as at least on hard mode I often just opted for the combos that gave the most healing back...) The main character has some cool-looking execution moves against a variety of enemies including mutants and security forces. The areas you explore while traversing the city are varied and have a neon sign / deserted metropolis vibe that is enjoyable.
If you want non-stop action this isn't the game for that, and its story you will likely either be very into or not, I don't think there's much middle ground to just kind of meander through the game if you're not initially sold on it, as its combat does become repetitive. I thought its concepts were interesting and found some of its scenes and characters very enjoyable. The  voice acting from one of the characters can be overdone at times, including their character nearly hyperventilating as he delivers a line late in the game in French. The character models are well-portrayed and have cool styles to them, but there are moments where their models look somewhat old at times. The main character's design is kind of wack at times in an ambiguous "appeal to as many demographics as possible in one character design" kind of way, and other characters can be a bit one-note in their brief portrayals, however other scenes have emotional impact and present interesting considerations of time, regret, and guilt.
I completed the game on 360 near when it was released, and am glad to be playing through it again on PC. Its soundtrack and setting are the standouts of the title for me, but I think it still holds its own as being a solid single player experience several years after its initial release.

The pure fact that memory exists is frankly amazing when you really think about it. Our wrinkled mass of neurons and blood allows us to process current information and store that data for further study or application. Some we retain for days, others we retain our entire lives. As long as that lump of protein gets the energy it needs, we can retain pretty much everything. Even the act of “forgetting” is sometimes just us misfiling a thought or experience only to be found later. More than that, the human brain is still kind of a mystery… We don’t know exactly how memory works really. We don’t know how we store specific thoughts and how they are really processed. We’re close, of course, and getting closer every day – but this game puts us into a time where the human race has already cracked that nut wide open, and is currently chewing up the insides like a rabid squirrel.
Remember Me (produced by Don’t Nod Entertainment and released by Capcom) is a game I’ve flirted with for a while. I bought it on the suggestion of Robert Bell (our wonderful SPOILERFREE movie reviewer!) but never really got into it at first. I thought it was a neat third person action game, but kind of boiler plate. Nothing too special. But I recently picked it back up – I wanted to play and review a game specifically with a black female protagonist, and this is the first one I thought of. Of that very short list. More on that later. As I installed it and started a new game, instead of just trying to stave off boredom for another day, I tried to actually experience the game. What the story was. How the characters were portrayed. What was my role in the conflict. And it turns out, it grabbed me by surprise.
The main thrust of the game is we are in a far future version of Paris, France. In the opening sequence there are ads for a device called a Sensen, brought to you by the Memorize Corporation. Sensen is an implant at the base of your skull that allows people to share their happy memories with others, remove sad experiences from their minds, and share information through that connection. It became so popular that Memorize the company basically became the government. They control the flow of thought and experiences. They experiment on people in secret factories, and in a small percentage of people Sensen mutates their minds and bodies into memory addicted monsters.
We play as Nilin, a woman who escapes one of those secret labs with the help of an underground terrorist group called the Errorists, who are trying to take down Memorize. But as we progress through the initial chapter we find out that Nilin was once part of their group, but was captured, and had her memories erased.
Usually I don’t spend too much time on the setup, but to understand this game, to really get into it, the history is pretty important.
The action is built around Nilin’s ability to adjust, distort, and remove memories using a device embedded in her glove and connected to her Sensen. In a fight, in addition to punching and kicking the hell out of her opponents, she can shoot blasts that disrupt someone’s thoughts freezing them in place. She can set off energy explosions that overload their minds. And one of my favorite parts – she puts her hand directly on the back of someone’s head to fry their Sensen completely. It’s pretty damn awesome.
Learning combos is key, because you get to build your own, which honestly I’ve never seen in another game. When you gather enough XP, you can unlock different powers connected to the X or Y buttons. So you can have a combo that heals you, or one that does massive damage, or a blending of the two. Its an interesting concept, that they implement very well. This makes customizing your character to taste cool and frustrating at the same time. Should I place this move here, or not? I don’t have enough of this to do that. What will happen if I… oh no that shouldn’t have happened what the hell.
I won’t lie to you, the story’s concepts and settings are really interesting, but the voice acting? It’s a bit over the top. Not as much as a game like Blades of Time (don’t worry I’ll be getting to THAT stinker eventually), but too overwrought. Every cut scene is dramatic or important. Every character interaction is filled with emotion and depth. It’s too much, and many developers don’t realize that part of the puzzle is pretty important. For the most part the story is fun. The fact that you aren’t just trying to save the city, you’re also trying to retrieve your stolen memories – your sense of self. I liked that a lot. But not everything can be important. Not everything matters as much as the next. Without a varying degree of drama the important parts are a bit drowned out.
All in all, I would suggest this game. Especially if you are into third person action games like me. And before you say anything, yes I do like more types of games than Metroidvania.
But not nearly as much.
1 out of 5 hours past bedtime. Relatively good, but it doesn’t blow your mind.

: I love all sorts of "not so great games", but I don't love this one. It's got an amazing cyberpunk setting, crazy awesome score, and passable button-mash combat. However, the hit or miss of the combo building system, incredibly aggravating camera control, and lack of any real depth leaves me disliking more than I liked. Which is a shame, cuz there's a lot to this diamond in the rough, but it's a little too rough even for me.
As much as I want to recommend this game, I really can't. Not unless you can get it for cheap.
I love all sorts of "mediocre" games. Bound by Flame, Technomancer, Of Orcs and Men. All sorts of stuff that doesn't review terribly well, but I still find to have enough spirit and enjoyment to make it a good experience for me. I have a real hard time finding that in Remember Me.
I -love- cyberpunk settings, and Remember Me paints an incredibly vivid and satisfying picture. It's punctuated by a great score from Olivier Deriviere, and a pretty solid voice cast. However, this is where the good stops for me. While I definitely don't mind repetitive button-mashing combat, I find that the interesting (and not terribly awful) combo system is hit or miss. Largely miss. It involves creating your own combos that offer different bonuses and then applying these in combat. What to heal more with your hits? Build a combo for it. Want to deal more damage? Build a combo for it. This mechanic is pretty great, but only when it works. I can't count the number of times I tried nailing the timing right for any mess of combos that involved back-and-forth light/heavy presses just to have the combo reset itself for no apparent reason. I would launch the first, second, third, and then the fourth attack, which seemingly came at the right time, would register as the first attack for a new combo. No amount of double- or triple-checking of the combo buttons allowed me to predict when it would work and when it wouldn't. While this isn't as dire for the normal attack combos, it's a deal breaker when it comes to healing and reducing special cooldowns, as the game is built around using your combos to their fullest potential.
I might be able to forgive the spotty combat if it wasn't for the fact that you'll also be battling the camera
. There's not a moment that the camera, which seems to auto-center to the worst vertical angles, will let you rest, as you're going to constantly have to be flicking it back and forth, not to follow the combat, but to push back against whatever automatic adjustment it tries to make for you. It's not good. I have played more than a few poor-camera games, and this one gives me trouble remembering any others that might be worse.
Then there are platforming moments that require a modicum of precision that the game cannot offer. I remember one instance in particular with having to navigate a minefield that left little room for error, but thanks to Nillin's inability to turn on a dime (no different than other games that put "weight" on how their characters move, but no one is using The Witcher 3 to platform [and you'll also remember they even patched in better movement for Geralt later]). This just added more frustration to an already frustrating experience.
The worst part about all of this is that I really, REALLY like the setting, and while I think the story is unnecessarily obtuse, I'm in for cyber thrillers. But all of the good is
mired down by the bad. I realize this is not true with everyone, but it is for me.
For completionists or gaming connoisseurs, this is worth a look at a cheap price, because it had a pretty big hype before release and then left little impact when it hit. It's noteworthy in the history of gaming, but not worth losing a lot of money over. Recommended at $5-10 at most.

God damn what a wonderful game! After recieveing this from a Capcom Humble Bundle ages ago, I kept putting this one on the backburner after all of those jokes about it being forgetful. I didn't even realise that it was full-on cyberpunk, especially with Life is Strange being so standard slice-of-life.
Now, it's not the greatest game in the world by any stretch. The combat is basically a VERY simplified Batman Arkham, the platforming is follow-the-orange-arrrow linearity, and the story gets a bit preachy. None of those things are bad however, and  this game is definitely better than the sum of its parts. First off, the graphics and art style are just stunning, even now in 2017 as of writing. Yeah there's little interactivity, but the attention to detail is astounding. I loved just being in the world at all times. Secondly, even with its preachiness, the story gets going very quickly with its cyberpunk morality questions and almost always hits the notes dead-on. The combat and platforming do their jobs well enough.  I pick the initial hardest difficulty on most games released from 7th gen onwards, and, aside from a few spots late game, I didn't have too much trouble. The game wound up being pretty short though, but the story beats definitely are paced right so there's no complaints there.
At the time of writing, the price is still US$30. I probably wouldn't pick it up at that price unless you've exhausted everything there is in every Deus Ex game and are still really jonesing for some good cyberpunk. Get it on the cheap and be pleasantly surprised. I grabbed the DLC halfway in my playthrough when it happened to be cheap, and it didn't really add anything noteworthy. You can skip that if you want.

On Saturday, I played the game To the moon.  A really good one! I cannot calm down until now. But how it can be so moved？
First, gameplay. It's no doubt that To the moon is good, but is it a good game or a good story? Many players have the same question like me. One obvious reason is that its gameplay is so simple (collect and puzzle) that it's more like an interactive novel rather than an RPG game. In another word, in the game, gameplay serves for narrative instead of the opposite. And this situation becomes a more complex question. As the video “Nintendo stated” provided in TGP，Nintendo believes game first (Gameplay first). They even ask writer to set story according to the certain gameplay. So, the question is what the standard of the good game is? At least, we cannot judge from the relationship of gameplay and narrative. In TGP, Prof. Ouellette stated that there are two types of game development, which one is Top Down, another one is Bottom Up. Obviously, To the moon is the former, which developed from story narrative to dynamics to mechanics.
Second, emotional experience. To the moon provide a unique and strong emotional experience. From the beginning, it has a mysterious atmosphere and a lonely feel. As the story developed, it looks like John bears unhappy marriage and takes care of River. And it’s confused why River crafted paper bunnies and what her illness is. There even some happy when I saw John and River riding. However, when Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts learned the truth, it becomes a deep emotion mixed with regret, sympathy and move. The reason “to the moon” and the yellow and blue paper bunny are thematic dissonances, which are powerful and successful. River is not a weird woman but a girl who loved John so deeply. What’s more, excellent soundtrack (such as main theme “To the Moon” or “Everything’s Alright” ) by Kan. R. Gao promotes this emotional experience.

The artwork was very well done, colorful, and overall impressive for the format. Personally, I do not like the sprite style. That was a hesitation when I bought the game, but I was willing to give it a shot. Nah, I just don't like it. If you like sprites, you'll love this.
Music. Yes, the main theme is really nice. Generally the music supported the feels.
Cons:
The pacing was dreadfully slow. This game has almost exactly four hours of content. You can speed that up a bit by tapping through all the dialogue, but you can't speed up the ponderously slow panning, animations, walking, etc. Be prepared to spend some time just waiting because you don't have any other choice.
This was a very story driven experience. The minigames were not needed and were just in the way most of the time. Its not like I got some sort of reward for solving them them faster or more efficiently so what was the point? I have enjoyed good minigames that added to the game experience - these did not.
The navigation. So bad. I'm talking about just walking around. I shouldn't be blocked by a *small* plant if I'm trying to get across a half acre property. And the entire screen shifting suddenly to track with the player in the center. Because you could only move up/down or left/right, it was so distracting. If I tried to use the mouse to direct teh characters, they would not go farther than about 6 tiles without needing more direction. Why was this? The player controls and navigation were what I hated the most about this game.
TLDR:
If you want a sweet boy+girl story, you like sprite animation, or just want a low-impact diversion for a few hours, you may like this game. If you want something challenging or faster paced, this is not for you.

is a very short story--scratch that, "tone poem"--disguised as a puzzle game. In comparison, the developer's earlier work,
, was a short story that started with after the end of the world and went downhill from there: what happens if a guy who's read far too much Nietzsche for his own good survives the end of the world? Mr. Szymanski's sense of horror is primary psychological, and the psychological trigger he enjoys pulling most is transgression.
was a story that started mundane and, as the player went through the motions of a puzzle game, it slowly transgressed the usual player's conventional morals. By the end, you
what's going to happen. You dread it, but, like craning one's neck at the grim-looking traffic accident, the sick part of your soul has to make sure.
also gets its creepshow factor from transgression. However, unlike
, it
walking past the line from the word go: you're a little girl. You're a nine-year-old girl, alone, locked in a shed by your mother. In Szymanski fashion, it all goes downhill from there. Lines are, of course, crossed and that is where
is most effective. It also does well with tension and suspense. There are one or two things that could be considered jump scares, but either they fall flat or I'm just not particularly susceptible to them and they're the game's weakest part.
Don't buy
for gameplay or expansive content, since it is only about an hour long. Those will inevitably disappoint you if you put much value in them. Buy it and play it if you want... a poem. A feeling. A theme. If
was about the potential barbarism in people well past the pale of everyday existence,
looks to things closer to home. By the end of the game, you'll realize you probably know at least one person that this tone poem comes dangerously close to describing. Depending on where you live, that person might live down the street and there may be a handful of them to boot.
If you're particularly unlucky, you might find it speaks to your own condition.

Played Assassin's Creed (AC) for the first time in 2017. Almost ten years after its initial release, the game still holds its own against more recent releases.  The protagonist is tasked with various types of missions - not just assassinations - to stop his enemies. Although some combat and some stealth are required at times, our hero more often finds himself eluding hostiles and performing feats of parkour.
Although the controls are not immediately intuitive for someone new to the AC series, they are relatively easy to learn and, most of the time, work well with keyboard and mouse control. After a while, running and jumping across rooftops becomes second nature and is one of the more enjoyable aspects of the game. Since combat is not the primary focus of this game, awkward skirmishes with guards can be overlooked. Although there are a few restrictions related to the unfolding plot, there is a surprising amount of freedom in how to proceed through the open world setting of the major zones. Most of the missions are fairly straightforward and not overtly challenging, with some exceptions; however, the more challenging missions are optional and not required to complete the game. The major drawback of the missions - and consequently of the game (and other games in the AC series) - is their repetitive nature.
The protagonist, while not entirely forgettable, starts off as headstrong and selfish. He does undergo something of a growth arc through the game. There is no customization, per se, although he does grow in power and gain new abilities, and all the growth is linear.
The game is set in the Middle East during the time of the Crusades and revolves around a secret war between the Templars and the Assassins. While the premise is intriguing, its delivery could have been better. The story generally moves forward when the protagonist visits with the leader of the Assassin order for further instructions, but in between, when completing missions, there are only sparse reminders about why he is going about his work. The atmosphere, on the other hand, is wonderfully presented through the lively cities with distinct architeture and various types of citizens on the streets, even if interaction with them is limited.
For its age, the graphics in AC hold up well. The AC soundtrack includes audio tracks and queues for various activities, such as discovering a new point of interest. To play the game, I did not have to install any mods or unofficial patches, and with one minor exception on an optional task (turning Vsync on/off), I did not encounter any technical issues.

It delivers upon what the name implies, and often that is all you should expect from a free game.
That said, there are flaws that left me not to recommend it.
-you can't use your mouse in the menu
-there is no volume slider
-the resolution can only be set to wrong and worse, and has no manual imput
-clicking "new game" automatically overrides your previous save without a confirmation
-mouse drag because the game has an fps cap (I'm assuming that's the reason, anyway)
-you cannot pause the game or otherwise access the menu during a cutscene
-you cannot move backwards in the menu by pressing Esc
-alt-tabbing leaves the game's audio on
-alt-tabbing while not having the game paused or in a menu traps your cursor in the center of your screen, which can only be resolved by opening your task manager and forcefully closing the application (without your mouse) or restarting your pc.
The last being my main concern, honestly.
It's a very minor issue if you know what's going on, but it's intrusive. And I could imagine it to be quite difficult to deal with if you're not the kind of person who uses the task manager frequently, or simply doesn't know how to use shortcuts. (except for alt-tab(though it could still be triggered by programs like skype))
All in all, it feels like a mobile port, and a poor one at that.

Recommended if you can overlook the many flaws and little annoyances. At this price it's several hours of good fun provided you adjust to how the game works.
- Beautiful retro graphics and not bad music.
- Once you adjust to the controls, some wonky gameplay elements and the way combat works it's pretty good for what it is.
- Combat is fun once you get the hang of it.
- Some nice boss fights.
- the game is not "fair" but I'm not sure if I should count that as a negative because I think it's supposed to work that way, you get the infamous "get-hit-mid-air-fall-into-instant-death-pit", enemies spawning out of nowhere behind you, enemies obscured by foreground graphics, instant-death traps you can't possibly see coming first time around, attacks that can't be blocked, attack that must be blocked, that sort of thing.
- CAN'T REBIND CONTROLS ON THE KEYBOARD. ARGH. 'W' is attack.
- platforming is easy. Way easier than the rest of the game. Unless you get pushed into a pit by an enemy it's hard to die when jumping, it's more of a time waster when you respawn at a checkpoint.
- Every now and then it's hard to tell if something is a wall/platform or just background decoration.
- You have unlimited continues and there are checkpoints all over, so even if you die every 30 seconds you progress unless you just can't complete some part, and the game is not THAT hard. So unless you go for achievements of not dying/not getting hit the challenge isn't really there in the long run, it's just trial and error and getting down enemy patterns.
- A few enemies have way too much HP, like the fireball gargoyles, you get down their pattern fast and it still takes a lot of hits to finish them off.
- You get 3 weapons but they're different only in graphics and damage to some enemies depending on the weapons. The attacks, parrying and magic work exactly the same with every of them.
- Your basic attack has several animation variants with different animation length. In a game where you sometimes need split seconds to react it's a death sentence. Also attacking pushes you forward even if don't press forward, often making you walk into traps.
- The story. The ending especially. At first the game is self aware then I don't even know what it is. It's not the most important thing in a game like this but somehow I was still disappointed.
Very old school. Very METAL!!! Probably very dividing; I like it, but can see why others might not.

TL;DR An enjoyable if short experience with cool graphics and sound, good controls, challanging but fun gameplay, and an abrupt ending. Buy it on sale.
+Excellent graphics and animations - You WILL stop playing from time to time just to oogle at the backgrounds, and when you purposefully kill yourself just to see what death animation that new trap is going to have, you know you made a really good looking game.
+Tight controls and fun combat mechanics - While a bit repetitive, combat never feels stale, and the controls are 100% responsive.
+Good Soundtrack - Nothing to write home about if you're a metal fan, but serviceable.
+The Difficulty - You're gonna die. A lot. But only on the first playthrough. Once you die a few times in a section and memorize what's ahead you will be able to breeze through with little problem.
-Too short - Even dying as much as I did, it took me just 4 hours to finish the game, and that's returning to an area in which I thought I missed a secret (I didn't). And speaking of secrets, they are too few and too easy to find, so any challange they offer is minimal.
-Not a lot of enemy variety - The foe roster feels a bit lacking. Even if there exists pallete-swap versions of previously encountered baddies with their own minor variations on attacks, they're still the same, and can detract from the overall experience.
-Weapon types feel pointless - The game recommends you to use your fire or ice weapon on different enemies, but I played through the game for a second time without using them and noticed little to no difference by sticking to my basic sword.
-Bad ending - While there's some resolution to the story (kinda) its basically a cliffhanger for a sequel. There better be some free/cheap DLC expansion comming for the game, which would fix my main two problems with the game as it currently stands.
Much like a high-end carnie haunted ride, its fun, loud, has some really nice, gory aesthetics and cool metal music, and its over before you know it, so its recommended with caveats.

I wanted to like this game. I really, really did. The art is awesome and unique (pixel, but almost like a pencil sketch), and I'm a huge fan of metal music and Nordic fantasy and imagery.  The artist of the game should be commended for his fantastic work; I look forward to seeing more from him. The music is serviceable, although maybe a bit too unsure of itself to ever really rise above average. It's metal, I suppose, but its a very tame, elevator style 'this has been carefully crafted to not offend non-metalheads' metal. A friend of mine quipped "This isn't metal - this is *butt rock*", and though I feel that's a tad harsh, there's a ring of truth to it as well. I would have liked to have heard it really break loose and command some attention.
The game itself, however, is poor. Painfully poor. You want to love it, because your avatar is a white-haired demon-slaying sexual tyranasaur and the world is literally dripping in blood and you're waving around a 5 foot sword and using it as a ping pong paddle for the bones of undead skeletons, but the gameplay is so nearly non-existent that you're going to be confused as to why you're not having the best time of your life 2 hours in and start to question what the hell is actually happening.
Here's what's happening:
Level design is flat. Enemies walk at you in a line. Projectile mages force you into the exact same question-and-answer volley of their projectiles, which at first seems compelling and then becomes tedious as you do it for the 1000th time. Parrying attacks and then delivering a walloping counter is awesome, until you find that its the answer to 75% of the bigger enemy fights so you're going to spend half of the game just sitting there waiting to be hit so you can counter. You want to tear like hell through hoards of enemies, but you only have one combo and its boring. Mastering the three main enemy groups takes maybe 30 mins, so the game just starts warping them all in together to add 'depth'; now you have to wait for counters while vollying projectiles from mages and avoiding on-hit damage from walk-in-a-line skeletons, who *have* an attack animation but its pointless because their entire hit box is an immediate attack regardless of if they're swinging or not.
Just as you start to think that the game is getting fun, you get locked in a room with a spawning wave of skeletons. You paddle-spank them for 10 seconds, and then a second group teleports in. You spank THEM, and then another group, this time with volley mages. Can I move now? NOPE - now its a boss skeleton, but he also has a slime-spitting dog with him. You need to counter block the skeleton, then volley-swat the dog.* The door finally unlocks, but 4 screens later you're being forced to do the same...exact...thing.
All of this is surmountable and even becomes trivial, but little by little you start to ask yourself "is this it?"
The game is trying to hide something from you by creating a complicated-seeming process of elimination for you to run through over and over again, and that 'something' is the fact that there is nothing else going on design-wise.
It doesn't feel good or fun. I feel like I'm knitting a sweater, not waging an undead genocide across a Cradle of Filth album cover (like i damn well SHOULD feel).
The last straw was when I did this semi-cool wolf run autoscroll stage, only to have the game lock me into a single screen with respawning ghost dogs that died in one hit. It was whack-a-mole. Straight up. Full stop. The game had me playing whack-a-mole instead of crafting clever levels and strategic enemies and letting me bang my head (which is PROMINENTLY featured in all of the videos but is barely in the game and feels out-of-place when it happens).
I don't blame you for buying this game. I fell for it too.
But be warned. The art is awesome. The writing is cheesy and fun.
The game, however, is a boring, uninspired slog, and it will lock you in one place for minutes on end because it has nothing else interesting to do with you, only to let you roam for another few minutes and make you wonder if you'd be happier just being locked up once more.
I do not, and cannot recommend.
*I know what you're thinking right now, I swear to god I do. "That sounds AWESOME. I love challenge, and I can master that♥♥♥♥♥♥and tear through that level like nothing! This guy sounds like he just sucks".  Please don't. This isn't Dark Souls. It isn't Devil May Cry or Castlevania. It isn't They Bleed Pixels. It isn't even Super Meat Boy. Its not challenging, its just boring. I'm trying to save you lol.

While the game quality has certainly increased and there are a lot more things to do, there is still room for more content (namely an imrovement on animal AI) but by the looks of it Hello Games has really been working hard to create a polished, fun game.  It`s too bad I spent the full $60 at release and had to wait many months for any considerable work to be done, but better late than never I guess.  The game certainly felt like it was early access or something when it first released, which put off a lot of people as it was marketed as a full blown title, so long as these free updates keep coming though I can overlook what was in the past, it was probably Sony who made them put it out in the original state anyhow.  While the price tag is still a bit steep for my liking for what the game offers, it definitely looks like it will be the game promised at launch over the next few updates.  I think once full blown multiplayer and co-op is established, and the animals (oh, those animals) get an AI overhaul the game will certainly be worth the $60+.
In conclusion, while the game has made an amazing recovery from the initial backlash it got on release, there are still some patches needed to really flesh it out as the game Hello Games wanted, but I am quite optimistic at this point which is great because it was hard to find optimism for this game several months ago.  Yes I recommend, but if you`re uncertain I`d say wait for a few more patches if you really want bang for your buck.

[The History of] Hammerfight is a game about combat using flying machines with maces, axes, guns, and other weapons attached.  The trick is, your movement imparts realistic momentum to your weapons.
After his village is attacked, a young hunter is the sole survivor of his clan.  Taken into slavery in the gladiatorial arena, he must work his way up the ranks until he can exact revenge on those who killed his people.  The game plays out as a series of missions, each a fight sequence either against a set number of enemies or for a certain amount of time you must survive.  Arena mode is an ever-escalating sequence of fights that allow you to loot weapons and money from enemies that you can then use in the main story.
Hammerfight can be played almost entirely with the mouse.  Spin it in a circle and you’ll fling your weapon around your machine.  Learning the correct timing on when to speed up and when to juke to deliver a crushing blow to an enemy is critical to your success.  Eventaully you gain access to a training hall full of weapons you can select from, each with their own style of play.  Swords are good against soft targets, and hammers crush armoured enemies.  Guns are a great multipurpose tool.  It is a unique and innovative control scheme that allows for a few different playstyles.
The graphics are pretty cool, but often it becomes difficult to tell what is going on in the heat of battle.  With all the effects from explosions, bits of the destroyable environment flying around, and the multitude of attachments you can get on your machine, the entire screen is just a blur of wood and metal and flame.  Often your machine will get trapped in a corner, unable to move while you take constant damage from touching the walls or your enemy, but you can’t see where you are to try and escape.  The soundtrack is awesome, though.  Just listen to the battle theme in the trailer above and tell me you don’t want to fight someone.
The story suffers from an over-abundance of Proper Nouns.  Events and characters are not described very well at all, and you will struggle to determine who each character is and how they relate.  Not that it really matters, you can just work your way through the game destroying anything that tries to kill you and you’ll win.  But the game wants you to take the story seriously and to invest in its narrative, yet it never gives you the chance to do so.  I still do not understand how to find gems to augment my weapons, or how that helps me, even though I stumbled upon three of them throughout the campaign.
I have mixed feelings about this game.  On the one hand, the gameplay is innovative.  But the nonsensical story, wild difficulty spikes, and visuals that easily obscure the action make me say you should take a pass on Hammerfight.
