This is a pretty good action-adventure game, but its not without its share of problems. The combat system ends up being quite fun but it takes a while for you to unlock enough combos and abilities to make it so. The game's 2084 Neo-Paris makes for an interesting setting with a bunch of good visuals (including its pleasantly sharp textures) and a solid soundtrack. The story is kinda interesting, but I didn't find the characters particularly memorable. The "memory remixes", which are essentially cutscenes that can be altered by the player, are a cool idea but they can get a bit irritating; their logic usually becomes apparent only after the fact. The maps are quite linear, making exploration pretty minimal as well, but they have enough variety to keep things fresh.
One major problem with the game is that it has the worst mouse controls I've seen in almost 20 years. There's considerable "dead zone" when using a mouse, which makes any kind of precision mouse movement impossible. It's obvious the game was designed for controllers, but that didn't stop titles such as Tomb Raider (2013) and the Arkham franchise games from having excellent mouse-keyboard controls (and these games predate Remember Me!). The camera angles are problematic from time to time as well, which too is unforgivable for a 2013 game.
In addition to this, every time I sat down to play, the game started to develop symptoms of a severe memory leak after about 40-50 minutes of playing, making it totally unplayable after about an hour. However, merely restarting the game solved the problem every time. (I also haven't seen anyone else mention this problem, so maybe it's just me.)
Even with these very noticeable issues, I'd still recommend the game. Overall it was an enjoyable experience with enough variety to keep you interested for its entire duration (about 10 hours on normal), especially since the combat system gets increasingly fun toward the end.

As great is the ambition, so is the fall. This game has incredible potential, a worthy and well-crafted background story about a bleak digitized-memory future, an original and satisfying combat system, Lara-Croft-esque environmental maneuvering, and yet all of this is made insipid and boring by an inability to tell a story and design a satisfying game.
The biggest problem is that it's just so stupidly linear. There's this big futuristic city as the backdrop, just aching to be explored, but all the levels have one entry and one exit, and you are forbidden from straying even slightly from the game path. Lara-Croft-esque jumping around might seem fun, but you can only go in the marked direction. There are no environmental puzzles. So it's not fun, just a chore.
To make things even worse, even the basic exploration is hampered by doors being locked behind you. You keep getting hints of cool secrets to discover, but if you choose the wrong path you cannot go back to find them. At a certain point you just give up, and randomly pick a direction and hope to find something new and interesting. More often than not, you guess wrong and are pushed back to the linear progression. Is this supposed to encourage you to replay in order to find the secrets? It encourages me to shut down the game.
About those secrets: many of them unlock more background story elements. They are all very interesting indeed, but if you miss the secrets -- so easy due to how you're forces to the linear sequence -- you will be deprived of these important details. Why punish players this way? Why not give players all the information? It boggles the mind that these intriguing tidbits are lockable and frustratingly easy to miss. I see no point in making this information a random gameplay reward.
There are so many other frustrating problems. Third-person angles are hard to get right, and this game utterly fails at the challenge. The camera is supposed to intelligently follow you around, but it's constantly in the wrong position, especially in combat. You will fight with the camera more than with your actual enemies. And of course, the heavy-handed linear narrative means that often you just can't turn the camera to look at things other than what the level designers demand. Again, you are encouraged to let go of your curiosity and just keep moving forward. It's a dismal sense of lacking any control over your character. It's the opposite of role playing.
The bad third-person angles also make it hard to enjoy the surroundings. The designers chose the worst possible field of view here, always narrow and incapable of grasping the magnitude of the vistas. It's a big futuristic city, but a you have only a tiny little keyhole from which to see it, and much of it is blocked by your character. And since the camera often won't let you even look around, it becomes an exercise in futility to even try. Little details get lost in the keyhole and big details are entirely impossible to encompass.
Another broken, but potentially cool innovation, is the memory manipulation sequences (this technique appears again in Dontnod's much better next game,
). Unfortunately, the controls for these sequences are especially abysmal. You are supposed to spin around your left joystick to manipulate time and catch certain moments, but it's awkward requires frustrating precision. Instead of immersing yourself in an evocative mechanism, you will be fighting your controls. What a sad miss.
I did finish the game, because I became attached to the background story. But I was bored and impatient to get to the end. And so it's worth mentioning that this game is quite long indeed. Usually I would applaud such a rich amount of content, but when the gameplay is so awful, it becomes a drag.
Final nitpick: though I heaped praise on the background story, it's also riddled with clichés. The characters are larger than life, as expected, but utterly unrealistically so. For a game that pretends to be grim and gritty, this makes it hard to identify with any of the people you meet.
So. Play this game only if you're really, really passionate about this genre of science fiction, or are really intrigued by the combat system. But know that the game itself is so frustrating that you might regret picking it up.

I'm going to preface this with a tl;dr: if you liked Darksiders II, the Deathinitive Edition is literally the same game.  It has an additional, harder difficulty, but the biggest change is a new coat of paint.  If visuals don't warrant the asking price for you, there's no need to upgrade, although this edition does come with all of the DLC.
That said, the game is very good.  Being an old vet, I went straight to the Deathinitive difficulty and found it genuinely challenging.  At times, I thought that certain enemies were unfairly tough, especially in optional dungeons, but the game is still fun and rewarding.  If you're coming from the original version, the mechanics are unchanged and you can still infinitely combo pop-ups to aerials to lock enemies and heal for free with the Black Demise weapon, use that info how you will.
The distribution of unique items is, I think, changed a bit, but I may be remembering wrong.  The Crow, Maker, Angel, and Shadow sets are now found in hidden chests or as rewards instead of distributed at the Serpent's Tome.  The sidequests are largely the same.
Speaking of, the sidequests are unchanged, and thus still absurdly tedious.  Chasing stonebites is a pain, as it always has been, while the rest are "go here, do that, come back".  Not worth it for completionist types, but they do provide tangible rewards for those that do.
Still, the combat is clean, the world is interesting if not vast, and some of the later puzzles are legitimately clever.  Clearing dungeons requires more button skill than cleverness, while secret hunting requires a good amount of both.  The narrative, while not great, at least makes the player's short-term goals clear.  It's a fun game to pick up, and for me has been worth it for four runs so far across the two editions.

As many have said, Hob is a very pretty game.  The first few hours of it are a pure delight!  I definitely do recommend this game to anyone who loves puzzle plattformers at all.  Everything looks amazing, and the areas are so imaginative!  This definitely touches on the same sort of otherworldly blend of nature and machinery seen in Portal 2.  That does however raise some small points.
First, this game is something of a metroidvania in that you will spend a lot of time revisiting places you've been before.  There will be a lot of running around.  The save points that were all over the place near the beginning will end up being very widely spaced apart in later sections.  The fast travel system is not as well distributed as one might like either.  This means the end game sequence is artificially extended by long, mandatory sequences of running, climbing, and jumping all over the map, and at the end of that, you have whatever it was that killed you the last time.  It was probably a fall since there are usually save points less than half a minute from difficult enemies.  I will give them credit for that.
Second, a lot of the puzzles are actually really easy IF you can find them.  That would be my biggest gripe is that even though you are given a map marker to where you need to go, you have to find the means to reach it, and since the whole environment is connected to machinery, the place you actually need to go next may not be near the place marked on your map, and it might not even be easy to spot.  I played through the entire first half of the game without a guide, but I admit to caving in and consulting a guide after wasting an hour running around trying to find a spot to use the final armament that I hadn't already visited.
My final complaint is that for all that you're changing the landscape, once you open up a new pathway, that's usually the extent of it.  There are a few puzzles that have you do A in order to do B and then undo A because B opened a way to do C, but once C or D is done, that's it.  You will probably never manipulate that part of the environment again.  Except for weak enemies, most enemies don't respawn, but annoying barriers like bushes and thorn hedges never go away (other than the few cuttable bushes), while only some walls and cliffs become passable.  You have a sword and three different tools by the end of the game, but not much to really do with them, so you will be running through mostly empty landscapes, climbing up and down because there are no stairs for this section of otherwise impassable terrain, and trying not to fall to your death in the areas where there is just no easier way through than to cross a narrow span or jump a gap.  It would have been nice if there was a little more interactability with the environment and especially a way to shorten some of the trips.
All that said, those are quibbles bred by long hours of hunting for obscure things that can be tricky to find even with a guide since nothing is labeled.  I still absolutely loved receiving this as a Christmas present, and I absolutely believe that it would have been worth it for me to buy it on sale.  Full price however?  Maybe not.  I certainly recommend the game, but if puzzle platformers are not your passion, you'll probably want to wait for a sale.

What a beautiful game, and what a shame Runic was shut down so quickly after publishing this.
Hob is all about puzzling through a beautiful, occasionally dangerous environment to reactivate old technology, shift and reconfigure old places, and clear out a strange corrupting force. There's clearly been some kind of apocalypse here, but none of the game's lore is conveyed in words - it's all environmental storytelling, gestures from mute characters, and a few light-based murals you can discover along the way.
I really enjoyed the environmental puzzling and the physical ways the character interacts with the world - punching open columns of rock to create ladders, heaving against levers to turn gears into place, and so on. The fighting is simple but feels weighty enough; though I never figured out how to perform complex combos, I never felt like I needed to either. This is not a combat-driven Torchlight at all. Mostly, I just spend my time traversing the world and finding secrets and unlockables, and just wondering at the mysterious beauty of the place.
Well worth your time if you're into that sort of thing, and a very respectable and daring final effort from Runic. It's a crying shame they were shut down because games that aren't as wildly profitable as microtransaction-driven online games don't appeal to corporate shareholders.
Also, despite the scare-warning, it plays perfectly fine with a mouse and keyboard after a short adjustment period. I alternated between right-mouse-movement and WASD movement as convenient for the level design, and aside from one particular oddly-constructed pile of rocks, I never had any noticeable issues.

Great design, fitting sound track, and just the right amount of achivement grind and difficulty to keep you occupied for 10h.
When they fix the performance issues and bugs it will be a very nice game, but even in it's current state very recommended.

What this game isn't: A difficult combat hack and slash that will have you repeating the same fights repeatedly over many hours that gives you that satisfying feeling once you finally beat a difficult fight (although certain enemies do require slightly different tactics).
What this game is: A easy to learn hack and slash title with an amazing storyline & beautiful graphics that impressed me from start to finish. This game is less about swinging your sword in a specific pattern and more of the psychological struggles of the main protagonist Senua. I won't go into the story too much as it should definitely be experienced yourself but Ninja Theory have done extremely well at entering the player into the inner turmoil of a grief stricken character's mind.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice includes very unique puzzle elements that make you think you're stupid once you figure them out, the keys to locked doors are locating symbols located in nearby areas and to progress through each area does require some thinking. Also some of the lorestones (this games version of collectibles) also have a few tricky hiding places that may require small backtracking (once you leave an area you can't return, so if you see a lorestone and you want it, you should get it, I missed 2 so had to play the game again). I do recommend finding the lorestones as it does give interesting overarching facts to characters, norse mythology tied to each area and collecting them all gives an interesting extra scene at the end of the game that makes the story more understandable.
As mentioned the combat is very easy to learn and you may find yourself relying more on heavy hits than light attacks (it should be noted that there are more combos then it appears by mixing light & heavy attacks) just because it downs the enemies faster (kick comes in handy with certain enemies too ;) ) and dodging/parrying will become your best friends. It is very forgiving though and generally only being surrounded by enemies or missing a timed parry at a bad moment can give you real issues.
The game's main strength is the story though, it is a fantastic tale where you won't be dissatisfied (confused yes) from start to finish. Made by Ninja Theory I was expecting an interesting story thanks to their other releases Enslaved & DMC but this game's story blew those out of the water. It isn't a game where you can control the direction of the story, and at times it may seem more of like an interactive movie but once you regain control of Senua you get pulled back in. The inner voices can be useful, annoying and occasionally troll like at certain points in the game, all it does though is make the game much more immersive in my opinion. You should listen to the voices if they get loud and rowdy though, generally they are doing so for a reason (lorestone you are about to miss for example).
While a short game overall I can't fault it for being so short except that I kind of wish I could play more of the story, the sheer quality of the game more than makes up for the short time spent playing it. It's a well rounded title that offers enough to keep a range of different players entertained and wanting more. Ninja Theory have once more proven that preordering a title from them is definetly worth the investment, I look forward to more titles from the studio in the future.

If you're old enough to remember the arcade game Lunar Lander, this works on the same principle. You launch a rocket (with limited fuel) and fire the booster to adjust your velocity and vector to intercept the targets, using the gravity wells of asteroids to slingshot your way around.
Crashing into objects (or your own mothership!) destroys your rocket but you can launch new ones as many times as necessary to hit all the targets. Flares from the mothership help you to plot the initial trajectory your rocket will take so you can hit the first target without much trouble but you need to try and hit multiple targets per rocket because each one costs money and if your overall profit falls short you fail the mission.
You can view the level in impressive 3D by moving the camera angle but the play itself operates on a 2D plane. There are 4 camera modes, some are better than others depending on the level layout.
On completion of a level you get a printout of your stats, including colourful ribbons for exceptional performance. You're graded Gold, Silver, Bronze or Blue (fail) and on the section overview (star system) each level (planet) glows at a different intensity for each grade, so it's easy to see which ones to retry later.
Main menu is laid out in a cabin scene (the Crow's Nest). Clicking desktop objects and monitors opens the menus for mission schedules, game settings, leaderboards etc.
E-manual: a huge library of documents relating to storyline, game mechanics, information about all the corporations and planets, mission logs and every other intricate detail of the game. Parts of it (eg. mission logs) are transcripts of the voiceovers. There's hours of reading if you're so inclined. I only skimmed a few items before I realised there were no clues or tips on how to tackle the difficult levels.
Graphics are not of the spectacular quality you'd see in AAA space games but nice 3D eye candy - Jupiter looks cool in section 7. You're concentrating hard on the job at hand so fancy, detailed space scenes would either go completely unnoticed or at worst distract you from the gameplay.
Storyline which progresses with cutscenes as you complete the sections. I couldn't tell you what it's about because these things go in one ear and out the other with me, but it's there if that's important to you.
Good voice acting for storytelling and level commentary.
Generic atmospheric background music. Twice in the game an original song bursts out from the commentary. They must have hired professional musicians for these fabulous tunes, with proper instruments and vocals, not the usual synth garbage you tend to get in these games. I wish there was more of it.
At the start of the campaign you select from 10 corporations to work for, each provides a different bonus. I chose 15% larger target ping radius, others give you profit boosts, increased rocket power and suchlike. This all adds to the replay value.
The essential game mechanic doesn't change, it's always the same action of firing your boosters. This could be seen as a game weakness but it's the level designs that produce the variety - new types of clouds are introduced at intervals and the asteroid configurations become ever more complex. The rich environment of audio, graphics and lore (if you can be bothered to explore it all) enhance the overall game experience.
Great hidden ending!
Fully integrated global leaderboards including individual rankings for each corporation.
In-game cloud support (not mentioned on store page) so you can continue your campaign on multiple devices.
Controller or keyboard/mouse options. Both equally effective.
Takes a while to load at startup but performance is smooth and solid, no problems.
I was drawn to this game mostly by the word 'puzzle' in the store page summary. It turns out there's no real brainwork involved, it's more about judgement and trial and error. This is not a criticism, it's my fault for not studying the description more carefully. Just bear in mind that it's not a puzzle game per se when making your purchase decision.
The zoom doesn't go out far enough. In Overwatch (top-down) camera mode you can't see the rocket and target on screen at the same time until you're up close which doesn't give you much time to fire your booster, especially if you're moving fast. The other camera modes help to see into the distance (I discovered this only after I'd completed the entire game in Overwatch mode, skewing the camera to see ahead!) and there are also indicators on the rocket to show the direction of the targets but neither of these features helps to judge your burn as effectively as being able to zoom further out in Overwatch mode would. Hiding the setup panel on the right during rocket flight would be another obvious way to increase the screen real estate - this seems to be a programming oversight to me.
Rage-quit potential: levels are unlocked as you progress and they become increasingly challenging so it's likely you'll get stuck at some point with no difficulty setting to dial down. My nemesis was level 33 (Zoom Zoom) when the guidance flares disappeared.
It's built with Unity so why no Linux? Come on guys, don't make me work on my 100% achievements in this horrid Win thing!
Harder than you'd expect. By the 2nd section (out of 8) I was already having trouble completing some of the levels but it's the type of game where your skills improve with experience so it's a case of "getting over the hump".
50 levels in the campaign which took me about 12 hours at a leisurely pace for a single (mostly low-grade) playthrough and there's a lot of replay value. Imagine that you are a child and go out the back door of your parent's house on a far away planet to *your spaceship*. You take off and fly straight into the sky, past the clouds into your home stellar system and then rocket to nearby planets to explore. You can land on them, walk around, gather resources, or just explore. Through all this there are no load screens; it's one continuous experience. You can walk around a whole planet if you want: it will take many days or even weeks.  Then you warp to other systems each with their own planets; there are trillions of systems from which to choose. At it's core, that's No Man's Sky: it is a chill exploration game of stupendous scope that pays off the most when you just slow down and look and let wonder sink into your soul.
This is possible because each planet is created from a different binary seed which is fed into a procedural generation system in a way that enforces uniqueness. There are probability density functions that control how common certain features or feature combinations occur. As a result, there are extremely rare creatures and planet types that can be found only by determined exploration. (By determined exploration, I mean hundreds of hours of play or getting very lucky!)  Finding these gems is one of the best-- and most underrated-- aspects of the game.
As you explore, you will run across aliens with their own languages which you can learn, along with their history from monoliths, plaques, and ruins.  You can buy ships from aliens using units you get from mining the enviroment, or selling objects you find. You find mysterious Lovecraftian lore in abandoned buildings and begin to discover the secrets of an entity called "The Atlas". All I have described so far is the No Man's Sky that originally shipped. But now there have three updates and there is much more.
Updates 1.1 and 1.2 added base building with the ability to teleport back to them; farming plants (for profit) at your base; the ability to visit other people's bases (and use their farm!) and as well as leave public messages; vehicles for driving around planets-- the hovering Nomad exocraft is my favorite--, create racetracks at your base on which others can compete; giant freighters where you can create a collection of different spacecraft, as well as build a base; an excellent photo mode for capturing and sharing any of the numerous beautiful scenes you will find in your exploration; different play modes were also created including a Permadeath Mode, a Survival Mode, and a Creative Mode.
Not long after the game came out, people noticed interesting Hex numbers on certain player constructed objects called "signal boosters". These Hex digits were decoded by players and discovered to be galactic coordinates. After the functioning of black holes (wormholes) was worked out, a method of rapid travel was created by players, called "black hole roulette",  that made moving in circles of fixed radius around a galactic center very fast. As a consequence of these group efforts, players began creating galactic communities, the Galactic Hub being the largest. Hundreds of players visited or built their bases in the Hub. Messages were left, gardens shared;  player lore created. The sandbox and social aspect of the game began really coming to life.
And now has come update 1.3.  This update *is massive*. As it is new, the implications of all the additions are yet to be understood. The beginnings of a more synchronous multiplayer are present: you can see a representation of a nearby person and hear them talk, while you occupy different instances. (I expect some sort of co-op mode in the future.) Portals, which function like "stargates", allow a person to relocate their base anywhere in galaxy with little effort, for which the person knows the coordinates. You can also, just visit for a walk, or drive around using your expcraft, but without your starship, if you choose not to move your base.  This will make the formation of communities even easier. Much more lore was added; aliens that give quests were added. A new race of aliens was added. The farming and manufacturing system was doubled in scope. The galactic economy was made deeper. New ships were added. Freighters were given warp engines.
I have been playing No Man's Sky (via GoG) since the game came out for PC (I have over 1000 hours played)  and got this Steam version so that I could start over without having to delete my old saves. The changes have been substantial enough that I wanted to experience the game from the beginning anew. I have not been disappointed. One note: because of the size of the update, there are currently a number of bugs. Hello Games has been releasing patches fixing the bugs at a terrific rate considering the small size of their teem. I give them high marks for their dedication to the game and its players.
I am very excited to see what the future holds for No Man's Sky!

[The History of] Hammerfight is a game about combat using flying machines with maces, axes, guns, and other weapons attached.  The trick is, your movement imparts realistic momentum to your weapons.
After his village is attacked, a young hunter is the sole survivor of his clan.  Taken into slavery in the gladiatorial arena, he must work his way up the ranks until he can exact revenge on those who killed his people.  The game plays out as a series of missions, each a fight sequence either against a set number of enemies or for a certain amount of time you must survive.  Arena mode is an ever-escalating sequence of fights that allow you to loot weapons and money from enemies that you can then use in the main story.
Hammerfight can be played almost entirely with the mouse.  Spin it in a circle and you’ll fling your weapon around your machine.  Learning the correct timing on when to speed up and when to juke to deliver a crushing blow to an enemy is critical to your success.  Eventaully you gain access to a training hall full of weapons you can select from, each with their own style of play.  Swords are good against soft targets, and hammers crush armoured enemies.  Guns are a great multipurpose tool.  It is a unique and innovative control scheme that allows for a few different playstyles.
The graphics are pretty cool, but often it becomes difficult to tell what is going on in the heat of battle.  With all the effects from explosions, bits of the destroyable environment flying around, and the multitude of attachments you can get on your machine, the entire screen is just a blur of wood and metal and flame.  Often your machine will get trapped in a corner, unable to move while you take constant damage from touching the walls or your enemy, but you can’t see where you are to try and escape.  The soundtrack is awesome, though.  Just listen to the battle theme in the trailer above and tell me you don’t want to fight someone.
The story suffers from an over-abundance of Proper Nouns.  Events and characters are not described very well at all, and you will struggle to determine who each character is and how they relate.  Not that it really matters, you can just work your way through the game destroying anything that tries to kill you and you’ll win.  But the game wants you to take the story seriously and to invest in its narrative, yet it never gives you the chance to do so.  I still do not understand how to find gems to augment my weapons, or how that helps me, even though I stumbled upon three of them throughout the campaign.
I have mixed feelings about this game.  On the one hand, the gameplay is innovative.  But the nonsensical story, wild difficulty spikes, and visuals that easily obscure the action make me say you should take a pass on Hammerfight.

Assassin's Creed was a landmark title for the 7th gen consoles. Alongside games like Grand Theft Auto 4, Mass Effect and Mirror's Edge, greatly shook up conventions in what action adventure games could really be. It innovated heavily in terms of technology, rendering highly detailed environments with dozens of npcs on the screen at any one time. And featured things we hadn't really seen before, like crowd dynamics where NPCs react differently based on how quickly you move near them. The 7th generation of consoles was like Santa's workshop for developers and we were all eager to see what was under the Christmas tree.
Naturally the original Assassin's Creed is very overlooked today. The historical context of the title is long forgotten and it is considered very bare compared to its sequels. What remains is a very interesting relic of a different era, both in it subject matter and its gameplay.
You play as Altair, an assassin of the Levantine order during the third crusade. He is given the names of 9 targets, and upon killing them will redeem his name during a botched mission you observe during the prologue. Altair is noticeably less charismatic than the later main characters in the series and the plot is noticeably more low key. I will say it's to this games benefit if you are interested in the history of the time period. The game is steeped in atmosphere and the plot, while fairly goofy does keep your attention if you're invested in it. If you are fascinated by this period of history it is a very enjoyable experience all around but if you're interested in it more as an aesthetic it probably will not keep your attention.
In terms of gameplay Assassin's Creed 1 is the most bare in the series. Side missions are more mandatory and repetitive, constituting the same mission types over and over. Thankfully the PC version does switch things around with adding additional missions that involve races across rooftops and a few others that break up the tedium here and there. Combat is also noticeably less fluid than later games, relying much more on visually watching enemy animations to know when to counter and when to dodge. It's one of those things that you eventually get used to but if you've already played the sequel you'll find this somewhat jarring.
At the same time this is a game steeped in personality and is significantly more nuanced than later titles, which swerved more into high fantasy and high camp. If you're a history buff or interested more in the historical context of the title I do recommend this game. But if you're more interested in just another open world action game I'd direct you to look into getting the sequel instead.

Remember Me? Nope. Someone stole my memories. Who? I don't know... they stole my memories? Oh... k. What now? Imma steal them back. How? Gonna beat up random bums on the street.
Remember me is your typical third person action adventure game. The
recipe of linear progression and button mashing fighting sequences with a lot of climbing in the style of
. Maybe throw in some
and
for seasoning in there.
takes place in future "Neo" Paris where memories can be digitized and traded. Societal collapse ensured! People are trading their memories away (or stolen) until they have none left and end up living as empty shells in slums. Our protagonist, Nilin, has had her memories stolen and delves into the quest of getting them back. Luckily she can steal and remix memories herself and can hit harder than Zangief.
The gameplay mainly consist of traversing makeshift sheet metal homes of the Paris slums, lustrous apartments of the privileged few, old city rooftops, an industrious prison complex and futuristically furnished office spaces. The heavy linear progression is done in the style of running and climbing ledges and various other environmental objects. Exploration is not rewarded as straying from the path laid out by the developers usually results in death. Wonder what is hidden below this ledge? Let's see... hmm... you just died. This monotony is broken up with frequently occurring fighting sequences. Fighting is done with combo building button mashing kicks or punches. Button combos  are fixed to four different ones (ex. one being : X-X-X) but can be expanded upon by adding abilities (called pressens) to them. Four such abilities exist; damage, heal, cooldown, link (multiplies the previous pressen). Meaning you can build a combo that damages more, heals you and cools down your skills. Pressens are unlocked by leveling up which is in term is done by fighting enemies. Skills are available to help in fights but are not upgradable. Fighting is fluid and landing combos not hard but can be frustrating when against large crowds as you will have to dodge hits and possibly mess up your combos. It works most of the time and is satisfactory due to needing to change your approach for different enemies.
On a small amount of story based occasions, you get the ability to remix memories. You enter the mind of someone and edit certain objects in a given memory to change the outcome of it and influence their actions in the real world. It is a fun way to explore the story behind Remember me and seeing different outcomes can be hilarious and sad. I feel like this was the strongest part of the game and it’s a shame so few of these sections are available.
My main problem whiles playing Remember Me is the janky movement and jumping, less than fluid control while climbing edges and pipes and a scripted camera that is all too willing to take control away from you. Looking at the story, I don’t see how any person would be influenced in such a way by such an insignificant event – in the grand scheme of things. A little more polish would have done this game good but some more time developing it, adding more choice based content would have changed it completely. Imagine if the remix sequences had different outcomes you could influence by changing memories characters have of certain events, therefore changing the outcome of the main story. It's nice to think of the what if but this is not that game.
All in all I was satisfied with my 12 hour playthrough. It can be janky at times but in the end its nothing game breaking. The game plays fine and if you liked any of the other games mentioned above, I see no reason you would not like Remember Me.
PS: Victoria Chase from Life is Strange is totally Olga from Remember Me.

Coming from someone who spends most of their time playing the Arkham series,
is actually a nice take on the classic beat-em-ups genre. Usually, fighting games are side-scrollers
. but this game shares a battle arena type
. The player controls the character into some area that's big enough for a brawl, and the mobs spawn in smoothly with no loading cutscenes
. The game is combo orientated up to 5 different combo sets, which the player unlocks one by one throughout the entirety of the game. In a way, the mechanics are actually creative by allowing the players to customize the move sets themselves. Named
are the different types of fighting move that the player can input into either a punch or kick. That are also uniquely categorized into having perks, such as causing more damage, heal on hits, reducing cooldowns for special abilities, or linked into chains to extends the previous perks and additionally increases their effects.
. Nilin, the character, also has special abilities that she can unlock throughout the game, which utilizes them very well. Every time whenever she uses an ability, it goes on cooldown-- this is where the cooldown reduction Pressons are useful. The mobs in the game make sure that you utilize every single one of your abilities and Pressons, which persists the player to experience the game mechanics by its full. There are also frequent incorperations of parkour
, where the character must continue with obstacles in her way. The game also experiments with a game mechanic that was implemented into a masterpeice of a game,
. During a "memory remix", the player controls a chain reaction of a butterfly  effect of the victim-- changing little things in order to have a different outcome. Finally, the collectibles-- an on and off taste for me. I don't mind finding them for extra content like concept art or scripts of the lore. It bothers me because it benefits the gameplay. It forces the player to scour in hidden areas for permanent extra HP, Focus, and even EXP
.
The story takes off with the character Nilin, a memory hunter and fighter. Unfortunately, she's an amnesiac at the beginning of the game-- having all her memory wiped besides her name. Bits and pieces of her past are restored throughout the game, which is a nice gesture since everyone loves a good mystery. Speaking of mysteries, Nilin allies herself with a mysterious contact named Edge, with no physical contact and only through comms. The two of them take on neo-Paris together, aiding Nilin to restore her memories and discover that this utopia is definitely a dystopia
. Of course, mysteries always have their twists and this game sure did have a few that the player will discover if they continue playing. Recovering the memories of Nilin, remove the facade of the the story's setting, and unvealing the secrecy of Edge. We get to see Nilin's questions, doubts, and struggles as she continues these missions deployed by Edge, wondering if he's ally or foe. The story attempts to be dramatic, but it will never be success than their other game,
.

A thing to note: I bought this game simply to have the OST, so I my play time seems a bit low that's because I originally watched a let's play and never really played through it myself.
And then. Uh. Yeah. I wish I could just give this game a seven or six out of ten instead of the current black and white function. Because like, I think fondly of this game. But it's not great.
A little before this game was published—or at least appeared on my radar—I found out I have autism. So to have this fictional character being described as acting a certain way and to recognise that as being what I have was…really nice. A first, and in the seven or so years since then I've only encountered such a character twice (once by a befriended author whom I pushed a little, and another time in a kinda weird (in a negative sense) set of short stories by a random internet writer). That combined with a good story and a great soundtrack (I love Laura Shigihara's music) made me love this game quite a bit.
But now, Gods know how many years later, it's really only that nostalgia that keeps me thinking somewhat fondly of this game's story.
I've learnt a lot since then, and thinking back the portrayal of autism seems really scrambled. River, if I recall her name correctly, seems incredibly classically autistic most times, in which case she should not be treated as allistically (is that a word) as she is. But then I feel like the story seems to want her to have something like Asperger's or PDD-NOS, which…those people are not that disabled.
And then like, much as I love that there's a prominent autistic character in it who's autism is actually relevant to the story, the story is not about her. It's about her husband; the people who have to deal with the autistic person. She's very evidently a burden to him. Which…happens really often in media. Either we're a burden to those around us, or we're socially inept genius white boys. Or both. So that makes me feel kind of sorry for my young self. I feel like she deserves to be excited about a story about her (a troubled smart biracial woman), not the people 'struggling' to deal with her.
I don't hate the game, certainly not. I just wish it's story were better. Kinder. More thoughtful.

RWR is an RPG-style top-down shooter. Your mission is to take over enemy territory until you are the only faction with territory left on the map. Pretty straight-forward, but it's easier said than done. If you're playing with vanilla settings (the way it should be), you'll find that going rambo like in all those other games won't work. At all. Working with all the other soldiers in the army is absolutely necessary if you want to succeed. You'll start as a grunt; not much more than cannon fodder. But as you learn the mechanics of the game and start killing off more than 2 troops a life, you'll gain ranks and soon, you can command your own squadron. When you get here, you won't need to follow the commander's orders that much; instead you think you could do more damage by leading a strike squad to that isolated base over there. From an expendable troop to a valuable leader - that's where the beauty of this game lies. Another important piece of this game lies in the RP (Resource Points) system. Using resource points, you can change your equipment as well as call down support from HQ in the form of artillery, paratroopers, etc. Getting RP requires you to gather information on enemy vehicles, capture territory, and safely delivering that chewing gum you found back to base. But the most important thing to remember about RWR is that it's all about tactics. If you and the enemy are locked in a stalemate, maybe you should try flanking them while they're preoccupied with your allies. If you've got a silenced weapon, put that to use by sneaking into the enemy base unaware. For an kinda silly game, RWR is perhaps one of the best war simulations to have ever been created.
If you like dying a lot, get this game.

First I want to get this out the way the game didn’t really need “Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice” as a title. “Hellblade” conjures up images of a brainless hack ‘n’ slash game, and sounds cheesy. The omission leaves us with “Senua’s Sacrifice” which feels more appropriate to the content of the game.
The games focus is the story it wants to tell. There are no moral choices, no filler fetch quests, no pointless collectibles – the lorestones serve a purpose – and no sandbox. Don’t get me wrong I love branching story paths and wide open worlds to explore, but they’re not necessary in every game, and this one certainly doesn’t need them. The game is no longer than it needs to be, and spending hours looking for Surtr’s fifty toenail clippings would only serve to detract from the story.
The visuals are stunning and stand up to any AAA game; I’m using a screenshot of Helheim as my PC’s background, but the star of the design is the audio aspect rather than the visual one. The ambient sounds and voices that haunt Senua are an important part on all levels. The story, the game and overall immersion, so don’t ignore the recommendation to play it with headphones.
The combat feels inspired by Dark Souls, as you don’t just flail at the enemy until it is dead but rely on dodging and parrying to create exploitable openings, and avoiding certain attack patterns. It feels a little bland at first, but as you progress through the game other enemy types appear. The weakest part of the combat is the lack of variety in tactics used by the enemy, they just walk toward you. They don’t really work together either.
The puzzles can be a little irritating at first. There is no real guidance about them but once you get into the idea of what you’re looking for the frustration factor drops off. For me the most irritating puzzle was in a house, where an unstoppable enemy chases Senua as she looks for runes. It isn’t clear where to go – obviously as that’s part of the puzzle - but its instant-kill feels bugged as it successfully killed her despite being nowhere near it. Or maybe Senua suffered a heart attack, the lass is having a bit of a rough time. That’s an Understatement of the Century Award candidate right there...
The quality and effort that has gone into this game makes it worth buying at its full price. It is largely unique and feels like the product of a team that wanted to make something; rather than one for whom game-design is just a job spent cranking out the yearly iteration of a franchise. That said Senua is so well rounded and relatable, something often lacking in gaming, that I hope we’ll get see her grow with a new story. I can think of at least one plot point that needs resolving.
Whatever they decide I hope that Ninja Theory will continue to give future games as much attention to detail as they have with Senua’s Sacrifice. If they do I’ll buy every one of them.

So I picked this game up not really knowing much about it, apart from the fact that Mental Illness plays a large role in it, due to the trailers and little marketing the game had.
The game is about Senua, a Pict warrior who travels to the Norse Underworld known as Helheim, in order to find the soul of her deceased lover Dillion.
Right off the bat you are introduced to Senua and your travel companions... these being the multitude of voices that reside within her head. 1 of which acts as a form of Narrator giving small bits of backstory while the others comment on the current situation, some being neutral, some being positive and the rest negative.
You accompanied by the spirit of your former friend / mentor called Druth who was once a Slave to the Northmen, as a result he has extensive knowledge of their culture and legends. In fact it is due to Druth's stories to Senua that she even knows of Helheim and the way to reach it, which started her on this quest.
The game instructs you that it is best played using Headphones in order to fully experience it, I also recommend this as it really adds to the atmosphere of the game as you will hear the voices in Senua's head as if they were in your own, they don't constantly talk all through the game but when they do, having multiple voices argue with eachother, cheer you on or belittle you all at once really helps you understand just how horrible it is for Senua to endure it. I can't begin to imagine what the game would be like without them.

Beautiful, The landscape and the rest of the enviroment was beautiful, it was very easy on the eyes and the deathinitive edition complimented it. The tutorial was very cut and dry about everything and even gave you a bird to help guide you wherever you needed to go and even in later parts of the game as well. The characters all had charm, like you could feel their emotions and believe them. They were very good at explaining their surroundings and potrayed a certain history of it that makes it feel it had depth. The button combo fights were very fun and you are able to summon spooky ghouls to help aid you and the weapons system is like Diablo 3...except less complex, but still interesting. This game looked promising at the start and I wanted to play it for a while.
Why does the world feel so empty? There is literally one area with nothing in it. It's so freaking huge, but there is nothing there. It only feels like I'm fighting 2 monster species in every area.  I swear there was only like 8 different monster species. Fighting the monsters at first are very satisfying, because you think, oh it's just the beginning, the fights aren't going to be too bad, but I better try to farm up and get better gear. Wrong. Dead wrong. Every monster you fight (Not including Bosses) feels exactly the same. A couple of autos and a super attack, that's it. Plus it makes the button combo fighting system feel very useless. Why do I need to use an AoE ability or a knockup? I could just easily press Square 3 times and kill them. It's not rewarding at all, AoE for example, You hardly every fight large groups of monsters in the game. There is no strategy or uniqeness.
I swear to god, I felt like I was in areas for half-hour to an hour, in some cases. All I would be doing is solving an easy puzzle, run back, fetch this, run around again, and so forth. I understand that the game environment is beautiful, If anything they did exceptionally well on,  it's how details that were put into like a statue or broken down stones, but for once, I wanted a Sprint system. Did I not mention how huge some of these dungeons are? I felt like I was running in Quicksand.
Storyline aside, if you play this game, you will soon find out how redundant these quests get. There is even one of Main Quests that makes you do the same thing except different part of the story WTH? I feel like these tedious quests are just meant for you to run around and kill time. Paired with the uninsteresting monster fights it doesn't bode well at all.
Now I think the point of these tedious quests and big areas was the puzzle solving. For the first few hours, it was sort of fun to do and made me feel like a champ, but they really limited the puzzles to where it just feels like another chore. If this was the first game you ever played, then this doesn't really partain to you, but if you played God Of War, The Legend of Zelda, Prince of Persia. You know that this is really just another copycat that only offers a half-written story.
So when you're first exposed to it after darksiders 1, It's interesting, because it's new and we like new things. Once you have acclimated to it, you start noticing things like why this, how, or this doesn't make sense. That's because there is only a partial bit of depth to get you where you're going. The plotline was Death needs to rescue his brother, but first he must fetch all this♥♥♥♥♥♥first, then he must solve these spooky puzzles, and after that you must defeat the ultimate evil.
I recommend that if you played games like Zelda, God Of War, or Prince of Persia to stay the hell away from this game and just watch the 2 hours worth of cutscenes on youtube rather than 20 hours of tedious, redundant, and non-unique gameplay. You're not missing anything by doing so which is why I said earlier that it has little depth and still understand that you can just do so. I didn't finish the game after 75% completion and just watched the rest and still made sense.

This game has much tighter controls now, and when I die, I feel like it is always my fault, which is what I really look at when playing this type of platformer. I've chosen not to read the extensive list of improvements so I wouldn't be biased or actively looking for how each of the fixes operated. Good job to the developer for all of this polish, and definitely good job to the publisher for taking this difficult decision!

Well this is my first review, so I\'ll make it interesting with a personal interpretation. Read this only after you've played the game and you have your own opinion of it :) Otherwise, you know - SPOILERS :)
So this game, I feel is obviously about the drama between a mother and her daughter. The mother has lead a heavy, very heavy life, full of mistakes, full of wrongs. She has only her pride left... barely.The daughter sences this and much more. She feels her mother's pain and wants to help her. But she's refused. The game takes place in a nightmare, hence all the tripping colours and weird machinations. At first I asked myself if this is a metaphore for a womb and escaping from it. Close to the end you cut some bloody ropes, which remind me of umbelical cords.
I believe the mother can\'t let her child go and wants to protect her from the evil in the world... I honestly feel for her. I have a friend for whom I have the same feelings. That's why Autumn is in a cage, going in circles, always thinkering with stuff. Which makes her mother furious: she can\'t control things she doesn\'t understand! That\'s why she stops her constantly.
At one point you are attacked by a spectre of a black wolf. I honestly shivered in my entire body, such a good moment. I believe the wolves represent the evils that might afflict women: abuse, a wasted life, dead hopes and so on. The game is both very sad and very scary, when you really think about it. If you know someone, a man or woman, who might be abused - help them, be there for them. And love your children... I think this game is about those things...
Thank you for reading, and to the creator(s) keep making games like this :)

TL:DR: *It's good in a lot of ways, but is not recommended, UNLESS it's really discounted in a sale*
OK, so, this game has a lot of things going for it, especially for the time. The premise is unique, the setting is really cool and the attempt to tell a story set within actual history is commendable. The story itself is also stronger than I was expecting, and the dialogue is also decent. For a game that is a decade old, it also looks... alright, all things considered. It even runs fine on a modern PC (Intel 6600K; GForce 1070; even on a 21:9 monitor). But its age really does become apparent in several ways:
- If you think the "climb a tower, mark an objective, execute, repeat" get's boring in current UbiSoft games, buckle-up, because it is much more of a grind in this game. It doesn’t even alert you to alternate ways of executing a target most of the time. 90% of them just let you know where 1 or 2 citizens need help, and occasionally a mission objective, all of which you can naturally just discover wandering around the city. At least Far Cry 3 tied gear unlocks to the towers in a lore-friendly way.
- Combat is pretty pointless. Just time counter-attacks and you'll be fine for the vast majority of enemies, even though you're supposed to be strategic and run from large encounters. One time I didn't feel like finding cover, and instead laid waste to a small army out in the desert with virtually no effort. The most difficult and frustrating enemy in the game is the controls. I can appreciate that they dole out moves over the course of the game so you can get used to them, but you get a hang on them really quickly, and then it inevitably becomes repetitive.
- Controls. Holy Hell. I was initially impressed with the way they organize the gamepad controls to fit with  areas of the body, but (like a lot with this game) that wore off early on in the game. Are you gonna climb that wall, or vault off of it? You gonna climb to that clearly visible hold-point, or just hang there while I pivot the camera around to try to find whatever arbitrary play-state you need to be in before you'll move? Are you going to run to sit in a hide spot, or clip the invisible hit-box of a person sitting there & ruin the whole thing?
- They were clearly in love with the pseudo-cinematic sequences in the game, because they don’t let you skip them. Not when you’ve rescued a citizen and you want to bone out before guards see the pile of bodies at your feet. Not when you biff a mission (probably because of the controls) and you want to retry it. The only one I’ve been able to skip in 12.5 hours of play is the opening, and only with the keyboard; not with the gamepad. (which is another control issue, but in order to play you have to navigate the first half of the menu w/ the keyboard, then with the controller. It’s wonky.)
- The game regularly lets you know that you’ve hit a “checkpoint,” but if you die you will get punted back to the same spot all the time. You don’t lose collectibles you’ve found or anything, but other than that the “checkpoints” are completely pointless.
- Speaking of collectibles, there are a bunch of flags and additional assassination targets strewn around the maps, but because they didn’t implement achievements on Steam, they are also completely pointless. No unlocks; no extra lore you can read through. Nothing. You aren’t even rewarded for exploration with new information about your target; the only additional tips you can get are via the tasks you’re REQUIRED to do before you are allowed to take out a target.
There are things in newer UbiSoft games that feel grindy, unfair, or just kind of out-of-place, but playing this game really drills in just how far they’ve actually come when it comes to game design. I wouldn’t say that this game is pointless, or even without its fun moments. But if I’d paid $20 for this I would be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Luckily I only paid $6, which in Canada is, like, one beer at a bar. So this has definitely lasted me longer than 1 beer would. That’s why when it’s on sale (and it frequently is) I wouldn’t discourage someone from getting it, but for $20 is not a recommendation.

My expectations for Remember Me were lower than how I ended up feeling about it. I completely forgot that this same dev developed Life Is Strange and is working on the upcoming Vampyr.
From other reviews, my expectations were that the story, gameplay, and design choices weren't that great. In my opinion, I think the story is ambitious and, in many ways, unique. While the combat is certainly repetitive, the story is in no way generic. The idea of a mega corporation controlling peoples' memories by altering the bad ones in order to preserve happiness is a bizarre concept. And the fallout of it makes sense as it crosses so many laws of reality. It's hard to talk about the story without spoiling anything, but Nilin, the protagonist, is an "errorist" and a memory hunter. She ends up finding it to be her goal to put an end to the corporation that has caused so much damage to society with their inhumane treatment of both patients and prisoners. By the end, I was actually impressed with the overall story and direction of it.
What makes the combat unique is the complete lack of weaponry for Nilin and the abilities she possesses in terms of hand to hand combat and the technical abilities she has as an errorist. She can cause glitches in robots, turn invisible, etc. While this combat system is different, it does become repitive rather quickly as there isn't much variance in the enemies and the enemies are incredibly predictable, making fighting a bit easy.
While I love the world design of Neo-Paris in 2084, the level design is only okay. There are eight chapters in the game and a lot of them revisit the same places, making it feel reptitive. The only difference in the locations you come back to is that they might be destroyed. And despite being set in Paris, the game didn't feel like Paris at all, aside from some of the first few chapters where you do walk through the "St. Michel" district. The rest of the game is set in slum, a futuristic version of Bastille, various futuristic buildings, technical labs and biological labs, etc. The backdrop of Neo-Paris really only serves as that, a back-drop.
I will say that the music, voice acting and writing, cut scene direction, and the animation in this game are incredible. The music especially.
Overall, this game was pretty good. The only downsides really were some of the level designs and the combat, which was often times repetitive. And those two do take up a lot when it comes to video games.

Oh, Spooky. Your mansion truly is terrifying especially when you don't know what's going to slaughter you in the special rooms. You and your games are truly an entertaining experience to work for. I have drawn out many positives and negatives of this game. I'll simply list them below:
Postives:
- Decent pacing; not too rushed, but a little slow at times
- Good design and affects used for the various monsters that await you
- Quite a lot of enjoyable easter eggs; includes references, minigmames, and other hidden little things
- Level design is generally fair
- Interesting stories for each monster (Well, the first just sorta came out of nowhere)
Negatives:
- Gets more tedious with the further you get; becomes more of a job
- Jumpscares become natural as you progress; more of an annoyance
Positives:
- Good sense of humor
- Adorbs art style
- Funny overall storyline
- The desks in the shape of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(one of the best easter eggs)
- The dead ends in some rooms give a shock of dreaddown your spine
Negatives:
- Monster Database ruins the feeling of dread from when you first meet a monster
- Becomes stressful when you die
Honestly, I love this game and I do think it would be fun to return to, even if the negatives may rule out replayability. I think this because the game's art style is the type to really make you nostalgic while playing it. Probably my biggest disappointment is the name change, but I'd rather have that than to potentially lose the game as a whole. Overall, I say that this game deserves a solid 8/10.
Thank you for reading my review and have a good day!

Y'know, I enjoyed my time with this game.  I liked the art style, and the overall atmosphere and world design.  There isn't much story to speak of, it's aching to be one of the more "evocative" type of games but can't quite pull it off.  The sense of scale and wonder isn't quite there, but they do a good job making the attempt nonetheless.  The story is meant to be told wordlessly, but there isn't much story there regardless.  The combat, once you get used to it, is decently satisfying.
When it comes to some of the technical issues though, I wish I could be more charitable.  My rig is pretty powerful, and yet the game has constant, noticeable hitching, even at sub-native resolution and installed on an SSD.  It crashed fairly often, and eventually (near the end of the game, of COURSE), the C++ Redistributable borked itself and could not be repaired after a reinstall, a game cache verification, and a manual reinstalling of the libraries.  I wanted to finish the game but now I can't be arsed.  Sorry, Runic.

First of all, Hob is cute af. That being said, let's move on.
This is a game suitable for anyone, of any age. The world is vast, colourful and a delight to explore thanks to a fantastic level design and smooth controls. There is enough collectibles to fulfill any completionist's dream, even for a rather short game (around 15h for me). The puzzles are pretty easy, but they are engaging and never feel out of place. They weren't just put there to say "hey wait, here's a puzzle before you go" : they are part of the architecture. Combat is a minor element of the game, but you fight just enough to remember that this world is alive. One regret though is that the unlockable combat abilities are not that useful, simply because you don't need them to win - I actually forgot that I had them.
Another regret is that I wish the game was longer. While its short lenght is not a flaw, it leaves me wanting for more. Should it have a sequel ? I guess not. Everything has a sequel and a prequel and a sequel of the prequel these days, and one-shots are refreshing and a good reminder of the beauty of ephemerality. Well, I'm getting carried away here, and the fact that Runic shut down pretty much answers that question anyway.
I find many similarities between Hob and Hyper Light Drifter : no talking, a vague story, a ruined land where nature meets thechnology, underground facilities etc. (also both heroes wear a red cape, but that's not relevant). Hob is much lighter and brighter though, and even if its world is broken and deserted, you rebuild it with joy and never feel alone.
It is very fun and easy to play it is very detial too.

Did you love playing wargames with little plastic soldiers when you were a kid? Perhaps you still do? Who am I to judge? Either way, this game is definitely for you!
RWR really captures the joy and playfulness of that familiar experience of messing around with little green toy soldiers. If you're considering purchasing this game and are currently thinking 'hmm, this looks like it's my kinda thing', rest assured it is because I went through the exact same thought process, bit the bullet and love it.
Speaking of biting the bullet... this game can be quite brutal! Every hit has a 50/50 chance to kill you unless you're wearing armour, which only mitigates a few more hits, so be prepared to die regularly! It's no biggie.
I've only played single player and can't understand why some reviews below say it's only good multiplayer; I can see how it'd be even better with a bunch of friends, but honestly single player is also immersive, fun and challenging. Sure, it takes some time to get used to how everything works, but that's part of the charm for me. Once you grasp the basics, the game's depth unfolds quite organically as you level up and unlock new options, begin to control a squad etc.
I think the AI is really good, they use some pretty sneaky tactics and coordinate their attacks really nicely. You are never left with that feeling of the AI 'cheating', for example it's actually possible to sneak up behind some enemies and spray them with bullets before they magically notice you! I've seen much worse AI in some AAA games, so this is impressive to me.
The game has a really nice, gentle humour that often raises a smile.
Another thing I love about it is how balanced the weapons are. I often find myself going back to the humble assault rifle that is your default firearm even once I have access to higher level stuff, because it still has its place and your weapon choice is more about how you choose to play than one weapon being inherently better.
I very rarely buy Steam games at full price as there are so many sales, but with a game like this I urge you to pay what the devs ask, as I did, so that this awesome team will continue to improve this game and also hopefully make more such games in future! The price is very reasonable anyway.
Please keep up the good work, this is my new favourite game!

After about 5-6 hours of playtime to finish the game (Not including time spent afk), I've decided to give Hellblade a review.
Senua's Sacrifice is a roller coaster of tension and beauty that has a special place in my heart. A must-have if you're a fan of atmospheric horror and high quality visuals, audio and storytelling. Also, many many bonus points in my book for Nordic mythology.
+Gorgeous graphics
+Well plotted storyline/narrative
+NORDIC MYTHOLOGY!!
+Voice acting is absolutely terrific
+Binaural audio is org@smic
+Combat mechanics are a breeze to pick up
+Atmosphere is created with great vividity in many scenes
+/- Combat could be a little too easy/bare for some people to enjoy
-Combat mechanics can be used to cheese some fights by dodge + Slashing repeatedly
-Beat it once and there's not much to play it again for, apart from collecting lorestones if you hadn't already
In my honest opinion, this game is definitely worth a pickup whether it's on sale or not. There's so much more to it than the fairly simple combat. It's the tension and emotion it creates within you, the panicked feeling you get when the voices start screaming at you to move.
Ninja Theory has created a very thorough portrayal of mental illness throughout the game, and I can only applaud them for it. Not only have they made psychosis an ever-present theme in Senua, they also manage to have players growing more anxious by the minute, with the malignant rot in Senua's arm threatening consequences stemming from your repeated demise. The binaural audio adds so much extra tension in tandem with brilliant voice acting and stunning visuals, I do hope more games start using binaural audio in future.
I loved the game without a doubt, but it's only my opinion as I'm a sucker for atmosphere in video games. Props to Ninja Theory for smashing this one out, and I can only imagine what they'll do next to knock this one out of the park.

The New Colossus marks the second of two highly anticipated games of recent memory that are seemingly missing an entire third act, the other being Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. As many others have pointed out, just as soon as the game gets into its groove, it ends like a sweaty middle-aged man collapsing after one thrust, as his partner (the player), stares blankly in dismay when the promised ♥♥♥♥♥♥ never comes.
Of course there are many great titles with shorter lengths and girths, however it's a shame that, unlike its predecessor, The New Colossus is marred with pacing issues, too-often restrictive level design, repetitive enemy types and severe performance issues during cutscenes. There are times where this game shines with the sort of seething set pieces Tarantino would be proud of, but these moments are few and far between in what is mostly a frustatingly tepid sequel.
Wolfenstein may initially impress you as it whips out its large lasergewehr, boasting of its ability to penetrate even sheet metal with its red-hot juice. But as you soon discover, its canisters provide only enough of the coveted virile stuff to tickle your surface, when what you truly desired was a full-scale invasion of your arseschwitz, no holes barred.

--FAMILY SHARE REVIEW... BUT SHARED OPINION--
Sure, it's not as good as The New Order or The Old Blood, but it's still plenty of fun, improving on the previous games in as almost as many ways as it falters.
First off, let's talk gameplay:
As far as the core gameplay goes, enemy balance is significantly improved (no more bullet sponges!) and level design is still solid. The enemy designs have been tweaked a bit, so while a few old enemies (such as the ricochet shotgunners) are no longer present, some new enemies such as the robo-crawlers and snipers have been added to the mix.
The perk system has been significantly improved, with you leveling up all the perks simultaneously rather than having to awkwardly complete X perk to unlock unrelated Y perk.
The contraptions are pretty hit-or-miss. Two are basically just perks that unlock access to new pathways in levels, with the third, the almighty Extend-O-Shoes, being the only one with useful combat application.
My main complaint about the gameplay would be the guns, which feel significantly less varied this time around. Each one sports an alternate fire mode but these don't make them feel like new guns insomuch as slight variations (the shotgun can fire 3 shells at once, the rocket pistol can switch between having a shot arc or firing a straight rocket, etc). It doesn't help that you only get one of the two "cool" guns on a given playthrough, depending on whether you chose to save Fergus or Wyatt. At the very least, everything feels significantly beefier compared to TNO, even if there's less variation.
Also, I've seen quite a few negative reviews complaining about game length and honestly found these pretty baffling, as the main campaign took me almost the exact same amount of time to beat as it took me to beat TNO, with roughly the same amount of cutscenes/interactive non-combat levels. Not only that, but this time around there's a bunch of bonus missions that provide fun reverse-retreads of levels with amped-up enemy placements, as well as playable versions of a few areas that were otherwise only used for interactive cutscenes, and even one fully original level.
Now, let's talk story:
First off, you've probably seen loads of people whining that the game is "overpoliticized" or "full of SJW and leftist agenda". I went into this game pretty wary that these rumors would be true, but thankfully they (mostly) fell flat.
The story is ridiculous to the point of being downright parodical. Half the plot falls apart if you try to look at it with any sort of logic (spoilers: they dislodge a boat that was stuck in some mud by FIRING A NUKE AND RIDING THE BLAST WAVE) but quite honestly, I was perfectly fine with that. It's kind of like how you never think about how Bruce Willis suffered permanent hearing damage from firing his pistol in Die Hard because it was just so damn cool looking. It's meant to be a fun action romp about the ultimate Macho Chad and his merry band of walking stereotypes killing completely over-the-top caricatures of Nazis, not some heady and realistic sociopolitical commentary, but thanks to the current state of irl politics we've been having a lot of people take this game way too damn seriously.
As far as the notion of the game pushing some sort of "♥♥♥♥ whitey" agenda goes, I'll say this: Yes, there's a character who clearly holds resentment towards white people. Yes, this same character uses the whole "I'll call anyone who I don't like a Nazi" technique that the modern ultra-far-left is known for. But what the angry reviews -won't- tell you is that these traits are clearly characterized as flaws, are often pointed out by other characters as such, and at one point in a surprisingly powerful scene this character gets absolutely BTFO'd by a side character for trying to call them a Nazi to dehumanize them.
As for the characters in general, as mentioned they're each following some trope or another (again, often to the point of parody), but again I don't really see this as a negative as they're still entertainingly written and feel like actual people with actual personalities/traits/flaws/etc.
If I had to pick one exception to this it'd be BJ's dad, Rip. Without getting too spoilery, he feels like a character who was written with -just- flaws, and it comes across as trying to hamfistedly force you into disliking him, leading to his scenes being the weakest in the game by far. This is about the only point where I'd say the angry reviews were right, so thankfully he's a pretty inconsequential character.
In closing:
Overall, the gameplay has its improvements and worsenings compared to TNO, landing overall at a net neutral change.
The story is entertaining in the same way mindless action movies are, though the bits where it tries to get serious fall flat on its face half of the time. A slight bit worse than TNO in that regard.
If you liked TNO you'll get plenty of entertainment out of this. Likewise, even if you haven't played TNO but are a fan of crazy action shooters, you'll still have plenty of fun.

So is this game still worth buying/playing? Having just beat Syndicate and awaiting Origins, I decided to replay it.
In short, surprisingly, yes. Despite all the thing's I'm about to say, I did enjoy playing the game and would recommend it to others.
The graphics were not so great, but it's expected. The story was decent enough, and worth going through if you've forgotten it for later games.
Another thing to note is that this game is not really a stealth game like the series later evolved into. For the most part, planting yourself and slaughtering the guards after you is more effective than running, and there are almost not true stealth kill missions. On top of that, the game is missing the nearly essential stealth kill moves like haystack kill, ledge kill, and even the drop kill. So go into the game expecting more of an action feel.
The thing that really ticked me off was the control scheme. There was a never ending stream of explitives as I accidentally jumped off walls, jumped into water, or jumped pretty much anywhere dangerous.
TLDR;
Decent game, especially if you plan to play the others, but expect to wrestle with the controls.

Slain: Back from Hell is a reiteration of its previous title simply titled Slain!. Slain: Back from Hell is a game developed by Andrew Gilmour and published by Digerati Distribution. This game has had an interesting story as originally, Slain! was a terrible game that didn't work well and had major issues one of which was the difficulty
Thankfully, unlike other developers who just give up and move on with other games, Andrew Gilmour and Digerati Distribution listened to the feedback and reiterated Slain! into Slain: Back from Hell and the game as a whole has improved greatly from the movement speed of the main character to even the level of extreme difficulty the original had, still this game remains very challenging
I will only recommend this game, if you want a very challenging but a good well designed game. If you are looking for a game that you can simply breeze through, stay far, far away from this game
This game is very responsive and accurate with its controls however it is strongly recommended to play with a controller
Overall, this is a well-designed, albeit very challenging, action platformer. It has stiff jumping mechanics, challenging level design, two-hit deaths, and a medieval/fantasy/heavy metal setting in the format of an action platformer
I would only recommend it to people who really want a challenge, otherwise, steer clear away from Slain: Back from Hell
