TL;DR - it's an incredibly fun game where you're one little dude fighting in large battles. The game lets you play pretty much any way you want, whether it be taking part in the intense frontline action, or sneaking behind the enemy and taking them out with silenced weapons. Very fun, highly recommended if you like the idea! Oh and there's multiplayer.
In RUNNING WITH RIFLES (RWR) you get dropped into the middle of a brutal and bloody war between the Greenbelts (USA), the Graycollars (Germany), and the Brownpants (Russia). You play as one soldier in an army of hundreds as you slaughter dozens of enemy soldiers, die a lot, get reincarnated each time as another soldier, and rise gradually through the ranks, battling it out across some unknown country trying to completely dominate the enemy. RWR is super fun, and the developers are friendly and dedicated to the game.
There is a campaign mode, where you go from one map to the next, completely capturing each one as you go,
There are about 10 maps (which are all very well designed) to wage war across in the campaign. You can also play any of these maps as a single quick battle, although there's no guarantee that it will be over quickly. Each map can take anywhere from 20 minutes to over 5 hours
with the frontline moving back and forth with each attack and counter-attack.
In multiplayer, you can play PvE or PvPvE, with a huge number of people (up to 64 I believe). Playing online is super fun because you can actually use proper teamwork with other players, to annihilate the enemy soldiers on the front lines or to stealthily capture a base behind the enemy lines.
When you start playing, the basics are obvious: run with your rifle and click in the direction of enemies to shoot at them. But it's not actually that simple, because the game is fairly realistic when it comes to dying. One bullet is enough to drop you where you stand, leaving you wondering where the bullet even came from. Running straight towards the enemy holding down the left mouse button will get you killed over and over with no reward. You have to use cover, utilise mortar and artillery strikes, call in airborne reinforcements, move with your allies, set up machine gun installations, and use tanks or other vehicles to break through enemy lines.
There are lots of different weapons and items that you can use, including shotguns, sniper rifles, grenade launchers, rocket launchers, riot shields, and flares. There is something for pretty much every playstyle. Need to get behind the enemy and destroy a comms tower? Get in a camouflage suit, take a silenced sniper rifle and pistol, some C4, and you're good to go.
The game lets you change quite a few game options before you start a singleplayer game, such as friendly/enemy accuracy, starting XP and RP, etc. This basically determines the difficulty. On higher difficulties, the game is very tough, and this is when battles become hour-long stalemates, the streets and fields quickly turning into blood-soaked killing grounds, until you successfully create an advantage by changing up your tactics.
Overall, if you like the idea of being an individual taking part in a large-scale war, you should definitely put this game on your wishlist. Keep in mind that you will die a lot, and it can be kind of frustrating at times, but it's always entertaining. It's also obvious that a lot of love was put into the game. Overall, just really good. Highly recommended!

The gameplay is fun though and playing Wars more agile brother has a neat, very different feel to it. I was never any good at blocking, so the dodge-centered approach comes natural to me. The artstyle is beautiful, the environments are diverse for the most parts and the world and lore are very well made. I really like the whole Hell-Heaven-Apocalypse-stuff, because it takes all the cool myths of christianity without adding the boring parts (looking at you, new testament).
So in short:
+ very satisfying combat
+ gorgeous artstyle
+ great world/lore
+ You play as one of the four horsemen!!
- story drags on sometimes
- awkward, diablo-like item-system
The Deathinitive Edition:
Now, what's different with the new version. First of all, the DLCs are fully included and woven into the main game, making them feel like natural parts of the game, which is the best a DLC can hope for. The visuals are enhanced too, but you wouldn't notice that unless you really look for it. The best thing might be the overhauled loot-distribution, that makes the obsolete item-system a bit less out of place. The menus are still awful though. Man, why doesn't anyone put any thought in menus any more...
So, all in all, if you havent played Darksiders before, play the first one, love it, come back and play the second game too. If you have played the first and have not played this one... seriously? what the hell is wrong with you? If you own Darksiders 2 already, you don't have to get the update. I think it was worth my 6 bucks, but i am a bit of a fanboy.

What can I say about this fabulous game. For me, it is Dan Dare resurrected. It is Buck Rogers brought into the present. (That will tell you something about my age :). NMSky takes me back to when I first played "Elite" the Amiga game created by David Braben and Ian Bell. I can never forget the heart-stopping thrill as I docked and the music of The Blue Danube carried me into the space station. Then came, of course: "Frontier: Elite Two"; "Frontier: Encounters" and eventually "Elite Dangerous". Elite Dangerous was and is a great game. The detail is amazing. The possibities endless.
However, now to "No Man's Sky". We all know it got off to a truly rocky start, with Sean Murray actually verbalising the potential as fact, when that was not, at that time, true. As I watched and read his comments and then the horrific realization that players revealed of the (then) actual game, I lost all hope - until now.
So here is my present review, after, as you can see, I have played approx. 86 hours. Even with that amount of hours I still have only scratched the surface and I haven't even started the Path of Atlas story-line. I did not choose it at the beginning and still I am having a ball. Eventually I stumbled onto the Quest Line, which, it seems does take you onto the Path of Atlas . Until then I can safely say to Hello Games: "Thank you so much for hanging in and turning an ugly duckling into a fabulous swan". Even with more patches to come, this game is now, (especially since the 1.30 patch), a definite winner.
So far, as I fly around the several planets, discover new things to do (no spoilers), see wonderful sunrises and sunsets, meet intriguing / interesting aliens, get my Hyperdrive and begin to explore outer space, nibble at the little hints which are gently steering me along my own, procedurally-generated path, find a crashed wreck once in a while, learn how to trade with different species, I am, once again, reliving my childhood space fantasies, although now with very acceptable and, for me, fabulous graphics.
For those interested, my PC specs are: Windows 7 Prof. 64 bit; Processor: i7 4790CPU, 3.6HGz; NVidia GeForce GTX 960; Memory: 16 RAM; I am connected to my TV Ultra HD and can run the game at resolution 3840 by 2160. However, because I then get quite low fps at times (even though still smooth), I choose to run it at 2560 by 1440, with some settings at Ultra and some low. Works fine and graphics are still great with good fps.
Here is my personal advice to any potential space traveler:
1. At this time (compared with a year ago), ignore the continuing negative comments. Hello Games have stepped up to the plate and are producing a winner.
2. As you start the game, take some time to watch Youtube (up to date) reviews and gameplay tips so you won't be too bogged down and frustrated and tempted to give up. Simple things like how to create stuff by, (on the PC), pressing "E" to bring up the list of what you can create or realizing that, when you leave your ship and the most recent save takes place, that you can choose (without ruining the story) to go back to it if you make the wrong decision out of the possible 3 answers in the space nodule which you have entered or which are the best places to find what you need, etc., etc.
3. Above all, don't be tempted to rush to get the best ship ingame or to quickly amass fabulous wealth or to become the best fighter overnight. There are some guides which will show you how to do these but as far as I am concerned, they destroy the possibility of you creating your own story - your own special life in your own particular world. If you follow other very detailed game guides, I believe you are missing out. Immerse yourself in this NMS universe. Be your own character in your own Alternative World. Enjoy yourself as you explore and find things out in your own time.
4. As I have just mentioned, take your time; wander around; soak in the atmosphere; be there, in that world, living your own self-chosen adventure. The possibilities are endless. Be prepared to be surprized, astounded, encouraged, relieved, happy.
Finally, I anguished throughout the recent Steam sale bacause of the original comments from a year ago until finally, one day before the sale ended, I bought the game. I have no regrets. Now, after 86 hours, I do not hesitate to say the game is worth full price.
Be reassured (Disclaimer) - I am not in any way associated with Hello Games. I have no axe to grind or ulterior motive in giving this review. I am having a fabulous time and looking forward to getting into my own world ASAP. Enjoy yours. :)

This is an exceptional experience. Is it perfect, hell no.
A lot of the negative reviews will say that it's basically an interactive movie. I love movies, and would love to be emersed in them more. Another criticism is that the combat is clunky. Well, it can be, but it is also pretty stylish, and, when you get to grips with it, not so bad. Thirdly, there are sections which are a bit frustrating (I'm looking at you, Sitr's fire), but you get over it.
Positively, this is some amazing story telling, superb voice acting, excellent motion capture (some of the best I've seen in a game; Andromeda should be ashamed), simply gorgeous set design and graphics, and engaging, fleshed out characters.
But by the end, the research, consideration, and inclusion of psychosis as a major plot element was simply stunning. I've worked with homeless individuals suffering psychosis, so it's not a new concept to me. This game just takes it to a whole new narrative level. It really was exceptional.
If you want a game about hack and slash "I'm the biggest badass" heroing, go elsewhere, this ain't it.
If you want a (as far as I know) utterly unique carefully storied experience that looks and feels just right, with a brutally spun plot, and fleshed out characters, this is for you.

Really neat little game if you have a bit of patience for it. Why? Controls and overall execution.
Here's what you *NEED* to do:
1. Change the resolution by editing the config.ini in the install directory(Steam\steamapps\common\Hammerfight). Change it to something like 1280x960 or similiar. The original is 800x600 i think, so just multiply both numbers to a same number. Don't make it wide as it will stretch and look ugly. Don't make it fullscreen as your screen is probably wide(unless you un-wide it somehow).
2. In options in the game(to the left) change mouse sensitivity to 100 or close to that. Probably 100 unless you want to break your wrist. Maybe increase DPI outside of the game, directly to your mouse. The controls are hard to get used to, so you need as much control as you can get. (Yes, it will be a bit hard navigating the menus UNLESS you have a mouse which has a DPI-switch button; mine is 1800 and 200, lol)
3. Make it windowed mode and restart. (I might be missing something about the options, so play with it a bit yourself, it's not much options there anyway)
4. OPTIONAL. Put grafics to 0.2 and in config.ini change all "GFX_RENDER_***" to "false". Maybe not all of them.
5. Be fu cking hardcore. Have patience, try over and over again, be ballsy, devious, smart. Not saying if it's worth it or not, just saying that if you like everything BUT the controls - trust me, you just need a little bit of time to get the handle of it.
I played it before like 5 or more years ago and I also remember being mad. But I also remember lots of fun too. I could've dropped it like many other people here right now, but I had too much love for physics engines and fancy graphics; and I still do. I will repeat - maybe it's just all about the taste.

Like other games in the 2D shooter genre, Booster Trooper gives you control of a soldier that has the ability to move in pretty much any direction with the assistance of rocket pack. The backgrounds and map detail are incredibly gorgeous. The graphic feel like you are playing in a completely 3D environment. The multitude of ordinance animations and blood effects are done with a surprisingly high level of quality for each player and weapon. Almost every single piece of audio included with Booster Trooper seems to have been designed to match the games intensity and in most cases it might even charge it up. The handful of screams when someone is finished off give the characters a little personality and round out the audio set nicely. Even if you're a pro in this area of gaming, the number of weapons available to you would take at least a few dozen games to get a basic handle on the entire set. If you've been a long time fan of this game type, or even if you're new to the party and are simply looking to test the waters, Booster Trooper is a solid choice. Guns, jet-packs, and beautiful scenery all make for a wonderful day.

Hammerfight is a physics-based fighting game set in a world where people fight in helicopter-like flying machines with hammers, guns, and other stuff. Like the description says. (My low playtime is because most of me playing this game was on the Humble Bundle distribution)
Pros:
--I don't care what people say, the controls are FINE. Just turn the mouse sensitivity all the way to max.
--Wide variety of weapons with various advantages and disadvantages
--Interesting storyline
--Challenging but not too hard once you get the hang of it
--Endless arena mode to show off your mad skillz
Cons:
--Hammerball is ridiculously difficult and honestly not that fun.
--Macelike weapons are overpowered and guns are too difficult to use
--Can't get all weapons in a single save unless you hack your save
Oh, and you can hack this game. After beating the game, you can be like me and try to figure out how the game's engine works by messing with the player save files, eventually allowing you to do things like my profile picture. It's also quite hilarious to ram enemies with 100000000 sharpness shields, get free hammer coins, or have the arena announcer call you absurd names.

Not sure how other people are putting in 20+ hours in this game. The campaign is only around 3 hours long. After that you can just fight in the arena however long you want, but it gets repetitive fast. Overall it's a fun game if you can get past the bad controls.

This is at its base a pretty fun game - it plays pretty smoothly, especially once you get the knack of jump boosting, the weapons give you a good range of tactical/playstyle preference options, while not perfectly balanced they are all viable options with benefits and weaknesses. The game modes cover all the basics - Capture the Flag, base defense, team death match, free for all, but there is nothing really innovative here.
The arenas are graphically fairly diverse, but probably most of them are a bit too similar tactically, while others are a bad idea if you plan on having bots due to the limited routes and the poor AI pathing - if set to low levels you should be able beat up on the AI with its slow reactions and poor aim, if set hard the bots are pretty challenging as long as they don't get stuck on scenery, or failing to find a route to the target when playing CTF or base defense.
Generally I wouldn't buy this to play against the AI, and decent random online games are rare nowadays, but if a group of friends wanted a fun lightweight action game to play against each other regularly, this would be a decent option.

Physics based combat game, you drive a flying machine swinging oversized melee weapons, destroying your opponents with overwhelming brutality.
The story is a little hard to follow because it is explained through text boxes between levels, but the world they created has good care put into it, took inspiration from ancent greek and medieval arabic civilizations, with a good deal of clockpunk and cosmic horror elements put in the mix.
the Campaign is enjoyable, with good variety, but you have little control over whats going on or where you want to go, I really wish this game was more like an rpg, that gave me the possibility to explore a little bit more of this detailed enviroment and get quests and sidequests.
now, talking about the combat, the titular "HAMMERFIGHT" which i guess is the main reason you even clicked on the storepage to begin with; all i can tell is: yes, it is awesome.
Now, all you need to do to score a hit, is your mouse: you control your flying machine by dragging, making it roteate a bit and once you have momentum you can smash the opponent.
it's quite simple, but difficult to master.
You've got a lot of choice regarding weapons, you get maces, swords, spears, waraxes, warhammers etc... everything has his weight and damage that directly influences your style of combat; the fights are frenetic, often chaotic if you don't know what you are doing, everytime you score a hit, the game simulates all you want to hear or see in a medieval fight: the satisfying "CLANG" of metal against metal, bits of armor or wood flying everywhere, fire, blood, down to the last messy bit.
Now, as for the negative, I just have to warn you that the single enemy warrior is more of a threat to himself than it is to you, that's why the game loves to set you up against handicap matches, where the AI will employ mostly dirty tactics to take you down, and you'll scream "But that's not fair!" a couple of times.
But putting that aside, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for something special.

I'd been meaning to replay this game a second time before submitting a review, mainly because of some plot developments that really demand a second viewing in order to contextualize properly the things that are happening in the game.
I did play the devs' previous games multiple times, but I have to admit, part of the reason why I'd taken so long here was because AWIA SCARES me. People may differ on what they conceive as horror, but for me, this is a horror game. Yes, it continues the sort of exploratory and puzzle style with focus on narration and story from the dev's previous games, but it is terrifying to me.
It begins with some text that appears straightforward, but then gets increasingly intense as the text screens progress, accompanied by some very aptly ominous music. And that's just the prologue before the game begins. You awaken to find yourself in a bright, oversaturated, and mesmerizing arboreal environment. And things seem pleasant again. Yeah, you're locked in a shed, but you easily get out, and you're able to communicate with your mom. But as you begin to explore your surroundings, things get more unnerving, and you find yourself feeling more vulnerable.
That's much as I can really describe of the setting without spoiling anything. The story in AWIA is a bit vague and unclear at first (and even a little after a second viewing), but it's not a disservice to the game. It's a very surreal experience, and the game does an excellent job of slowly giving more information to the player about who you are and what is going on. It's actually done very well, and adds to why the game is so scary to me. I can't really say much, but just the little bits of flavor text when you pick up certain items, or enter certain areas help to convey, although not so subtly, very organically, bits and pieces of your character (like why you can only carry one item at a time).
Speaking of flavor text, the dev mentioned to me in a previous comment how one of the things he added in The Music Machine, was a larger variety of objects in the world to interact with because he felt that it added immersion. I definitely agree, and it was one of the things I liked in TMM versus The Moon Sliver. It gets even better in this game. When you attempt to use certain objects to deal with certain puzzles, there's actually unique text describing why your item doesn't work, instead of a generic “this item does not work here”. It's great, and I could be wrong, but I think there are also different ways to solve some of the different puzzles. All this just adds to the immersion, that you really are a little girl just fumbling around trying to figure stuff out.
And as you try to figure stuff out, the game may seem a bit slow at the beginning (at least it was for me, because I could not figure out many of the puzzles without quite a bit of roaming about because the...trigger points aren't as obvious), but it's quite rewarding, and like many good horror films...it gets increasingly disturbing as you progress, until you get to the final sequence and it's just snowballing in your face.
Overally, I greatly recommend this if you're into the previous games by the dev. And even if you weren't, I feel like you might have a different opinion about this. The game is much more intense. The puzzles are much more interesting. And the voice acting is incredible (as I said, this game legitimately scares me. It's emotionally taxing for all sorts of reasons). The story and characters seem rich. I say seem, because again, it's a bit unclear. But as I said, it's not a bad thing, and I look forward to additional plays, and looking through internet discussions to piece together exactly what is going on between the girl and her mother.
The graphics are gorgeous, and very fitting as you'll find. The music is excellent as with the dev's previous works. And at the end of the day. It's cheap, it's a quick play (under an hour). If you're looking for a quick, immersive, horror experience but with more emotional and narrative substance, I'm not sure you can really do better than this.

Darksiders 2 is probably one of my favorite aRPGs in recent years/ Althought the Deathinitive Edition does currently have some performance issues, the support that Nordic Games offered for Red Faction: Guerilla makes me optimistic that they will continue to work with the community and patch it to work properly.
I enjoyed the original Darksiders, but the sequel expands and improves on every aspect. Some quick comments.
- The graphics are indeed much improved. Crisp, clean, and the cel-shaded inspired art style is lovely with the overhauled lighting.
-The music, as in the original version of this game, is outstanding, and easily some of Jesper Kyd's best work. Equal parts gothic and celtic inspirations make the soundtrack well worth remembering.
-The voice acting, and the characterization of Death in particular, is exceptional. My biggest issue with the original Darksiders was that War was basically a grimdark Space Marine. Death, on the other hand, is always handy with a bit of much needed snark, sarcasm, and even the occasional moment of sensitivity. This is the reaper as I like to envision him.
- The gameplay is quick, satisfyingly punchy, and has a gentle learning curve with a high plateau. Playing with various specs and active abilities is quite enjoyable, and finding an upgrade for your equipment is always nice.
Overall, I would wholeheartedly recommend the Deathinitive Edition for newcomers to the series. For anyone who already owns and has played the original release of the game, you will not find anything new here, but revisiting a fine game in revised form is very enjoyable.

TL;DR - it's an incredibly fun game where you're one little dude fighting in large battles. The game lets you play pretty much any way you want, whether it be taking part in the intense frontline action, or sneaking behind the enemy and taking them out with silenced weapons. Very fun, highly recommended if you like the idea! Oh and there's multiplayer.
In RUNNING WITH RIFLES (RWR) you get dropped into the middle of a brutal and bloody war between the Greenbelts (USA), the Graycollars (Germany), and the Brownpants (Russia). You play as one soldier in an army of hundreds as you slaughter dozens of enemy soldiers, die a lot, get reincarnated each time as another soldier, and rise gradually through the ranks, battling it out across some unknown country trying to completely dominate the enemy. RWR is super fun, and the developers are friendly and dedicated to the game.
There is a campaign mode, where you go from one map to the next, completely capturing each one as you go,
There are about 10 maps (which are all very well designed) to wage war across in the campaign. You can also play any of these maps as a single quick battle, although there's no guarantee that it will be over quickly. Each map can take anywhere from 20 minutes to over 5 hours
with the frontline moving back and forth with each attack and counter-attack.
In multiplayer, you can play PvE or PvPvE, with a huge number of people (up to 64 I believe). Playing online is super fun because you can actually use proper teamwork with other players, to annihilate the enemy soldiers on the front lines or to stealthily capture a base behind the enemy lines.
When you start playing, the basics are obvious: run with your rifle and click in the direction of enemies to shoot at them. But it's not actually that simple, because the game is fairly realistic when it comes to dying. One bullet is enough to drop you where you stand, leaving you wondering where the bullet even came from. Running straight towards the enemy holding down the left mouse button will get you killed over and over with no reward. You have to use cover, utilise mortar and artillery strikes, call in airborne reinforcements, move with your allies, set up machine gun installations, and use tanks or other vehicles to break through enemy lines.
There are lots of different weapons and items that you can use, including shotguns, sniper rifles, grenade launchers, rocket launchers, riot shields, and flares. There is something for pretty much every playstyle. Need to get behind the enemy and destroy a comms tower? Get in a camouflage suit, take a silenced sniper rifle and pistol, some C4, and you're good to go.
The game lets you change quite a few game options before you start a singleplayer game, such as friendly/enemy accuracy, starting XP and RP, etc. This basically determines the difficulty. On higher difficulties, the game is very tough, and this is when battles become hour-long stalemates, the streets and fields quickly turning into blood-soaked killing grounds, until you successfully create an advantage by changing up your tactics.
Overall, if you like the idea of being an individual taking part in a large-scale war, you should definitely put this game on your wishlist. Keep in mind that you will die a lot, and it can be kind of frustrating at times, but it's always entertaining. It's also obvious that a lot of love was put into the game. Overall, just really good. Highly recommended!

Janken, (Rock-Paper-Scissors for you Gaijins) is a competition that demands the utmost of determination and skill. Hosting endless layers of mindgames upon mindgames behind its deceivingly simple ruleset, it is not an activity to be partaken by the simple-minded. So imagine my surprise and delight when I would find such a game to be offered on a non-Japanese service such as Steam.
Unlike in countries with inferior cultures (take the United States for example with its barbarous sports like Football and Rugby where those primitive apes thoughtlessly throw themselves at each other. I imagine it is due to the resulting brain damage that the East has evolved to be more intelligent than the West), where it is treated as a mere children’s game, Janken is an artform in Japan, as obvious as it should be through the likes of manga such as "Kaiji"and "Liar Game" (Ignore the simpletons that recommend you to simply “watch the anime”. Their brains, likely atrophied by years of Transformers and Superhero flicks, cannot comprehend that absorbing both is integral to the artists’ intended experience).
In fact, I think the only thing that would make this game better is if it were made by the Japanese. They would take it a step beyond what the Western developers have created by tailoring a deep and intricately woven backstory for each character. The main character would be brooding and mysterious, if only due to his troubled past which will be revealed over the course of the campaign. Rocky would have had a rough childhood, having been teased all his life for his genetic deformity caused by the accident that lost him both of his parents. Randy would have grown up in the slums, and would have slowly risen to the top through sheer will and determination. And of course the female would have been a childhood friend of the main character who made a promise to one day marry him. With such modifications, the game could possibly exceed “G-senjou no Maou - The Devil on G-String” as the greatest game on Steam (a nod to my fellow G-senjou no Maou enthusiasts), but I digress.
I have seen several criticisms of the game containing only a single player campaign. These cancerous philistines are everything wrong with the state of Western gaming. A multiplayer experience cannot provide the tempestuous rollercoaster of emotional highs and lows that a precariously crafted single-player game can. I am immensely grateful that the Japanese industry does not so easily succumb to the demands of the degenerate masses and refuses to arbitrarily add multiplayer into games that clearly don’t need it.
In either case, the developers at Wholetone Games have proven themselves sufficiently competent by expertly building upon the existing Janken formula (a task I previously thought impossible). Through careful placement of strategic combo moves, players have to put infinitely more thought into their turn (a concept that may be difficult for our Western counterparts to comprehend). With its near-perfect composition of intellectual stimulation and emotional depth, I wholeheartedly recommend Ｊａｎｋｅｎ　ｃｈａｎｐｉｏｎ (Rock Paper Scissors Champion) to all lovers of high-quality entertainment.

The game that started a franchise with various sequels, many of which I haven't even played and probably will never get round to. I admit, it's silly to judge a game without playing it properly but from what I observed, it seems the cash-grabbing sequel-popping has made Ubisoft forget what made AC1 great in the first place. A stunning game on all accounts, with a few irritating flaws.
Positive:
The game's story establishes the whole Assassin's Universe, with you playing as Desmond Miles; a present-day prisoner of a modern-day Templar Organisation forced into the Animus machine that recounts memories of his ancestor, Altair, in order to uncover the location of a certain artefact. Altair is part of an Oriental Assassin Brotherhood, focused on fighting corruption amidst the chaotic time that is the Crusades, but having broken the Brotherhood's tenents he must undergo various missions to redeem himself. Most of the game focuses within the Animus as you step into the role of Altair. Both storylines, merging into one are quite interesting. A lot of material is covered, ranging from real historical figures and events during that Dark Age to certain fictional twists relating to the ancestor's experience. Despite a lot of content it still leaves just enough open questions for the inevitably released sequel Assassin's Creed 2.
All the real action takes place within the memory machine as the assassin. Altair, despite being a useless swimmer, is a Talented Swordsman and Parkour Master who can climb anywhere and jump meters down into haystacks. Combat is very entertaining, particularly as you witness gallons of blood ooze as Altair performs brutal counter-attacks from both small and large blades. Could this gameplay be any cooler? Only if you incorporate it within a massive sandbox world! The developers clearly worked hard to craft the landscapes. Whether you're roaming Damascus and Jerusalem, or riding the horse around the cliffs and country there is plenty to explore and breathtaking views to admire.
There's nothing to complain about regarding graphics and even sound. Whether it's the voice-acting, effects, or music; all are done well. The soundtrack consits of a wide range of styles, combining Middle Eastern ethnic sounds with electronic harmonies. Nolan North sounds like Nolan North as usual, but he still gives enough expression and emotion that makes it easy enough to feel for Desmond. Altair on the other hand, despite having a good voice often sounds very flat and rather odd that this Semitic person speaks with an American accent when no other Medieval character does (even the Crusaders). Nonetheless, this is passable when you take into account all other qualities.
Cons:
As everyone stated, this game can get quite repetitive. Main missions have very similar structures, with the only difference being the kind of cutscenes that play before you attempt to assassinate your target. Although the Director's Cut addition does include some extra side missions and the choice of when and which to do, it still doesn't feel varied enough. Fortunately the repetitiveness is something that was fixed in AC2, but for those that are really turned off by it well... AC1 is full of it.
There's another flaw that doesn't get mentioned much, and that's the tedious unskippable dialogue sequences. During the first playthrough I don't mind them for story-related purposes, but once you've completed the game and want to replay, almost every level starts with a boring cutscene before you can get into the gameplay. IMO, this is an even worse problem than the repetitive missions because at least those didn't stop the game from being fun. It's a shame because had those dialogue scenes been skippable on replay I would be much more forgiving but alas, is the reason why I add quite a few drops to my score.
Conclusion:
Everyone's talked about this game, and of course they did. The game was very new for its time and had a big influence not just on sequels, but on other VG titles to incorporate aspects of sandbox and third-person exploration. AC1 still does it better than a lot of those games. There's a great story to tell here, and great gameplay to experience. But I won't blame you if you're put off from replaying the missions due to unskippable cutscenes once you finish the main story.

Well this game is a hot mess. Seriously, I'm really not sure how the AC series took off, although I'm glad it did as the later installments are much, much better in a variety of ways. This is an older game, so I guess I won't spend too much time describing things in detail, so in the words of Inigo Montoya, let's "sum up".
Graphics:
For its time, this game had relatively impressive graphics. The attention to detail from the water, to the glistening sun, to the  stucco on the sides of buildings, the graphics are one of its only saving graces, and I'm not one to care about graphics particularly if everything else is fantastic. The only particularly awkward thing about the graphics is the unnervingly jelly-like faces (seriously, when they're in the lab talking to each other? That was weeeeird).
Rating: 7/10 (for its time)
Storyline:
I was lost through most of the storyline. It wasn't an enjoyable story, and it seemed convoluted in a lot of ways. It's difficult to describe an AC game without giving away plot details (really difficult), but if you've played any of the newer games, this one is really nothing special. It goes as predicted, and they seem to be prone to giving away things that'll probably most definitely likely happen later on; they're their own worst spoilers. So a predictable storyline with little originality, filled with "why?"s leaves little to the imagination. For example, you're an assassin, and you're wearing the garb of an assassin, running through cities. Guards randomly attack you for no apparent reason and call you an infidel (because of your clothes? I don't know), but yet other guards just let you run on by, and NPCs that you rescue will "tell the whole city of your bravery/sacrifice" (thanks? I'm so glad everyone will know I'm an assassin, except those few guards that really don't seem to care?) - Honestly, there was a lot of arbitrary dialogue that didn't make much sense in relation to the character you're playing. I'd say the storyline was arguably the least impressive element of the game, and the later games certainly improved the creativity, flow, and continuity tremendously.
Rating: 4/10
Gameplay:
Oh boy, this game wasn't that fun for me at all. For starters, the controls on the PC are horrendous. The camera bugs out all the time, your character will sometimes jump in random directions with little input from you, the parkour elements aren't that responsive, and... you can't swim.. You're a great assassin, but if you touch the water, you drown. I guess if you don't want to be assassinated, just find an island somewhere and hope the assassin randomly decides to jump into the water? Problem solved! Anyways, yeah, controls are all fudged up. Activating things in the lab sometimes takes a few button presses to actually make it "take", sometimes the camera spins around your head if it's obstructed by something close to you. Aside from the camera and controls, the gameplay is really repetitive. You have targets to assassinate, and in between those targets in the cities, you just go around and do these side-missions where you might escort somebody (where you're always attacked), race to an informant before time runs out, collect flags on top of buildings before time runs out (why?), assassinate minor targets like guards without alerting the guards (sometimes maddening, especially when they're in the middle of a giant group of people and rarely venture away, forcing you to sit and wait for them to move so you can have a chance - there are multiple targets, so if you succeed at one and alert the guards on the second one or on the way back to the informant, you fail the mission). There are pickpocketing missions, ones where you have to save citizens from a group of guards attacking them (why? I guess protection money or something, I don't know - every group of citizens is always needing to be saved from guards). Sometimes the citizen saving missions bug out and the NPC disappears (not dies, disappears. *poof*), so you have to wander away and come back and kill the kind guards again.
Another problem with the gameplay is the combat. The combat is *terrrrrrrible*. It involves trying to time clicking the mouse with when the sword hits. It's difficult to get it right all the time and pretty much guarantees you'll be parried at least once with every swing (why?). It's so repetitive that you eventually get to the point where you're just clicking the button non-stop and hoping someone attacks you so you can counter them (they can kill you much quicker if you're attacking than if you just stand still without attacking... I don't know). They'll knock you down and sit there and wait for you to get up (how nice of them!). Sometimes you'll be fighting 10 of them at once (I guess quite often, really, depending on how much of a risk-taker you are). They'll chase you if you run away, clear across the city, and you have to semi-hide from them until you can actually hide in the conveniently placed boxes with shades scattered around cities, or the random piles of hay everywhere. They'll then walk right up next to the box, stop and act like they can't find you (REALLY UBISOFT?), then all of a sudden run back down the side of the buildings. It's so crazy. Oh, and you'll be riding through the countryside and random people will just start chasing you for no reason at all until you have 987439873498 people trying to kill you for going too fast I guess.
Horrible, horrible gameplay.
Rating: 2/10
Sound:
The sounds in the game were rather detailed, except you'll be hearing that sword-clanging sound long after you stop playing the game. High quality, attention to detail. Music was decent and atmospheric. The only qualm I had was the absolutely atrocious voice-acting (hoooo-boy, it was terrible).
Rating: 5/10
All-in-all, I guess I'd give the game a 4/10, and really only recommend that you play it if you're wanting to see where the long (almost too long) Assassin's Creed series began. If not, you can safely ignore this title, or if you've played it before, don't waste your money getting it on Steam. I have plenty of unplayed games in my library and I'm slightly disappointed I wasted my time finishing this one, but c'est la vie.

What can I say about this fabulous game. For me, it is Dan Dare resurrected. It is Buck Rogers brought into the present. (That will tell you something about my age :). NMSky takes me back to when I first played "Elite" the Amiga game created by David Braben and Ian Bell. I can never forget the heart-stopping thrill as I docked and the music of The Blue Danube carried me into the space station. Then came, of course: "Frontier: Elite Two"; "Frontier: Encounters" and eventually "Elite Dangerous". Elite Dangerous was and is a great game. The detail is amazing. The possibities endless.
However, now to "No Man's Sky". We all know it got off to a truly rocky start, with Sean Murray actually verbalising the potential as fact, when that was not, at that time, true. As I watched and read his comments and then the horrific realization that players revealed of the (then) actual game, I lost all hope - until now.
So here is my present review, after, as you can see, I have played approx. 86 hours. Even with that amount of hours I still have only scratched the surface and I haven't even started the Path of Atlas story-line. I did not choose it at the beginning and still I am having a ball. Eventually I stumbled onto the Quest Line, which, it seems does take you onto the Path of Atlas . Until then I can safely say to Hello Games: "Thank you so much for hanging in and turning an ugly duckling into a fabulous swan". Even with more patches to come, this game is now, (especially since the 1.30 patch), a definite winner.
So far, as I fly around the several planets, discover new things to do (no spoilers), see wonderful sunrises and sunsets, meet intriguing / interesting aliens, get my Hyperdrive and begin to explore outer space, nibble at the little hints which are gently steering me along my own, procedurally-generated path, find a crashed wreck once in a while, learn how to trade with different species, I am, once again, reliving my childhood space fantasies, although now with very acceptable and, for me, fabulous graphics.
For those interested, my PC specs are: Windows 7 Prof. 64 bit; Processor: i7 4790CPU, 3.6HGz; NVidia GeForce GTX 960; Memory: 16 RAM; I am connected to my TV Ultra HD and can run the game at resolution 3840 by 2160. However, because I then get quite low fps at times (even though still smooth), I choose to run it at 2560 by 1440, with some settings at Ultra and some low. Works fine and graphics are still great with good fps.
Here is my personal advice to any potential space traveler:
1. At this time (compared with a year ago), ignore the continuing negative comments. Hello Games have stepped up to the plate and are producing a winner.
2. As you start the game, take some time to watch Youtube (up to date) reviews and gameplay tips so you won't be too bogged down and frustrated and tempted to give up. Simple things like how to create stuff by, (on the PC), pressing "E" to bring up the list of what you can create or realizing that, when you leave your ship and the most recent save takes place, that you can choose (without ruining the story) to go back to it if you make the wrong decision out of the possible 3 answers in the space nodule which you have entered or which are the best places to find what you need, etc., etc.
3. Above all, don't be tempted to rush to get the best ship ingame or to quickly amass fabulous wealth or to become the best fighter overnight. There are some guides which will show you how to do these but as far as I am concerned, they destroy the possibility of you creating your own story - your own special life in your own particular world. If you follow other very detailed game guides, I believe you are missing out. Immerse yourself in this NMS universe. Be your own character in your own Alternative World. Enjoy yourself as you explore and find things out in your own time.
4. As I have just mentioned, take your time; wander around; soak in the atmosphere; be there, in that world, living your own self-chosen adventure. The possibilities are endless. Be prepared to be surprized, astounded, encouraged, relieved, happy.
Finally, I anguished throughout the recent Steam sale bacause of the original comments from a year ago until finally, one day before the sale ended, I bought the game. I have no regrets. Now, after 86 hours, I do not hesitate to say the game is worth full price.
Be reassured (Disclaimer) - I am not in any way associated with Hello Games. I have no axe to grind or ulterior motive in giving this review. I am having a fabulous time and looking forward to getting into my own world ASAP. Enjoy yours. :)

To the Moon is one of those uncommonly rare games where the intensity of the player's emotional involvement is such that despite being a rather short game (the story itself is easily completed within the span of three or four hours) one feels as though they've spent dozens of hours playing.
In many ways, playing To the Moon is an exerting experience. Not that much skill is  needed or that it requires physical prowess, but rather that every action and task the characters - and through them the player - has to undertake is intrinsically tied to a grippingly gloomy backdrop.
Yes, To the Moon is one of those games which addresses issues still widely non-represented (at any rate as central narrative or mechanistic concerns) throughout the game industry: grief, regret and the relentless irrevocability of passing time. Underneath the cutesy and colourful pixel art and quirky characters and dialogue, To the Moon goes beyond the usual question "what if you could rewrite your own past" and asks "what does your past mean to you? How far would you go to achieve your dreams?"
Now I understand this seems hyperbolic, and I will amit there is much in the game to deterr potential players.
The controls tend to be simplistic and navigation through the levels is consequently not as optimal as it might be.
The narration, although (and I will avow that this is merely my personal feeling) usually spot-on can at times be slightly too forceful.
Perhaps what might deterr players most is the overall lack of freedom which is left to the player in deciding how to interact with the tale: the story is very much linear, and while this is a staple of the genre I would not be surprised if many a player found it repugnant, especially when the current trend is towards multiplicity of choice.
That being said, the positives seem to me to be so overwhelming as make these flaws menial.
The game's music is masterful: subtle when discretion is needed, powerful in emotional moments, ominous in the darkest moments... I have yet to find such quality in a game of such small a scope.
The characters are not only endearing, they - perhaps more importantly - human: they have complexity of emotion, and neither is quite as monochromatic as they might seem.
The main story is compelling and offers quite a few surprises and twists.
And most importantly the emotional impact of the narative is so powerful that there are very few games (at least among those I've played) which do not pale before To the Moon. The game's major subtlety is in the way it chooses to deal with its subject matter -  I'll refrain from saying more here so as not to spoil the suprise for those who have not played it yet.
In conclusion I heartily recommend this game to any of you who are willing to look beyond its inocuous aspect and experience a deeply thought-provoking narrative which, for my part, had me step away from my keyboard quite a few times to reflect on what my actions in the game truly meant. If this sounds like the kind of thing you'd enjoy, I'd say it doesn't get much better than To the Moon.

Hob is a mysterious experience, one that honestly should not be missed if you're a fan of an puzzle platformer that tries to immerse the player in its bewildered tale.
The story is told through environment alone, by your actions shifting the world, exploring and by glyphs or small details placed through the world. This will surely put a lot of people off, as its hard to keep track to whats going on if you dont pay attention or rush through the world. That being said, if you do take time to learn the world, its quite a good tale, assuming I understood it correctly. It wont blow your mind, but it is quite interesting.
Gameplay is mainly composed of platforming and puzzle solving with a bit of combat. Neither of those things are hard or annoying which was great. Camera is fixed so you will have to rely on the game to show you the environment rather than having a free look.
Atmosphere wise, its nice and its incredible how it all fits once you start "fixing" the world. Its like a giant puzzle with shifting lands and different environments.
Sound design is not something you'd praise, and while there is music and sound effects, they rarely make an impression, which is a shame for such a pretty world.
Overall while the game isnt something you'd praise, it is still quite the experience. if you're a fan of the genre, buy it and if you're not I would still recommend you at least give a try, if not for the obfuscated story but at least for the atmosphere and gameplay.  8/10

Some parts of the game suffer from tedium as they rely too much on timing and reflexes to grant you access to the next checkpoint but patience usually results in finding an effective solution to the problem. Slain is brutal, it’s metal, it’s unforgiving and a lot of fun if that’s what you’re looking for.

I stood up, controller gripped in my white knuckled fist, ready to hurl the accursed thing into the television, the ground….anywhere that might produce the catharsis that comes from rage-induced destruction. Then, as I calmed myself, I looked back to the screen where I faced the bold, bloodstained lettering I would come to know so well while playing Slain: Back from Hell, which simply read, "You have been Slain"
So, without further ado, allow me to introduce you to Slain: Back From Hell:
The story in Slain: Back From Hell is fairly simply gore pulp fare. You are a heavy metal viking all-around awesome warrior brought back from your restful, almost eternal slumber to once again vanquish the evil that has risen in the lands. You would rather just sleep, but the fates have determined that would not be so and as such you are determined to take out your frustration on said evil…and maybe even do some good while you are at it.
Often juvenile yet humorous, Slain  doesnt try to pretend the game is something it isnt. It is quite simply an over the top tale being told around equally over the top gameplay. In this regard, Slain carries itself well. Despite simplistic and (at times) intentionally bad writing which features a lot of “I’m the best”, “nah-ah, I’m the best” sort of banter, it works well given the intent and presentation. I would give the story an 8 out of 10. Could it have been better? Possibly. Should it have been? Probably not.
Gameplay is really the heart and soul of a game like Slain. So, how does the gameplay actually stack up? Quite well, as it turns out. This is not a game for the faint of heart. You will hack, slash, and cast spells on a path of gory destruction to the backdrop of chunky, guitar driven metal riffs. You will also die. Often. Like a lot. Probably every minute or two. Maybe even more frequently than that. It can be rage inducing without a doubt but when you finally calm down and get back to it,  you end up persevering and that comes with a definite feeling of satisfaction. This will be a rinse and repeat scenario however, so as I said before, Slain is not for the faint of heart.
Combat is handled in simple and yet effective fashion. You can attack, block, cast an attack spell, jump, and dodge left or right with the simple push of their respective buttons or trigger. There are also power attacks featured for both attack and spell casting which require you to hold down the proper button or buttons for a charge up. The spell will automatically discharge once it has charged. The power attack must be charged and then released with a timed second push of the button. Everything else related to attacking is simply based on judging space and terrain.
Slain also features light platforming such as jumping over traps and onto elevator platforms, jumping to trigger certain events, and of course jumping to avoid or better position yourself against enemies.
There is a fairly wide variety of enemies from your basic skeletons to spectral wolves to ghostly women with knives, gigantic bats, and so on. Each area features its own unique set of beasties and bad guys. There are also a fair amount of mini-bosses and each area also features an actual boss fight as well. Learning their patterns is essential to success although even having done so, you then must also execute your moves, sometimes flawlessly. I have found that sometimes after having died 20 or 30 times to a single boss or scenario, that often the best solution is the most basic. Increase your level of aggression and go for it!
Each enemy also has a weakness. For some, basic physical attacks or spells are the thing that will do them in quickly. Others require something extra such as spells. Fire, Ice, and so on. These spells become available one by one as you finish sections of the game. For example, you will receive a fire sword early on and an ice axe a bit later. These can be switched at will via the right thumbstick on your gamepad (and while I’m thinking about it….use a gamepad for this game. I can’t see wanting to play this with keyboard and mouse).
There are light puzzle aspects to this game, mostly centered around finding switches or defeating certain enemies to unlock new areas. There are also some secret areas you can find and unlock as well.
All told, gameplay was completely solid and highly intuitive in Slain. I think a 9.5 is the perfect rating for this.
As you can see already in the screenshots I have provided, Slain hearkens back to an older style of graphics in gaming. A bit muddier, a bit less distinct, but no less compelling and evocative. You are travelling through nightmarish realms and the graphics in Slain absolutely help to put you in the proper frame of mind.

Remember me is set in a very interesting world where, as I'm sure other reviewers have noted, memories have been commoditized. This allows for a number of interesting world-building pieces, including a particularly cruel prison (where memories are taken upon arrest and returned upon release) and broken "leapers" whose minds have been broken beyond repair due to constant tampering. One of the most interesting questions explored by the game is how we deal with trauma. Can trauma simply be deleted, or is it necessary to grow and learn as an individual? As a colleague once told me, "sometimes you just have to let people hurt." Though some have said that the game thinks it's smarter than it is, I can't say I found it particularly pretentious.
However, the game falters in some important gameplay and story aspects. The parkour elements are satisfying, but there is very little freedom in where Nilin can go. The combos feel smooth, but often the camera will swing around the make it difficult to see what you are doing, and the targeting of her projectile weapon is somewhat awful. You'll almost never target the enemy you'd like to if there are others in close proximity. Often, you must move as close as possible to the enemy you'd like to target. I enjoyed the creation of combinations, although I didn't unlock enough "pressens" (combo pieces, essentially) to really have a ton of flexibility. As you build focus, you gain the ability to do special moves, such as insta-killing robot enemies or planting a bomb in one enemy that damages all enemies in the area. These are extremely satisfying to use. Some of the stronger enemies (Johnny Greenteeth comes to mind prominently) require a bit of trial and error. For him particularly, as soon as you activate the special move that you must use to damage him, a message comes on screen telling you that "reconversion leapers" are immune to the move you've just activated. As you can tell something is different about the boss, Johnny Greenteeth, I just assumed that he was a "reconversion leaper" and wasted a ton of time hammering on his minions. I finally just looked up the strategy online.
The storyline, to me, felt very meandering. After I certain point, I gave up thinking about why I was going where I was going and doing what I was doing. Nilin seems to continually revisit the prison from which she escaped. Another big issue are the memory "remix" sections where Nilin must alter a memory to change the way a certain character feels about a situation. These are a wonderful concept, but boil down into simple time-consuming trial and error. You may alter a memory by turning on a television, moving a stool, etc., but it's basically impossible to imagine how that changes the scenario without watching the memory play out over and over.
Lastly, the final boss seems put in place simply to have a final boss. The entire game this entity has wanted to die, and at the end he seems very eager not only to fight you, but to kill you as well. No time is spent at all attempting to convince you to end his life. Your character has retrieved her own memories, sabotaged the memories of the most important individuals in Neo-Paris, fought some of the mightiest boss enemies, all to reach and destroy this boss that claims to want nothing more than to be destroyed (and who has helped you from the beginning - I apologize for the spoiler, but this is ludicrous). It wasn't a terribly difficult boss fight, but it certainly left a rotten taste in my mouth.

I just finished this game, and, overall, I quite liked it.  It had an interesting and compelling story, fascinating characters, and a mindblowing twist about halfway through (and another good one at the end).  It had one really big flaw: most of the game is just a climbing around the city and fighting random enemies.  The most interesting feature by far, the player-character's unique ability to rewrite others' memories, is something you only get to do four times throughout the entire game (and the first is really just for practice).  Stealing memories and using them to guide yourself past obstacles of various sorts, is also pretty interesting, and you get to do that a bit more often, but by far most of the game is spent in pretty generic combat.  I would add that boss fights in this game can get very frustrating.  Each boss requires certain special tricks to defeat, and the game does not really give enough information to figure it out.
No review of this, Dontnod's first game, could be complete without a comparison to its second game, Life is Strange.  Although in terms of story and setting, the two games could not be more different, they have a clear commonality.  Life is Strange is about altering the present by changing the past, whereas Remember Me is about altering the present by changing the way we remember the past.  The difference is that Life is Strange is much more focused on its story, characters, and unique concept, whereas Remember Me is mostly a fairly standard fighting game.  I could never escape the idea that Life is Strange was the game that Dontnod really wanted to make, and that it was Capcom that insisted on more conventional elements for Remember Me.  Bear in mind that I have no inside knowledge; for all I know, Dontnod wanted to make a standard combat-adventure game, and it was Capcom that was pressuring them to focus more on the unique memory-based elements, but that's not what I would guess.
Don't misunderstand me: assuming I am right about Capcom's attitude and actions, I would understand.  This was Dontnod's first game, the concept was unusual, and so I could understand why Capcom would have wanted some more conventional elements.  Also, given the story's setting and concept, and the nature of the player-character, having more combat elements was entirely reasonable.  I do wish that the combat had been more interesting.  The idea behind the Pressen combos was not a bad one, but if you are like me, and you are less than exceptionally coordinated, you will tend to rely on the punch-punch-punch combo a lot.
The only other thing I would say about this game itself is that it might have benefitted from a little more openness.  It was very easy to miss power-ups, and it would have been nice if they had made it easier to go back to get them once you realized you had missed them.  Sometimes, it made sense that you could not go back, as when you were going through a place where the doors sealed behind you, but it made relatively little sense when you were climbing your way around Paris.
All told, though, I enjoyed this game.  I had to make my way through some uninteresting combat and some frustrating boss fights to get to the good parts, but overall it was very much worth it.  I have heard that Dontnod is interested in doing a sequel, but that Capcom is not so interested, and that seems like a shame to me, since I think a sequel could make a lot of improvements.  But if Vampyr and Life is Strange 2, both of which I am very much looking forward to, both do well, maybe Capcom will reconsider.  In any case, for all its flaws, I definitely recommend this game, especially to those who like Life is Strange.

After playing until I completed the first "official" dungeon of the game (releasing the fire from the mountain), I feel I can now write a proper review.
Pros (as of 7:39 pm 11/12/15) :
- Game looks absolutely GORGEOUS, scenery characters and items included. (also, 5/10 things are shiny. That's an added plus in my book.)
- Adds a new difficulty, DEATHinitive. This is good for players like myself that plan on perfecting this game.
- For people that already own Darksiders 2, it's currently 12 dollars (was 6 up until 12:00 11/12/15). It's not much compared to it's soon to be $30 price tag.
- Despite its very rocky day one launch, Nordic seems very keen on listening to the Community and fixing any issues as soon as they can.
-The DEATHinitive Edition includes all the DLC (minus the soundtrack) already installed. If you didn't have all the DLC in the original, this is very much a plus. It'll make your new playthrough far more enjoyable and fresh.
-This version of Darksiders 2 adds Steam Cards. I don't think I need to explain why this is a good thing. (Gimme dat badge already...)
Cons (as of 7:39 pm 11/12/15) :
- As stated previous, had a very rocky day one launch. This means a handful of issues.
- As of 11/12/15, the DEATHinitive Edition isn't very optimized. Will change once game is properly optimized.
- Some hit detection issues against destructible items (i.e. boxes, ceramic vases, etc.), especially when framerate is fairly low due to sketchy optimization.
Now, I feel I should make this known, as it seems most of the community doesn't know. THQ, the original publisher of the Darksiders franchise, went out of business around 2013. That much a good 90% of us know, as well as the fact that the Darksiders franchise was created by Vigil Games, which also went out of business in 2013. Nordic Games bought the rights to most of the THQ IP's, including Darksiders. The new company that was put in charge of creating Darksiders 2: DEATHinitive Edition goes by the name of Gunfire Games, which as it turns out holds a rather large amount of Vigil Games employees. Essentially, it's the same people working on the upcoming Darksiders 3 that worked on the previous titles. The 6/12/30 dollar price tag is by no means a bad PR move, nor is it a robbery of the community. If it were some random company that had never even heard of the name "Darksiders", then it would, and I would fear for Darksiders 3.
Give this game some time people, Nordic is working on fixing it.
Update: I was incorrect. There are no new quests in the DEATHinitive Edition.

This game is an interactive experience, and one I find to be quite brilliant at times. Is it perfect? No; there are weaknesses in the gameplay aspect, as the gameplay is simple and mostly there to bridge the narrative experiences together. There are also some minor glitches that occur, unfortunately.
However, the game is built around delivering a narrative experience, and it succeeds wholeheartedly in that aspect. The story of Senua is gripping, and often haunting: I often played at night before bed, and I found myself dreaming about it (not so pleasant dreams).
I have also found myself interested in psychology, in dreams, and things of this nature in entertainment media and works of art. Ninja Theory did a great job representing the experience of what it would be like to suffer from psychosis. It is like a window into that world, so to speak. Also, the framing of the hero's quest is a perfect way for a player to travel in this sort of existence.
I really hope Ninja Theory continues in this style and touches upon another aspect of humanity, and all the while improving their game design even further.
Hellblade is definitely recommended, but expect a game of which the sole purpose to deliver the experience of a story--an interactive narrative.

Is it scary? You bet your butt, that game has areas that had me hiding behind my controller.

Some of the negative user reviews for this little game are not warrented at all. It's 3 bucks (sale) I mean come on!!! And yes it works on Steam/modern PC, you don't need a dedicated potato (sporting modern GTX1060 - no compat issues).
I wanted a hunting game just to chill tf out / different pace after my annual Paradox burnout, got suckered in by the negative user reviews of The Hunter Classic (which isn't remotely as bad as the cod crowd make out - fool me twice I know) and so bought this instead. Given I haven't played a hunting game since OG Deer Hunter / RMTH it is a pretty good sim and scary/atmospheric in places if you can ignore the late 90s polys and switch off the terrible ingame music (which isn't completely out of place if you have ever watched old school RL hunting videos with porno music).
Now find myself up for 30 bucks for Call of The Wild+DLC (THC is also great doing trial now), but HU2010 is also pretty good if you have no budget to speak off and can imagine textures / a decent grass draw distance in your mind's eye haha. The feel of the game (aside from the cheap ATV), range of weapons (a nice Lee Enfield model), huge parks, number of animals, equipment and Africa- all very nice and easily worth it if you need an escape and can't shell out for latest graphic$$$.

To put this into perspective, one of my favorite games of all time, Deer Hunter: The 2005 Season by Atari, was released in 2004. That game had great graphics for its time and it ran beautifully on my laptop that was more or less a folded piece of paper with a keyboard scribbled on it. This game doesn't look half as good despite being made five years later. Textures are oddly stretched on some maps, there's not much in the way of atmospheric effects, everything is pretty low-poly... if you're a visual gamer like I am, this game doesn't have much to offer.
I've had this game for several months now, and every time I load up the game, it feels like a fight from the beginning to the end. The mouse sensitivity when you're not holding your gun is really, really distracting. Trying to cycle through each item in your inventory can be a bit of a struggle, especially if you forget what you have equipped. If you're not paying attention you could accidentally fire at random, sending whatever you were sneaking up on in the opposite direction. Why in God's balls would you have 'Fire' bound to the same key as 'Activate'?
Shooting is very realistic; shooting the spine takes the animal down immediately, headshots kill it instantly, nailing a limb will slow it down... this is a feature missing in many big-budget titles (looking at you, Cabella's). You can decide what animals spawn on the enormous maps, and you decide the population of each species. You can choose the weather and time of day of your hunts. There's an enormous variety of weapons to choose and items to use, which will appeal to many people. There are plenty of animals to choose from, and each map comes with a true-to-life selection of animals that would inhabit the respective biomes.
I do have some hang-ups that probably bother me more than other people. Movement speed is really difficult to get used to. If the maps looked better, I might not complain as much, but my god, even sprinting feels like a crawl. This also makes tracking injured animals a real pain in the neck. The voice acting is atrocious, with dialogue like, "I'm so pumped!" and "Wait until I tell the girls about this!" and, my personal favorites, the over-exaggerated shrieks of "OW!" when you are attacked by some wild beast, or happen to run into a particularly sharp plant.
Do I like this game? Yeah, it's fun. Do I love it? Not particularly; it's just missing so much. Would I reccomend it? I mean, if it were a mobile game, absolutely - because that's what it looks like. But as a PC title, I just can't do it.
Overall, 5/10.

Well, this was another stellar game by one of my favorite developers, David Syzmanski. As with his pervious works, he takes a psychological horror concept and really drives it home using minimallistic and yet lush and evocative scenery with a short tale attached. To tell you any more than what is in the store page would be a disservice to a person wishing to play this, so I wont go into my personal thoughts on the story, but I will say that it is quite compelling.
This time around, the Unity 5 engine, but without using stock assets. This marks an evolution in Mr Syzmanski's development ideas and skills, as previouosly, he used stock assets (to perfection). Actually, if you were to play each of his games in order of release, you would easily be able to track a clear progression is ability and skill, with this game as the current culmination of his previous efforts.
As with previous games, this game makes heavy use of the interplay between light, darkness, and shadow to emphasize the desired atmosphere. Additionally, the original soundtrack and sounds further enhance the experience. All was done in outstanding fashion.
Another appealing aspect of this game was the 45 minute to 1 hour length. In my opinion, it was the perfect length to accomplish the goals it sets out to accomplish.
The controls are simple WASD with R/L mouse to pick up, use, and drop items, and shift to run, since walking around exploration games slowly is always something of a chore (in my opinion. I appreciate it when devs include running despite it not being strictly necessary).
The puzzles in this game werent too difficult to solve, but were clever, making good use of the items available in the game without getting in the way of the experience.
Anyway, I can go on and on about this game, but I will simply close out here by stating that this was a special experience and I was glad for the opportunity to play this game.
9 out of 10.

As this franchise enters 10 years of being beloved by many it's easy to overlook where everything started with this installment back in 2007.  Are it's controls clunky?  Yes.  Does it feel dated?  Yes.  But it's still Assassin's Creed, the game that started it all and this entry is absolutly a must play in the grand scheme of the franchise.  It's also the only true stealth game of the franchise in my opinion as combat can legitmately punish you in later portions of the game because at the end of the day you're playing an assassin, not a soldier that the likes of Ezio might make you think the protagonist is (I still love AC2 just pointing out the difference).
10/10 would leap to my death accidentally from that chruch in Acre again.

This first entry to the extensive Assassin's Creed franchise (how many of those games are there now?) still holds up well to today standards graphic- and gameplay-wise. While I encountered some weird glitches from times to times, those were more of the funny kind (guards walking on walls, citizens spawning out of nowhere in the middle of the street...) and I didn't encounter anything gamebreaking.
The layout for each city is amazing and it's really fun to roam the streets and navigate the rooftops. Likewise, gameplay for both parkour and combat is fairly solid despite a few hiccups here and there.
This game, however, isn't without its flaws.
The most noticeable one, I'd say, is that the free-roaming aspect is way underdeveloped and that the game gets dull and repetitive before you're halfway through the main plot. Each city serves you more of the same side objectives and the director's cut "extra content" does nothing to fix that. Each "playground" had potential for so much more so it's a real shame the different setting for each city and district doesn't make much of a difference. Why do guards unfairly brutalize citizens from the rich district the same way they do in the poor district? This doesn't make any sense and just shows lack of ideas towards more varied content. Even combat gets dull after a while despite the feeling of empowerment it provides, as you'll quickly end up using the same effective strategy to dispose quickly of enemies (a counter-attack with the hidden blade one-shots anything, even boss opponents).
The other, but less important, main flaw I'd like to mention, is that despite of its title, Assassin's Creed encourages you to play more like a mass murderer, and less like a stealthy assassin, as it provides you with zero incentive to play subtle. Successfully stealth-killing is in many situations downright impossible (not hard, it's actually meant to be undoable without getting noticed), and even when you succeed, it isn't rewarding. Most of the time, killing in the open any guard who noticed you will prove to be quicker and much more efficient than wasting time running away from them to find a hiding spot or an opportunity to blend in the crowd.
The story has its moments and intriguing hookpoints, but isn't overall that memorable either. Some dialogue scenes felt well-written, but that's it. Scenario could be summarized as "Kill that list of guys and we're done" (with a couple plot twists).
I'd still recommend it though, because I enjoyed playing through it from start to end and it's nowhere near bad.
Perhaps the fact I played other games at the same time rather than going through it in one single burst helped cope with the repetitiveness of it, but I'm also planning to go for the optional Templar and flag hunting objectives so I guess wanting to come back to it for that is proof the game IS enjoyable.
Oh yeah, and from what I got from the somewhat cryptic ending, the events in this one are a setup to the next installments in the series, so this alone should be enough of a reason to play it if you want to go through the rest of the franchise.

David Szymanski is one of those indie developers making "games as art." Even to open-minded players, that can be a turn-off. There is no lack of pretentious, patronizing, and often preachy nonsense out there, and that can understandibly sour gamers towards arthouse titles. But unlike those developers, Szymanski is creating profound, memorable experiences with compact, well-written narratives, and he is doing so with no agenda but his artistic vision.
My first of Szymanski's games was the free Fingerbones, which was strong enough to get me to pay for futher games. The second was the powerful The Moon Silver, which is by far my favorite of his stories. And the third is A Wolf in Autumn. All three games place an emphasis on psychological horror, and all three are short, playable in a single one-hour sitting. All three contain characters constructed through text, audio, and, for the playable characters, gameplay. You generally won't see character models on-screen, but that doesn't detract from the experience. Anyone who has played a well-crafted text-heavy game (or read a good book, for that matter) knows memorable characters are created through writing, not through visuals. Gameplay can be described, and not inaccurately, as "walking simulator with puzzles," and that's fine. That's all that needed.
There's not much I can say specifically without spoiling the experience of A Wolf in Autumn. When it intends to be beautiful, it's beautiful. When it intends to be spooky, it is. It's better than Fingerbones, though it doesn't live up to The Moon Silver, which does a better job of using its limitations to its advantage. Like all of Szymanski's games, it sticks with you. You'll be thinking about the story long after you finish playing. That's a compliment.
Bottom line: if you like psychological horror, aventure games, and you value games as a way to tell stories, you like A Wolf in Autumn. You'll like everything from Szymanski, in fact. My only suggestion is to start with Fingerbones, which, again, is free. If you enjoy that, you'll enjoy the rest. I can't wait to try The Music Machine!
