Alright listen up. I've read a lot of useless reviews about this game, and most of them contain misleading or just plain wrong information. I've played this game an insane amount (the number you see is only a fraction), so I feel like I should try to set the record straight.
If you have a mouse with adjustable DPI, put it as high as it will go. Put the in-game DPI at 100. If you still can't move around easily, buy a new mouse, because yours is horrible. You want a mouse with at least 800 DPI, which shouldn't be difficult to find. Pretty much any ♥♥♥♥♥♥ wireless mouse now days has that.
I'm not going to give this game an across the board recommendation. It's full of perplexing design choices: Really hard at the beginning, need 2 mice to trade items between profiles, can't un-equip gems without editing the game files, gem farming is really tedious,(just edit them, it's not worth farming), can't manually select levels in the arena, runs at 50 fps (why?), need to play through multiple times to unlock every game mode and weapon, and the giant hud gets in the way a lot because the game is locked at 800x600.
That being said, POWER THROUGH THE FIRST LEVEL WITH THE flying insects. Yes, it's hard. It's hard because you suck. It gets easier after that, and even easier once you actually learn how to control your momentum and spacing properly. Controlling the flying thing while wielding a weapon is weird at first, but once you get the hang of it, it works incredibly well, and the game has a ridiculous amount of depth. I'm still learning new techniques after over 100 hours in.
As for miscellaneous stuff you should probably know: Once you put a gem on a weapon, you can't take it off. You have to edit the gem away. There are plenty of guides on how to do that. Blood rubies are essential for arena (the best part of the game by far), and they are very difficult to get. I'd recommend not farming them and just editing them onto your weapons once you finish the main story.
This is one of the most unique and most satisfying games I have ever played, but it takes some time to actually learn how to play well. Give it 4 or 5 hours. If you can tolerate it that long but still aren't having fun, give it until you start doing arena fights. If you still don't like it, then I guess it's not for you.

The game does include a single player bot mode that will allow you to practice your skills and the game includes a nice variety of game settings, 24 different maps, and supports both the Steam Overlay and widescreen resolutions.  The music design is standard military fare, nothing particularly notable, but fitting and not too annoying.  Unfortunately, the games shooting sound effects, while somewhat realistic, really get repetitive quickly. For a bargain title though, the game is a competent although not particularly memorable entry, and worthwhile purchase for anyone who is looking for a quick diversion at a budget price.

Summed up, it's a great idea with a great story delivered in a poor excuse of an engine.
Glitches are, while tolerable to an extent, so bad that the game becomes unbearable after less than an hour of gameplay. Immediately from the start, you can tell things aren't going to go right, I'm about an hour in and I've already falled through thr ground twelve times; and that's just the tip of the iceberg. It's parkour system (if you can even call it that) is limited and restricted to specific interaction points and yet time and time again those interactions don't work. It tries to be something between Tomb Raider and Assassin's Creed in it's design and yet fails horribly at both.
Cutscenes are some of the least optimized and smooth things I've ever had the unfortune of seeing; getting through the cutscene after the first memory mix was like trying to watch a bad mime show over an even worse internet connection. Slow, stuttering and broken/intermittent audio sums this up; that's even if cutscenes ever load in the first place (over half of the time I've had to reload and redo something to get a particular scene working).
Graphics are mostly beautiful and one of the redeeming qualities...until you get out in the city and see how poorly optimized and developed the LOD system is, with opjects loading in as late as two-feet in front of you and distance objects often looking like something out of a 90's shooter. For all I know, this may be the cause of the falling and walking through objects and terrain issue, or it might not be, either way it's a catastrophe for a AAA company to put out something this broken in something as simple as LODs. We should not be having LOD issues in 2013.
Loading screens take far too long for the level of graphics in the game, and fail/freeze about 20% of the time forcing a hard exit and reload. My 200-mod Skyrim, Space Engineers and Rust loads faster than this; and those aren't optimized.
Story and dialogue are the only real redeeming factors here and even then it's a bit dry/cookie cutter in some places. If feels a little like the developers seen the success of Mirror's Edge and said: "Let's make something like that, with a strong female lead who's running from a corporate authority structure in a dystopian future" — and then they proceeded to hire the best writers out there but give them no other input; the result being a great story with great dialogue (when it's not stuttering in a cutscene) that seems to be lacking a strong motivation from the company itself. You can't just hire a bunch of writers and send them off without some sort of guidance; unfortunately that's exactly what this feels like.

I personally really enjoyed Assassin's Creed as a whole. Below I have detailed just what made this game worth playing, as well as what I found frustrating or undesireable throughout my playthrough.

Seriously, is Dontnod capable of a bad game? Nobody talked about this one, but after Life Is Strange I queued it up. What I got was the same level of incredible writing, time-bending adventure with an element of action. These people know how to make video games.

Surprisingly well-written protagonist strung into unfortunately underwhelming circumstances. Underwhelming in the sense that while you might be playing for the story, which is memorable but honestly slightly above average quality, you'll soon see yourself committing to a chore of an adventure to get back to the story.
We'll just do a simple pros and cons, starting with the pros:
+ Well-written female protagonist Nilin is surprisingly likeable despite seemingly gauged to fit that strong, witty character. She'll occasionally throw weird one-liners here and there, but they're bearable for the most part. There is very little hints of sexualizing or stereotyping Nilin's character; she's written in the sense that she happens to be female rather than just being a female character, which is probably why you'll still see people praising her despite giving this game a thumbs-down.
+ Gorgeous landscape that has aged tremendously well at the time I'm writing this review. Remember Me does the justice of tossing you into Nilin's world indefinitely.
+ Character design is an interesting blend of cyberpunk and modern casual wear. Even NPCs will feel somewhat individualistic to an extent. As for hair, don't ask me.
+ Memory remixing is a damn well interesting concept that is well-executed. Being able to observe a person's memory through mind-hacking and then reconstructing it to one's desired result gives one the tremendous feel of playing god.
And then there's the cons that kill the pros:
- Extremely linear plot in a world that begs for the ability to actually change it. Remember Me is misleading before purchase, in the sense that the game's advertising seems to boast that your decisions can bring about grave consequences for the world. You can only do so much.
- The plot itself is interesting, but underwhelming. There are a great many faults in this linear plot, and one is the lack of an explanation for certain characters being able to justify their current actions despite their previous actions after being mind-hacked. I say this because memory remixing does not focus on a series of events to change a person's attitude toward certain things; you literally only change one event that prompts someone to act differently.
- Lack of characterization depth for almost every character that has a name. Bosses will occassionally be introduced in one chapter only to never appear once defeated. Characters who seem to be playing supporting role will eventually have you realize how minor they are several chapters in.
- Lack of environment interaction. Gorgeous setting that you can neither destroy nor change upon conscious decision.
- Combat is lackluster after repetition. Cyber-memory abilities are interesting (I find them to be quite fun overall), but the combos you use as your main way of combat will quickly feel repetitive, hence the mention of chore of an adventure previously.
- Parkour. It's unfortunately not fun to do when you're directed to it.
- The price. If you choose to still get this game, wait until it goes on sale. I for one managed to get this game at 80% off, and you can do it as well. If you like to binge games, then make sure to know that you'll probably finish the game in 12-15 hours.
As for me, I'll probably still just play for achievements. I'm silly that way anyway. Overall, I don't regret buying this game. There are, ahem, memories to think of. But for new peeps who are just getting into the niche audience, I don't recommend this one.

Since this is a re-release, I will simply address the problems I encountered in the time that I've played the game.
The Cons:
1. Aim Mode
The biggest problem I encountered was Aim Mode. In the first dungeon, the Cauldron, you have to throw shadow bombs at switches in order to progress, which means going into Aim Mode. For some reason the sensitivity in Aim Mode is exponentially higher then when normally moving the camera, so moving the mouse like you normally would has the camera doing 1080 turns. After looking online and messing with settings extensively, I settled with having the aim sensitivity around a quarter of the bar and switching my mouse's DPI to 400 and moving extremely carefully whenever I had to use Aim Mode. Hopefully there will be a fix for this.
2. Controls/Key Bindings (My god this game needs a manual)
Some of the games key placement are uncomfortable, like dodge being on alt.
I personally started using my thumb on alt and got used to it, but others may find simply re-binding the keys to be easier. However, re-binding can be a hassle in itself. Due to the fact that you can not bind a key to another if an action is already bound to it, simply switching between two keys means binding the first to an unbound key, binding the second to the first, and then binding the first to the second. There's also the fact that there are multiple keys that are already bound against your knowledge, so finding an unbound key in the first place becomes more difficult.
3. Actions/Executions
The game doesn't explain about several mechanics in the game, some of them literally being key to move on.
Interacting with a person/object seems elementary, yes? But other then an icon popping up and telling me I could do an action, I wasn't told that "E" was interact. In fact I had to look online for this answer, and despite thinking I was an idiot for doing so, saw several forum posts of people asking this same question.
Similar to this is executions. Executions are animated instant kill strikes that restore all your gauges (health, wrath, reaper) and have increased chances to drop gear. This isn't a problem on console since the button you have to press appears over the enemy when you can execute it, but on PC you simply see a red circle and wonder "What the hell does that mean?", again not being told that the interact key solves the question.
4. Frames
There have been other reviews stating the game stutters, tears, and drops frames. The only thing that I saw was frames skipping from turning on default sensitivity due to the speed. Putting on V-Sync and lowering the sensitivity for Aim Mode seemed to get rid of this.
It should also be noted that upon entering the tutorial dungeon, the Crowfather's palace, my display drivers crashed. Everything worked fine when I reloaded the game and I was able to continue onward.
Overall I highly recommend you wait till patches come out and fix these and any other problems that may be prevalent in this game.
P.S. On a side note, I personally love the Darksiders series and can't wait for further entries. Hopefully they'll be more PC friendly in the future.

Disclaimer, I got this game for free because I had bought the complete package earlier on sale. I didn't play the first very much because I didn't like it, and haden't tried 2 yet.
I was initially surprised about all the negative reviews on here, since in the start I had no problems. The game is really good and fun. Then I came over more and more bugs and flaws, and I just can't recommend the game in it's current state.
Some bugs/big downsides:
- When changing video settings, you have to restart the whole game.
- When changing mouse sensitivity, the game freezes on a white background and you have to close it.
- Climbing on whines is often bugged in a way that you have to spam wasd in a dirrection to move because you won't move when holding the button down. It looks like the engine is treating it as many small whine-walls instead of one bigger one.
- In 7 hours, I had 2 random crashes. And I often crashes if I alt + tab. I use 2 monitors, and just moving the mouse over to the other monitor and clicking on Chrome to select it, does not crash the game.
- I can not progress the game any further because of a bug that is crashing the game everytime. When I follow the storyline and have to collect a certain key from a certain angel, if I let the cutscene play normally, the game crashed after a minute or two at the same spot, if I try to skip the scene, the game crashes right away. There's no way around this bug that I have found so far.
- The sound settings volum doesn't adjust certain sounds and scenes. The recap in loading screen when you start the game from a save is quite loud, some random sound effect are loud, and some boss cut-scenes are loud. I don't want to change Windows volum, since I often do more things while gaming.
Some general pros and cons:
Pros
+ The fighting in the game is one of it's best features, lots of comboes, different attack styles, special weapon abilities and dodging. When fighting bosses you have to observe and learn how to fight the boss you're facing, or you'll die.
+ Loot balance is good, different levels and rarities drop from all kinds of enemies and chests.
+ Fast travel and a decently large world.
+ Background music
+ No loading screens besides when you fast travel and "teleport"
+ Cool VFX
Cons
- Bugs
- The world is restricted, it's not open-world in the sence of WoW or Skyrim. There's also only characters that affect the main storyline, which doesn't help with the world building.
- Side quests are (so far, 7 hours in) only collecting certain items along the main storyline, there's no additional stories or fights. Also a downside for world building.
- A lot of people say they can't even run the game. For me it's not running too bad. (when it doesn't crash)
- Some inconsistencies in what cutscenes you can skip, I can often only skip the scenes I want to watch, like those with story.
I will update this review if bugs are fixed until I am able to finish the game. If the game is updated to stop it from crashing and I can actually proceed in the story, I will recommend it with a warning of the other problems.

After finishing the game, it's hard to recommend it.  It's somewhere between the amazingly engaging New Order and the dull, pointless slog of Old Blood.  Story is the only really enjoyable aspect; the shooter gameplay is very simple, the level designs are visually neat but honestly very linear and simple (especially with the MULTIPLE ways they want you to repeat every single level for pointless side missions and pointless challenges), and it's fairly stretched out for no real reason.  The entire first half of the game (after the amusing first level) is tangible time wasting, and my foot was tapping constantly for things to move along.  After that major event, it picks up til the finale thankfully, but that was about 7.5 hours of my playtime (which is bloated pretty badly since I AFK a lot with the game running, whoops) before that finally happened.
Shooter wise, it's not great.  The speed at which your armor and health are whittled away is absurdly quick, so even as a run-and-gun game, it's below Destiny 2 in my book, especially with how terrible the UI and audio are at indicating exactly where you're being shot from (since enemies really only approach when you aren't looking), so you honestly spend far more time having to sneak around at a snail's pace or camp a spot peeking out from cover and headshotting. And I was only playing on Do or Die.  I can't imagine how fragile you must feel on harder difficulties.
Even story and character wise, Wolfenstein 2 is flawed in comparison to its predecessor.  The entire Roswell arc is totally pointless. The entire game is spent connecting with resistance cells (i.e. the new characters of the game) who do nothing of significance besides brag loudly, and then the predictable but enjoyable finale.  There's never really a sense of risk to other major characters beyond the very beginning, and aside from one or two major events in the game, they don't do anything or progress meaningfully.
All in all, it's an OK game.  A simple shooter (with honestly far too few and too simple weapons; the new SMG is utter crap) and a decent but not great story follow up to the original.  Pick it up on sale maybe if you've got ~10 hours you want to burn sneaking and shooting.

Hunting Unlimited 2010 is a rather fun virtual hunting simulator, designed to allow you to hunt from the comfort of your computer. Various locations around the world are available, as well as various types of prey such as; Deer, Elk, Bear, Lions, Elephants, and more. I, myself enjoyed the simulated hunt in the Northeastern United States with a 30-30 Winchester Lever action, which also happens to be the same type of rifle I own and have hunted with in real life. Various scents, lures, blinds, and more are available to help you in your hunt, as well as an array of various weapon types from Rifles to Crossbows, designed to let you make your simulated hunting experience unique to your style.
I have played hunting simulators in the past and this one ranks up top with the better ones, for its realistic feel and approach. The landscapes are varied and immersive, the ambient noises are a nice touch and the graphics, while not great, aren't so bad  you can't enjoy the game. If you enjoy realistic hunting simulator experiences, I would recommend this over one of those Cabela's Hunting games any day.

When the game is first launched, the player is greeted by an original soundtrack that cleverly explains the game, the different combination moves and even provides a clever back story. The soundtrack itself is a masterpiece, it is catchy, upbeat and friendly for all ages.
The graphical design is also a major part of the game, the GUI is easy to navigate and works amazingly in practice, the characters are aesthetically pleasing and the game unlike many others has options for windowed mode and fullscreen. The windowed mode isn't fixed like many other games as it can easily be manipulated by left clicking and dragging.
The cost is free, a game that is designed this well should come with a price, the only costly feature about this game is the amount of time you will find yourself investing into perfecting the various combo moves and defeating the opponents with them.
The only cons that could be easily identified are the small amount of battles (the gang could have been expanded to extend the amount of gameplay) and the combo moves, they could have added a mana bar of some sort that allows you to play moves as you please without making you as predictable.
Rock Paper Scissors Champion, is an amazing work of art that goes completely unrecognised and due to the gameplay present I am rating it an 8/10. This game has the potential to be a 10 with minor tweaks and I am looking forward to any future updates/sequels or any DLC that may be released.

An incredibly beautiful - and at times frustratingly challenging - Metroidvania platformer. This is easily among the most visually stunning games I've played (though I'm slightly annoyed by the Windows 10 system font), and the soundtrack is phenomenal as well. The abilities that you gain throughout the game are really fun and make for some crazy movement options once you get them all. My only real complaint is that I'm not a huge fan of the design of the game's difficulty. Whereas in games like Metroid or Axiom Verge, you have a big health pool but limited save locations, in this game you have a very small health pool and are frequently in danger of being one- or two-shot to death, but you can save basically anywhere. Personally I prefer the former approach, but I could see other people preferring this system. That one complaint isn't enough to drag down the experience that much, though - Ori and the Blind Forest is a must-play for any Metroidvania fan - just remember to save often!

Ori and the Blind Forest Review.
Great visuals
The visuals in Ori makes you think like you are in a moving art gallery. from the dusky bluish forest to dimly lit jungles, Blazingly bright lava and stone areas, heck if the opening scene didn't wow you with its visuals, i'd have to call the police cus i think you"re crazy. The Art in Ori is sure to mesmerize you. Did i mention theres a climax scene for every section you finish? Those are just Breathtaking to play(and die) through.
Great Soundtrack
The Soundtrack In Ori is very very nice to listen to due to it incorporating hymns that evoke a sense of nature, all the stages share a "hymn" but there's a distinct melody for each section that just gives it enough flare to not feel the same.
The sound efffect for the game are also very crisp to hear. you will hear the sound of grass being stepped on, sound of diving into the water, sound of bashing onto foes etc. The sounds in Ori synergizes very well with the visuals.
Great Controls(maybe a bit too tight)
Controls in this game is tight, you aren't sure who to blame when you die, the Level? or the Controls? Thankfully the save system in Ori makes dying no problem and no hassle. Imagine the save system in Ori like a Save State commonly found in Emulators. Therefore Dying becomes a non stress issue in Ori, which makes Platformin sections in Ori(which are hard) non punishing and gives you the feeling of "One More TRY!! I KNOW I CAN DO THIS!". More platformers should do this save system especially if they're hard
Nice Gameplay
The gameplay is nice, very nice, Ori feels very polish in its gameplay, The way you beat enemies in this game isn't really conventional, so that's something to keep it fresh, as you progress more into the game, you'll gain new upgrades to traverse to places you can't before, that same upgrade also can be used to beat new enemies you can't before, you can also beat old enemies using new ways, i wont spoil the fun but once you get the "bash" upgrade enemies becomes 10x more fun to kill.
also did i say this game is quite hard, you will die a few times but nothing frustrating so dont worry.

The story is pretty black and white, even though there's a plot twist that tries to greys it out, didnt really help
eh, maybe i've just seen better stories then this.

I haven't completed this game yet but from what I've played so far I feel that I've gotten my moneys worth out of it and would highly reccomend Slain as a fun action oriented platformer. 1 to 10 I would give it an 8.
Wonderul graphics and pixel art, by far the best the best aspect of this game. The audio is decent with a metal soundtrack. The action in the game moves along in a good pace. The bosses and enemies are challenging but not frustratingly hard. There is a regular sword attack, a charged attack, a backwards dash to evade enemy attacks, a standard jump button, and a parry that can be used effectively when timed correctly. You also get a magic attack that has two different functions- a standard projectile and a charged 'needs and uses all your mana' attack. You can get different sword type. So far I have a freeze and a fire enchanted type sword. The different types of swords can be easily switched on the fly. Different types of swords do more or less damage to the different enemie types. I haven't found a way to know which type of sword does better or worse damage to which enemy other than what is mentioned in the game regarding only witches and knights. There are a few other minor gameplay functions that I won't mention but the gameplay overall is satisfying and fairly simple.
There are checkpoint that are spaced out fairly well. Usually one before every boss as far as I know. There are hearts for health occasionally that renew your health completely. You can recover mana by using a charged attack to finish off an enemy. There really are no items or inventory. The gameplay is very challenging with a difficulty on par with any Dark Souls game. You'll die a lot, but as mentioned above, the checkpoints are placed nicely and with a quick reload time to keep you in the game at a constant pace.
I am not a huge platformer fan but after enjoying Salt and Santuary I needed more platformering fun and Slain is surprisingly providing.
Game runs pretty smooth now, and it is lots of fun. Awesome sound. 9/10

So here is the deal fellow mortals: I saw this game's trailer at launch and I wanted it. But, I read the Steam reviews and was turned off.
We flash forward to several months later and a buddy sends me a free copy. I accept and download it. I end up falling in love. The game offers a great hack and slash with a vague Castlevania/Actraiser (Action parts of 1 and 2 in layout) element. So if that is something you have been wanting, this is your game. Couple that with a tacked on metal theme and I fell for it.
The metal theme isn't perfectly integrated, but it exists. It's like having bacon on a good cheesburger. You don't need it, but it adds to the enjoyment. This limp metaphor sort of sums up the game as well. It's a good and enjoyable meal if you choose to go get it. Is it healthy and perfect? No. But is it fun? Does it make you want to take one more bite, despite your best interests? YES.
The game's visuals and pixel graphics can sort of blend, but I hear they have been toned down. There is challenge and pride to be had from solving combat problems. On my fun or not fun scale, I rate it fun.  Watch the trailer and consider if this is the action/platformer you want. If so, you will have a good time.

Man, I've played this for about half an hour and this game totally got me. It's beautifully designed, the pixel art is amazing, so is the sound track. For me, which loves metal, it's an awesome 'plus' feature.
When the game launched I've noticed a lot of people complaining about bugs, control issues, gameplay, etc. I haven't played it until today, and in my opinion the controls are very fluid and smooth, the gameplay are excelente and until now I got nothing to complain. Seems like the devs worked hard indeed to fix all the negative aspects of the game, which is very nice because there are some devs who gives a f*ck to the game after launching it.
Slain is hard as hell, as it suggested on the reviews. But it's not that cheap, unfair and unballanced hard which makes you wanna stop playing the game, or even those boring trial and error kind of hard games which makes the game being difficult not because the challenge itself, more because its flaws and clumsy gameplay. When you die on Slain, you feel like it's totally your fault because you didn't mastered the controls mechanics, like the dodge and parry moves.
The game makes you feel like grinding into it to win, it's very rewarding when you defeat a hard enemy or got through a hard platforming section. I'm a sucker for hardcore/retro titles like Oniken, Shovel Knight, Bleed, Hotline Miami, Odallus, etc. I loved it and I'll recommend to all platformer fans, even casual ones who don't like that kind of difficult games. It's not that unforgiving as other ones, there's plenty of checkpoints and your life bar doesn't drain that fast when you get hit, except for the hard foes and bosses. Awesome game.
Edit: Forgot to mention that I'm using a Xbox one controller.

Finally back from development hell, Slain is the heavy metal sidescroller we all deserved. You see the title of the game, you don't expect much, if anything. You see screenshots of the game, and you REALLY might not expect much, if you're still allowing yourself expectations at all.
Then you start playing.
Despite its ridiculous premise, or perhaps because of it, Show With Your Dad Simulator is actually a game I find myself coming back to again and again when I need something to do. It's fantastic in short bursts, and even longer ones don't wear out their welcome.
Gameplay is simple, but addictive, and difficulty slowly increases over time, while still always being immersive and enjoyable. It can take you back to your childhood, no joke, back to when games were just score-a-thons, and the only thing that mattered was getting more points than last time, and it does so in the best way possible. Yes, I am still talking about the game where you're showering with your dad the whole time.
This game I bought on a whim for reasons I can't remember, if I even had any, has quickly become one of my favorite things to do when have a few minutes to kill and want those minutes to be filled with fun.
And dads. Lots and lots of dads.
If you've got some time and the spare change, I can't recommend showering with your dad enough.

A solid game with a Zelda-like overworld/dungeon structure to it. Doesn't deviate much from the first Darksiders apart from adding loot drops and the added layer of character customization that such a system would bring. If you haven't yet played Darksiders II, this is a definite buy. Just an overall fun game that may not do anything new, but delivers a very enjoyable experience that very few can dislike. It's a very gamey game, and a good one at that.
Unless you're really jonesing to play it one more time, it may not add enough for people who have already played through the regular Darksiders II. It's noticeably better looking and the folks at Nordic did a respectable job of modernizing its visuals, but beyond that it's still the same game. See for yourself if it's worth it.
Many of the negative reviews surrounding the game are a result of the way its developer handled the way it gave loyalty bonuses to previous owners of DSII. I didn't have any issues buying this edition as I didn't own any of the DLC. Those who did own all content for the original game but bought it piecemeal rather than in the Bundle were upset they didn't get the game for free like those who did the latter. Could've been handled better, but in the end it's small fee for the fans, especially if you'd like to see a Darksiders III.
The game does carry over some of the bugs of the original, unfortunately, and doesn't appear to be well optimized to run on a broad range of machines, but the developer has been doing an admirable job of pushing out updates since its launch a couple of days ago to address the game's issues. I personally don't have any performance issues, but I've got a somewhat beefy system so I can't really comment too much on this.

A game about flying machines propelled by a single engine that produces a sound which's calming effect is yet to be beaten by any of
.
Story starts right off the bat with, what seems like, no tutorial at all. You're ordered to pick up your sharp-swingy toys and go kill some flying worms.
Aforementioned situation lasts for several short levels and frankly gets boring quickly, fortunately the moment the player starts wondering if there's more to Hammerfight than vermin that define the rules of gravity it happens - the game starts for real and you get to confront airborne machines that resemble yours.
It's worth lasting those few bug infested levels so you can enjoy the rest of this beautifully crafted and unforgiving title.
Hammerfight already has a respectable amount of years under its belt yet it manages to age gracefully due to its specific, rich in detail, graphic style.
Controls are fully mouse based, both movement and weapon attacks are executed by performing circular, rhytmic mouse movements so it is vital that you have a perfect feel on them translating to in-game responses - start your adventure with this game by tinkering a bit with mouse sensititivy setting in the in-game menu and you should have loads of fun between dying by getting smashed with a rock on a chain or getting bitten right in the engine by an angry flying bug thingy.
Final aspect worth mentioning is that Hammerfight is a strongly physics based game, weight of weapons and defense modules affects both your speed and the way they feel and interact with enemy machines.
Blows or slashes dealt to foes are sensationally gratifying which combined with possibility of mounting two different weapons at the same time make you just want to see if it is possible to gracefully stab an opponent while trying to follow with more traditionall approach - smashing him with a boulder on a chain.

Hammerfight is a ludicrous physics game that is tough to get into, but rewarding once you get the hang of it. The story is convoluted and confusing, and is presented like the player is meant to know exactly what the hell everyone it jabbering about even though they do not - this is not necessarily a bad thing though.
Pros:
*The game is (usually) fun
*Physics combat is fun
*Campaign is decently long
*Branching storylines with varying rewards and endings
*Convoluted story that is neat, but takes a long time to get your head around
*Encourages experimentation with equipment and techniques
*Minigames are alright - though unlocking some involves playing against cheating AI (e.g. hammerball)
Cons:
*Game has a very steep learning curve
*Enemy choppers do not have to follow the laws of physics
*Enemies can do things you cannot (e.g. spin their weapons without momentum, manually aim their guns)
*Unlocking most minigames is a frustrating experience for first-time players
*Particle effects and smoke make it extremely hard to see what is going on at times
*Large HUD also gets in the way at times
*No new game+ options means starting from scratch every time you want to view the other story paths
*You need A LOT of room on your desk to be able to play effectively - clear out a wide area around your mouse or it will do it for you...

Running with RIfles is an excellent shooter. It rewards cautious players who stick to cover, advance slowly and plan ahead. I think that the co-op multiplayer experience is the high point of this title, and the pvp is fun - good luck finding a server with anyone playing, though. Co-op servers are always populated, in my experience.
You'll level up, earn a larger squad to control, unlock better weapons and body armor, etc, as you kill more and more enemies.
The depth of this game sort of reveals itself the longer you play and the more skilled you become - and the more skilled players you play with - setting up cover deployments, weapon deployments (more on this further on....) moving the frontline up with other players, calling airstrikes, reenforcements, relocating armory/communication/respawn trucks... it's all really good, co-op fun. The gunplay and sounds are very satisfying, and each weapon has its pros and cons. There is no super weapon... maybe the P90. My favourite assault rifle is the Famas.
This game has a ton of potential, and I realize it's a small time, independent affair, but there are a few negatives. (I'm aware that this game is being patched, but still, I review this as it stands today.)
Cover deployment and weapon deployment (stationary MGs, miniguns, TOW launchers) seem to deploy in a random orientation and with minds of their own. There is no option to rotate cover or deployable weapons, they are placed down in the orientation that you are handed. If the MG you spent your hard earned resource points on is facing the opposite direction that you'd like - well, tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's frustrating. Sometimes you will deploy a cover item and it will inexplicably roll onto you and kill you. Or deploy in a manner completely opposite the preview.  Sometimes it won't show up at all. Sometimes it will take ten times longer to deploy than it should and that ends up getting you killed. You will get good at timing the enemies approach vs placing a cover block. If you do get good at this, you can easily hide behind your sandbags and take out 30 enemy soldiers without breaking a sweat.  Out of cover, you'll be dead in one or two shots.
Does it seem like I am talking about cover too much? Maybe so, but it's the most important life extending aspect of the game, right after body armor. And maybe riding in a tank.
Anyways, it's not without its flaws as a game, the graphics are basic and leave a lot to be desired, but overall, I have enjoyed this title FAR more than many other higher priced games that I've played this year. It's incredibly addictive and incredibly fun.

Running With Rifles is a simple game of trial and error. You will start your career as a low-level grunt, throwing yourself into the front lines in an attempt to rambo your way to victory, as you have been trained to do in so many other games. You will try this and you will die. Quickly.
"Alright..." you think to yourself, "I get it: I should just sneak around back and take the objective from behind! Yes! I'll take this silenced pistol and...", and before you have a chance to finish your thought, you have been killed by a small patrol group on your way to the objective.
"I see! It's all so simple! I just need to move slowly. I'll get to the objective, bring a sniper rifle, so I can scan the field ahead, and silently take out any patrols along the way." As you make your way to the enemy objective, careful to avoid any unwanted attention, you see a group of two guarding what appears to be the only enterance to the objective. You creep up hiding behind bushes and trees, finally within pistol range of your targets. You quickly reveal yourself popping off two quick shots, killing the first guard, but missing the second. After noticing you, the guard runs behind cover. You move to flank his position, but you see other enemies are closing in. You are alone in the enemy base with dozens of rifles trained on your position, woefully underequiped for the situation. You decide to make a hasty retreat before the enemy is able to completely surround you, though in order to do so, you risk exposing yourself to enemy fire. You make a run for the exit, bullets whizzing by you. With enemies close behind, you set up a position, taking cover behind a small rock, sniper in hand, and begin cutting down their numbers. Just as they begin to initiate their retreat, you are killed by an APC that had run up behind you, while you were focused looking the other direction.
This is a good game. There is plenty of room for a variaty of tactics, more of which make themselves available to you as you progress through the ranks, earning weapons, arial support, troops, and equipment.
The A.I. is competent. You will find them assaulting, flanking, and retreating in ways that make your life far more difficult, though I will say veichle control is not something they have mastered quite yet.
The weapons all feel powerful, and all have distinct advantages and disadvantages.
Maps all feature similair features and terrain, however are made to feel distinct and unique.
Though frustrating at times, this game rewards thinking outside the box. Exploiting weak points in the enemy defense is just as important as maintaining a strong front line.
If there was one thing I would like to see added, it would be more game modes. To my knowledge, there is only the campaign mode, which is excellent, however can begin to feel a bit redundant after a couple of successful levels. Some sort of CTF, wave defense, or king of the hill game mode(s) would be very welcome, though with the one update we get every two months or so, I am not sure we will be seeing any of those soon.
All and all, great game. Good buy.

X-Tension is the expansion to X Beyond The Frontier and this is where the series really really begins to take the shape we know from the later games. Multiple starting points have been added as well as the ability to change ship at your leisure making this a much more smooth and enjoyable experience than Beyond The Frontier.
The graphics and interface have received a major overhaul not only making the game far more pleasant to look at but also much easier to figure out.
The addition of multiple starting points now allow you a bit of an advanced start if you have to restart as well as the ability to specialize before the game has even started. This all goes a long way towards making learning the game a much easier experience. Satellite control systems now means you have the ability to manage your interstellar trading empire from a distance without the need to dock with every station you own to check on it's progress and this automation feature also helps makes the gameplay feel much more smooth than it was in Beyond The Frontier.
A heavy duty AI improvement makes every part of the game better and the new addition of random missions gives a little purpose to those players that aren't completely satisfied with the open and unstructured nature of the game.
This however is all just an appetizer when put against the biggest change of all. You are no longer confined to a single ship for the entire game. In X-Tension you are allowed to change ship at a whip and practically every ship you see in the game can flown, from the light scouts to the heavy fighters and the cumbersome traders you can now chose your ship to match your mission and this makes the game much easier to play in a huge way.
All in all X-Tension is the game that introduced many of the concepts we now associate with the X series and in many ways it really is the game that made the series the industry standard it has become today. It's not a game without faults but for it's time it was a huge deal and a great game that holds many fond memories.

Pros:
- Realistic shots. Shoot the legs, that'll disable and/or slow them down. Shoot the head? instant kill. There's lung-shots, heart shots and much more. The animals can also bleed out! Sometimes you even have to put them down...
- A truckload of already-available guns for you to use in your leisure.
- Heavily customisable maps, weather, types of animals that spawn, and more!
- Tents to hide away in! Enough said.
- Would make a good game if it was ported to mobile/tablet devices.
- Bullet-cam options!
Cons:
- Minor bugs, though they shouldn't really have too much effect on the game, mostly AI-related. Nothing serious like crashing or resolution errors. They actually make the game a bit easier at times! This can be a good or bad thing, depending on the person. The animals running around endlessly in a circle is a notable bug.
- Graphics are a bit dated. Though those who really want to play the game are probably going look past it. Think a "late-2000's era budget game" graphic style.
- This may only be a problem for, or only be noticed by a handful of players, but the profile name text input bar is controlled by the left and right keys. Not a very popular UI design to some.
- Vehicle controls (horse and quad bike)
In short, if you enjoy hidden gems like these, I'd say give it a try. I reckon it's an 8.5/10.

It was 82 degrees on the afternoon of October 10th, 2011. I was debating if I should go out deer hunting or not. There was a particular stand set that my friend Dave and I hung in June that I had not been to yet this season. Most of the times the wind was not right or it rained and I did not feel like getting wet. I don't like the heat either but I knew cooler weather will be coming in the near future. I still had to attach a pull rope to this stand because I forgot to when my friend Dave and I put the stand up. Even though it was pretty warm out and it is still early in the season the wind was perfect for this stand setup. We had an east wind.
I decided to go. I jumped in the shower and used my unscented and bacteria killing soap. Then I got dressed and sprayed down each layer of clothing. I drove out to my hunting spot and sprayed down my outer layer of clothing quite liberally. I have always wanted to put a stand in this spot over the years but never have due to the walking distance. I know the big boys are in here but I just didn't want to take the time and put a stand here. Times have changed. I get more serious about my hunting every year and strive to shoot only mature bucks. I carry an extra bottle of cover scent with me at all times. Even though I took my time and tried not to work up to much of a sweat walking in, I pretty much was dripping with sweat by the time I got to my stand. Once I arrived at my stand I sprayed down very liberally again to try and cover the stench of my sweat. I then climbed into my stand, attached the rope and then hoisted up my bow. I then sprayed down a third time. Now, it was 4:30pm and finally time to start hunting.
I was quite surprised by the number of squirrels I saw. They appeared to be out in record numbers. I sat in the stand watching and listening to the squirrels until about 6:00 pm. Out of the corner of my right eye, I caught movement that was not a squirrel. It was a nice big doe. I talked to my son Mitchell (Deer Slayer on BGH) and told him I will not be shooting a doe tonight unless it was an albino or a piebald. We have seen an albino doe on the property in years past so we know the genes exist here to see another albino sometime. This doe and her 2 fawns were coming from a pond that is down over a hill. They must have got up from their beds, got a drink then proceeded to come up past my stand which is in a corner of a large oak grove. There are multiple trails coming and going in every direction in the corner where my stand is and there is water down over the hill and acorn and hickory nut trees that litter the hillside where my stand is. The doe and her fawns walked past my stand on the right. I had an easy 25 yard shot on her but chose not to take it. They then walked on and came up the trail 15 yards right in front of my stand. As the big doe was walking up the trail it looked as if her eyes caught mine and I thought I was busted. She only looked at me for about 5 seconds then continued on without any signs of worry. The doe turned broadside again and I chose not to take her again. This second opportunity was very tempting but I was able to hold off. I was there to see what would come out of the bedding area just as the light was fading, if anything at all. She walked down the trail a little way and she gave me a perfect quartering away shot. Again, I chose not to take the shot. By this time 15 minutes had passed and it was now 6:15. The next 45 minutes except for more squirrels was uneventful.
It was now 7:00 pm. The canopy of leaves in this area is still pretty heavy. Light was fading and I was going to give it about 15 more minutes. At 7:02 I heard a loud snap of a branch straight out in front of me. It sounded to be about 50 yards or so away. I intently was looking for what made the sound of that branch snapping. I was hoping it would be one of the big bucks that I know lives in this area. I saw a glimpse of brown passing through the trees. I now knew it was at the least a deer. I kept an intense stare on the area I knew the deer was at. It moved again and this time I saw antlers. At this point in time though I was still unsure if it was a shooter or not. The buck was continuing towards and about 30 yards away I finally had a full view of his rack. I knew at this point he was definitely a shooter. Right now he was walking straight at me and was about to walk up the same path the doe and her fawns took earlier. When he came up the embankment he stopped short of the top and looked in both directions. He decided to turn left and walk around to my right side. There was a number of trees lining the embankment so I could cautiously turn and hope he would not catch my movement. There is a large double tree off to my right and I would position myself for when he stepped out from behind this tree I would let him have it.
He kept slowly walking and stopped right when he was behind that tree. I was thinking to myself I need you to take two more steps and stop. The buck must have read my mind because that is exactly what he did. I didn't have to stop him or anything. I couldn't have asked for a better scenario. I had my crossbow up and pointed already and now it was just a matter of making a small adjustment until I had the crosshairs of my scope on the kill zone. The buck gave me a 15 yard, slight quartering to shot. I pulled the trigger on my Horton Legend crossbow and let the Easton XX75 arrow tipped with the Rage 2 blade broadhead fly. I watched as it hit it's mark. I thought ahh yes!!! It was a perfect shot. I watched the buck take off like a freight train. He ran down the embankment across a flat little area back up another hill then out of sight.
Once he was out of sight I began counting until I heard him crash. One thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three. Crash, crash, thrash, thrash, I heard the buck now rolling around on the ground and then I heard this deep aaaarrrrrgggghhhh. I call that the death growl. I knew he was dead. I shot him at 7:05 pm. I texted my son Mitchell at 7:06pm and wrote BBD BABY BBD JUST NAILED HIM!!!!!. My son immediately called and asked me the details. I told him at the time I think he was a big 10 pointer but I didn't look at the rack too much and I wasn't sure but I definitely knew he was a shooter and I heard him crash and he was down. I told him I would find the arrow and then call him back. I then called my friend Dave and told him and he asked me if I was sure I wanted to pursue him or wait until morning. I said I heard him crash and I heard the death growl and I knew he was down. I got down and went to the point of impact and could not find my arrow or see any blood. I walked the way the buck ran and looked for blood and any part of the arrow but I did not see any at all.
My son called me back and was wondering why I didn't call him back. I said I couldn't find the arrow or any blood and I was starting to second guess myself on pursuing the buck any farther. He asked me again what happened and I told him the details. I was positive the buck was down but just in case I was wrong I did not want to push him. My son said wait and he would be out to help me find him.
By the time  my son and I got back to the stand site 45 minutes had passed and it was now completely dark. But, with the help of the flashlight I won in a BGH grand slam contest I knew we could find the buck. This flashlight is awesome. It lights up everything. We walked the way the buck ran. Scanning back and forth looking for blood. Finally about 60 yards from the point of impact I spotted a drop of blood about the size of an apple seed. The blood was bubbly. The further we walked the drops were getting closer together and bigger. We reached the top of the hill where I last seen and scanned the area. We walked about another 10 yards on the blood trail and I scanned the area again. I said I see brown. My son said be careful but I knew he was dead.

First and foremost I want to thank the makers of this game for actually making a Metroidvania. I've been on a Metroidvania kick for about a year now, and so many of these things turn out to be super linear.
On top of that, this is actually a good game. It actually seems to understand what it wants to be and how to execute it. ANNND it's got lovely HD graphics instead of hiding behind the facade of "pixel graphics."
The platforming is pretty challenging, but I don't think it's that hard. Just learn to manage your save points and you'll be a-okay. Also make sure you use a controller. I can't fathom playing this with keyboard and mouse, but I guess some people try to do that.
The game does have faults, but I don't think they're big enough to turn down a recommendation. So here they are:
-Combat is not very deep at all. You essentially have a short range auto-aim. But how the game uses platforming inside of combat makes up for it.
-Personally I find the story a bit too... try-hard. Character motivations don't totally make sense either. It comes off as cliche to me, and maybe just a touch pretentious. But the awesome music had me buying into the emotion, even though afterward I thought about what had transpired and went, "Wait... what?"
-Sometimes the artistic design of the levels gets in the way of the layout. And I mean that literally. There are parts of the foreground blocking my view!
I think the last thing I'll mention is that it focuses a lot on platforming. I imagine that could be a turn-off for some. It might have been for me if I had known that before playing it. But, as I said, it knows what it wants to be and executes it well. So it's not like the janky stealth sections of Owlboy. Ugh.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a platformer with stunningly detailed areas, lovely music, and satisfying platforming. Don't let the short length put you off, there is absolutely no dull, filler content and it is a joy from start to finish.
The storytelling is kept to a minimum, but I found myself caring enough about the plot that I wanted to see what would happen next.
Using new abilities in combat and travel is rewarding and you'll eventually find yourself toying around with new ways to get around quickly.
In terms of visual and audio design this game is completely enthralling. Areas are full of things to look at yet never cluttered enough to hinder gameplay. Enemies have particular sounds which you'll find yourself immediately knowing how to tackle various situations.
Although I love the visual design, the music is probably my highlight of the game. Gareth Coker's evocative score perfectly encapsulates the beauty of the world design and the joy of exploration.

Remember the good old Zelda: Link to the Past? Hob feels so much like it and much better in some places.
You are a sword-like-thingy wielding creature that explores and changes the world around you. There is some combat but if you like exploring (i.e you get all the upgrades and have enough currency to buy them) combat will not be too difficult on normal difficulty. There are 2 higher difficulty settings and one lower but to me it felt very well balanced. But combat will never be just a senseless buttonmashfest. Block, evade, stun, remove enemy armor - even combat is part of the exploration/puzzle experience.
Other than that, you will be jumping, climbing, running and swimming to get to the next button, switch or lever. While there isn't much hand-holding - usually a general direction of where to go is all you get - most puzzles aren't very complex. From the offset you will immediately notice that Slain: Back from Hell looks spectacular. The intro screen itself is very reminiscent of any 80’s metal album cover you can find at your local record store (if you’re lucky enough to have one nearby). Unlike several other retro-inspired games, Slain: BFH takes advantage of every square inch of your screen by filling it with breathtaking Gothic artwork consisting of beautifully vibrant pixels. I was excited to complete each section because I knew the next section was going to offer new candy for my eyes and as expected, developer Wolf Brew Games never failed to impress. Consisting of creepy, blood-soaked castles, wolf-filled forests, and dank, goopy sewers, this is hands down the most gorgeously created 2D platformer I’ve ever experienced.
Please check out the rest of my review:

NOTE: I got my hands on this game AFTER the update, so here are my impressions:
Slain! Back from Hell is a 2D action/platformer with a good mix of adventure and heavy metal.
The visuals are well made, with good color contrasts and beautiful stages: From forests and hills to sewers and catacombs.
The soundtrack is catchy and fits very well with the game's atmosphere, transitioning from slow paced (but touchy) ballads to brutal and technical passages on stages and boss fights. Also, the OST is made by Curt Victor Bryant (from Celtic Frost, check it, it's pretty good).
The gameplay of it reminded me of Castlevania meets Dark Souls, due to muscular memory is a must for parrying and gain a upper hand in combat. Hitboxes works well. And there's a cool (but not so useful for me until now) back dash. As you progress, you will gain new powers to aid you on your journey, but still,
The difficult is on spot. Not too hard, but not too easy either.
Story is self explanatory and pretty straightforward, helps to make a connection between the stages.
In the end, Slain! Back From Hell delivers what it promises: A good challenge with many good elements. If you're a metalhead and/or like OG Castlevania games, this game is a must.

Now I've not finished the game yet, but I felt as if I'd try to geta review out there especially seeing as the game is currently on sale and might persuade people to buy this game. Now, I've only just bought this myself, so I can't tell exactly why the game previously had negative reviews, the Devs have sure changed any issues that there may have been previously, as it has been much better received this time around.
Right, into the nitty gritty. The game is a metroidvania style platformer, which should already give you a great indication of whether or not you are going to enjoy this game. What is unique here though is that this game offers a very unique asthetic, combined with a heavy metal soundtrack. The fact that you play as a sword wielding, leather clad, undead head-banging badass slaying all manner of foul beasts justs makes this game awesome. The game can be infuriatingly challenging, but at the same time it is very rewarding. After you have died to the same boss 6 times, but finally come out on top, there is a huge sense of simultaneous pride and relief. The mechanics of the game are important to learn, you cannot simply hack and slash your way through, or you'll be found out fairly quickly. You have to learn the individual enemy attacks, and time blocks/dodges perfectly, or you'll be swiftly cut down. Movement and attacks have a nice weight to them, as good as they could be in a platformer, and you'll soon be accustomed to slipping past the traps and hopping up the ledges of this dark and beautiful world. There are a few different weapons that have been added, but are a poor attempt at adding variety, it feels like they are just there for the sake of it. I also think that some of the puzzles could have been more well thought out, as they mainly seem to consist of pressing a switch, running to the other side of the screen, jumping up to a platform, pressing another switch, wait for the next platform, and this can grow stale very quickly. There are some different sequences which add a little bit of flavour, for example turning to a wolf and being chased across the level, which is a refreshing change from the usual slog.
If you are looking for a good Metroidvania style game, at a good price, look no further. Just don't expect anything exceptionally different from what you are used to. The Devs made a game, were criticised for their mistakes, but instead of giving up on it, have made the necessary improvements, and that in itself deserves credit. I can recommend this game at 9.99, and even moreso if you get it on sale.

So after waiting for a year and 3 (?) major updates, and a big enough sale, I went ahead and bought NMS. With all those caveats out of the way, here's the good, the bad, the ugly:
The Good:
- It's honestly really beautiful, visually
- The soundtrack is outstanding
- Cool first planet, big animals, ship upgrade just lying around, tons of ruins and an alien monolith, all that jazz
- Alien monoliths present a very nice break from just mining plutonium and iron
- Seamless, vast space exploration
- There are AI space battles, and they've happened with some regularity, and the bounty factor is nice
The Bad:
- Needs multiplayer
- Needs more depth in mechanics and a more structured storyline; the Atlas path is mehhhh
- Takes too long to upgrade gear; I'm 12 hours in and while I lucked out with an uber multi-tool from a random alien interaction... where's the loot?
- Animals are essentially boring, just moving parts of the landscape once the novelty wears off after 5 hours
- Sentinels aren't a meaningful deterrent and don't provide a compelling antagonist
The Ugly:
- Where are all the aliens?
- Why is every space station exactly the same?
- Upgrading gear makes exactly no difference to the experience of playing
- Combat mechanics, especially in space, are awful
- Bases are pointless without multiplayer: no one's gonna see your house, dude
- Inventory management is endlessly boring
- All voice prompts need to die
So in short, the game's not there yet unless you got it for $20, like I did. At $20 this is a game to occasionally graze in, but isn't a full meal. Perhaps with more updates and a few major expansions I could revise: otherwise, can't recommend yet.
Kudos to Hello Games for continuing the development of NMS. It's a lot of fun now!

Know what you're getting into. Sony has marketed this game as the greatest space sim ever, and fans went ballistic, expecting a great space opera like Star Citizen. But from the very beginning, No Mans Sky wasn indie game from a very inexperienced and naive developer for mobile titles. With that said, I'd compare this game more to Journey or Abzu. It's a relaxing and beautiful experience. Now when I bought this game at release, I was disappointed like many others that it was missing all the various promised features. Who would pay $60 for Journey? The price was unnaceptable. And when I explored a few of the procedurally generated planets, some of which looked unique, most of which looked the same, I refunded it. BUT I did promise to keep an eye on it, because I love what this game is. I love the concept. But the execution? It needed a LOT of work. Hello Games made a fatal mistake that would seal the fate of NMS forever. People lashed out at Sean Murray, the developer, calling him a liar and a con-man. All of these people had a right to be angry.
Now, Hello Games could've run off with our money or even start releasing paid DLCs of the features missing. But they didn't. They saw that players were infuriated. And I think it scared them straight. They stopped talking to us..They went off the radar. This made players even MORE infuriated. But unbeknownst to us, they were secretly working their butts off to try and rectify their mistakes..No more promises. No more talking. I think they realized actions speak louder than words. People want proof of concept. And that's what they're giving us. No Mans Sky has come a LONG way, with base customization, freighters, an all new alien species, an actual storyline, vehicles, more varied planets, AND my most favorite feature? Completely overhauled combat. The combat is now more in line with your average dogfighting sim. It's more challenging. Also introduced into the game(Although I haven't experienced them yet) are factions and faction battles.
Each free update is giving us more and more features that were promised to us from the very beginning. Should we forget about the broken promises and lies that Sean Murray told us? No. We shouldn't. But should we consider forgivng them? I genuinely believe we should. I think No Mans Sky was a wake up call for this naive team. And for the record, I don't know if all of this was their fault anyway. If you'll recall, their office DID experience a flood which wiped out god knows how much data..And Sony as usual has their deadlines. We shouldn't have expected much to begin with, considering NMS WAS their very first actual game.
Anyway, No Mans Sky is a beautiful and relaxing game. I've always loved the visuals, and I always enjoyed taking screenshots of the scenery. But I never expected it to be a simulator. You shouldn't, either. But you should still expect a LOT of mining..But this time, there's a point to it. You can upgrade your suit, your ship, do some trading to afford a better ship or even a freighter, construct any kind of base you want with different technicians focusing on exocraft, scientic research, or more construction..The list goes on.
My ONLY problem is the price. This still shouldn't be a $60 game. I strongly advise you to wait for a sale. I didn't buy this game again until it was $23. But who knows? Hello Games is working around the clock to bring us major updates for free. So maybe one day, this game really will be worth $60.
(Played on both PC and PS4. Currently all my playtime is on console.)

If you can get past the low graphics there's a very relaxing game here. The game goes like this:
1) Select your target animal(s), location and equipment.
2) Track your target animal(s). You can use an RV or a horse to get around the big maps, and binoculars/calls to figure out where your target is. You can also use decoy animals and scents to bring your prey to you. Most animals will smell/see/hear you from a long way off so you have to hide yourself well. You can bring a tree seat and hide up in the branches, set up a camoflagued tent or just lie down in some nearby bushes.
3) Wait. This can take ages so it's a good game for audiobooks/podcasts. Occasionally make a call (not too often or you'll scare it off). When your target gets close enough, bring out your weapon (there's a variety of rifles, shotguns and a few bows/crossbows) and shoot the bugger.
4) If you hit it in the right spot it'll die instantly, sometimes it'll run off and die of blood loss so you'll have to track it down. Tag your animal and it goes off to the trophy room.
There are also a lot of missions if you want something more structured, but there's a good variety of environments and animals to keep you occupied. You can also go to Africa and hunt elephants/lions for some reason. There's a modpack that adds new equipment, skins and weapons: go get that too. If you enjoy sniping games or enjoyed the hunting in games like Red Dead Redemption you might enjoy this.

I must say I was skeptical when downloading that game.
I was searching for some game that was cheap or even free, which wasn't a big killer for my disc space and I came across this amazing game.
The story:
You are playing as the protagonist, the former Rock Paper Scissor champion and you must fight your way back to the throne. On your way, you must beat various strategic geniuses.
The Gameplay:
You are playing a game called "Rock Paper Scissors" to regain your title as champion.
Rock-paper-scissors is a zero-sum hand game usually played between two people, in which each player simultaneously forms one of three shapes with an outstretched hand. These shapes are "rock" (a simple fist), "paper" (a flat hand), and "scissors" (a fist with the index and middle fingers together forming a V). The game has only three possible outcomes other than a tie: a player who decides to play rock will beat another player who has chosen scissors ("rock crushes scissors") but will lose to one who has played paper ("paper covers rock"); a play of paper will lose to a play of scissors ("scissors cut paper"). If both players throw the same shape, the game is tied and is usually immediately replayed to break the tie.
There is also some special combo moves you can do to higher your chances of winning.
My conclusion:
After hours of playing, I can gladly recommend this game to all of my friends and family and I think everyone should have tried it at least once. The OST is also worth buying, since the soundtrack is very well put together.

Hob is an action-adventure game where you play as a guy who just wants to go home. Unfortunately, home is pretty far away, and many puzzles and enemies block the path. I dove into this game blind, and I definitely enjoyed it.
Hob has a very Zelda-like vibe. You play a little guy in a tunic with a pointed hat hacking at grass with a sword. Of course, you'll find no rupees here, just health. That doesn't mean there is no shopping mechanic, however. As you defeat enemies and unlock rectangular stones with glowing symbols, you gain a currency. This currency is used to upgrade the abilities you gain along the way. There is no name for the currency.
Speaking of no name for currency, there's no names given for anything other than shop items. There is no dialog. On one hand, it's pretty great for those of us who get impatient while NPCs talk forever. On the other, it can make it a little harder to figure out where you're going.
A good example of this is when the stone golem that's been helping you motions across a large hole in the ground. You cannot jump it. You cannot fly. You probably have no idea what the big symbol in front of the gap means because you don't have that ability yet. You just know you have to get over there. You get over there by completing a different area completely first. They also won't tell you how to use your new abilities when you get them. I personally had to check the control map a couple times to figure out what I was doing. This lack of dialog can leave some people very lost for a while.
I played Hob with a keyboard and mouse, but there were a lot of times I thought "I should really use a controller for this". It works with the keyboard and mouse, but there are a lot of diagonal jumps. These jumps get a little awkward on keyboard when you're in the middle of a time-based puzzle (or if you're being impatient). They wouldn't be too bad, but you cannot change direction in the air. I found myself dying by falling off ledges more than anything (because I'm impatient). Otherwise, it feels nice control wise.
The combat in Hob in primarily done with your sword, but the other abilities you gain in your adventure can also be used. Punching a group of scorpions in the face can be quite satisfying. It also comes with a handy stun! Rolling, slashing, and punching your way through is pretty fun. Although, once you learn how certain monsters work, it can be a little on the easy side. That being said, I have been oneshot by a monster in this game. That’ll teach me for not following map markers provided by a sentient golem that doesn’t speak my language.
The puzzles usually involve moving large sections of the area. They’re not exactly Myst hard, and you won’t need to bring a notepad or calculator with you. They do make for some pretty cool sights though. Shoving an entire section of an area down to reach the other side is neat.
Overall, Hob is a nice game for people who like platformers and puzzles. It looks nice visually, combat feels good (as it should from Runic Games), and just exploring in general is pretty fun. Aside from anything mentioned above, the only real downside I can see (if you can even call it that) is that it probably isn’t for all ages. This is due to blood, violence, and some dismemberment.

TL:DR - Pretty but shallow.  Short to play through.
Graphics: For the most part the game is of outstanding graphical quality.  It does trip up at 2 points:
1. Senua's inability to fully close her mouth 90% of the time.  Minor but distracting.
2. The interspliced video.  In the 90s, we had FMV - basically real actors on a green screen that would be interlayed with the game's background.  Neat at the time, but not so fantastic by today's standards.  Somehow, they've managed to do this worse than it was in the 90s.  It looks really, really dumb every time its attempted and really hurts the experience overall.  It's like they ran out of animation budget so they forced an intern to stand in.
Gameplay: Meh.  Do yourself a favor and find something to hold down the W key, as you'll be using it a lot.  Senua has two speeds:  Walking, and slightly faster jog.  This gets really annoying when you're inevitably backtracking.  Combat reminds me of the Witcher 3, except with more cheap stun locks.  Spawning enemies can hit you before you even notice them, or are even fully formed.  This gets old rather fast.
Sound/Music: It was alright overall.  Nothing really stood out.
Story:   It has all the elements of the hero's journey in it.  I do like the Senua's supporting cast of herself, herself, herself and herself.  They did get annoying sometimes however.
Overall it's more art than game.  Keep that in mind.

TL;DR A work of art.  Buy for the story and experience.  OK combat and/or puzzle repetition may lessen some gamers’ experiences.
Hellblade is an amazing experience but I think you have to go into it with the right expectations.  This game is about the story first.  It is told through wonderful writing, acting, stellar sound design, graphics, and a soundtrack I wish was available for purchase.  The developers did a great job with the world building.  There were runes throughout the world that gave bits of lore that I actually enjoyed finding and felt added to the story.  Often times things like this in games become things I gather for the achievement or because I need them to move forward, but I quit paying attention after a while.  This didn’t happen for me in this game.  The puzzles throughout the game are interesting in concept.  Senua’s psychosis makes her see patterns and place meaning on objects others wouldn’t notice.  The puzzles are designed to help the player experience this.  The same kind of puzzles occure multiple times though.  While I wasn’t bothered by this in the context of the story, I can see where others will be.  It could be especially fatiguing if the game is played straight through.  The combat is ok. I bought this game whilst barely knowing anything about it apart from the premise, and in a mere 7 hours it has me feeling emotional like no game has ever achieved, while it's often used as a buzzword, this game is truly an
, no matter what genre of game you like or dislike, this is something I feel deserves a chance no matter what.
What Ninja Theory pulled off with this game is absolutely out of this world, the protagonist is so incredibly believable and human, you feel with her, you start to share her fears and doubts, you want to help her so badly to overcome them, so much so that you start to forget it's just a game after a while as you join Senua on this journey.
It also helps that the game looks beautiful, helping to immerse you even more, the voice acting is also top-notch and it really makes all the characters feel real, even simple grunts and sighs from the protagonist sound genuine.
The only flaws I can personally think of is that the combat is a bit clunky at times, but nothing that hinders the game in any way, and the combat-sections are relatively short so it shouldn't be much of an issue, though you should know that this is not a game focused on hack and slash action at all, despite the title.
The game handles some very serious themes such as mental health, loss and suffering, overcoming fears and your own demons, but it does it so incredibly well, it never feels forced, only later did I realize I learned from this game, and all of that is achieved without any text crammed in your face or recieving monologues from anyone.
This, to me, is in all honesty and with no over-exaggeration an epitome of what this form of media can achieve, I'm incredibly thankful to Ninja Theory for making this game, a product of creativity and care, and in my eyes a masterpiece in every sense of the word.

Know what you're getting into. Sony has marketed this game as the greatest space sim ever, and fans went ballistic, expecting a great space opera like Star Citizen. But from the very beginning, No Mans Sky wasn indie game from a very inexperienced and naive developer for mobile titles. With that said, I'd compare this game more to Journey or Abzu. It's a relaxing and beautiful experience. Now when I bought this game at release, I was disappointed like many others that it was missing all the various promised features. Who would pay $60 for Journey? The price was unnaceptable. And when I explored a few of the procedurally generated planets, some of which looked unique, most of which looked the same, I refunded it. BUT I did promise to keep an eye on it, because I love what this game is. I love the concept. But the execution? It needed a LOT of work. Hello Games made a fatal mistake that would seal the fate of NMS forever. People lashed out at Sean Murray, the developer, calling him a liar and a con-man. All of these people had a right to be angry.
Now, Hello Games could've run off with our money or even start releasing paid DLCs of the features missing. But they didn't. They saw that players were infuriated. And I think it scared them straight. They stopped talking to us..They went off the radar. This made players even MORE infuriated. But unbeknownst to us, they were secretly working their butts off to try and rectify their mistakes..No more promises. No more talking. I think they realized actions speak louder than words. People want proof of concept. And that's what they're giving us. No Mans Sky has come a LONG way, with base customization, freighters, an all new alien species, an actual storyline, vehicles, more varied planets, AND my most favorite feature? Completely overhauled combat. The combat is now more in line with your average dogfighting sim. It's more challenging. Also introduced into the game(Although I haven't experienced them yet) are factions and faction battles.
Each free update is giving us more and more features that were promised to us from the very beginning. Should we forget about the broken promises and lies that Sean Murray told us? No. We shouldn't. But should we consider forgivng them? I genuinely believe we should. I think No Mans Sky was a wake up call for this naive team. And for the record, I don't know if all of this was their fault anyway. If you'll recall, their office DID experience a flood which wiped out god knows how much data..And Sony as usual has their deadlines. We shouldn't have expected much to begin with, considering NMS WAS their very first actual game.
Anyway, No Mans Sky is a beautiful and relaxing game. I've always loved the visuals, and I always enjoyed taking screenshots of the scenery. But I never expected it to be a simulator. You shouldn't, either. But you should still expect a LOT of mining..But this time, there's a point to it. You can upgrade your suit, your ship, do some trading to afford a better ship or even a freighter, construct any kind of base you want with different technicians focusing on exocraft, scientic research, or more construction..The list goes on.
My ONLY problem is the price. This still shouldn't be a $60 game. I strongly advise you to wait for a sale. I didn't buy this game again until it was $23. But who knows? Hello Games is working around the clock to bring us major updates for free. So maybe one day, this game really will be worth $60.
