Not ready for prime time.  I'm only 2.4 hrs into the game and the performance/quality are fairly disappointing.  The game has crashed twice.  Textures disappear and flicker constantly as I move around the world.  Trees will lose all foliage, details on the ground will vanish then come back as the character moves around.  I'm not exploring a solid place but one where things can vanish and appear back again at any second.  It's very immersion breaking.  My computer is old (i7-3770 and Nvidia GTX 770), but exceeds the minimum requirements.  I tried turning settings down to medium, but the game just looked ugly for it; and the disappearing textures just got worse.
Otherwise the game seems fun, if not a little obtuse.  I've gotten stuck once right at the beginning in the tutorial and had to watch a YT video to figure out where to go.  Almost got stuck a 2nd time before stumbling across a place to climb.  Gameplay seems to consist of:  explore, fight some enemies, wander around looking for a way to progress, repeat.  It's something I could get into, but I think I'll have to set this aside for a few months and hope future bug fixes improve the experience.
edit:  I took opportunity of Black Friday/Cyber Monday to purchase a better graphics card which wasn't on sale.  I bought an Nvidia 1060 6GB which improved on the flashing textures somewhat, but introduced frequent stuttering and hitching of the game.  That's at 1080p and settings set to High (and vsync helped a bit).  Still, performance was disappointing.
I've since finished the game.  It's an interesting tale, decent combat, puzzles that aren't too hard, with some rather complicated jumping.  I'm changing my review to recommended, but with steep reservations.  If you demand performance look elsewhere. If you enjoy puzzle games and exploration, and are willing to put up with sub-par performance, Hob is worth a purchase on sale.

I paid $24 bucks for this game and I don't regret a penny of it. (In its current state, Atlas 1.3, it is still NOT worth $60 bucks/ full price)
It has entertained me for hours, its challenging yet its peaceful, it’s frustrating yet it easy. You cannot just easily progress or buy everything, you've got to work for it. Yes, sometimes you have to be repetitive... but its gets easier as things go on.
If you had doubts about picking this up just ask yourself "did you enjoy Minecraft?"  If the answer is yes, this is a very advanced version of Minecraft... in space.
You must spend hours slowly farming resources, which will in turn make gather the same resources a little bit quicker later.
If it’s your first time playing, DO NOT start on Permadeath or Survival. You will die... A LOT.
You need to know what to look for, how to look for it, and how to efficiently farm it. This game is about efficiency in the long run. There are multiple paths to take after you start off as a crash victim and repair your ship. You can be a galactic trader, explorer, pirate, or much more. Though the depths of each of these paths is now as deep as some would like, they can still be entertaining. (Pirates kind of go the path of GTA where each sentinel you kill brings harder and harder sentinels after you... until you run away or die)
Traders work their way up from small ship to Freighters, which cost millions of dollars, but allow you to own multiple ships and have a mobile farm and base.
Explores can keep it small with a variety of ships which allow them to quickly traverse the never-ending universe naming as many things as they want after themselves.
If they ever get the multi-player figured out, this game would make an AMAZING MMO universe.
I will say this, if you're looking for a game that has instant gratification (AKA a game you can completely figure out or conquer after 5 hours of play), this is not a game for you.

First things first: I knew what I was getting into when I purchased this, and updating my base edition of DS2 with none of the DLC to the Deathinitive for six bucks was a great deal. I was neither an early adopter nor had spent a great deal of money on the game beforehand even for the core version, so the update's price doesn't really bother me from a personal stance, though I can understand both early adopters' laments and the issues Nordic is having to deal with considering the license transfer from THQ for the property.
So! Is it worth it?
As a DLC update, yes, though I have yet to see any of this DLC in the game (I've got closer to 10 hours in the game including time in the original DS2 as I was in the middle of my first playthrough when I saw the announcement for this.) As for everything else, the changes are either quite small or I simply haven't come across them in a major way yet. SOme models seem slightly tweaked, but nothing extreme, and overall anyone coming into this expecting a world of difference will be disappointed. DS2 is a great game, with solid controls, a beautiful world, and some of the absolute most amazing music I've ever heard, but it is by no means a groundbreaking title, serving as a mixed-bag of Prince of Persia, God of War, and Zelda and mixing the three into a tasty combination that works well but fails to do any one thing as well as its inspirations. The Deathinitive Edition is the same game but with more content, so don't expect it to change your mind if you weren't impressed by the regular version.

Welp, figure I'd do a review of this despite it getting a good amount of backlash ATM. Now I'll be honest in this review since I'm judging the GAME and not the business practices the devs have pulled here, although those should be addressed. Check the negative reviews if you want to understand why, but given time they will be irrelevant since this version officially replaces the base varsion of Darksiders II.
I should also note my time spent is irrelevant because I have played and beaten both games multiple times back in my console days on the Xbox 360. Good? Good.
Pros: +An awesome story with an ever expanding universe full of well written and designed characters. It has humor, drama, suspense, horror, and even some well done sad moments.
+A visually stunning world. While the texture quality may be hit or miss given the year it came out, the game has an absolutely gorgeous esthetic that fits right at home with some of the best stylized games such as Borderlands, and many of Blizzard's titles. The colors are breathtaking and the character designs are somthing out of a good comic book, like Todd McFarland's "Spawn" for instance.
+A sweet soundtrack with excellent visual feedback all around for this game. Everything from the combat, to the voice acting, to the music ques oozes with ear warming sounds and makes the game feel even more satisfying to play. Audio is important to a title and this game passes with flying colors.
+Fast paced, well done combat system with lots of combos and flashy moves to unlock, and tons of enemy variety with some seriously well done BOSS BATTLES that highlight just what a crazy universe this all takes place in.
+Tons of content, especially with all the DLC now added into the game. You definently get your moneys worth with lots of varied locations, collectibles, quests, and a thoroughly long and satisfying main quest line. Don't let my P.C time fool you.
+LOOOOOOOOOOT! If you are a fan of Diablo/Borderlands style loot drops with tons of weapons that game weird effects and make your guy look like a BAD-A$$ than you have come to the right game!
+Interesting Zelda/Metroid style puzzle solving that isn't too complicated but makes you feel smart anyway for completing it. Tons of secrets to explore too so watch out for that chest marker on the map!
+The Crucible. Normally I don't throw in things like this in a review as a bonus unless it's a seperate mode, but the WAVE BASED Crucible challenge is filled with great endgame content. It has awesome loot drops, excellent challenge, and some sweet extra boss battles outside of the main game.
+ALL THE DLC!!!! I know I mentioned this when refering to the content for this game, but it begs mentioning again. One of the biggest issues with DSII used to be how expensive and how numerous all the DLC was for new players. It even involved things that SHOULD have been in the base purchase like some of the dungeons, and the Crucible.
No game is without it's flaws and Darksiders II is no exception.
Con: -The port. Despite this being the "Deathinitive Edition" this game still suffers from poor optimisation, a bare bones options menu, and frequent framerate drops even when little is happening. I get it to work stable enough myself, but if you are expecting 1440p 144mghz gameplay with a framerate that never drops with your two 980Ti's then you will sadly be disappointed.
-Sometimes very frustrating puzzles and confusing level design. This doesn't happen often, but I'll occasionally lost track of where I am going, what my objective is, and what I am even supposed to do for the puzzle. I used to stumble into areas I wasn't meant to and run around wondering what in the world my crow buddy is trying to tell me... speaking of which.
-The crow is freaking useless. He goes all over the place, often in areas you just came from, and his pathfinding is the most confusing thing I have ever seen as quest markers go.
-Occasionally cheap shot enemies.
-Bad keyboard and mouse controls. I'm sure some people can get around this, but I SERIOUSLY reccommend a controller for this game.
-Barely any graphical improvement. While the game's style more than makes up for it, the texture quality leaves a lot to be desired. Don't expect something like Witcher 3 from this. I can't stretch enough how good I think this game looks, but that opinion is entirely subjective and some people simly wont like the style and the texture quality wont help support that feeling.
-While the controls are fine overall, sometimes the movement suffers from hectic combat and I cannot COUNT how many times Death has flipped RIGHT IN FRONT OF THE BIG GUY WITH A DRILL FOR AN ARM during his heavy attack and had half of his health nuked due to some dodgy... well, dodge mechanics.
-Annoying and sometimes cryptic Quest markers. Quest markers are CRUCIAL in an RPG and the ones in this game desperately needed to relay information better. They often don't give you much information in their descriptions, and if it's designed for searching something it can be very frustrating due to the Zelda style level design. Sometimes they'll tell you to go somewhere and you'll be running around the quest marker hoping it'll move or give you a hint only for the objective to be under some underwater cave, in a secret room you have to find on your own. Combine this with Ash the Crow's crappy pathfinding and you will be left hunting the Darksiders Wiki for a lot of quests and puzzles.
Overall, I love Darksiders II, and this franchise as a whole. Now with a third entry in the series announced I simply cannot wait for this franchise to continue to grow and expand this awesome universe. I give Darksiders II a 9/10. What holds it back is some annoying Questing, and subpar P.C performance. Many of the Base version's issues are solved with the DLC which boosts the score a point or two over the older version. It's worth every penny regardless and I am happy to reccommend this game even at full price. On a sale it's a complete steal.

First review ever, but I think there's some justice to be done. This is not my mother language, so expect some (I hope) minor mistakes.
I'm not going to talk about the more than flawed release, just about the product as it is right now. First of all: it's worth it. If you're thinking wether to spend your money or not, don't think it twice and grab this. Here are the reasons why:
-Art is awesome. And yes, let's not fool ourselves; it's the main reason to play this game.
-Music is not bad. I've been listening to metal for more than 20 years so there is little room for surprises here, don't expect it to get better than most metal music you can find out there. But it's good enough and it clearly delivers what's intented to, without being too repetitive.
-Gameplay... Well, it has its ups and downs. It's fun once you get used to it, but during the first two hours or more timing feels a bit odd, blocking and reflecting projectiles is not as intuitive as it should, and a bit of practice is required. Also, it relies heavily on trial an error. If you don't like to be killed, reloading the game and trying something else until you find the way to survive, I'm not sure I'd recommend this; sometimes it can even get frustrating if you just go swinging your sword mindlessly, which is the top 1 thing you should never do.
-Story is meh. Epic ending though, pretty much what a heavy metal story should be.
-Challenging bosses, at least some of them.
-Sound desing is awesome. I still hear those banshee wails in my mind.
Personally, I think it lacks some speed. There are too many moments in which you'll find yourself waiting for that f****** platform to get closer, then jump on it just to be killed by an executioner after missing your block for 0.1 miliseconds: here we go again. Fortunately, there are moments like the Wolf Run too.
Keep in mind: the game only last 5-6 hours if you're good, but I'm replaying it quite a bit. As I've already said, it's worth it, as it comes with the best pixel art I've ever seen, and one of the best concepts too.
Hope you found this review useful.

I have mixed feelings about this game. It has an excellent and fairly touching story, and works great as animated pixel art. However, as a game, it fell a little short, and in fact the very few game elements and scenarios that were present were annoying.
All that being said, I recommend the game. The story is simple, but touching, and has several surprises. The backwards presentation of the events of the characters lives allows you to see the effects before you see the causes. But creators have structured it so that while you see the outward aspects, it's only as you get closer to the beginning that you understand the feelings of the characters.
I'd love to see more games with this kind of story, but I hope in the future that they put more effort into the game parts. For example, chronotrigger explored related concepts, but had really great gameplay.
To The Moon was a fantastic game. It had a great story line that made the players equally sad and intrigued to keep playing. I absolutely loved the soundtrack.

To The Moon manages to play with your emotions like how a professional pianist can recite a song from memory effortlessly. You'll find yourself heartbroken one minute and laughing the next.
I would try to make a more formal review of this but that doesn't do this game justice. The characters are nothing short of some of the best I've ever seen. Each character has their own quirks and flaws, but that's alright because it makes them all the more human. In my experience, the game will not make you cry solely because of the ending, but because the story is over. You'll find yourself getting so attached to these little pixels that you'll find it hard to let go, which I believe was the intentional result of incredible writing by Kan Gao.
The soundtrack? The soundtrack itself deserves a review of its own. What I love about this game is how well it manages to convey the tone of the situation by music alone. In a more light-hearted scenario the music becomes more energetic with brighter instruments. While in a more serious scenario, the music shifts to a deeper, more impactful style that makes you think to yourself: "I need to get out of here." Even though I first played this game back in 2011 - 6 years ago as of writing this - the music still manages to break my heart all the same.
In conclusion, To The Moon managed to convince me, along with many other people, that video games
be a form of art, as well as the first out of two games to ever make me ugly cry. Buy this game. It's one hell of an experience that you will never forget.

[SPOILERS] This game is decent, but a step down from TNO in almost every aspect. It feels like a rushed product. I really wish I didn't have to pick whether I reccommend or not, but since I've more criticism than praise I have to choose the latter. Loved TNO? Want a game that takes TNO to the next level? This is not that game.
THE GOOD:
-Music, mmmmmmmmm. Mick Gordon always delivers.
-The Cutscenes. Mein God. They're amazing. =
-The "walking simulator" and QTE levels are fantastic.
-The design of the Kreisau's HQ inside the Eva's Hammer is on point, Max coloring everything in and the Helicopters being named after him is great.
-BJ's physical character progression wheelchair -> supersuit -> *spoiler* was pretty neat.
-You're killing Nazi's, always great.
-Plenty of delicious collectibles. Come to me.
There's plenty more that's decent, I'm really trying to balance the good out with everything that will follow in my review, but I'll probably fall short. I do have a great many criticisms for this game, but only because I love this franchise, want it to be the best it can. Maybe I was too unrealistically hyped for this game, and that's where some of my dissappointment is coming from. Here goes:
LEVEL DESIGN:
Level design feels lazy and uninspiring compared to TNO.
-Bland washed out color pallates for most missions (which flavor would you like? grey and chrome generic nazi building interiors, brown and green washed out muddy dilapidated buildings, or just plain darkness (where all you can see is the tip of your gun and enemy headlamps.)
-TNO had levels that weren't afraid to actually have some lighting. (Belica, Nautica, Eisenwald, Moon, etc...)
-The most interesting levels are the walking-simulator ones (Roswell, Mesquite, TV Show).
-Levels feel like "move to this big area, now crawl through some pipes to this big area, ok now go ot the final big area.
-Just about every big fight constantly uses the "kill the commander" mechanic, which gets annoying.
-The backtracking on the last mission felt incredibly lazy. The Ausmerzer is a HUGE flying fortress, presumably with room upon room of stuff inside, but you're telling me the place we need to go is exactly where I was before?
GUNPLAY:
Gunplay is....just ok. Nothing new or improved from TNO or TOB. Just your standard set of weapons.
-Mixing weapons is useless. When have you ever needed the LKW and Shockhammer together?
-The coolest weapons are the "heavy" weapons that you can't carry with you, despite being in a super suit and genetically engineered supersoldier body all the time.
-The weapon wheel is incredibly clunky to use mid-fight.
-The LaserKraftwerk (havent played Wyatt timeline) is incredibly OP and dumbed down from its TNO counterpart, it can twoshot even the largest bosses (Zitadelle).
-The Uubergehwer, while cool, just feels like they wanted a BFG type gun for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles. And again, you can't even add it to your inventory.
DIFFICULTY:
-Difficulty is all over the place for different sequences, there are two in particular that are markedly harder than the rest of the game. IMO, the top 2 difficulty levels just yield tedium and repetition that severely hampers the flow of the story, not even worth playing.
-Damage feedback is pretty bad, only activating when you have 20 health left, which usually means you're one bullet away from death.
-On higher difficulty levels, Kampfhounds combined with the overall darkness of maps is insanely annoying. Unlike TNO there is no mechanic to lessen damage while a dog or crocodile is biting you.
STEALTH:
-You bought this game to kick the ever-loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of some Nazi's right? To run face first into a group of 20 Nazis while dual weilding rotating shotguns, right? Me too. Why then, does the game seem like it's setup for almost every scenario to be stealth-run.
-You'll finish a huge battle in one area, move through some pipes, up a ladder, and then boom...you're in the next area, the little "signal detected" graphic pops up and you're right back to everything being quiet again. Apparently none of the Nazis in THIS room heard what was going on in THAT room.
- While it was difficult as hell, I wanted MORE fights like the courthouse, where you there is absolutely no option to stealth your way through. You just have to gun through countless nazis.
CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT:
VILLAINS are bland, boring, and few.
-TNO had a good handful of nicely developed side-villains, unique bosses, and enemy types (Engel, Deathshead, MachineMan, The Knife, Herr Faust, London Monitor, Bubi, Keller). New Colossus pretty much has...Engel and the ALPHA, that's it.
-Engel just seems like your generic Nazi with some creepy sexual behavior thrown in. She was much cooler in TNO when her face was broken, dual wielding assault rifles shooting up your friends. Deathshead was more of a compelling, creepy, threatening villain than Engel ever was.
FRENDLIES are criminally underdeveloped.
-Characters carried over from TNO receive almost no additional development (Bombate, Max, Anya, Fergus, Wyatt).
-Grace is decent but replaces **spoiler** way too fast.
-Horton and his gang are underused and come into the story way too late.
-Exploration of BJ's past is a nice touch, but ended too soon, imo. It didn't seem like his father aged...at all? (Odd)
STORY:
It feels like they developed a whole string of INCREDIBLY cool cutscenes (seriously, they're all fantastic) and then were left scratching their heads, desperately rushing to pump out levels that do a bad job of stringing them all together. Too often I felt myself playing just to get to the next awesome cutscene.
-Both TNO and TNC have some pretty jarring transitions from cutscene to gameplay.
-The choice to have you playing as a debilitated, dying BJ for almost 2/3 of the game is...odd. Uninspiring. BJ whines and is depressed through the first 2/3, then miraculously is totally fine after a **certain** event. No trauma whatsoever, no regrets, no nothing, just "ok I'm back to normal, nevermind the ♥♥♥♥ing incredible things I just endured, next mission."
MUSIC:
Look, I love Mick Gordon's work. Everything he does is fantastic, and the music here is pretty damn good too. But like everything else I mentioned, it isn't as great as TNO, imo.
-The music/cue system feels less "complex" than TNO, with less cues and dynamic audio. if you unpack TNO's audio assets, you'll see that the entire game is composed of hundreds of looping 10-30 second pieces, all of which string together seamlessly based on a variety of in-game events or actions.
-The music itself also feels less complex, but more organic, which isn't a bad thing.
-There are quite a handful of themes rehashed from TNO (Gibralter Bridge, The Kreisau Circle, Ransacked, to name a few). This could either be a great thing, or a sign of how this game was rushed out the door (presumably rushing Mick to compose the OST), depending how you look at it.
-Quantity wise, I think TNO had many more memorable themes.
CONTINUITY WITH TNO (Nitpicking):
I understand we're in a different part of the world now, which might explain some of these points but:
- What happened to your laser rifles? Why no burst fire on the pistol anymore?
- What happened to parts of the Eva's Hammer that you specifically explored in TNO?
- What happened to the Guard Robots and Heavy Robots and their telekenetic energy-bust cannon things?
- Why does TNO's main menu feel 100 times cooler than TNC's
- Why does Frau Engel never mention her new face, or Bubi?
- Why is Deathshead or any events from TNO, not mentioned outside of readables or small interactions with tertiary characters.
It isn't a BAD game, imo. It just doesn't live up to the previous game. I wholeheartedly want to believe it was rushed through development, and that's why it falls short in so many categories. It feels like Bethesda pushed HARD for this game to come out FAST.

FFS, I didn't learn I could dodge until I made it to my first boss (I'd just been parrying everything up to that point). I played on the default difficulty and had a few close calls during encounters with multiple enemies. Overall, not very challenging and the only time I died was when I had to maintain Senua's balance while walking across a narrow beam (wasn't really paying attention).
While the environments are beautiful, there's not much to do in the way of exploration. Also, Senua moves pretty slowly, so if you're not the type to spend your time enjoying the sights, get ready to keep your finger held down on the 'Slow Jog' button. There are collectibles in the form of lore stones that recite some intriguing bits of Norse mythology to you. They aren't hard to find and I got most of 'em on my one playthrough.
Not a lot of replayability though. Not a huge gripe for me as the $30 price tag is pretty generous considering the quality on display here. It's also kinda short. I finished it in around 6 hours but I knew it would be a quick ride. Perfect game to knock out on a weekend.
I probably won't play it ever again, but it is still one of 2017's highlights (and quite the delightful surprise). This is a very strong single player title that I feel everyone should give a try.
Definitely worth a buy, in my opinion.

I'll start off by saying that this was one of the most impactful games I've played in recent memory.  Such a powerful and compelling story.  Buy it... and strap yourself in.  It is going to be an emotional journey.
Overall - 9.5/10
I can't say enough good things about this game.  I only cut the half star because of two things: there are some typos in the subtitles, and it did crash on me one time in nine hours of gameplay.
Gameplay - 8/10
The gameplay is pretty straightforward.  The controls are easy enough to wrap your head around although they deviate slightly from the controls I'm used to for this type of game.  The combat is pretty tight but can become a bit redundant and tedious at times.  Luckily, I found these sequences very tolerable and they did not detract much from the rest of the game.  I also noticed a couple of instances where some objects were difficult to interact with if the character isn't positioned properly.  Back up, approach again, no problem.
Graphics - 9/10
This game is really pretty... when it needs to be.  It is also very dark and forboding when it needs to be.  The character models are exquisitely done.  The graphics are everything I expected from a game as cinematic as this.  The environments and effects are excellent and very appropriate for the tone of the game.  Was able to run everything seamlessly at the highest settings on an R9 380 X.
Sound Design - 11/10
This is where this game truly excells.  They will tell you to wear headphones at the beginning of the game and I would highly recommend it.  Without giving too much away, they are necessary to appreciate the great amount of effort the developers put into every piece of the soundscape and even help mechanically in a few instances.

A story in a Norse setting about a woman trying to go to hell to save the soul of her deceased lover. Also, there are mental illness / the "darkness" / "voices in my head" / "what is real and what isn't" sprinkled in to make the game feel smart and sophisticated, to varying degrees of success.
On that last note, the idea is integral for the story, and it works; I'm fairly sure I understood the meanings and messages it tries to convey, and the characters and settings fit and change based on how those topics are handled and presented within the story. However, there's a seemingly smug "OR~ IS~ IT~?!" with all of those topics that are only danced around and not actually "Hinted at and then explained" that leaves a sort of sour taste in my mouth.
Without spoilers, the main character, Senua, obviously has a troubled past. Some of the trauma is hinted at, but is then later explained as she confronts those issues. A+. Very good voice acting, mo-cap, and overall presentation.
Then there are a few things that hint at “This journey isn’t even real~!” “It’s all in your head~!” “That-last-part-was-real-and-this-part-is-only-slightly-real-based-on-your-perceptions-of-reality-obscured-by-your-past~!” and just feels tired and cliche to me, personally. I chose to ignore a lot these instances, and taking the story as it was actually presented to me was a lot more enjoyable.
I mean, heck, you can always try and go 10 layers deep with Rick and Morty, but you don’t have to to still enjoy the show (for those that enjoy it). There are indeed sub-plots and hints that are actually, identifiably there, but you don’t have to read into the hints if you don’t want to. For this game, it felt like there were some grand sub-plots and ideas that were hinted at with all of the “psychosis” things in addition to what was identifiably there and dealt with, but there wasn’t actually substance to back up anything other than “What if?”
That just personally annoys me. Your milage may vary.
The gameplay itself mainly has two segments: fights and "puzzles"
For combat, you have a Light attack, a Heavy attack, a Block, a Dodge, a Sprint, and a "Slo-Mo" mechanic that fills the better you fight. Combat starts off a bit on the simple side with just dodging and blocking with some stabs, but then ramps up as you learn a few intricacies between light attack, heavy attack, dodging, and sprinting during combat. The ramp up for this learning was actually pretty fair, and felt like I was learning how to fight within the game's systems.
Enemy movesets can be a bit predictable, but the overall experience is balanced with having more enemies to deal with as the game progresses, each with their own cliche's (I'm slow but attack hard, I rush you and attack a lot, I have a shield and you need to wait for an opening, etc). Fights end up being more about seeing bounds of the fight area, discerning which enemies need to be taken down first, which are the highest threat, and maneuvering through everything without getting killed.
Overall, I found the combat pretty fun. I'm not too experienced with extreme hack-and-slash or fighting games, with only a bit of Bloodborne and Demon's Souls / Dark Souls I under my belt, but I was able to grasp it, and I had fun with it. The only issues I had were when the fight areas were a bit too small, and I ended up dodging into a wall or flat-out could not have dodged. This frustration probably could have been avoided if I blocked more, but I went through most of the game just spamming Dodge and moving to the Left and waiting for attack openings. It sounds a bit simple, but, with the above mechanics in mind, it is fun and, overall, satisfying.
The other major portion of the game comes from "Puzzle" sections. I say this with quotations, as they aren't really all
Puzzle-like? They're almost all different placements of the "Align-the-various-things-within-view-and-press-a-button" Shadow Box puzzles, "Oh hey, I need to make this symbol on a door. I can see these bright, shimmering things floating about. Oh darn, it doesn't fit all the way when I look at it from here! I better climb up here - oh darn, it's blocked! Better drop this bridge to cross it" sums up most of these.
Then there are blocked doors with "Runes" on them. It's mostly the same thing. Look at the runs, try to find geometry or shadows in the environment that match the shapes, look at them, move on. This is made (a lot) easier by the fact that, when you're close to the area to view a symbol, the symbol in question *floods* the screen to let you know you've reached the right area. There are a few MC-Escher-esque situations like this, but there is a sound cue instead of a visual one.
There were a lot of these "Puzzle" sections, and, overall, felt a bit drawn-out. The caveat to this is that these environments are often very well rendered, with a story to tell...and often with narration sorta-forcing the story at you. Between the world building, the quality of the voice acting, and the amount of detail put into everything, these sections went from interesting at the start to "All right, another one of these. Time to enjoy the modeling and texture work, get the Lore, and move on" near the end.
As an overall package, the game runs for around 6-8 hours. My first playthrough was very enjoyable. For $22.49, and a pc rig strong enough to render the game at full-glory, it was a worthwhile purchase and experience for me. The combat was fun, the world was interesting, and the acting and presentation were top-notch. Some more variation in the puzzle sections would have been appreciated, but all of the everything else going on more than makes up for that. I'm not sure when I'll play it again, but I'm very glad to have had a great experience the first time through for the price of entry (especially sale-price!).

Update: 11/22/15
So I've been playing this remaster edition of DS2 for a while and I'd like to say the game is actually better than what I thought previously. Although it had some really nasty bugs during its initial release, the developers had fixed them (at least in public beta) and now it runs very well on my laptop.
Current Issues: They are small and do npt pose serious problems to pro gamers.
a) On your way to the Drenchfort, there's a chance that you will fall infinitely and eventually die while you're riding the horse.
b) The Makers' chest area (Aylia) seem to have a resolution issue, since its texture was not smooth but made of chunks of small squares.
c) The game wouldn't stop running after you exit sometimes. It happens occasionally when you've played the game for several hours.
Let's talk about the pros:
Besides the apparent better texture and shaders, the gameplay system in this remastered edition  is well-balanced. Old players won't really appreciate the beauty of it until the later stage of the game. I personally had complained about not being able to access my DLC weapons instantly before. Now I actually think it is a well-considered idea to let players gain access to them "when the time is right". Trust me, it makes the gameplay so much smoother, because you get to use better weapons and armors when you really need them.
Comment: Changed my opinion from Not Recommend to Recommended. Still, looking forward to seeing the developers improve the game further.

Look, Nordic Games are doing their best to provide us with a genuine, fun, new experience with Darksiders 2, so cut them a little slack. They new they were getting to into a pretty picky fanbase, and they're trying their best.
Now, onto the review:
The game is the same as Darksiders 2. If you were expecting Darksiders 3, I'm sorry, but this isn't it.
There has been some changes here and there, graphical changes, UI tweaks, texture rises, as in, the textures don't look like absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥now, general tweaks to enhance what THQ left us with. Now, are they bad, or good? Well, they're kinda both.
On my end, the V-sync is almost completely broken, as it was in the original. AA is also broken, as far as I can tell. I didn't pay too close of attention, though. I alt+tabbed once and the game crashed. Got me a little pissy, but I remembered this is an active thing, and fixes are coming/will come. So we're going to have wait and see.
Nordic Game hesitated on doing things with this because they know how we, the fan-base, can get if not done properly. I have been a loyal fan of the Darksiders series since day one. Loved War's story, and I love Death's story. I love the gameplay and art style of both, these games were a dream come true in my own opinion. The develops though, ehhh...
Darksiders 2 was broken to begin with, even without this new Dethinitive edition. And Nordic Games are trying to remedy that. They're doing their best, and at the moment, they're doing an okay job at that.
People need to learn to be a bit more patient, and wait for more fixes. You people gotta realize this came out in 2012, and they're just restarting updating it. It's gonna take some time before they get it into a stable condition, all along adding slight changes and tweaks to it.
All in all, do I recommend this? YES. While it's on sale. If you're reading this when it's not on sale, wait until they apply more fixes to it, then buy it. If they already have applies fixes, and it already is in stable condition, then I can without a doubt recommend this to you at full price.
You're doing a fine job, Nordic Games. Just keep it up, and everything will go smoothly. We, the Darksiders community, believe in you.

I bought this game a while ago and completely forgot about it so I decided to give it a shot after a few years. I've played a few chapters and from what I gathered, I've experienced all the game has to offer and I do not recommend it.
Remember Me is a linear experience that is very similar in gameplay and structure to Enslaved: Oddysey To The West, however I have not played enough of Enslaved to give it a fair comparison. The closest comparison I can do is with the Prince Of Persia series as they seem to have the same type of linear gameplay and combat.
I don't have a problem with linear games. Uncharted, Prince of Persia: TSOT and Mirror's Edge are very linear games yet they are among my favourite games of all time. However, Remember Me is a game that I believe is too linear. From what I've played, The game holds your hand from platforming to combat over and over. Just that is fine as Prince Of Persia does the same but the reason POP succeeds is because of the amount of genuine player thought and effort that goes into each segment so memorable. Remember Me is too predictable. In platforming segments, you simply follow the obvious path (that is blatantly indicated via arrows) and you will progress. There is no thought from the player needed, just a continuous following of the path. There are some parts that are a bit different from the usual but after a moment of interest it becomes stale very quickly and still requires no effort to complete.
Now one thing that Remember Me has which is kind of interesting at first is the combo fighting system but ultimately fails. In the game, you must try and "remember" how to do combo moves and then you get to decide which moves to use in the combo. There are moves you can use that are powerful, can heal you, can cool down specials, etc. When I saw this I was excited to play with it but it failed when the "dominant strategy" became evident. This is when you find the easiest way to do something and you use only that strategy. All I had to do to easily pass combat segments is make a short combo with powerful hits and one with lots of healing hits so I ended up spamming one combo then switching to the other combo if I got hit. Messing with complex combos can be fun but is too frustrating to pull off so you just do what's easiest. POP's combat isn't perfect either but at least it lets you experiment in a fight to figure out what to do for yourself when the game throws you a curveball. In Remember Me, the enemy weaknesses is told to you and it makes them too boring to fight.
The only thing I can commend this game for is an interesting story (even if the characters are flat and boring), the puzzles altering people's memories which were really cool and a boss in which you had to fight a giant robot which was challenging and fun. However, none of this interested me enough to continue with the game. It was boring, too easy and never had a memorable moment (ironic, isn't it). If after reading this you still want to buy it, I recommend putting it on easy mode simply to get through it faster.

Personally, this is one of my favorite indie games. It has a lot of pros, and a whole lot of cons.
Pros:
SMASH! - You can smash pretty much anything, including many parts of the environment. Landing one of those perfect hits on the enemy, going blue, and just generally destroying everything is one of the most satisfying things in this game.
GFX - The attention to detail is superb, as seen in the environments, weapons, and "vehicles."
Story - While difficult to understand at times, I enjoyed it a lot, and though it interesting.
Weapons - There are a great many weapons available, and each is different.
Modes - There are 5 working gametypes: Solo: single player campaign, Hall: where you select and buy weapons, Grim: where you hunt flying worms, Arena: where you fight other flying machines, Hammerball: where you fight weird machines in some sort of soccer type game.
There is another gametype called Tribal Wars, but it doesn't seem to work (at least, for me).
Cons:
SMASH! - Sometimes, if you go blue and miss an enemy, you might wind up outside the map.
GFX - People are really weird sometimes. The animations can be... odd.
Story - Lost in translation applies here. Quite a bit of it.
Weapons - Sometimes the chain type weapons will break. No idea under what circumstances, and it doesn't happen terribly often.
Modes - Solo: The story can be very confusing and jumps somewhat. Hall:sometimes weapons can be lost if you drop them, Grim: the idiot AI enjoy dropping bombs on your head all the time, Arena: it often pits you against 3 AI at a time, and that can make it extremely difficult at times, Hammerball: Not for the faint of heart, this is the single most difficult challenge I have EVER faced in a game. More on that later.
As I mentioned, Tribal Wars seems to not work at all for me.
On the subject of Hammerball: For the first round, you have to face a single flying mechanical lobster. Not too difficult. Second round, you have to face two. One goes for the ball while the other uses some sort of taser on you if you don't dodge it. Third round you have to face three flying mechanical flying lobsters. One goes after the ball and the other two attack you with some sort of taser.
There are 4 different ball types I have encountered in Hammerball. The first, a rock, is easy to deal with and gives you one point per score. The second is a bomb that will go off after a time unless the game ends, or you manage to score. It's worth two points. The third is a flying buzzsaw that will get angry if you hit it, and it will move around. It's somewhat manageable and is worth three points. The fourth is some sort of flying tentacle monster that will generally kill you when it appears. I would assume it's worth four points if it's actually possibly to push into the goal. Bit of a spoiler here: it looks like the final boss of the game, but can fly around.
On the subject of AI: In general, they aren't too bad. Your allies like to throw bombs though, and sometimes, the human AI like to seriously "derp out."
Overall, I think that, even with all it's flaws, it is a GREAT game. It's incredibly fun to smash the AI with hammers, flails, axes, swords, etc. The graphics are amazing, and the AI can be dealt with. For only $5 I think it's a great game, and has entertained me for hours on end.

I usually don't put much effort into reviewing games, but this game is such a journey. I won't even bother to mention the game mechanics, because I feel like picking into that would destroy the absolutely beautiful image this game has painted for me. As someone who's mentally ill, struggling with depression, and surrounded by people in a similiar scenario -- playing this game offered me temporary relief, it was rewarding emotionally and mentally. (I'll prevent spoilers by trying to summarize this without giving away the details of the game.)
Regardless, as I've said, this game is a journey. It's grueling, my first play-through was on the hardest difficulty and without referring to a guide I'll admit it almost defeated me. Top that up with the fact that there is no achievement for beating it on any/the hardest difficulty, it made it even more grueling to complete upon that realization. However, I believe that's what made it even more rewarding and emotionally impactful at the end. Depression, and/or mental illnesses aren't an easy journey. There's no text guide as to how difficult one person perceives it compared to the other. And there's no Nobel prize for having a harder time than someone else and overcoming it. And I like to believe that is ultimately what this game is meant to portray.
It's stressful. It's sometimes irritating, especially when you screw up the same sequence a few times and have to panic about the inevitability of failing the game. But at the very end, when all is done, there is nothing but relief. So I'd definitely recommend this game, even if you're not someone who struggles with depression or mental illness. It's a totally different (and true) perspective, it tells a unique story unlike any other.

An exploration game with Metroidvania flourishes that sees you dropped into a world with no real context and left to clear it out of bad guys and some kind of creeping corruption that's fouling the place up. The action takes place both above and below ground but each part generally leads to you pulling a lever and watching massive chunks of landscape impressively spin, rise, fall, flip and generally reassemble itself into a configuration which allows you to press forward. There are collectibles which give you a number of advantages (i.e. longer health bar, new powers for your glove thing, etc) in combat but it's not a hard game at the best of times so I didn't even use some of the new powers I ended up with. The story is close to non-existent and even when I arrived without much fanfare at the ending I was none the wiser what was going on. Frankly it doesn't matter though because opening up the map and clearing out all the corruption is the main hook and it doesn't need anything else to grab you. It doesn't have the same beautifully lonely atmosphere of RIME and it's nowhere near as pretty but in some ways it's a more engaging game because it's less linear and has more stuff going on. Overall it's really good stuff and I loved the 10 or so hours it took me to finish it and open the entire map up. PSA: the performance on my PC at least was pretty ropey. It was generally fast and smooth but had blatant issues streaming in new parts of the open world as the frame rate would briefly crash through the floor with irritating regularity so maybe wait for a patch or pick up the PS4 version if it's better.

Hammerfight is surprisingly fun and if the creator was a much better programmer it would have been an instant indie classic. While this might not be the full version, the steam version is incomplete, it is worth the price.
Tip: Since you likely won't read this longer... If you play this turn up the mouse sensitivity in the games options. The game SERIOUSLY overestimates the power of your mouse.
In Hammerfight you play a flying machine with a flail, sword, or hammer attached that you can swing wildly. The gameplay at first is quite hectic but soon you get the hang of things and will be able to fight with the best of them, expect to stink a lot at first, it will be 2 hours before things click and until then you will feel like this game is unfairly challenging you. After this period the game is all about timing and finding your opening, and when you strike the enemies FEEL it, your weapons have actual weight and not only do they affect how you fly, heavy weapons do affect how you fly and when an enemy gets struck by one expect them to fly right into the wall with a satisfying SPLAT! You can even strategically attack the opponent's weapons to stop their momentum or even destroy them.
The game isn't without its flaws. There is no Newgame+ so as soon as you beat the game it is OVER and you need to start a new game... There is no way to grind crystals, they enhance weapons, in this game (only in the full version) so whatever you end up with is all you get. The game feels short and you can easily finish it in one afternoon... Enemies in the Arena have a large tendency to just blow up to kill you or use a "blow up the entire stage" attack, making the high-level Arena feel cheap rather than fun. As well there are a few game ending bugs in the game. Multiplayer would have elevated this game to instant greatness, but there is none.
All in all Hammerfight is a very fun game that is short but ooooooh so satisfying. This game could have been a great game worthy to be one of the greatest indie games of all time, but it falls short and becomes instead simply a very good game worthy of anyone's cash. If this is on sale BUY IT! there really is no excuse.

This is a really good cyberpunk game (and there are not too much of them) but somehow I got the feeling that with more love from the editor and more polish this game would have reached its full potential which is a 10/10. As it is now I would rate it 8/10.
The good:
- a well written story in the line of the best cyberpunk litterature you can find: things looks simple at first with the Big Evil corporation that is enslaving the world, but things get quickly more subtle and deeper.
- the universe is well thought and beautifully designed: there are some cut scenes à-la Blade Runner which are really breathtaking. There are lots of small details, references and puns that gives credibility to the story.
- the voice acting and the music.
- the Memory remix is a great idea and fun to play. I wish there was more of it.
- the powers you acquire through your initiatic journey are really cool: conceptually and visually.
The so-so:
- I really liked the platformer part since I enjoyed games like Prince or Persia, but highlighting the path takes away all the challenge. There should have been an option to remove the hints.
- the combo lab is really a great idea, unfortunately it's one of those ideas that didn't reached its full potential. I ended up spamming the same combo of 5 moves because it just works. I would have expected the choices to be more tactical.
The bad:
- the combat system is quickly boring and even annoying at times. The options are too limited: dodge or attack. Nilin can't pary or counter attack. So the fights are very repetitive and consists of dodging until you can land a combo without being interrupted, or start dodging again if you are about to be hit during a combo.
- it's too short and linear. First playthrough on Errorist level took me only 12 hours, even when trying to find collectibles.  There are too many questions left unanswered that would have deserved side quests to extend the game time.

A short but sweet cyberpunk action game that will likely leave you "remember"ing the storytelling far more than the gameplay itself.
In 2080-something, the world of Neo Paris is addicted to memories. All citizens have a device attached to their spinal cord that allows them to share and download memories from other people and other lives. Cool, right? Except for when the devices malfunction and spur mutations in the host, leading to "leapers", or half the enemies you fight in the game.
You're Nilin, a 20-something kung-fu pro that has had her memories stolen and has been imprisoned. You spend the game running, jumping, and kicking your way to reclaim what was lost.
The platforming is remniscent of the Tomb Raider games, except easy mode. There are AR-style icons to indicate where you need to jump next, and the magnetism is enough so that you'll very, very rarely ever miss a jump. If manual platforming isn't your strong suit, then no worries here, as it doesn't really add much to the game except a nice sense of verticality.
The combat is much stronger, but still not the game's strongest point. It's solid and snappy, and dodging is very fluid and easy to do, so no complaints there. Unfortunately, while you can customize your combos in the sense that when you press 'X' here, you regen health or do more damage, your combos themselves are static, and there's only four - a 3 hit, 5 hit, 6 hit, and 8 hit respectively that unlock through game progression, and the button patterns are always the same. While this allows you to learn the combos quickly, it leaves very little in the way of innovation.
More fun are the special abilities that you learn which allow you to take out certain enemy types with a consumption of Remember Me's equivalent of a Super bar. Without giving away too much, you essentially "hack" the world and enemies around you for extra-powerful attacks.
All of that takes a back seat to the storytelling though, which is where the game shines. The writing is never longwinded, the characters are (usually) interesting and have their own strong motivations and desires, and you'll even occasionally discover some fairly poignant quotes and very well-written lines of dialogue.
The plot culminates quite solidly at the end, despite some shortcutting in the final chapter that leaves a little bit more extrapolation of the final boss and his motivations to be desired, but all in all it's a satisfying and extremely pretty adventure that you might even want to revisit after the game's moderately short 8 hours with the new game plus feature.
Pros:
+Very good writing and interesting setting
+Solid heroine
+References to Gibson, Ghost in the Shell and other well-known cyberpunk franchises
+Excellent graphics
+Smooth combat
+Collectibles and worth replaying for completionist status
Cons:
-Platforming is not challenging at all
-Few puzzles with easy solutions
-A bit short

Would I reccommend this game, yes. Is it a great game, for the most part but does have flaws.
when this game tries to scare you, it does its job, for the most part, very well, starts off with very few jump scares of cute cardboard and slowly makes it more scary with each 50-100 levels.
BTW: MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD
This is a good horror game and does do a good job as posing itself as a cheaply made one at that, and to an extent does go under the guise of this very well.
Good parts:
I loved, and I mean loved, how they recycled rooms, and while at first I thought it was just a way to be cheap and save time, it made you overtime feel trapped and there was little hope to leave until the rooms started ticking up to a nice round number near the hundreds where you felt safe and prayed for salvation. The monsters, for the most part, also helped make this part of the game scarier where if a monster was trying to catch you, you had to hope for the right rooms or be fast to get to the door with your stamina not running out making stress something of an add on to the terror. The jump scares were also very intelligent, especially with the randomly generated rooms where at the beginning I found it cute, but while running from a hellish demon actually scared me so much I scared my dog from me jumping from my seat. Another part about this that had me on the edge of my seat was something most horror genres nowadays neglect, darkness because each hundred rooms there is more darkness and harder to see making the game feel more ominous, and in the last hundred rooms you can barely see in from of you, and when you get the lantern to see through the darkness, it is borderline scarier somehow so good job Lag Studios for doing something most horror forgets.
Issues:
One of the major issues would be the story, the story is all over the place and the thing was, from the middle of the game it helped create atmospere with you leaving notes of your sanity being ebbed away as you travel through the mansion, and given the brilliant yet short explaination of the monsters met, it had potential, but you wind up in a boss fight that comes borderline out of nowhere and you die no matter what and you join an army now, because DLC? I dont know I haveng played them nor intend to unless steam sales. It comes out of nowhere which is upsetting because of the potential lost and the boss fight was way too easy and felt a bit like pandering to a younger audience when the story could have ended with spooky taking the last of your sanity or something and make you another monster preying on others who come your way, which would have been really terrifying or make you a cardboard thing to scare a fake player.
There was also one creative idea for an enemy where it had to see you or else you would slowly perish, and while it was terrifying for a while, and brilliant, soon became a chore and for about 30-40 rooms, it was a bit too long without much change and my terror when from "crap he's going to get me" to "ok come on I just want to get this done".
Lastly, after my computer crashed this game for me two times (unrelated to game, computer updates) I completed it in less than four hours which is quite shocking to me because it felt longer even when it wasn't
Final Verdict:
would I pay for this game, for very little like a couple of bucks, sure. Was it worth, to an extent where it does much of the horror very well, my only real complaints would be length, one enemy, story, and the boss, but again due to this being a free game does put this higher on the list. This also has some replay value for the notes and the underlying story atmoshpere that is not really looked upon but overall is not a big motivation to go back to, but if you want to just spend an afternoon looking at creative enemies and silly yet effective jumpscares, this would be a good game for you.
Rating: 77/100

I'm six hours in to this game and have mixed feelings about it. The graphics are great. This game looks really, really good.
The animations match the verbal dialogue very well (except the crying baby), even if the teeth stand out too much. The animations for characters in the cut scenes are noticeably unnatural though. Anytime two people are physically interacting the animations are almost comically lumbering, ungraceful and synthetic. For as good as the design, models and textures are, they should have used motion capture for the animations because they are laughably poor at times (BJ's mother and father scuffle, the handling of the infant in the Neu York tower scene).
The level design thus far is counter-intuitive; you have to go up to go down and vice versa when navigating maps. Minor gripe. Paths are non-linear (which is good). There also seems to be a lack of realistic scale in areas (how big is this damn sub, and how is half of it separated by a foot locker?). How many nazi's went unnoticed for months on this sub?!
The camera is even more nauseating than previous installments though. In addition to the forced bob_pitch and bob_roll (which is turned to 11 in this family of games), the camera now rocks and tilts after turning left or right. I cannot conceive of any logical reason for this. It's disorienting and unnecessary. It adds nothing positive to the game, story or the experience in general.
Movement is decent. Strafing, running, turning, shooting are all functional. Physical interaction with the environment could use polishing though (jumping, climbing ladders, hoisting).
Aiming is okay and reliable. Shooting is decent , although off-hand aim in dual wield is a bit wild and wasteful.  The heavy weapons are fun so far.
The weapon wheel is absolutely horrid in design and function. It would be a non-issue if you could scroll through weapons faster than molasses in January, but nope.... you might as well file FOIA requests for your weapons because that's how long it takes to cycle through them.
The story is fairly straightforward thus far, with an unusually modern social conscience for a retro period setting.
This game is good if you get it on sale. Not for $60 though. I can't imagine replaying this game due to the poor camera and pitch/roll settings.

There are people who have reported technical problems with the game. I do not have any of those.
There are people who complain the game is racist or promotes a SJW agenda. I do not see it.
Then why a thumbs down? Because, frankly, i found the game boring. W2 starts off right after the end events of the first one. If you didn't finish it (or remember f**k-all because, let's be honest, it wasn't exactly Apocalypse Now) the game politely gives you a 5-minute refresher at the beginning, with a "when we last left our heroes" vibe.
The start is promising, with BJ gunning down nazis in a wheelchair, which I found a fitting metaphore for one of gaming's oldest franchises, but soon enough it descends into generic corridor shooting.
Which wouldn't be so bad if the focus was more on the action and less on the stealth. Sure, you can play your own way, but the game will actively punish you via bad game design choices if you don't go stealth when an officer is narby. Damage indicators are almost non-existant, meaning it's very hard to figure out where the guy shooting you is. You also have only 50 HP half of the game, so one of the soldiers being spawned out of the nether might get a chance to rush you in and kill you in 3 shots if you're armor is low, which can often be the case.
For people who think this is 'realistic' i'll remind them that this is a game where you shoot robot dogs with dual-wielding shotguns.
The Story? Sometimes decent, but BJ was apparently born under the sign of Ex Machina since the only way his escapes would be less believable would be if he were to pull out a weapon literally out of his a$$. No, THAT would be more believable. I know I said it's not meant to be realistic, but COME ON. (courthouse end cinematic if you really wanna see it). His monosilabic monologues in the first third of the game really don't help make him more relatable when, during a cinematic, he usually has the personality of a brick wall. The support characters are all over the place: some are stereotypical, some are interesting, some are just plain a$$holes. There is a good message underneath the facade about how no one is born a racist, we are transformed into it either by hardship or discipline, but it goes by fast; you'll miss it if you blink.
I really wanted to like the game, but the stealth, the design choices and the sometimes bland levels made it more of a chore than anything else. Remember that rosewell city in the trailer? Yeah, in the main game you're there for like 5 minutes. The game tries to lure you back with side-missions (more officer hunting, i.e. stealth) but i'll be damned if i can bother.
Right now i'm off-planet stealing some nazi codes, AGAIN. I'm 3 missions away from the end but I really don't feel like putting in the extra hours.
It's not a bad game, but it's just too much of the same mixed with bad game design and a mediocre story. Get it on sale if you're on the fence.

Other reviews do point out the lack of responsiveness in the controls, leaving them feeling sluggish. While this definitely feels intentionally designed, it can be mitigated very effectively if you adjust the mouse DPI slider to a lower number. The mouse DPI slider is basically a difficulty option, where the higher you go, the slower the controls become. Use it if you're really having that much of an issue with the game's controls. Also, don't be fooled by the first few levels. There's a much larger amount of customization and weapons once you unlock The Hall. Plus, the main story is only one part of the game, with two extra modes for each style of combat the game offers. This expands the game's life for quite a while after the main story ends. Overall, 8/10

CAVEAT: I waited and started the game after 1.33, which is a whole new game from version 1.0.
This game is simply incredible! This is above and beyond what I had wanted out of ANY space exploration game, and certainly 100x better than the initial release version. I had a day off and I put 9 hours into the game in one day (and that was all on the starting planet, after I received my first spaceship, and found a crashed/damaged Hauler which I proceeded to fix-up).
Right now, I have a cumulative of 13.3 hours into the experience, and I don't have a vast majority of the content or story unlocked. I am aware of the state the game came-out in and what was missing, but after reading the patch notes of the last 3 patches (really should be referred to as MASSIVE expansions!... did I mention they were free?!), the game is now a LOT deeper than it was.
I really wanted to get this game on pre-order, but my gut told me it may not live-up to the hype... and it didn't. After a MASSIVE over-haul, and when it was on sale for 66% off, it was a no-brainer for me to get this thing finally.
One of the early complaints I saw were about how people got bored with the game and just blazed through the (at the time) limited story narrative with nothing to achieve... I started my first game in Survival mode. I highly recommend it, as it is exactly as advertised. Death came early to me while I was learning that I could not breath the toxic atmosphere of my first planet and that I had to gather resources, dart from cave to cave, and look for bases and other points of interest rather than just running willy-nilly to my main objective and getting off the planet.
There were TONS of Points of Interest on my starting planet, and they were a pleasure to look for. Resources were available, but definitely scarce, so survival definitely played a huge part in the exploration even after getting a ridiculously great Class A Multitool by pure random chance from one of the aliens I encountered early-on. Sure, you could fly anywhere quickly, but would you have access to enough Plutonium to power your thrusters to get up in the air again? Most of the time the answer was 'no'... I had to venture through caves and explore minutes away from my spacecraft to gather what I needed. The wildlife was passive (thankfully), but the atmosphere was always choking me.
Going off planet to a hot moon for the first time was even more abusive (in a great way)... I was greeted by a fast howling creature which resulted in at least 3 deaths until I figured-out what the heck it was... and it was mean... and made me jump when I heard the scurrying sounds through my surround sound in the middle of the night. I would jump on top of my ship as soon as I would land just to scout the surroundings. It was a legit Aliens-type feeling, especially since the small moon was densely populated with other wild life which was constantly being spooked... and for good reason with that six-legged bas**** running around! Resources were even scarcer than on my first planet, and after several reloads (after I figured-out that I could reload saves >_<!), I managed to escape with next to no resources (which I felt were adequately stock-piled from the first planet), 1 health unit, literally drained Life Support, and no shields/resistance to the elements.
Next planet was in the new system and it was a beautiful Paradise planet with vast oceans and green islands... except it was crawling with ANGRY Sentinels that apparently destroyed all life... I was forced to run multiple times. Ultimately learned how to deal with them after a couple of near-deaths, and started farming as many as I could from a different location to net me some great loot. I have no idea how to survive going back to the central point crawling with Sentinels on this planet, but I gladly try! :)
I am pleased to announce that in Survival Mode, the game difficulty being 'too easy' is no longer an issue. There are multiple ways of farming money, and everything can kill you, but you always have a chance once you learn the basics. The game is difficult, but not brutal. I got a feeling of playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. in space on more than a few occasions as I explored abandoned buildings, way points, and crash sites... it was wonderful!
I saw what the graphics looked like before, and I have to say that they look incredible at 1440p and a 980ti now. I have the FPS cap set to 60fps with VSYNC on, and I feel like the game is smooth but may occasionally dip, as judged by moments when it the game runs like butter. It is a minor note, as the game plays very consistently, and I can't tell if maybe the frame drops are in my head or not.
I did find a base with an Architect I could claim on the first planet, but have so far decided not to build my first base prior to unlocking some more Blueprints and greater access to credits and resources. So yeah, I have not even touched on one of the largest aspects of the game, not to mention the freighters! All I know is that I landed on the first Class C Freighter I saw, and the captain offered to sell it to me for 192 million credits... I had about 200K at the time.
So at this point I am GREATLY looking forward to spending more time with this game, while my girlfriend is terrified that I won't see here ever again... well, for at least the next 100 hours or so. ;)
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Fairly easy to figure everything out, so the learning curve is not particularly steep... if you know how to play FPS games and may have played a Survival-type game, you will probably do well.
- Really great Survival Mode, which should be the default in my opinion
- Tons to explore
- Vastly improved planet types and creatures over the original
- New progression system
- Interesting economy mechanics
- Really fun exponential growth model that REALLY lets you feel like you are starting from nothing and growing into a force to be reckoned with
- Faction system that gives you additional unlocks
- Great spaceship variety (in terms of visuals, however I have seen pretty interesting stat and slot combinations also... this is always going to be subjective, though)
- Sound design gives weapons weight and startling moments when something sneaks-up on you (if you have surround sound)
- There are vehicles now, too?! O_O
- Plans for even more content, while the current build is already amazing!
Cons:
- Not a lot of details on how to actually survive when you first start... I had no idea caves could protect me from toxic gas, which is the exact opposite of what I would personally expect (greater gas in cave pockets, not less o_O... I can live with it, though).
- No explanation of the Quick Menu and all of the cool things you can do with it... pretty easy to use and figure-out at least.
- Still some optimization work may help performance on older machines and fix the odd crash (I only had 1 when I loaded a prior save for the first time), but still highly playable.
Conclusion:
The game has evolved greatly from its initial release, and this is exactly the type of game I wanted for the longest time. It seems to do things in an simpler/easier way than games like Elite Dangerous, but at the same time it does a lot of things better, and maybe a handful of things worse. It's a must buy for any lovers of space and survival genres, especially if you are looking for a great single-player experience as opposed to having to be surrounded by people in typically MMO's. You are truly a lost traveler and it feels like it in this world. I feel like it's finally worth full price, but it's a complete steal if you get it on sale! Two thumbs up! :)

I would like to start saying that this game was one of my favourite title of the past few years. That said, I'll try to be objective about it.
I really recommend the game, someone could feel it's a bit overpriced considering just its lenght (8 hours were enough for me to beat the game), still there are alot of other factors, let's say it's quality (very, very high) over quantity (8 hours, low replayability). I'll go using pros, cons and neutrals (aspects I feel worth to mention but that different players could judge differently):
- Every aspect of the writing it's deep and well balanced, background and references to myths and cultures are flawless, same for the innovative and effective portrait of mental illness (Senua suffer from psychosis) this game provide. The story itself is short and simple, but its thematics are important and touching. Senua is one of the most real character I ever found in a game (or in other media), her emotions are vivid and her actions are never some cheap choices to help the story go or to make it longer. The acting - yes, that's what it is imao - of the protagonist is perfect, also the other cast give a solid performance and this make a simple story a story you won't forget.
- The world in which Senua moves is beautifully portrayed, enemies are well designed and the atmosphere is great. But the game trademark is the main character model, Senua facial animations are simply awesome, something you could expect just from a live action actress, a good one.
- Senua hear voices, and if you use the right headset (I used a Logitech G430 7.1) you'll experience a great use of the surround effects.
- The game mix few solid elements - combat, exploration, puzzle - doing it good and achieving a good balance, the combat system may be simple, same for puzzle and exploration, but the "rhythm" used to mix them helps to keep the experience fresh, the ongoing storytelling fits and complete the pace of the game.
- This game give much, the experience delivered it's something enlightening as a lightening but also clear and short as a thunder. You'll think about the game and its thematics alot, but at the current state (no new content whatsoever - aka dlc and/or patch) you'll unlikely play more than one run, maybe you'll go for a second if you're missing an achievent and if you want 100% on this title (yep, I'll probably do it).
- I mention this just because I know it's crucial to some player. As I said before, I just needed 8 hours to beat the game, for someone this could be a flaw. While I point it out for the ones who could value this aspect much. I have to say I feel this is totally secondary in a game like this, it wasn't at all a problem to me, the experience delivered it's superb and I'm not sure how much I'm in need of games with 100+ hours to play. Also this game strikes hard and deep, so by its intense nature it make sense it's not a long game, it's energy would be dispersed if put into a longer game experience.
- You won't have choices to make, nor multiple endings. Same as before, I mention this cause many players want these elements be part of all their games. This wasn't a problem to me, the storytellig was great and the thematics were deeply explored, many ignore that having multiple choices - if not done perfectly - while providing more content for the player, can lead characters and story in directions uncompatible with their nature.
Ok, so yeah, I recommend it, even if I see it's not a game for everyone. I hope my review can help you understand is Hellblade is the right game for you. :)

It's very satisfying to solve the puzzles and watch giant chunks of land rise into place and fit perfectly with the existing terrain, like giant mechanical puzzle pieces. There's just something about Hob. I'm a crotchety old goat at the best of times, frequently overly critical of games - but this one has that rare quality of delivering me directly to my childhood. A sense of wonder, or the beauty of simplicity? I don't know what it is, but Hob has it. Despite not sharing much in terms of gameplay, it reminds me of Bastion in some ways.
It isn't for everyone, however. The most commonly-cited criticisms are broadly correct; the basic combat, thin plot, and linearity are all valid complaints. If you don't like Zelda games, and aren't taken by the graphical style and general game environment, Hob probably isn't worth your time. Although I must've fallen to my doom dozens of times in completing it, the game could easily be described as being quite casual, if only due to how simple it is. Go here, unlock this piece of environment with your power glove, beat these enemies - rinse and repeat.
However, it's how the familiar formula is delivered that makes the game shine. Everything about the world of Hob conveys a lush beauty that is rarely seen in smaller games like this one. I found myself staying at the various 'vistas' in the game for no reason other than to savour the view. See above...your mileage may vary, but I found the game world to be compelling in all the right ways. Even the way the grass moved captivated me, as ridiculous as that sounds - the animation really is superb across the board, with no wonky physics to be seen. The minimal, poignant soundtrack also does a good job of bolstering the sense of discovery and purity (for lack of a better word), as well as helping you empathise with your avatar at key moments.
The world is sprawling, but cut into neat sections that you unlock as you progress. This is somewhat linear, but that isn't always a terrible thing. Hob is an example of linearity done well, dressed up in a tux and obscured by the shifting environment. It isn't as simple as 'go here, do this thing', despite what I said above - the environment sees to that. FFX did linearity (mostly) right, while FFXIII got it wrong. Hob falls into the former camp, I feel. The combat is going to feel pretty basic to most people in a post-SoulsBorne gaming landscape, but it's serviceable and offers a sense of progression via weapon upgrades that alter combos slightly, and so forth. Nothing goundbreaking, but I didn't find it grating.
Give Hob a shot. It's a sad state of affairs that Runic has now closed down, but this is a fine game to leave as their parting gift - it's clearly made with a lot of passion, despite the flaws. 2017 has been a bit of a rollercoaster for gaming so far, and shockingly Hob is one of the most enjoyable games I've played this year, despite the heavy competition. Far be it from me to dictate how people game, but I feel that approaching it in the right way will help a lot - leave cynicism (mostly!) at the door and step into the lush greenery with an open mind. Hob doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it sure looks and feels fantastic to experience.
