Upon finishing (((Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus)))' story, I felt two things: awe, and wonder. An awe at what I had played - a shockingly brutal, yet blastingly fun first person shooter featuring the Nazis many hate so dearly. However, there was also the wonder - a wonder of what could have been. Don't get me wrong, I loved this game, and I will get into why I think it's incredibly good. However, some moments fell flat on their faces, and that brought me a bit of cringe.
To begin, and arguably the most important part of the game - the gameplay. It is freaking superb. They fixed the problems that the first had, and added so much more - the game downright feels AWESOME to play! It certainly took a lot of inspiration from DOOM (2016) with the speed and fluidity of the experience. This outstanding and masterfully crafted gameplay is accompanied by stunning locations which were truly breathtaking, and the graphics are phenomenally good. It looks just as good, if not better, than DOOM (2016). Some weapons were admittedly useless for more than one scenario, but I still found them to be quite cool to use.
Speaking of the scenarios; the locations that you fight in are filled with interesting material to read and propaganda to observe. The swastika is ever-present and it looks wonderful in a sick and twisted way (only against Nazis for this review). Sadly, there was not a single boss battle though. Not even at the end. The game however always finds a way to grip you and compel you to continue marching through this sprawlingly brutal experience.
A quite critiqued aspect of this game is the story. I have to admit that some scenes were painful to watch. Fergus for example was completely butchered - he is a useless character used as "comic relief" even though he was pretty badass in the first game. All characters are stupid stereotypes, especially the black lady, and I hated her. There was very little humour, and what was there was baffling. The story is undeniably brutal and some of the scenes in it are absolutely gruesome and AMAZING! I cannot stress this enough; some of the scenes in this game were of the absolute best quality possible and top all the other Wolfensteins combined. Loved, loved, LOVED some of the scenes. I really don't want to spoil it, but I guess any scene featuring Frau Engel was freaking horrific and amazing.
Hitler is in the game (if you don't want minor spoilers skip onwards to the next paragraph). Hitler is just portrayed in the most disgraceful way possible (though I doubt disgraceful is the right word). He is shown as an instable, feeble old man with a poor and degrading attitude. For the amount of time he is in the game, I wanted one thing - just have him be serious! Good God, is that too much to ask for? If he is the villain that is so woefully spoken of thoroughly in the experience, then have him BE that woeful villain. Instead we get an idiot that pisses in a ♥♥♥♥ing bucket and vomits in front of some people. Really? I'm appalled.
The trailers for this game also show much more than we actually see regarding the homefront (not the game). There's really only one key scene where you are seeing the world within a truly Nazi-like environment, which lasts 5 minutes at most. Other areas are simply "bombed" environments reminiscent of Fallout. The trailers for this game are stupendously superb and hyped me extensively for the game. Sadly, none of these are in the game. Either way I can't really complain since it's more than in Wolf TNO anyway. Word of advice to continue - I'd rather play and shoot while OUTSIDE and not within buildings... the buildings just make the game so... restricted. Please give us more open locations next time, while not removing the feeling the game gives us completely. Honestly at this point there's nowhere to go but up, right? Well. we'll see.
Anyway, to conclude, I think this is an amazing game continuing the great alternate-history that Wolfenstein The New Order and The Old Blood have created, even though some of the humour is pathetic and Hitler is complete♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game and a colossal disappointment to see. The fantastic graphics and splendid gameplay make up for any problems with the game, and also other scenes. The game is about 10 hours long.
Score - 8/10: Definitely worth it!

Great platform game! It rivals Rayman Legends as my all-time favourite, even though it's a very different game.
First off, the presentation is excellent. Especially the beautiful, diverse layered visuals make a lasting impression. Although I do feel it might be too covered in post process filters, making it look a bit on the blurry side. In comparison Rayman Legends has super crisp detailed artwork.
The music is really well made, but it's just not my cup of tea. I'd label it as fairytale muzak, and would've prefered something a bit edgier to contradict the visuals just a bit.
Maybe I'm just too old and cynical for this kinda spiritual fairytale gibberish, because the story didn't do anything for me, although it was told through gorgeous realtime cutscenes.
The main ingredient is, of course, the gameplay. And it's really, really good. It starts off very simple, but as you gain abilities through story progression and unlock nodes in the 3 branches of your xp based skill tree, you end up with quite the arsenal of moves. This means that near the end many parts of the non-linear world map can be traversed using different movement combos, giving you a great sense of freedom.
The difficulty is quite high and at times pretty unforgiving. There's not much hand holding, so I frequently ended up going somewhere I wasn't meant to, which often means you'll encounter something that requires a move you don't yet have. It just took me a stupid amount of attempts to realize this and assumed that it was a puzzle I had to solve, so after the 10+ hours I spent finishing the game, I had died 634 times!
It's not Super Meat Boy hard, but it's pretty challenging for sure!
I played using a Xbone controller, and sadly the controls aren't re-bindable. I would've loved to be able to rebind the stomp ability to a button, instead of analouge stick down (if you add a bit of diagonal, the move is not executed). In general the controls felt a wee bit unresponsive and sluggish, but I adapted reasonably quickly.
I was hoping to be able to just jump back in with the character I had completed the game with, in order to finish the skill tree and explore every remaning nook and cranny of the map, but sadly the game doesn't allow this.
Bottom line - anyone who likes challenging platformers with a hint of puzzle and rpg needs to get this game.

After awaiting this game's release for months, I bought it the week it was released and like many others, was severely dissapointed. I contemplated getting a refund which I've never done with a Steam game, but after seeing the developers' posts about recognition of the game's flaws and upcoming updates, I decided to stick it out. TL;DR: Remember Me is certainly worth a look for its interesting mechanics, but falls flat on its face in the story department.  If you have a gamepad, use that.
It's a real shame that Dontnod had such trouble finding a publisher for Remember Me, and even more of a shame that it ended up being Capcom.  Given the success and narrative complexity of Life is Strange, I don't doubt that Dontnod had prepared a wonderful, thought-provoking narrative surrounding the central mechanic: memory alteration.
Memory alteration is perhaps the most interesting mechanic in the game.  You're shown a brief memory of a defining moment in someone's life, and have to then alter it to manipulate that person in to doing what you want.  The truly interesting part is that you have the power to make the memory either better or worse depending on the variables you change.  There are achievements for the positive endings, and there's a great deal of satisfaction to be had in giving someone their happy ending.  However, in almost every case, the goal is to make your target remember something far worse than actually happened.
Somewhere, buried in the heaping mess of a plot, there's a plot that questions the morality of altering someone's memory and shows a culture lost in its own past, as its denizens relive only the best memories from their past and the pasts of others.  At some point, the vision was to force the player to make thoughtful moral decisions that could potentially alter the plot of the game.  That vision was sadly left on the cutting room floor to make room for flamboyant bosses that get announced comicbook micro-villain style and a final boss who will give one opinion, just to contradict it in his very next line.
The combat system is pretty neat as well, allowing you to build your own combos to maximize damage, heal yourself, or cooldown your abilities.  Abilities are varied and well thought-out (you actually have a need for all of them!).
Overall, it's worth playing for the first 3 episodes or so, or however long you want to keep going to the next memory alteration, but ultimately I'm not sure if it's worth finishing.  Pick it up on sale.

Quite a learning curve, and very difficult at times, but a very fun and interesting game.
The game's engine is heavily physics-based, with destructible envronments throughout, and realistic simulations of weight, mass, inertia, etc. which make the dynamics of the motion feel very believable; you can practically feel the jarring impact of a successful hammer blow.
The setting is quite unique. It seems to be akin to a steampunk Ottoman Empire, inhabited by a handful of tribes at uneasy peace with one another. There are also sentient malicious robots, giant bugs, and magical crystals.
Story comes second to gameplay, but is not nonexistent. In a nutshell, you control the last surviving member of you tribe, the Gaiars, in an attempt to fight back against the corrupt powers which destroyed your home. There's also something going one about three magic crystals that must never come together, a wall of fog fast approaching, and an incomprehensible Lovecraftian evil on the horizon.
Gameplay is where Hammerfight really shines. You use your mouse to control your machine, which has a weapon hanging freely from its side, and use your momentum and inertia to swing or stab or whatever. There are hammers, axes, flails, rocks tied to chains, long curved swords, straight pointy swords—each with their own fighting style to figure out. You can also mount armor to your machine, or use a cannon, or carry throwing spears, or mount two different swords and link them so that they pivot as a single item, or use a single sword with enchanted gems inlaid that allow you to phase through enemies while at the same time lighting them on fire and healing you.
It's not without its flaws of course: The AI (especially allies) leaves a lot to be desired, and the explosion effects need to be dialed down a bit, but overall Hammerfight is a fun, challenging, and ultimately unique game that is worth checking out.

CAVEAT: I waited and started the game after 1.33, which is a whole new game from version 1.0.
This game is simply incredible! This is above and beyond what I had wanted out of ANY space exploration game, and certainly 100x better than the initial release version. I had a day off and I put 9 hours into the game in one day (and that was all on the starting planet, after I received my first spaceship, and found a crashed/damaged Hauler which I proceeded to fix-up).
Right now, I have a cumulative of 13.3 hours into the experience, and I don't have a vast majority of the content or story unlocked. I am aware of the state the game came-out in and what was missing, but after reading the patch notes of the last 3 patches (really should be referred to as MASSIVE expansions!... did I mention they were free?!), the game is now a LOT deeper than it was.
I really wanted to get this game on pre-order, but my gut told me it may not live-up to the hype... and it didn't. After a MASSIVE over-haul, and when it was on sale for 66% off, it was a no-brainer for me to get this thing finally.
One of the early complaints I saw were about how people got bored with the game and just blazed through the (at the time) limited story narrative with nothing to achieve... I started my first game in Survival mode. I highly recommend it, as it is exactly as advertised. Death came early to me while I was learning that I could not breath the toxic atmosphere of my first planet and that I had to gather resources, dart from cave to cave, and look for bases and other points of interest rather than just running willy-nilly to my main objective and getting off the planet.
There were TONS of Points of Interest on my starting planet, and they were a pleasure to look for. Resources were available, but definitely scarce, so survival definitely played a huge part in the exploration even after getting a ridiculously great Class A Multitool by pure random chance from one of the aliens I encountered early-on. Sure, you could fly anywhere quickly, but would you have access to enough Plutonium to power your thrusters to get up in the air again? Most of the time the answer was 'no'... I had to venture through caves and explore minutes away from my spacecraft to gather what I needed. The wildlife was passive (thankfully), but the atmosphere was always choking me.
Going off planet to a hot moon for the first time was even more abusive (in a great way)... I was greeted by a fast howling creature which resulted in at least 3 deaths until I figured-out what the heck it was... and it was mean... and made me jump when I heard the scurrying sounds through my surround sound in the middle of the night. I would jump on top of my ship as soon as I would land just to scout the surroundings. It was a legit Aliens-type feeling, especially since the small moon was densely populated with other wild life which was constantly being spooked... and for good reason with that six-legged bas**** running around! Resources were even scarcer than on my first planet, and after several reloads (after I figured-out that I could reload saves >_<!), I managed to escape with next to no resources (which I felt were adequately stock-piled from the first planet), 1 health unit, literally drained Life Support, and no shields/resistance to the elements.
Next planet was in the new system and it was a beautiful Paradise planet with vast oceans and green islands... except it was crawling with ANGRY Sentinels that apparently destroyed all life... I was forced to run multiple times. Ultimately learned how to deal with them after a couple of near-deaths, and started farming as many as I could from a different location to net me some great loot. I have no idea how to survive going back to the central point crawling with Sentinels on this planet, but I gladly try! :)
I am pleased to announce that in Survival Mode, the game difficulty being 'too easy' is no longer an issue. There are multiple ways of farming money, and everything can kill you, but you always have a chance once you learn the basics. The game is difficult, but not brutal. I got a feeling of playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. in space on more than a few occasions as I explored abandoned buildings, way points, and crash sites... it was wonderful!
I saw what the graphics looked like before, and I have to say that they look incredible at 1440p and a 980ti now. I have the FPS cap set to 60fps with VSYNC on, and I feel like the game is smooth but may occasionally dip, as judged by moments when it the game runs like butter. It is a minor note, as the game plays very consistently, and I can't tell if maybe the frame drops are in my head or not.
I did find a base with an Architect I could claim on the first planet, but have so far decided not to build my first base prior to unlocking some more Blueprints and greater access to credits and resources. So yeah, I have not even touched on one of the largest aspects of the game, not to mention the freighters! All I know is that I landed on the first Class C Freighter I saw, and the captain offered to sell it to me for 192 million credits... I had about 200K at the time.
So at this point I am GREATLY looking forward to spending more time with this game, while my girlfriend is terrified that I won't see here ever again... well, for at least the next 100 hours or so. ;)
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Fairly easy to figure everything out, so the learning curve is not particularly steep... if you know how to play FPS games and may have played a Survival-type game, you will probably do well.
- Really great Survival Mode, which should be the default in my opinion
- Tons to explore
- Vastly improved planet types and creatures over the original
- New progression system
- Interesting economy mechanics
- Really fun exponential growth model that REALLY lets you feel like you are starting from nothing and growing into a force to be reckoned with
- Faction system that gives you additional unlocks
- Great spaceship variety (in terms of visuals, however I have seen pretty interesting stat and slot combinations also... this is always going to be subjective, though)
- Sound design gives weapons weight and startling moments when something sneaks-up on you (if you have surround sound)
- There are vehicles now, too?! O_O
- Plans for even more content, while the current build is already amazing!
Cons:
- Not a lot of details on how to actually survive when you first start... I had no idea caves could protect me from toxic gas, which is the exact opposite of what I would personally expect (greater gas in cave pockets, not less o_O... I can live with it, though).
- No explanation of the Quick Menu and all of the cool things you can do with it... pretty easy to use and figure-out at least.
- Still some optimization work may help performance on older machines and fix the odd crash (I only had 1 when I loaded a prior save for the first time), but still highly playable.
Conclusion:
The game has evolved greatly from its initial release, and this is exactly the type of game I wanted for the longest time. It seems to do things in an simpler/easier way than games like Elite Dangerous, but at the same time it does a lot of things better, and maybe a handful of things worse. It's a must buy for any lovers of space and survival genres, especially if you are looking for a great single-player experience as opposed to having to be surrounded by people in typically MMO's. You are truly a lost traveler and it feels like it in this world. I feel like it's finally worth full price, but it's a complete steal if you get it on sale! Two thumbs up! :)

First off I want to say this game isn't for everyone. If you're looking for a hardcore action-packed space adventure this game isn't for you. It has a hardcore mode, but in my opinion it just adds tedium, but I suppose I'm not the target audience for that.
What this game is for though is for exploring, building, and trading. They have come a long way since launch, and at this point I'd say the game is at a stage that it should have been on release, and it's worth buying now, especially since I believe they will continue to stick with it and provide updates. I have forgiven them since their abysmal launch due to the fact that they have stuck solidly with the game for a year to continuously improve it.
Anyway, this game is mainly for people who want to explore space, experience the huge variety of landscapes and creatures, find other player's landmarks and bases. You can trade your ship up slowly from a crummy starter ship to a marvel. You can even get your own freighter, and have a garage of exotic ships like rich guys with their lamborghinis. There are many ways to earn money in this game too. You can farm plants for money, scan creatures (you can get more money the more upgrades you get), or do missions. There are other ways, but those are the 3 main ones you'll find yourself choosing between, or even doing all 3.
The only problem I have with this game is sometimes it's like a jack of all trades, master of none. The base building is fun, but there a limits to what you can build (you can remove them on PC though). There is multiplayer, but at the moment there's limits as to what you can do (they have confirmed they are working on it). There are a large variety of ships, but you see the same variety on repeat and it begins to get old. There is a lot of randomised terrain generation, but sometimes it's too random, like you'll never see a nice flat plains that stretches for miles, or even different biomes. All planets are one biome, and have the same consistent generation throughout. That aside, there are some REALLY cool planets out there though, floating islands, massive craters with lakes in them, long snaking mountains to name a few cool features.
You won't find much in the story in this game, but no one plays this game for the story. It's about making your own story, as you are the traveller of this game, the main character, making your mark in your small area of a wider galaxy, of which there are several to spawn in. I was skeptical of this game at first, which is why I bought it on sale for under £20 which I recommend you do if you are the same, but in my opinion it's worth the £40 they ask for.

Great game overall. Gameplay is flashy and fast, stealth is buggy and stupid, but still fun, visuals are stunning. (I really dig the id Tech 6). Story wise it felt somehow alike the Mass Effect 2 back in the day compared to ME1 and ME3. Spoiler kinda-free (not exactly) it’s a transaction between Wolfenstein 1 and future part 3 in which you spend all the time gathering your crew (and collectibles). Then at the end, when everyone is together you do something to set events of third game in motion. Sounds somewhat familiar right? I know it is pretty vague description, but that’s how I experienced Wolfenstein 2.
All of this said the gameplay is fun. It doesn't have the hellish drive of Doom, but it is still great to kill Nazis. Downside though is that BJ talks A LOT like HOLY HELL SO MUCH at the beginning of the game, mostly some stupid gibberish too but closer to the end of the game he gets his stuff together and stops whining. Speaking of Doom, after listening to Mick Gordon's speech about OST writing process for Doom where he said "We don't want metal in our games, because of [cat memes]" - the weakest part about the Wolfenstein 2 would be the choice of endgame credits song which were some bad metal cover of  "We're Not Gonna Take It". I know I know, the song itself is symbolic and all but as much as I like to listen to metal every now and then hearing some guy growl ANYMOOOOOOOORE was a meh kind of experience after beating the game. In other worlds it was some average and cringy cover. About the actual game OST: it was pretty decent (I should listen to it some time) but mostly I couldn't even hear it because it was too quiet even after tempering with ingame sound settings.
My bet is that the next game would be called Wolfenstein lll: The New Revolution (or Frontier).
P.S. I'd aim for 100% achievements in the game for fun sake and to get most out of it, if not for the "Mein leben" achievement. Where you need to beat the game on max difficulty in ONE sitting without skipping any cutscenes and obviously with permadeath. It's snake meets Pac-man, but with no challenge and horribly imprecise and floaty controls. The developers seriously need to learn what a controller dead-zone is.
The real money microtransactions have at least been replaced for the Steam version, but you can still see that it was originally made as a tablet gamed designed to con children out of their pocket money.
It gets boring, fast. Don't be fooled by my play time, I left it idling for the cards; I was bored and done with the game in about 10 minutes.

This is a perfect example of how a game can be simple without being easy. Like other Snake-style games before it, Millie requires more strategy than you typically expect to use going in. The farther along you go, the more you need to start pre-planning your route before Millie even starts walking. I think it's cleverly designed and there are enough curveballs lobbed at you to keep you on your toes without it getting to the point that you start to feel beaten down. My only real complaints are that the controls become less responsive toward the end of the game (especially around Do Not Enter signs) and there isn't enough variety in the music to prevent it from getting tiring. Those two things aside, I think this is a great pick for gamers that like strategy and puzzle games.
I like the idea of making Snake a puzzle game, but I hate that you can see so little of the maze at once.  There is really no reason for it.

I'm a huge horror nerd and, though so far I haven't found many Heavy Metal artists that I enjoy, I really appreciate the aesthetic. I have also always loved the Castlevania games. From the origional on the NES, all the way up through the 2d DS classics.
I will admit I got scared off by this game's initial reception. Everything I read painted it as a real failure. I read that a big patch was coming in a few days though, and as a birthday gift to myself I picked this up. This is EXACTLY what I was looking for. Gorgeous pixel art, a heavy-handed, pulpy tale brimming with purple prose, geysers of blood, burning witches, vast lands of demoniac, blasted beauty, more Metal iconography than even King Diamond (Hallowed be his name!) can shake an inverted cross at.
Now, clearly you can tell from my time played that I've not beaten this, but there is a fair challenge that never gets TOO unfair in my experience. I'm an old guy and, well, ol' grey mare she ain't what she used to be. My reflexes aren't going to get me into e-sports anytime soon. We have here very generous load points that respects the player's time, though, so don't let the relative difficulty scare you off. Even when you get your head handed to you for the tenth time by a radioactive giant skeleton you'll find that death's sting is never too severe.
The music, as well, warrants mention. Chunky metal by way of Curt Victor Bryant, formerly of Celtic Frost. Maybe that means something in your world? I've not previously heard of them, yet I'm listening to them as I write this. The soundtrack is excellent and quite fitting. It truly helps set the grimdark mood.
Overall even at full price I suggest picking this up if you want to be transported to a world of monsters and steel, of blood and flame, of cheesy horror comic writing and album covers.

I first completed AC on PS3 back in 07 and this is my 7th time playing it, that's how good this game is. The storyline is amazing and you really connect with Altair as you follow his journey to becoming a ranked master Assassin.
AC takes place in Masyaf and several other holy lands (Jerusalem, Acre and Damascus), Altair's objective aim was to capture the Apple of Eden as he fails to do so his master and Brotherhood leader (Al Mualim) demotes him to rank novice and tasks him with assasinating 9 templars.
The combat in this game is good and up to standard but because it is set in a very old time most weapons were not invented such as a pistol rifle and the hidden gun etc... which are playable in the rest of the AC franchise so you only have a hidden blade and sword. The graphics are standard though I don't find it important as the storyline of this game just overshadows the rest of the qualities.
PROS
- Amazing storyline
- Great combat
- Teaches you history while you play
- Has a great twist towards the ending
- Graphics are good
CONS
- We're introduced to Altair as a master assassin already, it would be good to know his background and life before that
- In the game Altair has an american accent which is kind of cheesy, really he's suppose to have a middle east accent but I guess the reason for that is probably because of the glitch in the Animus.
Overall rating = 8/10

Full of hilarious and sometimes frustrating glitches - most easily fixed with a few adjustments to settings - Assassin's Creed appears to be a mediocre port of a great game.
Playing at a casual rate, making minimal mistakes, while also meddling around in present-day affairs, this game will offer you ~14 hours of true game time. For those completionists that enjoy spending time collecting hidden objects, the game may offer up to ~20 hours.
I would say the game is worth the $20, but I'm biased towards this part of the series. For most, I defintely recommend waiting until the game goes on sale; just be sure to pick it up if you haven't played it yet!

This game had the potential to be a heck of a lot of fun. The mechanics were refreshingly unusual, but not horribly complex, the violence level was just right to be cathartic and amusing, and it was (at first) challenging enough to be fun without having being utterly impossible. Sure, there were levels that took several repeat attempts to get past, but it was always possible to see that you _could_ succeed, if only you'd managed a better hit at first, or dodged a little more skillfully, or not hesitated so long in that one spot, etc. It got more difficult as I progressed, of course, but not so much so that my skill level couldn't progress enough to keep up with it, if I gave it enough tries. And then.....
Then I hit a level where I ended up dead in a pit somewhere. I won't give away the plot by saying how (and to be honest, I didn't pay that much attention to plot, other than to note that, surprisingly for this sort of game, it actually had one), but the only way out was to grab a disgarded weapon and fight several respawning guards. At which point the skill curve became a skill cliff... a skill cliff coated in ice filled with caves full of yetis armed with grenade launchers, while I didn't have so much as a rope. I spent an entire day trying to get past that single level, and I have no idea if I even came close. Three out of every five attempts ended before I even managed to pick up the stupid hammer. I enjoy a good challenge, but to go from levels that were challenging but possible to achieve in, at most, two or three repeats to something that a full day of cursing, teeth-grinding toil couldn't conquer isn't so much challenging as it is frustrating... and, of course, due to the game's linear nature, it makes it impossible to continue the game.
I played this game during the free preview period here on Steam, and had fully intended to buy it. If I had not reached that level during the hours I played for free, I would have bought it, happily, and been exceedingly disappointed. So, sadly,  I cannot recommeend this game unless you either believe yourself to be the ultimate god of arcade games, or you enjoy an exercise in frustration. I really wish I could.
~Velvet Wood

An entertaining 10 hour Cyberpunk adventure story that is worth playing through once.  The story itself involves a bleak futuristic Paris where a corporation called Memorize has taken control of the majority of the populace through their memories and allowed them to create a surveillance state.  You play as Nilin, a rebel soldier of the group called "Errorists", who is intially captured but escapes and trys to regain the lost memories taken from her.  All the while trying to bring the downfall of Memorize.  The graphics and art style of the game make future Paris a beautiful yet bleak place to explore through.  The orchestrated music score with it's mixture of techno is quite good, it's just ashame they didn't release an OST for it.  The combat gameplay itself is decent yet the Remix segments are by far the best parts of the game.  If you've ever played DONTNOD's other game, Life is Strange, then you can instantly tell that the Remix portions of the game helped influence the Rewind mechanic in that game.  I also found it interesting that the main protaganist, Nilin, seemed to inspire the appearance of the main character, Max, in LIS.  Overall, if you're like me and I decided to give this game a try because you enjoyed LIS then you may be disappointed if you were expecting a similar experience.  It's still a fun game and I give it a 7.5/10.

Remember Me features gorgeous (and colorful) graphics and excellent world design, as well as an incredible soundtrack. The "exploration" is pretty limited, unfortunately, essentially consisting of mostly limited (and narrow) paths that serve little purpose other than to corral you from battle scene to battle scene. It doesn't help that the story is really, really dumb. It's hard to recommend the game on the basis of any of these things by themselves, but I daresay that the combat makes this game worth playing.
I have a feeling that most people will disagree with me, but I think Remember Me's combat is the best part of the game. I don't know if I'm enjoying the combat for the wrong reasons, and I have a feeling that DONTNOD lucked into some of the more interesting aspects of the combat, but I think the combat in Remember Me hits its stride at the end of Chapter 4 and keeps you engaged through all of Chapter 7. Chapter 8 is absolute trash, though, and playing through it really made me wonder if DONTNOD even understands what makes Remember Me's combat so special.
The problem with the combat for nearly half of the game is in how the game doles out your new abilities and introduces new enemies. I usually don't like games that require you to fight a bunch of weaker enemies while dealing with a stronger enemy, but Remember Me's combat thrives on this idea, and it actually made me appreciate the ins and outs of the combat system. You can unlock up to four different combos throughout the game, and you unlock individual moves that you can add to any given combo in order to change your attack attributes. Some attacks prioritize damage output, while others will heal you or decrease cool-down times for special abilities. Dealing with mobs of enemies really helps you to see the value in this battle system, as you're rewarded for taking risks with longer combos and customizing them according to each situation in order to prioritize certain attributes.
For example, some enemies damage you whenever you hit them. You can kill them pretty easily if you don't mind burning some focus, but I think it's more interesting to simply customize a combo to prioritize healing. Alternatively, you can prioritize damage output for a longer combo for use against those enemies while milking other enemies for health with a shorter combo that prioritizes healing. It's actually really interesting.
I doubt that we'll ever see a sequel to Remember Me, but I'd love to see this combat system implemented in a more cohesive way. I think it's worth experiencing, but I can understand why people who are used to the more polished experience of the Arkham games don't care for it. If you can pick it up cheap during a Steam sale, then I highly suggest playing until at least the end of Chapter 4 so you'll know for sure if you should stick with it. If you're impressed by that point, then you'll probably really enjoy the bulk of the game.

In short - the thousands of existing reviews aren't wrong.
Knowing the reputation it had, I still had some interest in No Man's Sky and I finally got NMS on sale around the time of the 1.3 update. Right off the bat the game would crash at the loading screen. I thought maybe it was a graphics or configuration setting. Then I noticed you aren't given the option to make any configuration changes... There's no main menu, only a difficulty select screen. So I never would have known if that was the problem. Having to load the game before you can change graphics settings? That's a horrible design choice. After a quick internet search I found out that NMS has a known issue with my specific series of AMD graphics... So, in my frustration and research I found that NMS allows mods, and THANK THE INTERNET GODS FOR NOMANSSKYMODS dot COM!!!! One of the top listed mods was a game fix for my graphics card. Loaded it up and the game was working! After seeing trailers and other gameplay footage I was excited to see my starting planet - which was a barren rock. I quickly picked up the primary game play mechanics and started on the missions of repairing my stuff. That's where I quickly hit a roadblock. I needed 'Heridium' to repair my ship. I ventured out into a dangerous, freezing and barren planet walking towards every Waypoint in sight. I found nothing. I walked and scanned finding Carbon and Iron, Carbon and Iron, Carbon and Iron and nothing else. I looked online, thinking maybe I was missing something obvious or doing something wrong, but no - there was no Heridium to be found. So finally, after TWO HOURS of walking and scanning (occassionally hiding in a cave from the cold) I found Heridium. I mined all that I could carry, which is where I hit my next roadblock. I had to dedicate 2 more hours of walking back to my ship, while maintaining enough resources to keep my suit's life support online and having almost no inventory slots. This was a horrible and tedious process and if I hadn't already dedicated so much time to the game I would have just deleted the save and started over. So, after 4 hours I was able to repair my ship and actually start the "game." I took a break to watch some other players on YouTube and didn't find a single person who had the terrible luck I had. Most people had their ships repaired within 20 minutes or less even on their first plays. I immediately jumped to the next closest planet, knowing it couldn't be as bad as the planet I just left... and I was wrong. The next planet didn't even have enough Carbon for me to keep mining! No Carbon, no Iron and I could barely scrape together enough resources to launch my ships thrusters again so I could escape that hell. My confidence was pretty broken at that point. From, then I was playing a couple hours every night just to try and find the amazing planets and creatures I had seen in screenshots and videos. Occasionally I would break away from searching planets to follow the story line but the story seemed to take the "anything could be anything - it's so mysterious" approach and I wasn't into it. After 22 hours I finally found an interesting planet, with beaches and grass and creatures! Then I discovered I couldn't set a marker or any indicator to find that planet again. So, going back to the internet I found out that you can get the ability to set your own Waypoint IF you build a base. So could I build a base on this planet? No. So I warped around more planets until I found a place I could build a base... And of course it was on a hostile planet full of aggressive creatures and extreme heat. I did all of the grinding it requires to build it up so I could build a Waypoint, got VERY lucky and managed to find the 'good' planet again and setup a marker but by that time I was pretty burnt out on the grinding this game requires for progression. I will continue playing to finish the story but overall I couldn't recommend this game, based on the experience I've had. I give credit to Hello Games for what they have done and I think NMS is an amazing feat but I think a tighter, more focused experience would have made us all happier. It is my hope that they will develop a spin-off game with a small universe and a better focus on story telling. The game is beautiful and has some amazing moments sprinkled in, but those feel like a couple of strawberries thrown on top of the largest stale sheet-cake ever created.
Edit: The above experience was on the "Normal" difficulty setting. I did not even attempt other settings until much later.

After playing this game over 5000 hours in the non steam version i still enjoy it every day.
I strongly recommend using the DDNET client, since it has tons of skins and useful functions.
The game itself :
You wouldn't believe how this simple game can offer a huge variety of different modes.
You can simply play capture the flag / or Death Math and learn the basic dragging and shooting skills.
The most popular modes in the game are Block, DDrace and Gores.
You need to know, when you hit the dark tiles you get "frozen" and as soon as you leave the dark ( through someone else mostly ) you will be able to move after 3 more seconds.
In the Block mode the map is designed with a lot of dark tiles and players try to throw other players inside the dark and perform tricks to spin them around and dominate them. You loose when you land in the dark and get frozen.
DDrace is designed for multiple players to pass a map in the best possible time. There is a start and a finish line, between them you have lots of parts that can only be accomplished with multiple players. So Team work guys.
Gores follows the same system with a start and a finish line for each map. The difference at Gores is, that you can finish all maps without any help of others. But i strongly recommend playing with your friends, because you are all heading for the same goal : finish the map. ( maps are from the community. basically everyone can create maps).
About me:
I played thousands of hours Gores and it is still fun, because maps can be incredible hard and even the best players are not able to finish them with their friends. Just to give you an overview about that game.
Some hints at the end:
-do not use dynamic camera ( switch it off )
-use DDNET client ( tons of new stuff )
-play with friends!
-Since this is one of the hardest games to learn, don't give up because when you gain skill you will love it

Wolf TNC is a really good FPS, the only thing that holds it back is that it's simply worse than The New Order. Why? Because you get less when it comes to content and level / gameplay variety.
For example TNC is the first game in the series that has no bossfights. I was exctied to find out how MachineGames would top the fight against TNO's mecha-Deatshead so it was very disappointing to see that the last battle of the game is just about killing a few nazis and two giant robots while the villain of the game is not even present on the level.
The great secret rooms that were part of Wolfenstein since RtCW also seem to be completely gone: no secret switches behind paintings, no secret walls, just a bunch of dossiers, gold and so-called starcrads hidden on the levels. Audio diaries? Those are gone too, even if you pick up a recording you only get written text. But hey, at least the nazi spoof songs are still here. The side missions on the base are also minimalistic, uninteresting and accomplishing them doesn't reward you with small cutscenes and stuff.
The most interesting weapon of TNO, the Laserkraftwerk is gone. It's replaced with a generic sticky bomb launcher and the crazy sci-fi weaponry that was quite the extra in Wolfenstein games is missing too. The only thing resembling that is a "nazi BFG" but sadly MachineGames somehow managed to make such a weapon completely useless.
The level variety is not too great: you go from generic nazi bunkers to generic destroyed cities, only the last two levels manage to show something special.
The story is good and fun but even that manages to offer very little overall. The main problem with the game is that Frau Engel, the main villain is just one dimensional as hell: she's very cruel and enjoys being cruel + she really wants to get her hands on Blazko and that's all. What is she after? What is her big goal? Nothing, she's no "crazy nazi Dr. Frankenstein" like Deatshead was nor she has funny elements in her character like Rudi from The Old Blood when he wanted to get revenge for his stupid dog. You want nazi side villains and side characters? Forget about them, they don't exist here, you get only Engel and her faceless henchmen. Hitler turns up for a few seconds, he's used for laughs and that's all.
The other thing missing is the fantastic / mythological / occult elements that were always a huge part of Wolfenstein. In The New Order we had the Da'at Yichud storyline that seemed like an interesting one and something that would return here, in The Old Blood there was the good old occult elements etc. In New Colossus? Basically nothing, the very, very tiny bit about the Da'at Yichud only seems to be something that may or may not be used for a sequel.
The gameplay itself is largely the same as what you've seen the TNO with a few minor adjustments and a few extra options. New Colossus is better than TNO in this regard but not by much.
As I've said the game is very good so I wholeheartedly recommend it to every FPS and Wolfenstein fan, just keep in mind that if you've played TNO or last year's Doom you won't feel that enough is on offer here.

This year was my freshman year at college. I was in a new environment, without any friends, studying a degree that was created last year. The success of the degree itself is largely uncertain, but it's what I'm passionate about, so that's gotta count for something -right?
The first couple weeks of college were dull and uneventful. I would wake up, shower, have breakfast, leave for my lectures. Cruise through the day, learning and working well. When I got home I would type my notes, have some food, and then work on any assignments -if there were no assignments due, I would watch some TV or jam something on Steam.
And then I noticed a very peculiar game in my Library. I was intrigued. Perusing the reviews in the Store, my curiosity awakened as oh-so-many of the blurbs proclaimed this game's brilliance.
I couldn't wait. I couldn't idly pass my free hours merely watching television or tinkering with sub-par Valve endeavours. I hadn't found my purpose in life -could this be it, I hopefully wondered.
I hurriedly installed this tiny number, barely containing my delight as the "Play" button went live. Flicking Skype to 'Do Not Disturb', I closed and locked my door, drew my blinds, and dimmed the lights. A single click of the M1 button changed my life forever.
My behemoth rig pounded out the pixels at an alarming rate, filling my widescreen monitor with flickering and flashing animated effects. Adjusting the cups of my headphones, I navigated the menu and began my journey.
Below is a log of subsequent events in my life:
~2 mins in and two friends PM me demanding to know what I’m doing with my life.
~5 mins in and I receive a Steam Achievement.
~30 mins in and I’ve got a good feel for the game. I’ve already picked up several Steam Achievements, and I’m hooked. Good thing it’s Friday night.
~1 day in and those who live with me -and have Steam- all peppered me with questions about my gaming habituals.
~1 week in and my friends have attempted to set up several counsellor sessions. Every second person I talk to is curious as to why I’ve developed a passion for this game -word has now spread beyond Gabe’s elect.
~2 weeks and I’ve got half of the Steam Achievements. I’m still thoroughly enjoying myself.
~1 month in and I’ve made some choices in my life to prioritise my time spent showering with my Dad. I now type my notes up at college during the lectures, and rush my assignments to get them done within a few hours of being home. This has increased my play-time by roughly 5 hours a week.
~2 months in and I am consumed by showering with my Dad. I skip free periods and I skip tutorials. I now take my laptop to class and play windowed in an attempt to gain my last few achievements. Somehow my sound un-muted, and nearly landed me awkwardly needing to explain what I was listening to -fortunately someone triggered the fire alarm, causing enough noise for me to fluidly mute both my laptop and the game itself. I have since inserted headphones just to be safe.
A couple weeks ago my girlfriend walked towards the front door with her bags and said to me, tears in her eyes: “I'm leaving.” As she headed down the drive, I realised something dangerously important. I chased her down, yelling "JESSICA, WAIT!"
She turned towards me, hope filling her heart, and she asks why. I had to ask her a very important question: "What is the WiFi password?? You're the only one who knows it!”
“You’re ridiculous! All you care about is showering with your Dad! You never pull your weight around the house; you never clean up after yourself; you’re obsessed with tiling the bathroom. I have to continually replace the dish-wash detergent because you splash it all over the lino floors! Do you have any idea how many “Caution! Wet Floor!” signs I’ve had to cancel on the credit card?”
“So that’s why they never came?! You were cancelling them?! Jessica, this is my passion. This is what brings me home each day! How could you do this to me?”
The breakup was immense. The breakup was intense.
The breakup made no sense.
I had hit rock bottom. Withy shaky hands I booted my rig, desperate for the one thing that would abate my misery.
This game gave me a purpose in life, and continues to still do so. This game is there for me when no-one else is -unlike Jessica.
In loving memory: Jessica.

My oppinion on Slain! is....complicated. What I expected was a Metroidvania game with lots of variety in monsters, levels, and metal music. What I got was a game with FANTASTIC pixel art and meh gameplay and dissapointing music and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t twist.
First off, the game deffinetly does have lots of potential with level variety. Once you get past the first level, you are opened to a hub with several different worlds that you can enter with beautiful backgrounds and art to differetiate as well as a variety of bosses that are all unique to their own worlds. Other then that, that's all I really have positive to say about the game.
Many of the basic monsters are cut and paste with a couple of variations (poison, fire, ice, big, small, etc). The enemies aren't as much as a challenge as they are annoying and it felt like in order to parry some of the bigger monsters (more specifically, the poison whip skeleton) I had to block at a VERY specific frame with a controller that lags on input.
The weapon variety, while cool, adds no advantage or dissadvantage against enemies from what I noticed. I went through the entire game with mostly the fire sword and took down everything fairly easily. The mana shot that you can do, while useful at times, does seem like a waste to use since there is a giant mana blast you can do that sort of acts like an AOE smart bomb and it just makes me wish there was more variety in magic to spice up the gameplay.
The level design is laughable and acts more as a platformer with hoards of monsters and traps occasionally thrown into the mix and even those are lacking in variety. Most traps are the same, an obvious switch on the ground or pool of blood will trigger and insta-death scene that will squish your character into gibs.
At it's current state, I can not reccomend Slain! to any sane minded individual as it feels like an incomplete game at best. While the art may seem cool, everything else just feels void of quality. Monsters have no variety, your weapons mean nothing, and the music feels like it just loops over and over.

Slain's pixel art is on par with Metal Slug in terms of quality and distinct style. Everything has this dripping, practical-effects-in-an-80s-horror-movie look that brings satisfying kinesthetic weight to combat. The game has quite a lot of charm, which is why I put up with the lack of polish and its frustrations. The art style is incredible. The music goes really well with it, although it's almost all ambient music so I couldn't see myself enjoying the album by itself. The dialogue is also written to fit well with the theme. So now the downsides:
Lots and lots of what feel like cheap deaths.
Traps: The areas are littered with traps, but unfortunately don't stand out all that much from the background. This might be ok if they didn't insta kill you. So in many ways, getting good at the game is learning how to identify and avoid the traps. Some of these traps make sense: there is a trap where the floor has a red bulb sticking out of it, almost like what some of the very deep sea fish use to lure prey. This is great because as players, we tend to go towards lights. However once you walk over it, a creature grabs you from the ceiling and eats you. Nice. But then there are statues that you walk under and just insta kill you by letting a pillar fall on you. They look like normal statues. Why? And you will always die if you trigger a trap. There is no way to dodge them. Once I moved out from under it and was completely out of range of the trap and still died. So there were a few places where I keep running in to trap after trap after trap, so I had to memorize where they were to continue since they don't stick out much.
Attack Arcs Suck Against Flying Creatures: The ice weapon kind of has an overhead arc, but it misses a lot of enemies that it clearly passes through. Your jumping attack simply goes sideways, making it very difficult to hit things flying above you, however they tend to hit you very easily.
Attack Speed is Slow / Delayed: As long as you can keep some distance between you and the enemy, the attacks work just fine. But there were some instances that I felt were unfair. Like I was in front of a trap, killing a mob spawner. I kill the spawner as a mob spawns, but cant attack fast enough to hit the spawn before it moves in to me, knocking me backwards in to an insta kill trap. Or there is a section where a platform moves up and down through flying mobs that move sideways. The platform is moving so fast and your attacks are so delayed, you can't hit anything. When they hit you, it knocks you off the platform. This section just felt like a luck section where I just needed to keep using the platform until I got through all the mobs. There just seems to be a slight delay between when you press the button and your hit arc actually goes out. LIke you start the animation of attacking but dont hit things right away. This game is very timing based where you have to block right before being hit or knock projectiles back at enemies. This delay made things difficult. The game controls just don't feel as tight as they should, like you don't feel as in control of what's going on.
Lack of polish: Checkpoint before ice boss not having a health/mana refill, so you just go to the boss to read the dialogue and die basically so you can respawn with full health at the checkpoint.
And a final note, the side scrolling is a bit choppy. This is especially visiable when in wolf form since it moves so fast. The background seems to update in intervals. I tried forcing vsync and that didn't fix things. Again, I really enjoyed the game, but there were a few times I was ready to quit from frustration.

30+ hours in the game and all I can say is that it is an amazing game with some problems.
Story
I expected a more captivating story. For a game with that hype factor I expected a stroy that would consume me and keep me wanting more after each and every mission. Instead we got a main protagonist, his boss and a couple of minor characters doing the Groundhog day type of repetition. You see your boss, he gives you a piece of equipment and sends you off to kill a guy but before you can do that you have to save citizens, jump off of tall buildings and here and there you have to help your assassin friends in order to gather information on your target. You have some pickpocketing missions and interrogation stuff but that is just about it. And for every single target is the same.
Gameplay
This is the part where the game redeems itself. Gameplay is fantastic and this is the main atribute of the game. Controlls take some time to get used to but it is not much of a problem. Very detailed open world gives you the possibility to do anything and go everywhere. The world is detailed, very nicely done. Fighting is very beutifull to watch if you do it right but if you make a single mistake it is a pretty frustrating thing to go through. You have to time your moves right and really be engaged in the fight. You can not just randomly press buttons and see enemy fighters drop like flyes. Charecter movements are really nicely done but Altairs walking is the only thing that makes me cringe. He looks like he is a male model on the cat walk.
The story maybe is not top notch but voice acting is. Motion capture and animation really are good and voice actors really made the effort of projecting character personalities to us.
The game itself functions properly. No chrashes, only here and there I have expirienced minor audio glitches but that was about it.
All in all the game is highly recommended.

Ori, for all its visual splendor and promise of titillating gameplay, is both a misleading and frustrating game. Frankly I am surprised by the majority of positive reviews, as on many outside forums there are a slew of complaints and I feel like this product did not necessarily live up to its description or promises. As I know there may be those who will rush to the title’s defense I will say that I have, in fact, completed every map (but Forlorn Ruins) to 100% completion on my first run-through.

I have put a fair number of hours into this game, and I hope that, given this consideration, my below criticism can be considered fair.
To me this game, when first advertised, seemed both captivating and fun; I was enchanted and purchased Ori outright for the display of its visuals. Sadly, I ended up having to tuck my purchase away for a few years simply because my old laptop couldn't handle the game and would often crash given its poor capabilities... Sometime later I splurged on a shiny, new desktop and was ready to figuratively dust the game off and play it again… It played slow-mo lag on a native resolution of 1920x1080. I have managed a fix in that Ori operates well at a lower resolution, but still  it has its stutters in specific areas of the map. I grew ired by the fact that this game was never optimized for anything less than a very pricey 1GB graphics card, and that, upon subsequent re-release of Ori the newer version was not free and was only given a short-term discount.
I felt cheated by this tactic and audience preference, and I’m sure others have as well. While it is disappointing that the makers seemingly lack courtesy or foresight, that end does not entail my true and overall dissatisfaction with the gameplay itself.
This game is difficult, and anyone who tells you otherwise has been blessed with skills wrought of their dedicated practice with controllers. I think some forget that not everyone has the same acuity or dexterity for these types of platformers
. If you're one familiar with MegaMan
you may fair well with Ori -- in fact it’s likely a good fit for you or you’ve already played it. For those of us who are inexperienced with such franchises, or casual gamers, or very young -- do not buy this game. The pretty, inviting, story-book graphics are a façade of its tricky and monstrous levels of difficulty.
If for whatever reason you still want to try your hand at this game
be aware that rates of success first-playthrough are phenomenally low. Also be open to the idea of making Ori commit a few tens of seppuku as an act of revenge for your losses.
Fluid aesthetics, wonderful music, and a charming story are to sheep’s wool where gameplay itself is like leaping into the chasmal maw of a beast. Hazard placements, mob spawns, dungeons, abilities -- all meant to challenge and guide the player – for even the simplest of tasks often become hindrances which contribute to the chewing and spitting up of repeated missteps. The game calls for nearly pin-point accuracy with movement and landings -- failure delivers unto the player repeated deaths for near-miss jumps into hazards, or the unfortunate timing of an enemy projectile
.
Forlorn Ruins was a dungeon which seemed to encapsulate the issues with this method of trial and
error. The early-game of Ori is fun and introduces you to the manipulation of environmental factors (mobs/spawns, lamps, jumping, climbing, puzzles, etc.) to progress... For Forlorn Ruins it asks you to throw all that away for the gimmick of "functionality loss as challenge". This dungeon in particular felt clunky, slow, and the most unforgiving in its design. This area gives no forewarning to the sudden inversion of your movement controls, to your being forced to scale walls and ceilings laced with traps, nor to its inexplicably asking you to “slow-your-roll” to move a cumbersome object from point A to point B.
Forlorn Ruins, as a dungeon
, felt lazy and disjointed from the rest of the game. The later dungeons seem as though they ran out of ways to provide challenge and responded by inundating areas with nearly impassable terrain to simulate difficulty. You would think of dungeons
as a way to capitalize upon a player's current skills and accomplishments, mildly upping the stakes of their quest and ushering them towards rewards that increase their rank or ability...
Ori instead decides it a clever idea that dungeons be the places of torment and anguish they are classically defined to be. While each dungeon poses the suggestion of utilizing new skills and abilities, the introduction to these concepts are neither intuitive nor rewarding. The adventures through these levels bear no true prizes, as upon completion of a dungeon it is unceremoniously blocked off forever while
Sein does not hesitate to demand your next objective.
You
teased with a cute little cut-scene and story-progression, but that does not ring with the same sense of satisfaction found when you can progress the story
defeat a boss, plunder loot, or gain a new and crucial ability. The escape sequences from these dungeons, again, can be rather arduous as they ask for pixel and time perfect maneuvers. Inability to pull off these "sweet moves" results in being reset to an event's starting position.
While some issues I have with Ori relate to its marketing being inconsiderate towards buyers of the original copy, it too is partly bred out of my feelings of the title being misleading towards its audience about its content -- neither showcasing nor giving probable cause that it may not be for everyone. I have found, in terms of gameplay, that the unintuitive nature of Ori stems from the dissonance between its aesthetics and mechanics: Ori lacks specificity in assigning objectives to the player; its method of teaching the player is vacuous, unrewarding, and uninvolved; it provides no difficulty slider or learning curve for players of weaker skill; and to impose a false sense of difficulty many of its levels seem unnecessarily littered with hazards and spawns.
A first-time player may notice that, by leaps and bounds rather than by skips and hops, how disjointed the early levels can be from the difficulty of even the early dungeon stages.
Overall, I am an unhappy camper. I have gotten to Mt. Horu, but I cannot find the will to continue any further. I am once again stinted by the puzzle at the entrance of a cavern, where instead of spikes I have super-heated ground upon which I take damage and cannot save. If Mt. Horu is meant to be a test of user skill its design is ignorant to the pacing preferences and time by which individuals take to complete a game of their own accord. Ori at this point says instead go hard or bust. I think I’m for the latter option.

People have written many negative reviews due to issues when the game was first released.  Is it actually fair to do such a thing to cripple a game in that way when especially when there was a fix, posted on the forums and then then an offical patch to fix the issue with the game.
Also there is the issue that Is beyond people's control at this point.  and that's the discount vs gettng the game for free if you owned all the existing content for DS2.  I can understand that it makes people mad, but then again, not a reason to give the game a bad review.
So with this out of the way... On with the review.
What can I say about this updated an improved version of Darksiders 2.  Well one thing a lot of returning players will notice is the improved visual quality of the textures and the lighting.  and in a lot o cases, with the new lighting that has been added to the game it makes the game look complete different compared to the original.  Some might say that it is good, and some might say that it is bad.  to me, I am actually mixed about this,  seeing as how the new lighting can at times make it harder to pick out important parts of the terain that you need to move forward, such as ledges on walls etc.
What you also get with this version of the game is all the previously released DLC and weapons but unlike the previous version they have been seamlessly intergrated in to the game.  No longer do you get a whole bunch of weapons and armor, but instead you get these weapons and armor as the game progresses.  Also the extra DLC missions are unlocked as you progress through the story.  Which if you ask me is a much better and more thought out idea.  seeing as how you can't do some of the DLC without having equipment from the main game.  this makes the DLC more enjoyable when you go in to it with the tools that you need.
All and all I would say that this version is an good update to the original which had it's share of issues, and I will admit they still do exist in this version.  But hopefully now that Nordic games is activly working on the IP and the game itself a lot of these issues can be addressed and the game will finally be turned in to the game that we've all wanted for so long.
In the end.  if you're new to the games, both Darksiders and Darksiders 2,  I'd pick them both up,   They both are great games and tell a great story with lots of action.  If you're returning to the series after putting Darksiders 2 down for awhile.  I don't think that you will be disappointed by the visual upgrades and changes made to the game.

To The Moon has unique story and entertaining gameplay. There's not much repetitiveness, and if there is, it's story driven enough to not be a factor against the overall feel of the game. Very emotional.

To the Moon is a game that has a very fiercely passionate fanbase, so my thoughts on the game won't be popular.
I don't think it was a 'bad' game. It was okay.
However, all things considered,
for me to recommend it to someone else.
I'll start by writing that the game is pretty to look at (as pretty as RPG Maker pixel graphics can be, anyway), and even prettier to listen to. The piano soundtrack is just beautiful.
The writing is solid. It's witty, and the humor is clever. To be honest, I enjoyed the humorous parts a lot more than the emotional parts of the game, which is kind of odd for a story that focuses primarily on being emotional.
And yes, the story is emotional... kind of. I appreciate the uniqueness of time travelling through memories (I'm a big fan of time travel), so that was pretty cool. But the story itself is simply not memorable. It feels like a combination of 'touching' cliches. To me, personally, it felt more cheesy and predictable than actually sad... kind of like an okay-ish Hollywood movie. Maybe it's because I've been spoiled by so many deeply awesome stories in anime or in other games, but To the Moon simply wasn't gripping.
It is also terribly slow paced. It's a 4 hour game that felt like 10. Each scene appears like it is being drawn out to the maximum, and I found myself disconnecting from the story and telling myself "Okay, I get it, let's move on" way too many times. I believe it could have been compressed into a 2 hour game without losing its essence or message.
Oddly enough, the one part that did not feel drawn out, but instead rushed, was the saddest event of the story, which doesn't make sense, as I did not have time time to feel emotional about that particular event.
Finally, the gameplay is dreadful. Walking around with clunky controls, doing the same thing (clicking on everything to gather memories) in every scene was not fun at all. I can appreciate walking sims when the walking part isn't so awkward, but this was really rough.
Everything simply felt glitchy, even though it wasn't a bug.

I got stuck in the environment six or seven times where I had to respawn, which was a little annoying, but don't let that put you off. Also, even though the visual style is great, there was nothing really new in terms of gameplay, nothing you haven't already seen in games before, and it even 'literally' borrowed a few mechanics from other games; for example, if you're low on health, be sure to cut the grass and spawn some health (I'm sure you've done that in another popular game). It also drops in framerate on occasion and gets quite chuggy in places. I have a powerful PC too, so if you have a low spec PC, you might want to try it out first. The final thing is a little more feedback would have helped. I got stuck a few times and founf myself wandering, not sure what to do next, but these are minor things in the overall experience. All in all, it's a great little game, quite a large world in which to explore and play, great (dynamic) level design, lots of collectables and a nice character upgrade system. Thanks...

One might ask: how could this game succeed? It's single player only, story driven, basically no replay value and less than 8 hours long. Is there a place for such game in a market dominated by soulless and greedy publishers, spewing their CoDs, Battlefronts and Destinies to the mindless masses year after year? Yet here we are, 500k copies sold in 3 months and almost universal acclaim. For me this was one of the most harrowing and unique experiences I have ever had in gaming. Ninja Theory took on a great challenge of independent development of a game that's touching on a very difficult subject of psychosis and actually succeeded. Not to mention state of the art rendering of the main protagonist, the technology on show is just amazing. Sure, the gameplay is nothing special, pretty simple action/puzzle hybrid, but it is the story and presentation that will keep you hooked. This is the kind of game that will stay with you long after the credits roll. I highly recommend this game to anyone who can appreciate unique story telling and is looking for something different in their games. If you are like me, sick and tired of the microtransaction driven ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and looking for a game that offers something actually unique - buy this game, support this amazing developer, so that they can keep delivering these great experiences. Bravo Ninja Theory, bravo indeed.

I have anxiously waited for Slain! to be released. I am still waiting for it to be released on the ps4 and the Vita, but I wanted this game so bad that I joined Steam just to get it. I can't go on enough how much I love this game from the art style, and the music and the gameplay. This is exactly the type of game I want to make myself, and it inspires me. I love the gruesome brutality especially. I will be happily getting Slain! again when it does finally find its way to the Sony platforms to. I can't honestly go on enough about how much I love this game.

Slain! Is much more than a game, it is an artistic masterpiece! The creative bar on the art side is set so high, that no game that exists can even dare to approach this beauty. All the modern engines and their fancy whirlygigs stand in the corner and meekly watch as just a few hundred megs of pixel-art put them all to shame. The creativity and talent of the artist/s here is just unbelievable! It's like you are in a flawless Heavy Metal comic book! And if you like gothic fantasy and similar creative paintings - then you will love this.
Provided, that you also like side-scrolling platformers, like the ones in the golden age of the 16-bit systems. Castlevania Bloodlines, Altered Beast and Warlock definitely say hello here (Castle bridge, Wolf Knights to say the least). I have completed both the early version of Slain! and the Deluxe Edition and i can say that despite the negative reviews at the game's release - i didn't find any issues with it whatsoever. It played as smooth and responsive (joypad) as the immortal Castlevania Bloodlines. In fact, the game is pretty much identical to it in the play mechanics, and NOT to the Symphony of the Night, as other reviews seem to often claim. Unlike SOTN, Slain has no backtracking , no time-wasting, but also no RPG elements. It follows a classic Castlevania formula, although the hero is more able and more agile than all the classic Belmont family.
Each patch to the game altered the gameplay by changing some core features, but I found the later-added game mechanics redundant (the whole block-based combat thing) and they only slow things down. I seldom use it. Still, the patches add many other important elements and enhancements, so we'll look forward to each and every one of them.
Also, unlike what some people write - weapons do have different tactical advantages: steel sword is faster, ice axe has a better reach and a knock-back combo, fireblade is like a mix of the two and is useful against fire-vulnerable enemies. Gameplay is smooth and (at least to me) is really engaging. You always feel like you want more. I can only congratulate the makers of Slain! and say only great things about it.
However...the game is missing one stage, and a final boss - which hopefully will be fixed, since i'd really like this game to have as many stages as possible! But the only true problem is the music....
There have been so much hype about the fact of it being METAL, that you would almost believe it would be made by someone like Theodore Ziras or Buckethead....well, OOPS....it isn't! As a metal musician myself i was very surprised that after all the advertising bravado and bringing in some name from the Metal world we get...this. Oh well...
It's kinda trying to be metal, it uses distortion guitars - if that's a plausible excuse - but it is really lazy! A lot of copy pasting and lazy lame repeating riffs with no soloing whatsoever -  what kind of metal musician does this?! Man this is like...betrayal! After one boss battle in the game the old witch says "By the Horns of the Metal God - you've slain the mother beholder!" Well you know what? Metal Gods would be ashamed by this.

The abysmal launch of the game has hurt its reputation, that is for sure. But I think it's very admirable that the work is actively being put in to not only fix the issues, but also improve upon the game and add content post-launch. I've seen enough other games on Steam released in an unfinished or unsatisfactory state that are just abandoned and do not receive this luxury.
I'm sure there are plenty of reviews posted that say something along these lines, but after playing it again I definitely feel the game deserves a second chance and I wanted to add to the positive voices for the game. I hope this game gets fair recognition for what it is now as well as what it becomes, rather than only being recognized for what it was at launch.

RUNNING WITH RIFLES. An addictive and fun game that will have you playing for hours. Personally, I think this game is definitely worth the $14.99.
The game is not very demanding of one's PC. I believe it would only get mildly laggy if there were a number of explosions in one area. Also, the download size isn't large.
This game has a lot of cool features. RwR offers a "level up" system in which you soar through the ranks (Private, Private First Class, Corporal, etc.). In order to be promoted, you must earn a certain amount of XP from killing hostiles and from completing other tasks. Also, you can form your own squad out of soldiers who are around you. Your squad size will increase as you are promoted.  When you start a new campaign, be prepared to sit in front of your computer for hours on end (most likely for just two). I have only completed one campaign... It took me over two hours.
On the other hand, the AI can be a tad bit annoying. For example, an AI (on your team) may stand still in front of your moving vehicle. They won't move (most of the time). This will cause you to lose points. Also, quite a few of your fellow soldiers may stick around your base/spawn and never leave. Other than these minor issues, the game is quite perfect.
After the first 30 seconds of the game, I knew I made the right choice in buying this game. Though some may find it pricey, I find that the content of the game is well worth the price. I recommend this game to all people who like shooters.

RUNNING WITH RIFLES. An addictive and fun game that will have you playing for hours. Personally, I think this game is definitely worth the $14.99.
The game is not very demanding of one's PC. I believe it would only get mildly laggy if there were a number of explosions in one area. Also, the download size isn't large.
This game has a lot of cool features. RwR offers a "level up" system in which you soar through the ranks (Private, Private First Class, Corporal, etc.). In order to be promoted, you must earn a certain amount of XP from killing hostiles and from completing other tasks. Also, you can form your own squad out of soldiers who are around you. Your squad size will increase as you are promoted.  When you start a new campaign, be prepared to sit in front of your computer for hours on end (most likely for just two). I have only completed one campaign... It took me over two hours.
On the other hand, the AI can be a tad bit annoying. For example, an AI (on your team) may stand still in front of your moving vehicle. They won't move (most of the time). This will cause you to lose points. Also, quite a few of your fellow soldiers may stick around your base/spawn and never leave. Other than these minor issues, the game is quite perfect.
After the first 30 seconds of the game, I knew I made the right choice in buying this game. Though some may find it pricey, I find that the content of the game is well worth the price. I recommend this game to all people who like shooters.
