RUNNING WITH RIFLES
In one sentence it is a beautifully crafted minimalistic Top-Down Tactical shooter.
The closest similar games are Cannon Fodder and Warhammer 40K: Dawn of War, with the difference that you are controlling just one unit. I am recommending this game because I feel that it does an amazing job capturing "war". WIth this game I've experienced war at it's fullest.
Weapons here have a kill chance rather than taking off hp. It is possible to survive a full-auto M16 blast to the face, and then kill opponent with one shot. Such is war.
I started as a Private, with a firefight lifespan of 15 to 30 seconds. In my first death ever, I was run over by our own tank because I didn't get out of it's way fast enough. By now the game says I've played ~67 hours, and died 1086 times total, which means I die on average every 3.7 minutes. What do these 3.7 minutes consist of?
Running to the combat zone and getting shot right away.
Running to the combat zone with your squad, getting pinned by sniper fire, leaving your squad to flank the enemy from the right and throwing him a fragmentation grenade.
Running to the combat zone with your squad and straight into an enemy APC, which proceeds to mow you down in a matter of seconds
Running to the combat zone, hearing APC from the distance and dual rocketing it into oblivion, before it even does anything.
Getting thrown out of your own boat and knifed by enemy commandos.
Throwing out an enemy driver and hijacking an enemy tank.
Sneaking into enemy base, hiding behind trees from big patrols and killing small patrols with silenced MP5, then destroying radar jammer, and finally calling airstrike on everyone inside.
Having an airstrike called on you, and be the only survivor from your squad, as everything around you goes up in fireworks.
Doing drive-by in a jeep, going ~100 kp/h as your squaddies obliterate everyone on the sides, while you run over slow ones.
Running over to assist a wounded soldier, as enemy tank rolls into view and obliterates both of you.
Shielding machinegunner with riot shield while he reloads, holding back the advancing enemy until support arrives.
Blocking off passages for enemy vehicles with sandbags and car wrecks.
Mining the road and exploding charges with enemy tank right above them. Most satisfactory.
Lying wounded, watching your positions get overrun with enemy hordes, and then calling an airstrike on yourself and them. Because you were dead anyway.
The list goes on forever.
UPDATE:
90% of the negative reviews on this game are written by people who have not bothered to even learn to play the game.
Experience grind.
One of the biggest problems people currently identify is the that you need to level up in order to level up faster.
- Well, here is the easiest way to level up without having to "git good" - use shield. When you are wearing shield, you soak up 1 exp for every kill made by friendlies close to you. That means, if you are shielding a general, who calls heavy artillery strike on 30 people - you just got 30 exp in 30 seconds, doing nothing.
- Second easiest way is to heal people. you get ~16 exp per heal.
- A little harder, but the most profitable and best way to level up is to be in the capture zone when an area is captured. You get lots of RP and ~50 or something exp.
"Servers are empty" claims.

Story-
In Slain! play as a mighty warrior that was brought back to life by Ancient Spirits to save the land from the evil Lord Vroll. Armed with his Sword and his bravery, he sets off in a quest to beat he crap out of everything and anyone who gets in his way. Sadly that's all I can say since I don't wish to spoil anything to new players.
Gameplay-
The concept is simple, 2D sidescroller kill everything, dodge traps and die (a lot). You might enjoy it, or it might♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Me personally, Im enjoying the challenge.
You also get to unlock 2 power ups for your blade, Fire Sword and a Ice Axe which can deal more damage to certain enemies. And lets no forget your mana which allows you to fire spirits at your enemies or use all of it at once with he spirit grenade.
-Visuals
The pixelated graphics are very nostalgic, it takes me back to when I first played Ghost and Goblins, Splatter House and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.
As for artstyle, Im in love! The dark gothic horror mixed in with fantasy has always been one of my favorite topics to draw. So Im looking foward for Wolf Brew to release a Art of Slain! book in the future. I'd buy it in heartbeat.
-Animation
Thanks to the updates, the game runs smoothly as it was intended to be.
-Sound
A few months back this would have been different, but thanks to the updates, we sounds in the game are more convincing and it really draws you into the game more. Plus its is very satisfying when you counter attack an enemy.
The soundtrack... Loved it. Thats all I can say about it.
-Controls
The controls are simple, you move, jump, attack, block/counter, and use magic. This was another thing that went through  developmen hell. But once more, thanks to the updates, the controls are now more responsive.
-Overall
Slain! is a game that deserves a second chance, and I can vouch for this. I have seen the developers work nonstop to bring us the original vision that they had for the game and more! So, if you are looking for a nostalgic hack and slash game to an amazing tune. Then Slain! is your game.

This game... it completely blew me away right from the very beginning. The character designs, the voices, music and visuals gripped me from the beginning, and kept me going throughout wanting more. While the objective to restore the forest is quite simple, the level designs are so well made and challenging that I was so hooked that I finished the game within a couple of days.
The character designs are so beautiful, and I have to say adorable. Especially in Ori's case. The theme of forest spirits, nature and life really speaks to me, and the characters were so expressive and compelling even though half of them don't even speak.
The story is simple, but really excels in showing the emotional connection between the characters, even the villain. Though I like the fact that the "villain" isn't evil, just a character with tragic circumstances of their own.
The soundtrack and environments are so memorable that at times I would be content just to stare at the wide expanses and admire the love and work from the developers and artists.
Progression is very fast but each ability allows you to navigate the environment in more ways, eventually allowing you to travel nearly anywhere you want, even upwards. Ori is so agile that traversing long distances and navigating the world map from one end to the other is not so difficult as you might imagine.
A couple of things I would like to mention, though. I would have liked the ability to fast travel between Spiriti Wells. Even though I didn't really need it, it would have helped for anyone to navigate the world map to return to areas and pick up all the collectibles. The other is that I could have gotten a little bit more explanation as to how the "Light" works, as it drives the entire plot from the beginning.
All in all, if you like platformers, nature, fantasy, exploration, an emotional story, great game design, or a challenge, this game offers it. So much care and love went into this game that I can't help but love it back. Looking forward to any more games in this wonderful new universe.

Wolfenstein 2 is a brilliant game with some frustrating flaws. It's got the best story and presentation of any game I've played this year. The story and characters are pretty much exagerated versions of what they were in the first game.
My frustrations stem from how easy it is to get killed most of the time you're playing the game. I was playing this on the "Don't Hurt Me" difficulty (second easiest) and still got stuck in some fights. I had to check to make sure the difficulty hadn't changed on me. The dual wielding controls also feel sluggish and diffidult to change unless you find cover that you can hide behind for a good while. Lastly you can use a melee attack to kill anyone pretty much instantly but you get stuck in a cutscene where you can still get hurt and killed. I died like that a lot. You also don't seem to get any benefit from killing people up close and personal like you do with Doom. It's weird they didn't take that into account. Don't let these flaws keep you from experiencing one of the best stories I've seen told in a game.
The direction of the cinematics was top tier The transitions remind me of an Edgar Wright movie. The action sequences are pretty much what I was left wanting from Inglorious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The characters are well defined if a bit zany. They all seem to have their traumas which are explored in the game. It causes a bit of dissonance thinking about it now but in the moment, if you can suspend your disbelief, it's got a wild range of emotion made belivable by the fantastic acting.
The gameplay is satisfying. Instead of a tick on your reticule, you'll know you hit someone because there will be a blood explosion. Even if they can get you killed, the melee kills are gruesome and effective. The feel of the weapons are distinct if a bit underwhelming the bigger you go. The pistols with a magnum upgrade sounded and felt better to use than the shotgun. The machine pistols felt better than the assault rifle. Regardless of how they compared to each other, they all sounded and felt like the weapons they were trying to be. They can all be dual wielded in any combination you like. It can be too time consuming in too fast paced of an environment to change your weapons on the fly. Instead of a weapon wheel for each hand it would have been useful to let you save weapon combinations in 1 weapon wheel for quicker weapon swapping.
The weapon range is pretty much what you'd expect; Pistol, SMG, AR, Shotty and grenade launcher all of which can be upgraded in mundane ways. The more unique weapons are a lightning gun and Petrol bomb gun. Depending on which choice you've made early in the game.
I ended up beating this and the first Wolfenstein in a weekend. I've never done that before and I have the bad habit of hardly ever beating the campaign before moving onto the next game. I was completely gripped by the story Machine Games have done an astounding job of putting together.

The game took me about 10 hours to complete and I was mostly thrilled most of the way through.

FINAL REVIEW UPDATE (over 350 hours in-game): IF you decide to buy this game, you'll have to accept it, warts and all. For all the hours I have in NMS, I have yet to complete any major storyline. There are aspects of this game I truly enjoy (exploration, base building, etc.), so that's why I keep coming back. For me, the game collapses (either by crashing or some in-game lunacy that makes continuing impossible) between the 12 and 16 hour mark. So, taking it at face value, for my play style, I get a lot of entertainment per hour (currently at a cost of about $0.20/hour).
However, if you are a player who expects to finish a game storyline, be ready for some major frustration while you do so. The off-planet mechanics are geared more towards game controllers than for PC and are still very klugey for PC.

Where to begin, there just seems to be so much unconditional love for this game, that Steam even calls it overwhelming.

While this game has it's charms, it's drawbacks are just too plentiful too ignore. The good, the story is good, at least to the point I got to, but I ended up getting a summary since there so many other drawbacks I couldn't finish. Story has a nice sci-fi hook and the characters are all interesting and you genuinely want to know more about them as the narrative progresses.
The pixel graphics are nice, but not really incredibly distinctive and the graphics end up taking away from the gameplay ultimately for reasons I'll go into now. First, resolution doesn't scale well and there only three ways to set this. A default fullscreen, which is just the 640x480 stretched out on the primary display, a huge problem for multi-monitor. The base resolution 640x480 is just too small for a game, even when this was released 6 years ago, and the worst part is the window isn't even scalable so you're stuck with the enlarged fullscreen or the small windowed version (which you have alt+enter to go into, isn't even a game option). The only other workaround is using Windows magnifier but that again, messes things up on multimonitor setups, and should be something a game takes care of itself instead of leaving to the end user. The big reason it's a problem, is the windowed the interactable objects are very small and quite difficult to see, making it a guessing game of point and click. It also really just blurs everything and doesn't give the game the atmosphere it's looking for. If the creators went back and just fixed the graphics options after all these years to make it work dynamically, for a dynamic platform (the PC), I would most likely recommend this game.
The music is a clear highlight here as well. It's great mellow music that sets the tone for what's happening well and there are strong themes in the narrative it highlights.
The other really dreary weakpoint, and this is compounded by the graphics, are the controls and gameplay. It's your typical walking simulator with interactable objects, (which is a genre I typically enjoy, exploration and small details are great), it just doesn't work well as a SNES style sprite search with graphics options not setup correctly for modern systems. The gameplay loop is so samey and chorey that it you just want to rush through it to get to the dialogue. Find a few objects, solve a simple puzzle and off to the next vignette. Fullscreen and windowed, there are invisible borders everywhere and the art style doesn't lend itself to small details well. To top it all off, the characters move like 4 directional snails, games of this style should be adopting the 16bit Zelda style of movement rather than Final Fantasy VI without Sprint Shoes.
Ultimately, gameplay is king and a good narrative can be found in all media, and should be suited for the form the media is presented in. To The Moon is too tropey for it's own good when it comes to mechanics and art, and I'm saying this as somebody that moderately enjoyed Undertale.
If ever the game receives an update to the way graphics work, I would say check it out, but if not, just go watch a movie you've been meaning to watch instead of playing this game.

Did you ever like Pacman?
Did you ever like Snake?
Were you any good at either?
IF you think you are a God at both then try this game out for siaze as it combines both pacman and snake into one fun little puzzle game that will frustrate you beyond belief.
How does it combine both games?
Well from pacman you have the white blobs that you have to collect from arond the maze, upside in this you dont have ghosts trying to eat you.
From Snake each piece you eat makes you longer which makes going round harder as you cant walk into yourslef or its game over.
So add both of those together and you have Millie.
it starts out easy enough you are small but the more you eat the longer you get so you are then gonna have to make longer circles to get that last piece to get them all from the map and then of course get to your hole in the grond to complete the level.
It sounds simple until your body is so long and you have to go through all the twists and turns and hope you dont have run into yourself.
To top it all off there is a little bonus where you fly a plane and have to draw a shape in smoke, that i have only tried to do the heart and failed as its not as easy as it seems.
Great little casual game that even at $4 is worth it as it will give you a lot of joy and frustration for anyone who likes puzzle type games

Ori and the Blind Forest is a single-player platform-adventure game designed by Moon Studios, founded in 2010 making the company rather young and new.

You, as the player, assume control of Ori, a white guardian spirit. Through out the game, as Ori, you need to navigate the platforms and solve multiple challenging puzzles. Using Soul Link, the player can save the game and use experience to achieve new perks or upgrade current perks.

Despite that fact this game fits my lore/ story driven loving mind. Within the first 7 minutes I had been through a rollarcoaster of emotions.
The voice of the Spirit Tree in the forest of Nibel narrates that when Ori fell from the tree during a storm, Ori became orphaned and was then adopted by Naru, who raises Ori as her own. The love between Naru and Ori is shown by Narus affection.
Suddenly a cataclysmic event damages or "kills" the forest causing its food supply to wither. Here an act of affection performed by both Naru and Ori shows the affection between them.
Ori collapses near the Spirit Tree reviving it (sort of) and then becomes revived by the Spirit Tree, Ori later meets Sein, a being who guides and helps Ori against enemies through out the game. Sein is a part of the power of the Spirit Tree, as Sein explains itself
Sein is referring to Kuro, a giant raven-shaped bird whom stole the core of the Spirit Tree. When Ori was lost, the Spirit Tree released a flash of light to look for Ori;

The flash released by the Spirit Tree killed three of Kuro's hatchlings leaving Kuro vengeful. Kuro despises the light. Though depicted mostly as vengeful, hostile and cruel - Kuro has a fierce passion to protect her last unborn child.
Together Ori and Sein strive to recover the light of the three main elements which supports the balance of Nibel; Waters, winds and warmth.
Through out the game Ori and Sein comes across other characters, which I will not yet reveal here until I, myself, have completed the game 100%
I recommend this game because it has amazing, stunning and breathtaking scenery, animations and stages. Really the art of the game is beautiful.
The plot itself is amazing and when you're introduced to all characters, the game leaves you, yet again, stunned and speechless. Not to mention the soundtrack which functions exactly as any soundtrack should. It helps breathe life into the players immersion and emotion.
And when you have completed the game, you will speculate - does the game have an actual message? It probably has - and I will find it.

I rarely leave reviews. Hell, I rarely complete games because life gets in the way. But oh my gosh. This game is one I will judge all platformers by.
Pros:
- Simple but heartfelt story.
- Absolutely gorgeous graphics.
- Controls are a dream, even after you've mastered the many different actions and start getting confused between the various jumps.
- Challenging (I swore a lot), but not so much that you want to give up (and that's saying something coming from the most easily disheartened individuals) You can actually progress each life.
- Intuitive saving system.
- Simple Health/Energy/Levelling.
Cons;
- I downloaded the 'Definitive Edition' in the steam sale, apparently the original is no longer availible. Weird, because I ended up with both in my library, confusing and annoying me very much when I played 5 hours and then couldn't find my save file (as it was on the 'different' game). I ended up getting too far in to vanilla to bother starting the definitive (guess that's my own personality) so I feel I missed out on a bit. Saying that, this is only my first playthrough so I'm probably going to immediately start the next one on difinitive.
- Powerups are often too much of a faff to get to warrant the small reward. You have to go back a level/area with your new powerup to get a single 'vitality point', for example. As such, I just powered on with the 'main quest' and completed it with about 3/12 possible extra hit points. And thats certainly not down to skill. Too easy?
- Too short (vanilla, anyway).
- Made me cry over 2d shapes.
- Kuro was robbed.

(This review covers the original
. While most of it also applies to the Definitive Edition, I have additional thoughts about the Definitive Edition that do not fit here, so I will post a separate review for that.)
In the heart of a mythical jungle not unlike the world of James Cameron’s
, the majestic Nibel tree is the source of life for an odd race of light-rodents who are born as leaves on the branches and drift to the ground. A leaf named Ori drifts too far from the tree and is adopted by an odd motherly creature named Naru. While Ori is being raised by Naru, an evil owl named Kuro removes the tree’s source of light, leading to the death of all the other light-rodents and the destabilization of the forest. Ori and Naru remain blissfully unaware of their roles to play the grand scheme of fate, until one day when food becomes a bit too scarce and Ori is forced to leave home…
To call this game merely “beautiful” would do it a great disservice. This game is hauntingly beautiful. Disturbingly beautiful, even. The kind of beautiful that I sometimes forget even exists. And I’m not just talking about the visuals: the soundtrack, the themes, the feeling of complete fragility, the absolute freedom of movement, the nightmarish sense of scale and the cruel environments, the feeling of
when you survive something impossible, it all comes together to create something deeply frightening, something that transcends the player.
Aesthetically, it is beautiful in every way a game can possibly be beautiful. Every frame pops off the screen in haunting, striking colors. The stylized art will likely never show its age. The orchestral soundtrack is filled with showstopping masterpieces like “Naru, Embracing the Light”, “Completing the Circle”, and “Light of Nibel”. The story is a heartwarming, tearjerking tale of loss, legacy, and family. The character designs are memorable and adorable (mostly, but I’ll get to that later). Simply put, if you aren’t touched on some level by the way this game looks and sounds, you’re probably not human.
But it’s not just the look and sound that convey beauty, but also the game mechanics. The game is designed to make you feel the fragility of life itself, and to understand that it is precious only because it is so easily lost. The first third of the game is designed make you feel humble and powerless against unfair odds, making Ori out to be a tiny, unlikely force of light in a world which threatens to consume him at every wrong turn. But upon climbing halfway up the Ginso tree and acquiring Ori’s signature “bash” skill, you may start to feel something different: you no longer dodge and flee from your foes, instead you now jump fearlessly into them, sailing over hazards and climbing up impossible chasms with ease. You start to feel Ori’s confidence, an appreciation for his endless potential despite his tininess and fragility, a feeling you will spend the rest of the game exploring.
The playstyle is almost purely based on movement and agility. As the game progresses, you don’t begin to feel more powerful so much as you begin to feel more liberated, and free of the darkness and dread that surrounds you. The game creates a sense that you are spreading your light everywhere you go, and every place you visit becomes better because you were there.
The game is also very sound in programming. Unless you’re specifically looking up speedrunning tech, it’s highly unlikely you’ll encounter any glitch at all in a casual playthrough.
I do have some nitpicks, but none of them are bad enough that they can’t be overlooked:
* I feel that the game relies a little too heavily on stock sound effects. The bullet noise for bashing, as well as some of the enemies’ attacking sounds, are a bit on the distracting side when you recognize them from dozens of other games.
* I feel that Ori’s main weapon, the auto-aiming flame, is very strange, and almost a risky design decision. I understand the design principle behind it – to allow Ori to fight by avoiding enemies rather than attacking them – but even after all this time, it feels ever-so-slightly out of place. Perhaps Ori’s default attack could have been the stomp move and it would have felt more natural, but that would have broken the Metroidvania progression, so I’m not sure there’s a better alternative.
* Every so often, there’s a tiny sprinkling of outright bad level design, like that exploding slug that falls from offscreen after climbing out of Gumo’s hideout.
* There's a skill that lets you breathe underwater, but if you haven't researched it by the time you're out of the Ginso tree, it's basically useless because there's only one body of water in the entire game where you'd need it.
* I feel that most of the enemies are poorly designed. There are only about 10 types of enemies to encounter, and most of them are some variety of blob or frog. The most powerful enemy is, quite literally, a ball of rocks. In a game where the main characters are so memorable and full of personality, the enemies are all boring, dehumanized, and visually confusing. Their body masses slosh around like balloons full of paint, and it’s hard to even tell what kind of shape they’re supposed to be. Now, perhaps the enemies were intentionally dehumanized so you wouldn’t feel bad for killing them, but if that’s the case, I feel it was a poor move. Many games have adorable enemies which have become icons of the game. You know, like goombas and koopas?
There are some exceptions. I especially liked the charging rhinos and the mini Kuro birds. They had a soul and personality. Why couldn’t all the blob-frogs, spider-blobs, blob-slugs, and exploding blobs have been as cool-looking as them? (Although, to be fair, I’ve seen the Ori 2 trailer, and it seems like they might actually be addressing this issue. All the indigenous species in the new game look fantastic.)
Altogether, I can’t give this game anything less than a 10/10 for everything it has done. It has far surpassed all of my expectations, delivered powerful impressions and presented several game mechanics I’ve never seen before. Any nitpicks I have are totally overshadowed by my enjoyment of the game. And, perhaps more importantly, I keep coming back to it after all this time. It might wind up being my favorite game of the decade.

The advertising of Wolfenstein 2 made allusions to the current American political situation was in poor taste.

Not to mention, the people you have to ally with. An obvious allusion to the civil rights movements in early WW2. The way they acted, seriously troubled me. The way that they brought race into it, felt like stooping to the low of the nazis. In my opinion, they should have stated that race is irrelevant to one's personality. I respect that connection; but once again after what the soviets did to my family; I feel extremely dirty allying with them. However I understand that this critique is purely political and others are entitled to their opinion.
[spoiler over]
In conclusion, gameplay was awesome, had a few issues with message and that gun wheel, defineltely recommend.

Worth $60 now? Not really, but the recent updates are a definite step in the right direction. However, no matter how many updates come out, this is definitely not a game for everyone.
PROS:
-A practically infinite, procedurally generated universe to explore
-An advertised 30-hour storyline
-Side missions to keep you occupied while exploring
-Base building that is woven into the story
-Limited multiplayer allowing you to run into other players, as well as come across their bases and discoveries
-Relaxing music and atmosphere
-Multiple difficulty levels that caters to more hardcore and casual playstyles
-Regular patches and updates
-Mod support
CONS:
-Gameplay can be grindy and repetitive
-Every system has a space statiion, ruining the sense of isolation
-When flying, the game will try to adjust where to fly for you to prevent you from crashing. This doesn't always work out, and usually just prevents you from going where you want and you end up crashing anyway.
-Procedural generation can yield pretty odd results
-Mission objectives tend to just be fetch quests
-Inventory management can be a chore, especially during the early game
-Despite regular patches, the game still has its fair share of bugs
Despite a horrible launch, Hello Games has shown that they care about the future of No Man's Sky. I believe that even on launch day, there was a good game deep inside here, it just needed refinement to show. As of 1.3, No Man's Sky is beginning to find its identity, and is starting to deliver the potential it showed on launch. I picked up the game on sale last week, and have enjoyed a good majority of the 50 hours I've clocked in on it. For this reason, I feel it's safe for me to recommend this.
HOWEVER, I do NOT believe this game is worth $60 yet. There is still more that needs to be expanded upon before I can safely say that. If the price drops to around 30 or 40 bucks, then I say go for it. There's plenty of content here to make you feel like you've got your money's worth, but it's still not anything groundbreaking, and still has its fair share of problems.
As I've said, this is a game that definitely isn't for everyone. Combat takes a back seat to the exploration and resource gathering here. This is advertised as a chill exploration experience for good reason; it's more Star Trek than it is Star Wars. If you enjoy walking sims, survival games, exploration in Elite: Dangerous, and games similar to Minecraft, there's a chance you'll dig this game.

I received this version for free because I own the original version with all the DLC. This game is the same as Darksiders 2 with all the DLC except it has an HD make over and it also has some bug fixes and loot tweaks. I see a lot of reviews giving this game a bad rating simply because they didn't receive this version completely free which is just lame in my opinion. Depending on which version of Darksiders 2 you own you either got a free copy or a discount of up to 80% off.
Now as far as the game goes it's a very fun game with some issues. My biggest issue is with the camera. The camera doesn't always go where it should be. This games uses dashes and rolling manuvers instead of a blocking system, so sometimes when you roll away from an enemy it takes a second for the camera to catch up (you can move the camera manually). The games HD make over looks and runs nice on my I5 laptop with my 6 gigs of ram and 1 gig dedicated video card.
The gameplay is borrowed from some very popular games.In this sequel you play as War's brother Death. Most of the fighting and combo mechanics are borrowed heavily from God of War. The movement and wall systems are borrowed from Assassin's Creed or Prince of Persia. As Death you can run along walls grab pillars jumping from rock to rock. the games dungeons and puzzles are clearly Zelda inspired. I see alot of people say this is a zelda clone. Hob is a fantastic game boasting highly detailed environments, imaginative creature designs, and story telling that is VISUAL. The creators at Runic Games understand "show don't tell," and Hob does it. Probably the strongest statement I can make about Hob is that it does not have any major flaws for me, at least in terms of art and story. The story is simple and it works, there are questions that are never answered, but nothing that feels forced, awkward, or that logically breaks the story. The designs are consistent, the world is vibrant, and the puzzles are familiar to the genre of puzzle-games yet always have the unique "Hob" perspective. Some of the most challenging puzzles for me involved getting up to a ledge I could see, but could not reach, or finding a safe path down to a lower level. A lot of games can't manage the basics, but for me Hob shows just how important the basics are. Hob also features a new world design that I have never seen in any other game. The world of Hob is the most developed character in the game and it hides suprises around every corner. I have played this game for over 20 hours and I think there still might be some corner hidden away that I have not managed to find. I hope the devs will not leave this gem alone. DLC, or even a sequel would be fantastic, especially since there are enough blank spaces in the world map to add new content in the future. For now I will give Hob an enthusiatic 10/10. Buy Hob.

This game had flown under my radar until it was released and I read a glowing review on Eurogamer.  They likened it to Zelda, which firmly caught my attention.  So without hesitation I downloaded and started playing.  I'm very glad I did!  The world is like one great big Zelda dungeon complete with labrynthine puzzles that intricately link together.  I felt "stuck" on occasion, but I really just had to sit back and think logically about where I can probably go next and look for hints built into the world.  Solving some of the puzzles was definitely rewarding and not overly frustrating.  The game isn't perfect though, as you get severe frame rate stuttering as you transition from area to area.  (It's presumably loading in the background.)  It gets even worse if you Alt-Tab to other apps and come back to the game.  It's like memory gets all fragmented making the stuttering even worse.  If that happens, just save and exit, and it should be much better when you start fresh.  I thought the game was the right length, but after finishing it I wanted to keep playing.  Aside from simply playing it again you have the option to keep looking for hidden secrets you missed.

With a world that you explore changes and transforms as you experience it, giving ample variations of the world you thought may be set in stone (often literally). You know those little mechanical details you used to see in games and films? Well they actually do something here.
Great fun to explore and to play. Often games seem to be one
the other, but in Hob there's plenty to explore and to interact with. From the strange and cute wildlife (which you may cuddle or dice as you please) to crab-like mechanical platforms that even send the baddies fleeing in terror.
This game also boasts some of the best level design I've ever seen, which ties in with the exploration and puzzles brilliantly. But it's also far more vertical than you might assume from looking at the screenshots, and you'll often get to look over cliff faces to find there's something ahead/below. You might get stumped or lost for a moment, but their little visual cues and overall planning prevents frustration. The game rewards backtracking (which is useful once the world shifts or a new ability is unlocked) but it isn't required to complete the game. And there is an immersive fast travel system which you can use too.
It's also visually unique, having the look of a comic come to life. I feel like I'm playing in and with the concept art for games I grew up playing as a child. And I love the mesmerising soundtrack too - which sneaks out of the ambience nicely and emphasises discoveries. I just wish it'd be playing a bit more often.
Despite the simple style (which is not a bad thing), the game is quite demanding and can lag at times. To their credit, the developers are constantly improving the game; but the framerate often drops drastically - most commonly when the camera pans up for some cinematic views, or peers down to reveal the depths of the game; which I assume is from loading masses of content at once.
I hope the developers will find a way to improve pre-loading (perhaps by using more RAM) to prevent this. I'm sure that it will also ease the strain on the GPU, allowing less powerful devices to run the game (my Laptop for example, which only has integrated graphics, but a powerful CPU and plenty of RAM).
Other than that, nothing really bothers me about the game... apart from creatures/enemies occasionally
out if existence for seemingly no reason (they're not self terminating due to getting stuck).
It may be a little demanding, but Hob is the most fun I've had in a long time.
I hardly ever get to sit down and play for over an hour with all the projects I have going... and I just spent 3 in a row with my eyes wide and a smile on my face.
Need I say more?

Despite its best efforts, Remember Me is a game worth playing through. Once.
You're here for the same reason as everyone else. The game looks fantastic in trailers, in screenshots, and I'm happy to tell you that it remains fantastic-looking throughout the whole game. Any game that can make a sewer-level look good deserves some credit.
Pity the gameplay doesn't fair quite as well.
You have four static combos to choose from, that can be slotted with different effects ("pressens", the most made-up scifi name in existence next to anything beginning with "Z") - and while the animations for each slot is unique, outside of the general pool you choose them from every other aspect stays exactly the same.
There's damage, healing, and the cooldown-timer reducing effect for your static combos. Notably, though, are the chain moves, which have a multiplicative effect when stacked on themselves and "anchored" to a single effect. This means that you can heal your entire healthbar, touch-of-death any enemy and completely remove the cooldowns on all your abilities in a single combo.
The abilities are mostly situational, the few that aren't are useless compared to your regular combos (without the enemies introduced that are straight up immune to those).
Result is that it's incredibly underwhelming. On a first playthrough, where you're being dripfed the "pressens", you don't have enough tools to do anything with, and on any playthrough afterwards you just break what's there.
Luckily they balance this by introducing enemies that are immune to your melee combos completely and require either the peashooter projectile weapon or your "I Win" abilities (if they're not immune to those as well).
Sorry did I say luckily, it's awful.
You have a combo-extender (Think Dodge Offset except worse) wherein you dodge over an enemy and continue your combo otherwise, but ranged and melee enemies have absolutely no problem attacking in quick succession, just far enough apart that they will always catch you on the recovery frames. Not to mention the horrible hit detection on the enemy-dodge that means it's always a safer bet just to dodge into the enemy you're currently punching then to actually try to use the system for anything else.
No counters or parries or options to play well, don't be ridiculous.
This is not God Hand, this is not you juggling crowd-control viability, single-target damage, speed, reach, recovery, ancilliary effects for each move all under constant pressure. This is an incredibly sloppy game that just manages to scrape over the bar for being completely streamlined.
There's a fair few collectibles to halfway incentivize replaying the game, but don't. It's not worth it.
You cannot skip the cutscenes. And boy does Remember Me love to waste your time with cutscene, after cutscene, after forced walking segment, after cutscene.
The "remix" segments are just interactive cutscenes. You can't walk down a corridor without a cutscene. The entire last level is just cutscene followed by a solid 10 minutes of forced walking. It does not miss a chance to shove its plot down your throat.
Remember Me's plot isn't good, either. The world is fantastic, the setting is inventive, it has some great ideas, but the plot is just about the amnesiac non-character Nilin getting reunited with her parents and being really blandly angsty about it. With incredibly bland-to-poorly written dialogue.
I didn't even like going through it the first time, and the second time was absolute torture. No, you can't turn them off, skip them, fast-forward, you can't even alt-tab or bring up the overlay because it pauses the cutscene.
I've legitimately left the game running and gone to make coffee while cutscenes were playing while clearing out collectibles, this is not a game that expects nor desires you to replay it.
What keeps it going during that first playthrough is visuals. And that's it. This is not a game you want to be good at, or even wants you to be good at it.
That's whats to recommend Remember Me for, here. An eye-treat that's mechanically ambitious and suffers intensely due to continual compromises with a cinematic direction, compromises that drag it down an absurd degree.
That first playthrough, though? That ones alright. I recommend it for that one.

My favorite modern platformer. It boasts some absolutely beautiful and varied visuals, while having strong, consistent controls and a balance of challenges. I've full cleared it twice, though I've failed to 100% the entire game due to some missable credit during the three major 'dungeon'-esque scenarios (RIP).
The soundtrack is gorgeous and matches the visuals very well. "The Light of Nibel"--the main theme--is easily the most memorable track of the game.
Level design is a bit unwieldy for backtracking... at first, however the game offers a lot of shortcuts to open up to alleviate this in fuller playthroughs. Upgrades to your skills will ultimately make maneuvering the terrain much easier and fun as you unlock everything. Ori is quite nimble and can run relatively quickly baseline, so it shouldn't feel like a slog to move in and of itself.
There's no point in this game where the difficulty of the platforming feels unfair. The difficulty curve is also nice, and doesn't spike up considerably from any point to the next. You'll encounter gimmicks and challenges that the game will ease you into. The save command makes this game very casual friendly, and alleviates frustration of getting stuck by leaving the point in which you must backtrack/practice entirely up to you.
You'll acquire the Bash skill, and it's one of my favorite platforming mechanics by far. There's so much you can do with it. :>
The story is rather small, and overall the game can be very short in repeat runs, but I still enjoy whizzing through this on subsequent playthroughts from time to time. I went back to acquire most of the achievements and still enjoyed it.
Tragically, as of this review, I did not own the Definitive Edition (yet) and wasn't even aware it existed until a few days ago, so I definitely missed my coupon opportunity.
Without doubt, I recommend this for anyone that enjoys platforming games (Sonic 3 & Knuckles being my eternal favorite). It's not terribly long (my first 100% attempt was about 7.5 hours, but I can complete the speedrun in 2-2.5 hours), but it's worth trying to unlock the achievements for challenges. I'm absolutely looking forward to the sequel (which has even more gorgeous visuals) on the horizon.

A testament to what a small team can accomplish with a (relatively) modest budget. This game accomplishes what it sets out to do - deliver a 6-10 hour experience with laser focus on tone and theme, and do it at half the price of Triple-A titles. I genuinely enjoyed my time with Hellblade. It's incredible to look at, and the metaphor knocks me out. The combat is OK, and the puzzles are OK, but that's not the reason to play this game. Play it for the attention to detail in the graphic and sound design. Play it for the artists' dedication to the craft. Play it because there simply aren't many games that attempt to explore mental illness in a meaningful and nuanced way. Highly recommended.

Basic stuff:
Played it on a laptop (GTX 970M, i7, 6700HQ, 16 GB RAM) and with a PS4 controller on SCP DS3
Settings:
1080p with all settings at high (Though GeForce Experience wanted at few at very high strangely). FPS would hover around 30-45 FPS depending on the scene.
Issues encountered:
Controller failed to register at times but would be solved by tweaking general controller settings on steam and some crashes that would resolve when I would restart the game.
What I liked:
1. Breathtaking graphics - some of the best I've seen from an independent studio
2. Easy to grasp combat system
3, Sound design - best played with headphones in order to appreciate the way the game presents "Hearing voices*
4. Price - its less than $16 in my region and even far less if you buy it now on sale
5. Plot - it manages to really draw you in and has a very respectful depiction of the rather taboo subject of psychosis
What I didn't like:
1. See issues encountered section
2. Camera is pretty janky if you managed to be cornered
3. Length - it's kinda short

First off, this is a short game. I've played through the main game (there are 2 mini bonus 'episodes) in around 3 hours. That isn't necessarily a bad thing, just something to consider. Now, onto the review.
I thought based on other user reviews this game would be a masterpiece but I was sorely disappointed. The music is indeed stellar, and by far the best part of the game. The gameplay is more or less non-existent. Even for a narrative game like this there's almost no puzzles or anything to figure out. The game could be played on auto-pilot. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the story isn't nearly interesting enough to get away with lacking any real gameplay. The 'funny' dialogue is very hit-or-miss, and a few of the references are getting dated. Anytime I felt anything it was 90% because of the music.
The art is pretty, but it was hard to tell what you could walk through and what you couldn't. In addition to pathing problems, walking felt very slow and tedious - why not include some kind of run button or increase movement speed? Given that most of the 'gameplay' is walk around, the fact (well opinion, to be fair) that walking feels awkward is not ideal.
They're not exactly the same type of game but if you are looking for a narrative game with a good narrative and non-trivial gameplay, I'd recommend looking at One Shot.
EDIT: I forgot to mention, the game has a single achievement which is to beat the game so if you want to 'perfect' any ol' game, this isn't a bad choice. At least, not a long one.

Sadly, I've also lost all motivation to continue.
The underlying vision of this game appears to be centered around explorarion and adventure, where everything about the game is expressed in a non-verbal way.  The game deliberately avoids having any UI, button prompts, tutorials, direction, waypoints, or goals.  While that type of minimal-ui visual communication can be a fantastic tool for creating imersive gameplay, a significant portion of the time I was left quite confused, and I believe deliberately so.
Throughout my experience, if felt like everything in the game lacked purpose.  You hit buttons because there exists a button, so you should probably hit it, but it's never communicated why we're doing anything in the game, what our goal(s) are, or what we're supposed to do next.  Unfortunately most of my time with this game was spent wandering aimlessly, trying to figure out where to go next.
I hope to see more great work from this studio, and their $20 launch prices is amazing for what they deliver, but I felt this game fell flat.  Perhaps they'll put my $20 towards making another game that I'll enjoy, but I won't be blindly purchasing their next game based on reputation alone.

It is at times like these that not only did I wish there were more comprehensive recommendation option, neutrals, caveats and all, but also a more generous refund window - perhaps even an extra hour ought to be sufficient. I only hope that based off what I have written on this game - and not what I had to click in order to post the review - people will be able to understand just one person's experience with this game.
Based off of early footage, it would have been fair to assume that Hob would be a zen puzzle game. The setting appeared to pay tribute to the likes of Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli, whilst the art assets and sound design all appeared to build upon the signature Runic style, which is to say, a team heavily influenced by their experience with Blizzard, but with a Promethean flair about them. To say that the Torchlight series was anything other than an indie candle which was lit from the inferno of Diablo and WoW would be optimistic. The game's prized
says all that needed to be said there. However, it wouldn't be fair to Runic, who did after all work to the best of their means to keep their vision alive, and it paid off for them, and all the loyal players who came to warm themselves by Runic's captured heat.
It was a source of pain then, when I drew too close to Hob, chargrilled atop Runic's writhing flames. What I had hoped for was another quirksome puzzle game with a few twists, a unfolding narrative, and a creative game world with crisp mechanics and feedback that made progress intuitive and rewarding. In other words, I was hoping for a more spacious and open-ended S-xy Brutale. What I got instead, was a 3D platformer.
Et tu Runic
My desire to keep my experience as fresh and unspoiled actually left me ignorant as to the game's core operation. I could see why the store page brought with it such a strong suggestion to bring with it a controller. Imagine if one might, the agony of navigating down slippery platforms barely exceeding the width of the dainty protagonist with WASD. The scenery - whilst at first inviting due to it's alien and abstract geometry, becomes lethal and trecherous as only one might expect from decrepit abstract ledges in advanced states of ruin. How ironic.
It is actually possible to fall off platforms within barely a hair's bredth of error when least expected. After a while of traversing the terrain with minimal difficulty, it may well be possible to blunder into certain death half a dozen ways. I've been oneshot by a troll's club down a narrow chokepoint where the camera is obscured by foliage, I've slipped off a low wall and instanty died after landing on a cactus, and falling into the abyss after holding the line straight with the D key (no wobbly adjustments with a joystick involved). Perhaps my least favourite are the frequent occasions where the feeble character will drop off a ledge and plummit only 30ft or less to result in a torrent of blood. A grizzly, if predictable outcome for us mortals, but quite the contrary to how generous every other platformer from Banjo Kazooie to Mario has always been. I loathe platformers, yet even I was astonished by just how greasy and unforgiving fairly innocent platforms appeared. The novelty wore off bloody fast.
Clipping has also continued to be an issue in the game. The occasional moment of being lodged in place between two or more objects in the game has been an infrequent, if vexing experience. A cruel fate which even the QA testers of the game must have raised hell over, for avoiding a game ending bug such as comes from getting trapped in the scenery, is the only reason the respawn option in the main menu exists. After all the energy spent on crafting Hob's world - and the world is very pretty - I can sympathise with Runic's solution to the bug, even if as cynical patches go, it's a devilishly funny one.
Combat plain sucks. Beneath appearances, the core combat functionality is no different to Torchlight's method of click to win. The difference is that at least with Torchlight, the player's avatar could take a hit, and had limited, if sparkly abilities to cast. Hob has a bit of brass, and sure doesn't look like the little slugger ought to be capable of hauling around that impressive robot arm of his. The little guy has limbs that make spaghetti look like seqouia, and he's just as squishy as would be expected. The truth is, I think everybody could have done without combat in Hob. Finding creative ways to evade and defeat the zerg creep would have been enough, without having chittering goblins and those wretched cowards who toss infinite exploding slugs into cramped arenas. They're just the worst. Unlike the obnoxious platforms however, the mobs can be spanked into submission with Hobs aforementioned brass cudgel. It takes a while, but being able to trick mobs into launching themselves into hazards brings the occasional mirth, and after wrestling with the controls, mirth is very much needed.
Oh, and whilst I remember, the fact that the keys cannot be rebound is sinful. Runic overlooked one of the essentials of game design. That's a paddling right there, with a dinky brass bat.
Well thank you very much for reading this far. Please don't make the same mistake that I did. Invest in a controller. As pleasing as the world it to the eye, it's still a trecherous one, and even with a stick, expect to die a hundred silly ways. When all is said and done, it's possible to hug a sugar glider-rabbit hybrid. That's a teeeen outta teeeen right there. Know what you're in for, be safe, and please don't let the world stress you out.

This has the potential to be a fantastic game, but it's plagued by a couple major issues.
---Negatives---
- There are puzzles in this game, but most of the time it felt like I was just running around looking for something that I missed or following environmental queues like a trail of bread crumbs. Very rarely does the game clearly show you what your objective should be, so you are left looking for something to hop onto or looking for a path that you missed. The puzzles that are done well feel fantastic and are very satisfying to complete. I would have liked to have the game zoom in on the objective when entering a new area, then I have a direction to work towards. That small change would already make the game a lot more engaging.
- Camera angles are good, but not great. Too many times I was left wanting to move the camera manually in order to move my character around. The game does a good job 90% of the time, but the other 10% took me out of the game.
- Combat is not engaging or challenging. Movement in this game is fast enough relative to the enemies that it's not necessary to fight anything unless required to move on. When I do have to fight enemies I find myself mashing X and occasionally dodging an attack or two. Enemy variety was extremely low and I was disappointed that they did not significantly change upon entering a new area. I would have liked to see quicker enemeis with more varied attacks to match the protagonist.
- Upgrades are not substantial enough. I didn't feel compelled to get many of the upgrades because they just weren't that useful. The only upgrade I was excited to get was the green cloak which allowed me to move quicker. Combat upgrades saw very little use in my playthrough as I rolled my way through most enemies.
- Performance is inconsistent. I was regularly dropping a large number of frames at medium settings with a GTX 1070 @1440p. It didn't prevent me from finishing the game, but it was annoying at times.
---Positives---
+ The artwork is amazing, as you can probably tell from the previews. You can really sink into the charming world as it transforms, and boy does it transform.
+ Hob does a great job of showing you the story and how to play instead of outright telling you. This might be annoying to some new players, but you quickly catch on.
+ The controls in this game are well done. The character is easy to control and platforming is enjoyable, which I can't say about most 3D platforming games. New abilities are implemented well and gradually introduced in the way they should.
+ Save points are frequent and generally in a useful spot. I only ran into trouble with these when I was backtracking to previous areas.
+ The map does a good job of letting you know what you missed, where you should be going, and even providing hints at how to access specific areas.
---Closing Thoughts---
There is an amazing game hidden inside Hob that could be revealed if a couple major flaws are fixed, but as it currently stands I cannot recommend this game.

Hammerfight is a game that will make you scream in excitement and scream in frustration, often in the same play session.  Perhaps the most frustrating thing about Hammerfight is that it so bipolar: innovative and terrifically executed core mechanics make you want to play, then the significant frustratings and nagging issues make you want to stop playing, but then you get drawn back in by the core gameplay, and so on.  I'll recommend this game, but only to the buyer with substantial patience and forgiveness for a game that is in itself unforgiving.
At it's core, Hammerfight is a 2d aerial combat game.  Battles are fought between flying machines with attached swinging weapons (hammers, swords, flails and the like).  Here's the thing: there is no "swing weapon" button (except for the throwable weapons that I don't use anyway because they're not nearly as fun).  You swing your weapon by moving your ship in such a way that the weapon swings around you (side note: in the options menu, crank up the mouse sensitivity unless you like moving like a snail) and connects with your opponents.
The core combat fueled by this gameplay is exhilarating.  You have a massive variety of weapons to choose from, and while they are various takes on classic archetypes (e.g., sword, hammer, axe, etc.), they have a variety of nuances that give them distinct advantages and disadvantages.  Swords, for instance, require close-range flying and are repelled by armor, but carve up a flyer in no time on a direct hit.  Hammers and flails don't do as much hull damage, but can shatter armor and send enemies flying across the screen.  When you get the flying skill to start delivering massive hits, the results are extremely cathartic: the sounds of crumpling metal and splintering wood combined with the sight of your opponent hurtling into a wall and exploding rank among some of the most epic moments in any game I've played, let alone a 2-d one.
But underneath this overwhelmingly successful core is a wealth of nagging frustrations.  The UI is abysmal, often blocking your view of fighters that are well within striking distance.  Enemies and allies alike - especially in higher levels of play - have a tendency to pepper you with ranged weapon fire that, even if it fails to hit you, still blinds you (white screen) and produces an extremely annoying high-pitched noise (if you have tinnitus, you know).
But above all: the game is loaded with unexpected and seemingly unfair deaths.  You will die a lot in this game, and while many times this is because of poor piloting, on numerous occasions you are killed from full health for seemingly no reason at all.  As best as I can tell, the game's physics are such that sometimes a thrown weapon or environmental object can get "jammed up" in your ship's weapons, which results in it constantly hitting you.  In arena, some enemies explode when you kill them, often times killing you from full health.  I get that this is an intentional mechanic (suicide bombers), but in a game that's supposed to be about shattering impacts, punishing a player for attempting to deliver such an impact is unbelievably backward.  I have died many times in this game, and probably <1% of my deaths is from actually getting hit by an enemy's weapon; almost all of them are from random explosions, a single thrown weapon or environmental object, or unidentifiable cause.
I love this game, and I hate this game, and I can't stand how its bipolarity keeps me conflicted.  I play it because I love the gameplay, and while it's fun I will inevitably stop playing it out of frustration later.  I recommend this game with *extreme* caution; if you have the patience for the game's unforgiving, and at times seemingly unfair, nature, it'll be a lot of fun for you, especially at its price tag.

The button-mashing gameplay is what takes its toll on patience but thankfully its not the primary focus. Its not necessarily the action that makes it a great game but the personality that radiates from it. From the environments and the music, to the story and the characters, even the background lore that is uncovered by finding clues throughout the areas all come together to make a fantastic and engrossing game.
The weakest aspect IS the fighting: the combo system gets tired by the third chapter and sadly it never adds anything new besides punches and kicks. No weapons, just fist and feet. As you fill up the combo bar, shown on the bottom of the screen, each hit can replenish health, add damage, and reduce the time between Sensen abilities; player-activated special moves that induce major damage for a short time. The story advances in leaps and bounds during the memory manipulation puzzles. These parts are a way to slow the game down from all the ledge-hanging and button-mashing and its impossible to really fail these moments.
The graphics are fantastic and Neo-Paris *feels* alive and real. From the first moment you see the skyscrapers rising through an alleyway you get a sense that most of the care was put towards the details. Even the latter chapters that take place inside the technology-laden government buildings have been crafted and no one place feels repeated The music is both orchestral and techno blended together which elevates during fights and gives depth to the surroundings even when just standing around. The voiceacting is superb and never sounds phoned in. There aren't many ambient sounds, though, since most of the effort was put towards the music.
Nilin is a great character and never comes off as two-dimensional: she's haunted by her forgotten past and plagued by the actions of the present. The secondary character's personalities feel alive but there are only a few of them. The rest of the world is populated by enemies of varying difficulty and its sometimes a chore to have to stop and beat up a few of them only to traverse to the next area to do the same. Boss battles don't really vary it up either with predictable patterns and repetitive dialogue but thankfully only occur at the ends of chapters.
Its main focus is on telling the story and it succeeds in doing so. It only falters with the fighting. If you hate games that show and not tell then its simply not for you. As far as value goes, you probably won't find all the lore and collectibles in the first playthrough but its definitely worth it to try a harder difficulty level next time.

Author's Note: I've been a fan of Assassin's Creed for around 4 years and I recently decided to replay the entire series so, here goes my review for the very first game. The one that started it all.
Back before naval combat, Ezio, hook blades, and yes, even before two hidden blades came Assassin's Creed (1). Assassin's Creed follows the story of Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad as he seeks to regain his assassin rank. Like the future games, this one takes place in a historic setting, this one's Jerusalem during the Crusades.
Before I dive into the setting and scenery, let's first talk gameplay mechanics. So, the game gradually gives you back your original weapons, as well as skills. The weapons include a sword, dagger, throwing knifes, and of course the hidden blade. The combat is pretty good in the first one, but it's definitely improved through the years. You can block attacks, counter, and dodge. Now, if you're used to the newer games, you'll find the hidden blade a little different than what you're used to. The hidden blade can't really be used in a fight, it's only really for sneaking up on enemies. The sword combat is fairly good, but like I've stated before, they've improved throughout the series. One thing that may disappoint you is the lack of the crossbow that you see in the trailer. Sadly, the crossbow was cut out due to the fact that it made assassinations easier, but you'll do fine without it.
Now, you've got all of you weapons so, you need something to use them on. As you go through the game, you are tasked with gathering information and killing targets chosen by the master of the Assassins. This is done in different ways, and in different locations. First, you'll have to go up to a viewpoint and sync in order to see your choices. Usually, you have to complete three of these tasks to gather enough information for the kill. This information can actually be pretty useful and makes killing your target easier. These tasks kind of feel like mini-games and they're pretty fun! There's pickpocketing, gathering flags, and even killing targets. There's more than that, but I'll let you explore the other options.
Okay, so you've got all of the intel, now it's time for the kill! Your targets vary from either sneaking into their base of operations and (trying to) stealthily kill them or dueling them. If you fail at stealth, then you'll probably either have to duel them or chase after them (Just depends on how much they value their lives). This is pretty fun and never really gets boring. In reality, the game is a little repetitive, but to be honest, it never really felt that way for me. Just enjoy the moment.
Alright, so we've talked about assassinating big targets, now let's talk about their little henchmen. As you go through the game, you'll fight a variety of enemies, such as: guys with swords, heavy armor guys, guys with bows, guys with maces, and so on. The combat really isn't that hard and it doesn't take much to get used to it. The enemy A.I is fairly good, but sometimes a little laughable. They do sometimes pose a challenge though, which is always fun. Oh, and just like you, they can't swim! Looks like you're not that different from them deep down.
So far, we've covered killing, killing, and...ah...well, more killing! Now on to the scenery. So, the game takes place during the times of the Crusades (hench all of the Templars) in the area, and even in, Jerusalem. The cities you'll visit are fairly large and full of life. You'll usually see at least 4 people, usually a fair bit more, in most areas on the streets. The cities look great for its time and the game runs rather smoothly. How do you get to the cities though? Well, you'll eventually unlock the fast traveling system, which means you'll travel...fast. It's not too different from the one you'll find in AC 2, but you won't need a boat. As soon as you run out of the Assassin HQ, you'll get the option to fast travel. If you'd rather see the world for yourself, you can always travel by horse.
Now, on to the last bit of stuff. So, the voice acting's pretty darn good, even if Altair has an American accent for some reason...you get used to it though. The graphics, like I said, are pretty great. Even the soundtrack is pretty great, it provides even more tension to tense situations!
Overall, this is a really great game! If you haven't played any of the Assassin's Creed games before, this is a great starting point. You'll really appreciate the newer mechanics in the later games. If you've already played some AC games and not this one, this is a great chance to see what you missed! It may not be the best Assassin's Creed game ever *cough* *cough* Assassin's Creed 2 *cough* but it's definitely a great start to an amazing franchise.

Alright...it's time I reviewed.
Let me just right off the bat say that truly the only reason to buy any videogame is to help support the artist who struggled to make it (and, well, to get some entertainment in the form of a non-alcoholic beverage). And that's exactly what Assassin's Creed does...for like two hours.
So here's my issue: it's way too freaking repetitive. You meet up with Al Mualim (hope I spelled that right), your boss, get berated, get a mission, complete one of many repetitive tasks (such as jumping off buildings and saving insanely helpless citizens) in order to even be able to DO the mission, then you do the mission and head back to Al Mualim to start the process all over again. Seriously. You do it so many times you easily accumulate over ten hours (even if you speed-rush).
Yahweh, Allah, and God-- I'm just as unfocused and ADHD as the next guy-- so how the hell was this game so popular?!
Well, I've come to a few conclusions which I will highlight as the positives of this game:
1. It's historically accurate
2. Graphics are great. Still hold up after more than a decade
3. Has an interesting premise-- which is hard to get to because there are so many mundane and repetitive objectives that get in the way
4. Very diverse. Represents many cultures
5. Offers two sides of an argument that's been going on for thousands of years
6. You get to be a mother-loving assassin (or at least I hope Altair loves his mother)
It's for these reasons that I believe the Assassin's Creed franchise has prospered, and I hope to see improvements in the next game that I play, which will most likely be the second one...
I just hope I can be bothered.

Assassin's Creed. It's been 10 years since this game came out.. I've played it and replayed it over and over since 2012 and it's still one of my favourite Assassin's Creed games. But my views back then were different because there were only like... 5 main games. So what do I think now? well...
Story:
It starts off with Altair recovering an ancient artefact from Solomon's Temple. However, he manages to break 3 tenants of the creed. Once he returns with the artefact, the Templars track him down and kill the civillians and other assassins who live in the assassin HQ, Masyaf Castle. Everyone blames Altair for bringing them there so Al Mualim demotes Altair to a novice rank and makes him find and kill 9 templars who are trying to ensure the 3rd crusade continues. Altair kills all 9 but then the leader, Robert de Sable confesses it was actually Al Mualim who wanted to use the artefact to bring new world order. Altair then kills Al Mualim aaaand the rest is for Assassin's Creed Revelations.
Also there's a modern story with Desmond Miles but... not much to talk about.
Gameplay:
The gameplay in this game is probably the weirdest to talk about. It's not great, because the games that came after were far better but it's definitely not the worst. Honestly, I think this game got 1 very important thing right: STEALTH. Stealth is what Assassin's Creed is about and it seems only this game can do it properly. The fighting is a little bit clunky at times but definitely not as easy as the likes of 3, Black Flag or Rogue. It's only when I played it on PC that I managed to figure out that sometimes if you counter then quickly press X, you can finish them off while they're recovering. I also like how the side missions end up helping you in the actual assassination mission. It suprisingly becomes easier, plus it'll tell you what you should do.
Assassination missions:
Tamir: Definitely the easiest. Just walk up to him and stab him
Garnier de Naplouse: Make sure to stab him when he's talking to a patient. Otherwise he'll become Yoda and detect you while you're behind him.
Talal: He just runs away... hold sprint and then stab him ._.
Abu'l Nuqoud: Fat ♥♥♥♥er runs away and jesus christ he's like Dr Eggman in Sonic 2... faster than someone who should probably be the fastest.
William of Montferrat: One of the best targets to kill. Running around in a fortress trying to not get detected... niiice
Majd Addin: He looks like Bin Laden. And there's a bunch of soldiers trying to kill you. Also quite fun.
Sibrand: The worst ♥♥♥♥ing target ever. He's on a boat and you need to jump on ♥♥♥♥ing platforms to try and get to him. Don't get detected or he'll run away. Mistime a jump, you're falling into the water and dying. I've played this game like 5 times and every time, this mission ♥♥♥♥s me over. ♥♥♥♥ it and ♥♥♥♥ Sibrand.
Jubair: This one is just... annoying. There's like 7 different people you need to kill and you need to find which one is the real Jubair.
Robert de Sable: I used to find this one the most tedious. Both versions btw. In Jerusalem and Arsuf. But now that I basically know all the things you can do with the combat, I pretty much got past it in under an hour. I actually find it quite fun now. Cutting through a bunch of Crusaders and Saracens. It's good.
Rashid ad-Din Sinan (Al Mualim): Very underwhelming... although I do like the fight, it could have been so much better.
Music: The music in this game is really good. Very mysterious 'n♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not as good as 2, Brotherhood or 3 but still good. Jesper Kyd never fails.
Overall: The game is still good and honestly, if Ubisoft made an updated texture pack for the PC version like they did with Watch Dogs 2, I'd be okay with that. I wouldn't mind a HD remaster either but as long as they show this game some love since it's the 10th anniversary... then anything is fine with me. The game can be repetitive in terms of structure, but it's still fun and definitely worth trying out.

To start off the review, I want to say that this game, to put it simply, is magnificent.
You play the game as a warrior set to save her husbands soul from rotting in Helheim (what the Vikings called Hell). She goes through a long and dark journey that will test her will and strength to fight off her greatest fears, all for the name of love.
This game is amazing because the game knows what it is, and it isnt trying to be anything other than that, and that seems to be rare in a lot of modern games. You can tell that the Dev team spent most of the time developing a great story, focusing most of the time on the actual story line itself, and the atmosphere the game, rather than trying to compete with other games in the same genre. The story is heart wrenching to say the least, but as you near the end it just gets better and better. This is one of the best games to incorperate horror aswell due to the fact that it does not rely on jump scares to make it horrific. The sound alone in this game will put some people at unease. The visuals also add to this as every where you look seems to have a dark background to it.
I've seen people complain about how this game is too short, but honestly I think its perfect. The game would feel stretched out and dull if Ninja Theory tried to make the game closer to a 12 hour game or sometime related to that. This doesn't really have any down time, except for some puzzle's if im being completely honest. You also have to keep in mind that Ninja Theory is a small company, and they made this game with a budget of only 300,000 U.S.D and a team of just 13 people.
This game isnt perfect, no game is. The PvE is pretty lackluster. It gets quite repetitive after awhile (as there is only 3 attacks, a dodge, and a deflect) and the enemies are all similar in look for the most part. Also some of the puzzles can take up a lot of time only for you to realize that you were looking in the wrong area out of a massive room. However, even after these problems, the game is still pretty damn fun.
Even though fighting normal enemies in the game gets somewhat stale, there are times it is truly jaw drawping. As you get late into the game, there are times where there are enemies constantly thrown at you, giving a very intense battle.
The boss fights are quite epic, not only by how the bosses look, but because its a good challenge mixed that is also very entertaining. Also, NONE ARE QUICK TIME EVENTS.
I give this game a strong 4.5/5. This game is great due to the amazing voice acting, dark atmosphere, fantastic story, and a horror setting without any predictability. The only drawback, as I stated above, are some elements of the PvE that I felt were repetitive and aggravating at times.

This game takes you in from the get go. At the start you get a warning about the 'presentation of psychosis', and boy does it deliver on that. We follow the title character Senua through Hel, Vikings realm of the dead, all the while listening to the voices in her head. Voices antagonize, scare, curse and laugh at her, tell her where do go or not to go.
Gameplay is excellent, with some simple puzzle solving and great combat. Action is well done, fighting opponents one on one or sometimes multiple opponents. You have to be careful because they are clever and will get you on your every misstep and missed attack. Game play mechanics are simple and effective, reminding me of the Batman Arkham series, with only few buttons used to perform great looking fight moves.
Story is dark and weird, while at the same time being very personal. It shows you the pain Senua is going through, no holds barred. The psychosis that our heroine is going through is at the forefront messing with hers and our minds. The fact that developers dropped permadeath in all of that, pushes the tension even further.
All in all a great game that will keep you invested and on the edge of your seat !
