This is the first game I've ever taken the time to write a negative review about. It is TERRIBLE. TERRIBLE!!!
Before I start my rant, it looks really good (not top-notch, but good), the combat mechanic is unique and interesting, and the customizable combos are really refreshing in a game like this.
Now then...
The story is predictable, the combat is X/Y mashing (Xbox controller), and the BEST thing about this game, the combo combat mechanic, is completely ruined if you're fighting more than one enemy at any given time. The combos don't keep long enough for you to dodge and hit again, and if you accidently target any other enemy and hit them instead, the combo is lost. Like I said, it is the best IDEA in the whole game, but it's also by faaaaar it's biggest and most highly annoying downside.
The Elite Enforcers I just button mash heal combos on them because there's no other consistently-viable way to beat them, and again, the combo is ruined if you're hit once, meaning you're lucky to get a 3-4 combo, NEVER the 7 (or whatever it is) big one that is "so great."
At certain points of the game, I've gritted my teeth whispering under my breath "just finish the game, then you can uninstall it and never touch it again." I am on the EASIEST difficulty. If I were to try to play the hardest, my computer would probably be thrown out the window.
Every boss fight is AGONY!!! The first one with the boxing-match type deal wasn't that bad. Another one was a lady teleporting around and you just had to beat on guys (that do not even give xp when killed...) until you can use your DOS ability to hit her a few times. Rinse and repeat. A lot. Same goes for the twin uglies, the Greenteeth ugly, and I'm sure plenty of other bosses I can't recollect. And I remember one "boss fight" was just running from a ship that was shooting at you..? How is that a boss fight..?
There were minor bugs too, but not too bad. However, there was one that made me scream. Fighting the twin uglies that killed airship-dude, I killed them, the minions were still alive, and whatshisface started talking in my ear so i couldn't fight, dodge, or anything except walk EXTREMELY slowly until A. he was done talking or B. I'm dead and have to start the annoying boss fight all over again. Take one guess which happened to me... Had almost the same happen to me with the Greenteeth ugly, where everything was dead, but nothing triggered, so I had to restart the checkpoint and do it again. SO fun.
Also, all the cutscenes, talk-n-walk sessions, all unskippable. Even if you've saved and quit to play another day. Even if a TnW queues (cues?) happens at a respawn point and you have to listen to it EVERY TIME YOU DIE. Which is made far, far worse when the platforming is horrendous. Why put a bright orange arrow where I'm NOT supposed to go? Why make me die if I land on a floor too soon, even if that's exactly where I AM supposed to go? Why have I missed a jump half a dozen times, where she slides down a wall instead of grabbing onto it like the markers says she's supposed to? All the while having to rewatch a cutscene/listen to a TnW every time this happens.
For a $60 game, all these things are nigh-unforgiveable. I'd rather swallow some stranger's spit than subject myself to this infuriating garbage again, and no, I'm not kidding.
If you don't want to read all of that mess, Imma simply name the game what it should've been called in the first place: "Wait for Cooldowns: THE GAME"
......Can you at least see WHY I'm not recommending this game..? It's horrid.

A nice game with flawed joypad controls. As others have mentioned, this is a mixture between snake and paceman. I used to play snake on my very old Nokia mobile, it was superb fun and the best part of it was the open area, the speed and the responsive controls. Millie has closed spaces, a slow pace and extremely frustrating controls that don’t seem to respond. If you are walking between walls for example, pressing left or right for your next move sometimes registers but doesn’t always, leading you to lose the route you just preplanned in your head.
Overall I would recommend the game as there is always hope for the future that the joypad controls can be fixed. A game with poor joypad responses shouldn’t advertise as having full controller support.
I strongly suspect whats happening with the joypad is that the movement is registered but millie only turns on the grid, so it you are just a little too late then she carries on to the next space and then turns, which is very unforgiving. The should be some lee-way, a little forgiveness for the human reaction speed, all the play to move when you are actually on the space and moving slightly beyond it instead. Developers, if you are listening and even bother reading these reviews, please take note :)

Slain! looks like a heavy metal Symphony of the Night or Super Castlevania IV but it plays more like the original trilogy of Castlevania games for the NES. It's difficult, the controls are stiff and require precision & timing, and there's little in the way of explaining the game's mechanics. All of this seems to have been by design. You're definitely going to want to play this with a gamepad. If you're an oldschool Castlevania veteran you should feel right at home here but if you're expecting a more forgiving action-platformer or a Metroidvania you'll find yourself initially frustrated and possibly disappointed. There are some rough edges here in terms of presentation: sound effects v background music, minor performance issues, occassional crashes. These will likely get smoothed out in time. As mentioned by everyone, the aesthetic of the game is fantastic with great attention to detail. It's more Castlevania than Castlevania with gothic horror on display everywhere. The soundtrack is excellent and totally appropriate. Bottom line: if you love the original Castlevania or Castlevania 3 or if you're a fan of classic hard arcade-y NES titles (e.g., Ninja Gaiden) you should grab this. If you're more interested in exploration over platform puzzles this isn't really for you. If you're expecting inventory management & leveling up over tough action requiring persistence and precision then maybe this isn't the title for you.

When I first picked up Slain!, I was super exicted to play it. I've been looking forward to this game for a while now and in the first half hour, I was having a great time. The art is amazing, the music gets me ready for a gruesome adventure and the archaic setting is right up my alley.
I played and played, died and died and progessed further and further with each try. And after about an hour, I finished the first level. At this time I was thinking, "wow, that first level was extremely hard". But as I progressed further into the game, I realized that it's not challenging for the right reasons.
My constant deaths were not due to mistakes on my part. I would try something new each time. And I've given both of the first two levels PLENTY of tries. Here are the problems with the game (in its current state) that I see so far:
- The character doesn't always hit in combos like he should when I'm mashing the hit button.
- When I hit the dash back button, it doesn't interrupt the player attack animation, which causes the enemy to hit me before I can dash. The dash NEEDS to interrupt the attack animation to get rid of the unresponsive feeling of that specific mechanic.
- Each battle basically consists of hitting enemies while they hit you (partly due to not being able to dash properly). It's almost impossible to get through a fight without losing health or exploiting the game. (Getting enemies on a ledge so they can't hit you). This causes me to lose health with almost every single enemy encounter. Which leads to my next problem.
- The hearts. You regain health by hitting things that resemble tombstones. The heart then pops out and start floating away. Sometimes when the heart starts to float away, I can't jump due to me swinging at the tombstone. The heart gets away and I've learned that if you go into a battle without a lot of health, you die. So at this point, I restart at the checkpoint because I KNOW that I'll die.  "Repeated failure is a predictable cycle, and rather boring." - Raph Koster.
- Another problem with the health regen system is where they are located. Most of these tombstones are located right above enemy spawning points. So since I have little health left from my last battle. It's nearly impossible for me to collect this next heart because I dont have enough health to kill the enemies surround it.
- The last problem I have is with the enemies stacking on stop of eachother. I know it's kind of wierd for enemies to "wait in a line to attack you", but when they're stacked up, you lose SO much health when you're fighting because there are times when A LOT of enemies are thrown at you.
As a game dev myself, I respect the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of this game. It's awesome and has SOOO much potential to be great and I have faith that the devs are going to make it so. So my recommendation is subject to the tweaks, fixes and optimization.

I've had this game for awhile but I stopped playing for a bit while the devs at Wolf Brew Games addresssed some of the gameplay and functionality issues.  I'm happy to say this game is utterly fantastic!
Graphics
Without a doubt this is a very very gorgeous game.  The only way you can get a game that looks better than this is to go play Castlevania Symphony Of The Night or Rondo of Blood.  There is a ton of detail in the foreground and the background going on that is really amazing.  Swaying flowers, weather effects, lighting effects, rivers of blood, souls, traps, parallaxing, I can't stress enough how good this game looks.  Secondly, the animation is oustanding.  Everything from the NPC's to the monsters and bosses really shine.
Music
The soundtack is pure heavy metal but pairs really well with the gameplay, art, and over all feel of the game.
Gameplay
This game plays a bit like Symphony of the Night mixed in with Ghost and Goblins, and a small dash of Megaman.  Your character uses a sword to hack and slash his way through the game,  but can also can throw bolts of magic (when he has mana), block attacks, crouch, jump, and backdash (ala alucard).  While you don't technically pick up new weapons,  later on you get the opportunity to wield different elemental aspects of your sword.  This can be useful for certain leves/monsters/bosses that may be more vulernable to a specific type of element.  The game does a good job of telling you when to use different elemental aspects, although later on you will need to figure out which weapons work best or switch between them. The controls are precise (I use a USB PS Style controller) and fully customizeable in game.
Difficulty
The game can definitely be challenging at times (it's called Slain for a reason) but it's no Demon Souls.  The levels, subosses, and bosses have a good variety of difficulty so you'll need  a different  approach to each one if you're going to be successful.  Slain does of good job of keeping you on your toes while making you work just hard enough to make it fun without it being needlessly exacting.
Cons
Slain 2 isn't out yet....seriously I can't think of anything.  If I had to nitpick there are only a couple of abilities that I don't think the game tells you about (I might be wrong as I don't remember all the in game text)
1)Mana Burst (crouching down and holding the magical attack button) unleashes a burst of magic that kills most weaker monsters fon the screen and damages everything else.  You can only use it with a full mana bar but it also has the side benefit of temporary invincibility right before the burst.
2)You character can swat back enemy projectiles like a Jedi.

None, and I mean, NONE of the controls are a problem. This is not Cave Story or Dishwasher Samurai. The combat is not combo driven or twitchy. This is about taking time, learning, and dying alot. This is old school.

I honestly do not understand all the negative reviews here.   I purchased Slain expecting a (Gorgeous) sluggish sloppy mess that was going to be hopefully patched in the near term to address the major shortcomings in the gameplay.  I have been following this game for a long time, and the dev's seem to be very engaged and genuinely desire to provide the best product they can, so I decided what the hell - I'll give em the chance.  It sounds like perhaps there are some optimization issues that at the time of me writing this need to be resolved for some folks, but the devs are already looking into it.  Anyhow, I saw none of this.  Instead of a 12 buck gamble on a future quality product though, I was pleased to discover a very enjoyable game right out of the box!  I'm running on a i7, 16 gb ram with 2x 770gtx cards, and Im using an xbox 360 controller like a filthy console peasant would.  I have not tried with a keyboard but with that said, I have played the game on max graphics quality and it handled exactly like I hoped it would.  Volgar the Viking or old school early Castlevania games would be the best approximation of gameplay that I can think of.  Perhaps the old Blackthorne game from Blizzard?  These are all good things - they were all fun games!  The controls are simple, and the combo chaining crowd will likely be confused by the fairly straight forward approach, but that's the point - this is an homage to the classic 16 bit side scroller, and they were all about making the most of pretty basic gameplay.  The game is challenging, but the ballance is well done - some fights are intended to beat you to a pulp but if you play smart you will live through it  there is always a health pickup to keep you going.  The pace is good, and if you keep your cool, you will do just fine.   This game is dripping with atmosphere.  The graphics are absolutely stunning - some of the finest pixel art I have ever seen, channeling the very best of the 16 bit consol era along with the glory or the old VGA pentium days of platform gaming.  Every screencap is art.  The atmosphere is augmented by fantastic music and flavor narrative that complete the dark, Gothic environment and works on the same vibes that made Diablo or Symphony of the Night so engrossing.    This game by my observation is damned good.  It does what its supposed to do, and it does it well.  I don't understand where the negative posts came from, though they may well have valid points - what works on one computer may not work on another.  That said, from my own experience, this was exactly what I wanted.

The story is about 2 doctors - Dr. Eva Rosalene and Dr. Neil Watts.
They have the technology to travel through a patients' memories and alter them, so the patient will wake up remembering having lived an entirely different life.
However this will stop a patient from "functioning" afterwards, making them draw their last breath moments later - Meaning this will only be applied on their dying days, if they have a wish they didn't accomplish during life.
Their patient now is Johnny, and he wants to travel to the moon.
Sounds simple huh?
Well, it isn't.. Every action in life have a consequence, a cause, something it inflicts on, and of course you'll find out just why Johnny has such a wish.

The story made me really curious. You really don't know what has happened, because it's about an entire life - Hard to fully predict.
It stirs up touching emotions for most people, just read all the other reviews - Many agrees.
The soundtrack is really beautiful, you can listen to it seperately on evenings you just want to relax and reflect on life. I'd even say the soundtrack is what makes up the best and most important part of this game.
It proves a great storyline can beat gameplay.
A very unique story; I don't even recall seeing movies with a similar theme.
The fight scene cracked me up, I was laughing so much my neighbour had to ask what I was doing. It was a pleasant surprise.
You'll know when you get there, if we share the same lame humour. :p
The game is really short, it takes about 3-4 hours to go through (Was 3 enjoyable hours, but it's very short for 7.99£, Bundle for 11,99)
So however much I'd like people to support them, buy it on a discount.
Artwork
Well, it's created in RPG-maker so you can't expect more than pixel art. However it contains a lot of digital painted picture scenes, which could have used a little more polishing to really catch the eye.
It does its' business well enough, but I missed a few scenes to be as beautiful as the story.
A touchy story - We'll all feel differently about this, just like some people cry to the Titanic Movie, but I say this story hits homerun for most people.
You pay for quality instead of quantity. Short but strong game; however the soundtrack is infinite (If you don't find a replay-value in the game, you'll probably find it in the music).
"Sometimes I wish i'd done things differently or achieved more, but I'm also happy with my life as it has been..."
Is probably how I'll feel on my deathbed.
More in depth than their other game "A Bird Story".
In case you wasn't fully satisfied by that story.

Hob is a 3D top down action game that plays sort of like Hyper Light Drifter and Legend of Zelda, sounds pretty awesome right? Well not really because the core mechanics of what make those two games great are a filed down mess.
The majority of this game is walking around the map pushing buttons, and when I say majority I mean 98% of the game is spent doing this. There are no actual challenging puzzles in the game, any puzzle you come across is solved by walking around an area till you find a button you didn’t push, a ladder you haven’t climbed, or a cube you haven’t pushed into the right area. Most of these puzzles became incredibly frustrating because you would hit a button, then an area across the map would have changed slightly and you’d have to figure out what changed.

You don’t really have to think at all while going through the game, most of the puzzle go as follows. If you hit a dead end, there’s probably a button nearby, and you better push that button so that it lights up another button five rooms back. You spend around an hour in each area pushing buttons, so you can go to another section across the map to push more buttons. It gets incredibly tedious, and really starts wearing on you after you catch onto the fact that there is no more substance to the game.
Throughout the entirety of Hob there were zero bosses, which was a serious problem with the game. It would set you up perfectly for a boss fight, you’d push a button and a huge shutter would happen causing the platform you were on to shoot underground, straight into a massive robot manufacturing facility, were you’d ultimately have to battle a colossal robot scorpion. However, the scorpion never came, there was never going to be a boss fight. You never get to fight that grand robot scorpion, you enter this beautiful looking robot facility, push more buttons, and leave. There is never a boss to challenge your mechanics, and what you’ve learned through the monsters in the area.  Some would say this isn’t really a downside because the game was meant to focus on its story, which is understandable, but it doesn’t help the game from becoming stale.
There’s minimal combat and whenever you actually do get into a fight, the combat feels stiff and thrown in just as a distraction from the dull task of clicking buttons. You have a roll ability which is comparable to the dash from Hyper Light Drifter, or the Roll in Dark Souls, it grants you a few Invincibility frames and darts you in whichever direction you point the stick. There is no cool down or Stamina bar forcing you to use these rolls strategically. Every fight turns into rolling around until the enemy uses one of his two attacks, then you strike him until you see his attack animation start again. Rinse and Repeat.
The fighting became so boring and frustrating that I found myself just running past the enemies, because it was better than hitting them in the face with a sword thirty times till they exploded into bits. The only time I wouldn’t run past them was if the game deemed it necessary to kill them to open a door, or lift a platform. There wouldn’t be any indication that you needed to kill them either, you would just have to figure that out through elimination.
There are two weapons in this game, you have the classic sword, and a robotic fist which you can charge up and hit for damage slightly higher than a basic sword attack, which basically means you’ll never use the Fist unless you need to destroy an enemies Rock Armor. The charge up on this weapon is actually incredibly long for the low damage return, it’s a high-risk weapon with low reward.
There's also some upgrades to your character which grant you new abilities, the only ones I purchased was the Shield upgrade, which you’ll never use because it costs energy to deflect hits, and slows down the game to an unbearable crawl, and the Teleport behind enemies' ability, which you’ll never use because it costs energy, and you can just roll around practically making you invincible. There are also abilities to change some of your sword combos, like a stab while sprinting combo. This was the only one you would really use, but it never felt ground breaking. You wouldn't unlock the upgrade and say to yourself. “Wow, this ability is going to change everything!” It's just more of the same, you hardly even notice using it.
Now onto the worst thing in this entire game, the Grappling Hook. This was the worst thing by far in the whole game. The grappling hook uses energy for you to hold on to the “Hook” which in longer platforming sections will seriously frustrate you, it’s already hard enough just using the thing. To jump from hook to hook, you have to make sure your camera, slowly moves itself into position so the next hook is in view, while holding yourself up with the hook running your energy low. You then have to look at it with the left stick till it glows, then I think you press A to latch to it. I say I think because it’s so terrible that sometimes it will just jump you off the hook and you’ll fall to your death. Sometimes you'll jump to the next hook effortlessly, then you'll fly straight back to the previous hook. It’s awful in all regards. There’s a section where you have to do six grapple jumps in a row and after all that work, what do you get? A cloak that you don’t even get to use because it costs eight butterflies which is a ton!
Across the map there are hidden sections where you can find different Cloaks, each one of these has to be unlocked with a ridiculous number of butterflies. It took me till about three quarters through the game to unlock one of these cloaks. They offer a boost stat effect, for a downside of another stat you have, generally health. The one I bought was the Green cloak which increased your speed. It didn’t really change too much but it is there if you want to collect something to try and spice up your game.
While exploring this world you'll come across these Chests you can open, giving you ten green orbs, or a new schematic for an ability or cloak. Early on these chests are a life saver when trying to afford your initial upgrades, and I always felt relieved when I found one.  However, the problem that happens in Hob is the fact that enemies drop these green orbs as well, and they drop way more than the chests. This makes the chests feel like a waste of time trying to collect once you're further into the game, especially when majority of them only have ten green orbs in them.

The biggest enemy in the entire game is the perspective. The camera is constantly out to get you, making platforms seem in reach when in reality they’re incredibly far away. The cameras are in fixed locations that you cannot rotate, while walking it will snap to a new location sometimes changing the direction you’re moving in causing you to fall off a platform. Slight inclined platforms are some of the most annoying things in this game, you can’t tell where the edge is properly, you don’t know if rounded objects like the pipes you walk on will be collided properly. There is a section where you're climbing a colossus which is fairly broken, once you get to one of its joints it starts pushing your character off. You basically have to fight the game to advance past this section.
Ladders are also horrifying, they’re so frustrating it’s difficult to describe. When walking up to a ladder and pushing towards the left once attaching to the ladder it will force you all the way to the left on the actual ladder, forcing you to change the angle of the stick. It seems like a stupid complaint but through the seven-hour play time it really adds up becoming incredibly irritating.
One thing that gets incredibly annoying is the fact that when every you approach an object your character climbs on it, so you have to get in a very precise location to pull a lever, or you’ll just start climbing on it. Let's talk about bugs, in Part Two.

Hob is well designed and fun to play. It is a 3D platformer, living puzzle-box of a world, that evolves and changes the further you progress. As soon as I started playing Hob I wanted to know what happened to this place and what was going to happen next.
Visually, it is a work of art.
Exploration and discovery are key roles and none of the inhabitants of this world really tell you where to go or what to do. You get to figure that out for yourself. That's part of the fun and once you get it, the flow of the game really draws you in.
As a game, it is one of few I have played in several years (PC & Consoles) where my excitement to play consistently wasn't driven by some need to do "daily quests" or involve myself in some new weekly "multiplayer modes" just to climb tiers as a progression scheme.
I just enjoyed the game and wanted to see how it ended.
I recently finished the game and was more than happy with my time spent playing it and the price. Torchlight I/II were awesome, Hob was amazing, and I am already looking forward to whatever Runic Games has to offer next.
My only recommendations are:
(1) If you get frustrated, go back to areas you may have overlooked with a fresh eye. Don't rush - and resist the urge to "Google it". You're only cheating yourself from having that "Aha! I got it!" moment that comes from figuring it out for yourself.
(2) A game controller (PS4, using DS4Windows in my case) is really much more fun and natural than a keyboard + mouse. This is my own personal preference, although a game controller is also recommended by the developers. You may enjoy the game just fine without a controller.

At it's time of release, it was a brave entry with its mix of free running and stealth based gameplay. It is immersive, and gives you a real feel of the history and geography of the third crusade. The graphics arent too bad for its age either. One of the main reasons I would play this is the story, as it provides alot of the starting canon for the rest of the franchise. Each assassination feels purposeful, and taking a life has a consequence. Some of the targets I developed a personal anger towards when learning of their deeds, which indicates the strength of the writing.
However, for the good there must be bad. For a start, it runs badly. Freezes throughout loading menus and occasionally in game - often mid combat which is awkward. The investigations required for the assassinations are repetitive, and tend to turn the game a bit grindy when you are performing them. The combat for some reason I just cannot fathom. I appreciate not all blows would be blocked, but the counter system makes little sense in the type of attacks that can be blocked. It boils down to luck - or maybe I am missing something. Late in the game the number of enemies is honestly ridiculous, and when you are surrounded by enemies winning is nigh on impossible. It got to a point on a number of occasions when I rage quit and resolved to watch the remaining cut scenes online. The missions themselves are sometimes hit and miss, I can't tell you the number of times I fell in that damn harbour, I mean, an assassin that can't swim? Really?
For all this however, it probably is worth playing. Just dont expect an odessey, I went out of my way to explore and got less than 20 hours.

A long time ago this is a game I would've recommended to (nearly) everyone because of what it was at its time of release. Unfortunately, this legendary game, which spawned a huge franchise, has not stood the test of time and barely gets a pass from me now. The only reason this game gets a "yes" from me is because it's part of a series which has significantly better titles, and if you're interested in this series at all, I think you have to play the game that started at all. I assume it goes without saying that you should absolutely not buy this game unless it's on a big sale (50% or more).
-----
The great qualities of this game are: Wonderful setting and scenery. I personally think the game still looks quite nice! Some may disagree, but for its time the game was pretty and still looks good now. Another plus is the game's atmosphere and story are very cool. Assassin's Creed, AC2, and a few other titles in the series take a fun creative approach to history and I very much enjoyed the storytelling.
That being said, unfortunately this game has a few major downsides which nearly made me hit "no".
1) There are many issues with this game on current PC's. It took me numerous tries to get the game to not crash during the "animus tutorial" stage. Which brings me to #2...
2) Unskippable cutscenes AND NO SUBTITLES. These are one of my biggest gaming pet peeves and man do I hate them. This game is a big, big time culprit of unskippable cutscenes and MAJORLY hurts the replay value of this game. (You'll notice I only have enough to complete the game and do some collectibles).
3) The movement and gameplay don't feel as smooth as they used to. Perhaps this negative is not as major as the first two negatives. The game still feels alright and the movement is good as well as the combat, but in comparison to the innovations made in AC2 and beyond, this game feels stale and the combat/movement feels slow and jagged. If you've played AC2 and are coming back to play the original, you will be very frustrated with Altair's handling.
5) The assassination setups are cut and dry. At the time of this game's release, the game was so much fun many of us didn't care about the repetitiveness of the information gathering part of the game. Unfortunately, especially since we've seen far better, this really hurts the game's enjoyment if you ask me. You either pickpocket a message, harass a guy, or listen in on a conversation and that's about it for the preparation missions. They're boring and frustrating.
6) And speaking of repetitiveness, the collectibles are really, really boring. There's not really anything interesting about getting all the flags and kiling all the templars. These serve only as timesinks for the completionists.
7) Ubisoft and UPlay, stab me plz with a blunt object.
-----
All things considered, I think you should play this game. It's the first title in a legendary series of games, and was a well put-together game for its time. The story is interesting, the assassinations are fun, and the storytelling is wonderful (not to mention pretty damn good voice acting, which seems to be REALLY lacking in big titles these days).
Just be aware that the game has not stood the test of time as well as some others, and some things will be frustrating.

The long and short of it is that this game plays like a more linear, less interesting, less fluid Assassin's Creed. Despite picking it up on sale for 6 bucks, I still regret the purchase and the time I invested in the game.
-Potentially interesting world and concept
-Soundtrack is good but fairly repetitive
-Every aspect of the game is ridiculously easy. Combat is a piece of cake even on the highest difficulty, and the game completely holds your hand through the parkouring elements (seriously, the whole game feels like a tutorial level).
-English voice acting is pretty bad, and if you decide to use French instead with English subs, you miss out on all the side conversations/chatter that for some reason aren't subtitled.
-Annoyingly buggy. Hitboxes sometimes feel way off, and on multiple occasions I had to reload the game due to falling through the world or part of the area getting stuck when I should have been able to move it with my Spammer.
-Related to above: the game doesn't seem to play nice with controllers. Button prompts would show up with controller buttons half the time and keyboard buttons the other half when I was playing with a controller. Certain moves (targeted S-pressens) I found literally impossible to use with a controller during their tutorial phases and had to switch to keyboard for a short period.
-The story just isn't that appealing, and the characters are very one-dimensional and not terribly believable.
-The game feels riddled with terrible plot holes. For example, in the first chapter of the game you alter someone's memory to believe that their fiance was killed by the people who are targeting you, in an attempt to keep her from killing you. It works, and then... we never hear from her again. Seriously. She somehow never figures out that her fiance is actually still alive.
-Very very linear. It's impossible to even backtrack through levels, with doors immediately and permanently closing behind you as you make your way through corridors. Went the right way but wanted to look for collectibles/powerups? Too bad!
-The game raises interesting moral questions and the protagonist herself seemingly struggles with things she's done... and then it's all ignored as she brazenly continues on the same path without any seeming hesitation or regret aside from the interludes between chapters. It feels very unsatisfying and disconnected.
-Ugly. For a fairly recent game, the look of the game is honestly abysmal save for the character models and interface. This would be forgiveable if gameplay was good, but... yeah.
-The camera is pretty terrible in some parts of the game - strangely, more often in the open than in tight corridors. Not sure what's going on there.
In the end I couldn't even bother to finish the game, stopping about 75% of the way through and watching the rest on youtube while I was cooking. And yeah, the ending is pretty unsatisfying too.
Buy some of the earlier Assassin's Creed games (the most similar to this title without being bad, imo) or really any other action game out there. Unless you're scraping the bottom of the barrel, I wouldn't bother picking this up even on sale. And, not to disparage anyone's taste, but whoever is saying stuff like "great story" or "this game is like a good book" must be pulling from a pretty small sample.

A tremendously good story, well built characters and their developments, albeit a bit contrived. Totally worth it if not for the controls during combat and memory altering: in combat every action seems to be on a delay, and even though you get fair warning before an enemy attacks you if you are in the middle of a punch you can not break the attack to slide down. This style of combat would have worked great in other games, like Dark Souls and Monster Hunter, where these delays force you to take a strategic approach to your enemies. But does not work well against a cluster of enemies, where a Batman's combat style would be more fluid and feel more responsible. About the memory altering scenes, I believe it could have been simpler with a console controller, but moving the mouse in circles to move the memory back and forwards it's not the best way to do it. Had to that the need to pause the scene in an exact moment to interact with the memory and you begin to feel the impossibility of make fine tunes, ending up going back more than you really need just to try and catch that fleeting interaction moment - after you spotted it, which can also be frustrating. These scenes are beautifully scripted and are central to the story, but I feel they just can't be properly explored with the current scheme. I would suggest a two part game: first see the movie and spot the interactions points in the normal sequence (maybe press E when a sound or a shine pop up). Then you are given a list of those points and choose to alter them. When you do so, you go back to that point, see the change happening and the branching of the story, You can then let it play and when you return to the 'change select screen' you can now see your new branch with the new interaction points. I don't know, maybe it's just me. Another bad thing is how close to the character the camera is - you have a beautifully detailed world but you are given only a claustrophobic perspective to look at it. I understand this camera is probably easier to work with in tight spaces, but as with the combat you could have used Batman's camera. And turn off the blur...
The story is nicely done and this game deserves to be played for it.

Slain! is a 2D action platformer, releasing on Steam on March 24th 2016, being developed by Wolf Brew Games. Players will control Bathoyrn, a hero in the gothic world, seeing to liberate seven great towers from 7 deadly overlords.
Gameplay is played from a side view, and you have to hack and slash your way through levels, using heavy attacks, quick attacks or magical spells. A lot of the negative reviews on Steam are pointing out that the game has poor unresponsive controls. Whilst this is true in some points, I feel like it is not as big of an issue that people are making out. Not to mention the developers have already acknowledges the issues and are working on a patch to be released.  The platforming elements in Slain are few and far between, there is a number of jumping puzzles, but none that have you re-doing the stage over and over again because you miss a ledge, each of the jumping puzzles are concluded within a minute or two leaving it a stress-free challenge. I would of liked to have seen a little more in-depth combat mechanics in game, and maybe even some sort of talent tree/unlock system through levelling up to add some additional abilities, but alas.
Visually, Slain is absolutely gorgeous. The pixel graphic style hits all of the right notes and it is easily one of, if not the best pixel style game I have ever seen. The backgrounds of all of the levels are stunning and perfectly hit the mood of the game on the head. The character models of the player and enemies are all very high quality as well. The attack cycles of all of the characters animation are fluid and look amazing to see playout. The graphical department is definitely Slain!’s strongest point.
Slain! is hard, a lot of timing has go into when to strike your enemy, trying to remember attack patterns of your foes will also make the combat easier to overcome too. Thankfully each level has a number of checkpoints evenly spread out across the stage meaning if you do die, you don’t have to replay the whole stage again.
Now, I am not 100% sure whether I have finished the game to be completely honest. I got an ending cut scene, or so it felt like it, with a “To be continued” at the end, but looking at the achievements, I haven’t got any apart from one. I definitely haven’t defeated a giant spider; I haven’t defeated the “Mega Beholder”, Horge, or Lord Vroll. I am not sure how I fight these, and I am not sure how I go about seeing the rest of the content; is it even present in the game? I’m not sure.  For what I have played so far, and if it is the game I have finished, it only took me just under two hours. That for me is a little on the short side. Like I said, this could be a bug, with the game; I am just not sure and would welcome a response from a dev on the point.
Technically, the game is OK. I will mimic the concerns about the controller issues that people are having in that they aren’t hugely responsive at times.  Some sort of tutorial system would be welcome too, rather than being chucked into the game and being expected to know what all of the buttons do right off the bat. Slain also has an issue at points where invisible walls prevented me from progressing through the stage, when it is quite clearly the way I needed to progress - this only happened when I was trying to jump over traps though.  I was happily surprised I could play the game on 4k resolutions though which for me is a nice addition.
Slain is a game that I was extremely hyped over for a number of months. I was disappointed when the game was delayed a few weeks ago, and couldn’t wait to pick it up on launch this past week. Maybe I was a little too hyped for it because I expected a lot from it. In the game’s current state I can simply recommend it for action/platformer fans as it is an interested take on the genre, hopefully the developers can clear up the technical issues and shed some light on the content that I seem to have missed. The price tag of £8,99 may be a bit too high at the moment for only 2 hours’ worth of content, so this is one to watch out for when on sale.

Of all the negative reviews I read before buying this game, they all complained about the same thing: lack of "holding  your hand" with regards to the controls, but this game is guilty of far worse gameplay issues than just failing to provide a breakdown of the controls.
The player character "bathoryn" is exceptionally underwhelming, his attacks feel like a child suffering from muscular dystrophy attempting to punch their way out of a paper bag, larger enemies have entirely unblockable and unavoidable attacks if you get within Bathrobe's attack range and the projectile attacks that Bathrobe is capable of are laughable at best and as such have little strategic useage, the "spirit bomb" or "mana bomb" attack (carried out by holding down and pressing the decapitation button) has a charge delay that feels tediously long.
Ultimately none of the attacks feel smooth or responsive and if we are to believe that Bathrobe is a great hero of old then why does he have all the strength of a dry sponge?
The "you have been slain" that you are presented with should you die, is even more flow breaking as in a game that should feel fluid and fast you will find yourself repeating the basics over and over because every enemy has a very basic routine of "drudge forward and attack" and the only arc in difficulty is that the game throws "more♥♥♥♥♥♥to deal with at the same time." forcing you to attempt to jump/dodge/block while attacking.
Even Boss enemies have a monotonous slew of attacks that after the first 1-2 failures become blatantly obvious and so "dodge-wait-attack-wait-dodge-wait-repeat" becomes the defacto, which would be totally forgivable if Bathrobe felt powerful or fluid, but he just doesn't.
The controls are not nearly as responsive as they should be (with either keyboard or controller), the back-dash is utterly laughable (with almost a full half second delay in initiating, which is more than enough time for most creatures to hit you) and the movement feels very disconnected and a lack of being even remotely fluid causes Bathrobe to feel stiff and peasant like (as opposed to a trained warrior). I'm not even going to go into detail on how underwhelmingly useless the "decapitation" attack is.
Art style? Yeah, it's alright... it's a little unremarkable though, nothing in the game jumped out at me as striking or impressively constructed.
Music? It's run of the mill metal, at times it doesn't even feel like it fits the level design, speaking of...
Level design is exceptionally poor. Run forward, jump over the occassional trap, the platforming elements are tedious and for the pace of the combat the levels are entirely too long.
Ultimately Slain presents itself as a game with "stunning visuals and true old school gameplay" now if by old school gameplay they meant a throwback to the platformers of Spectrum Sinclair and Commodore 64 era with sloppy combat mechanics and terrible flow of design or gameplay then they definitely hit the nail on the head.
This game seems like it was constructed around the concept of "Darksouls YOU DIED! was really funny, hurr, lets make something that immitates that." but has completely failed to realize that responsive combat and a world constructed around death being designed to teach you a lesson rather than as a result of you not spamming the attack button fast enough results in an exceptionally sub-par product.
I cannot recommend this game to anyone and I am entirely doubtful that sufficient changes to the feel of the character movement, level design, combat or over-all pacing will ever take place.
Ultimately, this game is not fun to play.

Ok so I reviewed this game when it first came out, and I really hated it. I heard they re-released it and made some changes, and based on some of my friends' recommendations, I decided to give it another shot. And holy mother of Metal, am I happy I did. This game is great now. They almost fixed every problem I had with it. It doesn't feel like the same game at all. I mean, how does a game go from a 2/10 to a 7 or 8/10 like that? The sound design is a bit better, and the animations are a bit better looking. But the combat. The combat is what sold me. Rather than the huge mess it was at launch, the combat now is actually fun and challenging. The combos are easier to make, the options to deal with enemies are better, and overall, the combat is quite enjoyable now. I can finally bob my head to these awesome riffs without feeling bad about how awful the game is. I am not saying it's the best game of its genre, but it's certainly getting there. Bellow, you will see my original review of when it came out at first. Just to see the difference.
Although I had no problem whatsoever with the controls, I still hated the  game. And here's why:
First, let's talk about what I loved about it. The art style. The graphics. The visuals... That's about it.
There are two reasons I hated it, and a couple of nitpicks. First, the sound design is kinda messed up. Things that should to be loud are not, and things that should not be loud, are really loud. I don't know how to explain it. When you play it, the lack of any grunts from the character or enemies seems really weird in a game like this. And the music is either too loud or not loud enough, depending on what setting you put it on. There is no middle ground. And speaking of the music, it was a big let down. At first, it sounds awesome. But then it gets really repetitive real fast. To make my point easier, pretend that you are listening to a Behemoth song with no vocals and no solos... for like 15 minutes... It isn't as good as you would expect.
The second reason I hated it is the bigger one, which is the combat. Look, for a 2D action game like this, you should either have a 1 or 2 attack style like Castlevania or Rogue Legacy, in which you hit with 1 weapon and 1 move, but you have another attack like throwing knives or something. Or you have the second kind which is fluid combos like Dust: An Elysian Tale or Salt And Sanctuary. You can perform multiple combos with easy to handle timed button presses. This game has neither. Your weapon is too weak and too stiff to use like Castlevania's whip, and your character isn't fast enough to pull it off. And the combo system in the game is just too bad. It needs lightning speed reflexes to pull off a 3 hit combo which isn't even that good. I found that none of my hits give knockback to the enemies. And the fact that you have to be right in front of their pixalated face to be able to hit them means you will be taking a lot of damage as well. The only way I was able to progress without getting much damage is crouching and spamming the hit button, because that attack is the only attack that gives some sort of knockback effect on the enemy... Almost.
Overall, the game is a complete mess, and I was really sad about that. I was so looking forward to it, and it hurts me to see it in such an unplayable mess. I do hope they fix it, but I doubt they will. I'll give it a week... Then I'm gonna refund it if it is still unfinished.

NOTE: This game is NOT a Metroidvania. It is a series of levels and each one is 99% linear.
Slain! looks great, and it looks even better in motion. But that's the only thing any effort was put into. The controls are awkward and the enemy design is worse. Animation/collision bugs cause your combo to drop or your swings to not complete. 75% of the big enemies can have their AI broken by simply ducking and mashing attack. WHAT!
I feel like this game was not rigorously playtested. This is because when I beat the game in about 4 hours (I didn't finish the sewer level, I think that's an after game challenge level?) I was treated to invisible credits and a soft-lock. Really.
If you read the credits (via the menu, since the end-game ones never show up) there is no writer credited. Which makes sense, because the sloppy drivel is rife with grammatical and punctuation errors. Phrases like "BTW" and "THX" are used at certain points. Those lines freaking killed my soul. Was this written on a cell phone? Why would they be so lazy here? It almost seems like an intentional middle finger. The stupid thing is, the story could (and should) be completely removed and it would feel much better. Just like old Castlevania games or whatever. No reasons needed, just do some platforming and fighting cool monsters.
I also want to hate on the music, since every one else likes it for some reason. Yes, it is indeed heavy metal and it does use live guitars. But that's it. It's just a constant chug-chug-chug in the background with no variety or even solos. Remember how Symphony of the Night used rock organs and synths and had Baroque pieces, creepy ambience in the caves, and only brought out the rockin' when s*** got REAL? Yeah, that's why it was so GOOD. I guess it's not fair to compare this against what might be the best VG OST of all time, but WHATEVER man. The music in this game doesn't even loop correctly. Ever. Also, I've been a metalhead since my teens (about 20 years going) so it's not a genre thing. Believe me, I was hyped.
TLDR: Super disappointment. Sorry. Wait for Bloodstained to come out a year or so from now.

If Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is anything other than an enjoyable video game, it's a value proposition. Developers Ninja Theory are no stranger to big budgets; they made Heavenly Sword for Sony, Enslaved: Odyssey to the West for just about every platform, and the most recent Devil May Cry game for Capcom. They know how to spend money, so it's interesting that they've separated from big publishers to develop and publish Hellblade at a $30 price. The end product is mostly good.
In Hellblade, you play as titular Senua, traveling deep into Nordic territory to rescue the soul of your murdered lover. In the vein of what Ninja Theory does best, it's a third person character action game. What makes Hellblade unique is that Senua suffers from hearing disembodied voices and seeing things that don't exist.
A lot of the marketing around the game has to do with the challenge in trying to portray a character with mental illness. Plenty of games have tried and it's almost always a flat portrayal of someone who's zany or unpredictable without a lot of nuance. With the help of consultants in the neurological sciences, Ninja Theory has crafted a tortured, sympathetic character in Senua.
Another aspect of the game that reflects Ninja Theory's experience and skill is in the look of it. It's a beautiful game with some really incredible motion capture, particularly in the faces. They don't look like video game faces; they're expressive and emotional every time you see them. This really helps with connecting to the characters and feeling what they feel.
While they nailed the characters and look of the game, the game parts are kind of lacking. Each level of the game will have you doing one of two things: finding hidden objects in the environment, or fighting. The hidden object stuff is mostly clever, but it's almost always boiled down to aligning objects in the right perspective to find the symbol you're looking for. It doesn't change much from beginning to end.
The combat is also not very robust. There are five enemies, excluding bosses, that you will encounter in small groups. The challenge is to keep them away from your back as they'll try to flank you to attack. With infinite ability to dodge, and most attacks blockable, the only thing that has to be figured out is reading attacks to time blocks (or dodge), and how many whacks it's going to take to kill the enemy. It's fun for a while, but it really wore me down by the end. You've got one weapon, so once you've figured out how to use it, combat loses its shine.

Hob is a fantastic game that combines a number of genres into one.  Puzzles, exploration, item collection, it's all there.  What I liked is the emphasis on the exploration, no matter what direction you took, you always seemed to end up where you where supposed to go, so I never felt lost while moving towards the next objective.  Finding secrets/collectibles was very well implemented.  Some are obvious to find, others a little more obscure and more difficult.  And what I loved was stumbling on a room that a lot of detail went into made specifically just for a health, energy upgrade, etc.  Sound, music, and ambience are all very good.  The art style, aesthetics, character design are top notch.  And of course, the manner of opening new areas/shorcuts is very creative and imaginative, and I was always pleased to watch it unfold.
What I didn't like was the camera.  For the most part, it did it's job, but other times I would find my view stuck behind some object, or the angle itself would make me miss jumps.  The camera is just troublesome.  I've had some performance issues with framerate and vsync.  I ran 60 fps for the majority of the time, with skips in framerate during gameplay, and some areas that suffered framerate drops.  You'll also run into quite a few graphical glitches, bugs that broke immersion for me.  There wasn't a whole lot of variety in enemy types, as you'll see the exact enemies in every part of the game.
Overall, aside from the flaws and glitches/bugs, I had a blast with Hob and enjoyed every minute with it.  I highly recommend it.

TLDR: I went in with stupidly high expectations, and was ultimately disappointed.
Let me start off by saying that the game is not bad. The world is unique and interesting. The artstyle is enough to sell the game on its own. The mechanics are solid, if a bit lackluster. It also runs very well (at least on my machine anyway) with the framerate dipping below 60 only a couple of times. I ran into a few minor bugs, sure, but only one that forced me to restart the game in order to progress. All in all, it wasn't technically bad.
Now with all the nice things I have to say out of the way, I'm about to rip this game apart.
I was looking for a zelda like experience. 6 hours in, I was wondering where the dungeons where at, where where the boss fights? I've picked up a couple upgrades, but I'm still running with just a sword and a robo fist.
There are no dungeons in Hob. There's a couple (maybe 3) underground areas that might be large enough to count as dungeons, but they're all so straightforward that they're just a seriese of obsticals.
Once I got over the initial wow factor of the new areras springing into place, the exploration of the world just swung back and forth between follow the blip on the map, and hunt for the one square centimeter that you haven't stood on yet. Often, the route you're supposed to take is easy to miss, which left me frequently thinking "what do I do? where do I go?". That's bad conveyance.
Combat in this game felt like it was trying to be dark souls, and did not succeed. I feel one of the biggest detriments was the lack of variety of ways to kill enemies. You can slash enemies, and you can punch them, and that's pretty much it. Hob would  benefit greatly from some kind of ranged attack, even if it was extremely limited in use.
Enemies could be classified into two groups: Trivial enemies that where basicly no threat so I'd just ignore them, and Absurd enemies that would kill you in one or two hits (three hits if you have almost all the health upgrades) no matter what you do so I'd avoid them as much as possible. While it certainly didn't help that I'm bad at the combat of this game, I didn't feel encouraged to get better. The best solution was the avoid combat, unless of course an enemy sensor eye stalk was in the room. This is a shame, because I like good combat systems. I like killing monsters. I didn't like killing monsters in Hob.
I thought maybe it was because I was using a controller, maybe that's why the combat felt off. So I switched to mouse and keyboard and discovered CARDINAL SIN NUMBER ONE: you cannot rebind the controlls. There are two presets for mouse and keyboard, and one preset for controller. That's it. This right here is enough for me to condemn even the best game. It's 2017, ALL games should have completely rebindable controlls.
There is only one boss fight in the entire game, and it's at the very end. At this point, I just turned the difficulty down to easy because since I never really practiced the combat during the entirety of the game, I had no hope of actually beating that fight. Also, I just wanted to get to the end already.
On game length, I beat it in about 13 hours, although someone who doesn't suck could probably do it in half that time. While I'm totally fine with short playtimes  in games if I really had fun with it, I can't say that I really had fun with Hob. I finished it wanting more than it could offer. The last 5 hours of play felt like a slog, I was going through the motions without caring anymore why I was doing them. Knowing all the while that I wouldn't find any worthwhile challenge along the way (and then they spring the game's only boss fight on me, but I already went over that).
I would have loved to see what this game would have been if Runic gave it another year before release. I applaud them for doing something different from what they've done in the past, and I'm sad that I didn't like it as I thought I would.

Hob is set on a beautiful and dangerous unknown world, with buzzing life above and the whirr of mysterious machinery below. The more players delve into the world’s design, the more they uncover a planet in peril. Players must learn to survive, understand their true purpose through acquiring skills, and ultimately transform the nature of the world itself. Hob is presented without text or dialogue. Narrative is revealed as players explore and interact with their mysterious planet, and the strange life forms that inhabit it. Hob features smooth controller gameplay, multi-layered puzzles, and striking visuals.
Hob is the newest and most ambitious project of Runic Games, a developer made famous by the popular Torchlight franchise.
Moving away from the previous style of Diablo clone games Runic Games delivers Hob. Hob is the name given to a tool used to cut/manipulate gears. This word perfectly defines the main character as you roam through this beautiful world. Hob's world is a machine, and throughout the game, you must master puzzles and dungeons to rearrange the world to what you need it to be. This is a fantastic concept that makes the world seem like a living character on its own. Hob is not a game that will please everyone although I'm sure Hob will please the fans of a good Indie game filled with puzzles and some very subjective story telling.
Unlike the overwhelming majority of games, Hob's plot is transmitted subjectively and artistically. The path is pointed (literally) by the faithful squire of the protagonist and there is also a map to assist the player if he gets lost. Other than this you are on your own. There is no tutorial, which I find refreshing. Runic must feel the player is smart enough not to have their hand held during the opening areas of the game. I respect that. The overall story can be as deep or as light as you want it to be. There are optional rooms to unlock in game that give you a visual clue as to how the world became what it was, but doesn’t tell it to you like other games do. Now I quite enjoyed this as I explored the world more freely than I would have if there was a linear story or even waypoints put in front of me (give me a dot on a map and I will follow it). However, I can see this having the opposite effect on some players. They could become confused by the slow and very subjective storytelling, and find it difficult to progress through the game.  The game features well thought out puzzles that will require a bit of thinking. Despite the degree of complexity, the gameplay and the puzzles are intuitive and should not cause a headache for most players. Hob also has some satisfying RPG elements. There are a lot of collectibles scattered throughout the world. From sword fragments to improve the character's attack to Heart pieces to upgrade your overall health (Link to the Past anyone???) I must say, I fell in love with this game as soon as I saw the art work and E3 trailers earlier this year. The game world is beautiful and the use of colour is executed perfectly. The main world areas above ground are colorful, vibrant and seem full of life, but when you delve into the dungeons there is a distinct change in tone making each area feel ancient and abandoned. The music in the game is perfect with each area/dungeon having its own unique soundtrack.  Hob is a game that is fun and full of life (even if it is a little Zelda-esqe). I highly recommend this game to everyone. It looks and sounds beautiful; the puzzles and combat are satisfying and the dungeons are challenging and different enough not to come across as boring or repetitive.
I played Hob through Steam on launch day and I have held off on my review as there were initially some ‘bugs’ I encountered. There was an issue with GTX graphics cards that would make the game crash at launch and I also encountered a lot of dropped frames but after a few very quick updates the game now runs smooth as butter.
Hob is available now on Playstation 4, Steam, GOG and Humble Bundle

Millie is a blast to play, for the first couple of hours and if you need some time without having to think. It's a kind of remake on a large scale of the well-known snake-games, where you have to eat your way through labyrint-like levels of increasing difficulty and complexity. While Millie eats her heart out, she grows longer and longer, and so there is an ever-increasing chance of eating ... your own tail. Happily, there are several means provided to make life a bit easier: there are clocks to rewind the time, hammers to smash through walls and even scissors ... to cut a bit off your own tail. Ouch.
By going through tons of levels, one can obtain stars (needed to buy the extra items), and shoes. With these shoes, one unlocks new levels. Quite simple, well-tried, and still effective. Graphics are nice and colourful, sounds are pretty good - I love the sound of Millie eating ;-).
But it takes hours and hours to really progress through the levels, as some are really very difficult, and only the most stubborn will reach the end of it I suppose. I got bored after a couple of hours, but my daughter isn't yet ;-). The game has full controller support, which is nice, but the controls seems to be rather sluggish and get some time to get used too. All in all, a good game to kill some hours, but nothing more than that.

Longelivety: 14/20 (no multiplayer, but more levels than you'd probably ever swallow)
Technical: 7/10 (some points deducted for the controller sluggishness)
Personal appreciation: 5/10
Overall: 67/100

Do you know the game snake? Well that's what Millie is. Remember the anger you feel when you bite your own butt in snake? That's ALL that Millie is.
Now in general I'm decent at snake, I'm not one of those hyper good pros who can snake against themselves multiple times, But you'd think at least the first couple of levels in Millie (maybe 1-30) would be simple and not require you to be some kind of predictive expert at snake. WRONG! At level FOUR you're easily stuck if you're bad at planning your next move and it doesn't get any easier from there.
What makes this even harder than snake? Well you can't even see the entire map for one so you're literally on the other side of the map munching along and then, wait, what's that? The other end of your body... Then you walk right into it because you couldn't even see how big you were getting.
While this game is cute and has some weird... you're going to pilot school plot... It's not for those who are not experts at snake. It's frustrating and just not fun. It'd be different if they made the collectables (shoes) the main think you need skill to get, while they require a little extra effort, you still need to be extremly good at snake to even beat the level with the minimum amount of dots required to open the level exit.
Overall a very frustrating experience. There should be levels of difficulty such that your body doesn't grow as much if you choose medium or easy. This game is dropped for me which is sad since I do enjoy snake games and this was cute and fun the first 3 levels. I would not reccomend this game to anyone unless you play snake like a boss.

Story and characters are superb. Everything about Senua's world is perfectly crafted, from the voice acting, to the visuals, to the audio. The gameplay is nicely paced out and gives you some down time after intense sections, which is well needed as it fully lives up to the psychological horror potential of games that so many other games fail at.
On the negative side of things, the combat could get frustrating at times because the dodge button is a fickle mistress. Towards the end, they start throwing multiple enemies at you at once and the combat can really only handle two at one. Interestingly, combat difficulty has an "auto" mode which adjusts the difficulty as you play. I'd say it worked pretty well as whenever I felt myself getting frustrated with the combat, it only took another try or two to push past it. I really like the concept of a game's difficulty adjusting on the fly as it'll keep skilled players pushing to improve with progressively more difficult challenges while scaling back to avoid completely blocking a player's progress. All without the player even noticing, so it keeps the game feeling rewarding.
Puzzles rely almost entirely on perspective puzzles, aka find the place to stand in a certain spot and look towards a specific object. It's not especially difficult to solve these, but I found them kind of satisfying. If you're looking for something to puzzle your puzzler until your puzzler is sore, then you probably won't find them very satisfying. They do exactly what they're supposed to do, which is give you something to do during the slower sections of the game while building on the psychosis aspect of Senua's character.
Overall, I'd say even though the gameplay itself isn't amazing, everything else about this game more than makes up for it. This is easily one of my favorite games.

Wolfenstien the new order is among my favourite games of all time for its immersive world, well written story and characters but most importantly its balls to the wall Gunplay that sets it apart from every other FPS. The same applies to Wolfenstien 2 but I will explain the differences in the following paragraphs (without going into spoilers)
Starting with a minor to some but really appreciated part of the game for me and that is how it immerses the player in its enviroments. Some of the enviroments (often in the first 2/3 of the game) are incredibly well detailed and as a Games Design student I know how hard it is to make something look as good and realistic as this.
The game ran really smooth on my GTX 1060 on ultra settings which I find impressive when it looks this good and with the chaotic gameplay.
The story is just as good if not more well done than the first game with some much needed character development for BJ and a well handled introduction of a new cast which was pleasent to see when I have games like Halo 5 try to do the same thing but ♥♥♥♥ it up. This is because the cast is both very distinct and likeable with their own motivations and personalitys that are very colourful such as Spesh, Horton and Set to name a few. Unfortunatley I must mention that the game was among the best I played in 2017, the ending was really adbrupt and not satisfying only making me wanting more. That is why I insentivise you to wait till the price drops or get it on a sale Like I did.
The gameplay is where the game shines just as much as good looking enviroments and gun models. The Gameplay is perhaps improved in every way from the first game with upgradeable weapons to your choosing, duel weilding whatever combonation of weapons you want and badass abilitys such as charging through breakable walls and of course Nazis. If you like Doom (2016) then your also going to love this with its brutal executions that are made to feel very good and well paced with the gameplay. As a result this also makes the stealth in this game an oxymoron as you chop a guys legs off while no one seems to see the incredible amount of blood everywhere or the screams of their comrades. I dont think this is a bad thing at all as while stealth is an option and a good one for initally approacing combat, it clearly isnt the focus of the game when the main character wouldnt be out of place in Gears of war.
In conclusion Wolfenstien 2 is Almost as good as the first game. If you can get this on a sale and you long for singleplayer FPS games with a good storys then Wolfenstien 2 is definitley worth your time.
Update: Wolfenstien 2 is defintley not worth full price, it is an enjoyable shooter which what I found to have a good story but the new order is definitley a superior game.
Get it. If looking at all the information on it really interests you, get the game. You won't be disappointed.

I first played this game in 2010 and at first I thought it was amazing, however now after 7 years I have some different opinions about the game. Lets start with the good points about the game:
1. The story - The story line in assassins creed has to be one of the best in videogame histroy as the franchise has been successful from the debut in 2007 all the way to present day. If you pay attention to the dialogue you will find a griping story that continues across the other games.
2. The combat - The game has a very easy combat system to use with a veriaty of methods to kill your enemies, sometimes the counters are a little laggy but if your timing and reactions are good then you will have a fun time cutting down your enemies.
3. The graphics - The graphics in comparison to newer games are awful but for a game released in 2007 the graphics are quite good and work on a veriaty of systems without any type of glitchs or lag.
Now lets look at the bad parts of assassins creed:
1. The sounds - In general the sounds are great quality and have no problems but there is one sound I really dont like and thats the poor women that ask for "just a few coins" you seem to hear it nearly everywhere in the city at somepoint and it can drive you insane!
2. Climbing - Unlike newer assassins creed titles the climbing in this game is very slow and sluggish. sometimes altiar just stands aimlessly on a wall whilst you mash your keys trying to make him move. If you think that when enemies are chasing you that you will just climb to get away forget it! It is nearly impossible to climb away from the guards.
3. Guards - The guards can make the game fun at times but mostly they just get in the way, for example when you are doing a stealth mission such as assassination missions the guards will make it very hard for you to complete this type of mission.
4. Saving citizens - The game offers a little but not compulsory side quest where you save citizens from guards attacking them, this is very fun and you need to do it to achieve 100% sync in the game. The problem I have with this is that once you have killed all the guards the person you saved takes ages to finish talking (the things they say are the same for each type of character you save and irrelevent) and then after that the camera locks on to the people who will block guards for you (these people are unlocked over the city as you save more people) when you just want to climb away before more annoying guards arrive to attack you.
OVERVIEW:
In general I recommend assassins creed to anyone who is looking at buying it as it has to be one of my personal favourite games and is part of one of my favourite game franchises! The Bad points list does have more points than the good points list but if you read what I had to say then you will notice that the things in the bad points list are minor little things that are no issue to most people and all the things that make a game good are found in the good points list. It took me about 18 hours in total to complete the game with 100% synch and I enjoyed it as much as I did the first time I played it. So yes do buy this game!

Oh man, there's so much to tell about this game that I'll probably spend hours writing this review.
The game is pretty old already, so it won't you cost a lot of money. This is the first game of the Assassin's Creed series.
Graphics:
The graphics are pretty decent for the time the game was released. I played the game with everything set to highest. The landscape views (especially outside town) are a bit blurry (maybe on purpose).
Sounds:
Well I went back to Windows XP to play this game because the NPC's didn't have sound in Windows 7. But I can imagine that the developers did not expect people to play this game in Windows 7 because Windows 7 did not exist at the time of the release of the game.
During exploration of the game the music changes depending on the activities that happen. You have combat music, sounds of slicing weapons, people screaming when they discover dead bodies.
I also liked NPC's commenting on my failed attempts to climb buildings, falling and hurting myself and such.
Gameplay:
I'm very impressed with the gameplay. The game plays very smooth. It looks like they tackled all the bugs and it feels pretty natural to play. A controller is unfortunately not supported so I played with keyboard and mouse.
The most challenging for me were the battles. Best way to do battle is to defend and wait for the right timing to attack. This is also what is taught in the tutorial.
Sometimes the fights takes place in tight corners, which is more challenging than usual.
I liked doing both the main and side quests. I really love how they took care of these quests.
The game made me feel like a real Assassin. I could use stealth to accomplish a lot of my missions.
Bugs:
The game only crashed once during my entire game experience.
Economy:
I noticed a lot of beggers in the game asked for coins. I wouldn't mind giving them some coins if I had any. I did hear that the next game (Assassin's Creed II) would have coins.
Savepoints:
The game saves automatically after each mission.
History:
I think this game is a good approach to mix gaming and history. I never liked history in school, but while playing the game I discover and learn a lot about the past. Of course what has been written in the books is not always true, right?
Improvements:
I could not run in the Animus room, which was a bit frustrating.
The fields between cities were a bit useless to me. I could just use my horse to outrun all the soldiers on foot.
I did not collect all the flags. There were too many.
Also at the beginning I was not sure what to do with the Templars? Actually I'm still not sure...
Q Would you buy the next game in the series?
A Definately

"But millipedes can't fly", I can already hear you scoff. "Nonsense", Millie declares, the anthropomorphic arthropod protagonist of the maze navigating puzzle game of the same name. She's a girl full of dreams, which makes it rather a dreadful shame that my hopes for Millie were all but completely dashed in the end, leaving me sad and wondering what went wrong.
The developers describe Millie as a puzzle game, but it's easier to think of it as Snake meets Pac-Man. Running through mazes your goal is to devour a set number of pellets and make it back to start without running into your bum, which grows longer with each pellet you eat, creating a train of legs which follow your pattern and threaten to cut off your path if you don't plan in advance. As a huge fan of both the games it takes inspiration from this sounded fantastic, but Millie screws up in a handful of ways which managed to all but completely destroy the experience for me.
A bigger issue than anything, controlling Millie is an absolute nightmare. She's clunky to turn at the best of times, but more often than not fails to turn at all or does so too early, almost always forcing you to restart a level as you find yourself trapped in a maze of yourself. Adding onto this frustration is the deliberately inflated difficulty of limited power ups (most notably the one that lets you rewind time briefly to undo your mistakes), which I can only imagine are a carryover from a mobile F2P model given the inclusion of an in game store (though everything is purchasable with stars you earn from playing the game). It doesn't seem like it would be an issue at first, but despite the kid friendly aesthetic Millie is an astonishingly challenging game. I found myself having to meticulously plan my every move just to be able to finish levels, which requires a level of memorization and precision that felt far above what should be expected from this sort of game.
I had high (perhaps admittedly too high) hopes for what Millie could be, but after only a little more than an hour I couldn't take anymore of it. The unnecessarily high difficulty, pour balance of power ups, and astonishingly bad controls sucked away whatever fun could have been, which not even the extremely cute art direction could hope to salvage. I can only speculate at how much content the entirety of Millie contains, not having the stamina to finish it myself, but for all the levels it contains  and the appendages of its lead, Millie doesn't have a leg to stand on.
