This is more a mixed review than a negative one.
The gameplay is basically Snake, but in Pac-Man-styled levels. Navigate mazes filled with corridors, collect all the pellets, and reach the exit, all without running into your own body, which elongates as you eat pellets. Familiar with Rattlesnake from Windows Entertainment Pack, which I recall had easier levels, I wanted to see how this compared.
It was fun for me in the beginning, but this was because the levels started out small enough that you could see the entire playing field on screen at once. By the time you access world 2 of 3, they become so big that even the zoom button won't show you the whole thing. This is important, because as you progress the levels become trickier, with more bottlenecks that you have to identify and clear early before emptying the rest of the stage. So, there's an increasingly heavy trial-and-error aspect that I don't really like. In addition, Millie's body becomes so long in these larger levels that, in order to eat those last few pellets you're missing, you have to take the long way around the whole area multiple times, just to avoid running into yourself. I've gone from taking 1 or 2 minutes to clear a stage, to taking multiple 5-minute attempts to clear just one, and I'm not even halfway done with the game as of this writing.
The zoom button pauses gameplay, and because the default camera is often zoomed in too close to anticipate bottlenecks and such, you'll have to zoom out constantly to make sure you aren't going down the wrong path. Not only does this make the pacing tedious, it suggests the developers wanted to enforce a memory aspect, which again is something I don't really like.
There are powerups, like hammers that break cracked walls and sirens that let you go both ways on one-way streets. I was hoping these would add variety to the levels, since there are nearly 100 of them, but they never seemed to make enough of a difference in the gameplay. They activate instantly upon pickup and last less than 30 seconds, so you have to know where to use them first, but again, since the levels become so large, you often have to make a preliminary attempt just to discover all the noteworthy areas. I feel the levels become challenging less by creative use of different mechanics, and more by increasing level size and number of bottleneck areas.
If the premise interests you, and the above points don't bother you, go ahead and give it a try. Otherwise, be warned that it becomes much more difficult than the mood of its trailer suggests.

I CANNOT recommend to buy this game at its current state.
Why? I wanted a fun, tactical teamwork-based shooter with a high replayability (as it was advertised). Well it's kinda fun, but also mediocre and very quickly repetitive grind-fest with bugs and poor design-choices. Which is sad, because it really has a lot of potential.
So what is wrong about it? First, the game is pretty much dead. It isn't completly empty, but there is basically just one server with more than 4 people playing. PVP is non-existing.
At least this one server has usually around 20 people playing, but since it's co-op you don't really notice it much (because of all the bots running around).
Second, it lags a lot. This game got MASSIVE desynching problems, making it often completely unplayable. You run for cover or trying to shoot the enemy...desynch...and then you find yourself dead. It's just frustrating.
The dev says "the netcode is very sensitive for ping fluctuations", so basically if you are not at NASA headquarters, you are screwed.
Now to the gameplay itself.
In the first few hours, it's really fun. You run around shooting enemy soldiers, figuring out the weapons and trying to do a bit of crazy teamwork. Which mostly fails miserably, but it's still very fun to blow up♥♥♥♥♥♥together. :D
However after you played for a few hours, you have seen it all and the game just becomes repetitive and tedious. Basically all you do is grinding through endlessly respawning enemies while trying to capture positions on the map. Nothing really strategic is going on there and it's really just not fun to be stuck at some positions for an hour before you can move on to the next.
Then the controls, they are alright but also buggy.
To prone does often not work, so you push the button a few times. Usually you are killed by then already. You want to climb a ladder and you're usually getting pushed back for no reason until you manage to get up. The non-rotatable view and that everything is so small doesn't help either.
Also running and throwing a grenade doesn't work, you have to stand still. The AI however somehow is able to do that.
Vehicles are another point. The controls are VERY choppy, it's just not fun to steer them. Shooting stuff with the tank together however is really fun :D
Although the fun doesn't last long usually, because the enemy is quick to blow it up. Using them from the distance only helps a little, but due to the short very view range it's not always an option.
So far they seem to be more a fun gimmick, as they aren't really game changing tactical elements, due to the massive amound of enemy respawns.
Boats are pretty much useless and rarely ever used it seems, except for safely grinding enemies.
Which brings me to team-work. Man this game could be so awesome about this. You quickly gather a few people, hop onto a boat or jeep, drive around and flank the enemy, opening a second front. Or you call in an airstrike, clearing the path for your team to storm the base.
In theory this sounds great, but since so few people are actually playing this game, there isn't much tactical stuff going on actually. Everyone just rushes to the front trying to shoot as many enemies as possible, that's it. And since the enemy respawns so quickly, airstrikes don't really do much difference to a match.
I imagine if there would be actually PVP, this would be much different. Sadly there is none.
Spawning. Oh man, do I hate this. You re-spawn at certain points or at the spawn truck, which is a cool idea but it isn't really well though out. The spawn truck only works when there are no enemies nearby. And too often the enemies rush your position (because they spawn so numerous) or some idiot drives the spawn truck into the enemy base.. -___-
Then you get spawned somewhere else, which is close if you are lucky, or across the other side of the map so you have to run for a LONGGGG time.
The maps, some are really cool but some are just badly designed, especially the last map. It just takes foreeeeever to walk around and advance. Generally you will spend a lot of tim running around.
Then the point I hate the most. The RP's (resource points?), it's like an ingame currency that allows you to buy weapons etc. and order airstrikes, reinforcements or such.
This is just such a bad design choice, it really breaks the game on so many levels. You gain RP's by destroying enemy buildings or special vehicles, or spotting them and by objectives (I think moving into a zone). So if you don't play rushing through the map and you want to play more support / stealth / tactical style, you don't gain any.
Furthermore you lose RP's every time you are killed, and since you are killed often, your RP's are quickly gone. I literally killed hundreds of enemies, have ranked up quite fast and are still running around with zero RP's.
I never got so far to actually be able to buy "the cool stuff", or call in heavier things like a tank or artillery. When I am so good at killing enemies and I am not rewarded for it, that just makes me feel bad.
So yeah, hopefully the promised patch in June will fix all these things, because this game could be really awesome. I also hope some new vehicles and game mechanics come in, and the tactical elements to be reworked.
If not, then don't waste your money. Right now it feels more like a beta with only a few people actually playing it. $5 or maybe $8 is ok if you like to pay for a few hours of fun grinding, but 15 is too much.
I kinda regret giving my money for it. I should have gone eating ice-cream with a nice girl instead, at least I would have some nice memories from that.

What if you'd mix bioshock's aesthetics, zelda's adventuring/fighting and metroid's exploration together in a final synthesis of the 3 genres ? You get HOB!
The world itself is very abstract and teaches you how to go through your own inquisite nature and icons on the worldmap.
There's almost no hand holding. It's a bit confusing at first but after encountering world events corresponding to the itels you find, you get the grasp. Go to your work bench and see what "this full meter" does to your sword,  and how about these mysterious butterflies ? are these for crafting abilities ?
In the scenes you'll encounter power up stations, mysterious traps and corruption that you have to do away with in various ways. What's that ridable tripod that gives stuff power ?
In this game, you find out things by doing and it's sometimes frustrating but just when you're about to get stuck, you discover a new drop or ladder, path or action you have to take that will make you discover the world further. The game doesn't feel linear though, becuase you're mostly poking holes in the corners where you explored and go ever further on the scenario. This is a wonderous adveture to figure out.
Sometimes you'll access a passage and a dungeon which will make sense of the progress when you come out of its tail or top end.
So because there's almost no hand holding I call it "pragmatism simulator, the game."
When you are in dungeons you'll unexpectedly find new things you never thought you'd need before, and this is it's very mch like a metroid game, that with every ability found/upgrade, world layer raised or corruption removed, there's an other layer of exploration you can do in the same place. Hob's cuteness mystery and danger comes together into one of the most enjoyable games of this year,
Hob is the pragmatic "sherlock holmes" of action adventure games, while it adds a little hint of "pocket tomb raider/metroid" into the gameplay mix. You find out about the story pure by playing and deduction, nothing else!
This game is gorgeous, the world is absorbing, the puzzles are fun, and it's a genuine joy to fix the world and change the geography. Highly recommended.

Wonderful game, generally recommended. It can be completed in a couple of hours, but I had major fun throughout it all.

The puzzles are on the easier side I think, and much of the game is fairly linear in that it always pulls you to the next objective you have to solve. There were no place in the game where I got "stuck" and had to think about what to do next. This is both good and bad. Good, because progress is always being made. Bad because puzzles are then fairly easy. If you like hard puzzles, this is not a game for you. If, on the other hand, you want to chill on a couch, this is an excellent game.
There are some combat in the game. But it is built on learning what the opponent is doing and adapting to this, more than it requires fast reaction skills. I found the combat fair, and not too punishing. You will soon have a health bar which can cope and opponents drop extra health as you defeat them in order to help you going further.
When I was overwhelmed by countless 3A titles this linear puzzle solving adventure game became a temporary but decent resting place.

First and foremost, be warned: If you're using a GTX 10-Series GPU, and/or are on Windows 10 (the issue hasn't been fully narrowed down as of writing) there is a pretty high likelyhood that you'll encounter severe dips and stuttering throughout Hob. The only solution so far is to get on the Windows Insider program and update to the Fall Creators Update. This fixed a lot of stuttering for me, but there were still times where my framerate was halved on a GTX 1080.
Hob is a good game, but I was having a hard time deciding and started out this review with the intention of not recommending it for the combination of performance issues, and gameplay issues I have. Visual design is great in Hob, I love the Borderlands esque art style, and the world and characters are fully realized. I do have a minor gripe that they have some missteps particularly at the end of the game with the lack of voice acting, but my main criticism lies in the gameplay.
The core of my issues with Hob's gameplay is due to the camera. You have no camera controls, as it's always locked and determined based on your position in the world. This works very well when you're rebuilding the world and have long shots of entire land chunks coming into scene which is really cool, but in gameplay it feels clunky. It's hard to judge where you're going to jump, so whenever you're doing precision platforming you're at risk of falling to your death. Not to mention for some reason you're stuck with Castlevania jump dedication, meaning as soon as you hit the jump button you're locked in. You get no manueverability whatsoever, which really clashes with the decision to have a locked camera. And considering you'll be doing a lot of jumping, this becomes a major issue. I died multiple times or had to restart puzzles more than once because I wasn't able to judge which direction I needed to point the left stick upon jumping. The camera also obscures your view in multiple areas, but this wasn't nearly as much of an issue.
I really want to recommend Hob and I do if you aren't at risk of performance issues, and know that you won't be frustrated by dying due to camera confusion. I was able to really get into the Hob for the last 3 or so hours of gameplay, but before that it was more of a grind to figure out performance issues and fight against the camera, which was really unfortunate. The game definitely had a lot more potential than was realized. I definitely think the unique ‘world building’ concepts they have in Hob are worth experiencing, but maybe wait for a price drop and make sure it’ll run well for you.

[ [ Scroll to the bottom of this review for a list of positives and negatives and the conclusion ] ]
No Man's Sky was a game that, leading up to it's release date, generated a great amount of hype. Right from the very first trailer, the game presented a world where you could make your own adventure. Where you could fly from planet to planet, all unique, and face challenges and mysteries as you made your way towards the centre of the galaxy. In each trailer, they presented a unique planet with unique wildlife and unique events occuring around the player.
To say the least, when the game released, a lot of us were disapointed.
You see, besides technical issues like poor performance and so on, there was very little present in the game that made it enjoyable. All those cool scenarios that we had been dreaming of based off of what we had seen before simply didn't happen. No freighter battles alongside wingmen in which you chase down pirates to the surface of a planet. No encounters with rhino-like creatures charging through the trees at a heard of other animals. Nothing ever really happened. To add insult to injury, the variation within the game wasn't as impressive as we all thought it would be. There were simply too few models for the engine to work with and too many planets to spread them across.
The game became a joke. Hello Games became perceived as liars and scam artists. However, 3 months later, an update released.
Then another.
And now another.
Where do we stand now? Well, things actually ♥♥♥♥ing happen.
Now I'm zipping across the galaxy, discovering what the "Atlas" is, what species I belong to in the game and their origin, the history of the Gek First Spawn, where the sentinals come from, where the weird growths you find within abandoned buildings came from, and the very nature of the universe itself.
Altogether, we now have:
+ A 30+ hour long story that expands upon all of the tidbits of lore previously in the game and answers pretty much ever question I previously had and that I have yet to complete
+ A (somewhat basic) multiplayer system, which is to be developed futher in future
+ Missions
+ Greatly improved graphics
+ Base building
+ Freighters that we can purchase and build inside of
+ A trading system
+ MUCH better combat
+ The ability to actually fly into the ground
HOWEVER, it is still worth noting that:
- The game still has pretty horrible performance.
- The procedural generation system still doesn't generate enough "unique" planets, flora and fauna.
- The game still is NOT worth the price it's charged at. It needs reducing.
To conclude, should you get No Man's Sky? At this point, only if it's on sale and you have great interest in the game or it's genre. If you already own it? Play it, damn it. Most of my positivity in this review is due to the fact that I don't feel like I've been scammed anymore. That I've almost got the game I wanted, that Hello Games have redeemed themselves, and that I have recieved enough enjoyment out of it thusfar to justify the price I paid. But overall, it still isn't quite there, so once again, only purchase it if you really want it.

The gameplay and story is great, but what its limitations due to being a Vita game and a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥port makes me not want to recommend it. But first I'll list the good stuff and rant the bad stuff after that.
The combat is good, it is not god-tier Platinum melee combat but is enjoyable. You have three different attacks that target 3 kinds of clothing (Shirts, pants and hats) and you need to beat the enemies clothes out of them in order for them to melt in the sun or run away in shame.
The weirdness only adds to this game, you can do ridiculous things like beat people with a kebab (my favorite weapon) and things impossible to achieve in real life, like buying Hyperdimension Neptunia t-shirts. It is a fun game that doesn't take it seriously.
The location is also good, seeing giant posters of Neptune everywhere is always good, it is set on Akihabara, a real location in Japan, although I don't know how far the fidelity to the real world counterpart goes, it is great to take a look around and see what a developed country looks like, also the fact that random people can assault you on the streets at any time gives it some familiarity to my own home country (I wish I had permit to carry assault kebabs). The game also give you real-world scanned panflets from stores that actually exist, now you might see it as cheesy advertisement, but as someone starting to learn japanese this is great.
Now for the bad stuff that makes me not want to recommend it.
The port is a mess, to start, there is no way to configure video options while in game, you have to constantly quit and open the game until you find the settings that most appeal to you, this makes the game feel more like it is being emulated than is actually meant to be played on a PC.
There is no true 1080p resolution, if you choose it the game virtually scale the 720p resolution, making everything look worse than it is, also nothing in the interface is meant to be seen on a big screen (clearly made for a Vita), so everything in the menus and buttons explode pixels everywhere, making again everything look worse than it is.
The game is also locked at 30fps, you can search unorthodox ways to make it 60fps but it will probably break a lot of stuff. I have no major problems with 30fps games, but adding it to the upscaled resolution makes me ill, I can't play sessions longer than 1 hour or else my head starts hurting.
Which wouldn't be a problem if I could play it windowed, you "can" play it windowed but it will make the rest of your screen go black, and if you try to alt tab it is likely to crash (what is the point of windowed option then?), that means you can't reposition the game window to where you want.
These were port issues, now the Vita limitations, as I said the interface was designed for a mobile device (as it resembles a mobile phone), so everything is giant, exploded resolution and in your face, like someone is rubbing the menu in your face. Now something related to the game that annoys the crap out of me is the high quantity of loading screens, areas are too small (again, due to being a Vita game), and sometimes you have to transverse 3 or 4 areas to arrive at your destination, that means at least 3 loadings. If you think Postal 2 has a problem with loading screens, look at this game, it will make Postal 2 feel seamless.
So yeah, while I love the game I can't recommend this port, it has been abandoned over a year now and it is not likely to get any updates, the developer also gave up on porting the sequel to PC (♥♥♥♥ you too) probably because then can't be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to make a proper port, specially since there are other somewhat similar (beat the clothes out) japanese hack & slash games that function properly on PC, like Senran Kagura and even Hyperdimension Neptunia Action U, the later being even a Vita port, but actually playable.
One of the best games I have played. I would recommend using the Japanese voice acting.

I was both satisfied and proud as
which he showed throughout the game. Seeing him always sane and composed is refreshing to me because I, in contrast, am a highly emotional trainwreck.

I "sort of" recommend this game. There should really be a neutral buttom, because 2017, this game is a bit "meh".
See, when I first played assassin's creed, way back when it was first released, I was blown away by how beautiful the game was, and how awesome it was to be able to freerun. My entire first playthrough was just me being mesmerized by how awesome it was to be able to move more or less how you want to. But as I went to replay this game a second time, a year after my first playthrough, it was a lot less appealing. Now, many years later, I replay this game here on steam, and I can look at the game with a fresh set of eyes.
Playing assassin's game the first time is sort of like having a summer fling on a festival or concert when you're in your early teens. You're blown away by how good they look, and how much in common you have, and how awesome and open they are. But they're really only good for that summer fling, beause the whole infatuation is shallow and lacks content. That's what assassin's creed is to me. It still looks good after all these years... But behind the polished surface, there isn't a whole lot to be attracted yo. There's tons of bugs in spite of all time that has gone by, and the controls is clunky and unwieldy. You are still asked at time to do things which will be hard not because it's hard, but because you can't really make the controls do what you want them to. Did you enter a ladder at a weirld camera angle? Now W on your keyboard doesn't make the main character go up, but instead down. Did you run too close to a bench while being pursued by guards? Now your character will sit on it instead of keep running. Did you enter combat? Now your character will draw his sword, even if you would prefer another weapon and had a different weapon drawn.
These are just loose examples. Assassin's Creed is packed with these issues. Sometimes, carrying out certain missions is not a delight, but a chore, because you are aware that while you can come up with a good plan for how to perform the mission, the most likely reason you will fail it, is because of a bug. Not because of game difficulty or something similar, but because there are still issues with the game and when the game is sporting an ancient save system, it means replaying large contents of the game over and over.
Well on to other things.
The main character is both believeable and unfortunatley a bit boring. As an assassin, taking lives every other day, you can imagine that someone must become hard on the inside to cope with the problems. It takes a certain type of person to do those things, and even if you're not bent on murder in particular, that sort of life will likely bend your mind to a single purpose - the cause. So Altair is not a deep person, he doesn't seem to have a background which would be interesting to explore, and he doesn't have any meaningful personal relationships either. He sort of just... Goes through life, assassinating people, because that's who he is. And that's great. It's believable to me. But it's also boring. I never felt that I got to know Altair, I don't really know who he is outside of his knife stabbing personna. And that is a bit of a shame. Ubisoft does a better job with later iterations of assassin's creed and its characters.
The story is forgettable. There's a story twist, but you can spot it coming long long before it's "revealed" to the character. There's not a whole lot of side missions beside the main story, and for being a free roam game... There's not much to roam in. I mean, the maps are huge but... There's just you, the main story and some side missions to help you succeed with the main story, and ten million billion collectibles. Alright, not that many. But still, Ubisoft sure tried to fluff replayability of the game by having a lot of flags one can collect.
In either case, since the game is now pretty cheap, I do recommend it. But I advise seeing it as a prequel to the story about Ezio Auditore, which is the protagonist in the next three games (assassin's creed 2, assassin's creed: brotherhood, and assassin's creed: revelations), rather than a game of its own.

Personal Rating: 5.5 of 10
One of the most solid and stable Assassin's Creed game (up till III) in terms of performance. Its really cool to be jumping around roof tops doing parkour and killing people with awesome animation. It is also very unique and smart on how the game incorporates modern technologies into a game set in the medieval time.
Although the settings are really nice, the game don't really feel immensive. Example, rooftops and buildings are repetitive so you actually stop paying attention to them and refer to the minimap to get to your location. Combat is okay as they try to design it to be realistic as possible when taking several enemies at the same time but can be slow. The NPCs are there to make the city feels alive but that is it. They are like zombies wandering around.
Missions are repetitive. I actually reinstalled this game three times before progressing half-way or so because every mission does not have much room for exploitation for an assassin game. Even if your presence is made known before killing your target, it simply means you are going to have a tougher time getting away and each mission feels more like a puzzle than an assasination mission. Also, based on my understanding, assassination are suppose to be done discreetly and probably when there are less people as possible like night time maybe?
Again, side missions are simply there for the sake of existing. Meaning once the game is completed, side missions are fitted in to the game with minimal effort like collectibles, races, deliveries and etcs. The rewards are not that great to start with nor even the stories that comes with the side missions.
Weapons and skills are unlocked progressively but it is not that great. I can't even make out the difference between a sword and wrist blade except that killing people with the blade is really stylish and cool.
Cities are huge but you need to make several travels between them as the areas are unlocked progressively so yeah visiting the same place over and over again is kind of boring too.
Story is quite interesting however do note that the game is not historical accurate. Some references and event timeline may be correct but that is all. I think the progress of the story is alright considering the time it is set in but it is too draggy for me. Not much plot but if they can change the pace of the story and put in more plots it could be really interesting.
I think Assassin's Creed is an alright game if sword fights, stealth/puzzle, parkour, conspiracy and assassination in the medieval time is your thing, but don't expect something really hardcore here.

The storyline itself borrows elements of Ghost in the Shell, The Matrix, and Equilibrium while the game play itself is a blend of a brawler and ocassionally a third-person shooter (When using the junk spammer weapon). Certain enemies require specific tactics and can be a challenge. I found the ones who teleport some of the hardest.

What makes the game worth it for me more than anything else is the story really, followed by beautiful graphics and stunning music. This sort of review system is very important to me, and if it something that draws you as well, meaning that you can overlook technical problems. There are a lot of great ideas that could have been executed a lot better. The levels are a little too linear. The combat system at its core is fairly interesting, I personally found it easy to figure out and use which was a nice change from the usual headache when I start a game, but can get repetetive at times. Boss fights and more advance enemies offers some more interesting aspects of the combat system.
Along with the combat system, you get to jump around, remix memories and do some minor puzzles. The ability to not skip cutscenes the second time a round is frustrating, especially since you can go back to previous episodes to find the collectibles you missed. The camera angels can get a little strange at times and hard to follow, the momvement of the protag is for the most part fine, except for certain bits where it makes wider sweeps and has you fall off a platform. The game isn't long, took me about 10 hours on "normal" difficulty the first time, whether this is a bonus or flaw is up to you.
The atmosphere and the music, combined with a good level of lore and information on sociological issues that surrond the game, along with beautiful graphics, is what makes the story draw you in, and by far the biggest strength of the game.On a personal note, it was incredibley refreshing to have a biracial female protagonist whose mose significant relationship in the game is friendship, something that's considered a bold move, and something I genuiniely appreciate.
Overall, if you're the type of player who doesn't care much about the story, with music coming in second too, while foremost looking for an diverse fighting system, clean and polished movement and an open world type of game, the game doesn't pay off. If you get very invested in stories, care a lot about the atmosphere and music, and aren't bothered by linear levels and want a combat system that's interesting, but wont give you a headace, then I'd say its well worth it. Note, I bought the game while on sale, don't remember exactly how much but I'd say it was easily half the price. I'd recommend also waiting for it to go on sale, makes the buy feel more worth it.

Remember Me is visually pretty, has good to excellent voice acting, tells an engaging story and the memory remixing is interesting. These things pretty much save the game, as the mechanically the game is pretty mediocre bordering on tedious.
There is one way and one way only through most of the environments and the movement mechanics often help to shatter the illusion of choice: while you can climb like a limber monkey and leap like a flying squirrel during the designated parkour sections, even a stair case railing or a small box becomes an insurmountable obstacle outside of them. Plenty of invisible walls further help to make the player feel penned in.
Worse yet, the game absolutely adores taking control away from the player through frequent unskippable cut scenes (in-engine and pre-rendered). Save points seem to get placed before cutscenes a lot, so if you save and exit you may watch it twice. The camera works fine most of the time, but it too sometimes gets locked into position for no apparent reason. The game also does a lot of explaining mid-combat, ripping you right out of the action in the process.
The combat system is passable, though it gets very repetitive very quickly. New enemy types rarely require new tactics outside of boss fights. The latter culminate in a (to me) tedious quick time event which, if you fail, means repeating the last few steps of the fight to get back to the QTE until you succeed.
Interesting mechanics, alright story and unlikeable characters.

So if you are getting frustrated in a fight with 2-3 enemies and it seams impossible to beat them... it's because you're not using proper combo.
I can't stress how important it is to get 3 x combo changed very often... from health to cooldown.
Forget 6x or 8x in combat... (here and there on lonely enemy you can do them, or if other enemies are far away)
But basis of your fight should be 3 x combo, quick cooldown for that super powers and health boost when you need it.
That being said... game is f***** awesome!

This game is gooooood. I totally recommend it. It continues what made the previous 2 Wolfenstein's great, while keeping the same gameplay. It's still very unique and much better than CoD and mediocre Destiny, while having the single player story that makes EA's and Activision's lackluster single player outtings just all the more terrible.
The biggest (among ONLY a few) downside to me were the bosses. There just wasn't as many unexpected and "unique the first time" boss fights like A New Order and Old Blood had, and Old Blood was just a $20 bucks expansion. The other is the ending of the game. It does complete the story of The New Colossus itself in my opinion, everything that it shows from the beginning to the end. BJ's past, Anya, the resistance, etc. But it does leave more to be desired. But this is because the developers have stated they planned this series' story as a trilogy in an interview prior to this game's release. Regardless, it doesn't feel as complete as the first game does. First game developed the world and fiction a good amount and concluded that story satisfactorily, but gave plenty of room for a new story, or shall I say a new facet to the reboots' story. I still say buy this and play it though. It's a great shooter with a great fiction...with no microtransactions. It absolutley blows CoD: WW2 and Destiny out of the park because of ALL those facets.
As for PC running, in my experience with a 1070, Ryzen 1700, and a 144 htz G-Sync monitor, it ran great. For cutscenes screen tearing was an issue, like the faces were the sad recipients of the tearing the most lol (common for Free Sync and G-Sync monitors apparantly running over 100 hertz), but wasn't that bothersome to me. It didn't jar me enough to try and remedy it, which there are ways listed in guides, but milage will very. For how short the cutscenes are that extra time of work and reading just wasn't worth remedying it personally. It wasn't atrocious screen tearing and audio didn't desync or anything. The game itself though ran great and didn't crash.

I love how the game doesn't hand you things on a silver platter.  There is no tutorial that explains every single move and function in the game.  It gives you a hint or suggestion and the player is left to figure it out on their own.  The controls are pretty basic as is so it's not a problem, and it's fun when you figure out a new move.  I hit this button + this button and tada  you guys figured one out.

So if anyone out there wants a good old school feeling 2d side scrolling platform/hack and slash game definitely pick this one up.

Pretty cool game
Things I like:
- Graphics are metal - I really love the look of this game.  The art for the environment and enemies is all top-notch imo.  At times the grunginess of it all can make traps, etc hard to see, but overall - beautifully done!
- OST is metal and adds a lot to the experience (albeit a bit repetitive in the guitar riff dept)  There are times where I feel the music is marred by the distortion.  Mainly because I'm not a fan of the tone - it's a bit dry and high on treble.  It overpowers the rest of the music.  Just my opinion, either way, well done and it certainly fits!
- I love the overall theme.  Feels like it was ripped from a death or black metal album.
Things IMO that could improve with patching, etc:
- SFX are weak!  This game could really use some decent SFX - they're not terrible atm, but I would've loved to have just stopped in the middle of a level and bask in the ambience of evil winds blowing through the trees, far-off screaming, or when you hit something, you really hear it, which brings me to the next point...
- JUICE.  For a game where everything is in your face, when I hit or kill something, I want to FEEL it.  A little screenshake and more meaty SFX for hits and kills would go a long way in improving the experience.
- Enemies either get knocked back or stay put and chop when you hit them.  I don't see any consistant pattern, so it's a bit difficult to be strategic with some encounters.  Hit timing, knock-back, etc could be tightened up some more.
Overall, at this time, I would recommend it to fans of sidecsrolling action games who are looking to scratch that nolstalgia itch with something new.  I hope the developers take some of the player feedback and implement any suggestions they find worthy.  If they do, then the game would be definitely be better for it!

Hob is a beautiful game that instantly drew me in. It's polished and feels like a finished game (which cannot be said of all games these days).
I would recommend it to anyone who likes beautiful puzzle platformers with a bit of action and set in a unique world (so, most people?)
It reminded me of Journey, mixed with The Neverhood (or Armikrog), mixed with some of the charm and je ne sais quoi of old-school games such as Rayman, Jak and Daxter, or Crash Bandicoot; but with updated graphics and modern game design principles applied. That is of course coming from someone with a PS / PC background - someone coming from a Nintendo background would no doubt compare it to Zelda games or Super Mario 64.
I got from it a feeling I haven't felt from a game in a long time, it's a feeling I can't quite describe, but something akin to nostalgia mixed with innocent curiosity and fun - like I had the opportunity to be a child playing a favourite PS2 game during school break for the first time again.
This game will never be my favourite game. It doesn't quite stand up to the design and polish of Ori and The Blind Forest, the uniqueness of Journey, the puzzles and plot of The Talos Principle, or the combat of... well, most games with combat. But I loved it, so much. And I am so very glad I bought it and spent the time playing, which was about 13 hours for me, but it felt like 20 (in a good way). It was relaxing and interesting and beautiful and fun. It is, simply put, a good game.

Great game, good balance between solving puzzles and a focused linear experience.

The combat is a little weird for my tastes, doesnt feel responsive or "snappy" its a little "loose" if that makes any sense, that feeling also extends to other game mechanics like some of the plataforming parts, and other parts where the game feels a little buggy like getting stuck on some geometry or spazing out between some bushes.
I question the choice of camera perspective a little bit, doesnt seem ideal for this type of game, althought they clearly took measures to minimize the problems caused by it (jumps correct the angles if youre a bit off, and you can only fall off ledges if youre sprinting).
A lot could've been done to improve the world map, its already been said but theres no indication of dungeon entrances, I had to look at a map someone made.
Just be prepared to face some sort of glitch (hopefuly you won't, there are't too many), personally I was hit by an enemy while collecting a butterfly, the thing then became un-interactive but I didn't get it, makeing it impossible for me to 100% the game, since im missing 1 butterfly even though I uncovered all the map.
Those problems didn't prevent me to have a blast playing Hob though; watching the world assmble piece by piece and then exploring those places, or the new places formed by a part you previously explored and the new part is great fun.
I would say of you want a zelda-like experience pick this one up, even if its not 'a link to the past', its still an excelent game with a GREAT value (its 20$ but it really feels like a 30$ game).

I have not yet finished Hob, but I have played about 8 hours at this point, and I feel very compelled to review it. I don't post a lot of Steam reviews, but for a gem like this I feel like I want everyone to know about it. It's SUCH a crowded year in gaming in 2017, and I fear amazing smaller games like Hob are going to get completely overlooked. But I'm considering putting this in my top five this year, and I've played nearly everything across handhelds, PC and consoles. It's just that good.
Hob is being described by many as something like the old top-down Zeldas. But it's much more complex in its RPG elements and combat, and perhaps a little less complex in its puzzle solving and dungeon-ing. Yes, it's linear, but I like that I'm constantly being pulled along and discovering new areas. There are plenty of little hidden upgrades and things for those who want to go the extra mile figuring out how to get to every little area.
What initially sold me on Hob was its beautiful, colorful art style. But the gameplay is keeping me thinking about this game even when there are much bigger titles out there like Shadow of War out right now. I just love Hob.
Two things it could use: More story elements. And fewer bugs -- I've encountered a few 'stuck' moments that required me to reload the game. Hopefully those will get patched out soon, but they are no reason not to play the game because it has frequent save points that automatically save when you walk past them.

Brilliant execution. I loved the amount of research and effort the devs put in to representing the experiences of real people with mentall illness (specifically voice-hearing and psychosis). They did a great job condensing those expierneces into a story about a Pict warrior woman undergoing the trauma of loss as she continues to deal with the darkness she fights.
I loved this game. Horror hack-n-slash with puzzle elements, and great catharsis, while not leaving the player feeling that her victory somehow fixed her psychosis - it is a constant in her life, and it played a role in both complicating her journey as well as framing her success.
Make sure to watch the "Hellblade Feature" afterwards - it discusses the story and efforts of the devs to make this game a real representation of a character with mentall illness.
Regardless of the measure of their success in accurately presenting it, they without a doubt put more care and effort into respecting and validating the experiences of those plagued daily by these experiences. Ninja Theory also included a URL to go read more about psychosis and mentall illness.
Can't recommend this game enough. Take the plunge, and don't walk away.

The game is a beautiful work of art, really. I applaud the narrative and the fact that I genuinely cared for Senua and wanted to see her story finished. It's a lovely story despite all of the surface horror and its message is deeply human, which is why I think there are so many positive reviews. Now, that said:
What I would say to you is ignore the lackadasical reviews blindly saying "work of art" with a couple of hours in the gameplay. If you look at the trophies, 1/3 of the players actually finish this game. And herein is the major problem with a game called "Hellblade": the combat is utterly terrible. It's simple and somehow fails. You will be backed into corners for repetitive fights where you can't tell WHY your character can't dodge; you'll just die. You'll mindlessly hit F to stun an enemy and left click/right click so often it becomes second nature.
Worst of all, in my playthrough, I ran into three serious bugs involving combat. The first time, I ended combat but could not do anything or advance as my sword was still drawn. I restarted, and the game luckily saved my progress. The second time this happened, it did not save, and I had to redo a massive section of the game. The third time I saw a bug in combat, the enemies literally would not stop coming. I stayed in combat for 35 minutes as they endlessly spawned before I realized "this doesn't seem right". A reboot, and that fight was over in 5 minutes.
I want to give this a positive review, I do. It's a beautiful game and the payoff and the end will stick with me a long, long time. It pains me not to give it a positive reivew because the combat is so terrible I had to walk away at some points absolutely furious at the gameplay. As such, the emotional payoff of the game was diminised.
If you don't think that will bother you, enjoy a really beautiful game. If you actually plan on finishing this, the last couple of hours might leave you so incredibly frustrated that the payoff at the end may not negate the damage that's done. It didn't for me. And that greatly frustrates me.

... You know, when I first bought this game, I went in with expectations of hating because it was pandering to fans of a big-name YouTuber looking to make a quick buck. Ten minutes in, I was surprised to find myself actually enjoying it.
The game itself is relatively simple, in both gameplay and plot. Pewdiepie's fans have been kidnapped by Barrels, and now he has to team up with his friends (Marzia, Markiplier, CinnamonToastKen, and so forth) to get them back. The game is mostly a platformer, jump on enemies to beat them, grab coins for upgrades, get special weapons and all that jazz. Sometimes, there are levels where you have to survive a horde of enemies until escape arrives, and a few shoot 'em up levels in the sky, so there's at least variety. The voice acting is pretty standard (I mean, it's not awful, but given the personalities behind said voices, it could be better), and the game itself is full of in-jokes fans of these YouTubers will greatly enjoy.
I'm not praising this game as a god among titans, especially as an indie title, but it's a fun little game I used to pass the time. It has its moments, and can be genuinely entertaining at times. My final verdict is a 7/10, a game I would recommend to fans of these Let's Players and as a fun platformer for kicks.

I followed the development of this game for years, but when it was finally released last year, I didn't have a gaming PC to play it, and thank god for that! I watched as many bought the game and streamed it online. At first it was mesmerizing. Then it became redundant and rather dull. It seemed it became a race for all streamers to make it to the center of the galaxy, because they had nothing better to do. There were many features that were promised by the game's developer that simply were not there. And the total lack of communication . . . yadda yadda . . . there's no point in continuing down this thread; it's all been covered by many before me, so let's jump to the present:
The game has been updated three times since launch, and each update brings a missing piece to the No Man's Sky puzzle. I have a gaming PC now and I bought the game during the launch of 1.3, and I don't regret it at all! I have almost 21 hours of gameplay in, and it's been spectacular.
At the heart of NMS is a survival game, so Permadeath mode makes the game incredibly challenging and engaging. Minor accomplishments that go unnoticed in the Normal (day one launch) mode feel like massive achievements, e.g. just finding your ship.
The mining aspect of the game is plentiful, but in Permadeath mode it's not mindless and boring but a challenge. You want to mine. You need Units so you can afford to build a good base purely for survival and future growth in the game.
There are mission givers now. This alone adds hours upon hours of game play in Permadeath mode. (Should note that these things exist in other modes but are less engaging because of the lack of mortal danger.)
And with the threat of dying and losing your saved game, you will feel the need to avoid conflict and move about more peacefully, which I think is kind of an objective of the game's developer.
Also, there's now some version of multiplayer, which was really important to me. Multiplayer is going to eventually open up a really interesting dilemma for players when they cross paths in Permadeath. I have a feeling interactions will work more like our real world interactions and less like GTA V (kill, kill, kill).
All in all, this game is shaping up quite nicely and if you're interested in the above mentioned things, I would definitely get the game. I'll also note that I mainly recommend the game for people who are not afraid of Permadeath. Without the constant fear of dying, this game is actually pretty easy and a bit boring.

Disclaimer: I have not encountered any bugs in my 40 hours of playing Update 1.3, I did, however, start a new save.
I've had No Man's Sky since day one. Last time I played the game was 2 months after launch. I did come back after Pathfinder, but never made it off the planet and quit. I've put in about 40 hours into my current save since Update 1.3. I see a lot of threads about how the game is not worth $60, how it is little content to justify the asking price, some even saying it's not even worth with the 60% discount it had a week ago. These claims are absurd from my point of view, here is why:
Story: More than 30 hours of new story has added to the game. The Atlas path has been revamped and tells a mysterious story which I won't spoil here.  I'm still in what I would describe as the early parts of the story and it has me intrigued far more than it ever did in 1.0. I'm enjoying it and looking forward to uncovering more of the mystery. Think the origins of the universe and what it means to be alive. I will leave it at that.
You also have monoliths and ruins spread out across the galaxy. These tell the history and background of whatever race inhabits that system. It's a great source of lore and it informs the player of the history of this universe they are in. These monoliths give you an understanding of that race's culture and customs. It gives the universe a lived in feel. Some of the races are distrustful of one another, some are sworn to help the Traveller (you) whenever possible.
Then you have the bases. You get to recruit people to help you build your base. They are not just some random npc's with no personality. These people have back stories and their own quests. They give you schematics and things you need to improve your base but at the same time, you get to know a bit more about each of them and how they are coping with the demands and expectations of their race and culture. They also give you more insight about their race. You end up caring for them.
Gameplay: Gameplay has also been improved upon. You have ship classes for explorers, traders, and fighters. You can choose whatever ship class fits your play-style or buy yourself a freighter and store your favourite ships on it. Scanning fauna and flora grants higher payouts when you install the appropriate upgrades, making exploration not only fun but also rewarding and lucrative. Upgrades can be acquired in many ways; some can even be bought, cutting down on the rng we had back in 1.0. Combat has also been revamped making more fun and challenging. Combat has never been the focus of No Man's Sky but it is a welcome improvement.
We now have quests that can be acquired aboard space stations. These range from explorer, combat or delivery missions, something for everyone. They give you units or specific items, as well as reputation for faction specific quests. Planet generation is vastly improved. Planets now have more varied biomes thanks to improved high resolution textures and foliage. It's fun to actually spend time on a planet and find something new, instead of seeing all you will ever see with the first few minutes of landing. More flora has been added as well allowing for absolutely beautiful garden worlds. The creature generation has also been improved and a lot of the creature bugs that were seen in 1.0 are non-existent.
The bad: Like every game No Man's Sky has it's own set of issues. Performance has decreased with the 1.3 update. This I believe is tied to the high resolution textures and should be optimized soon. AMD owners have had the most issues with texture bugs and the like. Some Nvidia users are reporting less than stellar performance as well, but far less than those with AMD hardware. Some quest bugs have been reported as well, some which I contribute to people not reading the quest and ending up stranded with no warp-cell to leave the starting system and having to farm to get the necessary component to build one. It is advised to start with a fresh save if you are a returning player. In my 40 hours with the update I have not experienced any bugs.
Is No Man's Sky worth it? Definitely. Update 1.3: Atlas Rising has raised the game to a whole new level. It is the game that should have launched a year ago. Hello Games have worked tirelessly to improve the game and it shows. They should be applauded for that. No Man's Sky os not just a game, it's an experience. It really satisfies the explorer in me. As a kid I always dreamt of living on the Enterprise D, travelling the galaxy, now I finally can.
No Man's Sky launch ver. 1.0 = 5/10
No Man's Sky Update 1.3 = 8/10

First of all, let me tell you guys why this game is a hidden gem!
This game supports cross-platform functionality so you can transfer your progress from or to Android/iOS/Windows Phone/Windows Store/Steam. Also, it means that every other people you see in the game are either playing from Steam/Android/iOS/Windows Phone/Windows Store. All mixed up into this game. Consider it as a melting pot of all major known platforms. What? How cool is that!
This game has been around for two years and it's still growing strong. It has a huge community of players still playing this game. Those millions of players can't be wrong. They still enjoy this game and this is one of the strong points of this game: The sheer numbers of users playing it simultaneously from all different kinds of OS & devices.
Give this game a chance, play it for a while, then you'll see the beauty of it. Collect resources, join allies, raid other castles, build structures and wait for it to complete while you do other things, even outside the game. Just enjoy the progress. Embrace yourselves to the game and let it absorbs you. Get away from reality and ascend to your throne.
For those of you who are afraid of Pay to Win scheme, well, let me tell you: It's not the case! In fact, you don't need to spend anything and still be competing very strong, if you know how to play it right. You see, it's about the priority. Which one you need first, a huge resources so you can build and expand quick or strong army so you can raid other castles and take their resources. I personally prefer the aggressive style :)
There are many interesting events that, to be honest, keeps me getting back to this game. The coolest event now is the Atlantis, where the map gets flooded with water, drowning everything on it, slowly.
One thing I'd like to highlight is the progress transfer functionality. You can transfer your progress from any kinds of platforms mentioned above to any kinds of platforms mentioned above. I found this to be useful for instance, I've made a good progress of this game on PC and suddenly need to take a couple of days trip with no access to PC, I can easily transfer the progress to my Android Phone and keep playing on the go.
The nature of this game is progress. Big or small, progress is still progress. Play it anywhere you like, jumping from platforms to platforms, one OS to another OS, and keep the progress going.
Now if you'll excuse me, I'll be going back to the game now and crush my enemies that threatened my clan.

I bought this game for PS3, Vita, PS4, and now PC.  Needless to say it's one of my all time favorite games.  Vampires are weak to sunlight.  Vampires are wearing clothes.  Obviously we need to undress them.

I wouldn't blame anyone for thinking, "this has got to be really, really bad."  At best, the title, "Undead & Undressed," might conjure up memories of campy B movies from the 1980s mashed into an anime.  At worst, this
be something so lewd as to have no reedeeming value.  But I must remind everyone of the ol' adage, "do not judge a book by its cover."  Or in this case, "do not judge a video game by its title."
Appreciating Akiba's Trip, first and foremost, requires the player to not take it too seriously.  In fact, the plot's overall premise is entirely silly.  The protagonist is an otaku (anime obssessed nerd) who predictably gets the raw end over a shady promise for rare and expensive swag.  Certainly not much of a textbook hero.  The badguys?  Energy vampires who want to drain people of their willpower to get through a regular day.  Oh horrors!
Leave your stakes and crosses at home, folks.  Battles are fought to strip an adversary of their clothes, thus exposing them to the sun, which evaporates said adversarial vampires into smoke.  And if stripping your adversaries to defeat them isn't silly enough, a sweatband on the head is enough clothing to ward off photonic fatalities.
Clothes have hit points that must be depleted before being ripped away.  You don't have to go at it totally unarmed, either.  There is a variety of "weapons" to use – posters and toys, gloves, wooden swords, and even laptops and flat screen monitors (hope you got the extended "accidental damage" warranty!
).  And did I mention this is equal opportunity stripping?  In the few hours I've played before writing this review, there were just as many vampire men as women.  Besides, the action is a bit too fast to spend it oogling your adversaries' physical appeal.  Defend yourself or lose your own polyester!
Really – this is a game that doesn't take itself at all seriously.  And to get the most enjoyment out of it, neither should you.
Other features of note:
The setting is a sandbox version of Akibahara (a section of Tokyo), supposedly faithfully recreated from real life Akihabara of 2012-2013.  As with any sandbox game, you can travel freely and utilize fast travel.  There are main story missions and a variety of side missions to do.  Unlike most sandbox games, this game world is split into several hubs where you must load the next area upon crossing a boundary rather than scrolling smoothly from area to area.  That can get slightly disorientating, but it's really not too bad.  Loading times are acceptable.
The plot is told through visual-novel style cut scenes where you get to choose
to react to various situations.  Sometimes, its not what you say, but rather
you say it that is important.
you react to various encounters will impact how other NPCs will come to regard you and influence the game's ending.  You can be polite, sarcastic, or downright antisocial.
In my opinion, definitely recommended.

Play Hob if you like adventure games told purely via visual storytelling where there's no dialogue (that can be understood at least), where you're put in a world of ancient machinery. Has a lot of similarities in feel to Legend of Zelda, Ico, and Hyperlight Drifter. If you love turning cranks, inserting power cubes, stone doors opening, discovering collectibles in little nooks of the map, and also some light combat to round it out, PLAY THIS.
I love games where you can seamlessly explore and unlock an entire world. There are loading screens for exterior to interior transitions, but in the main world map you're never stopped to wait for a loading bar to finish.
There are indicators for where you should go next, but none of it hits you in the face unless you've opened the map. Even the menus have no language in them (except for essentials like settings, and tutorial prompts). The delight of exploration, and uncovering new areas is sooooo much fun!
I ran into framerate issues here and there, but the game was so much fun to play, I didn't care. Occasionally the camera angle made platforming difficult (especially deciding which way to point the thumbstick when hanging from edges), but again not a dealbreaker. If the thought of framerate drops makes you want to gouge your eyes out, this might not be for you, but I think you'll be missing out.

As a pen & paper enthusiast I though I could utilize this tool to make up character images for the PCs I've created and played. Yes, ePic basically can do it, but basically is too much of a compliment in this context, and ePic doesn't deserve it. After all ePic isn't doing very well. Don't get me wrong, the templates are well designed, but that's pretty much everything positive I can say about it.
The downsides are:
- Barely any content in the free version, everything to create a proper character must be bought as a DLC.
- Character templates cannot be altered in any way, save for the clothes. You cannot change color of hair and eyes, pick another hair cut, or even alter the facial features. You get a stiff 2D doll to dress, with a small amount of clothes you can choose from, that's it.
- The stance is always the same, within one DLC each body is identical and only the faces slightly differ.
- If you've ever seen one character from ePic, you've seen them all.
Again, the artists have created quite beatiful templates, and the idea of this program is promising. But as it is (and I don't expect anything to change about it), with the lack of options to create a UNIQUE character that is actually yours, it's neither worth your time nor your money. Trust me, I'm an engineer.

This is a terrific program for easy to create characters for avatars for roleplaying games. I have been using it to create them for my fellow players.

I've been using ePic to make PC avatars and tokens for table-top RPGs and management software (MapTools). It's simple to use and you can create images quickly. The downsides are the (humanoid) models can be samey, as they all have the same pose and build; they look like they're from a 2000s-era videogame. But the big downside is that there is a very limited choice of clothing and items for male models - the female models seem to have double those for the men - and items which are unisex - like Hellraiser cenobite chains bursting through chests and angelic wings - are only available for one gender. If you want to create a full-colour avatar for a game quickly, and you can't draw (like me), ePic does the job, and it's faster and less fiddly than using HeroMachine. But there's a distinct lack of variety. For the money being ask for, ePic is good enough.

I hate to have to leave a negative review for this game, it had so much potential. The last thing I want is to discourage the developers, because their heart was in the right place here, it just didn't work this time.
First and foremost, the controls are beyond clunky, and not in a charming Castlevania 1-3 way, where it's an art to adjust to the slow pace and deadly jump mechanics. but this is more like you're never sure if what you're trying to do is actually going to happen when you press the button. It just makes the game really frustrating to play, especially when you get lucky and make a lot of progress only to have the unresponsiveness and poor hit detection fail you at the worst time, and then have to start all over again. Also, it's kind of strange to be thrown into the game and have no idea what the controls are. I understand it's a relatively simple game, and I appreciate being spared an annoying unnecessary tutorial, but at least an option to view the controls in the options menu would have been nice. For example, there is text early in the game telling you to block projectiles...but no mention as to how to do so. If you're going to break the fourth wall by giving the player text instructions on the screen, you might as well go all the way and tell them how to do it, otherwise it's pointless. Of course I WANT to block the projectiles, I don't need to be told that. I only found out by accident about 20 minutes later that crouching is apparently a block, at least I think so. I managed to block about 50% of the projectiles by crouching. Also, when you go to quit the game, the character jumps upon selecting Quit from the pause menu. Not a big deal, doesn't take away from the experience, but just seems like another weird control thing that makes the game seem rushed and unfinished.
In addition to the control issues, I felt like the overall gameplay was very one-dimensional. You have 2 melee attacks, but the longer attack seems completely useless. There is nearly a full second pause after the attack ends where you are left vulnerable. No matter how I tried to use it, or how quickly I backdashed away from the enemy after, the...I guess we'll call it the red attack, led to me taking damage 100% of the time, and doesn't seem to do any more damage to the enemy than the basic attack. Or at least, not enough to justify taking damage yourself in exchange every time you use it. The level design was also kind of generic and unexciting. Not visually so, but the layout was predictable and didn't keep me interested, mostly just a direct line from left to right, jumping a few gaps along the way. The monsters were fine, decent enough variety early on, but without much audible feedback when fighting them, they also got tired quickly.
On that note, the sound is another major issue. The music is ok, but a bit more repetitive than expected, which gets old very quickly when you're stuck trying to trudge through one area for a long period of time hearing the same 2 power chords chugging for 15 minutes. As for the sound effects, they are barely there at all. By default, both music and sfx are set to 10 volume. After a few minutes, I turned the music down to 9, then 8, then 7, and kept turning my speaker volume up just to be able to hear the sound fx at all, but they are rather bland and generic sounding, which is a buzzkill. Sound is a big deal in a game like this. You want that big violent explosion of sound every time you kill something. Not to keep comparing to Castlevania, but in Symphony of the Night for example, every one of the 100+ monsters in that game had a unique death sound that was percussive with some burning noises and occasionally some howling/screaming that matched up perfectly with the dying animation...it makes the kills incredibly satisfying, and pulls you into the world. SotN wouldn't be nearly as legendary without the incredible sound design. Not that I held this to the same standard, obviously a very different situation, but in Slain, the only thing you hear is some soft clinking metal sounds and whooshing. It really cheapens the whole experience.
In spite of the poor gameplay and sound, I do have to say the game looks amazing. This is some of the best pixel art I've seen in recent memory. Everything about the game is visually beautiful, and before playing it, I thought even if the game wasn't stellar, it would be a pleasure to play just for the visuals, but unfortunately that wasn't the case. I wish I could have enjoyed more of the scenery, but after about an hour, I'd had enough.
I appreciate the effort that went into this, and I can tell what the intent of the game was, but it has too many problems to be enjoyable in this state. It just feels incomplete. If I had played this as an early access title, I could give a pass to a lot of these problems while the bugs are still being worked out, but it was sold as a complete game, and it really could have used a little more time in the oven.

I'm kind of torn about this game, regarding my recommendation. On one hand this game has a beautiful scenery and fun gameplay but on the other hand it was hella buggy for me, to the point it made me mad. I played the entire game with the controller.
CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS.
A few examples for bugs I encountered:
1. In the first 30 Minutes of the game, after you leave the starting area and the two doors get opened by the robot dude, you're able to go back into that area without going back through the doors. This causes the game to keep the doors closed and without the fist you're not able to make the ladder appear to leave the area.
This got me stuck for like 20 minutes because I just couldn't figure out how to open those doors, of course it was a bug because those doors should have been open the entire time, you just need to to the right and trigger the opening scene before heading down or else you're basically screwed and have to begin a new game.
2. Enemies suddenly went invisible after they killed me, this was especially annoying with the big guys who have a wide area attack, at one point I couldn't pass an area because I kept getting killed by the invisible enemy. The only solution to that was restarting the game entirely. This happened quite a few times actually and it was gamebreaking.
3. Enemies disappeared in walls, this made it impossible to trigger scenes, like situations where you have to defeat all the enemies in order to make a ladder appear or anything alike. The only solution to that was getting into a teleporter and then teleporting back to the area again, sometimes I had to restart the game too. Pretty time consuming.
4. When starting the game with the launcher, the game got stuck at the first logo sometimes, to the point I had to go back to the login screen to avoid having to restart my PC because it was totally frozen. I avoided this by starting the game without a launcher.
5. Killing certain enemies in some way, I don't know how, causes their death sounds to be played in a loop, for example the guy that throws the exploding blue thingies at you. It was kind of funny though so I wouldn't really want that one to be patched out, it also fades away once you're gone from the area where the enemy is in.
The jumping in this game is incredibly annoying, mostly because I personally dislike the idea of linear jumping, from the beginning it didn't feel "right" to me. I'd have preffered to have air control in a game like this and I still think it would have been better after finishing it. Sometimes it just didn't really register your direction input right and you ended up jumping somewhere you didn't want to jump, especially into an abyss or on the top of thorns and once you're on the top of thorns, you're screwed because you can't jump for some reason and you'll die.
The enemies are a bit too easy in my opinion, I played the game on very hard and once you got all the patterns down they're really not that hard to beat, it's just a 1 2 3 pattern each time and easy to avoid by rolling. The only difficulty comes up when the game just spams enemies at you but that doesn't really have to do with difficulty but more with mashing your button and teleporting around the area.
Blocking is so goddamn useless in this game, I maybe used the shield like 3 times and it was really unreliable each time, so I always preferred rolling or teleporting over blocking. The upgrade that gives you energy orbs with blocking is pretty nice but that also brought up the question why energy orbs weren't just a normal part of the game? They were pretty useful but I only got to use it in the last fight, where it pretty much saved me.
The story is really confusing to me unfortunately, to be honest I still have no idea what is going on there or what happened, who the roboter guy is, who the burning lady at the end is, who that silent girl is that you can kill at the end.
What happened when you chose to reach out for the hand of the burning lady? I mean the  game just ended and I got an achievement saying something but I was only baffled and was like "what the fu*k?". Those lore rooms didn't help me either, it were just some shapes that moved on a wall so I started ignoring those rooms entirely and stopped looking for "swordkey" parts.
Then there are these "vantage points" where you can sit down or lean on a wall and look at the scenery I guess? I just thought they were kind of unnecessary because I was admiring the whole landscape the entire time anyway, I love floating islands and stuff like that so the game got to me anyway.
Ok, of course the game also has positive aspects, as I already said the scenery is beautiful and I love the whole art style of the game, which is heavily based on shapes.
The music was really nice too, harmonized well with the surroundings and everything.
But yeah I couldn't get the bad taste out my mouth from all the stuff I mentioned before.
Still I would recommend this game because after they released some patches it already started to run better and I got it quite early after release.

Runic Games, creators of the Torchlight series, are back on the market with Hob, a puzzle/combat-light game with a few RPG elements thrown in. The beautiful visuals and stunning soundtrack don’t make up for some clunky gameplay and a story that may fail to engage players. A team brave enough to change completely genre moving away from a golden goose like Torchlight in order to create a little gem of level design and exploration. A puzzle game full of mysteries and wonder. Runic Games take you on a wondrous mysterious journey through fantastic environments making Hob well worth your time.
In terms of gameplay, Hob feels like a close cousin to
. A pretty good action-adventure, with a fantastic world eager to be explored with satisfying puzzles and fun. The creature design in this game is so fantastic. The combat system is a little bit too simple, but the experience is really positive. Hob never loses momentum as you dive deeper and deeper into the game. It constantly rewards you by making the game easy to consume and feeling like you can go for just a little longer.  As a result, this is one of the few games that I’ve ever had trouble putting down. The gorgeous artwork might draw you in but the content will not let you leave. All in all It's a really great if at times a little frustrating puzzle/platformer full of Henson-like characters and moodiness reminiscent of films like The Dark Crystal or animated films like Don Bluth's Secret of Nimh. If you have ever played an action/adventure game and felt like exploring the map was a waste of time after a few hours, welcome to the explorers dream.

I'm not sure what I can add to the reviews here that hasn't already been said a hundred times already. The visuals are amazing. The story is fantastic. The characters are engaging and a lot deeper than you'd imagine. The gameplay is a bit more on-the-rails than I'd like, but it works well for this type of setting. The whole things is just... good. Damn good. It's winning awards, breaking sales records, getting positive reviews, and this game, and the devs, deserve it. All of it. They put a lot of time into getting this right. And they got it VERY right.
But.... you've read this all before. This review looks just like the last 250 reviews you just glanced at till your eyes started watering. All this praise, and you're afraid that the hype will be played up till you just feel let down when you go to play it. You'll get so worked up over how many people said you should play it, that you'll feel the need to avoid it simply because you don't want to follow other people. You don't want it to be another No Man's Sky, Duke Nukem Forever, Tony Hawk 5, Or that Sonic game from 2016. You'll avoid it because you've learned that you should. I wish I'd learned that sooner.
So here's a different review. From a different perspective. One I don't usually give often to strangers. See, I have Psychosis. ( Schizophrenia for those of us in the states) I hear voices, I hallucinate things that aren't there. I have experienced a lot (not all) of the things that Senua deals with in the game. I view the world very differently than a "normal" person would. I found the puzzles, controls, hints, visual, and audio cues perfectly natural. Ninja Theory did a lot of research about Psychosis and about what it would mean for a game's player character to have such a condition. They talked to people like myself (like me, but not me) who helped them develop the game into a realistic expression of what it would be like for a "normal" person to suddenly develop Psychosis.
And from my own fairly unique point of view, they knocked out of the park, into another park. A different park where that game isn't even a thing and all the players are looking at this weird ball going "wtf?!".
Seriously, get this game. It's technically an Indie game, but I would easily call this a proper AA or AAA title. The regular price is $30. And steam is running a 25% off sale right now.
If you still need convincing, let be put it this way, I initially pirated this game. I played it all the way through. And when I was done. I deleted it off my PC. Deleted the torrent file. Started up Steam and paid my $30 to a developer to had EARNED my money. And I've been blasting this game's name on my social media accounts ever since.
