AC Review:
Wow! It took me a long time to finally get into the AC franchise, but I'm very pleased that I did.
Basic info on equipment: HP Pavilion dv6-6123cl entertainment notebook. Processor AMD A6-3400M APU w/Radeon HD Graphics 1.40 GHz. Installed RAM of 6 GB. 64-Bit Windows 10 OS. Wired external mouse and keyboard. No additional equipment used or upgrades made to computer.
Gameplay & Controls 5/10: Definitely the most challenging aspect of this game, many times to the point of being tedious and irritating because you end up repeating some tasks multiple times before succeeding. (Another reviewer mentioned something about yelling and/or pounding on the table because of frustration with the controls. That may have happened more than once with me as well...) This was partly due to the fact that I was playing this on a PC and the controls really don't translate well from console to PC. It was exceedingly difficult to coordinate some of the movements, especially during combat scenarios and when you were sprinting. To say that I sprinted into walls a few times while trying to turn sharp corners would be an understatement. This was the only factor, in my opinion, that made the game unpleasant to play. If I tried it with an XBox 360 controller or something similar installed, it might have made a big difference.
Graphics 9/10:  Holy mackerel! For the year in which this game was released, I was totally blown away by the quality of the graphics. Given that it was released only two years after Elder Scrolls Oblivion, I was expecting graphics only slightly better than that game, but not even Skyrim -- which came out four years after AC -- is this realistic or amazing (and I happen to really love Skyrim, so that's saying something). Huge positive factor for this game, as it really makes you feel immersed in the world. *Side note: For the horse-lovers out there (like me) you're going to want to spend as much time in one section of the game as possible because you get to ride some of the most realistic in-game horses I've ever seen. Did I mention Skyrim? Yeah. It doesn't hold a candle to AC in terms of the horses.
Storyline 7/10:  While the story within the game is fascinating and entertaining, it's also not terribly accurate in some ways. If you're not at all concerned with that sort of thing, then this rating means nothing, but for those of us who appreciate history, it can be frustrating to see otherwise excellent games not get something right or deliberately alter important events just to suit the story. And honestly, the Templars are a rather misunderstood group, and it was dismaying to see them so badly maligned in this game. They really don't deserve it. *Side note: Christians, be aware that this game holds morality to be a thing relative to the person. (Of course, if you're okay with playing a game like this in the first place, then this aspect of the game shouldn't really surprise or bother you.) There are characters who deliberately state that certain things we hold sacred and true are nothing more than illusions or lies. Just be prepared for that when you play and remember that you *don't* have to buy into everything the game says in order to enjoy it. It's just a form of dynamic storytelling.
Overall Rating 7/10:  I found this game to be tremendously enjoyable to play, especially once I started to get the hang of the otherwise frustrating controls. Said controls remained difficult enough that they distracted a bit from the game, but the amazing graphics and engrossing in-game story balanced it out so much that I would play it again in a heartbeat and am looking forward to continuing in the franchise.
(Oh, and the only other complaint I have -- a minor one at that -- is the fact that you have to travel through about five or six different game screens before you can exit. Tedious, I tell you!)

Pros:
+Amazing graphics, compared to Old Blood and New Order it has increased tenfold and is quite possibly one of the best looking games of 2017.
+Combat. If you liked the combat in The New Order and The Old Blood, you'll like this games combat.
+Main characters are well voice acted and cutscenes are well made to the point to where you'd think these were believable people.
+Music, literally anything Mick Gordon composes is never bad. The soundtrack is something to write home about in this game.
Cons:
-Story is very uninteresting and too short of a campaign compared to The New Order. (I will not go into story details)
-Characters may be well voice acted but are completely forgettable and unlikeable.
-Weapons, there may be more but there is little veriaty to them with an added weapon upgrade system where some of these upgrades make the guns boring to use or downright useless and you'll most likely use 1 or 2 of these weapons through the entirety of the game unless the game forces you to use said weapon to proceed.
-Perk system has been dumbed down and feels like something straight from a call of duty multiplayer. It's no longer fun to earn perks.
-Difficulty is based around how much damage you do and how much damage you take. The harder difficultys can just become unfair to play on, and enemies will never change up combat strategies. This is very annoying on Call me Terror-Billy and I am death incarnate as enemies just dish out insane amounts of damage even on Do or die! (the difficulty I played it on)
-Boss fights revolve around throwing out smaller enemies along with the boss having a massive weak spot or just become cyberdemon like. (the "shoot it until it dies" format)
-The ending was just a build up to a big let down. There was no well thought out fight, just a button press and a cutscene. Speaking of cutscenes...
-There is an absurd amount of cutscenes. The game (if played on easier difficulties) is about six hours long. Three and a half of those hours are cutscenes. Proof:

Side notes:
*People have had issues with running the game but i've never had any problems with low framerate or crashes and freezes.
*I've heard complaints of SJW propaganda and as someone who's played the game I couldn't disagree more. Yes, there is some dumb bullcrap SJW stuff but it's not being forced in with the plot. It's there but it's nothing big or of importance.
*As someone who loved The New Order, liked The Old Blood, and praised DOOM (2016), I was hyped for this game and to see it be such a let down really makes me sad. I'd recommend you buy and play the 3 games I've just listed instead.
*Instead of telling me there is going to be more with the hero chronicles and making me buy the damn season pass, how about you give me more in the base game so I can come back and consider playing more. (yes my dumbass bought the season pass edition when I should've bought the base game)
*If you're willing to turn off your brain and just kill nazis, and you've played The New Order and The Old Blood, then go ahead and buy this game. I mean, atleast it's not the new Battlefront 2. I'll give it that. The New Colossus had some enjoyment.

Slain! looks like a fun heavy metal inspired throwback to Castlevania, but that all changes when you actually play it.  The rocking metal music, which at first sounds cool, quickly loses its luster as it's looped continuously ad nauseum.  I will say I love the look of the game and the concept behind it.  The whole experience feels hollow, like a skelton for a decent game is there, but not fleshed out.
I played this with a gamepad, so the controls were fine. Be warned, the game won't tell you the controls, so you'll have to figure it out on your own or look them up in the menu.
There's no sound effect for defeating enemies. Which leaves you feeling like you haven't accomplished anything.  The enemy AI is so basic that you can cheat your way to victory by exploiting their limitations.  There was a large skelton boss with a sword on a platform that was unable to move off of, that I just stood back and pelted him with projecticles.  Speaking of skeltons they can be obnixous to take down as they take several hits to defeat, and there's no skill involved so you end up mashing the attack button.
Maybe with some updates and tweaks this game could become something resembling a decent game.  As it is, it's just not fun to play, and there's little incentive to continue playing it through unless your a masochist.

I woke up this morning to find a message in my inbox saying:
"Thanks for your support, we hope you enjoy the game! Please leave a review on the store page as soon as you have installed and played to help us gain some early momentum"
So here is my review.
This could have been a great game, except for a number of flaws. The most prominent of these, is that NOTHING is ever explained to you; which would be fine, but the control scheme is almost entirely unintuitive. To add to that, the UI in this game was definitely not designed well, going through the menus, the only indication to what option you have selected, is that the option turns a slightly different shade of red, now I imagine the irritation of this is compounded because I am colourblind, but I can't see this being pleasant for anyone else either. Any other flaws past this, I can't really elaborate on, as they might just be parts of more unexplained gameplay. For example, flying enemies up higher than my jump attack, that very rarely descend while raining down attacks? I have no way of attacking them, but perhaps I have an unexplained vertical ranged attack.
I was looking forward to this game, and UI aside, it really is a beautiful game, and I really wanted to like it, but I can't play this as it is. If you are thinking of buying this, do yourself a favour, get something else.

I barely write reviews, and I may have less than five written in my years of Steam service.
That being said, this review is necessary, and it's just as much (if not more) for the developers as it is for potential buyers.
I WANTED Slain! I WANTED Slain! to be good. I had phone reminders set for MONTHS to check for a release date and bought it regardless of the negative reviews to really try this game for myself.
Shame on you, Wolf Brew Games. This game was my most anticipated title of 2016 thus far and it is awful. AWFUL. None of this lived up to what it was advertised to be, and it is due to gripes that are apparent within the first 15 minutes of gameplay. I view preview material with a good amount of wiggle room, as I know how much can change within development, but this is unacceptable. Let me break it down in bullet form:
- This was toted in many different outlets like it was going to be a Metroidvania styled adventure. It was not, and that will become apparent with subsequent bullet points.
- The graphics and certain animations are GORGEOUS, but the game as a whole is a mess. It lacks personality, and right from the opening cutscene there's none to be found in the game. Just because a few idling animations and sword swings look pretty doesn't mean the game feels cohesive.
- The sound design is virtually nonexistent. Even after turning down the (so far, repetitive) music, there was almost no sound to be heard. Super Meat Boy has more sound effects for running and squishing than Slain! has for "epic" combat, and Super Meat Boy's are louder.
- Like some other reviewers mentioned, this game feels like a Flash game in many regards, and not in a good way. The intro contains poorly written dialogue, with horrible text formatting. The animations that weren't the few good ones featured in previews are janky and quickly repetitive. I found myself walking past areas that triggered popup text and even dialogues from NPCs, that quickly vanished without allowing me to stop and read them. This included what looked like it would be useful gameplay information, if I could finish reading it.
- There is no reliable way to find out what Bathoryn can do. The controls are trial and error, and from what I was able to figure out, there is no depth to combat. I'm okay with simple combat, if it has flow, but killing enemies is actually boring; hacking and slashing is boring in a hack and slash game. I see what you were attempting with the button timing for the sword swings, but it feels unresponsive instead of rewarding.
- The challenge is horrible. I think in all the battles I fought with enemies both large and small, I died ONCE to combat, and did not struggle at all aside from that. At the same time, however, I found myself in situations where I did not have any techniques at my disposal to adequately deal with the combat at hand. In one room, there were a bunch of flying enemies near the ceiling, so I had to awkwardly keep jumping off of a platform and swinging blindly to kill everything instead of being able to properly engage them in combat. Bigger enemies can be dispatched by walking away and mashing your spell attack until they crumble, like other reviews point out. The only things that really ended up killing me were the ridiculous traps and pitfalls, not because they're treacherous, but because they're random and uncalled for. The moving platforms are incredibly tedious, and some of them even move randomly and require blind faith when you jump since you can't see the next one from where you stand. It doesn't really matter anyway, since there are overly convenient checkpoints whenever a real threat presents itself. Now for the traps. Yes, they're "hidden" but they're not cohesive with the layout of the level. They're placed where you can either see them easily and avoid them, or where they're not actually "hidden" so much as "there so enemies can push you into them." It's just a treacherous one hit death jump, not a trap. They're fancier versions of the aforementioned pits.
- The game over screen doesn't even have unique sounds and music. It just keeps playing the same song from the level until you respawn.
- There's no inventory system or map, you just mindlessly go right and sometimes find a weapon that the game vaguely describes without giving you a choice of using a weapon you already had. Just like the dialogues from earlier in my review, you can blink and almost miss the text.
This game feels incredibly rushed and unpolished for a game that had countless positive press, a successful Kickstarter, and extremely promising preview material. I'll be keeping my copy for the Deluxe Edition art content, but I'm warning everyone to stay away from this game until further notice. What a shame.

If you are looking for a captivating story with a VERY interesting concept, then Remember Me is one such game. It will have you questioning the morals of what you are doing throughout the entire game. The scenery, the city that you platform your way through is amazing, there is so much detail. So much thought has gone into building up the society that you witness. So, overall, if it is on offer, I would highly recommend you buy it.
HOWEVER! The game is not without its own flaws. Although Remember Me has an amazing story, I felt there was parts of what you could see that was left untouched. I won't go into detail as to what I'm refering to, but I simply hope you can take my word for it. Apart from some parts of the games world being left out, the combat and perhaps gameplay is a little easy. It is not very difficult to put simply. The combo's give it a little bit of customisation, but I only really stuck with the two short combo's that I could customise, as I found it rare to be able to kick off a full 8+ combo hit (so much dodging).
Still, it is a game that I would highly suggest you give a try. If you find the gameplay is too irritating, I ask that you TRY to look past it. I know for some of you that may be a little hard, but you will NOT regret it if you can. And for those who have finished the game but are intrigued by it. I suggest you look up two books, one is a 10 page one off comic called Remember Me: Cubed. As well as Remember Me: The Pandora Archive.

It is hard for me not to recommend that game, despite all the time I've spent on both the steam and flash versions (and the time I am likely to keep spending). Let me explain why though, as it is not that I did not have fun, but more that I see the missed opportunities to make this game a much more enjoyable one. On the graphic side, its sprite based (wonderful fantasy artwork) and very basic animations occur to make all this abstraction feel more living.
Monsters' Den: Godfall remain true to the core gameplay of its flash predecessors while adding a few very good ideas and features to the mix, as well as new bugs (like dungeons disappearing from the world map). It is possible to play the game in several difficulties, including a custom one making enemies from -30% up to +300% weaker or stronger than the standard challenge.
Unfortunately in terms of challenge, the game present little as soon as you understand the mechanics and survive the hardest part which is get a few levels at start. Both UI and actual gameplay mechanics offer the player ways to outsmart or softcheat the game.
- The difficulty can be changed at anytime and does not provide any notable difference in terms of rewards (it just makes the game grindier than it already when it comes to getting full legendary/mythical gear - not required to beat the story though). That fight is too hard? Change the settings. Steamrolling everything and having no sense of accomplishment, change it back!
- Reputation items can be bought from merchants and resold to factions for twice the price. Talk about a loophole, although the game is based on a timed economy, there is very little penalty (upkeep cost is ridiculuous) for letting months pass and generate money and reputation in this way (instead of actually playing the game as intended).
The gameplay, from what I recall, has not really been improved from the previous version, with many redundant or outright useless skills (i.e. Dire Wolf can be unlocked at level 3, why the hell go for the normal wolf then?), despite the inclusion of several arbitrarily unlockable classes (i.e. why no nature-warrior?). Despite many limitations there are still many viable party and character builds which make the customization one of the fun inducing elements in this game. Of course beside leveling up your characters to achieve that setup you aim for, it is the complementary loot that keep you going hunting for that piece of gear. And if gods have fallen, for sure not the RNG god as this is a mechanic that made the success of this game and basically any fight, any chest can provide you with the same enormous range in variation of quantity and quality than any other. A few events (especially overland encounters, boss encounters) offers guaranteed higher tiers of gear and part, but mainly if you were to run a dungeon floor and sell everything, then re-run it from a save from the entrance (same layout) you could still end up with difference in value ranging above 8 or 10 times more value in gold.
As part as the new "company" meta-game, you will manage more than one party of adventurers. Well, one only will be active and there is very little actual use in using the assignement features as usually by the time you can afford multiple parties, the benefits they provide are already insignificant. You company will also level up and for each of the 7 levels you can choose a bonus from a rudimentary 3-ways themed skill tree. While some levels offer you useful skills, some are completely non-sensical like willing to have your new recruits to start at level 3. Indeed, the game offer a stat boost system in the shape of potions (tonics) you can drink once per character level. When you can afford it, you want to restart a fresh party and boost them every level. Unfortunately, the game design decision was to not allow you to retroactively drink tonics, so if you really want to breed your uber-heroes, you have to babysit them from level 1 and pay due attention to their experience gain, so the last thing you want is them to gain more than one level at once, rendering such already pretty useless company skill even counterproductive (level 3? common, thanks for saving 3 minutes of my time to level up the recruit myself).
I could go on with the sarcastic critiscism on the many design decisions that are "meh" if not outright bad, but the game being still founded on its succesful core remains enjoyable as the endless time sink and ritual to honor the RNG god it is. Besides it is very important to highlight that the developper is interacting frequently with his community and is definitely dedicated to his product, so things may possibly get better rather sooner than never - especially now that he could be making slightly more money than with the flash version - and I for one would be more than pleased to change my recommandation to a positive one in the near future, which is just like the game, on the edge.

I can't believe I'm saying it, but this game has too much loot.
I loved the original flash
series for its rather challenging fights, that made you seriously consider your party composition and pray for healing shrines in a dungeon. So, naturally, I jumped at the opportunity for a bigger, better installment.
Well,
has surely become bigger, with (I assume) randomly generated missions, an overall worldmap, a global reputation, and a bunch of other additions that sound good... in theory.
In practice though,
has become an unbearable treadmill. You are drowned in loot you can't be bothered to check and quests you can't be bothered to read, and you know full well the supply is endless. Worst of all though, the challenge is gone completely, since now you can heal out of battle and just abandon quests you don't feel like overcoming. It's all just unsatisfying and pointless, and every dungeon feels exactly the same.
I like to keep a smaller mouse-only game installed at all times, to play it in short 10-minute sessions when I need a pause. I hoped
could serve that purpose.
But it makes me want to bash my head on the keyboard with boredom in five.

TL;DR: Loved the originals, but this game doesn't add enough to make it worth the asking price. Cannot recommend.
So, I LOVED the original Monster's Den games. I easily put hundreds of hours into both Book of Dread, and several hundreds into Chronicals. I remember seeing the announcement for Godfall, and I was so excited! I thought "Wow, if I can play Book of Dread and Chronicals for free, imagine the kind of content we'll get in a full release of Monster's Den!" This was back in 2010, when I put a big majority of my time into Book of Dread.
The years went on, and I would watch the Monster's Den: Godfall like a hawk. At some point--maybe in 2015--I had sort of forgotten about Godfall. Then, it's 2017, and I see Godfall release. All of the hype suddenly rushed back in, and I felt like I did back 2010; I couldn't buy this game fast enough. I launch it up, and for the first maybe 5 hours, it was everything I hoped it had been! The honeymoon was lovely, I guess you could say.
Then, I rolled over to see my lover the next morning...something wasn't right. I remember having so much fun playing BoD and Chronicals, but Godfall wasn't scratching that same itch. The skill trees seem kind of small and limited; is it just me? Have I become more cynical? The classes seem limited, too..you can unlock "new" classes, but they're more hybrids of what we already have than actual new classes.
The core gameplay is improved and refined from the original games, but the content? It only feels like there's the tiniest bit more, as if they did the bare minimum for a full release. The game did take seven years..is this what the seven year wait got us? Monster's Den Chronicals 1.5? I'm sorry, but that's not good enough for me. I may come across as entitled, or jaded, but I really wanted to love this game. But as I kept playing the game, I felt like playing the game less and less as time went on.
I feel like more is going to be added to this game as time goes on to make it feel more like a fully released title, but as of 1.131? I cannot recommend it; go play Monster's Den: Chronicals for free. The dev deserves your support, but not for this game as it is now. I wasn't REALLY disappointed, but I was disappointed enough to write this out.

This game offers a good representation of what a casual space survival sim is all about.
That being said, there is only 1 BIG issue that prevents me from playing this game any further. (until it's addressed)
Your spaceship? The one that is supposed to maneuver in a weightless environment? Free from the restrictions of conventional flight (thrust, drag, lift, gravity)? It is absolutely unable to strafe side to side or up and down. The VERY things that distinguish a spacecraft from an airplane are missing, creating an EXTREMELY clunky flying experience in space and in the air.
You see, when one is able to hover 50 feet off of the ground, one NATURALLY feels that they can move in any direction. Much like a helicopter. So, when you play this game and you can't do what feels natural it becomes a burden, a frustration... for example, it might usually take you 20 seconds to whip your spacecraft around a space station and dock or land in other games that allow full 6-axis movement. In this game, it might take you 60-120 seconds to move along a single line of bearing, change direction, then move again, then change direction, then move again etc. etc. etc.
I seriously don't see how a space game doesn't have this as their highest priority. Don't get me wrong, I'm glad they've done as much as they have and have tried to make this universe as fun as possible to play in, but they're missing some key components. It all starts with the ship. Everything you do in this universe revolves around you and your ship, so why does that seem to be the least thought-out part of this game?
If you play any other space flight simulator at all, you will be out of your element. You'll literally have to relearn how to fly, or just pretend you're flying a terrestrial flight simulator.
What's kind of funny about it is that at some point they created animations and code for ships landing on the surface of planets... which requires a downward strafe. Your ship comes to a relative halt and strafes down to sit nicely on the planet. So, why'd they stop there? Did they not see the application or necessity of 6-axis movement? The only practical reason I can think of is a flaw in the base design of the game that won't allow them to allow us to do these things. If that's the case, then they NEED TO LET US KNOW or TRY TO FIX IT.
More features and content are great, but they're useless if people don't like flying their ships.
I still recommend this game. It can be fun. I just wanted to give everyone a heads up of what to expect.
And to the developers of this game. I mean no disrespect. What you've accomplished is worthy of our time. But I think you missed a step. Please do something about it?
Thank you.

One of the best games that I ever played! I'll explain the basics. when the game starts, you'll start of as a private. in order to rank up you'll need XP or Experience Points. in order to get XP you'll need to eliminate enemies as much as you can, hopefully depending on your top down shooting skills you should earn a promotion which then allows you to have your own squad, getting a promotion also allows you to call air strikes and other supports.
Another similar thing to XP is called RP or "Resource Points. RP are points you receive during the game while completing different tasks. Those RP can be used to buy different equipments at an armory or to use different radio calls. you can earn RP by:
+capturing a base
+spotting an enemy vehicle
+selling valuables at an armory. Those are dropped with different commonness from the enemy +soldiers and have also different values
+selling rare weapons (those can either be used or sold). Those are either dropped by mini-bosses or +found in special crates (metallic boxes)
+destroying enemy vehicles.
+destroying mission targets such as comms truck, radar tower, prisoner bus, radio jamming tower, water tower, fuel tanks, mortars, ammunition crates, anti-air emplacement results in a good RP reward
+Stealing the cargo truck of the enemy team and bringing it back to one of your armories
+being promoted to a higher military rank
Anyway, moving on. there's also a range gamemodes you can choose. From Quickmatch to campaign, From playing SP to MP. quite good isn't it?
Overall: 9.5 / 10 (It can get a bit boring sometimes lol)

I had exactly 5 minutes of game time before I requested my refund.  I'm sorry, Wolf Brew Games, but this needs a lot more work before it's ready.
1. Get rid of the awful looking "high res" blood that comes out of enemies when you hit them.  Having your beautiful spritework clash with stuff that looks like default after effects is really jarring, and does the game no favors.  This actually really irked me.  Pick an art style and stick with it, man!
2. Combat needs massive improvements to impacts.  We need hits to really connect, make high quality "chunky" sounds and visibly stop or slow enemies, as it stands they react like an older Newgrounds flash game, where you swing wildly and the enemy kind of sort of backs up a bit but shows no indication that you're murdering it.
3. Music is good, but repetitive.  Get some more tracks made!
I'm sure there'd be more for me to say if I had played more, but that I already have a list that damning in 5 *minutes* of play is... not good.  It's not unsalvageable by any means, but you really gotta work on it hard if you want to turn this around from mostly negative.  This really bums me out.

Played a little over an hour, beat the first level and got to the point with the ice axe. First impression is that this game has lots of potential, but really feels like a beta release. I can tell that a lot of love went into making this game and I'd be happy to update the review if the game is also updated/improved.
Pros:
Beautiful art and animations (particles are very loud though)
Music is solid, but the sound mixing is pretty far off (had to turn the music down to 7 just to hear game SFX)
Great thematic. Skulls and blood and metal!
Cons:
- No viscerality. This is my biggest disappointment. When I hit or get hit with a huge♥♥♥♥♥sword, I want it to feel like that. Give me audio feedback when I flip a switch. I want to hear that platform move. Etc. Lack of feedback makes the gameplay feel hollow.
- No invulnerability frames and I get stunned on hit? What was the thought behind this? It adds some artificial difficulty, but mostly just feels bad. Getting stunned out of the spin and being unable to move but having no indication as to having been hit other than unresponsive controls is no fun.
- Sound effects are all but non-existant. I muted the music to hear the SFX and it seems like half of them just aren't there. Like I mentioned above, lack of sound really detracts from overall feel.
- Basic attack combo is untuned. Thrust hitbox projection + knockback is super strong. Decapitation move gives back mana, but mostly feels like a trap. 3rd part of combo, the down slash, is nigh on inaccesible. X spammed my way through the first level. The Anubis guys in the woods seemed less susceptible to that method, but only played a bit.
MINOR GREIVANCES
- Moveset between sword and axe is identical (aside from knockback)? More of a missed opportunity.
- Why tell me I should block if you don't tell me how to do it?
- Dash only goes backward, but it functions as a move cancel as well. Odd design choice that doesn't mesh with the rest of the controls.
- Menu control is sluggish and also still controls you in game while it's open.
- Badguy says "BTW" at one point. The cheesey metal story is kinda fun, but this was really jarring.
- Enemy collision is unintuitive. Hit detection feels right, but some mobs you can just stand inside of. I literally stood inside the volcano dogs and spammed X to kill them.
- Changing settings to 'fastest' makes the controls slightly better.
Awesome.

The cyberpunk aesthetic and music go really well with the premise behind the story, and the dissonance between the classes of citizens on Neo-Paris is very striking and thematic. The combat is not way over the top nor is it terribly bland. That being said, the game is easier to get a handle on with a controller rather than keyboard and mouse.

A biggest surprise for me this year.
I went into this games thinking it would be somewhere between bad and average (it was on sale). Luckily, I was wrong.
You plain Nilin, who lives in the world where memories are a commodity since there is hardware which can add or take them. In this world, people buy memories, sell them, anything but create them in reality. This brings a lot of problems for the society and Nilin is a part of a group that's fighting back, in the world you see many side effects this "trend" has.
The graphics is real good and you can actually mod it if you don't feel it's good enough.
You get attacked by... mutants?, police and guards and more. To combat them, you use martial arts moves put together by combos and you execute them during the fight so you have to be very present and conscious of what you press during the fight, it's not a one button masher for sure. Some moves can do specific things like break guard or heal you so you have to be careful when putting combos together.
The sound and music work very well together to bring you into Neo-Paris and I enjoyed the tour and seeing the differences between the slums and the high class. It all feels very appropriate.
Nilin herself it alright and is one of those girls that you enjoy watching from behind as well as from the front, her character is quite simple from the start what with being mind wiped but she takes off and grows on you, although it was hard to get over her British accent, in a game like this I'd have expected an American or otherwise (French?).
To be fair, you spend most of the time climbing or fighting but there are also some interesting passages involving rewamping other people's memories, following memory messages and look for secrets.
If you don't mind dishing out whatever cash the game's asking, you won't be disappointed, though you will need a lot of patience in the fights later on, so be prepared.

I've seen a fair amount of people complaining about this game, in part for its combat, in part for a missed potential.
While I agree the game doesn't achieve its full potential, I would refrain from really putting it down as such. Yes, it can be clunky. Yes, combat can be easy. Yes, the remixes should have been a bigger part of the game. And yes, the story is only ok, as it is too conventional and too scattered. I might even add that the platforming is really kind of unecessary.
However, I still must say that I found the game to be very enjoyable, because for all of those flaws, it still had a great atmosphere, it had some cool concepts, and despite its relatively easy combat, I still had a lot of fun with it. So while this game may not be a contender for game of the year, I'd still recommend it on a sale, because honestly it's still a fair bit of fun while it lasts. Oh, and props for a mixed race female protagonist. Not the best female protagonist in any video game by far (her physical prowesses are completely unexplained, and she still feels a bit sexualized), but still good to see some representation.

In particular, I don't think you've heard anything quite like this game's "glitch orchestra" score. The memory hacking sections are clever and emotionally powerful, but there aren't as many as you'd hope for a game centered around that concept.

Linear, unintuitive combat system, questionable exploration, and unimpressive characters. And yet the world imagined in Remember Me and the story it tells kept me playing for hours. There was a lot of untapped potential in this game, but it's worth seeing through.

Monster's Den: Godfall is a tactical turn-based dungeon-crawler and an all-around improvement of the previous games in the series.
Unlike the previous games, Godfall offers an open-world conquest with lots of places to explore and dungeons to delve in. Dungeons can have special properties like "lost," preventing you from seeing how many enemies you face before battle, or "ancient," increasing the quality of loot. There are various prizes for completing the given dungeon objective, such as special class ability manuals to unique pieces of equipment.
There multiple races of monsters with racial abilities, prompting players to adapt their battle strategy. Certain items have relic propterties and can be kept in the player base to give certain buffs to the whole party during their expedition. In the late game, players can discover the locations of unique and extremely powerful equipment known as 'artifacts." And of course, there are fearsome bosses to face, both new and familiar.
What I like most about this game:
There is a lot to discover. The intricate equipment system and large variety of special items kept me searching for new powers. Unique equipment plus scary new monsters is a great formula, and the tactical possibilities for team building are vast.
There is a lot of flexibility. You can unlock special character classes that offer exciting new skill combinations, allowing for deep team-building, or you can simply blast away with powerful weapons and equipment. With the new addition of "custom" difficulty, players now have complete freedom to chew through dungeons of pitiful monsters or to slowly overpower diabolical hordes with careful training. This is currently my favorite feature of the game, as I now have worthy opponents to combat my meticulously constructed team.
Story mode isn't long, but its also not boring. It has special encounters and an intruiging plot.
The devloper gives thoughtful consideration to player input and continues to make the game a better and better experience.
What I dislike:
You can't reverse your ability upgrades; you have to recruit a new character instead. I've raised nearly two copies of my team because I wanted to reverse some poor upgrade choices. Subclass skills are not understood until you have the means of using them, which is somewhat fun but too perilous since you have to make irresersible choices to learn about them. (To prevent this, I've made a subclass skills guide in the "guides" section.)
Faction armor and most of the enchantments in this game communicate that stat bonuses matter above everything else, which makes it so. There is not as much use for creative bonuses or armor set bonuses at the highest levels of difficulty. Bosses are very accurate, making evasion based strategies hopeless. Certain bosses have degrees of healing and armor piercing that seem excessive.
Ability trees and upgrades could use more variety and balance. Rather than certain skills being overpowered, multiple skills have effects that are too minor to be useful.
Dungeons could use more unique features to mitigate the experience of "grinding." (I can testify that there are NO secret passages, no matter how suspicious some walls look.) The option to reduce difficulty has somewhat reduced this problem.
These inconveniences don't deter me from describing Monster's Den: Godfall as a really great game! I've enjoyed exploring and battling my way through its expansive world. I fully recommend it, and I look forward to its continued development!

I'm having a lot of fun in this game so far. Assorted thoughts to follow.
- The open-world feels strange, I'm not sure why there needed to be a traversable map instead of just a list of locations
- The combat is as enjoyable as every other game in the series
- The skill trees for each class are interesting, a solid improvement over the previous system(s)
- Maybe it changes later on, but the item class requirements are odd. "Requires sorcery to equip" seems meaningless, when ALL mages start with both sorcery and arcane. Why not just say "Requires mage to equip"?
- Rep grinding seems kinda boring, but I guess without the grind, there isn't much meta gameplay outside of the dungeons.
Surprisingly, the worst thing about the game is the performance. This isn't really a top of the line, graphically intensive game or anything, so you wouldn't think there would be any performance troubles. However, After playing in a single session for perhaps an hour, the average framerate has dropped from a smooth 30 to an irritating 10-15, and it only gets worse.
Overall, it seems good enough. I would give it 3/5 stars. An easy 4 if I didn't have to close out of the game ever half an hour to maintain a smooth framerate.

I have noticed that the game difficulty is all over the place sometimes. On the start of my second playthrough, I bumped it up 2 difficulty tiers, because why not? Until I got to level 4 or so, I had to use the consumable limited-use healing supplies after every encounter to make it through even a single area. Now, at level 17, I am able to take on even the strongest enemy parties without taking a single point of damage quite often. I haven't felt truely threatened by any enemy groups at all for the past 4 hours of gameplay. It's fun to see my strategy panning out, but... where's the challenge?
I don't see myself doing a third playthrough, but this game was unexpectedly more fun than I imagined it would be on my first few hours of playing it. I change my rating to a 4/5.

Original review:
This review is based on the latest version of the game available to me, which is v1.0 for OSX (and I believe it’s also the latest version for Linux). Since the release the developers released a number of patches, Windows only. For a Windows review read somewhere else. I’ll update this as / if game gets updated.
From the developers website: "Slain! is affectionately inspired by games such as Ghosts and Goblins, Altered Beast, Shadow Of The Beast and Golden Axe"
Played all of those as a kid. The only thing that's better in Slain! are graphics. Everything else is much, much worse. So sad I backed this on Kickstarter, can't get the refund. If there was only a bug here or there, I would have hope that it can be fixed. But it's not about the bugs here (actually haven't encountered any), it's about poor game design, really bad controls, missing sound effects… In the games mentioned above there was at least some feedback / knock back when you get hit by an enemy, in Slain! enemies walk through you. Sure, all this can be fixed but it’s not a question of days but rather months. At this stage, I would suggest to the developers to slap the “early access” badge on this and take it from there.
EDIT #4:
As of 31 May developers "hope" they'll have OSX (that probably means Linux too) update ”in the near future". Thanks for the kick in the balls, again.
EDIT #3:
Hoooraaay! Patch 1 is out! It fixes sooo many things! Oh, wait... it's just for Win. No patch for OSX and Linux. But the store page says the game supports OSX and Linux? Well, it also says there are trading cards and achievements.... but you know, who cares anymore.
EDIT #2:
Achievements are broken. You can get the first one, but that's it, the rest of them don't work. Store page states "trading cards", but they are nonexistent.
EDIT #1:
Try turning the music off and you’ll find that this game is almost mute!
Except from generic footsteps and sword sounds there are no sounds when you pick up power ups, die from spikes, break stones or fall down. On the menu screen you see the rain falling and flashes on the screen (lightning) but can’t hear any of that, it’s all quiet. At the beginning a monster spawns from the ground, blood sprays from the pit, visually very dramatic… no sound… no ground rumbling, no sound of blood spraying, the monster is mute. Fire gargoyles spit fireballs from their mouths… no sound at all.  Monsters make engine revving like sound which starts quietly, then gradually goes louder, then ends abruptly and then starts over in a loop. Skeletons make a fireplace crackling like sound (bones?) but die without making any sound… The list goes on and on. And I’ll remind you all that one of the Kickstarter stretch goals (which WAS reached) was hiring “dedicated professional audio designer”.

I'll explain the basics. when the game starts, you'll start of as a private. in order to rank up you'll need XP or Experience Points. in order to get XP you'll need to eliminate enemies as much as you can, hopefully depending on your top down shooting skills you should earn a promotion which then allows you to have your own squad, getting a promotion also allows you to call air strikes and other supports.
Another similar thing to XP is called RP or "Resource Points. RP are points you receive during the game while completing different tasks. Those RP can be used to buy different equipments at an armory or to use different radio calls. you can earn RP by:
+capturing a base
+spotting an enemy vehicle
+selling valuables at an armory. Those are dropped with different commonness from the enemy +soldiers and have also different values
+selling rare weapons (those can either be used or sold). Those are either dropped by mini-bosses or +found in special crates (metallic boxes)
+destroying enemy vehicles.
+destroying mission targets such as comms truck, radar tower, prisoner bus, radio jamming tower, water tower, fuel tanks, mortars, ammunition crates, anti-air emplacement results in a good RP reward
+Stealing the cargo truck of the enemy team and bringing it back to one of your armories
+being promoted to a higher military rank
Anyway, moving on. there's also a range gamemodes you can choose. From Quickmatch to campaign, From playing SP to MP. quite good isn't it?

Essentially you try to match the son with the correct dad. It may seem simple, but as you progress through the levels, more obstacles appear. The obstacles are fun, humorous and contextually relevant (most of the time), and make the game increasingly challenging but still enjoyable.
When you first start there are a few gameplay modes:
- Endurodad: Match the same son to the correct dad each time;
- Dadathlon: Match a different son to the correct dad each time, within a given time limit;
- Dad Divisions: Match the correct son to a slew of dropping dads.
As you play more, or reach certain scores, more modes are unlocked. One of these modes is a short point-n-click type mini adventure game ("Soapico"); another is where you control a son in a bathtub, who has to shoot down incorrect dads while simultaneously picking up correct ones ("Inglorious Bathdads"). Each mode (except for Soapico) tests essentially the same matching skills, but in different ways.
- Bonus objects get unlocked with more plays or high scores
- Amusing minigame fillers between level-ups
- Various entertaining modes of gameplay
- Each mode poses a different kind of challenge
- Good humour, jokes & general cheesiness
- Just the right amount of difficulty

I make a lot of 3D renders, for various reasons, so I'll be a little biased towards programs like DAZ Studio or SFM. However, I still feel that creating a 3D model to render from is much more convenient than using ePic, which is a shame. It has potential, and I have used ePic to make some art for a non-commercial game project I worked on, but I keep going back to DAZ for my renders and character art. My computer isn't even that powerful, but I can get a high-quality render done in almost no time at all.
On the other hand, if you don't actually care about the way the art looks and simply want a generic character render, ePic is still worth keeping in mind.
I personally recommend ePic, but only to people with no other options. Stick with DAZ or a similar piece of software if you need versatility in your renders, but use ePic for concept art or generic renders if you want to.

This is all good and well for a quick lark, but it would appear this product isn't much use until you spend at least tens if not hundreds of dollars on DLC packs. So you'd best be the type who LOVES customising the look of your character in video games just for the ♥♥♥♥ of it; or, perhaps more practically, a keen tabletop RPG gamer who can't draw. At present I'm neither of these things, so I was clearly never going to be the ideal target audience for this product.
The free "demo" version is pretty basic, with not a whole hell of a lot of options on offer...but you might get an hour or two's entertainment out of it, and can't complain about the whopping great starting price of FREE. Quite who would want to pay full price for the DLCs is beyond me, but I have put one of the packs into my wishlist on the off-chance it pops up for, say, 75% off in the future.
It's certainly a user-friendly enough program, even for dumb-dumbs like yours truly, so I'm happy to give it a thumb-up. Just one, and a weakish one at that, but it's a thumb just the same. But definitely check out the demo in detail before you even CONTEMPLATE shelling out the crazy prices they're asking for the add-ons...
Verdict: 6.5/10.
UPDATE: Ooookay...ah-he-he-hem. In light of my now curiously high number of "hours" in this program, it seems that an update might be in order. Again, though, my initial observation remains essentially unchanged: it's only going to be worth spending money on if you're either someone who adores customising characters for the sheer heck of it, or someone who has a definite "use" for the finished results. Since writing my initial review, I've found myself unexpectedly falling into the latter category (nope, not going into any details, haha), and have found it surprisingly versatile...especially after a good chunk of the DLC content was purchased. I still wouldn't recommend said DLCs at full price - they're definitely overpriced, in my opinion - but there's no denying that it's a useful and competent product for what it is, and what it sets out to achieve.
Revised Verdict: 8/10.

The game focuses on being a psychological and suspense horror while trying to give an earnest portrayl of someone who is suffering from psychosis in the form of extreme paranoia and auditory and visual hallucinations.
As far as the story goes you play as a young pict woman who descends into norse hell to retrieve the soul of a lover.   The game doesn't have a HUD so relies on visual cues in the form of "voices" warning you about being attacked form behind while offering commentary, criticism, and insults as you play the game.  They voice has a fairly distinct personality.  One is clearly narrating  and is friendly, one is always questioning you, the other is echoing the question in an answer, and etc.  It's well done and thoughtful.
The gameplay isn't very deep.  It's got a simple 3 phase forumla per area.  Puzzles relying on a unique mechanic for each area with combat that acts more of a reset in pacing and refreses your palette finished off by a boss.  The puzzles aren't terribly difficult, the combat is fairly straight forward, and each boss is different and unique and has their own mechanic involved.
The game does a GREAT job at creating anxiety, fear, and suspense through its mechanics, music, sound, and visuals.  There are no jump scares, no cheap thrills, just very thoughtful game design that was used to tell a compelling story and metal illness.  There are concerns about save deletion if you die too many times and all i reccomend you not worry about it.  The game very careful monitors your skill, adjusts difficulty (leave it on dynamic), and will always keep you flirting with the edge no matter if you're good or bad.  To give you an example I got to the end with minimal deaths (read none really) died once and the rot on my hand grew massively.  My friend who died multiple times (read 50) had half the rot on his hand at the same point.  I can't say where the game over point is but it's really generous and is a mechanic that helps add anxiety to each fight, but you're relatively safe at all points.  This isn't to add artifical difficulty as the game becomes easier but is meant to have you emotionally invested in to game.
Either way I highly reccomend it if you're into story driven experiences and are more cocerned with a compelling experience than just gameplay itself.

I read some of the early reviews before I started playing so I already had an idea of what to look out for - and what a lot of people are calling negatives I'm actually more inclined to call choices that the designers made that just may not have been well-received, so I'll address some of those early on.
Controls: I'm playing with a Steam controller and I don't find a lot of lag within the game itself, but I do find there to be lag within the game menus (which is kind of weird).  Controls are simple, but strategic: you have a 3 hit combo, a slight backwards dash, a jump (you can attack during your jump), a ranged magic attack (can be cast midair), and what looks like a backhanded slash.  Others have complained of input lag, but I didn't feel any per se, I felt like my button presses were in time with the animations - which is maybe less responsive than some would have wanted, but felt very natural to me.  One point where I think the creators of the game may have "suckered" some people is there isn't an ability to animation cancel: if you're in the middle of an attack and someone swings faster than you, you can't dodge or jump.  This was frustrating the first two or three times it happened to me until I realized it was intentional: you can't just bull your way through some areas and you need to actually use some strategy.  The only part of the controls I'm not particularly fond of is the backhanded slash, which doesn't actually appear to do much: it's less useful than your normal attack, it's shorter ranged, and it doesn't seem to do more damage.  It looks cool, but it doesn't appear to have a use.  I'm not very far though, so maybe it's some sort of required execution for bosses or something.
Animation is gorgeous; there's tons to look at.  I wish it was a little better defined, but it feels like somewhere between an 8 bit Castlevania and a 16 bit one.  I know that's a weird middle ground, but it feels very appropriate.  Music is a bit repetitive - I didn't mind it as much as some other people seemed to, but I did mind that it was very LOUD and the settings were either LOUD or almost muted.  I ultimately turned it down to hear the ambient noise and found it more pleasant and helpful.
Difficulty level seemed to be about what I expected from a game that seems to pay homage to 8/16 bit classic Castlevania platformers: it's not particularly forgiving, but it's also not particularly difficult, either, with tons of health and mana vials to be found easily.
Overall, I'm recommending this *with caveats*; I think with a couple good patches, some of the day one issues will be cleared up (like that weird input lag in the menu and the music issues) and it'll be a lot better.  It reminded me a lot of Volgarr the Viking, albeit much easier.  I'm super happy it works with my Steam Controller without having to fiddle with it too much.  I also haven't found it to be much of a Metroidvania (yet); it honestly plays like an original Castlevania title from the NES - that's not a knock at all, but if you were expecting a large map with back tracking and finding new powers, I can't say that I've seen anything to that effect (yet).

Have you ever been really excited for a game? Like so freaking excited for a game to come out. But when you finally get to play it it leaves a bland taste in your mouth? Well that game would be Slain for me. I really wanted to love this game. Art style is rad. Music is rad. Yet the gameplay is flat. Levels are incredibly boring.

Slain! is a beautiful artistic game with a wonderful soundtrack. The pixel art is top notch and wonderful that portrays a Gothic atmosphere. From the screenshots and everything I saw, this felt like a winner. So, I gave it the chance. Boy was I wrong...
The game starts in a Legacy of Kain-ish style in a tomb. Which caught my eye, as I was looking around the tomb awestruck. Then, I walked outside. The graphics were indeed what was told. Breathtaking game and great example what an indie studio can do. You play Senua who is trying to enter Hell to save a loved one from the clutches of Hela - Goddess of the Underworld. The game plays in third person and consists of two main parts, a calm part where you explore and solve somewhat easy visual puzzles, and the combat part which is very similar to the Batman Arkham Asylum/Witcher 3 mechanic, consisting of sword fights. Because of financial constraints the developer trimmed the fat what you usually see in AAA titles, such as progression or crafting system. In doing so they created a much more tightly focused game - with emphasize on story telling and the mo-cap performance by the actress who plays Senua.
What makes this game utterly unique is its attempt to depict the experience of mental illness, such as being depressed or schizphrenia by using sound and visual manipulation in the game. Throughout the game you can hear your own voice and others doubting, mocking or encouraging you. Landscape may change depending on from where you look, constantly making you doubt whether what you see or hear is real.
This game is a fantastic achievement for a 20 person indie developer who self published its game. While the puzzle part and fighting can become a bit repetitive, its visuals and the impressive performance by the mo-cap actress make more than up for it. Well worth the full price.

The problem with RWR is essentially misleading advertising. The game supposedly touts replayability by way of being a sandbox and declares it has RPG elements.
*RPG Elements*
Not really. While you gain experience to unlock radio calls for reinforcements and basic guns/gear, you have no choice or customization options (you can't even name your soldier). Each time you want to swap out guns/gear you need to go to an armory and do it manually, which gets irritating as you'll generally have either a long trip to the front or can, with bad luck, die a few seconds after customizing your loadout.
*Sandbox*
Again, not really. If your definition of sandbox is "you aren't penalized for failing to do what the game prompts you to do" then I suppose it qualifies, but for me sandbox generally means freedom to do what I want, when I want, where I want in a fashion that can be meaningful, enjoyable, or fulfilling. While it's certainly possible to swap in a silenced submachine gun and try to 'sneak' behind enemy lines, there's really no stealth feature, nor is there anything to do behind enemy lines that has any real value. Additionally, it's entirely possible for your NPC allies to win each map area, turning it into a safezone devoid of anything to do or any enemies to fight. In one game I wound up advancing through two maps without actively attempting to do so. The computer forced me to move towards completing the game.
*Replayability*
Unless you're big into multiplayer, nope, not really. It gets pretty routine after about five hours because all there really is to do is collect a squad and run up to the front and shoot enemies until you die. Rinse, repeat. Finish up a campaign? Awesome! Now it's over and the next time you want to play you have to start from scratch.
If you're looking for an open world sandbox military shooter with RPG elements... this is not it. If you want something to screw around on for a few hours, you might like it. But for me this was definitely not what I thought I was buying.

You can choose how to do things - Do you want to command 20 soldiers to charge a base, or do you want to sneak around with a silenced pistol and take out some high-valued commanders? Do you snipe encoming soldiers, or blow up radio towers to disrupt communications?
There are lots of things to do, and the battles are intense. It's also a very long game, battles often lasting up to an hour, sometimes more. Despite the drawn-out battles, it doesn't really start to feel boring - You always have a goal to work towards, and if you find fighting on the front lines growing boring, you can grab a silenced pistol and sneak behind lines to take out valuable targets and blow stuff up, only to come back and find your assistance has allowed your men to push forward and take the zone.
The game also has a very robust multiplayer system. Holy crap, multiplayer is fun. There's co-op, competitive, etc. This game is jam-packed with replayability. I'd strongly reccomend it to anyone.

A truly new and fresh game back in the days, where parkour meets pseudo - historic fights with evil templars.
That game was a really nice distraction from most of the stuff released back then. But what it has to offer now?
First of all this is really part of trilogy (pentalogy?) depicts a story of one guy, named Desmond Miles, snatched by some organization, locked in a room and forced to relive past lives of his ancestors in search for... Well that would be a spoiler, so I let You to find out.
Game take place in two different places, one being today reality and second in middle ages Holy Land. While present offers some background story of Desmond and his story, the Animus part is where the fun really happens. You're an Assassin named Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, sent by Your order to kill cartoonishly evil templars in attempt to free Holy Land from their grasp. Altaïr also slowly reveals their true purpose there and his job became one of finding something hidden through generations... Overall story is pretty good and makes almost no effort in captivating player.
Now little about gameplay - it is a third person perspective, where You're allowed to climb almost every building in game. Unfortunately the climbing itself is a little clunky, but if You can grind Your teeth a little, You will get satisfaction quickly. Apart from this there is some horse riding, running on rooftops and many fights. Altaïr slowly gets better weapons and means to fight more enemies at once, without dying. Fights themselves are pretty spectacular, with many different finishers and moves, depending on weapons used. They are also pretty intuitive, if one learn their moves.
Main quests are done very good, but side quests are really boring and repetetive, and that is very unfortunate, as they do very little to expand the story, and they can be just ignored.
While game aged a little, some vistas still are magnificent. Animations of fights are done very good too. You will notice that many building looks the same, but that can't be avoided in a game that big and somewhat complex. Overall graphics are pretty good.
Do I have to tell You that the preferred way to do that is by playing with a controller? No, I think not.
P. S. Remember - water is Your most deadly enemy, and You can't counter it;)

The setting: In cyberpunk Paris, memories are bought and sold as a commodity, and you play as an 'errorist agent', stealing and altering memories in order to tear down the corp that monopolizes the memory technology. Unfortunately for such an awesome premise, the game itself is fairly mediocre. The main gameplay is 3rd person brawling, and while being able to design your own combos is novel, overall the game mechanics are shallow and toward the end of the game it was somewhat tedious. I really wish the game had capitalized more on the "memory tech" premise - there's some cool moments like using someone else's memories to navigate a safe path past sentries, or when you get to "remix" memories (basically playing through a scene and finding ways to modify the scene so that you alter its outcome), but those moments are too few and in between you're platforming or beating up dudes. The storyline is serviceable, though the lack of agency in the main character is frustrating (for 99% of the game she goes around doing what someone else is telling her to do). Other than that, the visual designs of cyberpunk Paris and the "memory landscapes" are fantastic. I really hope they make a sequel and make a game worthy of the great premise.

First off, I have a fear of the paranormal, so this kind of game is effectively my worst enemy. That's why I decided to start off with Spooky's House of Jump Scares. It's a seemingly cute and cuddly parody of modern horror games, where you travel around a massive mansion full of terrifying monsters. For the first few minutes you wonder why you though of getting it. For the next few hours, you're running for your life from the freakiest things ever. Think cardboard cutouts aren't scary? Just wait.

its addicting and it doesnt have those high quality graphics like other horror games do just to make up for their game not being good at all, but this game shows that you dont need fancy graphics to be truly a horror game, and that even the cutest of things can scare anyone if the setting and music is just right.

SHOJS is definitely a game that is defined by its nickname: it's spooky and FULL of jumpscares. You start off fairly easy, with the jumpscares being very cutesy and the specimens relatively easy to avoid. As you progress, however, and meet more specimens, the scenery gets creepier, the specimens tougher and the story more apparent. Sadly, it also ruins the fear factor, as most of the game's scary aspects are on its ambience and incredible music score.
While many of the specimens are creepy, scary, and draw lots of inspiration from other horror games, creepypastas, etc., after a few hundred floors it becomes a game of "run from the monster and don't look back"...or at least if you don't defend yourself later like I did xD It really loses that sense of fear and helplessness (except for a select few specimens), and becomes quite predictable. However, at the beginning of the game I was utterly petrified because I definitely didn't know what to expect. Looking back, I definitely don't regret playing, as it was 4+ hours worth of YouTube videos, but it definitely wasn't as scary later on. If anything, it got kind of frustrating with certain specimens...especially if you died multiple times because you weren't sure how to escape them.
All in all, I do recommend Spooky's. The art style, the music, the characters, the sense of the unknown, the game's length and its inspiration from other media of the genre make it a must-play. However, be aware that it becomes somewhat predictable later on, with some suspense still evident. LAG Studios, awesome job!
Also, the edition of DLC is great. I'm just a cheapskate and a scaredy-cat xD
Score: 8/10

Full review below this paragraph. First of all the community for this game is TOXIC. The moderator of their forums even tried digging into my account to make fun of how many hours I played X and Y because they have no argument for why this game is good. It isn't good mostly due to all kills being luck-based RNG, that alone negates any claim of skill so deal with it this game sucks for multiplayer on that basis alone and they disagree but in a bad manner. I was even banned from the forums and my posts deleted while the even worse posts from the community stayed, then was unbanned after Steam decided to step on the dev for this unacceptable behaviour. From the dev himself no less. Shameful. And now on to a deeper review of the game itself:
Short version: Attempt at top-down 2d Battlefield, key word attempt.The many positive reviews are either cooked up and fake or those other players must exist in a universe where crappy gameplay seems fun. That or the game has wide appeal but it did not manage to appeal to me specifically. If this looks interesting to you wait on sale at least, not worth full price. It still feels like it should be Early Access and in Beta still because of lack of depth, you are doing the same thing over and over and what you are doing is not interesting enough to count as good gameplay.
Longer version: The lack of first person perspective and the 3rd dimension ruins this game (and yes I know you can climb buildings and it is pseudo-3d, still top-down perspective) and this is a big failing in design of this game. The damage system is very dumb and is the #1 problem with this game, there is a chance that your bullet will kill and will roll the random number generator (RNG) to see if your aimed hit counts, no joke it's that bad quite literally. This leaves the game open to many times where you can hit a guy 6 times and he stands and they hit you once you die. The RNG is all you depend on, no matter how accurate your shot it rolls the dice to see if that shot does anything. Very stupid system, big mistake on part of the dev who did not think this through in any way. The RNG damage system alone is a good reason to walk away from this game and never look back, it doesn't require skill to kill if you can hit someone several times and none count. As for lack of first person perspective you will get shot in an imperceivable manner all the time. You look like you are behind cover and then get hit from a direction by stray bullets while still obviously in cover. This is a constant in gameplay and I cannot recommend this game to anyone I like. This would be 10x more of a fun game if we had first person perspective and no RNG-damage with this style of gameplay but it is what it is. The attempt at fixing this issue with perspective is a crosshair that shows a line where you cannot see between your character and cursor but that doesn't work well at all. Shots that should hit don't, shots that shouldn't hit do. Those two problems are the crux of my main issues the game and it is crippled because of it.
As for the gameplay singleplayer is just a back and forth. Mindless grinding worse than an MMO in here for exp. AI is too dumb on your team to take objectives properly, and the flawed spawning system means you will be shot at behind and from the side of places that should be secured. Any attempt at being smart you get smacked with several guys spawning from where you just snuck around from and them shooting you through cover more often than not. Overall uninteresting gameplay. I tried it several times on a friends computer and never got it, finally after enough harassment from him I finally bought it and that was $15 completely wasted. Do not trust the Steam review system like I did, I typically read the negative reviews first but at the time it only showed one on the store page which is deceptive. I repeat what was stated above: If this looks interesting to you wait on sale at least, not worth full price.

In RWR you are a grunt, a simple soldier, cannon fodder, expendable trooper trying to survive on the battlefield.
You can make a difference, but it will probably never be a major one, in this way the game is actually quite different from most, where you the player ends up winning single handedly against impossible odds.

Don't be fooled by the simplistic graphics; this is a very fun war game.   It is a war of attrition, as your man on the field can only really take one hit; you have to use cover, line-of-sight, flanking, supressing fire, all of it to stay alive and push the enemy back.  With vehicles and a large selection of weapons, there's a lot going on here.
You will die - over and over and over again, but respawns are very fast though.  If  your team is working together, you'll advance across the battlefield, taking objectives.  Totally addicting - I've played hours until I couldn't anymore because my hands went numb.  I've mostly played the co-op Invasion mode, where 32 players and a host of NPC soldiers battle an enemy AI.  The AI isn't always the brightest, but throws hundreds of soldiers at you making each battle intense.
Highly recommended.  If you do get it, be sure to read the guides in the Steam community hub, they'll help make sense of it all.

First thing you will notice about Slain is the gorgeous pixel art graphics and amazing metal soundtrack, animation is also pretty darn good but do bear in mind that it's keeping with traditions so may appear to the perfectionists out there to be missing a few frames but it works well and as intended.
Difficulty is something i'm delighted to see in this game, it pays homage in a really good way to classic platformers of the past in that it's a very challenging without being insanely difficult that it wouldn't overly frustrate you so that's all good. Pixel perfect is a good way to describe the collision detection in this game, that is to say how close to an object you have to be before impact occurs, this is somewhat important so i would describe it as being tight in this regard so do be careful and time your jumps to perfection.
Controls are spot on, for reference i am playing with keyboard which uses cursor keys for control of your character and other keys for slash etc. This isn't a control system that gets used these days but something you would have seen years ago but for me this just feels very natural, didn't try gamepad controls but it's there for those who prefer it and also i didn't have any control issue's and any kind of input lag either. I will just say that keyboard bindings are not listed in the launcher/configuration and there is virtually no options ingame apart from music and sound fx volume.
I won't spoil what the rest of the game has to offer as that should be for you to discover but there are some great little features and surprises in store.
Metal soundtrack
Pixel art graphics (amazing really)
Slick controls
Great difficulty
Lack of options
Some achievements are currently bugged
Just to sum up would i recommend this game? Yes i certainly do especially if you love and remember classic action platformers but do bear in mind that it's a challenging game too so if that's your thing then you could do a lot worse than giving Slain a shot and i rate it 8.9/10.
For reference i purchased this game myself and didn't receive a free key from the developer or publisher and in no way related to them, thanks for reading and hope that you all enjoy your experience.

An absolutely fantastic, one of a kind, unique game... if you play it with HUD turned off. I explain it in detail here:
But the short gist of it, AC1 was clearly designed to be played without a HUD (except some of the missions that were added in the PC version, they didn't take HUD-less design into account), and it provides a whole different experience. As an example, you're not going to an eavesdrop icon to listen to a minute of conversation and that's it, mission done. You're going to the Jewish Quarter because that's where the Rafiq told you there might be information, and you find the Jewish Quarter by seeing in the distance the Star of David on a gateway, while you're on the rooftop, and then you explore and use your Eagle Vision to see who knows something.
As soon as the HUD is introduced, a lot of this is lost, and the cyclic nature of the game is seen (which is why a lot of people call the game repetitive, because HUD makes the cyclic nature obvious, but without it you NEED it to learn patterns and to investigate what's out of the pattern).
Even if you've played and like the game already, but have never played it with HUD fully off... do it. It won't be a perfect HUD-less experience on PC (mainly because, as I mentioned, new PC missions don't take HUD-less design into account, but you can ignore those because not every mission is required for game completion), but it will still be great and unique.

It's been a long journey waiting but the wait was very much worth it. This expands on the Monsters' Den universe in the only way it could, by allowing you to venture onto the surface world! I love love love old Monsters' Den games, they're nostalgic to me because they defined those countless hours you'd spend on sites like Armor Games, Kongregate, and Addicting Games just browsing the hundreds of games until one piqued your interest enough to try.
Now onto the game, it's essentially Monsters' Den Chronicles with a fresh coat of paint and a bunch more bits and bobs attached. It can be a bit overwhelming at first given all the content there is, the large map, and all the little factions spread across the world. But once you get down to it it's really just old school Monsters' Den. The dungeon-crawling, loot-gathering adventure that I've known and loved for years.
If you've played other Monsters' Den then this one will feel very familiar, just more expanded. There's a new Skill Tree similar to Dragon Age, each character has 2 "subclasses" full of active and passive abilities that allow you to choose how you want to play that character (for example, you can have a healer archer with the Nature subclasss, or have them as a damage dealer with the Archery subclass, or a mix of the two).
If you haven't played other Monsters' Den then I suggest you go and play Chronicles before investing in this one to see how you like it. If you like Chronicles then odds are you're definitely going to like this one, both games are built the same way this one just has much, much more content.
As for other aspects of the game, the art style is nice, huge step up from Chronicles. Each combat encounter has a nice backdrop. The art for the characters is really detailed, and the dungeons are creepy and dark. Character and enemy design is also very nice.
Music and sounds are very Monsters' Den. Visceral and satisfying when your attacks and abilities land. The music adds tension when it needs to and eases up during the lulls.
I would say the one thing that might turn people off is the naturally repetitive gameplay. It's is simple and works for me but it might not work for everyone. You go from dungeon to dungeon, defeating the enemies and looting the place before moving on to the next one. The quest system and overworld bring much needed variety to the game, but it does boil down to the dungeon crawling aspect pretty heavily. If you were content with how the gameplay was in previous installments then this one is a no brainer because it gives exactly the same thing but with a much better foundation and sprinkles even more onto that foundation.
Fun game, however quite a few bugs, one of which happens quite frequently in dungeon - screen goes black and you cant open up the menu and have to force close the game. Be sure to save often!
