At first, Monsters' Den: Godfall seemed alluring in its promise. It's a turn-based RPG with base-building elements and a slathering of subsystems. It's got a real solid set up for its game world, one in which the various deities of its Grayhawk-y pantheon have all been killed off except for the goddess of revenge, and its promise of customization in party makeup and skill loadout is appealing.
Unfortunately, Monsters' Den's biggest problem is probably its biggest asset as a Kongregate title: it is really, really same-y and boring. If you want a timekill that will require minimal conscious thought, Monsters' Den will put you in a zen-like state of RPG clicking. On Normal difficulty, single ability spam with the stock party that the game assigns you right out of the gate (in my case, complete with a fighter named Chad) is enough to surmount all mobs, once you've figured out what order to target them in. To compensate for that, (slightly) tougher enemies are damage sponges. Combats drag.
I'm not sure if I ever lost a fight, and I deliberately challenged dungeons outside of my level bracket in an attempt to see if there was any cool peripheral stuff outside of the main plot. There are sidequests with plotlines and occasional sites of interest on the world map, but like the rest of the game, they're not very interesting.
The core plotline, after its righteously awesome setting fails to deliver any further information or worldbuilding, is a bit tedious. Mostly you stand in the presence of people that the designers want you to know are really important and listen to them panic about cosmic things, waiting for the inevitable instructions to go to a dungeon or kill an extraversal being.
If you want immersion, check out Darkest Dungeon. If you want tactical crunch, there are oodles of other games on Steam. If you want narrative development that engages your characters as principal actors, rather than slightly awkward bystanders, most other RPGs have this down.
What Godfall is good for is spacing out while staring at your screen, clicking idly, and paying more attention to the podcast you're listening to than the game itself. It's not objectively bad, especially if what you want is a timekill, but every aspect of the game feels just...kind of flat.

Where do I stand on this one? Think I'll start on the positives. The game, when it works, plays great. For a franchise whose protagonist for the longest time was a head at the bottom of the screen they have surely understood character creation. They've made absolutely sure to give all major and sub-major NPCs a full personality, making the inbetween-sections and cutscenes full of life. Sprinkled with B.J.'s inner monologues both in and out of missions, there is a certain depth that you just wouldn't expect out of a game that is about slaughtering hordes of Nazis. This does not mean that it's without it's humor, both in the extremely over-the-top plot devices, and with some bits here and there that proves that it's a game capable of not taking itself too seriously. The levels are also sprinkled with collectibles where a large part are readables that give you tiny glimpses into the minds of the denizens of this dystopia which helps color in whatever the story leaves out. Gameplay, gunplay and visuals are also as stunning as you'd expect from Machine Games at this point. There is real satisfaction in most combat elements, whether you like the sneaky playstyle or the blazing glory of dual-wielding shotguns, and the game provides you with customizations that allows you to play as you want really. All in all, when the game works it is great.

So, this is a very early review because I feel like some of the early negative reviews are not fully thought out. I will try to keep it simple.
I:
I have no issues with controller lag. I use an Xbox 360 controller to play, I do get a second or so of lag with the keyboard (left and right direction only) so this must be a keyboard issue only, for now. I was about to see what they meant after I got the first sword powerupgrade to realize that these specific enemies, not going spoil anything, are better to fight without the powerupgrade. Sword powers are interchangeable or can be turned off. This adds a little tactic and strategy, which is a positive in my eyes. Also, people might be trying to play this game on to high of a setting for their computer, which unsurprisingly could cause input lag and FPS drops.
IMPORTANT NOTE Before playing the game you get a box that lets you choose graphic display such as resolution, quality, window or fullscreen, and Display 1 (2,3, etc.). The same box also shows you the controller and keyboard setup, which you can reassign the keys (Only movement keys can be reassigned). So, knowing which keyboard keys to press can be a mystery. Seems that QWER (attack), 1234...(Mana attack/swordupgrade), P (pause) and ENTER are used but I haven't played much with the keyboard controls.
II:
Sound, yes the soundtrack is great. However, I agree it is a little loud. So what I did was go into options and turned it down a notch and guess what?! it made sound way better and I now hear all the little game sounds as well (e.g. foot steps, swinging sword, etc.). I also have good headphones so that might help. Also, if the soundtrack bores you than change how you play and try to get past that specific area instead of getting slain or mute it until you get past that area you keep having to repeat. PS the slain death screen is great.
III:
I have read discussion forums that GOG had an earlier build on release date and most people seem to be writing reviews off of that wrong release or not realizing everything offered to them; Or, some other technical issue that I seem not to have.
IV:
You can exit the screen withOUT Alt+Tab, no idea why someone said that only Alt+Tab will let you exit.
V:
Some letters in the game are hard to read due to the font choice, but logical guessing from storyline and other words I can make out what is being stated.
VI:
The pixel art is beautiful and I cannot wait to see what other enemies await as so far there has been a good mix.
VII:
Variety in attacks, including mana and weapon upgrades seem adequate and rather more than I expected them to include. I expected something closer to Castlevania but get a lot more and I am talking about NES castlevania style/types of weapon and attack choices.

This game has the potential to be great, but ultimatly it falls on its face. You are given a taste of nuanced strategic combat, defensive base building and the progression from a lowly priviate with a rifle to an officer calling in artillery and reinforcements. Sadly, all of these mechanics are in the game but the meta-game renders them useless.
One of the worst parts is the total lack of a real tuturial. I had to spend an hour surfing the wiki to figure out some of the basic mechanics, which are actually pretty important when it comes to performing decently in the game. I don't know how I even would have figured most of the game out without a guide. Simple things like knowing you can click the yellow dots on the map to choose where you respawn, or the ways to obtain in game cash are never told to you and without knowing about it, and many other things, you end up having a worse time when you first start playing.
RWR turns into a major grindfest with no end reward. Without going into the gameplay details, which will make little sense without having played the game, many of the mechanics become very frustrating and repetitive after a couple hours of play. You are left with nothing to do but spawn, kill as many bad guys as possible and hope that your army doesn't get stuck capturing a base, moving on and then losing it, over and over. It's not an epic battle over a single position, it's a game breaking, virtually unbreakable cycle in singleplayer.
The multiplayer technically has PVP but I've never seen a lobby with more than one or two people in it. The PVE lobbies are hectic battles and can be fun for a while but they soon become boring once you realize that human victory is inevitable, always.
I honestly think that if another year of dev time had gone into the game it could have been one of my favorite indie titles of all time, which is the worst part. The idea is amazing, even the individual in game concepts are great, but it is the way they are implemented which makes RWR fail.

Rogue Entertainment gives us Quake's second official mission pack, which would be as good as the first were it not for its hearty share of unique fumbles. A few weapons have alternate "firing modes" (they really are separate weapons) in this, and they all use unique ammo: Both nailguns have Lava Nails (just plain extra damage), the Grenade Launcher has Multi-Grenades (shorter fuse, explodes into a cluster of five smaller bombs - direct hits are functionally identical to regular grenades), the Rocket Launcher has Multi-Rockets (four rockets in an even horizontal spread) and the Thunderbolt has the Plasma Gun, which fires an energy orb that acts like a more damaging rocket and that will, on impact, shoot electric tendrils at nearby enemies. The problem is, the game gives you way too much ammo for these new weapons, in addition to generously providing supplies for your old arsenal. The end result is a rather easy game on any difficulty, a game which allows you to indulge on using extremely heavy firepower very often. Multi-Rockets in particular will turn most encounters into a joke, as they make short work of anything short of a Shambler and the final boss.
Dissolution of Eternity comes with many new enemies, though other than the two new bosses, they're essentially just remixes of the classic ones. There are also two new pickups, both of temporary effect: the Anti-Grav Belt, which lessens the effect of gravity over the player's movement, and the Power Shield, which reduces the damage and knockback of attacks received from the front. Level design is somewhat inconsistent in its quality compared to both the original layouts and those from the first mission pack, and the game opens with a rather dreary looking level, perhaps the ugliest of the lot. That said, some levels look and play like the best of 'em, and the new texture sets, based on human antiquity, are really nice. An easy recommendation, even if it is the weakest among the first Quake's official offerings.

There will be spoilers in this review.
This game is what happens when indie storytelling meets some solid visuals.
The art is impressive, the gore feels weirdly consistent with the otherwise beautiful vistas and the setting is memorable. The puzzles are straightforward, but engaging. The combat feels fair.
The gaming experience is minimalistic in its approach. There is no HUD at all, there is no health bar, no quest pointer and there is no tutorial either. Beside the keymap on the main menu which explains which button does what, there is no explanation for some intricacies like getting up after a knockdown, switching between enemies, being able to parry ranged attacks and shieldbreaking. The controls are mostly conveyed to you by the voices in your head. It's not a complaint, the confusion of the learning process really adds to the atmosphere.
The narrative is not particularly deep, but explains the complicated subject of mental illness in the simplest terms and puts you into the shoes of a troubled Celtic girl in a believable and immersive way. One could argue that as mad as the main character is, her condition would be more debilitating than helpful and thus the depiction is not as realistic as claimed, but then there would be no game mechanic and the disbelief can be easily suspended.
That is all nitpicking. To be fait, the game has only two major issues.
First of all, the decision to have parts of the cutscenes live-action. There has never been a good live-action part in history of video games. Movies can often get away with CG and even when it is at its least subtle like in Sin City or Immortel Ad Vitam, you end up with unique, albeit corny, visuals. On the video game side of things, you have bad acting ruining the experience of Myst and Phantasmagoria or just feeling out of place, like in Enslaved and Hellblade. The effect is just jarring, especially considering how far motion capture has gone and how well it is done in this game and you just have to ask yourself, why not have those cutscenes motion captured too. The immersion would certainly stand to benefit from it.
Second and last is the permadeath mechanic or rather the lack thereof. After the first combat sequence we are treated to a message that we can only die so many times before the save is wiped. At this moment the game breaks two of its own rules. It explains a game mechanic and it lies about it. The combination of the two feels like the cheapest shot in an otherwise great game. If that mechanic would be explained by the voices in your head and then turn out to be a lie, there would be no problem, they are an unreliable narrator by definition after all. If the mechanic was actually in place, I would be slightly peeved by the message on screen breaking immersion, but not much. Even if the permadeath would occur, it would not be too bothersome, since the game is short, the puzzles are simple and the experience is fascinating enough to go for another round. And yet, your save will not be deleted no matter how many times you die and the lie is given to you by the only words on screen you see between starting and ending credits.
In spite of the aforementioned, I have to say that this is one of the best games  I played in the last couple of years and I would certainly recommend it to anyone who values a cinematic experience in a videogame and misses the spacial trickery of games like Portal and Prey (The original one, not whatever we got this year)

I think in order to fairly and objectively review a game, you need to look at it in four section: Graphics, gameplay, sound, and story. These four elements make up a game. By this reasoning, let me review To The Moon.
Graphics - N/A
Graphics are arguably the least important aspect of a game, in my opinion. To The Moon is created in RPG maker, so graphics are even less important. 16 bit, familiar animations, etc.
Gameplay - 3/10
TTM is not a game, per se, but more of a collection of cutscenes. This is fine, because it is heavily story driven.
Story - 5/10
Unfortunately, I was disappointed. The story is creative, but no where near the level of depth and emotions that I was led to believe existed here. The dialogue is boring at best and the majority of time incredibly cringey. References to Animorphs feel out of place. The dialogue is full of colloquialisms and phonetic spellings which are awful.
Sound - 10/10
The soundtrack for this game is amazing and it's only saving grace. Mostly piano based, which works nicely with the dialogue and triggers an emotional connection. Unfortunately for TTM, that's the only good part of the game.
I paid 1.99 for TTM and finished it in two sittings in about 3 hours. I feel like that's a fair value for what I paid, but I wouldn't pay much more. In my opinion this game is completely overrated and feels more like a high school play than a 'brilliant' game.
Overall Rating - 6/10

The puzzles themselves as far as difficulty goes are challenging at times but definitely not "difficult." I bought this on sale after the Atlas Rising update because people were excited about it and I appreciated that the developer put time into fixing their game.  I read a review a while back that said no amount of work could ever fix this game because it is a fundamentally bad game at its core.  I think that guy was right.
There really isn't much game here at all.  People like to say it's a "chill" game, but I think that's misleading.  It's not so much relaxing and enjoying the atmosphere as it is zoning out because you're doing the same pointless thing for the 600th time.
Pointlessness is what this game is all about.  The worst example is the pulse drive.  You need iron to travel between planets quickly.  If you run out, you stop flying at crazy fast speed and it will take several real life weeks to get where you're going.   Better stock up on iron while you're on planet, right?  Nah.  Any time you run out of iron mid-flight, your ship will stop in the middle of an asteroid field and you can just shoot a couple asteroids to get all of the iron you need.  Of course, it would be awful if you ran out of iron and had to spend the next few weeks of your actual life getting back to a planet.  That's your cue to remove this pointless system from your game, not take away all of the consequences of that system.
All of the other resources are basically the same way.  A few of them will require a bit more searching, but you never really feel like you're stocking up on resources for your journey.  It's all just part of the same boring routine.
But hey, searching for resources gets you to go explore all of these crazy planets, right?  Yes it does, but that's not a good thing.  This game might have billions of places to land your ship, but every one of them it basically identical.  It has two main colors and maybe a couple more secondary colors, but they're laid out basically the same.  The 3D models look different on each planet, but just barely.  The animals look different but they behave identically and none of them are actually interesting to look at.  There are all kinds of different weather hazards, but the only difference between them is the icon that shows up next to your suit's hazard bar.  The only real difference you'll find is that sometimes a planet has water.  Woo!  Space stations are the same way, but even more blatant.  Each one is unambiguously identical aside from placement of the aliens inside.
Exploring these identical planets is even worse.  It's the same awful "points of interest" system that bad open world games have been copying since the first Assassin's Creed game.  Fly to a point of interest.  Press X to <do thing>.  Get reward that wasn't worth the time it took to fly there.
There lies my main complaint.  No Man's Sky has no respect for your time.  If it's not wasting your time by making you fly all over for lousy rewards, it's wasting your time by making you sit and wait.  Want to fly from one planet to another?  Max out the throttle and it says it'll take several real life weeks to get there.  Turn on your pulse drive and it drops down to a minute and a half.  Wow, technology is amazing!  Now you just have to sit and do nothing for a minute and a half while you wait to arrive.  Cool...
No Man's Sky is a game of good ideas, none of which are executed well.  It tries too hard to slap a game on top of its poorly-built systems and fails at every attempt.  To the guy who said that this game is unfixable, I should have listened to you.

I'm one of the ones that liked the game when it first came out, but probably because I didn't follow all the hype leading up to release. I knew about the 18 quintillion planets procedurally generated and that was enough to convince me to buy!
It wasn't until after that I realized how much more was meant to be included. I understood a lot of hate toward the game and developers for the misleading advertising. I wasn't mad, just a little disappointed because even before I learned about all the missing features, I was starting to notice that the game seemed unpolished, unbalanced, or just plain unfinished in some places. I kept on playing, but it became more and more tedious. Landing on planets became a chore, just to restock so I can jump to the next system, making my way to the center. I lost interest before I got there. I would play every now and then when I heard about new updates, but never more than an hour or so, then go back to some other game. I racked up about 60 hours at that point.
But now! I followed some other folk's advice and very apprehensively deleted my precious save. Starting fresh, this is an entirely new experience. Now it feels polished, definately feels more balanced. It still doesn't feel quite finished, but in that good way that you know there are so many possibilities to make the game even better. An entire universe gives a lot of wiggle room to expand. MAJOR props to the developers for keeping at it. It couldn't have been easy with the angry mob demanding their heads.
I'm officially addicted again. I put in 30 hours just since the last update and I'm going to make it to the center this time.

A challenging turn based tactics game.  (Played on veteran difficulty: 125% hp and 125% damage boost for foes)
Cons:
-The game is still buggy and unbalanced. The bugs sometimes are what cause the balance issues. (some skills are currently OP, others are more or less pointless.)
-It is not an easy game. The boss fights in particular are the biggest problems you will face.
-The pacing is slow, and everything takes time to progress.
-It gets repetitive. There just aren't enough monsters, and events.
Pros:
-It's a sadistic sort of fun (imagine dark souls)
-The feeling when you beat the unkillable boss is amazing.
-Tons of items that can be used differently. (Allowing for multiple types of playstyles)
-Interesting story and lore.
-Dev is bug fixing like a madman.
Final verdict.
I recommend the game for people who loved the other monsters den games, but I doubt a general audience would put up with the bugs, and nigh unfair difficulty at the moment.

Not gonna lie, it's hard for me to recommend this one.  Out of the three campaigns I've started, I've never been able to get very far.  Primarily it's because of three reasons.
Reason 1: Your guys start off weak.  I mean, super weak.  As in, your clerics can't even heal until they've levelled up.  Nobody can do anything but attack for the first couple of fights, which kind of defeats the purpose of the battle system, tbh.  Meanwhile, all the enemies can still use all their skills, including group heals that can restore them from near empty to full (♥♥♥♥ING ORC SHAMANS!).  Not so bad when you have the ability to mitigate some of the bull later, absolute hell when all you can do is attack, wait, and run.
Reason 2: Your starting guys are random.  Sure, most of them can learn how to heal eventually, but in the early game when you've only got one frontline fighter against three frontline orcs, it doesn't matter how much damage your back line can do.  It also doesn't explain how to create new characters, which it really should do the second you walk inside your keep doors.
Reason 3: The dungeon modifiers are seemingly weighted to screw you over.  The ratio of fetid to non-fetid dungeons is inordinately high.  For the information of everyone who hasn't played this game, each dungeon is randomly generated, both in layout and in the form of special modifiers which change the conditions affecting your party in each battle within said dungeon.  The "Fetid" modifier cancels your guy's health and mana regeneration, basically killing your chances of winning any battles at low levels.  It doesn't show up too often there; though it shows up what feels like every dungeon as you get higher up, where its only function is to basically stretch out the battles from the challenging and fun area to the "Screw you, I'm throwing fun out the window because you've played this run too long" area.  I've started just dropping the quests that make me fight in fetid areas the minute I find out about it, just because it's not fun at all.
That said, on the one game I managed to push through that first hurdle, the game really showed its polish and shine.  Once you get some skills, the tactics really start to open up, and once you get some decent equipment, you really start to feel powerful when you steamroll a group of bad guys that would have ripped you apart in the early-game.
I'm gonna give this one a tentative recommendation, provided something gets rebalanced in the start of the game.  Maybe include squad-hiring/making in the tutorial.  Also provided he adjusts the spawn rate of "Fetid" from "Every other level" to "One in a hundred".

Bethesda Software's Wolfenstein II: Thew New Colossus refines what was built in the previous entry into a well crafted first persons shooter-with a few problems.
Wolf II continues the story of BJ Blaskovic's Nazi killing adventure where it left off in the previous game. We get to finally see what a Nazi controlled America looks like and it does an alright job showing it, but the game does too much telling. The characters and collectables in the game are well written but a lot of the stuff they talk about in a Nazi controlled America would have been interesting to see. An example is, you hear a conversation that slavery has been re-insituted in the country, the Ku Klux Klan are being used as Nazi enforcers but you don't really get to see any of that. All of the enemies are Nazis or robot Nazis, if they mixed up some variations in the game, it would add a whole lot more flavor in the game and an more fleshed out world.
The story for the game is more personal, focusing on BJ's allies and not so much on the world. We get insight on his thoughts on seeing his country being turned into a Nazi state. He is going to be a father and he wants to make sure they don't grow up under the Nazi flag. He is trying to start a revolution and "put the fighting spirit back in America" by recruiting resistance groups. I feel the story for the first game is much better and just a lot more interesting. They only tell you all of the horrible stuff happening in America, but don't show it. I have to wonder why the developers decided not to show how the Nazis are treatening minorities while in the previous game, they showed a concentration camp and you had to fight your way out of it. A lot of missed opportunities in my opinion. Be warned, there are moments were you have to toss away all logic and if you can do that, you'll be fine.
The gunplay is amazing as expected from a Wolfenstein game. You can kill enemies with a nice selection of weapons, three barrel shotguns? No problem. Propane tank launcher? You bet. You can mix and match and dual wield a shotgun in one hand and a propane launcher in the other for some hyper violence. It isn't a big arsenal, but the quality and unique weapons will make killing Nazis fun regardless.
You can approach the game however you like, gunsblazing or stealth through the game. Skill progression and abilies in the game allows you to play how you like. However, in my playthrough of the game, I feel like I was being shoehorned into going loud and shoot my way through. The auto saving system seems to be almost random. There were times when the game autosaved at points were I kept dying every time it reloads. Needless to say, it was very fustrating.
Overall, the game isn't too bad. There are things it does right and there are things they could have done a lot better. I was happy with the purchase but if you want to wait for a slight price drop, I understand. But I know you'll have a good time in making America Nazi free again.

POST-BACK FROM HELL EDIT:
Well, they did it. They fixed the game. The controls have been made to actually work, and as such the combat is now not only functional, but fun, as well as fairly skillful. Enemies now have different behaviors that actually make you react to what you're facing, and running in and swinging wildly is likely to get you killed. The protagonist has also recieved some rehauling, and your attacks now feel a lot more calculated - The clunky and sorta pointless-feeling heavy attacks are gone, and have been replaced with an awesome charge move that requires you to carefully position and time it, but delivers massive damage if done right. The spells also feel like they're more worthwhile to use, the block feature now has a dedicated button, and the backdash is now actually usable as a dodge.
All of your moves, which you now actually know how to perform due to a new and improved tutorial system and a control screen, feel a lot more responsive and satisfying to use (the spirit bomb is particularly fun) This, along with the variety of enemies and situations and occasional acquirement of a new thing, keep things fun you make your way through the pretty, pretty levels. Also, a major fix that I didn't even mention neede to be made previously - the "You Died" screen, which was previously about 5-6 seconds long and unskippable, is now gone in less than a second.
The dialogue is still a little bit cringy (although still way better), and there are spots that are a little janky, but overall the game has been transformed from a mess to a really solid and enjoyable game. True to my word, I'm changing this review to a positive one, and now recommend this game to those who are interested, as it now actually plays as good as it looks.
I will, however, keep the outdated negative review below, for posterity. Those who fail to learn from history etc.
=================================================================
Allow me to start this review by saying that the game is gorgeous. The art direction is great, and the sprite and animation quality is top notch. The music is also pretty good killin' metal, if you're into that. This concludes the positive part of this review. I am also prefacing by saying that I played with a keyboard, as I feel that controllers might have a better go of it.
(EDIT : I have tried playing a controller, and the input delay is gone on that. Everything else said in the review still applies, however)
There's a phrase I've heard several times now regarding Slain! : "I really wanted to like this game".  And I did, honest! I was instantly sold on it when I saw how it looked. But as it stands as of this review, it is just terrible. I will of course immediately change this review if I see improvement.
The first problem you'll notice after launching the game is that the controls work only when they feel like it. Navigating the menu is the first obstacle of the game, as hitting the buttons only works sometimes. Once you start playing, you will realize that this is not an isolated issue.  For some reason, certain actions, particularly running, have a significant delay before they come in. I can't imagine WHY, but this sort of feels like it might be intentional, as other buttons work perfectly well, such as the two attack buttons.
And I had to personally discover what those buttons are, because the game provides absolutely no insight as to what the controls might be. Arrow keys move your character, and Q and W are the attack buttons. You can press R to do a backdash (a pointless one, by the way, which I'll get to in a bit), and the 1 button shoots a ghostly fireball. You can also duck and hit the W button to expand a full bar of energy to cast a screen-clearing smart bomb. I think there might be a third spell, but I have yet to see it.
I might seem like I don't know a lot about how to play the game, and that's because it's arcane secrets are skillfully hidden by the barely helpful handful of tips you recieve at the top of the screen. As someone who's pretty seasoned in terms of playing video games, though, I can say with confidence that either I completely do not understand how combat in this game works, or the combat system is a broken mess. You have a light and heavy attack button, and you seem to be able to do some combos (I use the word "seem" because I have yet to make them come out reliably), and decapitating opponents gives you more energy for spells. Actually fighting is a joke - Your attacks have hitstun, but the hitstun doesn't always work, either by design or through flaw, which means enemies will often be able to hit you while you're swinging at them.
The game implies that there is a block in a hint, which I have not yet discovered how to perform, and the backdash is essentially useless because enemies just stand there rapidly swinging, which means you're either going to backdash out of the range of your own attack, or not backdash far enough and just get hit by the next attack that comes. If there is any technique to the fighting, I have not discovered it, and the only way I've made any serious progress through the game is by just running forwards and mashing the light attack button, trading health with enemies as I move along, and using the smartbomb when there's too many of them. The developers apparently expected you to do this, as the levels I've seen so far are generously sprinkled with collectables that fully restore your HP and Energy, further cemeting my theory that this is what I'm supposed to be doing.
There are three things that will stop your progress- traps, which kill you instantly. Clumps of enemies who hitstun you to death, which I guess can be construed as the player's fault, and Bosses. I have yet to defeat a boss enemy in Slain!. I have encountered two in my time playing, the first of which I was able to just run past and proceed to the next area, and the second one which hurts you when you touch it, which is as far as I got in the game. Bosses are not fun or interesting, they're just big (admittedly cool looking) roided versions of the regular opposition which hit harder and have much more HP.
Outside of the biggest problem which is the gameplay, the game has other issues. There is no way to rebind the keys, and the options menu contains nothing except a single submenu, which is volume control. Aditionally, the dialogue is not only incredibly simplistic and written like a bored forum post, it's also in dire need of a spellcheck. Additionally, whereas the " solid " objects in the game look great, there are some particle effects of a much lower quality that really stand out as an eyesore.
I would describe playing this game as a chore. There is no fun in slaughering your way through the opposition, as the combat is just flat and unimpactful even when it doesn't feel broken. The two areas I've seen are not exactly inspired either, both being a series of alternating flat areas full of monsters and pits full of either monsters or spikes.
There can be a good game here, there really can. But the very core of the game, the only thing you do in the game, which is the fighting, is just bad. And as such, I cannot recommend this game for anyone, not even as eye candy, because you won't be getting far enough to look at anything significantly pretty. It's just a punishing, janky, unsatisfying screensaver.

Slain! was a game that I had been waiting for and looking forward to enjoy for quite some time now, but unfortunately there's too not much I find enjoyable here.
The one good factor this game has going for it is the art design. Lots of great colours splashed about gothic-medieval architecture paint this game wonderfully. This game is wonderfully bright and dankly dark at the same time, and that is shown well with the levels of scrolling seen between the foreground, midground and background.
Sadly, the art is the only thing I find great at this time. The controls, in which I'm playing with an Xbox One controller, are clunky. It's as if the developers grew up, like myself, playing Castlevania. Now, I love Castlevania. I will gladly play some hardcore Castlevania or Super Castlevania and then cross the bridge right into some Symphony of The Night or Aria of Sorrow. However, that's what this game's gameplay feels like to me: that bridge.
The developers seem to have created their own bridge, but it's a little rickety. Slain! is a cross between the old school Castlevania and Symphony of the Night, but unfortnately they didn't find the right balance between the two. In Castlevania, the devs understood that enemies needed a wind up and to be kept at a length, hence the whip or the long arc for the sword. Slain! gave me a fat sword that doesn't really seem like this amazing warrior would use (except to butter his toast) because the range is laughably short and he swings it like I have to tell him how.
And he can't block unless he crouches.
I assume maybe there will be longer, better weapons in the game, but at this point, with the game telling me nothing about how to play the game, ie. crouching makes you block and the B button is for decapitations, I don't exactly care to play that far into it. The mixture of slow, unresponsive controls and sludge metal is not a good mix. I enjoy grindy metal at times, but when your game feels like a gelatinous cube, and it's okay to have a game feel that slow, it may be best to tuck away the sludge metal for later.
In some way I want to recommend this game, because it looks gorgeous and maybe with a fix to the responsiveness it could be a lot of fun, but I can't do it. I cannot, in good conscience, recommend this game. The problems with Slain! bum me out as I was so very much looking forward to an ultra-dark heavy metal kind of vibe in a video game, but this is a whoops.

There is nothing quite like the feeling of staying up late into the night, putting on your favorite album (The Fragile, or Kid A) and blasting through the atmospheric yet action packed world of Quake. In the third part of the original Quake saga (Quake 1, Mp1, Mp2) developer Rogue Entertainment (same team that made Quake 2: Ground Zero) sorta-twists the original Quake concept in an attempt to keep fresh. Of course, you're still blasting through the same way you did previously, but the massive steps in content that Rogue Entertainment stuffed this expansion with makes this the better of the two expansions, and arguably on par with the original game.
Level design on this expansion is great. Some levels can be a bit maze-y at times, however it never felt as though I was going nowhere (which was an issue in the base game at at times in the first Mission Pack) I personally had no issues completing the levels, and the "switch of doom" which haunts the reviews of this game never game me issues, in fact it was not until after I finished the game that I realized the "switch of doom" worked for me. Although I won't lie, the levels were far more interesting in the second half, "Corridors of Time", than in the first half. Levels like "Curse of Osiris" and "Elemental Fury Part 2" take the player on a journey in a way that the previously mission pack failed to do (most of the time) the levels bring their own unique architecture and enemies to make for a refreshingly Quake experience. The best way to describe the second episode of this mission pack is... imagine Tomb Raider meeting Quake, that is about how it goes.
Unlike the first mission pack, Dissolution of Eternity brings a whopping 14 new enemies (over half of these are new bosses). You have flying swords, statues that come to life, a flying demon, and even a bunch of mummy guardians which serve as checkpoint bosses throughout the mission pack. From the axe wielding flying Overlord to a F******G Dragon, the mission pack wears the gothic ancient vibe of the original Quake with pride, and in turns makes it a much more interesting experience than the prior mission pack (Which wore the base aesthetic and style from the original Quake.)
If you enjoyed Quake 1 then I highly recommend picking up this mission pack. If you just finished the first game and are thirsty for more Quake action I actually recommend this over the prior mission pack due to its larger amount of variety and level tweaks that makes it a more enjoyable experience.

I think in order to fairly and objectively review a game, you need to look at it in four section: Graphics, gameplay, sound, and story. These four elements make up a game. By this reasoning, let me review To The Moon.
Graphics - N/A
Graphics are arguably the least important aspect of a game, in my opinion. To The Moon is created in RPG maker, so graphics are even less important. 16 bit, familiar animations, etc.
Gameplay - 3/10
TTM is not a game, per se, but more of a collection of cutscenes. This is fine, because it is heavily story driven.
Story - 5/10
Unfortunately, I was disappointed. The story is creative, but no where near the level of depth and emotions that I was led to believe existed here. The dialogue is boring at best and the majority of time incredibly cringey. References to Animorphs feel out of place. The dialogue is full of colloquialisms and phonetic spellings which are awful.
Sound - 10/10
The soundtrack for this game is amazing and it's only saving grace. Mostly piano based, which works nicely with the dialogue and triggers an emotional connection. Unfortunately for TTM, that's the only good part of the game.
I paid 1.99 for TTM and finished it in two sittings in about 3 hours. I feel like that's a fair value for what I paid, but I wouldn't pay much more. In my opinion this game is completely overrated and feels more like a high school play than a 'brilliant' game.
Overall Rating - 6/10

I have heavily-mixed feelings for this game.
I absolutely loved the syntax content of the game - it's story, characters, lore, etc. - as it all fit in well with each other. The world it set up was intriguing to want to learn about but not overwhelming you to the point where there was too much to care about. All of the characters (however few there are) felt memorable and capable of having a connection with the player. By the time the game ended I was blown away by how much the experience of witnessing such a game unfolded.
So why do I have mixed feelings? Because everything about "Remember Me" was fantastic except actually playing it.
With the exception of the few 'memory-altering' sequences, the game is basically a button-mashing single-player fighter game where you fight essentially waves of enemies that you just combo again and again. The game occasionally feels clunky, both with the fighting and the platforming aspects. When I finished the game I wanted to go back through and investigate any secrets or bonuses I forgot or passed, but I did not want to face playing the game once again.
This review for "Remember Me" is not intended to be positive. It's not intended to be negative. I generally refer to this game to people as "the greatest mehh game ever"; it falls in the dead-middle between being a good and bad game. If somebody from Steam or Valve is reading this, please consider creating a 'neutral' review option for games that are neither good or bad, but just ARE.

I've spent a few hours with Hob, and though I haven't finished it yet I can say that this is definitely one of my favorite games I've ever played. Without a single word said, it tells the story of a broken world ravaged by war against the disease spreading across its surface. Lost in this world you move forward, never quite knowing what's going on beyond the path in front of you until finally it starts coming together. Literally. The world is made whole again by your hand as your actions add up to restore everything you've fought through.
I've never played a game where you changed so much of the landscape not just as a result of playing it, but as an actual game mechanic to solve various puzzles and challenges. The art style is amazing, the gameplay solid. My only complaint lies in some framerate drops during loading of new areas which can be especially annoying during combat. Beyond that continuing issue despite a couple optimization patches, there's nothing else that bothers me about this game at all. That's a rare thing to be able to say.

The principal strengths of this game are its story and atmosphere, and the way all of that is portrayed: the ordinary people, the beggars, the drunks, the various military factions, the sounds, the languages, the architecture, the events unfolding around you, the events underneath those events...

Without exaggeration, the story is at least as good as The Da Vinci Code and to whomever I retold it (non-gamers included), they were interested to play or, at the very least, discuss the various ideas that occur in the game.

Dissolution of Eternity is the second and final Quake 1 mission pack. It's a very fitting end to the game's official content and dovetails nicely with the previous expansion pack, Scourge of Armagon. It was developed by Rogue entertainment who also developed Strife and American McGee's Alice.
Dissolution is much more fantasy based than Armagon. There's a distinctly mythological slant to the whole thing. You fight fantasy enemies like statues that come alive, these wraith like grim reaper creatures, magical swords that float and attack you, and the final boss is even a Dragon. It reminds me a lot of the original Quake's roots as a medieval fantasy game before the developers redesigned it as a first person shooter.
Indeed looking at Dissolution like that it really does make the game feel like it comes full circle with the original Quake. It has a few really good boss encounters that fill in the gaps of quality that were unfortunately lacking in the original. It is also legitimately challenging and several of the levels are very long and feel almost epic length.
The main negatives I would say about Dissolution of Eternity are the additional weapons they added weren't as impressive as Scourge of Armagon. You have things like a nailgun that shoots slightly more powerful nails, a rocket launcher that shoots three rockets at once, a lightning gun that just shoots a single projectile. If you play it back to back with Scourge you'll start to miss MJOLNIR.
But besides that. The levels are all good, the action is still fresh, and it has a final boss encounter that more than makes up for how easy Armagon was. It makes for a fitting end to the original Quake, and it only makes you want to play through the entire saga again to experience it a second time.

The main reason that I purchased this game was to play co-op with my bro. We spent the first 45 minutes trying and failing to get co-op to work. This is a game made for multi-player and the store page lists co-op as a function. So I would expect there to be an easy “Invite Your Friend” option. Nope. Let me check the wiki. That didn’t work. We haven’t had this much trouble connecting to play co-op since Rainbow Six: Vegas 2, but that is Ubisoft and we were playing it long after the official servers had been shut down. This is a recent release and co-op failed to work.
When co-op failed us we decided to try a mass multi-player game on an official game server. First we were going to try an Invasion game but the last two slots closed up so we chose Dominance. Running With Rifles is a “top-down tactical shooter with open world RPG elements. In RWR you join the ranks of an army as a common soldier, just like the thousands around you.” We were thrust into a chaotic war scene with no idea of what to do. We ended up on different teams so we still weren’t getting any sort of co-op experience. I chose to follow some dudes wearing the same brown uniform as me. We all look exactly the same. Killed. I guess should hide behind a rock next time. Killed. At least I respawn instantly and fairly close to my last position. Let me take a quick look at the map. Killed. Game ends. Never even got to see my bro. New game starts. Let’s see if there’s some leaders or organization to this chaos. Well, there’s definitely lots of uncensored swearing in the game chat. In one screen shot that I took I didn’t realize it until I was going to use it for this review, but it had the “N” word in it. Delete. There is the option to turn off chats, but for a tactical game with 32 players in it one would assume that you would need to communicate with your teammates in order to win. If only co-op had worked…
It’s my personal choice for home defense and I was glad to see it in this game. The game does offer lots of choices for weapons, but you have to gain experience and level up to be able to use most of them. At least the Mossberg 500 is one of starting choices. One shot and your target is down! And reloading only puts one shell in so you have to hit “R” eight times to fully reload it, but that’s a good thing. Makes it feel more like a shotgun. I finally went on a 5 kill streak, but I still ended with 34 kills to 79 deaths. And each death gives you negative experience thus making gaining experience and leveling up towards the better weapons difficult.
While the multi-player mode was crazy with bullets flying everywhere and me dying every three seconds, the single-player mode was a breeze, a boring breeze. There was no tutorial to explain what to do and no sense of a story or real campaign so I set off following everyone else. I rarely died although still didn’t earn enough experience for better equipment. And when I completed the first level…nothing…There was a quick pop-up window showing some level stats, but no cut-scene and no new level loaded. Me and my bot soldier pals just hung around commenting about the silence before the storm yet there was clearly no storm. Finally, after driving around in a supply truck (and running over two of my buddies who failed to get out the way, perhaps the best part of my game experience!) I realized that there are these white icons on the map with names of locations. What are those? Oh, those are the “warp gates” to new maps and levels. The lack of a tutorial had me thinking that there was a bug. I don’t need hand-holding, but a little direction would have been nice.
The graphics for the vehicles and environment are simple yet pleasing, but nothing to write home about. At least a super power graphics card isn’t necessary meaning just about anyone should be able to play the game just fine. The top-down view is different from most tactical shooter games, which I’m fine with, but the soldiers just seemed really small and indistinguishable and I felt that there wasn’t enough line of sight. I could only see a few feet in front of me when I should have been able to see further in order to better avoid enemies and gunfire. One option that I did like was the “gore level” slider. While I enjoy shooter games I’m not a big fan of over-the-top blood and gore. Some games will give you an on/off or a “less gore” option, but I had not seen a slider before where you can choose exactly how much you want to see.
If you still feel that this might be the game for you, do yourself a service and download the demo first. It’s received rave reviews on Steam so clearly others are enjoying the game.

This is my first game review.
I can't believe it took me 6 years to play this game. I spent a day looking at the "overwhelmingly positive" games in the steam filter and noticed this game was on sale for $2.  Oh boy, the experience was worth 5-10x that.
Negatives:
-Puzzles at start
I will start with the only negative to get that quickly out of the way. Personally, I was not a fan of the puzzle elements at the start of the game. I thought they really didn't bring a lot of value and were added as filler. I used a guide to quickly blow through these and you should do the same if you are not a fan.
Positives:
-The story
This story hit home personally with being a twin, but by no means do you need that personal connection to enjoy it.
This game is an emotional rollercoaster. There were times I was laughing out loud, and there were times where I was almost moved to tears. I don't really want to expand to much on this section to avoid spoilers.
-The music
One of the best soundtracks I have ever heard in a game. Most of the tracks are insturmental, which fits perfectly into the overall theme of the game. I work a job that allows me to listen to music as I work. Months after beating the game, I still queue up this soundtrack on Youtube every day.
Closing:
Now some people will argue that this is not a game. Though the game is light on "game mechanics", I truley believe the writing in this game was one of the best I have ever seen. I would recommend going into this game thinking you are going to watch a great 3.5 hour interactive movie and I would be supprised if you did not enjoy it.
This game/experience is in my top 25 ever played.

LONG REVIEW! Reason? I want more of these games and I want them from this company.
Even though I only play FPS games...my favorite games of all time are Chrono Trigger, Ocarina of Time, Ori and the Blind Forest. I try to step out every once and a while to see what else is out there and to have a good time away from being online. This is rare for me, so it has to be right! I completed Hob, and I am very happy that I was able to have this experience. :)
I played with a mouse and keyboard and honestly, it's the only way I prefer to play games. Even though there is a recommendation (strongly) to play with a controller... kb+mouse was excellent for me. Outside of the jumping mechanic, which I still feel should be a free movement.
When it comes to the comments of framerate dropping, I did experience this often but I don't wan to rule this as a huge problem as I am on vacation playing on my mothers computer, which is a AMD 4300fx - Geforce 1050ti... which is not the greatest system for gaming ;)
One thing I LOVED about this game... was not knowing anything. No dialogue or hand-holding to tell me where to put the spoon of cereal. :) YOU MUST play this on a higher difficulty. Well, you don't... yes you do!! Do it! It just makes it more fun. The enemies aren't like super-tanks, they are actually more responsive. I DO wish there was a lot more to do with combat+story and that the combat was a bit more seamless.  I think of Zelda boss battles and how the story was just that much bigger because of them.
The Lore was beautiful. The game design is beautiful. Do I wish someone made the grass, which I look at often, had a slightly more grassy design? Sure... but I accept it as is. Something to slash when I need health. I wish the desert portion was more desert and the lands-to-connect were vastly different... but I still loved it. I wish the areas you're blocked by weren't short enough for me to jump through (with invisible walls!!!!!???) but I got over that too.
There is just something about this game. Something about linking this world together and the atmosphere that just makes you want to keep playing. The puzzles weren't really challenging and I did grow a little tired of *put your hand here and everything happens, The monsters were actually really cool and I want more of them! And more reason for them. The designs were outstanding.
I have a bunch of other things I LOVED and didn't love but I don't want to drag this any further. AMAZING game. WORTH the experience. It doesn't have a real replay value for me (price totally makes that fine), but it will not be forgotten!

This game came over from the Playstaion and Vita, and while the concept of the game is well, umm, very Japanese, the game play itself is actually rather good. Yes there is a reason why the title is writen in a way to look like Akiba Strip as a pose to Akiba's Trip, it is a fairly enjoyable fighting game with a mediocre story to be an excuse of why you are striping people, yet doesn't make any sense when the enemy can be down to their knickers and a small bow in their hair and their skin is perfectly fine to the sunlight, yet once you remove the bow from their hair instantly they burn to death. I understand mechanicly why since it's head armor, body armor, and leg armor that you need to remove,but still makes the mediocre story just seem that much more off when you're suppose to believe that a small ribbon in a maids hair who has otherwise been totally striped can protect them from the sun.
All in all if you like the idea of enemies basicly having 3 health bars (head/body/legs) with a semi death's door mechanic where 0 hp on the armor doesn't instantly mean it's dead you still need to strip off the armor but if they can heal it before you strip it then you need to get it down to 0 again and try to strip before they heal again, then it's a good game. If you don't mind a cheesy story it plays well. Even though the game is locked to 30FPS I never really felt any input lag the game still felt fine. And don't be fooled by the scrreenshots on the Steam store page which make it look like a visual novel, none of the conversations seem to long and while it is the main way the story is told it is not the majority of the game time. Only reaon I really see why they did the story parts to look like a visual novel the only thing I can think of is because it was originally on PSP and so had to tell the story with limited memory and hardward power and so the Playstation, Vita,  and PC versions just got stuck with the same story telling because of it originally being on the PSP.

I bought this game on sale after the Atlas Update. I played it today for roughly 9 hours, and I will give the most honest review I can.
Picking the game up at this point, and at the price I did (it was 23 dollars), All I can think is that either they must have cleaned up a LOT or folks are way to harsh on this game.
For the first few hours,  I was dumped on a mysterious, hot planet. my ship was broken, and all i could do was wnder from place to place looking for parts. I enjoy exploring, and this was satisfactory. It really was an entire planet with dilipidated bases, cave systems, flor adn fauna. Periodically I'd encounter a base that had been covered in vegetation and interacts with weird old computer systems.
Then I fixed my ship.
Taking off from the planet was definately a holy-smokes moment. It was fun and I set course for another nearby planet
Next planet was na ice planet, like hoth from star wars. This one was even more dangrous, but I eventually found a trading post. I was able to wrk my way up to a better ship, and I explored the surface for a long time. Eventually I felt confident to explore the third and final planet in the system.
The final planet was a big lifeless husk, sort of like landing on a moon. On the surface....
Below the surface were these dense caverns filled with geodes, mushrooms and crystals. Ultimately I did not stay long on this dead planet, but in a desolate way it was beautiful.
Each planet was interesting, had their own personalities.
Then I went to the stars again and to a space station. By this point I've learned some alient words, and I'm growing more confident. Eventually I finish the big task of creating  warp drive.
Then the second "holy smokes" moment - I went to a new galaxy. this time with 4 new planets, each differnt.
Right now, I am on a jungle planet. It isnt teeming with fauna, but does have some 'gentle beasts' (large herbivors). I started a small settelement, and I'm beginnning to explore tthe surface.
My traveller has a home now, at least for a while. As I was ending my first day, I got to see the sunset on this new jungle planet. It was at this point I "got it" about this game. Its not a very goal oriented game, its a game about exploration, and to some degree, lonliness. I'd say its an aesthetic journey. I am alone on this bueautiful planet, carving out a small spot for myself. Its my own little corner of the universe.
Maybe this game launched too soon. Maybe it was marketed a tthe wrong sort of thing. It has mos tin common with subnautica right now, but, on a galctic scale.
To me, this game is very good. Its exactly what I wanted, and I hope that the team working on it continues to build more and more content.
If you see it on sale, my honest advice, is buy it if you haven't. If you did buy it and only played it right at launch, maybe give it another chance, with new eyes and new content.
I can't way to see where the game goes next.

Damn.  Let me get out of the way that I recommend the game if and only if you were a fan of the original.
Performance and bugs:
Ultimately, I can't recommend this game for the majority of folks.  I'm quite a few hours invested in the game and I can't bring myself to finish it.   The truth is the bugs are a real problem.  The developer has done a lot to fix the major one quickly.  So major, in fact, that people couldn't progress in the game after about 10 minutes of play.   I still from time to time get stick in the same type problem and have to reload.   I also occassionally get crashes in full screen mode.  And perhaps most annoyingly, I do a lot of multitasking while gaming.  I'll get a "game lost application context" and have to shut it down whenever I start up certain other programs at the same time.  First time I've ever seen that one.
There's also countless irregularities that affect gameplay.  Like chance to hit on UI being nowhere near what it claims to be.  If your chance to miss is low, like 1% you might not notice, but once it's 50% chance to hit you actually hit about 10% of the time.  Very annoying and I can't figure out what or why this happens.
gameplay:
This one is the most disappointing for me.  For every step forward, trying to bring this game into an actual world and not just an endless dungeon crawl, there's two steps backwards.   I feel like it lost the magic of the original in a lot of ways.  Even now I'm tempted to just go back and play the old Monsters' Den game.
Party balance is really off.  You might not notice it if you just go with your standard party, it seems to be built around this, but you'll find some classes just useless and others godlike.  You can easily run 3 and maybe 4 archers and do all content without ever worrying.  This can be fixed in patching, fine.  At the pace the game was developed I'm very concerned when the patches will come and if it will ever be right.
World balance and looting...it's just all off. How you spend your time isn't rewarded even close to right.   You can go grind for hours and get a few good items, or you can just spam search ruins on the world map and get maybe 10 in 1 hour without much effort.   Stuff like that.
The original classes were simple enough.  I'd like to have seen it expanded on, but the new systems are just not my cup of tea.  And maybe not yours either.  My primary complaint is the masteries.  You get to the end of a skill tree and it locks you out of the other skill tree you have, kinda.  You keep any abilities you've invested in before going into mastery.   I can live with that even though it's sort of strange.  What I hate, though, is the mastery itself gives you no information or hints about what it might offer in return.  The decision you are making is completely on the name of the class.  Then you have to randomly get lucky enough to find rare tomes to give you abilities for that mastery.   No way to know what they abilities are going to be.    Not even searching the forums gets you there.  Really annoying if you like to carefully plan your team.
I could go on and on about lackluster features, but the truth is everything but the original core mechanics of explore and loot is worse.   All of the added extras are so underwhelming.   You get a keep to upgrade in various ways, it's cool, but it doesn't feel like it adds anything.  You can manage multiple parties but they just give you a little gold, or rep every month.   Reality is it's still optimal just to use one party.   And the economics around expanding the teams don't make sense -- you have to pay so much in precious resources to slowly farm more resources with the teams.
The only addition from the keeps I really like is the relics.   It's quite fun finding and using relics.
The last thing I want to touch on is the combat system.  It's almost the same, but maybe a slight downgrade from the old original monsters' den.   It uses turn based for affects now that manifests is weird ways.   It just doesn't feel as sophisticated as the original.  But for the most part, it's the same.
I know this is sort of rambling at this point.  I'm not very good at reviews, but I wanted to warn others who might feel the same as me to think carefully about the purchase.  This game has an endless number of fans who will defend it no matter what the reality is, but if I were giving it a generic rating it would honestly -- as a HUGE fan -- be slightly below average.   I'll revise the recommendation after it's patched a few more times.  I'm hoping patches are forthcoming that improve the game, because I truly love the franchise.

This game has succeeded where many shooters/war games have failed.  It has the feel of an actual front line fight where cover, high ground, suppressive fire and reinforcements all play a huge role.  Starting as a Private you will not have access to any special weapons or even a radio to call in fire missions or reinforcements, but with skill and experience you can still have a big influence on the battle.  Level up a bit and you can have a major impact on the battle.  It is very rewarding to be able to break an hour long stalemate by attacking in force from an unexpected direction, calling in waves of paratrooper reinforcements at a critical time to hold recently captured territory, calling in massive bombardments on huge troop formations, throwing the driver out of a tank that has been dominating the field and knifing him, destroying a communication tower behind enemy lines that prevents AI counterattacks and allows your front line to finally move forward etc.
In the beginning it can feel like all you do is die, but if the battle has turned into a stalemate, that just means it's time to put your commander hat on and try something different.  Sometimes sneaking to the back of the base and placing a single sandbag can make all the difference.  Now you've drawn attention away from the front.  Every person that comes to attack you is one less reinforcement headed to the well defended front line.  The enemy front line weakens, then breaks as your guys come swarming in to mop up: game over and a very satisfying victory.

How's THAT for a metal title? The second expansion of the original Quake held nothing back in the naming, and similarly holds nothing back in the challenge. Whereas Scourge of Armagon felt at times like The Lost Levels to Quake's Super Mario Bros, Dissolution of Eternity sometimes seems like The Loster Levels. This isn't necessarily down to good design, either, so if you're here looking for more quality Quake, you might want to read on before pulling the trigger.
Whereas Quake had four episodes to choose from and Armagon had one long campaign, Dissolution has two themed episodes to frag through. The first, Hell's Fortress, is a series of sprawling castles, caves, and catacombs. The second, Corridors of Time, is an assortment of historically-themed touching on Egyptian tombs, Mayan sacrifices, and, uh, wizard towers. You might note that none of these lineups contain anything techy or eldritch, and that's an important thing to keep in mind. Dissolution's 14 levels are all roughly castle or tomb themed, skipping two of the major Quake aesthetics and leaving most of the grunts behind.
A strongly-themed pack isn't a bad thing as long as the levels are executed well, but for the most part I can't say they are. The first level of Hell's Fortress is a prime example of the pack's shortcomings. It's a castle you infiltrate through towers and tunnels, but all the architecture is flat, featureless, and relies too heavily on single textures. You're going to get very, very tired of olive brick and brown caves after just a few levels, owing in part to how much longer and larger they are than base Quake maps. The later parts of episode one and parts of episode two have more interesting designs but they feel like the exception, not the rule.
The gripes don't end at the architecture, either. Encounters throughout Dissolution tend to happen in cramped spaces like narrow corridors, rather than the platforms and arenas you'd expect from the prior Quake maps. Part of this is obviously owing to the heavy reliance on knight enemies, but once ogres and fiends start getting mixed in you'll find fights ending very quickly, often not in your favor. The new enemies only exacerbate this, with most of them having wide attack patterns and several exploding on death. And if that wasn't enough, most levels rely heavily on traps like collapsing floors and swinging axes to up the ante, but instant death in a lava pit only leads to frustration given the length of the levels.
At least the new weapons help blunt the painful combat. They're not really new weapons, but new ammo types for your existing weapons that generally do more damage. Nailguns get lava nails, launchers get cluster explosives, and the lightning gun can be switched to a BFG-style projectile. For some reason the ammo placement doesn't seem to take the new ammo types into account, so you'll be topped off on most ordnance even through pitched battles. There are some creative item additions like shields and gravity belts, but the levels are never really designed to take advantage of them, as if the item and level designers had no idea what the other was doing.
Overall, Dissolution of Eternity plays like a more immediately lethal form of Quake without much else to add. The levels are longer but not as expertly crafted in look, feel, or mechanics. Between the cramped combat and obnoxious traps you're more likely to run into bouts of frustration, and the new enemies, ammo, and items don't make much difference in the face of that. It's more Quake and more Quake is good, but if you're still jonesing after the base game and Scourge of Armagon, you might be better served with community maps.

There's no one tactic fits all here, and while this does feel awkward at first, you  soon realsie that's because you've become conditioned to multiplayer FPS. You can't just run around spraying bullets like a lot FPS. The bad guys are intelligent here and will punish you fast. Often you don't even know what got you it comes so fast. This, and the music puts you masterfully on edge. The difficulty level feels horribly retro at first, with it's unforgiving quickness of your death. You seldom survive a big battle on the first attempt. Or the second. Or the third ... But then it starts to feel nicely retro as you get into it. Games used to be harder and less forgiving. Your brain remembers ... and it likes it as it adapts!
It wasn't easy to set up though. My laptop spec (listed below) was below the minimum requirement graphics card (NVIDIA GeForce 840M 2GB with Intel Integrated 1GB) wise so I was curious how well this game would perform on it. Having noticed that DOOM well outshone the Nintendo Switch on it with a smooth 60 FPS and very crisp more detailed images even on the lowest settings, I thought i'd give this a go. Whilst alot of various settings were fine and worked excellently with DOOM, not so with Wolfenstein II.
After some trial and error, it was worth it. Turn everything to the absolute lowest setting and fix frame rate at 40FPS. Any other setting and the play speed was noticably up and down like a yo yo making it horribly hard/unpleasant to play. At 40FPS however, the frame rate is incredibly consistant, allowing for a good experience and everything still looks good to me - I play it windowed in 1280x720. I hope this saves someone somewhere some time and uncertainty :)

It hurts to say I can't recommend this game even though there is so much to love here. However, the technical instability in the PC port is just not acceptable, not currently at least when PC is becoming more mainstream and port quality is getting higher and higher. In my 13ish hours with the game it hard crashed or froze on me 6+ times (once requiring a hard reboot of my entire PC) and this seems to be a prevalent problem throughout the community. Until these issues are addressed I cannot recommend this game. However, if they are, and you are reading this in 6 to 12 months than yes, I can recommend the game, but not at full price. This is a sale purchase. More on that to follow.
Technical issues aside, this game has a lot going for it, and a lot not. As for the positives: it is beautiful; this game is a marvel to look at and ran very smoothly on my 970 outside of one area (the massive elevator) luckily you are not in that area for long. The lighting and character models are top notch, however some of the textures, even at high and ultra were kind of muddy and I do not believe it was due to loading as I am running this on a Samsung SSD.
The art style is a treat, the Nazi interiors are exactly what I would expect from a technologically advanced culture in the 60s. A perfect blend of real world 60s style with retro futurism. The guns and enemies all look sick and have wonderful dark sleek designs. I hope it doesn’t say too much about me that if I was starting up a militia I would emulate the style of the Nazis in this game long before I’d emulate the childlike scribbles adorning the walls and helicopters of the Kreisau Circle.
The feel of the game is top notch, I have been away from first person shooters for a long time, burnt myself out on them last generation, and this and Destiny 2 are the first I have played since Fallout 4, and I have to say Wolfenstein 2 has a better feel to it than D2 does when it comes to firing weapons. Which says a lot, when it’s the only thing about D2 that Bungie managed to get right. The sounds, animations, and reactions from enemies as they are getting shot are visceral and make the firefights a lot more fun.
Also since it won’t fit anywhere else, Mick Gordon knocks it out of the park again with the soundtrack to this game.
Now what doesn’t work, well, in short aspects of the story and the stealth.
In case you didn’t know, Wolfenstein is a stealth game at its heart, in part because the original game (not 3d, the one before that) was a stealth game and also I assume to set it apart from DOOM. This really hurts the game in my opinion. Because the game is balanced for stealth, BJ is built like a frail paper door and uninterrupted fire from an enemy can take you from full health to dead in less than 3 seconds, at least on normal (Bring it On). Now, this isn’t a huge issue most of the game because as long as you practice the stealth you will get better at it and will be able to take out most enemies before you are caught, if you are caught at all. However there are a number of sections where you are forced into combat and forced combat combined with a low Damage Threshold leads to rage inducing sections that really drag down the overall enjoyment of the experience. There’s also weapon upgrades, some are very useful (charged Lazerkraftwerk and silencers for the machinepistol and regular pistol) the others don’t add much, and a perk system. The perk system is so tertiary to the game that I almost forgot to add it to this review and only did when proofreading it over. It may be more useful if you play on harder difficulties, but I cannot see why you would want to, with how rage inducing the game is on normal.
As for the story, it is told wonderfully, but it feels toothless compared to the previous game. Deathshead was a true psychopath, while Engel just felt like a parent you’d read about on /r/raisedbynarcists. There is no equivalent in this game of the concentration camp scenes from TNO and I must heavily agree with Superbunnyhop’s analysis of the story. To sum it up, he feels that the game is much less cohesive due to it taking place in America instead of Europe; and because the devs are from Europe they were much closer to the material in the first game and could write what they knew. Whereas with this game in America they thought it would make sense for a southern Baptist preacher type to be leading a group of Bolshevik Communist Civil Rights Revolutionaries for some reason. Also it seems the vast majority of white America seems to be cool with the new leadership and reintroduced segregation and slavery, and they need to be woken up by the strong, smack talking, breast feeding, soul sister. Who put Grace in charge anyway? She just walks in and takes over…., OK? Also, can someone explain to me why Anya felt the need to take her shirt off before shooting the Panzerhound? I get that it made for a cool, strong female image, seeing a pregnant topless woman covered in blood, somehow managing to dual wield machine guns; but these situations and images when done for no reason other than to have ‘strong female characters’ come off as forced. If you want to see how a good female character is written, I will point to The Boss from MGS 3. She is strong, believable (unlike Anya), and her sex matters and is not just disregarded (unlike Grace, who could have been any race or gender), her femininity matters and shapes her character as it is revealed. The ham-fisted attempts at contemporary parallels to current day politics and the resurgent far right are a bit on the nose as well and come off a bit too cartoonish for my taste and fall into the same category as Deus Ex Mankind Divided did last year, with its comparisons to SJW’s and LGBT rights.
Overall this is a game of massive highs and lows. With a few tweaks if we get a Wolf 3, it could be a game of the year contender. Lay off the social commentary, even out the difficulty, and either get rid of the stealth (preferably) or make every combat encounter optional. This game is best purchased during a sale as I said before, or one of the few that may be better for one of those edited down youtube movie versions of a game. 6.5/10

The concept is
intriguing, which is all the more frustrating when you realize that it's not working out at all in this horrible, unfinished and overpriced catastrophe.
Although the level design is insanely hideous, missions ranging from uselessly easy to sadistically difficult during the first ten minutes, the controls take the cake.
If it's not baffling enough that pressing spacebar in the menu for some reason opens up the game website, which I really have no interest in especially after actually playing the game, everything else besides the menus is just as glitchy.
For the first couple of minutes, I actually had a feeling of control and was compelled to play - until I realized that the more I tried to influence what would happen, the more frustrated I would eventually become.
I was fooled into thinking that perhaps I simply should play more because hey, I probably suck, which still is kind of the case. But after I got comfortable navigating the cramped levels while trying to fling whatever useless weapon you are cursed with, the controls seem as glitchy and unreliable as do the physics feel artificially handicapped or simply buggy.
The idea of flying around and crushing things with huge rocks or hammers is great, but the only thing you get to destroy in this game are your expectations and stuff right next to your mouse.
As unfinished, glitchy, unnecessarily random and hideous this game is, I can't believe this game is not early access. In it's current state, I personally can not recommend anyone should buy this game without trying it out first.
Who knows, maybe you'll want to like it bad enough to actually fool yourself into enjoying it.
