I've been playing this game for quite some time before I bought it on Steam and for a reason. It doesn't matter that it's just singleplayer and local MP (and boy, this game could sure use network MP), Hammerfight somehow made me play over and over.
In Hammerfight, you pilot a tiny helicopter that can have weapons hanging out from it. Swords, axes, flails, hammers, even guns later on. To use the weapons, however, you usually don't use buttons. You need to move yourself in order to make the weapons swing and hit your enemy. You start out in a campaign mode with an interesting and mysterious story about an original world and unlock new modes depending on your progress and decisions in the story with multiple endings.
The sortiment of weapons is vast and even different weapons of a same type offer quite a variability. As if that is not enough, you can also socket them with gems with powerful abilites, such as elemental enchantments, heal on hit and even temporary ghost form that makes you pass through enemies and ignore damage. Other equipment includes throwable weapons, shield plates that are normally hanging too until you hold a button, when they equally spread and hold, making a turtle. Speaking of which, these weapons can be activated handily, by holding LMB, you can press any key that is defined as that item's shortcut, which is great and makes you more efficient.
The feel I get from the game is both satisfying and frustrating. It feels awesome to swing your hammer, sending your enemy into ground, blowing him up by the impact. When I pair two weapons together, forming a staff that stretches to both sides out of your copter, it actually looks graceful and deadly and it's a kind of a challenge as it requires different handling. This game is a challenge from start to end for players of any level of experience. But it's an experience not worth missing.
The developer has abandoned the game and this is probably the last version you will ever see. Too bad. It deserves a sequel to an amazing story, or a prequel to enlighten us to the origins of the world, or networking to play on LAN or Online. Also, quite certainly, there are bugs. So the game can sometimes play on your nerves, but if you ask me, you'll keep coming back. It's too fun to miss.

is an interesting story that's been walled off behind hostile game mechanics - a harsh reminder that interactive fiction and twitch action don't always mix.  It's a beautiful game with a great concept and fantastic performance, and it's
crippled by tedious, rage-inducing, fun-destroying "combat."
I have
reflexes.  I managed to pull off a five-hit combo once, by accident, after countless attempts. I tried to persist but my patience ran out when the "invisible" floodlight-sensitive enemies were introduced partway into episode 3.  There's no place to practice, no way to actually improve or get good at the game mechanics without pushing forward, automatically unlocking new complications that you have to master on the fly.  It's all on-the-plot training and if you can't get a handle on it the game stops being fun very, very quickly.  Quick load times don't help.  Tutorial tips don't help. .  Even reduced to the easiest difficulty setting I just get shredded.

So, I've just played through the game, and it has a lot of good qualities. Interesting story, good graphics, decent fighting system, though it is a bit repetitive and predictable after a while.
The main issue I take with it is the very linear path you are forced to follow with approximately no wiggle room. You can't do anything along the path your own way, only the exact way that the game designers wrote. You have a very athletic character that can climb and jump and back flip around any obstacle, so long as it's scripted... but if it's not, you can't step or jump over a footstool, because it's not part of the precise story. There's many hidden easter eggs to pick up through the game that I was fed up trying to get to because of some invisible obstacle that I illogically couldn't get past, rather I would have had to find it in exactly "their" way.
Likewise you can't engage enemies on your own terms like in some games, you can't avoid a fight for example, or race to a fleeing boss without being forced to defeat every minion along the way. Rather, you step across some invisible line, the music changes, all the doors lock and you're in one of their many scripted cage fights.
That's my beef with this game. I was excited to play it, and still got some enjoyment out of it, but the tightly scripted nature of it really limits the interaction. This made it feel less like a game and more like a frustrated movie that you power with a treadmill. I don't know if I'd recommend this game to people, if you enjoy stories, give it a shot, otherwise, buyer be warned. The game was ok, but with some tweaking to it's gameplay it could have been great.

Gameplay and story are divided and kept on two different planes, one for the player, one for the composers to tell their story. That disconnect that the fact that nothing important ever happens when the player is in control is where the game failed to utterly and disappointingly.
The game tells a nice little sci-fi story that has great idea no depth but a neatly fleshed out world around it. All in all it's not worth watching a million little cut scenes, non needed, to play mediocrely implemented Arkam-style combat.

This game follows a story that is at times deeply angers you and at others, fills you with sorrow but at all times, is quite intense. The depiction of an Orwellian world in the future is terrific, as are the powers that be and every other person who is surviving in the regime of Memorize. Each chapter's story is very well crafted around the checkpoint based gameplay and even though the story is totally linear, it's a journey you don't want to miss and must finish. This is one those games in which you're living a part of the protagonist's life as in a novel or movie.
The best parts of the game are when you get to remix memories. Although it would have been interesting if I could create armies or create total anarchy by remixing anyone's memories I chose, the developers chose not to trivialize memory remixing by limiting it to only some select people and moments in the story. Those parts draw parallels to Inception, to say the least.
The action is the only part of the game that can get a little repetitive and monotonous, but not if you keep changing the combo moves to suit every battle sequence, which is something I learned. The very fact that the combos could be modified as and when the player chooses was a fantastic idea.
A very beautiful game with an intense plot.

Combat is incredibly satisfying and the combo lab is elegantly designed. DONTNOD has set up a system with multiple approaches and strategies in regards to its combat scenarios - and they let you go to town with it. I can't compliment it enough. They striked a balance between developer control and player control, and it makes you feel creatively responsible for the outcome of the fight.
Also, the different avenues of gameplay provided by incorporating memory into the equation are all refreshingly interesting. Remixing memories, in addition to stealing memories, memory overload, remembrances, etc......It all lends a great deal to exploring the latent power of memories - and frankly I think the way it was tied into the game was genius.
The Story itself was the best I've experienced in years. And it was delivered by top notch voice acting, animation, and lore. This is one of the first games I've actually read into with journals and the sort. There was a lot of heart put into this futuristic interpretation of our world and it can be felt with every detail.
Visually, the game is stunning. There are moments where I would stand still and it was like watching a painting. It's worth playing for its artistic merit alone - but it also knocks it out of the park with its story and gameplay.
All this being said, I could care less for Uncharted-esque climb sections in games. And I wish that playing through it a second time would at least let you skip tutorials and cutscenes. But these are minor gripes. I will REMEMBER this game as one of my favorites of all time.
On paper, I would've called this game way too ambitious to actually work. But they did it with flying colors.

Ok. I felt I had to write a review of this, even though I'm not yet even through my first playthrough. This is a really great game, which is why I want to get the negatives out of the way FIRST:
NEGATIVES:
Ok so first off, the camera SUCKS, like it really really is very bad. There are some awesome vistas. You know the kind you just want to look at and appreciate... but the kind that the game decides it's going to take over and control the camera for you so you can only see half of it... That and the control scheme for the platforming sections adjusts directions depending on the camera rather than the character, which makes it a hard to adjust, matter of trial and error in platforming. Also, I found this game to be horifficaly optimised. I can play Witcher 3 on med-high graphics at a solid 35FPS on my laptop, but I had FPS lower than 30 with real lag spikes playing this game at the most random times even on the lowest settings. Granted I've only played thus far on the medium difficulty, it it's also worth mentioning that this does not seem to be a difficult game, even the boss battles are not particularly challenging. Things like chaining your attacks give you health back even when the enemy/boss has blocked them, make it less challenging than it might otherwise be.
POSITIVES:
With that said, if you have a good computer/latop and can deal with the camera and controls sometimes bugging out on you - GET THIS GAME. I don't know why this isn't a more widely advertised game. I've found the graphics to be beautifully stylised and really thematic at times. The sci-fi setting is bang on and highly believable. The environments you are exploring are true to their names, setting and highly evocative. The fighting, while not unique, is well executed and requires some degree of thought - a nice departure from the usual smash and grab type games.
As well, I really have to emphasise the brilliant sounds across the board. The soundscape is very evocative and relatively varied. I loved the addition of so much background noise that despite the linearity made the city feel very vibrant, alive and real. The music is wonderfully unique, and like the sounds fit straight into the world. The music seems to make sense, and while usually music fades to the background; in this it comes straight to the front in fight scenes and exploration as it seems to mean something. The voice acting, though nothing to phone home about, is good at times and average the rest, but does nothing to take away from the rest of the game. I also like the boss battles so far (I've only done two, some say they get repetitive, they have a better perspective than I on that to be fair), they're not challenging, but they are fun, relatively unique, graphically beautiful and give you a nice power boost/addition along the way.
Finally, there are some brilliantly brilliantly unique and well done aspects of the game, such as memory re-writing. I was actually in awe and felt very real and powerful the first time I did it on this game. It really is a totally new concept, visceral, has an impact and the 'rewinding' with your mouse was a moment of brilliance for the control scheme which otherwise wasn't particularly reliable.
CONCLUSION:
If you have a decent PC/Laptop, and don't mind some bugs, buy this game. If you like Sci-Fi, buy this game. If you like Platforming, buy this game - but be prepared for it to slightly annoy you at times ;). Basically, I highly recommend this game for an interesting story, realistic and visceral world, and engaging, beautiful graphics and soundscape!

The first thing you will notice are the vastly outdated graphics, which just hurt your eyes and are nothing like the trailers and the screenshots. Everything is downgraded as usual. However, this is not the biggest of surprises in the game industry these days, so in my generosity, it can be forgiven.
What I and many others fail to understand is the concept of the game, for it simply isnt very well thought out before put into use. This is very obvious when you really start to understand the gameplay and try to execute the things you observe the game showing you, which eventually feels clunky, outdated and sometimes, unfortunately, even flat-out depressing.
Gameplay-wise, the game holds your hand almost all the time and it becomes really annoying, when you start to notice you have no real difference in the course of action. There are moments where you just feel completely lost and get annoyed at how everything doesnt quite fit together.
The controls dont feel fluid at all, and occasionally you feel like you're either stuck in the mud or glue, or the game intentionally was made hard and frustrating to control. Why would anyone want to offer the players of their game an experience like this?
And what's really frustrating are the sounds. It's like someone literally wanted to hire one of the worst composers, voice actors and the sound designers for this kind of a game! Could it be simply a bad decision from the lead of this project or very, very dark humor from the entire team of the game developers? You decide!
And dont even get me started on the AI. It's rather non-existent. Some games are famous for their silly bot-AI that keeps doing mistakes and failing at the only thing it was designed to do. The only difference between those games and this is that the AI here isn't even funny. It just wants to make you shout at it's actions in utter rage.
The performance of the game tends to be lackluster. Ive seen it perform badly on many different specs and machines, which cannot garner much respect, but at this point it doesn't really surprise, either.
All this could be fixed with at least a long, interesting story that would give content for your money and/or time, but it doesn't really offer either.
When you thought it couldn't get any worse, the game has more bugs here and there, hindering your already non-existent progressing and sucking the last drops of joy out of the experience
On top of all of this, the game is insanely difficult to progress in. Everything has been made non-intuitive for the average gamer, to the point even hardcore difficulty masochists will find it unpleasant to experience.
It all makes you think: Where is the gaming industry heading these days?

I like the characters and the story, but the fighting...the fighting mechanics are so bad.
I know the protaganist is not supposed to be a bad♥♥♥♥♥at fighting, at first anyway.  At least that's what the story makes you think, as I haven't gotten too far into the story, but I don't think I'll ever get used to the fighting in the game.
The auto lock on to enemies is just annoying since you're almost always getting swarmed by at least 2+ enemies.  You can't just attack the person behind you by pointing movement stick in that direction.  No, instead by doing this you end up doing a big wind-up attack to the enemy in front of you, leaving you open to get smacked in the back.  This just goes against my intuition for fighting mobs in a game.
You tap the attack buttons to do regular attacks high, middle, and low.   Sounds good right.  Then you hold the attack buttons down (once the article of clothing is weakend) to do a grab/strip.  Oh, but when you do this grab/strip move you are again left wide open 1. during the time your holding the button down, and 2. while the move itself is performed.  It would be one thing if the move could be performed while the enemy is downed, but the only thing I seem to be able to do while the enemy is down is low attacks, not grab/strip?  I would think when the enemy is down would be the best time to perform a grab/strip.
I get fighting games that require timing.  I'm a big fan of the Dark Souls games, but this game is just bad in my opinion for a game that is centered around fighting.  Some may argue against this game being fighting centered, and I understand why, but it's still a huge part of the game.  I find myself only using the glove and regular sword type weapons because the large sword type weapons are just way too slow for fighting swarms of enemies with these fighting mechanics.  I'm usually all for oversized weapons.  Usually you need to be spot on with your timing, and you get a big pay off because of it with large weapons, but not in this game.
Some may say that this game is awesome because of it's location, and it's true that the location is good.  However, certain spots on the map have a locked camera angle.  Usually one that is high, at a bad angle for fighting, but looks good for a scenic view when your just running around.  So, if you end up smacking an enemy into one of these locations you'll need to either 1. back off and let them come to you, or 2. somehow deal with not being able to see what you're doing anymore.
Sure, I could always play this game on the easiest difficulty, and just pound through the enemies so that I can focus on the story...and the ecchi.  However, I find that you tend to get less of a reward for playing on the easiest difficulty (especially with the ecchi).  This might not be the case for this game, but I'm wavering on whether I want to spend the time just to find out I get less.
To sum it all up again, I want to like this game, I really do, but I can't.  It's just too frustrating in regards to the fighting.

TLDR:

I watched and waited for No Man's Sky for years after seeing the initial trailer. I was so excited by the concept that it was one of the only games I have ever pre-ordered. I was dissappointed by the repeated delays, but was fine with them taking the time to get it right. Then, after all the waiting and excitement, the game finally released...
It had bugs, but that was okay, they began working on them quickly. I sunk hours into the game. Little by little, my wonder began to wear off. There was no real plot other than to fly to the center of the universe. The Atlas. Nada & Polo. You met these two potential story lines with excitement, only to find there wasn't much to your future encounters with them after the initial meet and greet.
I kept flying. I wanted so badly to like the game. I finally admitted defeat and stopped playing before the end of 2016. I tried to forget about No Man's Sky. They released updates, but none of them were interesting enough for me to pick up the game again.
Enter update 1.3. I decided to start a whole new game to fully experience wat all the new content had to offer. I now find myself truly enjoying this game. There is a story to folllow. It ties in with the content added in the prior updates. I feel a sense of purpose now as I play. I'm having fun. I am very happy Hello Games didn't abandon this game. It has so much potential that it is now beggining to live up to. I hope they continue to add content in the future.

In short, I believe that No Man's Sky is defiantly worth the purchase when it goes on sale!

To start with the punchline, this game is incredible. The atmosphere is captivating, intense, and pulls you right in. The story, narrative, and decent into this world of madness is incredibly well realized. Anyone who has ever delath with real depression, for whatever reason (I have), will understand this kind of walking on the edge.
This is the way narratives should work in a game. If ever you watched a horror movie, you will know that sound makes and breaks immersion; often far more than visuals. Mute sound, and suddenly that scary movie doesn't feel quite so bad.
Hellblade realizes this, and uses it to the fullest extend. The overall physical and voice acting are superb, and the design choices are beyond reproach.
The game runs well, even on an older rig, and while, for me, the controls required some config file editing, that's nothing new for me, and does not incure any penalties from me. If you want, and enjoy a game with superb narrative, visuals and sound, then this is for you!

Gorgeous and thoughtful, this puzzle adventure game oozes with life.
The art involved in the obviously loving creation of this game is fantastic. From the hybrid creatures with endearing animation, the environment which seems alive, to the sound engineering, everything fits together perfectly.
Initially a little confusing, as the game does not fall into the all too common pattern of exposition that we see in so many games, you are thrown into a world where there is little of what we would consider 'traditional' language. The characters don't speak in any traditional sense, yet they communicate, through noises, gestures and animation, the environment provides audio and visual cues. This may make initially playing it a little jarring, as you don't get someone telling you specifically what to do, which includes telling you what your purpose is.
Not knowing your motivation you can ignore the guidance of the construct that greets you on first starting out - in fact you are free to explore. Whether following the guidance, or exploring on your own, you will quickly discover that there is a corruption blocking your way forward. This corruption, or at very least the existence of it, is perhaps the least original part of the game, but only because it is somewhat of a heroes journey staple, something we've seen before in games. It works, however, as these things often do. It likely reminded various players of different things, but I was reminded of at times the "flood" from Halo or the Zerg. Reminiscent but not a carbon copy.
As you progress the story unfolds through scripted moments and some of the discoverable areas, plus history built into the landscape you travel through - imagine being an archeologist or anthropologist visiting an area where you didn't speak the language, you look for knowledge in the world around you. You also get a sense of the story from interactions with the other inhabitants; the passive creatures you meet may provide their own guidance, and for me the gestural cues delivered by a combination of the art, animation and sound were superbly done, feeling like being communicated with rather than just present for a monologue.
The world itself is a construct, moving as you visit and engage new areas, shifting previously inaccessible areas to make them available, sometimes taking areas from undergound and knitting them into the world above. Awesome to watch as massive chunks of landmass move and shift, sometimes flying past you.
Opinions may vary on the puzzles, some feel them too easy, others find them too cryptic, others too linear. My opinion is that if you view it from a more overall perspective they strike an even balance.
I haven't finished the game, I would estimate I am about half way through, however I've definitely taken my time to soak up every discoverable vista, spent time trying to befriend beasts and look for every hidden rune, marker or half-obscured fallen giant. With a speed-run achievement set at 5 hours, the general consensus, and I'd agree, is that a typical play through might be around the 15-20 hours if you aren't lingering to just enjoy the world.
In summary I feel like this game represents what artists can achieve when they are working on something that they are passionate about. The art, the direction, the design, the emotion and the sound, everything is just done so well that on their own each is great, but when taken as a whole the sum is greater than the parts.
And finally, the developers. Engaged. It's not unique for developers to engage with their players, but it's certainly not the norm. From them posting feedback, and responding to it, on their live Discord server, to the blogs and developer interviews, they demonstrate that they love what they do.
With the sad news of Runic Games studio being closed by the company which owned them, I can only epilogue this review with:
The final outing from Runic Games demonstrates their passion for *creating* games, not just churning them out. The work the team achieved was amazing, it's just a shame we wont be seeing more from them as a family (but we'll undoubtedly see them all move on to other projects which they will bring their passion to).

TL:DR A good (but short) game that respects its predecessors and delivers a technical tour-de-force and an interesting movielike-gameplay experience. Not your typical shooter, I'd recommended when on sale, not at full-price.
Listen, I honestly don't understand the bad (mixed) reviews this game is getting. Sure, I can understand people arguing it's short or "too many cutscenes" -- that much I'll agree with. That said, BJ really is back at it in true-to-its-ancestors, Wolfenstein fashion. Personally, and I know many don't share this opinion, i love the cutscenes. I came into it knowing I'd be enjoying a cinematic shooter, so there was no surprise there. The characters are back and the gruesome antagonist is back with a thirst for blood and it's certainly enjoyable. I won't spoil anything here, check it out for yourself, I think it's worth it.
The weapons (includng the tasty Lasergewehr) and the well-executed dual-weilding is just really fun to shoot with and weapons really do feel like they've got impact and precision. The only issue I've got so far is the sound design around them -- it's somewhat lackluster in that it's unable to provide depth, a strong attack and a sense of loudness, power and definition. They sound... meh, just typical, on par with other shooters - which is a shame considering its a AAA title and the weapons you shoot hundreds-of-thousands of rounds with should really be meticulously delivered to players -
innovative and interesting audio included. #audiophilenitpicks
On another note though, the graphics are, well, as we've come to expect from other Bethesda titles, complete, well-defined and overall just super interesting and masterfully well crafted. The level design is of course linear but so interesting to look at that it begs for closer attention. Overall, I think the look and feel is spot-on in capturing the players' attention and driving the story and experience. On that note, the technical prowess is off the charts with a smooth Vulkan implementation that delivers astonishing framerates and oh-so-silky-smooth gunplay. I mean heck, I'm running an i7-6700k + a gtx 1080, and I'm pushing an unwavering 144fps+ at 1080p with every graphical option completely maxed out, including v-sync, anti-aliasing and deferred rendering. From a technical stand-point, the game really does shine as a fantastically-well executed triple-A title. Dare I say, the technical execution is almost as clean as Doom - which is a ridiculous standard to live up to. Vulkan is really... really impressive when well implemented and it's always a treat to play games delivered by a dev team that knows what and how to build. To say i'm impressed is an under-statement, there's just something so awesome about playing a game that feels so damn smooth.

This is a very creative game. It is fairly cute, but that is balanced with genuine scares, and creepy plot points, which are explained through letters collected throughout the game. The name is completely honest, and takes place in a ghost named Spooky's house which is full of, you guessed it! Jump scares! I've played some twisted scary games, but quite a few things in this actually startled me. The game also is smart, because like P.T(The dead Silent Hills that could have been great) it feeds off the eerie feeling of walking down a dark hallway, not knowing what to expect. It also feels like an old arcade game in a way, because you get a score for how many rooms you go through(Basically all the rooms are hallways, so, you don't really get anywhere), and people try to beat others' scores. The art style is nice and the gameplay is smooth. There are very few things "wrong" with it, and they're really just me complaining. For instance, I don't like that almost all the rooms look nearly identical, and the jump scares do get old after a while, but the game keeps you intrigued with the thought of beating scores and being better at it than your friends and other people. And also, trying to out run crazed ghosts is kinda nerve wrecking too, so the devs deserve props on that too. Altogether this is a very well made game so, let's get down to the "verdict".

I just finished my second play-through of this game, my first being shortly after it came out. I stand by my opinion that this is a great game that is well worth playing.
First, the game's flaw (and there is only one major flaw): the missions are unashamedly repetitive. If don't mind that, or mitigate it by performing only one or two assassinations per evening, then the game should be very enjoyable. If this is likely to be a huge issue for you, perhaps skip ahead to ACII instead, which has (almost) all the great elements of this game but with much more varied missions. AC has no game-breaking bugs for me, but minor bugs include bodies occasionally flipping through the air.
Now for the reasons to play: 
The voice acting varies in quality, but it is generally high (with the notable exception of Altair, unfortunately).
Some people dislike the way you can fall of ledges when jumping to them: while this can be an issue in the early part of the game, once you relearn how to grab onto ledges it becomes simply an additional skill the game requires, making free running a little more challenging if you want to avoid falling to the ground.
Overall, I strongly recommend this game as highly enjoyable stealth action game with a great story.

Assassin' Creed, this is where your long journey through the entire series begins. You start off as an ordinary bartender who is kidnapped and utilized for his ancestors' heritage. Through this process you are placed in a machine properly named the 'Animus', through which your ancestors' memories are viewed. In this game you see through the eyes of master assassin Altair, and the trials his must face to regain his master rank within the brotherhood. You travel to three familiar locations we have all heard about in history class, Acre, Damascus, and Jerusalem. Here you fulfill tasks and assassinations to progress the story. Spend your time wisely because there are plenty of viewpoints, citizen saving, and challenge missions to complete in each location, as well as uneventful flags to find. By collecting flags, you unlock additional memories of Altair.
Pros:
- Combat is easy to master.
- Parkour responds well to your path.
- The landscapes are beautiful for an 2008 game engine.
- The story is engaging to follow and fully voiced.
- Weapon upgrades are easy to obtain, you just continue through the story to obtain the next piece.
- Controls respond extremely well, recommend using a controller.
- The game is short if you just focus on main tasks. I don't recommend, however, if you're just in it to learn the story you could spend maybe an entire weekend to complete the main story.
Cons:
- It is dated so some players may dislike the old graphics compared to games of today.
- Side-quests are heavily repeated and bland.
- Bugs, especially when anyone hits the floor the game tosses bodies all over the place. Sometimes even you go flying somewhere and glitch out. Though it is also hillarious!
- The transition between Desmond and Altair can get sort of annoying, especially when you want to progress during the story's juicy parts.
- Flag collection. Very tedious and not so rewarding.
- Uplay. I only dislike this for achievement purposes, and having another game software running just to play this game.
To wrap it up, these are my opinions of the game. I enjoyed Assassin's Creed and I am planning to play through all of them the rest of the summer. The stories appear to get way better and I for sure would like to play through them all. The start of the series is short, but it educates the player well enough to understand what is conspiring between Assassins and Templars.  I recommend this game to anyone willing to start at the beginning of this promising series. Plus, Altair is pretty cool and his assassin attire is one of my favorites.

I played this game because I'm a fan of Runic and their previous games, and they did really well with the new direction they took in Hob.
Hob follows a nameless protagonist and his golem companion as they remove some sort of rot or disease from the world. The world is pretty large, and is only made larger by underground areas, the removal of rot which opens up new pathing, and the ability to literally rearrange the world; blocks of the world rise and fall by your hand to allow access to regions that were otherwise inaccessible.
Main points:
- The world is pretty open for exploration. There will be objectives marked on your map, but it's up to you to figure out how to get there and what to do once you're there.
- The combat is smooth and satisfying. I feel that "simplified Souls-like, but still requiring skill" is a good description.
- There are upgrades and whatnot for your character: new moves and different costumes which slightly change how difficult the game is. Personally, I chose a costume that limited my health, but increased energy recovery speed.
- IT HAS A WATER LEVEL!
- The puzzles are satisfying. I heard a youtuber describe the world as fixing a jigsaw puzzle which someone had put together incorrectly, and I'd say that's pretty accurate.
- It seems to draw influence from Journey/Abzu (storytelling), as well as Hyper Light Drifter (storytelling and environment).
Overall, I love this game. It was really peaceful and a beautiful, fun experience.

This is a game of exploration and discovery. You run around the landscape seeking things to interact with. You do a lot of leaping and climbing, parkour-style, to reach various types of glowing or metallic mechanisms. When you approach one of these hotspots a blue X appears (or kb/mouse equivalent) and you press X to make something happen. There might be a handle that you use to pull a giant stone circle into position, drag a block into an alcove to activate something, or punch a button to send something spinning.
The target items are dotted around the map, and when you discover/activate them they disappear from the map, so it's always populated with yet-undiscovered targets, and new areas/items are revealed on the map as you unlock them in-world. The route towards these items is never as straightforward as it appears on the map, it always turns out to be convoluted, festooned with obstacles and requiring mechanisms to be activated to open the way.
Many games have 3D graphics, it's not a big deal. However, this is not just 3D graphics, the world has vertical DEPTH. You're always climbing to high points and descending into caves and secret passageways. Finding your way up and down is just as important as pinpointing your location on the map overview. It's a labyrinth full of weird and wonderful contraptions, monsters, animals and fairies. Every time you turn a corner there's something new, hour after hour. Did I mention how massive this game is?
As you move through the world you collect powerups, hidden butterflies and artifacts. You battle enemy monsters. You pet friendly wildlife. You activate all manner of giant mechanisms made of stone, shining metal and glowing buttons. But most of all, you explore every nook and cranny, high and low, punching your way through walls (and the ground!) to reveal hidden tunnels and pathways, and dragging blocks and contraptions around, fitting them into inactive mechanisms to bring them to life.
Every so often you come across a group of enemies. I'm playing on medium (default) difficulty, there is also easy, hard and very hard available. Medium is an apt description. There's enough challenge that you have to make a few attempts but it never reaches the point of frustration.
Each type of monster has its own weakness. [snip] They all have their individual victory cries and gestures when they win the battle, but once defeated their death is permanent and they're cleared from the map never to be seen again regardless of Hob's respawns. This makes them the best indicator of new areas because if you find a monster it means you haven't been there before, and once you've defeated them you can look around for new collectibles and mechanisms in that area. The corpses take a while to decompose, so you can even identify recently-conquered areas from the older ones which are clear of bodies.
Keyboard/mouse is an option, but this really must be played with a controller. I can honestly say that this is the most satisfying use of a controller I've ever experienced... [snip]
The piece de resistance is the controller rumble. It's brilliant. You jump from a height and you feel your landing. Get too near a lightning emitter and it'll tingle to warn you. When big stone mechanisms are activated, the grinding sounds are complemented by a heavy shake. I can't get enough of it.
There are many good things to say about Hob, but if I had to pick one aspect that really sets this apart from other games it's the world-unlock animations... [snip] the 'cutscenes' can't be called that because they don't cut away from the game. [snip] The camera zooms out and the whole vista erupts with giant stones and grassland rising up from the depths or water pouring into dry beds to form lakes, changing the whole landscape. It's a sight to behold, I tell ya. And it happens a lot.
At strategic positions on the map, usually in very high crows nest positions, there are vista spots. These are places where you sit on a ledge and the camera slowly turns and pans out to reveal a particularly spectacular view of the world with impressive distance perspective. Sometimes they're vertical views, and if you suffer from vertigo watch out for those!
Most of the game has only ambient sound effects. I say "only", but these are fantastic subtle sounds that connect you with the environment to make you feel like you're there. [snip] There is very soft music occasionally but you have to pay attention or you won't even notice it... [snip]
Once you get over the aforementioned initial hump, I'd say the challenge is still medium/hard.

This game was obviously released to disastruous reviews, broken promises, lack of content, and the players got an underdeveloped game and everyone was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Understandable.
With this 1.3 update, I would say that No Man's Sky has become a damn good title. I remember everyone asked before the game released "Well this looks cool, but what do you DO?" I'll tell ya. You can follow the quest lines that were added in, and while they are not the most narrative experience ever, they are told in a very nice way. You can do base building which is neat and all, nothing crazy, but it leads to farming which is exactly what you'll do if you like grinding. You can also do the typical exploration of the various planets with their new biomes and activities to take part in on the planet and catalog the flora and fauna of the planets you visit. You can also do missions that are given out on the various space stations scattered throughout the systems that you visit.
There are still some issues that are being ironed out with a pretty quick pace by Hello Games, and the information on the various wikis for the game is hilariously outdated, but all in all this is a great indie title that was unfortunately touted before release as a AAA game and still has a AAA price.
I don't think anyone should forget the state in which the game released, but I strongly suggest that potential buyers look at what the game has become and not what it was. Hello Games has quietly improved it and are continuing to do so.

I already have this game for the PS3 but, thanks to the hackers, I came here to see if the PC version was "cleaner." I got it for $9.99 during the recent sale and I can say it was definitely worth it now that I'm able to play on servers that aren't hacked beyond playability.
Aside from actually being able to play legitimate games in multiplayer, the PC version has a lot of other great things to offer, including:
1. a Command Console - Like most PC games you can open up a command console and mess around with the singleplayer. If I actually wanted to waste my time digging into this feature I could easily spend hours entertaining myself.
2. Optimization - unlike the console version and like every single PC game, you can change the settings including sounds, controls, textures, resolution, etc.
3. Servers - on the console version of this game you'd be thrown into a lobby; the PC version has a huge server list with games holding up to 40 players. You can choose what kind of game you are looking for with the included options such as "hardcore mode, classic, friendly fire, full games, empty games, etc." which makes finding the game you want much easier.
4. Great controls - Call of Duty® has been known for its great controls on console and on the PC version things just get better when you're playing with a keyboard and mouse. It's just a lot easier to kill someone on PC.
There are probably alot more things that make the PC version of Call of Duty® 4: Modern Warfare® the best way to play, but I've only played the game for 3.5 hours.

Disclaimer: Don't worry about my small ingame time count - I played this game long before it was available on Steam and I usually just forget to launch it through Steam.
The game itself is a very dynamic shooter game, with really enjoyable and fluid movement, supported by the grappling hook - which is what makes the game so special and movement in it very different than in other, slow games. The maps are also really nice and well balanced.
But it's the mods where this game really shines. They can be accessed by disabling the "Standard map" and "Standard game mode" filters in the server browser. There is a lot of mods, ranging from speedrunning parkour maps (DDRace), through game modes with one-hit kills (OpenFNG, zCatch, iCTF) to driving tanks and flying helicopters (Battle).
I personally like DDRace one the most (especially the DDNet servers network, which has its own optional, improved game client). It revolves around passing a dexterity/thinking-based (more dexterity though) parkour maps, usually in teams. Maps are designed to require a good teamplay, except for the Solo and Dummy ones. It's really fun, because there are always new maps with new challenges and every player is able to find ones appropiate for their skill level. The community is also really nice and usually very friendly.
The game may be quite hard at the beginning - especially the shooter modes (in DDRace there are at least some easy maps, like StepByStep or Just2Easy on Novice servers),
. It's also much easier to learn, if you ask some player to show you around (especially in DDRace mod). While at start it may feel insane how some players move like rockets and aim almost perfectly, it becomes really fun to do it yourself once you learn the basics. Also, if you don't like shooter game modes, you can always play DDRace - which is mostly cooperative (except for the Solo and Dummy maps or Block servers).
- always check ping of the servers you join. Most servers, which are far away from your location, will have high ping. Try to play on servers with low ping (below 60) when possible.
So... to wrap it up - the game may be hard at the beginning, but it's really rewarding and enjoyable once you learn to move around the maps using the grappling hook.

Ah, the first amazing game in one, if not the most, amazing game saga of all time. Assassin's Creed: Director's Cut Edition is so amazing, with a gritty and brooding atmosphere. The game is fully open world, allowing you to fully explore the dark depths of actual places such as Damascus, and Jerusalem. There are plenty of opportunities to save helpless obese guys and screaming young Arabic girls. This game is very realistic, in which if you do anything socially unacceptable, such as stabbing people, the guards will take notice and chase you. In this case, you must break the line of sight by either climbing to the roof of a building or hiding behind your intimidating vigilante friends. This is not a game for the impatient though, as it takes time to slowly stalk a target and slide a blade into his rib cage without the citizens seeing you. If you are the type of person who would rather run in screaming, and wildly slash your way through the sword-wielding guards, then I would recommend some other game. Although, hacking guards is a large part of this stealth game. One of the largest building blocks in this game, (and every other AC for that matter) is parkour. If you like jumping over benches, scaling large walls, and swinging on beams to escape the soldiers who really don't like you, then this is your game. Although the controls are a little foreign at first, they become natural soon after you finish the "tutorial" level. The story is good, with many twists and turns, with a suprise ending. One thing this game lacks is cutscene quality, I mostly slept through the long discussions with the Bureau Leader. Although this game was made in 2007, it still holds its ground as very well constucted, with very good graphics (for 07) and a deep story. And, if you enjoy the other AC games, this is a great place to return to. Would stab and slash again: 8/10

The only other character in the game is a blonde who tells you a basic mission and says good job when you do it (Like Roll). IT IS A UNFINISHED GAME! But every level introduces new mechanics. The floor is destructable which can lead to some strategy on some level. The levels are basic, but have a general mechanic they are built around. Later missions I actually died. You are getting swarmed by flying enemies and little ground swarmers, and the chaos gets pretty fun. Seems like this game was made by a few people in thier free time. It's a shame nothing more came out of it because with money and polish if feels like it could have been a series. First 3 levels are meh. Then it gets more interesting. It is bland, but what is there is interesting and endearing. It's just sad because more resources could have turned a good tech demo into a great game. It's definitely worth a peek if on sale, you are a diehard megaman fan, and can appreciate the simple things. I shouldn't like this game as much as I do, but it grows on you. Which seems to be the general sentiment in reviews.

A visually stunning, incredibly atmospheric, and mentally taxing game.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice aims to tell the story of Senua, a Norse woman with severe psychosis looking to save her dead lover.
Hellblades atmosphere and attempts to make the player feel like they're experiencing a psychotic episode truly makes this game shine.

Beautiful graphics and incredible sound design take a fairly straightforward adventure game up to a level few other games have achieved.  This is a game crafted with love and it shows.  The character of Senua is one of the most fully-realized in recent memory, and the story, while not unique, is very well presented.

Upfront answer, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a good game. It's not a great game, though.
It is, however, an amazing experience that I cannot recommend more. This is one of those things that as soon as you are finished you'll want to find someone else who's played it just so you can gush about what you just went through.

Hellblade Senua Sacrifice is an indie short adventure through the darkness of your own mind and it's background of Nordic Folklore is a perfect combination for a perfect game.
Although it's short, it's memorable and it gave me a lot of sunspense and sense of disbelief. The puzzles are well made, not too easy...but not too difficult too. Senua is an interesting character to play with, combat is...alright... But thats okay, the atmosphere and the enemies are very well made, character models are high quality, but the world texture is not.
4/5 is what i'll give to this indie game.

This game was obviously released to disastruous reviews, broken promises, lack of content, and the players got an underdeveloped game and everyone was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Understandable.
With this 1.3 update, I would say that No Man's Sky has become a damn good title. I remember everyone asked before the game released "Well this looks cool, but what do you DO?" I'll tell ya. You can follow the quest lines that were added in, and while they are not the most narrative experience ever, they are told in a very nice way. You can do base building which is neat and all, nothing crazy, but it leads to farming which is exactly what you'll do if you like grinding. You can also do the typical exploration of the various planets with their new biomes and activities to take part in on the planet and catalog the flora and fauna of the planets you visit. You can also do missions that are given out on the various space stations scattered throughout the systems that you visit.
There are still some issues that are being ironed out with a pretty quick pace by Hello Games, and the information on the various wikis for the game is hilariously outdated, but all in all this is a great indie title that was unfortunately touted before release as a AAA game and still has a AAA price.
I don't think anyone should forget the state in which the game released, but I strongly suggest that potential buyers look at what the game has become and not what it was. Hello Games has quietly improved it and are continuing to do so.

What to say about No Mans Sky?

On release I refuseed to buy this game but recently I decided to give it a go after 2 major updates, and after 10 hours of gameplay, here's what I think:
Pro's:
-Fun concept
-The first time you enter space you are overwhelmed with happiness
-The basebuilding isn't intuitive but still fun
-The graphics are beautiful
Con's:
-The grind even from the beginning is mind-numbingly boring
-The story is forced upon you at first when you want to explore and still somehow manages to move slow
-The procedural generation is lack-luster and bland to explore
My verdict:
After the 2 major updates the game has enough content to warrant a full price, it is a complete game in an over-saturated   alpha/beta testing "game" market.

I did NOT own No Man's Sky before the big update; I bought it after the fact when I saw the reviews were positive and it was on sale.
It took me some time to get into the game and figure out how to operate everything.
Once I got ahold of what I was supposed to do I found myself overwhelmed with the
universe. There's so much to do and go and explore. And from what I've heard, the new update added so many new features. I find myself flying all over the place collecting different elements and trying to survive on whatever the planets throw at me.
I know a few other reviewers mentioned this as well, but there is a LOT of mining. It seems ridiculous at times, but even when I'm mining my heart out I still feel so involved in the game and the universe.

I haven't enjoyed a game as much as this for some time. It is highly original in a number of respects (even the way that objects animation when clicked), full of charm (the little creatures are delightful, and the bad guys laugh over your bleeding corpse), with a good level of puzzling and platforming challenge but not punishing. It looks gorgeous, and the cell shading gives it a cartoonish charm. There are additional save points are various scenic locations, where you can sit and enjoy the view, which is cute, and original.
If you love metroidvania, you'll love this, so expect quite a bit of backtracking, but if you love being in the game world, as I did, it's no hardship. It is called an "open world" game which might be seen as a little misleading, as the main story is fairly linear, but you can take time out to explore, hunt for that elusive power up, scythe the grass with your sword, interact with the animals, or go and pick a fight.
If it has a downside, its minimal storytelling sometimes left me wondering what to do next, as not all keypoints in the main narrative generate mission markers on the map, and I have a short memory.
It really does need a controller though, as some parts are close to impossible with a keyboard, and when you are navigating along a narrow ledge or platform, which twists and turns in odd directions, there is sometimes no key combination for the required direction, so you have to tap the two relevant direction keys in varying amounts to generate the right direction. I managed to get through the game, with a good degree of completion without a controller, but it does get very frustrating sometimes.
The back story and characters don't really have a lot of emotional depth however, it's really the PLACE with all its charm which provides the depth atmosphere.
A delight to play, close to perfect, but not quite. The map is a bit too minimal to be useful sometimes, and some of the animations e.g. when emerging from a save point, are too lengthy when you are tapping the keys in frustration after your latest failed precision jump, waiting to get to it again.
Also it's a bit buggy at the moment but the devs are sweating blood to polish it up, so full marks for effort.

Original Review:
After plaything through the game, I cannot recommend this to anyone.
Hob is a 3d platformer light on puzzle solving and frustrating combat.
Pros:
- Stylized world and character
- First two hours really fun
- Fun exploring
- Interacting with the world and creatures
- Exploring initially
- Interesting story initially
- Lots of checkpoint initially
Cons:
- Stylized world really is showing age with the Torchlight engine.
- Lots of clipping issues
- Character falling through the ground with instant death
- The game feels like it was designed in blocks.
- Once you have done one block, you have done them all.
- Find the butterflies, health upgrade, energy bar upgrade, sword parts.
- Find the “spirit imps” and release it.  Go to next block and do the same.
- Rinse and repeat.
- After exploring past the lightning area all the Areas look the same.
- Check points in later stages become further apart.
- Often leading to retrying difficult jumps over and over again.
- Doing the same complex jump sequence 20 to 30 times.
- Made my thumb hurt.
- Frustration does not equal Fun!
- Combat
- The dreaded micro-pause when dodging.
- This causes the player to be hit often with instant death.
- Instant death does not equal Fun!
- Energy bar depletion is never an issue.
- Game can be completed without using blocking.
- Combat upgrades are useless and do not add anything to the combat.
- Camera
- This is the fundamental flaw of the whole game.
- Turns the game into a “find the button and push it.”
- Because you cannot look around, you cannot solve the puzzles.
You just run around looking for a button or switch to press and see what happens.
There really isn’t much puzzle solving.
- Story
- There is no story mid-game. None.
- Mid game is all about collecting items and finishing the blocks.
- So boring.

Hob is a delightful gaming experience lovingly crafted and creatively executed.  Exploration and puzzles steal the spotlight while combat actually work much better than I've come to expect in a game like this.  Watch the world change around you and slowly discover the secrets necessary to save it.
This game is absolutely worth the time and money invested into it.  The visuals are absolutely breathtaking as you watch the world transform around you.  I found myself awestruck at the sheer imagination put into this universe at several points throughout playing.  Creature, character, and especially environment design in Hob is truly something to marvel at.
Puzzles were relatively simple most of the time, but required quite a bit of exploring, which was rather fun.  Jumping, grappling and warping around was very fluid and the intuitive mechanic of following the power lines was the perfect amount of instruction.
Combat was relatively standard for a little action RPG, which isn't a bad thing at all.  Enemies were challenging at time (I played on "hard" on a scale of easy, normal, hard, very hard) and it felt like the perfect degree of challenge.  Find schematics that you can use to unlock new abilities and upgrade your weapon for a more in depth experience -- but to be quite honest, you're not necessarily going to feel a huge difference.
The storyline of Hob was more of an implied world-building scenario rather than a narrative.  Elements of the world unfolded and unveiled themselves to you and the background of the universe was more implicit than solidified, leaving it open to thought and deliberation.  To me, this perfectly fit the tone of the game -- finding yourself in a universe full of otherworldly imagination.
I got 15 solid hours of gameplay before "beating" the campaign (of course there are always things that you miss that you can opt to go back and find if you so desire).  I was very peased with this -- I was honestly expecting to get about half of that.
Overall, I highly recommend Hob to those looking for an explorative, imaginative, atmospheric experience.  To those who favor combat and exciting gameplay over world building, maybe wait for a sale.

So this is where it all began, the first AC...
Please keep in mind that this game now is almost 10 years old, and it is showing it's age. So if you have played more recent ACs and want to check out the very first one, be prepared for some major differences.
However, the game still looks nice... it's colorful, the animations still look cool and it's still fun to run around in Damasc, Accra and Jerusalem.
Some differences though:
- The parcouring/freerunning works quite well, but it's pretty...clunky compared to that in, say, Unity or Syndicate. So accidents will happen, you will experience some misjumps and will prolly fall a couple of times. Still, it can be quite fun.
- The combat system is a bit spammy. Mostly, you hit x to strike and, while holding the block-button (shoulder button on a controller), hit x as well to block and counter-strike.
At first, combat is rough, but with each sequence, you learn more abilities (or get them back), so you can fight more efficiently, and a counter-strike will often result in one-shotting a mob.
- You have your sword, throwing knifes (which you can fight with), your fists and the hidden blade (which you can't fight with really, it's only used for stabbing people who are unaware), that's it... no smoke bombs, rope darts, guns, bows, xbows etc. It's limited, but that does not bother me much.
- The cinematics/conversations are rather long, and can not be skipped. However, if you play this for the very first time, that's ok, as it's interesting to listen and learn about the story and background.
- There are some bugs and glitches... occasionally, you'll die when you hit a haystack, which of course is a bug.
- The sequences are a bit repetitive... climb towers to find activities, do those to gather information on your target, report to your fellow assassin at the bureau, then head for the assassination of the target. It's like that until the end of the game.
- There is some side activity, but not as much as in recent games. No money, no purchasing of gear upgrades etc.
The game is showing it's age, and of course, AC II later hit the ball out of the park, BUT:
I still think that, if you like the franchise, you should play this first one at least once to see the start of the series. It's not all that long, and I think it's still a fun game with a lot of atmosphere and a wonderful soundtrack by Jesper Kyd.
And to be frank, I enjoyed replaying this much more than the most recent, IMO horrible Syndicate, and even the very spammy combat in AC I is better than the one in that new game.
So... check it out. It's old, has quite a few flaws and is missing a lot of the things more modern ACs had, but it's a great start to the series. I REALLY REALLY recommend to use a controller though! I played all of them with a controller, but especially for this one, I don't think you'll get much out of it if you try to play it with kbm.

Altair's voice is some of the worst voice acting I have ever heard to date in all the games I've ever played.  It's painful to listen to.  Most other voices are just ok.  I turn music off so no comment there.  The beggars, guards, and other people are numerous but their voices aren't numerous enough, so you'll hear the same recordings over and over again, though each map has different voices for the same types of people.
The controls are a little awkward, and i'm not referring to the difficulty matching up each action to a button.  It actually plays pretty well once you understand the High Profile mode which some people have difficulty adjusting to.  The awkwardness is with the camera angles.  They get stuck a lot in tight places, where you will often find yourself in, and it causes you to stab innocent people or jump off a ledge when you don't intend to.
I was hoping the fluidness and abilities would match that of the batman series, but it doesn't at all.  You can't aim the angle in which to throw a person off a ledge, forcing you to line your character up correctly, which may not be possible the way the guards move or other objects that may be in the way.  You can't pounce from a ledge to kill despite the opening sequence alluding that you can.  (You also cannot hide amidst the schollars while being watched as alluded to in the opening sequence as well.)  Hiding only works when you're not watched, which I feel is more real anyway.  You can't extend your hidden blade while swordfighting.  The knife throw and knife slash is the same button, so if they dodge your attack and land too far away, you'll reduce your inventory of throwing knives if you keep smashing the button.  You can pickpocket for more though.  Your character is a bit limited in what it can do.
Despite its age, the game holds up pretty well.  the pixellation is apparent in the scenes but the models are full and detailed.  the maps are maze-like and feel like a corridor may or may not be present while running around, and if you run down a dark alley, you may have a 50/50 chance you'll hit a wall and have to fight the people you're facing.  there is plenty of z-axis also. A Flawed Dose of Nostalgia
In 2016, it seemed like to play the original 2007 Assassin's Creed was to revert to the rough draft of the AC formula, but that is where I found myself loving the core gameplay of AC. The first game in the franchise hadn't yet been bogged down with the extra bloat most evident in the later titles like AC Unity, from the challenges and side missions to the rendering of visuals. The seminal Assassin's Creed succeeds today in 2016 because it benefits from being the innovative first in a formulated franchise.
The balance between a solid storyline and mindless side activities kept me moving towards finishing the game without feeling like the completionist challenge was unsurmountable (a personal problem I find with modern open-world games). I typically started with viewpoints, moved to "Save Citizens" missions, and then began my formal investigation into my assassination target. In my mind, I was learning the city, its people, and then solving the overall problem plaguing them. The objectives could be completed in any manner, but the approach I took felt the most natural for a stranger entering a city.
The combat felt great when my timing synced up well,  It felt good to be that overpowered, yet it was too easy and didn't involve much strategy despite being trained in-game with various techniques. Occasionally, I would find myself on-top of various things like market stalls with six other men on the same stall with three other men attempting to climb up to the "battlefield" . The AI scripting felt like the enemies were simply and mindlessly piling on. All I had to do was time the counter attack successfully to take out any force.
The stealth felt unrefined and was frequently undermined by a stray AI stepping into the shared environment or a drunken NPC shoving me into a group while I was attempting to blend in. While it helped to utilize stealth from time to time, the behaviors which broke my stealth usually threw me into another fifteen man battle. It was most useful when traversing the map to avoid battle engagement, but detrimental to all the investigations crafted into the story when a major assassination would down spiral due to imprecise stealth mechanics. This is best illustrated when I attempted to throw a knife at my target and pressed the lock-on button. It alerted everyone in the arena to my presence with the simple lock-on and a twenty man battle ensued.
After bouncing around to various AC games in the past year or so, the GUI in this original game felt so in touch with the premise of the Animus technology. The HUD and in-game menu never appeared gaudy or clunky, but the main menu unnecessarily required me to briefly switch to my mouse to make a character profile selection before I could begin playing with my gamepad. The map was a delight to engage with, but the investigations give the player various map information such as where guards are during the assassination's preceding event and the safest path for extraction after killing the target, that was ultimately undermined by an under-detailed HUD map.
I played the original version of Assassin's Creed to completion on PS3 around 2009 and it left a nostalgic feeling in the back of my mind. The nostalgic thirst was quenched with this latest 2016 playthrough on PC, but not without some stumbles along the way that reminded me that some serious gameplay mechanic overhaul occurred in the past 7 years. This game innovated at the time, but was refined greatly with the sequel.

This combat system has a different approach to others with similar setup like Devil May Cry. In Remember me you don't go for the highest combat combo for an S-Rank score. The combo's are too short to make that even work. Once you complete a combo string then the counter starts anew. How combo's work in this game is too simply combine damage, cool down or health regen to it.
And that shows right away how they're supposed to function in combination with the Sensen skills. You don't use the combo's to actually kill hordes of trash mobs like you would in similar games. Sure you can kill some and then overload their brain, but the majority of damage output comes from using the Sensen. So the combo's are there mainly for health regen so you can survive hordes of opponents with ease... combined with coold down reduction till your next Sensen attack is possible. This reduces battles often to tedious tests of patience where I want too attack, but have too wait for the right Sensen to come off cool down to deal with the specific opponent. On top of that the protaganist is nice and mobile as well as reactionairy in controls when dealing with many opponents at once. You can easily jump over them while maintaining the continuation of the combo. All opponents, even those invisible or off screen, have a noticable "gotham arkham"-ish indicator to show their incoming attack.
This change in mindset isn't what people expect from games with this style of combat. Thus they have trouble grasping it and finding it frustrating. That is not too say there aren't frustrating moments in the game. In some boss fights the QTE's aren't always visible enough. This can result in a repeated sequence until it is noticed by the player. I had such a moment that took me almost a dozen times too repeat and had no idea why. Which brings me to the point of communication information to the player. There are moments where the game keeps repeating the fact you need to use a certain attack, but other times no information is given on what to do. Personally I didn't find this bothersome since I enjoy solving situations. On top of that I look at which mechanics are introduced and then can come to the right conclusion on how to proceed.
The other part of the game relates to what you see in many action-adventure style games such as the new Tombraider reboots and Uncharted...namely the platforming and scaling walls. This works really smooth. So smooth even that I hardly feel involved most of the time. Only issue I have is that graphically the ledges aren't always clearly visible to indicate what path too take. Therefore the yellow indicators come into play in order to guide the player forward. Personally I find this at times helpfull when stuck, but other times insulting. I'd rather have seen a bit more contrast in which ledges could be used as part of figuring out the route to go.
I quite enjoyed many design choices in this game, but some don't really get fleshed out fully it seems.
Still it is a very enjoyable game with a cool story and some amazingly beautiful vista's. The story uses elements you'd normally see in time travel related stories. Since it now takes part in the minds of people this same element feels more at home and properly utilized. There are puzzles and lots of different things to do during a lineair progression.
Definately a game worth grabbing. It isn't a top of the line game in my opinion, but for a sub-maximal game it is still a lot of fun.

Remember Me is a game developed by DONTNOD Entertainment and published by Capcom. Remember Me was developed by the same people that created Life Is Strange and this game was the company's first game before venturing to Life Is Strange
The story takes place in Neo-Paris and you play Nilin, a memory hunter who has her memory erased in the prison of La Bastille and becomes a new person altogether, however, a person known as Edge manages to move her through escaping La Bastille and into the slums of Paris. Throughout the nine episodes (named Episode 0 through Episode 8), Nilin will discover what happened to her before she entered La Bastille, her past and the big corporations taking care of Neo-Paris
The story is well written for the most part and some of the characters are likeable, however, the characters are not really well fleshed out as opposed to other DONTNOD games such as Life Is Strange. Most of the characters just appear and are never mentioned again
The graphics are stunning and makes Paris look believable as a futuristic city, together with drones, robots and artificial intelligence. However I did notice some poor texture work here and there and at some moments the game's framerate did dip around here and there
The sound effects were okay however the music was really well done. It was almost as a mixture of both a blockbuster movie soundtrack and a glitchy futuristic world. The game managed to blend in these two types of genres together to make some enjoyable background music
The game mixes both platforming with action. The platforming was okay but nothing to write home about. You jump around Parisian buildings and scaffoldings and try to solve some platform bits to carry on. The big emphasis was the combat and this was the weakest segment of the game
The combat was really poor, clunky and awkward. The game emphasizes you using combos, each you do you can either perform an action strike, a health regeneration, and so on, however, with the brain dead A.I. and annoying, clunky, awkward combat system and the huge repition of enemies, it made the game's combat pretty boring
Another issues was the annoying camera. The camera was way too close to Nilin, so much so that whenever you wanted to see what was next to you or move the camera around especially in combat, it is extremely awkward and fixed too close to Nilin, also sometimes the game's camera would just freak out and go all over the place
Overall, Remember Me is a mixed bag. It has some interesting aspects such as the story, the graphics and the music but also has some flaws such as the awful combat mechanic and camera and the usage of poor texture work and dips in framerate
However, if you like futuristic stories/settings or like Sci-Fi, then Remember Me is worth a shot!

It's not the next Braid, but mechanically it's a decent game. There's not much to fault it for other than being short and the over-the-top fan pandering which, as indifferent, I found to generally be off-putting or not make sense (a rock named Jennifer?), but at the same time I commend it for aiming to please and be memorable to its fans rather than something generic. Needless to say if you despise the guy then you'll despise this game.
Pros:
-It has a nice high-res pixel art aesthetic, looking something like an HD GBA game.
-The music is pretty great. It sounds like it's going for an NES style and comes off as authentic to me.
-Fully voiced, though you may consider that a con as they're not voice actors by trade.
-Collectibles and unlockables to give you stuff to do while/after beating the game. The collectibles are put into tricky-to-reach or hidden areas throughout the levels.
-There are a number of small touches that make it feel like a polished game with care put into it. Picking up hearts when your health is full turns them into coins so they're not a waste. Changing your costume changes the character portrait in cutscenes. Replaying a level with an unlocked character changes things if that character normally appears in the level. There's a level where you get picked up in a helicopter to escape and
Cons:
-It's short. There are 27 levels total and if you just do a single playthrough and don't worry about collectibles/unlockables or the 7 optional levels then you'll only get a couple hours out of it.
-Too easy on any difficulty less than "Bro", probably due in part to its mobile origins. Your upgraded HP tops out at 16 hearts and enemies do 1 heart of damage on "Easy" and 2 hearts of damage on "Hard", but the checkpoints in the levels fully replenish you. "Bro" doubles the damage to 4 hearts and removes the checkpoints, providing a good challenge, though I feel there could be a happy medium between "Hard" and "Bro" for those looking for a slight challenge.
-When you replay a level the intro/outro cutscenes play again, forcing you to skip through dialogue. About half of the levels have some sort of intro/outro.
-Of all four YouTuber cameos in the game only one of them is really worked into the plot. The others are forced in and only relevant for a single level.

Hammerfight is an enjoyable concept that is hampered by large swaths of poor execution.  I greatly enjoyed progressing rom a lowly captured slave to a revered warrior during the campaign, though the plot was indeed wonky at times.  The physics are awesome and there is nothing like a perfectly executed blow that either destroys your opponent outright or sends him careening around the level like a living cannonball.  The arena mode in which you lay waste to waves of progressively harder opponents is a distilled version of the enjoyable combat and can make for many extra hours of gameplay.  The selection of weapons and the ability to dual wield leave the game open for nearly unlimited experimentation with different "loadouts."
Despite these strengths, the game has several rough edges.  The menu uses a touchy sliding mechanism which, though artistically unique, can make it hard to even select a game mode when you use a highly sensitive mouse.  Technical anomalies are common and pervasive, and despite the fact that my laptop handily exceeds the stated system requirements, I would often encounter game breaking slowdown and crashes.  These issues were even more vexing when I was unable to fully overcome them even after hours searching through forums and tweaking the .config file.  Also, I was not able to find any recent activity from the developer anywhere online, so I wouldn't hold out hope for any new updates or patches unless they come from an ambitious fan.
While I definitely feel like I got my money's worth out of this game, I should not have had to work so hard just to make the game playable.  When Hammerfight is at it's best it's a fabulous experiment in fast paced physics based gameplay.  At its worst, it's a tragically unplayable mess that is resistant to a solution.  Try the demo first and if you can get it working, dive in.

This game plays like a real-time version of Frozen Synapse, positioning, teamwork, and situational awareness are key.  At its best RWR is fast paced, engaging, and fun skill based tactical gameplay.
There are some problems with RWR, namely the graphics don't always adequately reflect the respective heights of different pieces of cover, sometimes making it difficult to know whether or not you can be shot.  This is even more troublesome when using rockets or grenades, as an object you believe you can fire over (or the ground) will sometimes stop and explosive meant for the enemy resulting in your death and the teamkills of any number of your squad mates.
The modding scene for this game is starting to spin up and means there are even more exciting options for gameplay around the corner for Running With Rifles.  Get a 4-pack and play with your friends and their squads for even more tactical and strategic action!

I've not had the chance to try a co-op session yet so keep that in mind.
I want to like RWR, there's a great game somewhere in there but it is such a frustrating experience.
It plays more like an early beta, the groundwork is there but the rough edges haven't been sanded down. It straddles the fence between tactical and arcade in a bizarre fashion. TTK is quite low and HP goes only one way so in theory positioning and teamwork is key. However at the lowest rank you don't have your own squad to command and you're not grouped into an AI squad, while the AI is fairly clever it struggles to work as a cohesive group with or without the player. It's not unlike playing in a pub server.
Due to the implementation of AI the front line is highly amorphous and you can rarely rely on any one area to be safe. Combined with AI that won't watch your flanks, the way mouselook is implemented and the lack of a minimap the more open maps will have frequent deaths that feel arbitrary.
The tactical/arcade dichotomy is furthered by high spread on weapons, this makes long distance engagements a bit of a roulette and prevents you from effectively locking down areas. Additionally it's very difficult to judge what is and isn't and will or won't be in your line of sight which makes trying to shoot without exposing yourself too much quite difficult. This could be solved with some very minor UI changes.
I have further gripes but these issues are the make or break of it.
