Hob is a beautiful, expansive journey through a world literally torn apart by war. The remnants of a long lost world are scattered across lush green forests, and dusty brown deserts. Ancient temples and copper pipes protrude from the natural canopy that has covered up the secrets of the past. Discovering these secrets is what drives you forward in Hob, and it makes the game an ever evolving mystery right up until its final moments.
With no exposition, Hob’s main menu fades into the first moments of gameplay. You are freed from a tomb by a hulking mechanical automaton. You’re not told to follow it, but you know it is what you’re supposed to do. These moments teach you that this robot is your guide, and friend. Your new friend’s will becomes clear over time: It wants you to restore the world to its former glory and destroy the blight poisoning the land.
Throughout your journey you will literally rebuild the world by repairing the ancient machines that rest just below the surface. These serve as the game’s dungeons, and upon completing them you are rewarded by watching the world literally rise up from the abyss. Every time I saw the intricate puzzle pieces shift and move into place I was amazed. Hob has a stunning art style, but the ever changing level design is what really steals the show.
You’ll also come across upgrades in these dungeons. Chief among them are Armaments that enhance the giant robotic hand your character has. These Armaments upgrade your traversal abilities allowing you to access previously inaccessible locations. In addition to Armaments you will also find health and energy upgrades, as well as schematics that allow you upgrade your combat abilities.
The combat is a bit of a mixed bag. You have a sword and the previously mentioned hand to attack with. You also have a simple dodge that provides a few frames of invincibility, and you can unlock the ability to block with a shield. When the encounters work as intended, the combat can be fun and challenging, but it does get repetitive over time. The real issue that I ran into where enemies that would get stuck on the game’s geometry or lose aggro for no reason. These glitches totally broke the flow of the combat encounters when they arose. They sometimes led to untimely deaths that felt out of my control. Thankfully, the game uses an in-world resurrection system similar to the Vita Chambers in BioShock, so you rarely lose progress when dying.
There’s a big world hiding just below the surface.
Hob features a fixed isometric camera that locks your field of view. The camera only moves when the game wants you to pay attention to something. It will drop down to a more conventional 3rd person view at key parts of the story to provide you with a grand view of the adventures ahead. Other times it will shift just enough to give you a peak at an area you cannot access yet, showing you a secret you may want to investigate later. Generally, the camera serves the game’s style well, but can sometimes be a nuisance during later platforming segments. The camera can sometimes make it difficult to judge depth and this can cause jumps to miss their mark. In addition, I ran into a few instances where I clipped through the ground when performing a jump. These moments were rare, but frustrating.
You must solve puzzles to reactivate the mechanisms that bring life back to the world. The tools you use to solve the puzzles are fairly traditional; you have to move blocks around or reach certain destinations in a short amount of time. While the tools are ordinary, the solutions are not. Just like the story, you have to pick up on context clues to understand what the game is asking of you. Many of the puzzles are seamlessly integrated into the natural flow of the game, and you may not even realize you’re solving one until you complete it.
The inevitable conclusion here is that Hob is a masterwork of exploration and puzzle solving. All of the game’s aspects come together to form a cohesive whole that is both entertaining and awe inspiring from start to finish. There may be a few hiccups along the way, but they’re easily overlooked when compared to the nearly flawless execution of the rest of the game. Hob is an adventure that will keep you enthralled right up until the very end, and even then you may not be ready for what it has in store.

Initial impressions after a couple hours:
I came in to this game with zero knowledge of what the game was about - other than the guys that made Torchlight made this.
The world of Hob is very mysterious, there isnt any spoken word or written dialogue in the game.  The game has many callbacks to the classic Zelda feel. You are plopped down on unfamiliar territory and you are to use your wits to unravel the world around you.  There are two main weapons in the game, your glove, and your sword. Both of which seem like they have upgrade paths - but only after you have found fragment pieces of each of them to upgrade.
I have been to what feels like 3-4 mini dungeons, in these they give you an upgrade for your glove ala the items you find in dungeons in classic Zelda. These glove upgrades are much like the Zelda items where it is used to help solve the upcoming puzzels,  not only that, but they are used in unlocking areas in the outside world as well.
I love classic Zelda, and sometimes I wonder why there aren't more games like it in the genre.  The only time where I am frustrated at times is when I am lost at what to do next. Since there is no dialogue or voice acting, you are encouraged to explore every nook and cranny of the world.
There were times where I felt like I stumbled upon a place way too high for my charachters skill level - where enemies were taking my whole life bar away in one swing - it is moments like this that provide a sense of wonder in the world of HoB and I can't wait to see what I uncover next.
One of the minor gripes I have so far is that there is no motivation for the charachter to traverse this world. Why were you plopped on this piece of land, so what if you collect sword and glove upgrades? What does that entitle? Why are you doing these things,  is there a greater evil, are you trying to save the world from the monsters that roam the land? Motive of why you are doing the things you do is unclear at the moment; hopefully that clears up as I progress through the game.
That notion however is a double edge sword - it just makes me want to continue digging deeper in the world of Hob.

This has been revised as my experience has grown.  Overall, I would still recommend HoB, but here are my thoughts on some of the more talked about features.
First, the game world.  The game world of HoB is pretty exquisite.  The art style, creatures, and sense of grandeur are extremely well done.  Watching the world change, based on your in game actions, is really neat and satisfying.  The way the different pieces of the puzzle-like world fit together and change over time is seamless and I'm pretty blown away.  I actually cannot imagine trying to make something like this work.  In my eyes, it's quite an achievement.
Second, the story or lack of one.  For me, this isn't an issue.  I'm actually having a great time with the mystery of the world.  I feel like the character, I'm just trying to figure out what the hell is going on while piecing things together through the puzzles.  It's pretty refreshing especially since I'm a bit of a snob about writing.  I'm not done with the game so I don't know how it unfolds, but right now (4-5 hours played) it is not an issue.  In fact, I think it works incredibly well because of the World's mysterious atmosphere.  That said, a lot of others have expressed frustration about this.  Their sentiments have been akin to, "I'm doing this just because."  To those people I say, "use your ♥♥♥♥ing imagination."
Third, the combat.  Combat is pretty similar to Zelda (much of this game is similar to Zelda).  You swing your sword and punch your way to victory.  Some mobs die in a couple hits, others take quite awhile to kill.  Some aren't very dangerous, others kill you in 1 hit if you incorrectly time a dodge.  The progression of your sword skills/glove skills are noticeable.  Enemies explode when they die, combat sounds are present, and when a club smashes the ground, you feel it.
Fourth, the puzzles and secrets.  I don't play tons of puzzle games, but I've been enjoying the ones in HoB.  I haven't found one that has completely stumped me for ages, but they don't feel insignificant either.  Thus far, I'm finding them pretty satisfying and with a reasonable amount of variance.  I imagine this is because most of them fundamentally alter the layout of the world and for some reason being able to see the impact makes them feel good to me.  I've discovered several secret areas, and I'm sure I've missed others.  It's exciting when you find one.  You feel like a small child that has figured out how to get into cookies.  Suck it, game.
My gripes:
Fifth, the controls and camera.  In general, the controls are fluid on the controller.  Your character is responsive, turns well, and moves well in combat.  The one caveat to this is during some of the jumping puzzles.  Your character cannot turn in the air.  Once you jump, you've jumped.  I cannot tell you how many times I've jumped from one log, to the next log, clipped the edge and fallen to my death.  It is frothing-at-the-mouth-maddening.  Absolutely livid.  The veins in my neck look like the forearms of a ♥♥♥♥ing gorilla.  I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, I was backtracking earlier and came to a log jump and died 8 times in a row because my stupid character can't just stick his giant bionic arm out and grab the side of a log.  First jump, wide left.  Second jump, wide right.  Ensuing jumps, all over the place.  Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥  I was freaking out.  This happens a lot.  Oh, nice ladder there.  Walk up to it, expect HoB to grab it, instead go flying off the ♥♥♥♥ing cliff to my death and have to run back.  Are you kidding me with this?  COME ON, MAN.
Which then, of course, brings me to the camera.  It's fixed, you can't move it.  Which isn't that bad, exceptt when you're behind something and literally just have no idea what your character is up to.  Whoops, "goodbye cruel world" as you parasail to your death.  Lots of weird situations where you're just running aimlessly, have no idea what's near you and then smash into something (like thorns) that hurts you.  I'm sure there are very good reasons for the camera being fixed, but be prepared to flip your♥♥♥♥♥♥  Between the camera/controls while jumping, you'll be rage quitting for sure.  I've rage quit a lot.
Lastly, the performance.  Performance has been a bit of an issue for a lot of people.  Some players cannot even start the game.  Fortunately, I've avoided those severe issues.  In my time playing, I've crashed twice.  Well, my game has frozen and stopped responding, forcing me to close it out.  And you will absolutely experience stuttering in some areas/chugging in some areas regardless of your computer's power.
Overall: I've really enjoyed HoB thus far and I am looking forward to continuing to explore the World's mysteries.  I'd probably rate it 84/100, but that score would easily be in the 90s/100 if they fixed the controls and the performance issues.  The camera is only mildly irritating and mostly comounded by the controls.  The atmosphere of this game is incredible.  Pick it up.
Update: Regarding game length, it took me just under 10 hours to complete the story with roughly half of the steam achievements.  I am nowhere near completing all of the puzzles for health, energy, etc.

To start this review off, let me say that I am a huge fan of the Assassin's Creed franchise. Even considering some missteps, concerning the latest direction the games have taken, I will still look at AC games through rose-coloured glasses. Except the first game of the franchise, that is.
It is the game that introduces us to the overarching plot of Templars versus Assassins. This is all very interesting and Desmond seems kind of cool. The way of how this story is told is also innovative and cool. Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, however, who is the 'real' protagonist of the game, is bland to say the least. The way he is written, does not allow the player to easily identify with him and thus makes him a bit annoying.
Gameplay-wise the game suffers from some very annoying problems as well. The jumping and climbing, which has become a trademark for the AC franchise, is not that polished in the first game. Very often jumps do not work out as planned and the stealth can sometimes be hindered by exactly those quirks. Furthermore, the missions are extremely repetetive and the travel-system in this game is god-awful.
For anyone, who wants to get into the AC series: Do yourself a favour and skip this one. There are tons of videos that give you a summary of the story, so that you can get into the second game, without having missed anything from Desmond's story. Keep your hands off this one, jump into the next one and fall in love.

The short:
This game is a work of art. It's done something I've never seen a game do. It puts you in the shoes of a schitzophrenic, and tells a story of a woman facing hell to save the one she loves. If you like games that do something outside of the box, buy it. If you like beautiful cinematic storytelling, buy it. If you want to experiece mental illness without going mad yourself, buy it. If you want to run around 360 noscoping zombies, this isn't the game for you.
The long:
Hellblade puts you in the mind of Senua. A celtic warrior on a journey to Hel to ressurect her lost love. The thing is Senua suffers from schitzophrenia. The story is one of a battle with ones mind. The developers actually went to mental health experts to accurately portray schitzophrenia. Although linear, the story and dialouge within is deep and gritty. Don't come into this expecting an rpg or a standard game. Hellblade is a cinematic experience at its heart, peppered with exellently animated, satisfying combat.
The atmosphere of the game reflects the turmoil in the protagonists mind. Often I would find myself looking at the scenery or walking instead of running to absorb the world and listen to what was being narrated. It is not a fast paced game, it's meant to make you think. There are lore stones within the game that tell of old norse mythology. Though not deeply tied to the story they are interesting and help immerse you in the setting.
The combat is pretty straightforward. It's stylish and satisfying. I did not find it difficult but it was very enjoyable and animated very well. The voices you relentlessly hear throught the game can trick you at times. Occasionally I would hear a voice shout "Behind you!" while in combat only to find nothing there. The combat wasn't the foucus of the game but served to immerse you and highlight Senua's struggle.
My only complaint in this game is the runes. Periodically you are tasked with finding the shape of a rune or runes in the environment before you can progress. It can be a bit tedious at times. If it was spaced out more or filled with other puzzle types instead I wouldn't complain. But overall its a minor complaint.
Overall the game took me about 7 hours to complete, I wish it was longer. But I'll take quality over quantity anyday.
Ninja Theory created a work of art and deserve my $30. Bravo Ninja Theory. I hope to see more from them in the future.

This game is free, and while the graphics look kinda crap-tastic, in the same vein that Minecraft did, it is a serious venture into horror and blood-pumping adrenaline. It starts off slow, but builds suspense and terror. It succeeded where so many "horror" stories failed. I'm not saying that it's terrifying. No, I'm saying that at some points you may fear for your life. Running down a dark hallway with an unkillable monster chasing you, when suddenly a cute cardboard ghost pops out of the wall with a scream sound effect playing alongside the jumpscare. When you focus and try to move on, you are blocked by that cute ghost cutout, all while Satan is closing in. You finally step to the side and bolt down the hallway with all your strength and pass through the door...but you are not safe. No. You are never safe. 1000 rooms of eery terror. It's an amazing game. Why the hell is this free? TAKE MY MONEY.
This developer understands horror. They understand humor too. I found this game nearly as funny as it was scary. They somehow found a way to blend true horror and suspense, with quirky humor in the same vein as games like Portal. Make no mistake, this game might not be for everyone, but it is something to be treasured if you don't dislike horror and humor. Oh, but if you can't stand games where you are more or less helpless, or with no explosions, then this isn't for you. For the most part, you run or hide. You always have that feeling of moving forward, even when hiding and there is very little hiding to be done. Mostly, you make like the Doctor, and RUN.
TLDNR; This game is a real gem. Keep it in your treasury, and an eye on this developer in the future.

Alright for starters, this is my very first review for a game, that's how good it is.  (Sorry if my review isn't on par with how good this game is.)  Now normally, I wouldn't pay more money for a game than how long the game even is but I can assure you it is well worth the price.  I'm sentimental at the best of times, a wailing snot nosed baby at the worst of times.  I cry at Disney movies, at all my favorite old time RPG's like the Final Fantasies, Grandia's, Wild Arms and so forth; however I have never cried so hard in my life at a game than this one.
The story is why you buy this game.  Do it, buy it now!!
And the music, also that.  It's really amazing, I couldn't help but be on edge everytime when it became haunting.  Unlike some games where the music is just 'there', it really sets the immersion in this.
Maybe I'm just too easily amused but I loved the humor in this and thought it balanced the seriousness very well.  Not too much to take away but enough to make you stop blubbering for a minute.
The protagonists you play have pretty good personalities and while it's not about them you still get to know them a bit so they're not neglected.
But the gameplay itself is a bit clunky so be forwarned.  Not terrible but you control movement with either mouseclick or arrow keys, not ASWD keys.  (I always assume I get to use ASWD because that's what I'm most familiar and comfortable with.)  Not that I'm complaining mind you, just know that's how you move.
Their Icon hit boxes could use a little work as well, not that you need to go serching for many items because it is a short game but you'll find some of the icons to be off center or missing in case of speech bubbles.
The menu could use a little work in the notes department, I don't know if anyone else had the same problem but it was kind of impossible to scroll through the notes section once you had enough to scroll.
I also found it a bit disappointing that there wasn't a drawn animation for a certain close up cutscene earlier in the game, like the later one.  And since it's pixelated it just looked quite blurry and kind of bad (and slightly out of place since it could have matched the other animations).  Just a suggestion perhaps if they could ammend that or avoid it in the future.
Now that's mainly everything, I played it for 5 hours straight, cried for probably another hour straight after that, immediatly got my husband to play (albeit grudgingly) waited several hours more while he played and since he is soulless he did not cry, but he indeed said it was worth the time he put into it.
It's so good.

Not to put too fine a point on it, but: there is not enough Dungeon Keeper in the world. Impire looks like a decent-enough clone of Dungeon Keeper, but it is sufficiently unique in most respects to be its own game. This is both good, and bad.
The good side of things is how Impire handles dungeon management. By zooming out or pressing a hotkey, you’re given a flat top-down view of your dungeon. Here, you can queue up units, build rooms, order upgrades and place traps. Units, like minotaurs, vampires, imps, warlocks and such, can be put into squads of six. Squads in turn can be moved around as a single unit, and coordinate their attacks. A well-formed squad of a tank, some ranged casters, a healer, and a general damage-dealer, are highly effective at handling almost any situation. Ladders may randomly appear in your dungeon, bringing adventurers that’ll try to destroy things. You can build things like a Tavern that lure adventurers in and gets them drunk, making them weaker, but it’s not really necessary.
You are limited in exactly what types of units and rooms you can build initially, and here is where things get idiosyncratic. As you complete set objectives removed from the main mission objectives, you earn DEM points which can be placed into a Diablo-esq skill tree, which resets each mission. If you want minotaurs for this mission, you may have to sacrifice gaining some spells, or a type of room, etc. It gives the genre a kind of build-order strategy, which isn’t bad, but it can rub you the wrong way. Squads can be sent off on raiding missions using an overworld map, which removes the squad from your dungeon for a time. If they succeed at the raid, you gain much-needed resources, as a dungeon is not entirely self-sufficient. There is no ore to mine, like in Dungeon Keeper.
The game can be played cooperatively over network or Internet, up to four players, or competitively if that’s your thing. The cooperative mode works well enough, each player gets their own dungeon, and each dungeon has it’s own entrance into a kind of common battle area where mission objectives are usually located. The plot is amusing, in a 90s video game kind of way, and while it innovates where it counts, Impire fails in the areas it needs most.
For everything Impire does right, with its own spin on the dungeon management genre, it gets equal amounts wrong. This is the type of game that’s best bought while on sale, and only if you really want this kind of thing.
Bonus: Is this Majesty’s Ardania?
You are correct, sire! Impire takes place in the fictional fantasy realm of Ardania of the Majesty series. Much of the design, how things look and act, are direct nods to their counterparts in Majesty. The plot even involves you playing as a subservient demon in the employ of the son of a certain Scottish-sounding Advisor...
Finally the game becomes what the developers / people promised. The graphics are better, there is more to explore and to do and more action than at the launch. Not bad! :)

This game is an interesting concept of physics based fighting. You control a big flying machin with a giant weapon attatched. Then you swing that weapon into other flying machines. It took maybe 3 hours to beat the campaign and with the arena mode there's plenty of gameplay left. The story isn't amazing, but the combat is flat out addictive. The game has tons of weapons that range from boulder on a chain to giant sword to giant hammer. There are even big bombs and spears you can hurl at opponents.
The downside is that this game begs for multiplayer which will most likely never exist. The closest thing you can get is if you and a buddy play on the same PC with 2 mice.

It's actually a very clever concept for a PC game--just poor execution. They've tried to create a game where the mouse acts like a Wiimote and you use it to directly control a flail attached to a flying machine. It kind of works, but a mouse is really too clumsy to be whipping around in continuous circular motions--it just feels unnatural.
Fun, challenging game, yet a cheap buy.  This is not your game if you hate steep learning curves. Also: Set your mouse speed to 1/2 of the reccommended setting,; it helps.

Hob is an adventure game with RPG, platforming and puzzle elements.
The game does a great job at making you feel like you are constantly progressing. Whether it's through new enemy encounters, upgrades, new abilities or locations, you are always doing something new, which I really appreciated.
One major aspect of the game is combat. It's relatively basic, but feels quite meaty. I would compare it to Bastion. Most enemies can be killed relatively quickly through simple button mashing. Where as some larger enemies will be a bit more akin to Dark Souls. Where one swing can do massive damage, and you really need to time your dodges and attacks. However this is much more rare, and most of the combat I've encountered so far has been more like the first example.
You've got a basic attack button, where your character will go through a sword slashing combo. Another button will allow you to charge up your fist. This is needed to open cracked walls, activate heavy switches or break stone armor on enemies. It feels really cool to use. You can also do aerial attacks, and have the ability to purchase new moves like sprinting attacks, or a shield. Again, adding to a nice feeling of growing stronger.
As you play through the game you will earn major new abilities that allow you to traverse new obstacles. Such as a "warp" that allows you to traverse over huge gaps or terrain, and is needed to progress through the game or access new secret areas.
Speaking of secrets, there are a lot of them. You do a lot of platforming in this game, and if you have a keen eye, you can find a lot of different types of secrets. Either a chest that will give you a bit of extra money, or a permanent health/energy upgrade. The game is open world, so you can always retrace your steps or teleport to an older area to find missed secrets.
The third and final element of the game is puzzle solving. I would say this is the majority of the game, and it's done quite nicely. I haven't encountered anything that stumped me for ages yet, but they are tough enough to make me feel accomplished when I solve them. A lot of the times, after solving a puzzle you will open up a shortcut to a previous area, or shift the land entirely so that major areas connect. It's a really nice feeling since it gives you that feeling of long-term progression.
Onto the story. There isn't much of it. There's no text, or dialogue. There aren't many major characters, and the story isn't in your face. At the moment, I'm just doing stuff because... why not? There's a little bit of character interaction and an intro cutscene that gave me a bit of a drive to actually feel motivated to do what I'm doing, but I don't see the end goal. That's not to say that's a bad thing, I have no problem with it, but some might. There are a few "lore rooms" that you can find that will tell stories in the form of hieroglyphics, but I haven't encountered anything more than that so far.
Overall, I'm absolutely loving the game. Everything feels great. It feels like a good Zelda adventure. My only gripe is that I feel like the game can use some optimization. Even on medium graphics, on my 1060 I get frame drops quite consistently when I reveal a new area.
Other than that, I can strongly recommend the game if you like the look of it!

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is about a Celtic warrior who embarks on a nightmarish journey into the underworld to retrieve the soul of her murdered beloved. There is no loot, or crafting, or open world here. It is simply a strong, immersive story, exploring one characters descent into darkness. It is insightful and genuinely mature; in the sense that it deals with challenging themes in a realistic and thoughtful way. It's also a deliberately stressful, unpleasant experience at times.
So my Head tells me, Hellblade has several issues that are likely to turn some people away. It is short, and very linear. The puzzles are somewhat limited, with not much variation, and it can feel repetitive. The camera during combat can be a pain, and there are only a handful of enemy types. The game also deliberately withholds information, which can lead to some frustration when it does introduce new mechanics.
But my Heart says - I loved every single second of Hellblade, absolutely loved it, even the frustrating parts! It feels like someone went away and designed a game just for me. If it all clicks for you, it has such a powerful impact, you will be thinking about it for days afterwards. Personally, I felt any drawbacks it suffered were completely eclipsed by its strengths.
Visually, the game is stunning. The environments are atmospheric and detailed, and Senua herself is particularly impressive, as the motion capture provides a nuanced and compelling performance that you don't usually see in videogames. Certain visual effects illustrate her psychosis, as colours begin to shine and glow, the world around you blurring, tearing, or even kaleidoscoping outwards. Often the game will use these effects to literally challenge you to see things from another perspective.
The gameplay consists of puzzles, broken up with combat as you are guided from area to area, unlocking doors and making progress. These sections are solid - not bad, but not exactly great either. However I think the developers have chosen to risk frustrating players, in order to reinforce the stories themes, and encourage you to see things through Senua's eyes. For example, throughout the game there is no HUD. There is no tutorial. Only basic controls are provided in the pause menu. It throws you into combat without warning, and it's only throughout the course of the game that you discover more advanced combos, counters, or special abilities. Which helps put you in Senua's position - they want you to feel disorientated, and unsure of yourself. The 'rules' of the world are never quite clear; what's real and what isn't, what's dangerous and what's not, and a result Hel feels like a mysterious, hostile place.
The puzzles also encourage you to participate in Senua's psychosis, as you accept her logic, hunting through the environment to find obscure patterns and symbols. This does get a bit repetitive, mainly providing you a reason to explore,but as you get used to it you also start to see  them everywhere. This also serves to subtly engage you with the voices in Senua's head. At first you'll probably try to ignore the constant stream of doubting, mocking, and questioning comments. But as you fight, a voice might alert you to circling enemies "Look out!", "Don't let them surround you!" or during a puzzle might offer advice "She doesn't see it - look up!" As a result you do find yourself listening, and taking in what they say for better or worse. It builds a more complicated relationship, that elevates them beyond a simple gimmick.
Speaking of which, I really strongly recommend you wear headphones to play this. The binaural audio works brilliantly, and the sound design is superb throughout. Playing without headphones would be like playing a racing game without a wheel - you can, if you want, but you lose out on a big part of the overall experience.
The story is emotionally complex, but actually quite a simple and universal one - I think a lot of people will relate to Senuas struggles to come to terms with grief, or overcome trauma. The symptoms of her psychosis reflect her internal conflict, and allow us to visualise her guilt, her fears, her self-hatred as monstrous forces. It's a harrowing journey, and Senua really suffers along the way, but it's also an inspiring one, and Senua is such a well realised character you can't help but join her as she perseveres against overwhelming odds. Hellblade is a work of real empathy, an intimate character study, rather than yet another power-trip where you save the world. There aren't enough games like this

This game has a very unique concept and storyline that catches your attention right away.
The story line is fantastic and will take you on many turns of emotion. You follow the main character Nilin through her journey of self discovery. Luckily, it's not nearly as boring as it sounds.
The special "Remix" mechanic that is the signature of the game, used to rewrite people's memories, always makes a huge impact on the story when used. I'm glad the "Remix" mechanic isn't used in every chapter of the game, as it adds to the significance of the plot. However, be prepared because due to the game being a PC port and not originally intended for PC use it can seem clunky or overall impossible to use until you get accustomed to preforming the action with a mouse.
The combat is overall simple, using predetermined combos that are unlocked as the game progresses. Some of the battles seem to be drawn out, lasting longer than needed and requiring you to save up "Focus" to use the same special moves in order to progress in battle. This causes many of the bigger battles to be a little grind intensive. Also, many of the boss battles end with quick-time events so be ready for anything. The actions are predetermined, but don't give you a particularly long time to preform them.
There are also a couple riddles thrown in there as well, adding to the variety of the game. You spend a decent amount of time swinging from building to building, ledge to ledge, which also helps break up the monotony of battle.
TL;DR
-Great Story, Unique Idea
-Badass female lead, wicked good voice actress w/ accent
-"Remix" memories, watch out for funny mouse antics
-Easy to grasp battle system, monotonous battles sometimes
-Riddles and Scaling walls/Hopping fences

Never before has any game or even any other product motivated me to write a review. When it comes to that I'm usually the kind of guy to think "well, someone else is gonna write something and there are enough reviews out there anyway". But man this "game" is just something else.
It's hard to even call it a "game" because it simplifies things too much. It feels more like an experience. You know that feeling after reading a really good book or watching a really good movie where afterwards you find yourself sitting there for half an hour staring at the wall and thinking back at what you've just experienced. Well the same is going to happen after you are finished with Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice.
Now let's start with the ratings:
Visuals (10/10) - The visuals of this game are fantastic. The character details and animations are the best I have ever seen in any other game. The facial animations actually convey emotions like horror, pain, happieness or sorrow as effortlessly as if it was live action and the different visual "tones" of the different seetings always create a very dense atmosphere.
Sound (10/10) - First off: you should play this game with headphones to profit from the directional soundeffects in this game. Other than that the sound is what you would expect and more with celtic music and really good voice actors.
Story (10/10) - Really the heart of this game. You are taken into a nordic/ celtic world while following Senua's quest to reclaim the soul of her beloved. What sound's like the typical "find the princess" story line from Super Mario with a female lead develops into a complex character study of Senua and her past aswell as her psychological state. That being said, It's not an "easy" story to pass the time. This♥♥♥♥♥♥is heavy and deals with psychosis, PTSD and lonelieness so maybe not the best material for an evening of relaxation.
Gameplay (7/10) - Now as much as I wish this game to be perfect, it has its flaws. The puzzles are very repetetive at lenghts aswell as often predictable. "Oh well there is a closed door, I bet I'm gonna have to find some symbols to get it open" is what you will find yourself thinking quite a lot. Overall the puzzles have a fresh take for the first hour or so, but become stale after a while with some new elements being added later on.
The combat on the other hand feels really good after a while. It is fast, gritty and depends on good timing and combinations. The only annoying thing is that you always have a lock on an enemy and have to lock onto another target if you want to attack a different enemy which feels really unintuitive and is super annoying when fighting multiple opponents.
Overall however the gameplay flaws are swept away by the sheer beauty of the game and the intense story and character development.
Final rating: objective 9/10; subjective 10/10.
*Objectively looking at the gameplay flaws I have to take some points away, but subjectively they didn't impact the general experience of the game in any way and therefore didnt influence my personal experience negatively.

It may seem though as if the game is constantly interrupting you in your Nazi killing flow, whether it is a cutscene or a pointless postcard from a soldier to his mother. The texts generally don't feel very thought-out and do not shed much light on the world's historical background, like in the first game.
What I mean by solid work is how well done is the absurdity, insanity and grotesqueness of the current world order and its main players. Frau Engel is one of the most ludicrous and monstrous villains I have ever met. The game throws at you one wow moment after another and the violence and horror are over the top most of the time. The whole part with Hitler is phenomenally well-done as it captures him in both terrifying and comical light. Swastikas are stamped on literally everything you can think of and the game doesn't know the term censorship unless you are playing the German release. There are many new characters, but you still have to have at least a rudimentary knowledge of The New Order in order to better understand the character development. Sigrun, the daughter of Frau Engel, is by far the most interesting one but isn't given much space until the last part of the game. Grace is a swearing machine and deserves a slap.
The gunplay is somewhat insipid when compared to the first game, as the guns feel weak and their sounds don't have the right impact (apart from the laser, which is brilliant). You can now dual-wield any two weapons in your arsenal. I found switching weapons to be painfully slow, plus the models have their FOV far too large and they cover most of the screen, making non-combat situations a bit clunky. The enemies on higher difficulties can now kill you with a few shots, which makes the newly added quicksave button an absolute necessity as you'll probably die way too many times. I don't like that your armour or superbody takes as many shots to fail as a regular Nazi soldier. You'll use Overcharging way more often than in the first game. The excellent automatic cover system from the first game was replaced with a manual one and you have to press Alt + WASD to lean from a cover, which is very clumsy and I honestly didn't use it much.
The game performed very well in the departments of graphics, optimization and various PC-specific settings. However, I had to fix like 5 things before being able to play and still there were many crashes, especially when using the Steam Overlay. The release was flawed with a lot of people experiencing graphical glitches, crashes or they were not able to play the game at all. But much of that was fixed and there are still many fixes about to come as the DLC unlocks over time.
It was a solid experience and I liked it, even though it is not that fresh and awe-inspiring as The New Order.

This is written by someone who pre-ordred... *sigh*... but still enjoyed and played the game intermittently.
No Man's Sky is a game that is for a specific group of people. It wont appeal to all, much like a lot of other games, it has a community of people that enjoy it for what it is and others that dislike it despite the new updates. The new updates add a lot of features to add either story content and emotion into the game or add brand new traversal mechanics, or even entirely new things like calling a planet your home and building a gek'nip farm on it.
The game features hours and hours of content, this varies from following the newly added story to creating your own path through the stars. Each player can experience wonders, some by having an intense dogfight, others from finding a planet with an interesting environment.
Some of the survival aspects may feel repetitive at first like constantly refueling the launch thrusters, but after you play for a while and understand ways around making specific treks out just to get fuel for them it becomes less of a worry and more of an idle thought.
If you are planning on buying the game, do more research into the game, into its mechanics, into the general vibe you get when you play, and remember that it is built around survival mechanics, so that you will be fueling/ recharging things along your journey.

When it comes to the Call of Duty franchise, it seems like everyone has a different opinion; some people love it, some people hate it, some people love to hate it, some are indifferent, and some are absolutely obsessed. Whatever the case may be, it's hard to deny the fact that Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare changed the game for shooters when it released in 2007. At that time, the market was over-saturated with World War II shooters; even the first three Call of Duty games took place in that era. There were precious few current-era war games to be had, and that's when Infinity Ward stepped up and took control of the situation.
Modern Warfare takes place in 2011, and a civil war has erupted in Russia between the government and ultra-nationalists who are looking to send the country back to the Soviet-era days. At the same time, a separatist group in the Middle East has taken power in an oil country, and this causes the United States to invade. To be quite honest, the plot is very confusing since you play as six characters throughout the campaign, there's a lot going on to pay attention to in terms of story. However, out of the interwoven tales the one that has stood out the most to fans and critics alike is the one that revolves around British Special Air Service recruit Sergeant John "Soap" MacTavish and Captain Price.
Let's face it, the story isn't what brings people to the Call of Duty franchise even though this game spawned two story-related sequels. Modern Warfare was the first game in the franchise to have such an explosive, action-oriented campaign that involved more than just killing as many enemies as possible. Who could forget such classic missions as Charlie Don't Surf, Death From Above, All Ghillied Up, Heat, and the iconic Mile High Club? Not to mention the spectacular prologue. It has been at least eight years since I've played this title, and many memories of these hard-hitting missions came flooding back. Although some think that it takes "no skill" to play Call of Duty, Modern Warfare's campaign is a brutal experience even on Normal settings; and Veteran mode is enough to make you want to break your keyboard.
For a game from 2007, the graphics are exceedingly lavish. When compared to other titles from the same year, Modern Warfare retrospectively feels and looks like it was pushing the limits of the Xbox 360, Playstation 3, and Wii. The game is filled with lush environment detail, atmospheric fog, incredible lighting for the time period, and more explosions and enemies than anyone can begin to count. Needless to say, the game has aged incredibly well over the last decade. I know that it's getting a remaster later this year, but honestly it doesn't need one. I should also note here that the soundtrack is, as always, incredible; it's performed by an actual live orchestra that does a splendid job in capturing the horrors of war in audio form.
The controls and basic gameplay are what you'd expect from any FPS, and the game performs just like every other Call of Duty title that has been released. It all feels really solid, and one of the most addicting aspects of the franchise is that the kills are very satisfying. Press F to plant bombs, G to throw grenades, 1 and 2 to switch between weapons, C to crouch, CTRL to go prone, spacebar to jump and stand up, shift to run; it's all pretty standard. If the controls aren't to your liking, you can always rebind them which is a major plus in any game. As well, the optimization here is top notch and I was able to maintain the game between 80-140 FPS at all times.
Aside from the single player campaign, Modern Warfare really changed not only the Call of Duty multiplayer, but online FPS play in general. It is the first title in the series to introduce a leveling system where experience points are gained through performing various feats. Players unlock new items, challenges, perks, and weapons the higher they level up, and once the max level of 55 is reached the gamer can enter a "Prestige" mode that lets them do it all over again up to 10 times. It is my understanding that Prestige mode is available on the console versions only, but I have not played multiplayer on PC so I cannot accurately confirm this information. You would think that online is dead after this many years, but there are actually a few hundred people who still play. Beware, though, as this title doesn't have VAC protection; it relies on Punkbuster, which doesn't always get the job done.
You can bash, glorify, hate, or enjoy the Call of Duty series as much as you want, but the fact of the matter is, is that Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare completely revamped the FPS genre as we know it today; not only within a single player campaign, but also the online multiplayer aspect. Some people really take enjoyment in being derogatory towards not only the series, but anyone that plays it, but without this particular installment I highly doubt that MLG and e-Sports would be where they're at today. So forget what the haters say, even though the Call of Duty franchise has become way too commercialized in later years, Modern Warfare stands as a solid classic with an amazing campaign. This is one experience that shouldn't be missed by any FPS fan.

At first glance, the game looks as if it's a successor to Dungeon Keeper ..If you go in thinking that, you'd be wrong.
Sure, it seems to have the look that could be perceived as a spirtual sucessor to Dungeon Keeper however only the atmosphere and humour could be loosely based on Dungeon Keeper.
To summarise, you play the role of a demon known as "Baal-Abaddon", whom of which is summoned by a not so smart sorcerer named Oscar, into the lowly form of an Imp. The gist of the game is helping Baal to gain his lost powers and to terrorise the surrounding land of Ardania in the ol' "Evil is good" sort of way.
You start each level with a handful of workers and Baal, building up your dungeon with pre-laid out rooms and creating/summoning units to form squads to go raid for materials/gold/food and to defend from hero invasions from the front and/or ladders (With the addition of choosing random/fixed/no ladders, thank god!).
The game can get tedious and rather monotonous as the general tone of each level is essentially build up dungeon, build up troops, raid, rinse and repeat until you're strong enough to go into the main part of the level. The main part of the level is usually the same (With an ending "Boss" of sorts) however getting there can change from level to level. The most part is the same, however on some levels there are some puzzles which can be somewhat challenging to start with.
With the patches that were released since the release of the game, it seems to be a lot more stable compared with release. Fortunately there doesn't seem to be as many crashes/problems/bugs which was ultimately frustrating for those that first had the game as there isn't a save game as such.
On the whole, I enjoyed the game. Sure, it gets a bit repetative but I enjoyed the cheesy humour.
TL;DR - Not a successor to Dungeon Keeper but is loosely influenced by its atmosphere and humour. Game can get very monotonus and tedious but is fun at times. A lot better than what it once was on release due to bug fixes.

Patches 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 combined have made this game quite an addicting experience for me.  If you like open world, I mean really open world, combined with a sense of direction in the form of quests or missions (added by the recent patches), this game should easily give you 60+ hours of content.  The quests take you along nicely through the various things to do such as repairing and fueling your warp drive, getting started on your base, and adding components to it on a need-driven basis.
If you like a challenge, survival mode pulls no puches (and permadeath is the same difficulty);  It is brutal.  It will kill you.  You will start on a planet that wants to eat you alive, and when you get off it and think you're over the hump, one wrong move such as being caught without the resource or fuel you need and you're dead.  You're going to give up and go back to Normal mode (I did) unless you're a boss.
The distractions are what give you (or me at least) zen-like moments-- scanning the flora and fauna around you; drifting serenely across the landscape in your ship, with a vague objective but mostly just taking in the view and losing track of time; walking along on foot from one resource or landmark to the next, while listening to the background music which creates a perfect blend of mystery, wonder, and calm.

The first Assassin's Creed was the most promising game in development, and shined brightly from every games exhibition. When it was released, though, the hyped expectations of the whole gaming world were... turned down, sadly.
While without a doubt that was a high-class, AAA product, with prodigious depth of open-world gaming experience, fascinating visuals, thoroughly reconstructed medieval cities and intriguing story. Yet all that was not enough. The creators of Assassin's Creed made almost everything right... but lose the fun-out-of-the-gameplay somewhere on producing stages.
I remember playing the game right after release, and I was grown tired of it in second city, no matter how much I was stunned by the prologue and the first city. Inglorious Re-Peeat-Ability is the thing that killed the hype of the game and downgraded its undoubted merits. The most usual Ubisoft story, as it seems.
But, as we look now, after the dust is settled, the first Assassin game was not bad. Quite contrary, it is still pleases us with visual feast. The reconstruction of medieval world is one of the best in known fiction worlds, would that be games, books or films. The fighting theme is ten times bested by the Shadow of Mordor title... but it is still engaging. Stealth is no match in terms of cunning and diversity with games like Hitman... But you know that too, you get used to it so long ago!
So, that that's I'm gonna tell you: if you've missed that game so far, try it now, it is definetely worth a shot. Just... don't play it like an open-world game. I can't believe I write something like that, being a huge fan on open-world gameplay, but in case of AC1 that's the point. There are just not enough rewards for the whole additional activity Ubisoft added in the game. No point in opening chests, collecting flags, and so on. That's that killed my fun when I was making my first approach there.
Just play the scenario missions and kill occasional tampliers on your way, while exploring and sightseeing the great cities which was putted into that game. As I said already, there are no other thing, which will give you so complex experience of life in the medieval Mid-East. Just for that Assassin's Creed 1 deserves a place in your games collection, aside from a fact it was a father for superb Assassin's Creed 2, which stands proudly as one of the best games ever created.
My mark 7.5. Not a diamond, but still glimmering and even shines, if you know, how to look at it.

I only recommend this game if you have an interest in playing all the games through, because on its own this is a pretty terrible game. The quests are repetitive, glitches are numerous, combat is worse than Arkham Asylum's, and the story has some cool twists but is altogether predictable. The voice acting is also horrendous, something that doesn't seem to improve for a few Assassins Creed games, and nothing takes you out of a game faster than bad voice actors.
But being a decently-original game idea when it was released and probably the best of its time, it's hard to argue that playing it isn't worth it especially if you're interested in the series. The graphics also hold up pretty well to today, and in some instances I believe the graphics are better than in Assassins Creed II, but besides that it's a ~18 hour journey (or shorter if it doesn't keep crashing) that's worth it for Assassins Creed fans.

Hellblade is a treat. If you enjoy adventure, compelling narratives, difficult combat, or horror then you should definitely play this game.
Hellblade is a horror action/adventure which will last you somewhere around 10 hours of gameplay. Spoler-free, Hellblade sets a strong baseline for atmosphere by way of voice acting and graphical effects; the game gracefully walks a tightrope of moody Norse mythology weaved all around themes of psychosis and supernatural elements. If you are not a veteran of horror games, Hellblade will scare you. If you are, Hellblade will still likely scare you - later on in the game.
The game offers a series of trade-offs between puzzles and combat. Spoiler-free, the puzzles are fairly straightforward, or at least well assembled so that you begin to instinctively "get" what a room's goal might be as you enter it. Tedious? Maybe at parts, but due to the game's modest length I believe any tedium is short lived as you move between chapters.
Hellblade's combat is where the game offers the bulk of its challenge. Your character is fragile, and combat appears to favor your enemies when it comes to landing blows. That's not to say you can't engage in a flashy, aggressive fighting style, but you must earn the opportunity. Expect to die. Also expect to experience mild-to-moderate amounts of frustration, as select combat scenarios lead to sub-optimal camera angles and/or unavoidable flanking. It's normal, but you'll be fine.
Horror isn't for everyone, but the best horror games will reward you for persistance and the struggle. Hellblade's rewards come not only in audio/visual form, but also from a skillfully told traditional narrative woven around traditional Norse mythology. This is not your buddy's Skyrim or Amon Amarth album. This is Hellblade.

This game is a top down shooter. They some how did every thing just right, so that it's a lot of fun. It's easy for any kind of play style, and you don't have to let your teamates cramp your style if they aren't team players. Most people will play for the mindless fire fights, but it actually has a very indepth stealth game mechanic built in (that takes a little patience to get the hang of. It's difficult, but mostly because video game's have not prepared us for enemies with eyes/ears in a stealth game).
It's not an MMO. Not truly. There are persistant stats, like your xp, your stash, and your resourc points (money), but there's no hub town, and the game is all about combat (many different kinds of combat, but still combat. You wont find any crafting mechanics). My big criticism of MMO's though, is that if you stripped away the MMO part, you'd just have a very veery boring game. This game is fun solely on it's own merits. A single player game or campaign could be enjoyed endlessly. That's what I found playing the Demo. After playing the demo for 5 hours, I realized the game was a blast, and bought the full version. But incase the game play wasn't enough, they do have xp and levels and loot. So that addictive element is there for those sorts of people.

The story takes place in a partially believable future Paris, France in about 70 years. The Neo-Paris is beautifully created as a delightful mix of the actual historical Paris and various sci-fi elements. Overall the graphics are good and have a nice unique touch. For decent gameplay a pad controller is highly recommended. Although classified as "FPS" there is stricly no actual shooting, only lots of punching and kicking and firing various gadgets (firearms will be abolished in Paris in 70 years). The difficulty level is quite high, as a fairly experienced gamer I had to switch from the normal difficulty level to easy after completing only 20% of the game to avoid excessive frustration. Still I felt the battles were quite difficult at times towards the end of the game.
The biggest reason why I enjoyed the game was the decent plot, and the somewhat philosopical approach at the subject. At best, it may give you a few things to think about regarding existence in general and the future of mankind and our planet.
The game is not perfect, there are a few minor annoyances like sometimes accidentally not being able to go back in the level in those places where they aren't completely linear. Also the battles get a bit repetitive eventually. For a single-player game it's perhaps also a bit short. Nevertheless, I enjoyed it and would highly recommend it.

This is one of those games that can't decide wether it wants to be a game or a movie. It's a shame I have to give this a no too because there's some legitamately good things about this game. Remember Me is an interesting but flawed game. It's mostly useful as a curio in the context of being Life Is Strange's predecessor. It follows the linear structure commonly seen in third person action games of the period.
The combat is functional sub-Arkham fare with an enjoyable but underutilised combo system in which the player chooses the effect of each button press. The combos are set, for example X-X-X, but you can assign HP, Focus (mana, essentially) or extra damage to each press. The further along in a combo, the stronger the effect. This dovetails nicely with enemies who sap your health as you hit them, forcing you to juggle HP returns with damage dealing. But the system is somewhat limited in scope. Focus attacks are cast like spells, allowing you to inflict lots of damage or alter the battle briefly. But in reality you use whichever attack the tooltips are telling you to use to finish the fight.
The story is underdeveloped but unique, a stylish sci-fi tale about the commoditisation of memories which draws some heavy metaphors but is never quite fleshed out enough.
The game has some striking visuals reminiscent of DMC, Mass Effect and Dead Space, whilst maintaining a style unseen elsewhere. It looks great at a high resolution on maximum settings, but still suffers from an overly consolesque presentation.
It features a likeable female protagonist and no love interest (always nice) but alas she isn't massively interesting, and still falls into the playboy bunny category of body type.
After the relative commercial failure of this game, DONTNOD bravely switched gear to the episodic and extremely unique Life Is Strange, putting their talents to better use with notably more commercial and critical success.
All in all, worth picking up in a sale and just about worth the time it takes to finish, but mostly exists as a precursor to bigger and better things.

After thoroughly enjoying Dontnod's superb Life is Strange, I decided to give their first game a try too.  The two games certainly share many similarities between them. They both explore similar themes, both have a young female protagonist and many of the design elements are also easily recognizable.
The gameplay in the two games is very different though. Remember Me is a third-person action-adventure game with combo-based combat. Unfortunately the combat is not very satisfying and gets repetitive quickly. The ability to customize your own combos adds a little bit of depth, but the novelty soon wears off.
The issues with the combat are made worse by boring level and encounter design. Levels are extremely linear and there's no real chance to explore the world. There's some collectibles strewn around the levels, but for the most part they are not particularly exciting, simply minor ability boosts and lore entries. The encounters are not much better, in most locations you are fighting several waves of very similar enemies with little variety. Bosses are bit more interesting, even if some of them can get bit frustrating.
Despite all these flaws, Remember Me is still worth it for a single playthrough. Both the audio and visual design are great and the cyberpunk city of Neo-Paris is well-realized. Nilin is an interesting main character and the story is pretty decent, too. However, this is definitely a game that should be bought during a sale, it's much harder to recommend if you paid a full price for it. Especially since the game is fairly short with minimal replayability.
I finished the game on Errorist Agent (normal) difficulty and found the game for the most part fairly easy. However, as the combat is pretty unsatisfying I see little point playing through on the hard difficulty.
The good:
- Great audiovisual experience
- Well-realized cyberpunk world with decent story
- Interesting main character
- Memory Remixing sections are great, unfortunately they are only a small part of the game
The bad:
- Weak combat
- Poor and extremely linear level design
- Platforming elements are extremely simplistic, most of the time the game simply highlights the spot you need to grab next
- Minimal replay value
- Some frustrating encounters
- Terrible quick time events, especially boss finishers are extremely annoying
The ugly:
- Camera can be annoying at times
- While the game was quite polished and bug-free for the most part, there was one boss fight (Johnny Greenteeth in Ep 6) where you are unable to progress if you defeat the boss in a certain way. Having to reload and redo the boss because of a bug was rather annoying

I think this game received an awful bum rap for what turned out to be a good effort at taking the Dungeon Keeper minion game style and turning it into something a little more unique, with some effort to make the game less about operating progressively harder dungeons and more about following a quest line -- it can conceivably be thought of as an underground version of Overlord, albeit with a crappier avatar and point-and-click strategy-RPG style combat instead of action-RPG combat.  That said, it's still not a top performer.
With an absolutely atrocious and unimmersive lobby system that tries to convince people to play co-op, it's really hard to get into and play.  Realtime strategy co-op is almost unheard of -- it's almost always TvT, free for all, or 1-on-1 adversarial.  By attempting to push the boundaries, they came up with a great idea but of limited utility to the typical fan base.
The graphics are very good, for an independent title from a now increasingly un-independent publisher, and the subtle touches are all fantastic.  The main problem is that the gameplay itself is somewhat kludgy.  It is quite obvious that the developers intended to make minions move around the dungeons on foot and then got bored of how long it took, so they added "ladders" which spawn heroes inside your dungeon, and the ability to teleport to avoid sitting around waiting for your minions to navigate.  Speaking of teleportation, their pathfinding is pretty poor for a game with astoundingly simple prefabs that should be a cakewalk for an A* algorithm with well-selected nodes.  A lack of waypoints and patrol routes and other RTS staples really makes the game into a micromanagement fest, which is so unfortunate because it would have taken so little time to improve upon the basic accessibility features to make the game more playable.  A little bit of effort in streamlining the back end would have made the content and gameplay itself massively entertaining.
Impire can really be thought of as an experimental effort to break from the standard and to introduce a whole whack of new gameplay features.  The problem is not so much the ideas as the lack of conceptual integration: it's like a giant smorgasbord where people forgot to keep things consistent, so you have the Chinese dumplings right next to the tray of Louisiana dirty rice and adjacent to a tray full of nachos with chili con queso.  All three are bloody well delicious, but they just don't go together.
The game gets better as you go on, but it's such a slog through the early levels that it really makes you wonder whether it's worth it, and even then, better is a relative term.

I've found this game to be thoroughly enjoyable. It's the perfect fighting game for those who can't afford the high-end consoles. The animations are creative, the art style is colorful and pleasing to the eye, and even when playing the game alone, I couldn't help but smile.
Unfortunately, not everything is perfect and there were several aspects that really killed my experience. My first issue is Sephi'ra. I did not have an issue with the balancing of any of the characters until I fought against Sephi'ra. Her kit is incredibly unbalanced and allows for cheap and unfair advantages. I fought AI versions of her and found myself losing 5 lives in stock within the first couple of minutes. Before you go and say "Emily maybe you're just bad" know that I did not have this issue with anyone else besides her. No matter how many times I used the dodge or counter mechanic, I found myself in her infinite flurry of kicks until my HP was over 150% before I reached my inevitable death. I went and fought actual players using the character as well to confirm my suspicions of an issue with her AI, but that was quickly disproven, as the same issues arose. I hope that some rebalancing of Sephi'ra hit soon
Another mechanic I found quite irritating is the "rage" mechanic. Now, Angry Mob Games is not the first dev group to come up with a mechanic like this in fighting games (some noteworthy uses of a similar mechanic include "For Honor", "Mortal Kombat", etc.) My issue is the way in which they implemented it. I found that the rage mode lasted far too long to make the perks of the mode balanced. For someone to be invulnerable to damage and have increased damage output for THAT long is something I found myself grunting with frustration at.
Besides those two things, the game was quite fun and the perfect party game to play with friends! I was hoping I could get in contact with a developer directly, but I decided to write a review instead, in hopes that they may see it. I should also mention that maybe I don't have the right to judge, as I only bought the game due to the addition of The Drifter from Hyper Light Drifter.

On launch I think we can all agree this game wasn't up to scratch for such an eyeball popping price.
Hellogames are working to remedy this, as they rightly should be, and have been updating with features that should have been in the game in the first place. AND FOR FREE. I applaud them for it. If this were a proper triple A game it would have been abandoned to sink and be slowly forgotten.
Hellogames are not a triple A company though, and this game is not exactly triple A either. It's a seriously amazing feat that's done what ED and SC are already trying to do and in quite a nice way.
Now onto my experience with the game: I got it on sale for 16 of your British pounds which is a real bargain I realise now.
I boot up the game for the first time, fiddle with the graphics settings for a little while trying to get the resolution right.
I don't know why but you have to restart the game for ANY of the graphical settings to change, which is a bit annoying.
I started on this planet mostly devoid of interesting life, get straight to fixing up my ship and admiring the view, getting used to the silly hold down button controls.
I'd just gotten off world and into space and it was absolutely awesome, a flurry of freighters warped in (rather loudly and brightly) as I sped up to the local station. I met my first lifeform, a robotic thing tapping at a datapad and not taking much notice of me.
"Ahh this is how I'd always imagined first contact"
Next I hit the galactic trade hub to see what I could sell, only to find that all the prices for alot of things weren't very good sales wise, which is the same in my local area it seems.
I explored the station for a good 20 minutes, attempting to communicate with the aliens, swooning at ships landing in the launch bay, and wondering what I should do next. What's this? An Atlas you say? OFF TO ADVENTURE.
I pretty much left that adventure as soon as I started though, as I'd learned how to make warp cells and the views of these alien planets were just too enticing. I found this icy planet with pine tree forests and a few funky creatures, I explored for quite a while on foot taking in all the beautiful sights. Sunrises and sunsets are absolutely one of the best things about this game, it's SUPER picturesque, I've already taken about 200 screenshots.
Anyway, I'd just come over this hill when I saw a the smashed shell of a frieghter strewn before this quite large snow covered mountain. After seeing what I could salvage from the freighter I made my way climbing up the mountain and to my joy there was a base module just half way up, overlooking this broken freighter, facing the sunrise. I knew this is where I'd make my home.
It's pretty much been just exploring and scraping together units since then, building up my base, going off on mad rambles through the frozen forests every now and then.
This game really is a mind bogglingly beautiful thing, but I still think the price is too damn high. perhaps 30 instead of 40 pounds would be better. I'd never have gotten this game if it was full price.
it's really a game you should buy if you love exploring, cresting hills to see what the next horizon looks like, chatting to sweet smelling lizards and swooning over how cool that one ship looks.
If you want to be a space trucker or an ace fighter pilot then this is not the game for you. Combat is crap, economy isn't as good as ED.
Tl;DR: BEAUTIFUL GAME. VERY NICE SIGHTS. COUPLE GLITCHES. BUY ON SALE.

The 'mostly negative' reviews made me not buy this game for the first year after release, but after 3 major free content updates I decided to take the gamble.

So far I am having a good time in the game with exploring on the different planets and trying to find out more about the alien spieces. There is suposed to be a 30 hour story mode in the game too, but I haven't even started it yet as I am still busy with trying to setup a home planet and a base. I bought the game and basically played the whole day without noticing it, I looked at the clock and saw it was already 4AM in the morning :)

From what I can tell the game is huge. I haven't even left my home solar system yet and there are hundreds or even more other solar systems out there to explore. No doubt you can spend hundreds of hours playing the game without even reaching the 'end goal' of the game.
So far (first dozen hours) the game has a lot of grinding (mining), because you basically start with nothing more than an environmental suit and a broken/crashed space craft. Starting with nothing you have to gather resources to craft components and repair your ship and after that you have to grind a lot more to get enough money to buy other 'needed' goods. From what I have read the grinding mainly exists in the starting phase of the game. Once you have setup a good functioning base with alien staff and workers the resource gathering will become partially automated.

I love this game. I'm the type of guy who can roam around for hours making no progress in the story, but loving every minute of it anyways. Which is what I've done so far... I think I'm approaching the end of my first run, though.
Personally I enjoy the combat system, but I know some people don't. You target your enemies' articles of clothing individually, getting as many pieces on the verge of breaking as you can, then can tear them all off in rapid succession. If you get a long enough strip combo, you are rewarded with the underwear of your opponents being dropped to the ground in a flash of light, free for you to pick up and keep in your pocket. And nobody even thinks you're weird for it!
There's a lot you can do to customize your look, too. If you see someone wearing something you like you can take it and wear it for yourself (though you need to raise your skills for each type of clothing to max before you have 100% chance). As you progress into the game, you can even dress up like a girl (initially to beat up and strip other creeps on the street. Because they're bad, and you definitely aren't creepy at all, you're the protagonist.).
The weapons don't really change much, once you find one you like, you can just keep upgrading it. Another part of what makes this game so awesome is you get to be an otaku roaming around Akihabara (otaku central) with your choice of cute anime girls, stripping whoever you see fit, eventually being able to take their clothes for yourself, all the while staying within the comfort of your own home like a true otaku.

For being the foundation of a wildly-successful series of games, the original
isn't really all
good.  While the gameplay was novel, the series was still finding its feet here, and made a few missteps.  Controls can be a bit aggravating, and the menu structure is frustrating.  Also, the game shows pretty-much all its cards in the first third, leaving the remainder of the game to feel repetitive.  The various forms of progress, like collecting hidden flags, are rewarded only by the sense of completion, and Altair's progress through the game is rewarded only with a few new weapons; nothing game-changing.  The original
is still enjoyable, just a bit underwhelming, given how successful the subsequent series was.
If you want to play the entire series, then you should start here, where it all began, and just keep in mind, if the game becomes a little tiresome, that this is one of the weaker entries and the later sequels are better.  If you don't plan to play through the entire saga, however, you're better off giving this one a miss and jumping straight to AC2 or AC4; those two represent the series at its best.

Hellblade is a treat. If you enjoy adventure, compelling narratives, difficult combat, or horror then you should definitely play this game.
Hellblade is a horror action/adventure which will last you somewhere around 10 hours of gameplay. Spoler-free, Hellblade sets a strong baseline for atmosphere by way of voice acting and graphical effects; the game gracefully walks a tightrope of moody Norse mythology weaved all around themes of psychosis and supernatural elements. If you are not a veteran of horror games, Hellblade will scare you. If you are, Hellblade will still likely scare you - later on in the game.
The game offers a series of trade-offs between puzzles and combat. Spoiler-free, the puzzles are fairly straightforward, or at least well assembled so that you begin to instinctively "get" what a room's goal might be as you enter it. Tedious? Maybe at parts, but due to the game's modest length I believe any tedium is short lived as you move between chapters.
Hellblade's combat is where the game offers the bulk of its challenge. Your character is fragile, and combat appears to favor your enemies when it comes to landing blows. That's not to say you can't engage in a flashy, aggressive fighting style, but you must earn the opportunity. Expect to die. Also expect to experience mild-to-moderate amounts of frustration, as select combat scenarios lead to sub-optimal camera angles and/or unavoidable flanking. It's normal, but you'll be fine.
Horror isn't for everyone, but the best horror games will reward you for persistance and the struggle. Hellblade's rewards come not only in audio/visual form, but also from a skillfully told traditional narrative woven around traditional Norse mythology. This is not your buddy's Skyrim or Amon Amarth album. This is Hellblade.
