On launch I think we can all agree this game wasn't up to scratch for such an eyeball popping price.
Hellogames are working to remedy this, as they rightly should be, and have been updating with features that should have been in the game in the first place. AND FOR FREE. I applaud them for it. If this were a proper triple A game it would have been abandoned to sink and be slowly forgotten.
Hellogames are not a triple A company though, and this game is not exactly triple A either. It's a seriously amazing feat that's done what ED and SC are already trying to do and in quite a nice way.
Now onto my experience with the game: I got it on sale for 16 of your British pounds which is a real bargain I realise now.
I boot up the game for the first time, fiddle with the graphics settings for a little while trying to get the resolution right.
I don't know why but you have to restart the game for ANY of the graphical settings to change, which is a bit annoying.
I started on this planet mostly devoid of interesting life, get straight to fixing up my ship and admiring the view, getting used to the silly hold down button controls.
I'd just gotten off world and into space and it was absolutely awesome, a flurry of freighters warped in (rather loudly and brightly) as I sped up to the local station. I met my first lifeform, a robotic thing tapping at a datapad and not taking much notice of me.
"Ahh this is how I'd always imagined first contact"
Next I hit the galactic trade hub to see what I could sell, only to find that all the prices for alot of things weren't very good sales wise, which is the same in my local area it seems.
I explored the station for a good 20 minutes, attempting to communicate with the aliens, swooning at ships landing in the launch bay, and wondering what I should do next. What's this? An Atlas you say? OFF TO ADVENTURE.
I pretty much left that adventure as soon as I started though, as I'd learned how to make warp cells and the views of these alien planets were just too enticing. I found this icy planet with pine tree forests and a few funky creatures, I explored for quite a while on foot taking in all the beautiful sights. Sunrises and sunsets are absolutely one of the best things about this game, it's SUPER picturesque, I've already taken about 200 screenshots.
Anyway, I'd just come over this hill when I saw a the smashed shell of a frieghter strewn before this quite large snow covered mountain. After seeing what I could salvage from the freighter I made my way climbing up the mountain and to my joy there was a base module just half way up, overlooking this broken freighter, facing the sunrise. I knew this is where I'd make my home.
It's pretty much been just exploring and scraping together units since then, building up my base, going off on mad rambles through the frozen forests every now and then.
This game really is a mind bogglingly beautiful thing, but I still think the price is too damn high. perhaps 30 instead of 40 pounds would be better. I'd never have gotten this game if it was full price.
it's really a game you should buy if you love exploring, cresting hills to see what the next horizon looks like, chatting to sweet smelling lizards and swooning over how cool that one ship looks.
If you want to be a space trucker or an ace fighter pilot then this is not the game for you. Combat is crap, economy isn't as good as ED.
Tl;DR: BEAUTIFUL GAME. VERY NICE SIGHTS. COUPLE GLITCHES. BUY ON SALE.

I am not one to get Hyped for games, I am also one that doesn't buy games day one.  I waited over one year to buy No Man's Sky, and it was a good wait.  Only paying just over $20 for this game, is about what it should of cost.  It is not a AAA game but was priced as such.
I have played many many games in my 30+ years of gaming, and I find this game to be good, not great, but an enjoyable experience.  Sure, it gets very same same, very quickly, and you spend more time outside your ship than in it, but there is a nice relaxing simple game here, that just got the wrong marketing thrown at it.
Most of the game is about mining minerals to fuel your ship and earn money to upgrade, with a very mild story that drives you towards a very simple end game.  This game is worth a look for it's current price.

The 'mostly negative' reviews made me not buy this game for the first year after release, but after 3 major free content updates I decided to take the gamble.

So far I am having a good time in the game with exploring on the different planets and trying to find out more about the alien spieces. There is suposed to be a 30 hour story mode in the game too, but I haven't even started it yet as I am still busy with trying to setup a home planet and a base. I bought the game and basically played the whole day without noticing it, I looked at the clock and saw it was already 4AM in the morning :)

From what I can tell the game is huge. I haven't even left my home solar system yet and there are hundreds or even more other solar systems out there to explore. No doubt you can spend hundreds of hours playing the game without even reaching the 'end goal' of the game.
So far (first dozen hours) the game has a lot of grinding (mining), because you basically start with nothing more than an environmental suit and a broken/crashed space craft. Starting with nothing you have to gather resources to craft components and repair your ship and after that you have to grind a lot more to get enough money to buy other 'needed' goods. From what I have read the grinding mainly exists in the starting phase of the game. Once you have setup a good functioning base with alien staff and workers the resource gathering will become partially automated.

I can see myself playing this game for a long time to come and I am happy that I took the 'gamble'. The 'mostly negative' review tag is really unfair to the game in it's current state. The game feels really immersive and fairly fleshed out so I can only tag it as 'positive'.

The game does seem to be really heavy on the GPU. With an OC'd 970 I get around 40fps (high settings) when I am on a planet. Though, it does not feel sluggish or anything. I can only really tell be looking at the fps counter, the game plays and feels smooth at 40fps. When I fly into space the fps recovers and I get that 60+ fps again.

I think that 60 bucks for this game is still a pretty steep price, but if you see it for 40 bucks or less I highly recommend picking this game up (if you like this kind of gameplay and genre).

Edit after 65h gameplay:
There are quite a lot of bugs and glitches I ran into and some aspects of the game are not greatly designed, such as the inventory system. And the grind is real so far. I spend 80% of the time mining for stuff so that I can craft basic things and to get money to upgrade my exosuit. I still don't have biodomes where I can auto farm basic goods. So be aware of this, you will be grinding a lot in this game. You can minimize the grinding by playing 'Creative Mode', but you will not get achievements nor milestones in that game mode.

The "Secret locations" are always just two meters away from your route. - nothing special about the game itself, it feels like playing some reskinned console "beat'em up"

I was gifted a copy of this game but I happily would have paid full price for it.  The backdrop is really interesting, if you like dystopian settings, and the story and characters are engaging.  Also, I'm going to come out and say it, it's wonderful to have a really good female protagonist, where the gender of the player character *isn't* a specific plot point.
The combat can be frustrating at first, but after a while it just sort of clicks and you find yourself chaining devastating blows together while gracefully dodging enemy attacks in a way that would make River Tam proud.  The fact you can customise your combos is another nice touch.  I personally went for a quick 3-hit pure damage one, then a 5-hit combo that did hundreds of damage thanks to the multipliers you can use, then the two longer ones were for regen.  I found you end up using your enemies to your advantage more than just hammering them into submission.

I would stealthily sneak around  my living room, surprising my family members with a cardboard dagger, I created from a produce box..
I would pounce from behind the couch and pretend to slash my father, my mother, my brothers, it didn't matter who.  Ahh those glorious days when I was a wee lad and my imagination could run wild for hours.. or until the ADHD compelled me to find something else to do.
Well Assassins Creed may be just the game to fill your childhood role-playing fantasy's in reality.. after all it's far better and cheaper than trying to actually become an assassin am I rite?
To start off with it needs to be said that Assassin Creed is the grand daddy of the Creed series, so the AI is kind of dumb and undeveloped, the game play is repetitive and the combat is slightly boring.  Yes I said it Assassin Creed on paper isn't a very good game at all....  I'm talking in 2016, where as in 2008 when the game came out it was fresh and new, so quite a few of the issues which plague the game were forgivable.  It wouldn't be a good review if I left out that the game feels very dated now.

Starts you off as Altair an assassin on a mission, I won't spoil what you're after, but if you put two and two together you'll figure it out (It's pretty much a tutorial getting you familiar with the game..)  After the fairly short tutorial mission you'll awaken to find yourself in the shoes of a man named Desmond Miles..  He's being held hostage and forced to enter the Animus, a machine which can somehow bring out the memories of your ancestors.. I won't go into anymore detail as I wouldn't want to spoil the fun of discovering the story.
This is the meat and potatoes of any game, the actual game play.  In Assassin Creed unfortunately the gameplay gets rather repetitive, it's set up on a series of memory blocks, which are self contained stories which combine together to form the story arc.  In the game or the Animus you are greeted with 6 or 7 different investigations, 3 of which are required to access the unique Assassination.  These are generic Eavesdropping, pick pocketing, Interrogations (nearly identical to pick pocketing, only this one requires you to beat up the target for information).  The few others scattered in are timed flag captures, assassinations, and destruction mission..   This wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't repeated on every stage, about 3 times per map.
You also have two types of collectibles, each of the 5 major areas has it's own set of collectibles.  Flags, view points and citizens... the flags offer little to no reason to actually collect them, I suppose on the console versions collecting all of them would net you an achievement or trophy, but the PC version offers nothing.  I guess this was just left over from the console version..  Competitionist will probably enjoy tracking down these little boogers, but the rest of us will just ignore them as you gain nothing from collecting them.  The view points are far more valuable as each one removes fog off the in game map, and reveals the locations of investigations, and citizens which you can rescue from harassment.  The Citizens unlike the flags actually have the added benefit of placing either a roving band of Scholars which allow you to easily escape from guards or citizens who grab and stop guards from chasing you.

The combat appears to be a button masher at first, but you'll quickly discover the true way to be a master assassin is using Counter Attack, which often times turns combat into a long drawn out affair.  Instead of mashing down the buttons and quickly ending the guards, you're left to wait for an attack.. It can take the Guards anywhere from 5 - 15 seconds to attack.  Early on in the game you're assassin seems much more capable of killing guards, normally a counter attack means the guard dies.  Later on the guards can take three or four counters to actually die.  Many encounters have the potential of having 10+ guards.  So do the math... the game is called "Assassin" Creed though, so you'll figure out that it's much easier to run away and hide than try and fight them all..

in 2008 when the game was first released, I'd give it an easy 9/10, it was revolutionary for it's time, and presented a unique experience which was fairly lacking at the time.  In 2016 the game feels very dated.  Considering video games aren't wine being dated isn't a good thing.  So I'd say it's probably a 6/10.  Not a great game but certainly not a bad game either, far greater choices exist in 2016 which were absent in 2008.
I'll recommend this game as it's the game which started the Assassin Creed franchise, and most people like myself just can't hop into a series in the middle.  So be Leary if you buy the game you may very well find yourself going gah, I have to do this again?  Just suck it up and plow through, the second game is only 15 - 17 hours away...

I remember scouring through every possible source I could get my hands on in reference to Assassin's Creed back in 2007. Whenever I came across a morsel of information or a rare screenshot I couldnt help but salivate over the article. The concept was new and invigorating. I said to myself that this would be the game that got me to purchase a console. However this was not to be ( me purchasing a console ) . In fact it wasnt until several years later on steam that I got my chance to play Assassin's Creed for the first time , and I was not dissappointed.
Assassin's Creed  is a sandbox style action-adventure-stealth game that centers around the protagonist Desmond Miles. We learn that Desmond is abducted by a pharmaceutical company called Abstergo who forces him into a machine dubbed the "Animus". This "Animus" allows its user to view the genetic memories of its ancestors , and in Desmonds case the memories of Altair Ibn-La'Ahad. An assassin who lived in the Holy Land during the 3rd crusade.
As Altair you will travel through Masyaf , Acre , Jerusalem , and Damascus in search of what Abstergo called "A Piece of Eden". While in the Animus Desmond uncovers an age old conflict between the Knights Templar and the Assassins. Through the Animus and Altair , Desmond learns a terrible truth about Abstergo and must find a way to stop them.
Assassin's Creed was a novel attempt at a first in what has become a long series of games. It was , and still is a great looking game. Visually you can take in breath taking views of the various cities by scaling the largest buildings , and gazing out in "Eagle View". The structures that you climb are mostly accurte representations of actual buildings. Scaling up said structures was a favorite part of the game for me.
Combat was fairly simple as you could quite easily dispatch a mob of gaurds easily even in the early game. Most of the side quests were repetitious and of little relevance to the overall progress of the game. However the main assassination quests were intriguing and an integral part in unlocking the secrets of "Eden".
Overall I think Assassin's Creed was a novel attempt and was a much better game than some of its sequels. If you are the type of gammer that needs stellar graphics and tons of quests then this is probably not the game for you. But if you enjoy exploring and gathering intelligence to unravel a mystery then I would advise you to give Assassin' Creed a play. Overall I think this is a 7/10 game and worth playing to any real fan of the series.

Although the game has definite charm and originality, it has several flaws that undermine everything good in it. The most annoying are the controls, which are HORRIBLE. Extremely stiff and sometimes infuriating, even, since the game has a LOT of walking around. The bad controls mean the going of the story slows to an excruciatingly dawdling pace. The automatons are less stiff than all the live characters in the game.
The other major drawback is that the player character won´t pick anything up that she doesn´t need right at that moment - which again means that the majority of the game is spent trekking back and forth through scenes that have been revisited time and again, to get that little item that is needed for the story to progress. Which again mean that the player will have to demonstrate utter patience whilst battling the controls. Also, there are many locked doors in nearly every chapter, which underlines the points I´ve been trying to make even more.
That being said, the story is charming, which is why I´ve started my second playthrough after all these years. There are truly beautiful elements - the art nouveau style, the automatons, the eminent cutscenes, the music. The whole of it drowns in the considerable flaws, leaving the player feeling like it is more work than play. A pity, really.

Syberia is a tour-de-force in the point-and-click genre of the gaming world, maybe not just even within its own genre. The story is both intriguing and compelling, the graphics still look great and hold their details, and the characters are awesome, interesting, funny, and tragic.
This game shows off the artistic talent and genius of Benoit Sokal, a Beligian comic artist and the game developer for Syberia I and II. After my last time playing it, I began to realize the small details that make a game's story great and its characters equally so. Our main protagonist, named Kate Walker, is an international lawyer from a law firm in New York...and her life there is less than satisfactory. Granted, these details are revealed through short phone calls with her doting, somewhat air-headed mother, her so-called "best friend" Olivia, her impatient, jaded boss, and her fiance, whom Kate discovers over the period of the game she is not compatible with. Good thing too, because her fiance is a total ***hole.
The stark contrast between her life in New York City as a lawyer (which, like I said, is only revealed through a series of phone calls over a period of the gameplay) and her travels throughout Europe looking for an old man with a fierce imagination and an obvious genius as she visits the *often* sad, small towns with their eccentric residents show us that our main protagonist is evolving a newer, more enlightened perspective. She starts out cynical and jaded, yet as she continues on her journey to search for Hans Voralberg, a brilliant inventor with a child-like mind and personae, she becomes more aware or her surroundings and the people she encounters, and begins to realize that there is more to life than crony, greedy bosses andcheating partners. She found a whole new world of wanderlust and the mechanical dreams of a brilliant progeny, and you bet she's going pursue it. Syberia absolutely shows our heroine evolving as the train she's boarded on plunges deeper into the arctic tundras of freezing, desolate Russia.
This game has a steampunk aesthetic, and has an acute sense of small, mechanical detail. Of course, this is one of the highlight;s of Syberia. Steampunk is a very difficult genre to work with, as it relies on both fantastical yet realistic, mechanical elements. Of course, Benoit Sokal knew what he was doing and not only used steampunk in an aesthetic sense, but manager to interweave its elements to♥♥♥♥♥highlights to the importance of the story.
Syberia is a brilliant, beautiful, imaginitive game. This game had a lot of love, effort, and creativity poured into it. This is a game where once you start, you don't stop until you realized you've been playing for 4 hours straight. This game isn't that long nor is it difficult...it's just right. Highly, highly recommend for the intrepid fan of the Adventure and Strampunk genres of gaming.

At the time of this review, I'm only 4 hours in, but I think it is a decent game.  For me, I work in the industry, and I know it is pretty complex, which explains why there isn't good simulators for it as opposed to aviation, rail, or even retail industry.  What I found great about this game is even in its simplicity and cartoony style; it does capture the following:
- The oil business is about optimizing processing.
- Optimization is not a simple accomplishment, as the measurement of each processing segment doesn't match with adjacent pieces.
- It not only includes exploration, development, processing, storage, and transport logistics, but marketing, mainenance, and safety.
- When played fully, you need to get license to operate in different countries, you have to develop those regions differently, and the regions are not cookie cutter to other regions.
- Contract management and ullage is well done.
- I haven't been successful enough to develop the corporate offices yet, but from what I've seen of the build options, I think that was well considered, especially as a separate and segregated piece of regional development and processing, because that's how it is the major oil companies.
There's some cons (graphic artifacts, some unnecessary menu clicking, maybe a bit too cartoony for the subject) about it as a game, and it does look like it could use a little more polish.  And if the developer is considering an updated version in the future (thinking new paid release), then competition would be nice, even if it is just shown in the marketing aspects (something that explains why prices go up and down).  But the cons are superficial in my view, because the game plays well and every other attempt I've seen for simulating the oil industry is far worse and completely unplayable.
If you want to understand something about the business of oil, then this is the best game I think you can find.
If you are just looking for another strategy/city builder game to play, then this might not be your best choice.

I finally decided to give this a go. I must say it is much better than I had anticipated. It combines a number of scenarios and games as far as setting and gameplay are concerned. The envrinoments remind of Deus Ex, the combat and upgrade system is very close to the Batman Arkham series (memory restructuring equals 'Detective Mode' etc.), it also has something from Dead Space as far as the camera angles and mechanics are concerned, and of course there's a side of Assassin's Creed with perhaps a pinch of Tomb Raider.
This does make for a great combo. The game itself is quite linear (meaning not open world), but the pace and storytelling are very compelling, and you don't mind the linearity of it at all. The various locations are introduced with a nice camera swoop, and the use of light and shadow does add drama.
If you are expecting a 'but', you're right. While the in-game combat very much reminds of the Batman Arkham games, the controls are not as fluid. The same goes for the usual walking around. The best way to describe the controls would be to say, 'a little clunky at times'. This is not a game breaker by any means, but I wish they would have chosen better camera angles, and that the movements felt more fluent, especially since the protagonist, Nilin, appears quite athletic and believably capable of all the moves without the 'superhero flair'. Another gripe I have are the boss fights, but that is the same for the Batman games. I find them unnecessarily complicated, and the overwhelming count of 'foot soliders' is just ridiculous at times. You can't click as fast as you ought to, but, with some practice and patience, you eventually get past all of them.
I have not yet completed the game at the time of writing this review, but I can already recommend it to anyone who liked the games I mentioned above, or simply enjoys a good game in a Sci-Fi setting that's neither improbable, impossible, nor too far in the future.

This game is... unique, let's put it that way. Hammerfight is a game in which you pilot a small helicopter-like vehicle, attached to which is a giant freewheeling hammer. Or sword. Or pickaxe. Or giant rock on a chain. You control your helicopter by moving the mouse (this will probably require some in-game DPI adjustment to get it working to your liking), and the challenge is in learning how to move your vehicle so that your freewheeling weapon hits things. Preferably at a high velocity.
There's a very fun unlockable arena mode early on in the game, with an additional monster-hunting one made available after you've beaten the game. There's also Hammerball, which is honestly not very fun.
Cons: While it has a somewhat interesting plot, the backstory is just confusing. The dialogue isn't the best, though it's been translated from Russian, so you can't expect perfection. The difficulty curve is rather high, hitting its first, rather severe, peak around the fourth level or so.

Running with rifles is hands down the most interesting game I have played in awhile. It seems like a simple game, but the depth of the combat system is realized after playing a couple hours.
Vs AI, the game makes it so even the best of players have to be careful. One shot usualy means death, and you smile when a shot hits you but somehow it was not lethal (there is a kill probability). Other times you scream at your monitor when your shot hits but doesn't kill, and the enemy only shoots you once and you die. The AI is surprizingly good, and the game is addicting even only in single player.
The game's combat system is rewarding when you are experienced, there are a lot of different tricks and game mechanics you will learn while playing online/offline. For example, it may seem like silenced weapons and stealth is not implemented in the game, but oh boy it sure is implemented. Silenced weapons attract less agro, crouching and going prone make it harder for the enemy to spot you unless you are a couple feet away. When you are firing a non-silenced weapon behind the enemy lines, literaly a horde of 40 enemies come swarming you from the base. With a silenced weapon, only the closest people to the guy being shot at start looking for you, and if you stop firing, they will soon cut off the chase (unless you are in plain sight and not hiding) and start going back to walking around.
On the official dominance server, there are many different playstyles that are all rewarding. Sniping is very intense. You hide on top of buildings, snipe other players, and the best part is when another sniper decides to counter snipe (or you yourself initiate the challenge). The sniping duels are amazing, sometimes it ends with one distinct shot that kills the opponent, other times it is a game of hiding behind cover, maneuvering, and setting up a area to snipe.
There is not much to complain about this game, but there are still some cons. First of all, the spawn truck. Online, new players drive the spawn truck as if it were any other expendible vehicle. Spawn trucks can only spawn players when they are not near a firefight, so it should be kept behind the frontlines. Playing through Assassin's Creed Brotherhood a second time has inspired this review. That is a great game, but the ending of it is really rushed, and because ACB puts so much emphasis on advancing a story, the rushed ending really hurts the game.
Assassin's Creed (1) gets criticism for being repetitive. But all AC games---and games in general---are repetitive. AC2, the pinnacle of the series, has a lot of stuff to do, but all of that stuff outside of story is centered on making money, which ultimately makes the game feel repetetive for repetition's sake since skills granted by money don't help your progression through the story (the most fun and straightforward way to finish AC2 is with your hidden blade, so all other purchased weapons are peripheral).
In AC1, repetitiveness arises from the structure of the game. There are three cities, each with three different districts. You have to complete about five (or six, if you include the vantage points) different kinds of missions to advance the plot and unlock new territories (whereas the feeling in subsequent AC games is that story unlocks new areas). One question then becomes: is the repetition of the structure of AC1 too simplistic? For me, the answer is no, because the variety of settings, combined with the challenge of stealth (it is harder in this one) makes AC1's repetition more complex than AC2's wait for a timer to increase my florins. (Fortunately, AC2 relies more on story to keep you playing.)
So the next question is: if story can make repetitive gameplay satisfying, is the story of AC1 good enough? AC2 has AC1 beat by a country mile in story. The anthology/Dickensian approch used to tell Ezio's tale is compelling. But AC1's story is much more open ended. In AC1, you keep chasing after something very mysterious. Each target you kill tells you something as they are dying that upends your first impression of them. The motives of your enemies and allies becomes complicated as the game progresses, and you feel like a tool caught in the middle. Most later AC games kind of miss this mystery, as the villains and heros are more clearly (and frankly better) defined. So the open-ended story-telling makes up for the rather shallow character progression.
So I think AC1 is a really good game, especially compared to later AC games (which I like a lot). The repetitive elements of the game are okay because they aren't too simplistic. The straightforward story is supplemented by great atmosphere.
Highly recommended.

I came expecting something similar to
, was I wrong. I ended up making it mid-way through the 2nd chapter and gave up. It's a micromanagement hell. There were several things that frustrated me with the game, here they are:
Combat
Micromanagement of your troops is non-existent. Healer getting mashed? No quick way to pull him out of battle, hotkeys are terrible. You end up just teleporting all your squads in and letting it resolve itself. When the fighting is over you have to teleport your troops to the kitchen to feed them. Feeding them refills their "aggression", if the unit's aggression is too low, they suffer combat penalties. Doing this over and over is mind-numbing.
Story
Painful. I can't believe I sat through those cutscenes. Voice acting is mediocre, the slow pacing and grade-school writing make it even worse.
Tech Trees and Resources
You basically get points for each achievement in the dungeon (e.g. Killing a hero, building 2 traps, building 10 traps, raiding a village, etc). Those points unlock buildings, units, unit special abilities, etc. The problem is having to do that in
make it especially painful. Most of the tech tree items are worthless--All you need to do is make a beeline toward some combat units (tank, healer, damage-dealer) and some key structures (to do things like upgrade armor).
Resource gathering is another pain point. While the idea of sending squads to raid nearby villages sounds cool, it ends up being a major chore. The map sucks and you are limited in the number of squads you have, yes more squads are unlockable but you already have most of them them tied up in combat to advance the storyline. (And you have all your troops in combat because: read above, combat sucks).
Hero
Annoyances
So you've started on a new map and all your troops are tied up gathering resources or fighting to advance the story. Now you have random ladders spawning across your dungeon to slaughter your workers. Traps? Traps are worthless. Another ladder...great. Teleport troops over, wait for fighting to finish. Teleport to kitchen to feed your troops, then teleport your troops back to where they were. More ladders? Wash, rinse, repeat.

My Impire experience was terminated prematurely by a corrupted save game, leaving me time for a quick review. Luckily it was my second playthrough, so I already finished the game.  I didn't play dungeonkeeper a lot so I wasn't stuck to that concept. Don't be fooled by my hours ingame. Many of them were replays due to bugs.
Even after the patch it seems to be quite buggy (or some may be features, I honestly can't say). But the problem of this game is best described by Baal himself "oh how tedious". The game seems bent on ruining any chance of having fun. Managing will mostly be clearing ladders, feeding your peeps, killing heroes that enter your dungeon - rince and repeat. In between you might be able to play the game ... a bit. There is some fun to be had in the cutscenes, though they get old really fast and you'll be waiting them out at the end. The graphics don't help, though I liked the rooms with the imps running around doing what imps do. Building an optimal dungeon would be nice, but there are usually fixed rooms in the way. The units are ok, but there just aren't enough. Halfway in the game you've seen them all. *spoiler* I highly recommend going with Velvet so you can play with some other units even though the differences are small. Units might respond to your commands but 50% of the time they decide what to do, damn smartypants Trolledons! In the chaos it's hard to click anything anyway so it might be for the best. Some corridors I couldn't enter until I carefully maneuvered my camera in just the right angle and by them "heroes have entered your dungeon".
It looks like the game got stuck in beta. Even after the patch there is no load button. Only one save game (which after the patch still gets corrupted). And the ladders omg the ladders, who thought that would be fun? Yes, I played most of the game with the 'no ladder' setting but still ... do you like commercials during your favorite movie? Of course you do!
Maybe some day with a lot of player input it might be a nice game. Until then, be sure to spend your money and time on another game. If only the game would let you play...

This game is a masterpiece. (But hold on, there's some bad things you should know too.)
The storytelling in this game is phenominal. Moving and powerful. The intersection of ancient religions (mythologies), cultural battles, maddness, inner struggles, with psychosis expertly used to build the atmosphere, makes for one of the grittiest stories I've played in years. The depiction the character struggling with her maddness is shockingly accurate and holistic, invoking a sense of dread and vulnerability, rather than just making the character alien. I have worked with people with mental illnesses in the past, and so I might be biased, but Senua may be my favorite game characters now. I truly applaud the developers on this.
There are some problems. The game has "find the rune" puzzles where you have to look in the area for a symbol to unlock a door. Typically there's some tree branches or broken lumber that, when viewed from the proper angle, make the rune. It's not really fun. I agree there should be puzzles in a game like this, but this mechnism was unpleasant. I just played with a walkthrough, and if it took me more than a few minutes to find, I'd just look up the answer. With that approach, it didn't detract much from the game.
Also, a minor note... Senua has some rather unpleasant facial features: buck-teeth and bulging eyes. There are alot of scenes where she's looking around with her mouth hanging half-open, and all I could think was "wow, that's an unflattering look." I think it would've broken the realism of the game and made her less relatable if she were crazy hot, but as it was, the visuals were a real distraction for me.

After having completed a play through of this game, I would like to commend the creators on a job well done.
This game is entertaining, and the story is fun to play through. The play style of the game is fast paced, with a lot of climbing and jumping. The action sequences are interesting, although the combo system is lacking, and leaves much to be desired.
Pros:
Fast paced action
Easy to follow guidance hints with ledges and such
Plenty of tutorials
Entertaining Story
Interesting concepts with the memories
Cons:
The controls are a little clunky (Feels like it was designed for controllers, plays weird on mouse + kb)
Combos are in a preset order
Menus are clearly designed for controllers, and do not translate well for mouse + kb
No proper counters for certain enemies
The graphics in this game are beautiful. A lot of the city backdrops, and surrounding environments are amazing to soak in while you're playing the game. There are parts when the game locks you into a super slow walking pace while you're engaged in a conversation. I have no clue why this was done, but it's incredibly frustrating since you're talking over voice comms, not face to face.
The fighting sequences are both fun, and frustrating at times. This is normally a good thing, because you want some challenge. However some of that challenge just comes about due to the poor targetting system, when it just randomly launches you to hit the wrong mob. There's one particular mob in the game that deals damage to you when you hit it, and the only counter you have to use an ability that lets you kill him instantly. However they toss multiples of these guys at you, and sometimes it's not practical to recharge that ability.
Thankfully, this game isn't super punishing, and when you die you start back with full health again. There's lots of checkpoints where it auto-saves. Almost every major battle, and even between sequences, it auto-saves. So even though there's frustrating parts, the game isn't overly punishing. You can also setup combos to heal you, which can sometimes work to even out the damage you take from them. There's a lot of give and take going on, and overall I found it tolerable.
My biggest complaint is that a bunch of the later boss fights require specfic mechanics, and until they finally decide to throw you a bone, you can end up bashing your head against the wall for a good deal of time. Also, I'm not a big fan of QTE which are littered throughout a lot of boss fights.
On the whole, this game was a lot of fun to play. I would recommend people to give it try, and enjoy the story as it unfolds. Probably best if you play with a joystick, but I used a keyboard and mouse so it's still playable that way.

+ A pretty nice and relaxing soundtrack
+ A great tutorial, easy to learn, and the user interface and clean and simple
+ The gameplay mainly consists of building a pumpjack, refinery, pumping station, and storage unit. Once you have these you will start gaining barrels of oil each day which you can sell on the market or take out contracts. Contracts are far more profitable, but if you fail to meet the daily quota you will be hit with some very heavy fines. The goal of the game is to reach a certain amount (example: $10million), and you fail if you go negative $1million or stay negative for more than 12 months. (Which is surprisingly easy to do if you fail contracts. Overall it's pretty relaxing and quite engaging as you try to get the maximum amount of contracts possible without running out of barrels of oil.
+ Some neat mechanics later on where you can buy licenses to drill in other countries with different biomes and real-world perks like cheaper labor / construction costs. You can also build up a headquarters which are large research buildings that improve your structures.
- At some points it becomes a waiting game where you just wait a long while for your contracts to finish, and to raise enough money.
- There are some bugs in the game. At one point I had over 7,000 barrels, and it randomly said that I failed to supply enough for a 300 barrels / day contract, which fined me $1million and I ended up failing the scenerio and had to restart.
- Feels a bit too basic, I would have liked to have been able to build pipes to transfer the oil, or at least see people working or transporting oil below. Even when a station breaks down nothing really happens you just have to wait. I  would have liked to have seen more animations in the building process, and perhaps more unexpected disasters or events.  Although these are just minor things.

The game is also a lot smaller than it seems.  You see the giant map and all the possible places you can expand to when you suddenly realize.... none of the levels are long enough to actually go into two different regions.  It's a really really small game and probably isn't worth more than $2.

Caster is a 2009 game that would have been a big hit on the Nintendo 64. I'm talking about the good old Rareware quality before Microsoft turned it into just plain Rare. In spirit the developer should earn a Miyamoto award! I think the developer was a senior programmer at Hidden Path Entertainment, they are known for games like CS:GO and Defense Grid 2.
Instead of writing a long review (which I may semi-do anyways ;P) I'd like to show some gameplay footage. From this hopefully you can deduce things like how quickly you can pass Caster and level of fun.
The game directory contents is quite interesting. It uses SDL (Simple DirectMedia Layer) and some other familiar DLL files. The assets are open to look at. For example the levels consist of two image maps. One for depth and one colour coded that represents the actual design. Essentially you could just create a level in Photoshop or Paint.
The biggest problem with Caster is that it freezes my PC randomly. It may have something to do with the graphics since the game works fine in safe mode. The only thing you can do is press the reset button on your PC when it happens since Ctrl + Alt + Del won't even work.

This is more of an intellectual and philosophic experience than a game. That said, it is highly recommendable. You will feel cultured while being more engaged than watching a movie.
Pros:
Lovely scenery and voice work. The music, too, fits the ambience. I particularly enjoyed the theme in the communist factory.
The story. As I said, this isn’t so much a game as a guided experience. Syberia has been described as “a journey through the failed utopias of the 20th century” which is a wonderful explanation. I would add that it is an exploration of the topics of obsession, disappointment, age, and lost potential. A deeply melancholic and thoughtful experience with a well written story and characters.
Cons:
The puzzles weren’t particularly challenging. Some had a bit of a forced logic to solve them or went a bit against intuition, which can be frustrating. However, the game doesn’t resort to the too common “push the boxes” or “arrange the pipes/wires/yarn” kind of puzzles so at least every problem is an original one.
On occasion I felt that the pace was a bit slow and that I had to do a lot of reading. However, take this with a grain of salt. Since the steam version comes with six languages I used the game to improve my French (very good voice work, by the way) so I may not be totally fair here. You will have to read, though, and pay attention to details.
Playing Syberia is like being inside one of those independent films that get the Golden Lion in Venice’s film festival. Sweet, gentle and meditative.

Wow. OK... Where to begin?
I stared at this game in my Wishlist for about a month, and then I finally decided to give it a go after needing a break from the usual. In hindsight, I feel good about buying this game at full price; anything less and I would be overcome with guilt as I type this.
What you have here is, first and foremost, a recognition of the single most important aspect of any RPG--a damn good story. 8-bit titles rise and AAA titles fall every day, and yet some devs
never figure it out, but Ninja Theory seems to have gotten the memo. Senua is a character who's easy to empathize with, and her story draws you in deeper and deeper as you go... I had a hard time walking away from it the other night and leaving it unfinished because I had work the next day. I
to know how it ended, and I wasn't disappointed in the end.
The next bit of good news is, this is definitely not 8-bit. The game's motion-capture is
impressive, and the visual and audio effects all contribute to some dramatic moods and mood changes. Combine the lack of a combat interface with Senua's size in comparison to the stature of her opponents, and you get a strong sense of immersion and maybe just a bit of anxiety from the fighting.
More good news--the fighting is good, but the game's not all fighting. Combat is used almost sparingly, when it's appropriate to the tempo of the game rather than simply when there was an excuse to throw enemies in your way. Hellblade's puzzles are interspersed with its battles, and they all fit in with Senua' state of mind because they revolve around perception--seeing things from a new perspective, through a different lens, etc.
Thematically, I'm not sure I could think of a more cohesive game. Hellblade is almost like a musical symphony in its design and layout, where every aspect of it contributes to the whole and nothing is wasted or superfluous. Every little piece is used to control the tempo and the mood. Aside from being a useful education in Norse mythology for the unitiated, even the stories of the lorestones found in-game serve as a subtle parallel to Senua's struggle.
And I consider myself to be something of a cynical/ruthless guy... but I will confess that this game gave me feelz.
Top this all off with the fact that you've got an incredible team doing amazing things with a difficult subject that you'd
see from a more massive studio, and you've got an overall winner. I will tell you that I'm writing this review as much out of a sense of obligation to the devs as to the Steam community.
Regarding some fearful remarks I read about permadeath in the game... Yes, it exists, but I played through once on Hard and never experienced it. It did add to the sense of tension and fear over the consequences of my actions, without me regretting that it was put into the game. So there's my two cents on that as well.

This game has both cute things and very scary things! For such a cute little ghost girl, Spooky really knows how to scare people with what's in her mansion! Other than that, if you try to get immersed, the atmosphere is incredibly solid and terrifying, the story unfolds quite nicely, and it has the feel of those horror garry's mod maps.
So, if you do like jump scares, absolutely get this game. It's great.

It's a fun game...alot like some of the older tycoon type games. You have to buy all the equipment needed to extract and sell the oil and manage profits and production wisely to not go bankrupt.
However, This game needs more depth/strategy to it for it's price tag. (It is still early access and the dev's do seem to be still adding to it) After completing a few of the intro scenarios and 2 failed (bankrupt) attempts at free play I was able to devise a strategy that had great results for every new field I created and the game started to feel repetitive and a lot of busy work trying to keep an eye on all the logistics of the game instead of expanding further.
The game is great small scale, the first couple hours of free play, but after you get a couple fields  and maybe a second region going there isn't much strategy in expanding, mostly just a lot of busy work.
Since it's still early access and I'm assuming the dev's want feedback, here's afew additions I would like to see in the game. (I'm not sure where elese I could post/send these)
I think it would be great if there was a central location to look at all the logistics/data without having to jump between regions, oilfields, or buildings. If the contract page could be added to so I could just select what region I want to view the open and active contracts for. Also, in the contracts page I'd like to see a breakdown of what each fields production is and how long they have until they are depleted because signing a large 180 day contract when a field has less than 6 months before it's depleted has some expensive penalties. It would also be great if there was another window that again has a place to select a region and it shows all the logistics of that region. Basically a condensed location to see the condition, performance characteristics, and operating costs of each building in the region.
Also, as for strategy additions. It would be great if buildings could be put into an idle mode where they require minimal operating costs so when prices are low in a certain region operating costs and production can be adjusted to wait it out instead of depleting the reserves with oil prices that make it hard to profit and expand...Also, it would be great if I could pack up and ship equipment/buildings to another field (for a fee of course). This way once a field has been depleted, the equipment can be repurposed instead of sitting around costing money or having to pay to take it down.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a beautiful experience.  All of its elements come together just perfectly to create a truly cathartic reaction. Few other games can say they so perfectly blend story, music, visuals, and gameplay.
At it's heart, Ori is a masterwork platformer with deceptively challenging puzzles that take an enormous amount of player skill and dexterity.  The creativity put in to these challenges is something truly respectable. Despite the challenge, Ori never feels unfair because deaths are always the result of the player rather than luck. Furthermore, the game gives you control over where you establish your reload checkpoints which allows you to avoid having to repeat too much content except for specific end of location events. Considering the number of times I failed at challenges, I was surprised that I never felt cheated, nor did I feel frustrated that I'd have to do parts over because of how easy the game makes it for you to do so. It doesn't punish you for failure, it only rewards you for success. This should be a standard philosophy for such games.
Visually, Ori is without peer. The art style is exquisitely beautiful throughout. If heaven were half as beautiful, what a wonderful place it would be. The muted colors and numerous, vibrantly themed locations always ensure you have something new to feast your eyes on. Each location evokes a specific emotion through its brilliant art design. Players will find themselves unwittingly admiring the landscape almost as much as playing the game.
The Music of Ori is ethereal and almost other worldly. it fits the visuals precisely, and helps to seal the mood. It is a powerful score that is carefully crafted in such a way as to not be overdone which is often easy to do for many games. The music never gets in the way, never betrays the mood of the environment and always fills the empty space that visuals alone cannot fill. Truly a wonderful score worth listening to even outside of the game. It is relaxing, powerful, and consistent.
Ori's story is one that blends classic tropes with a unique setting. In short, it is a story of love and redeption. There are moments where crying is almost a certainty and others where a smile can't help but grace the player's face. One excellent and unique aspect of Ori's story is that it is told with very few words. One could say it is quality over quantity. Most of the story is told through visual ques and haiku like statements that grace the screen while playing. The result is a story that is powerful, yet not distracting. Rarely will the storyline pull the player away from playing. Instead, it is usually up to the player to fill in the blanks with their imagination, and to allow the powerful, emotional message within be uniquely absorbed by each player. In that way, Ori's story is unique on some level for everyone. No two people will experience it the same way, yet all players will find something truly cathartic about the experience.
Ori is a wonderful game. As time goes on, it will stand shoulders above the competition as a true classic. Few games can achieve the level of brilliant cohesion amongst its systems that Ori achieves. It is a game that every gamer should play from start to finish. If more people played games like this, society may very well become a better place. Sometimes, powerful introspection can be had while being thoroughly entertained.

Hammerfight will quickly wear out your mouse and that's because the game uses it extensively, but in a cool and unique way. The original idea of steampunk war machines and their heraldry, the storyline and nice graphics are the major virtues of Hammerfight. Although the game may seem to be very hard at the start, nothing is more gratifying than smacking enemies at full speed with your weapon of choice.

Hammerfight is fun and funny - I literally laughed out loud when first playing this game. It's very satisfying to whallop the computer opponents with a rock on a chain.
However, this game is not without problems. Menu navigation is an afterthought. The HUD is frequently in the way. The HUD is stylized to the point that you can't read it at a glance. There's too much story. The "learn as you go" elements appear to still be under construction.
Worst of all, sometimes there is so much happening on the screen, you can't find your ship among all the layers of smoke, explosions, sparks, friendlies, and bogies. This game requires precise control and timing to succeed, but the busy-ness of the game takes that precision away from you.
I really hope the developers clean this game up. It has great potential, and I look forward to trying it again in the future. But for now... I'm uninstalling.

WHAT!? You mean that even after seeing that trailer and the overwhelmingly postive reviews, you're still not convinced!? Alright... THIS GAME WAS AMAZING!!!!
Our story opens up with two doctors who don't have the job of saving patients - rather the job of helping their patients leave their world with a smile on their face. How you ask? Our heroes change their patient's memories so that they can grant one last wish. Dr. Neil Watts and Dr. Eva Roseline have met an old man by the name of Johney who asks for the stangest thing - to go to the moon. With no explaination or context, our heroes set out deep within Johney's memories in order to do their job.
I cannot begin to tell you how much I loved the story. Seeing John's life really was heart-wrentching. Each new twist added to the story were complete shocks. And that ending. I'll say, very few things make me - not just tear up - but actually make me sob. That is how an ending should be done and it is what I consider to be the best ending of all time. There is, unfortunatly, one scene that went right through my head and I think it could have been explained better but oh well. This is, however, about a four hour game but for how the story never slowed down, every hour and all ten dollars spent into this game were more than worth it. As for the characters, each one was done well. I loved Johney and his wife. I loved Neil and Eva and their interactions. There's another character later down the line that I really liked but I cannot reveal their identity - lest I spoil some of the story. Even the side characters were written well. Another thing that I'd like to touch on were the jokes. There were a lot of legitimently funny jokes that played out throughout the adventure. They had me laughing throughout the journey.
The gameplay is mostly exploration and puzzle based. If for whatever reason you could not possibly care about story, then this won't be for you. The puzzles, however, do a good job of balencing the difficulty scale. Earlier puzzles helped later puzzles very evenly. unfortunately, there is no reset button so you are unable to try a puzzle again should you make a mistake. A thing I didn't like about the puzzles is that I didn't like how it felt like they slowed the game down when I just really wanted to get to the story. Exploring was nice. During your trip down memory lane, you would go around, interacting with objects in order to get little memory links that would allow a momento to jump you down a memory. I do wish I got a bit of context for why this was a thing. Another problem was that sometimes I get lost when exploring a memory because there was no indication of where to go. Granted, it's not hard to check every nook and crany, but sometimes there was something that I missed and a hint button would have
ed.
The graphics were very solid. The layout of the maps looked good, but the music! Every scene the music was in felt very appriopriete and I would highely recomend getting the soundtrack because they are timeless! About the soundtrack, some songs were really short when they were full length songs and I would have been fine if they looped them. Also, some songs just cut off when they end and a fade really would have been nice. I suppose now would be a better time than ever to note there were a few bugs to be found, but nothing too major to take away from the experience.
Alongside the game comes two 30 minute minisodes which take place after the main story. Minisode one is more about developing the world of
and their characters and skipping it wouldn't be as drastic as skipping anything else (but don't do that). Minisode two focuses on developing Neil and Eva as well as the overall story of the series (yeah, I should mention this is comfirmed as a series). One problem I have with minisode two is that I feel like the end spoiled a little too much for a minisode and I feel like they should have saved that shock reveal for episode two or further. Just keeping the mysteries shown in this minisode would have been more than enough for it. furthermore, the reveal really didn't shock me as I had already figured it out and I think they could have revealed it in a better way.
I can't stress how much I loved this game. For that reason, I gave this game a positively, maximum LOVED IT!!! This was my first game of this style, so although I didn't enjoy it as much as I have other story-driven games, I think it's because it's a personal preference in game styles for myself.
Art/Style: 9/10
Despite not being a huge fan of 2D pixel-style games, I cannot argue that the style was beautiful. The art reflects the various moods presented throughout the game and is quite detailed. I'm particularly struck by the richness of the blue sky. The lighting is gorgeous although some parts are a little dark.
Music: 10/10
There's a reason this game has been placed in the "Great Soundtrack" tag. The music is hauntingly gorgeous and stays with you even when the game is over. It goes from heartbreaking to creepy and back to heartbreaking.
Story/Content: 7/10
The story is arguably the entire point of the game. It is a story driven game. However, I found that the story sometimes fell short. Don't get me wrong, I did love it. Especially having personal connections to some of the themes presented, which I found quite exciting because they're themes I don't see brought up enough in many media forms. The reason I gave story a 7 is because it wasn't always clear. When I went back to read about the plot, I realized there was a lot that I had either not understood or just plain missed. Now, maybe that's a testament to how much I need to be spoon fed information as opposed to being able to figure it out on my own. I don't know. I did, however, enjoy having to figure things out and wondering and theorizing about what was going on. And perhaps multiple playthroughs would have revealed more and more to me each time.
There's a fair amount of puzzle solving, which isn't usually too difficult (although sometimes you attempt to click on things and it doesn't allow you to, making you think you have the wrong answer) but it is rather repetitive. Although you're looking for different things each "level" your solution to the puzzle is exactly the same each time.
I didn't find myself as immersed in the game as I have other story-rich games. I didn't really connect to the characters, and when it finished, I didn't feel like I was going to miss the characters or the story. The story itself didn't stay with me.
The playing time isn't very long (about 4 hours) however I found it felt much, much longer for me. Perhaps because I wasn't as immersed.
Mechanics: 9/10
Controls are simple. You use the mouse and keyboard. You can use primarily the keyboard or primarily the mouse, but you will have to use both at some point. I ended up switching between both. I cannot give it a perfect 10 because there were times it did not work as it was supposed to, which led me wandering around for much longer than necessary because the game was not responding to me clicking certain items.
Ease of Use: 9/10
Again, other than some parts of the game not responding as intended, the game is easy to navigate and laid out in a simple and direct manner. Instructions are clear and does not leave you frustrated, trying to figure out what is supposed to be done next.
Overall: 44/50

Being the first in the AC series, this definetly set a new bar, broke some conventions, delivered solid gameplay and all the while setting the foundation for what we know what will be a good story.
The graphics are mindblowing, considering it's age. The gameplay is a bit slow, stepping back from the Prince of Persia series' crazy acrobatics that seemed to have inspired much, and does everything with a more realistic pakour-like approach, it can at times be irritatingly slow, considering the sheer scale of environs one has to cover, but that is then addressed in the the newer releases.
The setting itself (Third Crusade), is one of the things that make this game particularly interesting. Not only do you interact with a well-portrayed medieval society at war, but you also encounter all the different cultures that were present in the mixing pot that was the Holy Land at that time. Having Crusaders yell in German, French and old English, with Saracens doing the same in Arabic (and Hebrew? I can't tell) adds another level of immersion.
I would reccomend everyone play this at least once - but bring a controller along for the ride. The AC games do not lend themselves well to keyboard controls, this one does so better than the later installments, but one might as well set a trend and get used to the persistent scheme.

While this game does have its moments, they're buried behind some bland missions (collect the flags!) and WAY too much time spent running from guards. The core gameplay, running around, hiding, and climbing is a good idea, but is not refined until later games. By comparison, Assassin's Creed II is far better.
On sale, however, this game may be worth it.

I think Assassin's Creed is such a weird franchise. It has so many cool things going for it, but then there's a whole heap of things that bring it down. I guess I would give it a Yes as a recommendation via Steam reviews, but from what I've played so far, my overall opinion on the series is more neutral.
Anyway, this is the first game in the franchise, and there are some really interesting things about it. No other game has really done free running so openly like Assassin's Creed, or approached history with such a expansive and imaginative point of view. The time period is very unique and well realized. The simple mechanics (some of which are okay, and others which unfortunately are not well polished) are also surprisingly welcome, because for someone like me, the combat and gameplay isn't exactly what draws me in, it's the world and history, so I don't want to waste my time learning some complex systems.
I think the problems lie with the combat and movement which are extremely hit-or-miss and the storytelling. Having most of the cutscenes take place from a static third person perspective is really off putting, and gives a really poor B-movie vibe for any story that is present. As well, the whole modern timeline thing is just ridiculuous. This game (and the series as a whole) needs to do without it. Especially considering there are zero likeable characters (in my opinion) in the modern timeline. I just don't care about any of them.
Overall, I'd probably give this game like a 6.5/10. I think it's a really decent game, and it's definitely worth a look, but grab it on sale.

Received a copy of this for free from my buddy after the 1.3 update, and played the original GoG version upon release. The game has really come a long way since the initial release. I have put in over a dozen hours into the 1.3 update thus far and performance and stability have improved drastically. I have experienced only a single crash to desktop in that time (used to crash every 20-45 minutes) and overall pretty smooth performance, some textures load in late or just in a weird/funny way before correcting themselves.
As for the gameplay, the cornerstone of this has always been just zipping around in your spaceship and exploring the different worlds. In the initial build I can recall it being extremely monotonous after a few hours of doing the exact same thing, visiting many planets that all felt mostly the same. Since playing the 1.3 update, the gameplay has become more varied and fun. A previous update added in land vehicles and base building, allowing you to have a homeworld where you can stash and harvest supplies. The addition of the questing system is a welcome change, allowing players to keep a log of what tasks certain entities have given them, and even hints players toward how to complete each task. These new additions are very much welcome and there are others that I have yet to experience for myself (such as the big Freighters). The core gameplay still revolves around the continous exploration of the galaxy for answers.
The story itself is very vague and I just click past most of the text because it comes off as just silly nonsense, slowing down progress towards my next self-imposed goal. However, the story does do one thing very well and that is to allow the player to fill in some blanks and make their own story. You are simply a traveller, wandering the galaxy in search of answers, but the questions are for you to create.
As of right now, this is still a tough sell for full price ($60). However, the developers have put continued effort since the initial launch to improve the game and thus far have done quite well in doing so. There are many features that I would still like to see, such as improved variety of ships/structures/creatures/planets. I have heard the biomes vary more as you progress, so the planet variety may improve but for now many of them have a very similar feel to them. The ships would benefit greatly from customization options, even if they are just aesthetic. There are plenty of other wild new gameplay mechanics that could be added and considered improvements, but I believe the devs need to focus on perfecting the kernal gameplay element, exploration.
Increasing the number of and quality of the places and things the player may encounter in their journey through the stars is paramount to improving the exploration element of the game. I am definitely having fun with the game now and would recommend it at a sale price (Price < $30). If you like space and exploration then you should find many hours of fun with this game. Also, posting pictures of the whacky, strange and occasionally phallic things for your friends to see allows you to share your experience....
Which leads to the final point..... ADD MULTIPLAYER!

I've been thinking of how to rate Syberia as there is a great amount of the Good as there is of the Bad. But which part outweighs which is the real question. Well, let's break it down.
You play as an American lawyer Kate Walker who's on a trip to a fictional village in France to sign a contract for a toy factory takeover. Unfortunately, its current owner passes away and there's only one person left in the family to give her the signature. However, their whereabouts are unknown and so Kate's journey across Central and Easter Europe starts.
Going further into the plot would reveal major spoilers so I'll leave it at that. The locations in the game are built around the steampunk aesthetic and come with a huge attention to detail. Highly immersive ambience and a beautiful soundtrack. As you traverse the areas, you stumble upon several characters, documents and of course occasional puzzles that progress the story. Nothing groundbreaking about the dialogue and not only do you have to read A LOT, you also have to memorize certain bits as they hold clues to some of the puzzles. For someone who loves to read, this isn't a minus but it does extend the playtime artificially. The game ends abruptly with a cliffhanger and leaves just enough room for a sequel.
Now, since this is an interactive adventure and not just a movie, I have to address it's problems in that department. First of all, the pacing. It really puts your patience to the test, running between interest points takes forever...and you will hate the stairs here. Absolutely everything takes too long to execute. There is another game made by the same developer, Still Life, which shares some similarities with Syberia, except that it never felt like a drag. This is a huge deal and I don't need to explain how awful it becomes when you get lost or just can't find the next clue. Speaking of, the puzzles range from simplistic "use the items you found along your path" to frustrating "how in hell would you figure that out". As stated earlier, the solution is sometimes to be attained from the found documents, but you never really know when you make use of it. Which again leads to thinking whether you could have missed something when in fact it's right there in your inventory. Another issue I didn't have to deal with in Still Life.
All things considered, if you are up to experience a memorable narrative taking its painfully dull and slow progress into account, this might be a good pick for you.

Brawlout is a platform fighter game that appears to be strongly influenced by games like smash bros and brawlhalla. There are a few things I thought were pretty cool about the game, the graphics look really nice and seem to be really well optimized as my pc could run the game on max setting at about 400-600 fps the whole time. The character design is pretty interesting too with strongly cohesive kits that fit stick to and make use of the characters look to create an imersive fighter.
However there are many more things about this game that just didnt make it stick for me and made me want to stop playing. First the player base is very small taking around 5 to 10 minutes just to find a short 3ish minute match, this is not something that is really the developers fault and may improve over time but as of now online play just doesnt seem that fun because it takes twice as long to find a match as it does to play one. Next in single player vs cpu there are no differences in difficulties to my knowledge making it so once you've mastered beating the cpus it is no longer challenging and as I said with the queue times earlier its not even very worth it to switch to online multiplayer. Third, their are very few character (which is expected mostly of early access) but they claim that they plan to add two or three more by release, that will total in around 10 characters. Arguably that could be enough for I fighting game since games like lethal league thrive with only 6, but the magnitude of competetive play this strives for versus lethal league is very different as lethal league is meant to be a much simpler game at its core. The amount of characters put into this game doesnt even take much time to learn them all. Once again without higher cpu difficulty levels and with sluggish online play I believe this game would benefit greatly from at least having more characters game like smash start you out with around 30 characters to play allowing for much better replayability as you learn to master all of the different character and playstyles. Further more and this may be purely my personal opinion but the movement in this game feels a little clunky whether with controller or keyboard the characters feel rather unresponsive often resulting in a move executing to late, not at all, or the wrong move happening. Lastly another personal opinion is I dont care for the way abilities chain, it feels like there are to many true combos in this game with no frames for recovery in between with these inescapable combos and nearly map wide moves like those seen on king apu and gancho puncho the gameplay seems kindof broken and slightly unfit for competitve play.
I very well might try this game again in the future once its out of early access but as for now I do not think this game is worth playing as what it does games like smash and brawlhalla still do better and with higher player bases.
Good luck to the development team, I'll be back.
TLDR:
Character design and game optimization are solid, but between clunky gameplay, broken abilities and combos, lack of depth to cpu fights, and low playerbase game is not worth in its current state.
